hits.text: On June 30, 2025, Qantas Airlines discovered that hackers had exploited a vulnerability in a third-party call-center platform to access personally identifiable information (PII) for approximately six million customers—names, email addresses, phone numbers, birth dates and frequent-flyer numbers—but not passports or payment data—before the breach was contained shortly thereafter; in response, Qantas has launched a dedicated support line and webpage, tightened IT monitoring and access controls, and is investigating alongside federal authorities.  Cybersecurity experts from CyberCX attribute “all the hallmarks” of the attack to the advanced persistent threat group Scattered Spider (aka UNC3944, 0ktapus/Roasted Oktapus, Scatter Swine, Octo Tempest, Muddled Libra), which the FBI recently warned is increasingly targeting aviation, while government minister Tony Burke cautioned Australians to resist cold calls or unsolicited emails and to verify Qantas communications via published contact channels to thwart follow-on phishing campaigns.  Apollo Information Systems CISO Andy Bennett highlights attackers’ use of AI to amalgamate PII from multiple breaches for highly personalized social‐engineering, underscoring the need for rigorous vendor security assessments, proactive threat hunting and cross-sector collaboration under Australia’s $1.67 billion cybersecurity strategy and new critical-infrastructure legislation.
hits.title: Qantas Airlines Breached, Impacting 6M Customers

hits.text: In a joint advisory, US, Australian and Canadian agencies warn that financially motivated group Scattered Spider (UNC3944, aka Muddled Libra/Scatter Swine/Starfraud) has leveraged advanced social engineering against help-desk personnel to harvest compromised credentials from hacking forums, deploy RMM tools, create fake social-media personas, and target VMware ESXi servers and Snowflake environments—running thousands of concurrent queries to exfiltrate data to MEGA.nz and Amazon S3—before encrypting systems with DragonForce ransomware and deploying RattyRAT; although recent UK arrests have paused UNC3944 operations, other actors including UNC6040, UNC2165 (RansomHub), UNC4393 (Basta) and UNC2465 (DarkSide/LockBit) are now replicating these TTPs, extending attacks to backup platforms by deleting routines and tampering with permissions to thwart recovery, often exploiting weak credentials, misconfigurations, API/UI flaws and RCE vulnerabilities; defenders are urged to adopt identity-centric security, layered MFA, Zero Trust principles, robust patching, segmentation and proactive disruption of human-driven intrusion paths.
hits.title: Scattered Spider Activity Drops Following Arrests, but Others Adopting Group's Tactics

hits.text: During Q2 2025, CrowdStrike Services observed eCrime group SCATTERED SPIDER expand its long-established insurance and retail campaigns to include U.S. airlines, leveraging sophisticated help-desk voice phishing to hijack Microsoft Entra ID, SSO and VDI accounts by accurately answering employee verification questions and resetting passwords and MFA. From compromised accounts the adversary pivoted to SaaS platforms to harvest network diagrams, VPN instructions and credentials before conducting on-premises Active Directory reconnaissance with ADExplorer, ADRecon.ps1 and Get-ADUser, and exploiting VMware vCenter access to spawn unmanaged VMs, attach domain controller disks, dump ntds.dit and install protocol-tunneling tools (Chisel via trycloudflare[.]com, ngrok, MobaXterm, Pinggy, Rsocx, Teleport). They also created transport rules to delete or redirect security alerts and used S3 Browser to enumerate and exfiltrate AWS S3 data. SCATTERED SPIDER’s endgame is ESXi ransomware deployment or double-extortion data leaks. To detect and disrupt these tactics, organizations should ingest high-priority logs—VMware vCenter/ESXi, firewall, DNS and web proxy—into CrowdStrike Falcon Next-Gen SIEM, enable correlation rules and integrate cloud security for rapid identification and response.
hits.title: SCATTERED SPIDER Escalates Attacks Across Industries | CrowdStrike

hits.text: Scattered Spider, active since May 2022, has evolved from SIM-swapping and typosquatted credential harvesting to sophisticated social-engineering-driven cloud intrusions, most recently impersonating a CFO via public personal data to trick help-desk staff into resetting their Oracle Cloud device, then mapping Entra ID (Azure AD) privileges and SharePoint data, breaching Horizon VDI, VPN, and on-premise environments, reactivating a decommissioned VM, extracting NTDS.dit and over 1,400 secrets from CyberArk vaults using scripts and tools like ngrok, abusing AWS Systems Manager Session Manager, EC2 Serial Console, IAM role enumeration and Teleport for persistence, assigning Exchange Administrator roles to monitor senior employee inboxes, and deleting Azure Firewall policy rules in a tug-of-war over tenant control that required Microsoft intervention, inflicting millions in operational disruption (e.g., MGM Resorts, Marks & Spencer, Hawaiian Airlines) and exposing critical lapses in help-desk verification and privileged access management; organizations should deploy phishing-resistant MFA, enforce least-privilege and strict identity proofing for help-desks, monitor cloud and endpoint activity, and conduct regular social-engineering training to mitigate Scattered Spider’s fast, multi-vector ransomware preparation tactics.
hits.title: Anatomy of a Scattered Spider attack: A growing ransomware threat evolves

hits.text: On June 30, threat actors exploited a vulnerability in a third-party call-center platform used by Qantas to exfiltrate 5.7 million unique customer records—none of which involved direct compromise of Qantas’s own systems—and on July 7 the airline confirmed a likely extortion attempt when the hacker made contact; after deduplication Qantas found 4 million records contained names, email addresses and Frequent Flyer details, 1.2 million contained only names and emails, and 1.7 million included additional data such as addresses (1.3 million), dates of birth (1.1 million), phone numbers (900 000), gender (400 000) and meal preferences (10 000), while no credit card, financial or passport information was stored on the breached platform. The company has begun notifying affected customers, deployed enhanced security controls, and is collaborating closely with the Australian Cyber Security Centre, the National Cyber Security Coordinator and the Australian Federal Police to investigate the supply-chain weakness, reinforce third-party risk management, and bolster monitoring and incident response capabilities to mitigate future breaches.
hits.title: Qantas Confirms 5.7 Million Impacted by Data Breach - SecurityWeek

hits.text: Since mid-2022, Unit 42 has attributed over 100 high-value cryptocurrency and BPO incidents to Muddled Libra—a fluid subset of the Scattered Spider collective—initially executing structured smishing and 0ktapus phishing campaigns (leveraging over 200 realistic mobile-auth portals) against large business process outsourcers, then evolving in 2023 into an ALPHV/BlackCat affiliate with multi-million-dollar extortion demands, later resuming high-profile attacks in late 2024 and expanding through May 2025 into software automation, telecom, hospitality, finance and retail verticals; their adaptable tradecraft blends social engineering of IT helpdesks to reset passwords and MFA, inside BPO access, legitimate remote management tools for CRM exfiltration, NSOCKS/TrueSocks anonymizing proxies, custom virtual machines, the open-source “bedevil” rootkit on VMware vCenter, email-forwarding rules to hijack incident response communications, and AI-driven voice spoofing for vishing, with members cycling via Discord and Telegram to refresh niche skills and spawn offshoots such as Scatter Swine and Octo Tempest, while leveraging deep incident response framework knowledge to persist in environments and repeatedly reclaim stolen data before affiliating with DragonForce for ransomware; defenders should deploy interwoven modern security architectures (Cortex XSIAM/XDR, Advanced URL Filtering, DNS Security, App-ID), enforce strict access controls, conduct rigorous awareness training, and maintain vigilant MITRE-mapped monitoring (T1566, T1556, T1215, T1562) to thwart these multifaceted, evolving extortion campaigns.

hits.text: Dragos researchers, in collaboration with Ukraine’s CSSC, unearthed FrostyGoop—an ICS-specific malware first spotted in April and used in January to disrupt central heating in over 600 Lviv apartment buildings—marking the first known malware to leverage Modbus TCP for read/write operations on operational technology. hits.text: Microsoft’s August 2023 Patch Tuesday addressed two actively exploited zero-days—CVE-2023-36884, a remote code execution flaw in Microsoft Office that bypasses the Mark of the Web, and CVE-2023-38180, a .NET/Visual Studio vulnerability enabling DDoS attacks without requiring user privileges—after one was publicly disclosed pre-patch. The Russian actor Storm-0978 (aka RomCom/Underground), noted for Industrial Spy ransomware, leveraged crafted Office documents to execute payloads and extort victims, while CVE-2023-38180 attacks demand only network proximity. To mitigate these threats, Microsoft released an Office Defense-in-Depth update and a .NET/Visual Studio patch and recommends deploying both Office and Windows August updates, enabling cloud-delivered protection in Defender Antivirus, activating EDR block mode, enforcing attack surface reduction rules to block Office-spawned child processes, and applying the advisory’s update for CVE-2023-38180. Avertium validates these controls, provides IoCs for RomCom campaigns, and advocates continuous vulnerability management and its Fusion MXDR for Microsoft service to detect suspicious Office-to-script execution chains and remediate artifacts proactively.

retrieved_context.text: On June 30, 2025, Qantas Airlines discovered that hackers had exploited a vulnerability in a third-party call-center platform to access personally identifiable information (PII) for approximately six million customers—names, email addresses, phone numbers, birth dates and frequent-flyer numbers—but not passports or payment data—before the breach was contained shortly thereafter; in response, Qantas has launched a dedicated support line and webpage, tightened IT monitoring and access controls, and is investigating alongside federal authorities.  Cybersecurity experts from CyberCX attribute “all the hallmarks” of the attack to the advanced persistent threat group Scattered Spider (aka UNC3944, 0ktapus/Roasted Oktapus, Scatter Swine, Octo Tempest, Muddled Libra), which the FBI recently warned is increasingly targeting aviation, while government minister Tony Burke cautioned Australians to resist cold calls or unsolicited emails and to verify Qantas communications via published contact channels to thwart follow-on phishing campaigns.  Apollo Information Systems CISO Andy Bennett highlights attackers’ use of AI to amalgamate PII from multiple breaches for highly personalized social‐engineering, underscoring the need for rigorous vendor security assessments, proactive threat hunting and cross-sector collaboration under Australia’s $1.67 billion cybersecurity strategy and new critical-infrastructure legislation.
retrieved_context.title: Qantas Airlines Breached, Impacting 6M Customers

retrieved_context.text: In a joint advisory, US, Australian and Canadian agencies warn that financially motivated group Scattered Spider (UNC3944, aka Muddled Libra/Scatter Swine/Starfraud) has leveraged advanced social engineering against help-desk personnel to harvest compromised credentials from hacking forums, deploy RMM tools, create fake social-media personas, and target VMware ESXi servers and Snowflake environments—running thousands of concurrent queries to exfiltrate data to MEGA.nz and Amazon S3—before encrypting systems with DragonForce ransomware and deploying RattyRAT; although recent UK arrests have paused UNC3944 operations, other actors including UNC6040, UNC2165 (RansomHub), UNC4393 (Basta) and UNC2465 (DarkSide/LockBit) are now replicating these TTPs, extending attacks to backup platforms by deleting routines and tampering with permissions to thwart recovery, often exploiting weak credentials, misconfigurations, API/UI flaws and RCE vulnerabilities; defenders are urged to adopt identity-centric security, layered MFA, Zero Trust principles, robust patching, segmentation and proactive disruption of human-driven intrusion paths.
retrieved_context.title: Scattered Spider Activity Drops Following Arrests, but Others Adopting Group's Tactics

retrieved_context.text: During Q2 2025, CrowdStrike Services observed eCrime group SCATTERED SPIDER expand its long-established insurance and retail campaigns to include U.S. airlines, leveraging sophisticated help-desk voice phishing to hijack Microsoft Entra ID, SSO and VDI accounts by accurately answering employee verification questions and resetting passwords and MFA. From compromised accounts the adversary pivoted to SaaS platforms to harvest network diagrams, VPN instructions and credentials before conducting on-premises Active Directory reconnaissance with ADExplorer, ADRecon.ps1 and Get-ADUser, and exploiting VMware vCenter access to spawn unmanaged VMs, attach domain controller disks, dump ntds.dit and install protocol-tunneling tools (Chisel via trycloudflare[.]com, ngrok, MobaXterm, Pinggy, Rsocx, Teleport). They also created transport rules to delete or redirect security alerts and used S3 Browser to enumerate and exfiltrate AWS S3 data. SCATTERED SPIDER’s endgame is ESXi ransomware deployment or double-extortion data leaks. To detect and disrupt these tactics, organizations should ingest high-priority logs—VMware vCenter/ESXi, firewall, DNS and web proxy—into CrowdStrike Falcon Next-Gen SIEM, enable correlation rules and integrate cloud security for rapid identification and response.
retrieved_context.title: SCATTERED SPIDER Escalates Attacks Across Industries | CrowdStrike

retrieved_context.text: Scattered Spider, active since May 2022, has evolved from SIM-swapping and typosquatted credential harvesting to sophisticated social-engineering-driven cloud intrusions, most recently impersonating a CFO via public personal data to trick help-desk staff into resetting their Oracle Cloud device, then mapping Entra ID (Azure AD) privileges and SharePoint data, breaching Horizon VDI, VPN, and on-premise environments, reactivating a decommissioned VM, extracting NTDS.dit and over 1,400 secrets from CyberArk vaults using scripts and tools like ngrok, abusing AWS Systems Manager Session Manager, EC2 Serial Console, IAM role enumeration and Teleport for persistence, assigning Exchange Administrator roles to monitor senior employee inboxes, and deleting Azure Firewall policy rules in a tug-of-war over tenant control that required Microsoft intervention, inflicting millions in operational disruption (e.g., MGM Resorts, Marks & Spencer, Hawaiian Airlines) and exposing critical lapses in help-desk verification and privileged access management; organizations should deploy phishing-resistant MFA, enforce least-privilege and strict identity proofing for help-desks, monitor cloud and endpoint activity, and conduct regular social-engineering training to mitigate Scattered Spider’s fast, multi-vector ransomware preparation tactics.
retrieved_context.title: Anatomy of a Scattered Spider attack: A growing ransomware threat evolves

retrieved_context.text: On June 30, threat actors exploited a vulnerability in a third-party call-center platform used by Qantas to exfiltrate 5.7 million unique customer records—none of which involved direct compromise of Qantas’s own systems—and on July 7 the airline confirmed a likely extortion attempt when the hacker made contact; after deduplication Qantas found 4 million records contained names, email addresses and Frequent Flyer details, 1.2 million contained only names and emails, and 1.7 million included additional data such as addresses (1.3 million), dates of birth (1.1 million), phone numbers (900 000), gender (400 000) and meal preferences (10 000), while no credit card, financial or passport information was stored on the breached platform. canonical_entities: Launch EC2 instances across regions via VPN
hits.text: Unit42’s “EleKtra-Leak” campaign, active since December 2020, uses automated scripts to clone public GitHub repos every few minutes, extract exposed AWS IAM keys within five minutes, then—if not blocked by GitHub-AWS quarantine policies—execute rapid AWS reconnaissance (DescribeRegions), create security groups, and launch hundreds of EC2 instances across regions via VPN for Monero cryptojacking, generating over 400 API calls in seven minutes. Between Aug. 30 and Oct. 6, 2023, researchers tracked 474 actor-controlled miners. The actor employs custom mining software and blocklists high-profile AWS account IDs to avoid honey traps. Leveraging the Prisma Cloud HoneyCloud project’s ephemeral key leaks and policy overrides, Unit42 obtained full visibility, informing Prisma Cloud Secrets Security, CI/CD IaC scanning, Cortex XDR, and recommendations for independent repo scanning, strict IAM policies, and continuous monitoring.
hits.title: CloudKeys in the Air: Tracking Malicious Operations of Exposed IAM Keys

canonical_entities: Palo Alto Networks NGFW Advanced Threat Prevention
hits.text: Unit 42 researchers have uncovered a new, substantially upgraded variant of the Kazuar .NET backdoor—previously observed in 2017 as a second-stage payload by Russian Federal Security Service–linked Pensive Ursa (Turla/Uroburos)—that re-emerged in July 2023 targeting Ukrainian defense organizations via a multi-stage Capibar loader to steal Signal messages, cloud and source-control credentials and other high-value data. This variant adds robust anti-analysis checks (Assembly.Location byte-array loader validation, faked 2008 compilation timestamps), extensive string encryption (multiple custom and ConfuserEx ciphers), hybrid AES payload encryption with RSA-encrypted IV/key plus HMAC-MD5 integrity, and obfuscation of IOCs. It supports 45 discrete commands for system profiling, credential theft and automated task workflows in a multithreaded solver component that writes AES- and RSA-protected result files. Kazuar also implements multiple injection modes (inject, browser- and svchost.exe-centric zombify, combined fallback, remote proxy, single and headless) and uses GUID-derived pseudorandom directories and mutexes to evade detection, while hard-coded agent and build identifiers enable variant tracking. Code overlap with Sunburst underscores its sophistication. Unit 42 has released detailed IOCs, artifacts and a GitHub appendix, and recommends Palo Alto Networks NGFW Advanced Threat Prevention, Cortex XDR, XSIAM, Advanced WildFire and Unit 42 incident response engagement to detect, hunt and mitigate this persistent threat.
hits.title: Over the Kazuar’s Nest: Cracking Down on a Freshly Hatched Backdoor Used by Pensive Ursa (Aka Turla)

hits.text: In early April, Palo Alto Networks’ Advanced WildFire and Cortex XDR uncovered SnipBot—a new v5.0 iteration of the RomCom RAT family—employing advanced window message–based control-flow obfuscation and anti-sandbox checks (filename hash and HKCU\…\RecentDocs entries) in a multi-stage chain beginning with a PDF-labeled EXE downloader signed using a likely stolen certificate; the downloader contacts xeontime[.]com for config-pdf.dll, which uses registry-based COM hijacking to load keyprov.dll from drvmcprotect[.]com into explorer.exe, decrypts payloads stored in HKCU\Software\AppDataSoft\Software, and opens a TCP listener on port 1342 for commands to update, delete, or execute modules. The main backdoor single.dll (mutex “SnipMutex”) supports 27 encrypted commands for drive and process enumeration, file upload/download, and remote module execution, facilitating network pivoting and targeted file exfiltration. Active since December 2023 (RomCom activity since 2022), SnipBot’s tactics, stolen certificates, unique obfuscation, and sophisticated loader underscore a high-risk threat actor likely focused on intelligence gathering; Palo Alto products classify its samples, URLs, and domains as malicious to prevent compromise.
hits.title: Inside SnipBot: The Latest RomCom Malware Variant

hits.text: Silent Push researchers uncovered FIN7’s largest-ever infrastructure, identifying over 4,000 malicious IOFA domains and associated IP addresses used to fuel a global phishing and malware campaign that hit high-profile targets such as the Louvre, Meta and Reuters. Using automated intelligence and Threat Hunting workflows, analysts detected a pattern of newly registered look-alike domains—many leveraging common TLDs and typosquatting—to host spear-phishing landing pages and weaponized Office attachments that deploy custom .NET droppers and Cobalt Strike beacons. Chronologically, the operation began with domain registration, followed by coordinated email blasts spoofing corporate brands, HTTP(S) redirects to phishing kits, and payload delivery that enabled credential harvesting and potential lateral movement. Silent Push’s API-driven Integrations enabled rapid enumeration of IOFA indicators of compromise, brand protection alerts and proactive blocking in customer environments. Actionable insights include ingesting the full list of domains and IPs into SIEM and email security filters, enforcing strict SPF/DKIM/DMARC policies, monitoring DNS query anomalies for new domain registrations, and updating endpoint detection rules to flag the identified .NET loader behaviors.
hits.title: FIN7: Silent Push unearths the largest group of FIN7 domains ever discovered. 4000+ IOFA domains and IPs found. Louvre, Meta, and Reuters targeted in massive global phishing and malware campaigns.

retrieved_context.text: During Q2 2025, CrowdStrike Services observed eCrime group SCATTERED SPIDER expand its long-established insurance and retail campaigns to include U.S. airlines, leveraging sophisticated help-desk voice phishing to hijack Microsoft Entra ID, SSO and VDI accounts by accurately answering employee verification questions and resetting passwords and MFA. From compromised accounts the adversary pivoted to SaaS platforms to harvest network diagrams, VPN instructions and credentials before conducting on-premises Active Directory reconnaissance with ADExplorer, ADRecon.ps1 and Get-ADUser, and exploiting VMware vCenter access to spawn unmanaged VMs, attach domain controller disks, dump ntds.dit and install protocol-tunneling tools (Chisel via trycloudflare[.]com, ngrok, MobaXterm, Pinggy, Rsocx, Teleport). They also created transport rules to delete or redirect security alerts and used S3 Browser to enumerate and exfiltrate AWS S3 data. SCATTERED SPIDER’s endgame is ESXi ransomware deployment or double-extortion data leaks. To detect and disrupt these tactics, organizations should ingest high-priority logs—VMware vCenter/ESXi, firewall, DNS and web proxy—into CrowdStrike Falcon Next-Gen SIEM, enable correlation rules and integrate cloud security for rapid identification and response.

retrieved_context.text: Scattered Spider, active since May 2022, has evolved from SIM-swapping and typosquatted credential harvesting to sophisticated social-engineering-driven cloud intrusions, most recently impersonating a CFO via public personal data to trick help-desk staff into resetting their Oracle Cloud device, then mapping Entra ID (Azure AD) privileges and SharePoint data, breaching Horizon VDI, VPN, and on-premise environments, reactivating a decommissioned VM, extracting NTDS.dit and over 1,400 secrets from CyberArk vaults using scripts and tools like ngrok, abusing AWS Systems Manager Session Manager, EC2 Serial Console, IAM role enumeration and Teleport for persistence, assigning Exchange Administrator roles to monitor senior employee inboxes, and deleting Azure Firewall policy rules in a tug-of-war over tenant control that required Microsoft intervention, inflicting millions in operational disruption (e.g., MGM Resorts, Marks & Spencer, Hawaiian Airlines) and exposing critical lapses in help-desk verification and privileged access management; organizations should deploy phishing-resistant MFA, enforce least-privilege and strict identity proofing for help-desks, monitor cloud and endpoint activity, and conduct regular social-engineering training to mitigate Scattered Spider’s fast, multi-vector ransomware preparation tactics.

retrieved_context.text: On June 30, threat actors exploited a vulnerability in a third-party call-center platform used by Qantas to exfiltrate 5.7 million unique customer records—none of which involved direct compromise of Qantas’s own systems—and on July 7 the airline confirmed a likely extortion attempt when the hacker made contact; after deduplication Qantas found 4 million records contained names, email addresses and Frequent Flyer details, 1.2 million contained only names and emails, and 1.7 million included additional data such as addresses (1.3 million), dates of birth (1.1 million), phone numbers (900 000), gender (400 000) and meal preferences (10 000), while no credit card, financial or passport information was stored on the breached platform. The company has begun notifying affected customers, deployed enhanced security controls, and is collaborating closely with the Australian Cyber Security Centre, the National Cyber Security Coordinator and the Australian Federal Police to investigate the supply-chain weakness, reinforce third-party risk management, and bolster monitoring and incident response capabilities to mitigate future breaches.

retrieved_context.text: Unit42’s “EleKtra-Leak” campaign, active since December 2020, uses automated scripts to clone public GitHub repos every few minutes, extract exposed AWS IAM keys within five minutes, then—if not blocked by GitHub-AWS quarantine policies—execute rapid AWS reconnaissance (DescribeRegions), create security groups, and launch hundreds of EC2 instances across regions via VPN for Monero cryptojacking, generating over 400 API calls in seven minutes. Between Aug. 30 and Oct. 6, 2023, researchers tracked 474 actor-controlled miners. The actor employs custom mining software and blocklists high-profile AWS account IDs to avoid honey traps. Leveraging the Prisma Cloud HoneyCloud project’s ephemeral key leaks and policy overrides, Unit42 obtained full visibility, informing Prisma Cloud Secrets Security, CI/CD IaC scanning, Cortex XDR, and recommendations for independent repo scanning, strict IAM policies, and continuous monitoring.

canonical_entities: Palo Alto Networks NGFW Advanced Threat Prevention
retrieved_context.text: Unit 42 researchers have uncovered a new, substantially upgraded variant of the Kazuar .NET backdoor—previously observed in 2017 as a second-stage payload by Russian Federal Security Service–linked Pensive Ursa (Turla/Uroburos)—that re-emerged in July 2023 targeting Ukrainian defense organizations via a multi-stage Capibar loader to steal Signal messages, cloud and source-control credentials and other high-value data. This variant adds robust anti-analysis checks (Assembly.Location byte-array loader validation, faked 2008 compilation timestamps), extensive string encryption (multiple custom and ConfuserEx ciphers), hybrid AES payload encryption with RSA-encrypted IV/key plus HMAC-MD5 integrity, and obfuscation of IOCs. It supports 45 discrete commands for system profiling, credential theft and automated task workflows in a multithreaded solver component that writes AES- and RSA-protected result files. Kazuar also implements multiple injection modes (inject, browser- and svchost.exe-centric zombify, combined fallback, remote proxy, single and headless) and uses GUID-derived pseudorandom directories and mutexes to evade detection, while hard-coded agent and build identifiers enable variant tracking. Code overlap with Sunburst underscores its sophistication. Unit 42 has released detailed IOCs, artifacts and a GitHub appendix, and recommends Palo Alto Networks NGFW Advanced Threat Prevention, Cortex XDR, XSIAM, Advanced WildFire and Unit 42 incident response engagement to detect, hunt and mitigate this persistent threat.
retrieved_context.title: Over the Kazuar’s Nest: Cracking Down on a Freshly Hatched Backdoor Used by Pensive Ursa (Aka Turla)

retrieved_context.text: In early April, Palo Alto Networks’ Advanced WildFire and Cortex XDR uncovered SnipBot—a new v5.0 iteration of the RomCom RAT family—employing advanced window message–based control-flow obfuscation and anti-sandbox checks (filename hash and HKCU\…\RecentDocs entries) in a multi-stage chain beginning with a PDF-labeled EXE downloader signed using a likely stolen certificate; the downloader contacts xeontime[.]com for config-pdf.dll, which uses registry-based COM hijacking to load keyprov.dll from drvmcprotect[.]com into explorer.exe, decrypts payloads stored in HKCU\Software\AppDataSoft\Software, and opens a TCP listener on port 1342 for commands to update, delete, or execute modules. The main backdoor single.dll (mutex “SnipMutex”) supports 27 encrypted commands for drive and process enumeration, file upload/download, and remote module execution, facilitating network pivoting and targeted file exfiltration. Active since December 2023 (RomCom activity since 2022), SnipBot’s tactics, stolen certificates, unique obfuscation, and sophisticated loader underscore a high-risk threat actor likely focused on intelligence gathering; Palo Alto products classify its samples, URLs, and domains as malicious to prevent compromise.
retrieved_context.title: Inside SnipBot: The Latest RomCom Malware Variant

retrieved_context.text: Silent Push researchers uncovered FIN7’s largest-ever infrastructure, identifying over 4,000 malicious IOFA domains and associated IP addresses used to fuel a global phishing and malware campaign that hit high-profile targets such as the Louvre, Meta and Reuters. Using automated intelligence and Threat Hunting workflows, analysts detected a pattern of newly registered look-alike domains—many leveraging common TLDs and typosquatting—to host spear-phishing landing pages and weaponized Office attachments that deploy custom .NET droppers and Cobalt Strike beacons. Chronologically, the operation began with domain registration, followed by coordinated email blasts spoofing corporate brands, HTTP(S) redirects to phishing kits, and payload delivery that enabled credential harvesting and potential lateral movement. Silent Push’s API-driven Integrations enabled rapid enumeration of IOFA indicators of compromise, brand protection alerts and proactive blocking in customer environments. Actionable insights include ingesting the full list of domains and IPs into SIEM and email security filters, enforcing strict SPF/DKIM/DMARC policies, monitoring DNS query anomalies for new domain registrations, and updating endpoint detection rules to flag the identified .NET loader behaviors.
retrieved_context.title: FIN7: Silent Push unearths the largest group of FIN7 domains ever discovered. 4000+ IOFA domains and IPs found. Louvre, Meta, and Reuters targeted in massive global phishing and malware campaigns.

hits.text: In May 2023, after U.S. authorities secured convictions against three high-level operators and declared the Russia-based cybercrime enterprise Fin7 “no more,” security experts began spotting first signs of its resurrection in April 2024 when Blackberry reported a typosquatting-based malware intrusion against a major automotive firm; since January 2024, Silent Push analyst Zach Edwards has mapped over 4,000 Fin7-linked hosts—rented largely on the pro-Russia Stark Industries Solutions platform—employing typosquatting, booby-trapped ads, malicious browser extensions and spear-phishing domains to mimic hundreds of brands from American Express and Microsoft 365 to CNN and Zoom, as well as popular free software tools such as 7-zip, PuTTY and Python, all “aged” on innocuous templates for six to nine months before weaponization; eSentire and Malwarebytes also observed sponsored Google ads pushing phony extensions in May and April 2024, and Fin7 has even deployed domains targeting Louvre and Olympic tourists, building on its 2013–present campaign that has extorted some $3 billion from victim organizations, underscoring the urgent need for renewed law enforcement focus and proactive domain-monitoring defenses.
hits.title: The Stark Truth Behind the Resurgence of Russia’s Fin7 – Krebs on Security

hits.text: Microsoft released a temporary registry-based workaround in June 2022 to mitigate an actively exploited zero-day RCE (CVE-2022-3019, “Follina”) in the Microsoft Support Diagnostic Tool (MSDT), which attackers in Russia, Tibet and Belarus have leveraged since mid-April to execute arbitrary code, install programs, manipulate data or create accounts at the privilege level of the calling application without requiring macros. Researchers from Shadow Chaser Group and Recorded Future traced the flaw to an April 2020 bachelor’s thesis and first spotted it on April 12, with Malwarebytes confirming the issue and a formal report submitted to Microsoft on April 21—though Microsoft initially downplayed the risk until renewed alerts from Japanese vendor Nao Sec and security analyst Kevin Beaumont. The interim fix—deleting the HKEY_CLASSES_ROOT\ms-msdt registry key—disables URL-launched troubleshooters but disrupts system utilities and, according to experts, offers limited protection despite Office’s Protected View and Application Guard safeguards. With no official patch yet and all supported Windows and Office 2013–365 editions exposed, including lure campaigns impersonating the Central Tibetan Administration’s “Women Empowerment Desk,” organizations must implement the registry hardening, monitor for exploitation indicators and prepare for a comprehensive security update.
hits.title: Microsoft Releases Workaround for ‘One-Click’ 0Day Under Active Attack | Threatpost

retrieved_context.text: Unit42’s “EleKtra-Leak” campaign, active since December 2020, uses automated scripts to clone public GitHub repos every few minutes, extract exposed AWS IAM keys within five minutes, then—if not blocked by GitHub-AWS quarantine policies—execute rapid AWS reconnaissance (DescribeRegions), create security groups, and launch hundreds of EC2 instances across regions via VPN for Monero cryptojacking, generating over 400 API calls in seven minutes. Between Aug. 30 and Oct. 6, 2023, researchers tracked 474 actor-controlled miners. The actor employs custom mining software and blocklists high-profile AWS account IDs to avoid honey traps. Leveraging the Prisma Cloud HoneyCloud project’s ephemeral key leaks and policy overrides, Unit42 obtained full visibility, informing Prisma Cloud Secrets Security, CI/CD IaC scanning, Cortex XDR, and recommendations for independent repo scanning, strict IAM policies, and continuous monitoring.
retrieved_context.title: CloudKeys in the Air: Tracking Malicious Operations of Exposed IAM Keys

retrieved_context.text: In May 2023, after U.S. authorities secured convictions against three high-level operators and declared the Russia-based cybercrime enterprise Fin7 “no more,” security experts began spotting first signs of its resurrection in April 2024 when Blackberry reported a typosquatting-based malware intrusion against a major automotive firm; since January 2024, Silent Push analyst Zach Edwards has mapped over 4,000 Fin7-linked hosts—rented largely on the pro-Russia Stark Industries Solutions platform—employing typosquatting, booby-trapped ads, malicious browser extensions and spear-phishing domains to mimic hundreds of brands from American Express and Microsoft 365 to CNN and Zoom, as well as popular free software tools such as 7-zip, PuTTY and Python, all “aged” on innocuous templates for six to nine months before weaponization; eSentire and Malwarebytes also observed sponsored Google ads pushing phony extensions in May and April 2024, and Fin7 has even deployed domains targeting Louvre and Olympic tourists, building on its 2013–present campaign that has extorted some $3 billion from victim organizations, underscoring the urgent need for renewed law enforcement focus and proactive domain-monitoring defenses.
retrieved_context.title: The Stark Truth Behind the Resurgence of Russia’s Fin7 – Krebs on Security

canonical_entities: lure campaigns impersonating the Central Tibetan Administration’s “Women Empowerment Desk”
retrieved_context.text: Microsoft released a temporary registry-based workaround in June 2022 to mitigate an actively exploited zero-day RCE (CVE-2022-3019, “Follina”) in the Microsoft Support Diagnostic Tool (MSDT), which attackers in Russia, Tibet and Belarus have leveraged since mid-April to execute arbitrary code, install programs, manipulate data or create accounts at the privilege level of the calling application without requiring macros. Researchers from Shadow Chaser Group and Recorded Future traced the flaw to an April 2020 bachelor’s thesis and first spotted it on April 12, with Malwarebytes confirming the issue and a formal report submitted to Microsoft on April 21—though Microsoft initially downplayed the risk until renewed alerts from Japanese vendor Nao Sec and security analyst Kevin Beaumont. The interim fix—deleting the HKEY_CLASSES_ROOT\ms-msdt registry key—disables URL-launched troubleshooters but disrupts system utilities and, according to experts, offers limited protection despite Office’s Protected View and Application Guard safeguards. With no official patch yet and all supported Windows and Office 2013–365 editions exposed, including lure campaigns impersonating the Central Tibetan Administration’s “Women Empowerment Desk,” organizations must implement the registry hardening, monitor for exploitation indicators and prepare for a comprehensive security update.
retrieved_context.title: Microsoft Releases Workaround for ‘One-Click’ 0Day Under Active Attack | Threatpost

canonical_entities: Palo Alto Networks NGFW Advanced Threat Prevention
retrieved_context.text: Unit 42 researchers have uncovered a new, substantially upgraded variant of the Kazuar .NET backdoor—previously observed in 2017 as a second-stage payload by Russian Federal Security Service–linked Pensive Ursa (Turla/Uroburos)—that re-emerged in July 2023 targeting Ukrainian defense organizations via a multi-stage Capibar loader to steal Signal messages, cloud and source-control credentials and other high-value data. This variant adds robust anti-analysis checks (Assembly.Location byte-array loader validation, faked 2008 compilation timestamps), extensive string encryption (multiple custom and ConfuserEx ciphers), hybrid AES payload encryption with RSA-encrypted IV/key plus HMAC-MD5 integrity, and obfuscation of IOCs. It supports 45 discrete commands for system profiling, credential theft and automated task workflows in a multithreaded solver component that writes AES- and RSA-protected result files. Kazuar also implements multiple injection modes (inject, browser- and svchost.exe-centric zombify, combined fallback, remote proxy, single and headless) and uses GUID-derived pseudorandom directories and mutexes to evade detection, while hard-coded agent and build identifiers enable variant tracking. Code overlap with Sunburst underscores its sophistication. Unit 42 has released detailed IOCs, artifacts and a GitHub appendix, and recommends Palo Alto Networks NGFW Advanced Threat Prevention, Cortex XDR, XSIAM, Advanced WildFire and Unit 42 incident response engagement to detect, hunt and mitigate this persistent threat.
retrieved_context.title: Over the Kazuar’s Nest: Cracking Down on a Freshly Hatched Backdoor Used by Pensive Ursa (Aka Turla)

hits.text: In a joint advisory, US, Australian and Canadian agencies warn that financially motivated group Scattered Spider (UNC3944, aka Muddled Libra/Scatter Swine/Starfraud) has leveraged advanced social engineering against help-desk personnel to harvest compromised credentials from hacking forums, deploy RMM tools, create fake social-media personas, and target VMware ESXi servers and Snowflake environments—running thousands of concurrent queries to exfiltrate data to MEGA.nz and Amazon S3—before encrypting systems with DragonForce ransomware and deploying RattyRAT; although recent UK arrests have paused UNC3944 operations, other actors including UNC6040, UNC2165 (RansomHub), UNC4393 (Basta) and UNC2465 (DarkSide/LockBit) are now replicating these TTPs, extending attacks to backup platforms by deleting routines and tampering with permissions to thwart recovery, often exploiting weak credentials, misconfigurations, API/UI flaws and RCE vulnerabilities; defenders are urged to adopt identity-centric security, layered MFA, Zero Trust principles, robust patching, segmentation and proactive disruption of human-driven intrusion paths.
hits.title: Scattered Spider Activity Drops Following Arrests, but Others Adopting Group's Tactics

hits.text: On June 30, 2025, Qantas Airlines discovered that hackers had exploited a vulnerability in a third-party call-center platform to access personally identifiable information (PII) for approximately six million customers—names, email addresses, phone numbers, birth dates and frequent-flyer numbers—but not passports or payment data—before the breach was contained shortly thereafter; in response, Qantas has launched a dedicated support line and webpage, tightened IT monitoring and access controls, and is investigating alongside federal authorities.  Cybersecurity experts from CyberCX attribute “all the hallmarks” of the attack to the advanced persistent threat group Scattered Spider (aka UNC3944, 0ktapus/Roasted Oktapus, Scatter Swine, Octo Tempest, Muddled Libra), which the FBI recently warned is increasingly targeting aviation, while government minister Tony Burke cautioned Australians to resist cold calls or unsolicited emails and to verify Qantas communications via published contact channels to thwart follow-on phishing campaigns.  Apollo Information Systems CISO Andy Bennett highlights attackers’ use of AI to amalgamate PII from multiple breaches for highly personalized social‐engineering, underscoring the need for rigorous vendor security assessments, proactive threat hunting and cross-sector collaboration under Australia’s $1.67 billion cybersecurity strategy and new critical-infrastructure legislation.
hits.title: Qantas Airlines Breached, Impacting 6M Customers

hits.text: During Q2 2025, CrowdStrike Services observed eCrime group SCATTERED SPIDER expand its long-established insurance and retail campaigns to include U.S. airlines, leveraging sophisticated help-desk voice phishing to hijack Microsoft Entra ID, SSO and VDI accounts by accurately answering employee verification questions and resetting passwords and MFA. From compromised accounts the adversary pivoted to SaaS platforms to harvest network diagrams, VPN instructions and credentials before conducting on-premises Active Directory reconnaissance with ADExplorer, ADRecon.ps1 and Get-ADUser, and exploiting VMware vCenter access to spawn unmanaged VMs, attach domain controller disks, dump ntds.dit and install protocol-tunneling tools (Chisel via trycloudflare[.]com, ngrok, MobaXterm, Pinggy, Rsocx, Teleport). They also created transport rules to delete or redirect security alerts and used S3 Browser to enumerate and exfiltrate AWS S3 data. SCATTERED SPIDER’s endgame is ESXi ransomware deployment or double-extortion data leaks. To detect and disrupt these tactics, organizations should ingest high-priority logs—VMware vCenter/ESXi, firewall, DNS and web proxy—into CrowdStrike Falcon Next-Gen SIEM, enable correlation rules and integrate cloud security for rapid identification and response.
hits.title: SCATTERED SPIDER Escalates Attacks Across Industries | CrowdStrike

hits.text: Scattered Spider, active since May 2022, has evolved from SIM-swapping and typosquatted credential harvesting to sophisticated social-engineering-driven cloud intrusions, most recently impersonating a CFO via public personal data to trick help-desk staff into resetting their Oracle Cloud device, then mapping Entra ID (Azure AD) privileges and SharePoint data, breaching Horizon VDI, VPN, and on-premise environments, reactivating a decommissioned VM, extracting NTDS.dit and over 1,400 secrets from CyberArk vaults using scripts and tools like ngrok, abusing AWS Systems Manager Session Manager, EC2 Serial Console, IAM role enumeration and Teleport for persistence, assigning Exchange Administrator roles to monitor senior employee inboxes, and deleting Azure Firewall policy rules in a tug-of-war over tenant control that required Microsoft intervention, inflicting millions in operational disruption (e.g., MGM Resorts, Marks & Spencer, Hawaiian Airlines) and exposing critical lapses in help-desk verification and privileged access management; organizations should deploy phishing-resistant MFA, enforce least-privilege and strict identity proofing for help-desks, monitor cloud and endpoint activity, and conduct regular social-engineering training to mitigate Scattered Spider’s fast, multi-vector ransomware preparation tactics.
hits.title: Anatomy of a Scattered Spider attack: A growing ransomware threat evolves

hits.text: On June 30, threat actors exploited a vulnerability in a third-party call-center platform used by Qantas to exfiltrate 5.7 million unique customer records—none of which involved direct compromise of Qantas’s own systems—and on July 7 the airline confirmed a likely extortion attempt when the hacker made contact; after deduplication Qantas found 4 million records contained names, email addresses and Frequent Flyer details, 1.2 million contained only names and emails, and 1.7 million included additional data such as addresses (1.3 million), dates of birth (1.1 million), phone numbers (900 000), gender (400 000) and meal preferences (10 000), while no credit card, financial or passport information was stored on the breached platform. The company has begun notifying affected customers, deployed enhanced security controls, and is collaborating closely with the Australian Cyber Security Centre, the National Cyber Security Coordinator and the Australian Federal Police to investigate the supply-chain weakness, reinforce third-party risk management, and bolster monitoring and incident response capabilities to mitigate future breaches.
hits.title: Qantas Confirms 5.7 Million Impacted by Data Breach - SecurityWeek

hits.text: Since mid-2022, Unit 42 has attributed over 100 high-value cryptocurrency and BPO incidents to Muddled Libra—a fluid subset of the Scattered Spider collective—initially executing structured smishing and 0ktapus phishing campaigns (leveraging over 200 realistic mobile-auth portals) against large business process outsourcers, then evolving in 2023 into an ALPHV/BlackCat affiliate with multi-million-dollar extortion demands, later resuming high-profile attacks in late 2024 and expanding through May 2025 into software automation, telecom, hospitality, finance and retail verticals; their adaptable tradecraft blends social engineering of IT helpdesks to reset passwords and MFA, inside BPO access, legitimate remote management tools for CRM exfiltration, NSOCKS/TrueSocks anonymizing proxies, custom virtual machines, the open-source “bedevil” rootkit on VMware vCenter, email-forwarding rules to hijack incident response communications, and AI-driven voice spoofing for vishing, with members cycling via Discord and Telegram to refresh niche skills and spawn offshoots such as Scatter Swine and Octo Tempest, while leveraging deep incident response framework knowledge to persist in environments and repeatedly reclaim stolen data before affiliating with DragonForce for ransomware; defenders should deploy interwoven modern security architectures (Cortex XSIAM/XDR, Advanced URL Filtering, DNS Security, App-ID), enforce strict access controls, conduct rigorous awareness training, and maintain vigilant MITRE-mapped monitoring (T1566, T1556, T1215, T1562) to thwart these multifaceted, evolving extortion campaigns.
hits.title: Threat Group Assessment: Muddled Libra (Updated May 16, 2025)

canonical_entities: Remote Code Execution via ms-msdt URI in Word/RTF documents
ms-msdt URI-based RCE in Word/RTF documents
hits.text: In late May 2022, Symantec identified multiple threat actors exploiting the MSDT Follina bug (CVE-2022-30190) through ms-msdt URI-based RCE in Word/RTF documents that load a malicious HTML via Word’s remote template feature to launch msdt.exe, sdiagnhost.exe and ultimately PowerShell—bypassing the need for macros—to install a digitally signed AsyncRAT remote access Trojan that performs anti-analysis checks, collects hardware IDs, user names, execution paths and OS details, and maintains C&C communications, alongside parallel deployments of a browser infostealer targeting cookies and saved credentials in Firefox, Chrome and Edge. Symantec customers should apply Microsoft’s advisories or disable the ms-msdt handler, update Symantec Endpoint definitions (File-based-Downloader-Backdoor:Async, InfoStealer) and monitor for related IOCs to thwart these rapid, damaging campaigns.
hits.title: Attackers Exploit MSDT Follina Bug to Drop RAT, Infostealer | Symantec Enterprise Blogs

canonical_entities: Bypass authentication by sending empty or invalid USERNAME and PASSWORD parameters with requirePasswordChange=Y
hits.text: A critical zero-day flaw (CVE-2023-51467) has been identified in Apache OfBiz’s login functionality—stemming from an incomplete patch for a prior high-severity RCE vulnerability (CVE-2023-49070, CVSS 9.8) tied to a deprecated XML-RPC component—that allows attackers to bypass authentication by sending empty or invalid USERNAME and PASSWORD parameters alongside “requirePasswordChange=Y,” effectively granting unauthorized access and enabling simple SSRF attacks against internal resources; discovered by SonicWall Capture Labs, the bug follows observations by The Shadowserver Foundation of active exploitation attempts against CVE-2023-49070, and SonicWall reports exploit traffic for CVE-2023-51467 spiking from 235 attempts on December 27, 2023, to 26,928 on December 29 and 3,129 on January 1, 2024, underscoring urgent need for organizations using OfBiz versions prior to 18.12.11 to upgrade immediately to mitigate further data exfiltration and system takeover risks.
hits.title: Critical Zero-Day in Apache OfBiz ERP System Exposes Businesses to Attack

canonical_entities: Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Tools
OS Credential Dumping: Security Account Manager
hits.text: Water Ouroboros is a Ransomware-as-a-Service operation that exploits public-facing Oracle WebLogic vulnerabilities (CVE-2019-2725, CVE-2017-10271, CVE-2019-2729) or drive-by installers for initial access (T1190, T1189), then executes remote Windows commands (wmic.exe, bcdedit.exe, wbadmin.exe, vssadmin.exe) to delete backups and disable recovery (T1490, T1562.001) before encrypting fixed, removable and network drives via a Go-based custom routine that uses RTLGenRandom to generate a symmetric key, protects it with embedded RSA public keys (App_ExportKey), appends “.locked” (unless suppressed with –E), excludes over 60 file extensions, and accepts credentials (c {user}:{pass}), logging (–a), non-aggressive (–A) and size filters (–m). Victims find Contact Us.txt ransom notes pointing to a TOR payment site and Hive Leaks data-dump threat. Post-infection, actors maintain access via compromised admin accounts (T1078), disable security tools (PCHunter, ProcessHacker), dump credentials from registry hives (T1003.002), move laterally over RDP/SMB (T1021.001/002), discover assets via AdFind (T1595.002) and exfiltrate data over C&C (SharpRhino RAT/T1071.001, T1041). With 136 incidents in the US and notable impacts on construction, IT, manufacturing and healthcare SMBs, the campaign underscores the need for timely patching, hardened public-facing apps, least-privilege access, MFA, robust backups and advanced threat detection.
hits.title: Ransomware Spotlight: Water Ouroboros | Trend Micro (US)

canonical_entities: injected commands via a malicious URL
hits.text: CrowdStrike researchers in April 2022 uncovered that ransomware actors exploited a critical remote code execution flaw (CVE-2022-29499) in unpatched Linux-based Mitel MiVoice appliances (SA 100, SA 400 and Virtual SA) to gain initial access, plant malware and pivot laterally: the exploit chain began with an external HTTP GET to a “get_url” parameter in a PHP file (to bypass IP restrictions) followed by a device-originated GET that injected commands via a malicious URL, enabling an SSL-enabled reverse shell (using mkfifo and openssl_client) and deployment of a “pdf_import.php” web shell and the Chisel tunneling tool. Although the threat actors deleted evidence from the VoIP filesystem, CrowdStrike recovered the undocumented exploit, downloaded tools and anti-forensic measures. With some 21,000 MITEL devices worldwide still exposed (per Kevin Beaumont’s Shodan string “http.html_hash:-1971546278”), organizations are urged to apply Mitel’s April advisory patches for MiVoice Connect 19.2 SP3 and earlier, enforce strict network segmentation around perimeter devices, conduct threat modeling to detect anomalous GET requests, and prioritize timely firmware updates to thwart zero-day exploitation.
hits.title: Mitel VoIP Bug Exploited in Ransomware Attacks | Threatpost

hits.text: Since at least May 2023, BlackBerry researchers have identified a technically sophisticated Chinese-speaking threat actor—dubbed Silent Skimmer—that after over a year skimming card data from Asia/Pacific e-commerce and point-of-sale sites has expanded its campaign to North and Latin America, compromising organizations across multiple sectors by exploiting known web application vulnerabilities—most notably CVE-2019-18935 in Progress Software’s Telerik UI previously used by China’s Hafnium and Vietnam’s XE Group—on IIS servers to upload a malicious DLL and achieve remote code execution; using a multi-stage toolkit comprising privilege escalation exploits, a remote access tool, stagers/downloaders, and post-exploit utilities along with open-source binaries and scripts to inject card-skimming code into payment pages; and dynamically rotating short-lived, regionally co-located Microsoft Azure VPS-based C2 servers (each active less than a week) to blend exfiltration traffic with normal operations, mirroring Magecart tactics that have impacted hundreds of thousands of sites (e.g., British Airways, Ticketmaster, Newegg), and highlighting the imperative for prompt patching of third-party components, comprehensive web-app security audits, and vigilant monitoring of anomalous C2 infrastructure to thwart credential and payment data theft.

hits.text: BlackBerry’s Research and Intelligence Team has uncovered “Silent Skimmer,” a year-long, financially motivated campaign by a Chinese-fluent actor exploiting Internet Information Services (IIS) vulnerabilities to breach online payment and PoS web applications across Asia-Pacific, North America and Latin America, achieving initial foothold before leveraging open-source and living-off-the-land tools for privilege escalation and executing a PowerShell-based RAT (server.ps1); this malware connects to geolocated VPS C2 servers to download additional utilities, deploy web shells and inject scrapers into checkout pages, stealthily harvesting payment data via reverse proxies and Cobalt Strike beacons. In parallel, Sophos detailed a “pig butchering” crypto scam using dating-app social engineering and liquidity-mining lures—no malware required—to trick victims into connecting wallets to malicious Ethereum contracts, netting actors millions; these findings highlight the urgent need for patching IIS, monitoring PowerShell and Cobalt Strike activity, enforcing least-privilege controls, detecting web shells, and training users against DeFi phishing.
hits.title: Silent Skimmer: A Year-Long Web Skimming Campaign Targeting Online Payment Businesses

hits.text: Researchers at NCC Group have identified SnapMC as a new rapid-strike extortion group that eschews file encryption in favor of pure data theft, leveraging the Acunetix vulnerability scanner to pinpoint and exploit unpatched PrintNightmare LPE, Telerik UI for ASPX.NET RCE and SQL-injection flaws in VPN and web-server applications, then running SQL export scripts, compressing stolen CSVs with 7zip and exfiltrating them via the MinIO client—all within 30 minutes—before delivering standard extortion emails. By making data theft the primary leverage, SnapMC renders backup-based recovery moot and heightens the risk that victims who pay ransoms will face repeated extortion or public data sale, as seen with Sodinokibi, Netwalker, Mespinoza and Conti, and echoed by Coveware’s advice never to pay. Effective defenses include prompt patching of known CVEs, deploying well-configured web application firewalls around vulnerable services like Telerik and maintaining rigorous vulnerability management to thwart this growing threat.
hits.title: SnapMC hackers skip file encryption and just steal your files

hits.text: The SnapMC group, newly identified by NCC Group, uses its mc.exe exfiltration tool to rapidly compromise unpatched VPNs and webserver apps—exploiting CVE-2019-18935 in Telerik UI for ASPX.NET and SQL injection flaws—to steal sensitive data and demand extortion within a 24-hour contact window and 72-hour negotiation deadline, often escalating pressure before expiration. Without deploying ransomware, SnapMC publishes a list of exfiltrated records and threatens breach disclosures to customers and media if victims fail to comply, exemplifying a streamlined “smash-and-grab” model that requires minimal technical effort. Observations of related exploits—such as CVE-2019-7418 against SonicWall and CVE-2021-1609 on Cisco VPN routers—underscore the critical need for timely patching, zero-trust network access (ZTNA) policies, cloud access security broker (CASB) controls, and a ready incident response plan to detect and mitigate these accelerated data-extortion attacks.
hits.title: 30 Mins or Less: Rapid Attacks Extort Orgs Without Ransomware

hits.text: Since December 2020, the relatively new APT group ToddyCat has conducted multi-wave intrusion campaigns against high-profile government and military Microsoft Exchange servers in Asia and Europe, first targeting Taiwan and Vietnam via China Chopper-deployed web shells to drop a multi-stage chain that installs the Samurai passive backdoor on ports 80/443, uses obfuscated C# modules for arbitrary code execution, lateral movement and registry hijacking to load iiswmi.dll and a .NET loader, and in some cases launches the Ninja post-exploitation toolkit—which, like Cobalt Strike, offers HTTP-camouflaged command and control. From February to May 2021 the group scaled up by abusing the ProxyLogon vulnerability to compromise organizations in Iran, India, Malaysia, Slovakia, Russia and the UK, then post-May expanded its scope to desktops and additional government and military targets in Indonesia, Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan. Independent telemetry from ESET (“Websiic”) and GTSC has partially mapped ToddyCat’s infection vectors and dropper delivery, though full chains and later stages remain undocumented. Researchers noted overlaps with Chinese-language groups using the FunnyDream Exchange backdoor against the same targets—sharing staging locations and directories—yet found no conclusive link, suggesting multiple APT interests. This campaign highlights the urgent need to patch Exchange servers, hunt for China Chopper web shells, monitor anomalous registry modifications and HTTP indicators, and enforce network segmentation to mitigate high-impact geopolitical espionage.
hits.title: Elusive ToddyCat APT Targets Microsoft Exchange Servers | Threatpost

canonical_entities: Launch EC2 instances across regions via VPN
hits.text: Unit42’s “EleKtra-Leak” campaign, active since December 2020, uses automated scripts to clone public GitHub repos every few minutes, extract exposed AWS IAM keys within five minutes, then—if not blocked by GitHub-AWS quarantine policies—execute rapid AWS reconnaissance (DescribeRegions), create security groups, and launch hundreds of EC2 instances across regions via VPN for Monero cryptojacking, generating over 400 API calls in seven minutes. Between Aug. 30 and Oct. 6, 2023, researchers tracked 474 actor-controlled miners. The actor employs custom mining software and blocklists high-profile AWS account IDs to avoid honey traps. Leveraging the Prisma Cloud HoneyCloud project’s ephemeral key leaks and policy overrides, Unit42 obtained full visibility, informing Prisma Cloud Secrets Security, CI/CD IaC scanning, Cortex XDR, and recommendations for independent repo scanning, strict IAM policies, and continuous monitoring.
hits.title: CloudKeys in the Air: Tracking Malicious Operations of Exposed IAM Keys

hits.text: NCC Group’s RIFT team has tracked a previously unknown extortion actor, SnapMC, which conducts sub-30-minute data breach attacks—eschewing ransomware to steal and threaten to publicly leak data unless victims pay—by scanning for and exploiting public-facing vulnerabilities (notably CVE-2019-18935 in Telerik UI and SQL injection) to deploy a reverse shell, executing reconnaissance via PowerShell (whoami, wmic, net users), occasionally leveraging privilege-escalation scripts such as Invoke-Nightmare and JuicyPotato, then collecting data with 7zip and Invoke-SQLcmd before exfiltrating compressed CSVs to cloud storage via the MinIO client (mc.exe) configured through config.json in C:\Windows\Temp; extortion emails grant a 24-hour contact window and 72-hour negotiation period, with SnapMC raising pressure early and notifying customers and media upon non-response, illustrating a low-skill, high-impact modus operandi poised to grow as data-only extortion demands less time and expertise than ransomware—mitigations include prompt patching, rigorous vulnerability scanning (including third-party components), properly configured WAFs, and robust detection and incident response processes to counter T1190, T1560.001 and T1567.002 techniques.
hits.title: SnapMC skips ransomware, steals data | NCC Group

canonical_entities: RansomEXX activity from March 31, 2021 to March 31, 2022
Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Tools
hits.text: Trend Micro’s analysis of RansomEXX activity from March 31, 2021 to March 31, 2022 reveals a predominantly human-operated ransomware campaign that hit the manufacturing sector hardest (followed by education and banking) with the highest attack attempts observed in the U.S., France, and Brazil—driven in part by a high-profile 2021 breach of a Taiwanese hardware manufacturer. Initial access is achieved via malspam delivering multi-stage payloads that leverage IcedID and TrickBot for footholds, deploy Cobalt Strike beacons and PyXie RAT for code execution and data exfiltration, use SMB to propagate a VATET loader for lateral movement, and employ Mimikatz and LaZagne for credential harvesting. Upon execution, RansomEXX evades defense by disabling tools (T1562.001), skipping encryption of critical Windows paths, file names, and extensions, and terminating hundreds of business and security processes to maximize impact (T1486, T1490), then encrypts data and demands ransom. Recommended mitigations include strict audit and asset inventory, hardened configurations and least-privilege access, macro and email sandboxing to block malspam entry, regular patching and virtual patching, multifactor authentication, advanced behavior-based detection (e.g., Trend Micro Vision One™), and continuous employee training and red-team testing to disrupt the ransomware kill chain and protect against future RansomEXX intrusions.
hits.title: Ransomware Spotlight: RansomEXX | Trend Micro (US)

hits.text: Karakurt, active since June 2021 and also known as Karakurt Team/Lair, has extorted over 40 small and midsize companies in North America and Europe by skipping encryption to steal data via brokered or stolen VPN credentials (often from unpatched devices without MFA), establishing persistence through service creation, AnyDesk or Cobalt Strike C2 beacons, and harvesting credentials with Mimikatz and PowerShell dumps of ntds.dit. They compress data with WinZip/7zip and exfiltrate via Rclone or SFTP to Mega.io, then threaten public leaks—backed by 11.6 BTC moved into Conti wallets and shared file-tree.txt artifacts—highlighting ties to Conti’s rebranding post–May 19, 2022 “shutdown.” The group’s pure data-extortion model renders backups ineffective, demanding that defenders deploy intrusion prevention systems, enforce VPN MFA, continuously monitor for unauthorized remote-management tools, and strengthen credential hygiene to foil initial access, lateral movement, and exfiltration.
hits.title: An In-Depth Look at the Data Extortion Group, Karakurt

hits.text: FARGO ransomware (aka Mallox/TargetCompany) is actively targeting unpatched Microsoft SQL servers, with threat actors evolving from deploying Cobalt Strike beacons in February 2022 to hijacking vulnerable instances for proxy bandwidth by July 2022 and now encrypting databases and extorting owners. The infection chain begins with cmd.exe and PowerShell scripts to download a malicious .NET loader, followed by retrieval of additional malware, execution of a batch script to terminate critical services, disable recovery features, and kill related processes before encrypting files with a “.Fargo3” extension and dropping a “RECOVERY FILES.txt” ransom note demanding Bitcoin payment. These attacks leverage brute‐force login attempts against weak credentials or exploit known SQL vulnerabilities, threatening non‐payers with public data exposure via Telegram. To mitigate this risk, organizations should enforce robust password policies, apply the latest SQL patches, monitor login anomalies, and deploy threat detection for IOCs such as specific MD5, SHA‐1, SHA‐256, vhash, and imphash signatures to prevent severe disruption to business‐critical services.
hits.title: Flash Notice: FARGO Ransomware Attacking Microsoft SQL Servers

retrieved_context.text: The SnapMC group, newly identified by NCC Group, uses its mc.exe exfiltration tool to rapidly compromise unpatched VPNs and webserver apps—exploiting CVE-2019-18935 in Telerik UI for ASPX.NET and SQL injection flaws—to steal sensitive data and demand extortion within a 24-hour contact window and 72-hour negotiation deadline, often escalating pressure before expiration. retrieved_context.text: Researchers at NCC Group have identified SnapMC as a new rapid-strike extortion group that eschews file encryption in favor of pure data theft, leveraging the Acunetix vulnerability scanner to pinpoint and exploit unpatched PrintNightmare LPE, Telerik UI for ASPX.NET RCE and SQL-injection flaws in VPN and web-server applications, then running SQL export scripts, compressing stolen CSVs with 7zip and exfiltrating them via the MinIO client—all within 30 minutes—before delivering standard extortion emails. canonical_entities: Launch EC2 instances across regions via VPN
retrieved_context.text: Unit42’s “EleKtra-Leak” campaign, active since December 2020, uses automated scripts to clone public GitHub repos every few minutes, extract exposed AWS IAM keys within five minutes, then—if not blocked by GitHub-AWS quarantine policies—execute rapid AWS reconnaissance (DescribeRegions), create security groups, and launch hundreds of EC2 instances across regions via VPN for Monero cryptojacking, generating over 400 API calls in seven minutes. Between Aug. 30 and Oct. 6, 2023, researchers tracked 474 actor-controlled miners. The actor employs custom mining software and blocklists high-profile AWS account IDs to avoid honey traps. Leveraging the Prisma Cloud HoneyCloud project’s ephemeral key leaks and policy overrides, Unit42 obtained full visibility, informing Prisma Cloud Secrets Security, CI/CD IaC scanning, Cortex XDR, and recommendations for independent repo scanning, strict IAM policies, and continuous monitoring.
retrieved_context.title: CloudKeys in the Air: Tracking Malicious Operations of Exposed IAM Keys

retrieved_context.text: NCC Group’s RIFT team has tracked a previously unknown extortion actor, SnapMC, which conducts sub-30-minute data breach attacks—eschewing ransomware to steal and threaten to publicly leak data unless victims pay—by scanning for and exploiting public-facing vulnerabilities (notably CVE-2019-18935 in Telerik UI and SQL injection) to deploy a reverse shell, executing reconnaissance via PowerShell (whoami, wmic, net users), occasionally leveraging privilege-escalation scripts such as Invoke-Nightmare and JuicyPotato, then collecting data with 7zip and Invoke-SQLcmd before exfiltrating compressed CSVs to cloud storage via the MinIO client (mc.exe) configured through config.json in C:\Windows\Temp; extortion emails grant a 24-hour contact window and 72-hour negotiation period, with SnapMC raising pressure early and notifying customers and media upon non-response, illustrating a low-skill, high-impact modus operandi poised to grow as data-only extortion demands less time and expertise than ransomware—mitigations include prompt patching, rigorous vulnerability scanning (including third-party components), properly configured WAFs, and robust detection and incident response processes to counter T1190, T1560.001 and T1567.002 techniques.

retrieved_context.text: Karakurt, active since June 2021 and also known as Karakurt Team/Lair, has extorted over 40 small and midsize companies in North America and Europe by skipping encryption to steal data via brokered or stolen VPN credentials (often from unpatched devices without MFA), establishing persistence through service creation, AnyDesk or Cobalt Strike C2 beacons, and harvesting credentials with Mimikatz and PowerShell dumps of ntds.dit. retrieved_context.title: An In-Depth Look at the Data Extortion Group, Karakurt

retrieved_context.text: FARGO ransomware (aka Mallox/TargetCompany) is actively targeting unpatched Microsoft SQL servers, with threat actors evolving from deploying Cobalt Strike beacons in February 2022 to hijacking vulnerable instances for proxy bandwidth by July 2022 and now encrypting databases and extorting owners. The infection chain begins with cmd.exe and PowerShell scripts to download a malicious .NET loader, followed by retrieval of additional malware, execution of a batch script to terminate critical services, disable recovery features, and kill related processes before encrypting files with a “.Fargo3” extension and dropping a “RECOVERY FILES.txt” ransom note demanding Bitcoin payment. These attacks leverage brute‐force login attempts against weak credentials or exploit known SQL vulnerabilities, threatening non‐payers with public data exposure via Telegram. To mitigate this risk, organizations should enforce robust password policies, apply the latest SQL patches, monitor login anomalies, and deploy threat detection for IOCs such as specific MD5, SHA‐1, SHA‐256, vhash, and imphash signatures to prevent severe disruption to business‐critical services.

hits.text: Last week Google’s Threat Analysis Group, in partnership with The Citizen Lab, exposed an in-the-wild exploit chain developed by the commercial surveillance vendor Intellexa in Egypt that leverages a man-in-the-middle injection on HTTP traffic to silently redirect targets first to c.betly[.]me and then to sec-flare[.]com, delivering Predator spyware without any user interaction; on iOS this chain combined Safari RCE (CVE-2023-41993), certificate validation bypass (CVE-2023-41991) and XNU kernel local privilege escalation (CVE-2023-41992) and was patched in iOS 16.7/17.0.1, while on Android initial Chrome renderer RCE (CVE-2023-4762), delivered via MITM or one-time links, was patched on September 5; this campaign highlights the serious risk posed by proliferating commercial spyware, underscores the urgency of enforcing universal HTTPS and enabling Chrome’s HTTPS-First Mode, and demonstrates the critical need for organizations and users to apply the latest OS and browser updates, deploy encrypted-traffic protections, and monitor for anomalous network redirects to mitigate future attacks.

hits.text: Cuba ransomware, first observed in late 2019 but only drawing widespread attention in November 2021 after infiltrating at least 49 organizations across government, healthcare, IT, manufacturing and finance, has since expanded its scope to compromise 101 victims globally (65 in the U.S., 36 abroad), demanded over $145 million in ransoms and collected more than $60 million. Operators gain initial access via Hancitor‐delivered loaders, phishing emails spoofing entities like Ukraine’s armed forces press service, unpatched Microsoft Exchange SSRF vulnerabilities (CVE-2022-41080/41040), compromised credentials and legitimate RDP, then deploy Cobalt Strike beacons via PowerShell and PsExec to execute memory‐injected payloads (“pones.exe,” “krots.exe”/KPOT), use Mimikatz for credential theft, and abuse Windows services to encrypt files with a “.cuba” extension. From 2022, affiliates such as “Tropical Scorpius” have employed the RomCom RAT (rmtpak.dll) for data exfiltration, industrial Spy ransomware tie-ins, and a kernel‐mode dropper (ApcHelper.sys, signed with a LAPSUS-stolen NVIDIA certificate) to terminate security tools, while adopting double-extortion by threatening public release of stolen data. High-impact incidents include attacks on Chilean government VMware and Microsoft ESXi servers, unpatched Microsoft Exchange environments, and The Philadelphia Inquirer in May 2023, which disrupted newspaper distribution and business operations. To counter this evolving threat, organizations should promptly apply Exchange and software patches, enforce multifactor authentication on RDP, restrict PowerShell/PsExec use, deploy EDR to detect Cobalt Strike and memory injection, monitor for malicious driver loads, and implement FBI/CISA mitigation guidelines.
