retrieved_context.text: On March 2, 2025, CyberMaterial’s report on Void Manticore (aka Storm-0842, linked to the cybercriminal Storm-1811 cluster) details a coordinated espionage campaign that began in late 2024 against aerospace, defense and government organizations in Europe and North America: operators initiated intrusions via spear-phishing emails embedding weaponized RTFs exploiting CVE-2024-4113 to drop a custom loader (“VoidLoader”), which in turn deployed the “ManticoreShell” backdoor; post-compromise activities included credential harvesting (Mimikatz), lateral movement via PSExec and WMI, privilege escalation through a signed kernel-mode driver exploit, and persistence using registry Run keys and scheduled tasks; C2 communications leveraged HTTPS with a domain generation algorithm (DGA) and fallback to TOR. Over a three-month window they compromised at least 15 organizations, exfiltrated more than 20 GB of intellectual property, and triggered system outages exceeding 48 hours in critical environments. Key mitigation measures include immediate patching of CVE-2024-4113, deployment of EDR solutions to detect anomalous IOCTL and PowerShell activity, network segmentation to contain lateral movement, strict monitoring of DGA-style DNS queries, and implementation of multi-factor authentication to thwart credential abuse.
retrieved_context.title: Void Manticore (Storm-0842) – Threat Actor - CyberMaterial

retrieved_context.text: Since mid-September, unknown cybercriminals have been conducting large-scale brute-force attacks against internet-exposed instances of Foundation Accounting Software—widely used by construction sub-industries such as plumbing, HVAC and concrete—by targeting the default “sa” administrator and a second high-privilege account within the MSSQL database accessible via TCP port 4243 (opened for Foundation’s mobile app). After an observed peak of roughly 35,000 rapid login attempts to obtain valid credentials, the attackers enable an extended stored procedure (e.g., xp_cmdshell) to execute OS-level commands and scripts, automating lateral movement and data theft across multiple unrelated victims. Huntress has identified just 33 hosts left with unchanged default passwords, alerted all impacted and at-risk customers, and urges organizations to rotate all Foundation credentials, remove direct internet exposure, and disable the exploited stored procedure to mitigate further compromise.
retrieved_context.title: Threat Actors Target Accounting Software Used by Construction Contractors - SecurityWeek

retrieved_context.text: Evil Corp–linked operators began by abusing the open-source Responder tool to poison LLMNR and NBT-NS name-resolution queries on Windows hosts, harvesting NTLMv2 hashes and cleartext credentials, then used pass-the-hash techniques alongside PSExec and WMI for rapid lateral movement and privilege escalation to domain admin; once established, they deployed WastedLocker ransomware via scheduled tasks, encrypting over 95% of critical servers and workstations with AES-256, causing 72 hours of operational downtime and a $10 million ransom demand. Cynet’s automated threat detection flagged abnormal name-resolution traffic and excessive SMB authentication failures, enabling immediate host isolation, credential resets, and network segmentation. Key mitigations include disabling LLMNR/NBT-NS, enforcing SMB signing, monitoring NTLM authentication events, and strictly enforcing least-privilege service accounts to prevent similar intrusions.
retrieved_context.title: Cynet | Threat Detection Report: Wastedlocker Ransomware

hits.text: Since at least 2019, China-linked Winnti APT (aka APT41/BARIUM/Blackfly) has run the stealthy CuckooBees campaign against technology and manufacturing firms in North America, Europe, and Asia to support Beijing’s Made in China 2025 initiative, exploiting ERP platform vulnerabilities for initial access and deploying a “house of cards” kill chain—including an undocumented Deploylog backdoor and updated Winnti malware concealed via rare Windows CLFS abuse—to maintain persistence through a VBScript WebShell (up_win32.jsp variant), modified WinRM HTTP(S) listeners, a signed kernel rootkit, and side-loaded DLLs via IKEEXT and PrintNotify services; after reconnaissance with built-in Windows commands, attackers stole credentials using reg save to dump SYSTEM/SAM/SECURITY hives and a custom MFSDLL.exe loader of mktzx64.dll, leveraged stolen domain admin rights and scheduled tasks for lateral movement, then exfiltrated hundreds of gigabytes of proprietary data in password-protected WinRAR archives renamed as rundll32.exe; Cybereason’s discovery underscores the need to patch ERP systems, monitor unusual CLFS writes and service modifications, detect script-based web shells, scrutinize registry hive exports, review scheduled-task anomalies, and flag renamed archival tools to thwart similar state-sponsored espionage.
hits.title: China-Linked Winnti APT Group Silently Stole Trade Secrets for Years: Report

hits.text: Security researchers at Cybereason uncovered that since at least 2019 a Chinese state-sponsored APT group known as Winnti (also tracked as APT41, Barium, Wicked Panda, Axiom) has been running “Operation CuckooBees,” a multi-year, multi-stage espionage campaign targeting technology and manufacturing firms across Asia, Europe and North America to steal hundreds of gigabytes of trade secrets. The attackers exploited both known and zero-day RCE flaws in a popular ERP platform to deploy JSP web shells, enabled WinRM for persistence, dumped registry-stored credentials to move laterally via scheduled tasks, and used a sophisticated loader chain—Spyder Loader (disguised as SQLite3 DLL), STASHLOG (which hides payloads in Windows’ proprietary CLFS logs), SPARKLOG (which extracts and side-loads PRIVATELOG via DLL hijacking for SYSTEM privileges), and DEPLOYLOG (which abuses Transactional NTFS to overwrite dbghelp.dll and hijack the AMD K8 kernel driver)—to install WINNKIT, a kernel-level rootkit signed with a stolen BenQ certificate that hooks TCP/IP at the NIC to receive commands for shell execution, file enumeration, SOCKS5 proxy, RDP and process control, all while evading detection for years.
hits.title: Chinese APT group Winnti stole trade secrets in years-long undetected campaign

canonical_entities: trading and brokerage firms in Hong Kong, the UAE, Jordan, Lebanon and Malaysia
hits.text: First observed in September 2024 and active through at least August 12, 2025, the GodRAT campaign—attributed to an APT likely linked to Winnti—targets financial institutions, particularly trading and brokerage firms in Hong Kong, the UAE, Jordan, Lebanon and Malaysia, by distributing malicious .scr and .pif files via Skype messenger disguised as legitimate financial documents. Evolving from the AwesomePuppet RAT on a Gh0st RAT codebase, GodRAT employs a two-stage loader architecture: an initial stub invokes SDL2.dll to allocate memory and extract XOR-decoded (key 0x63) shellcode hidden via steganography in image files named to mimic authentic financial reports, then searches for the “godinfo” marker and uses the authentication string “GETGOD” to contact C2 servers, download UPX-packed GodRAT DLL modules and launch browser credential-stealing and remote-access payloads. This advanced steganographic delivery evades signature-based defenses and underscores the need to inspect .scr/.pif attachments, monitor Skype channels, and deploy detection rules for “godinfo,” “GETGOD” and related shellcode patterns.
hits.title: New GodRAT Weaponizing Screen Saver and Program Files to Attack Organizations

hits.text: Last week Google’s Threat Analysis Group, in partnership with The Citizen Lab, exposed an in-the-wild exploit chain developed by the commercial surveillance vendor Intellexa in Egypt that leverages a man-in-the-middle injection on HTTP traffic to silently redirect targets first to c.betly[.]me and then to sec-flare[.]com, delivering Predator spyware without any user interaction; on iOS this chain combined Safari RCE (CVE-2023-41993), certificate validation bypass (CVE-2023-41991) and XNU kernel local privilege escalation (CVE-2023-41992) and was patched in iOS 16.7/17.0.1, while on Android initial Chrome renderer RCE (CVE-2023-4762), delivered via MITM or one-time links, was patched on September 5; this campaign highlights the serious risk posed by proliferating commercial spyware, underscores the urgency of enforcing universal HTTPS and enabling Chrome’s HTTPS-First Mode, and demonstrates the critical need for organizations and users to apply the latest OS and browser updates, deploy encrypted-traffic protections, and monitor for anomalous network redirects to mitigate future attacks.

hits.text: In September 2024, a Winnti-linked APT began targeting trading and brokerage firms by distributing malicious .scr/.pif screen saver files via Skype that use steganographically embedded shellcode to load GodRAT—a new Gh0st RAT variant evolved from the AwesomePuppet backdoor—into legitimate processes. Two loader types (one with XOR-encoded shellcode bytes, one extracting shellcode from JPG images via an expired Valve.exe/SDL2.dll signed binary) allocate memory, inject the decoded first-stage shellcode, decode configuration data (single-byte XOR key 0x63, “godinfo” header), and fetch a UPX-packed GodRAT DLL from C2. GodRAT launches under a “-Puppet” flag in curl.exe or cmd.exe, collects OS, host, AV, process and user metadata, and communicates over zlib-compressed, triple-XOR TCP channels. It supports in-memory plugin injection—deploying a FileManager plugin for file enumeration, manipulation and 7zip-based extraction—and installs Chrome and Edge password stealers in %ALLUSERSPROFILE%. AsyncRAT serves as a secondary fallback implant. Ongoing detections (12 MD5s across Hong Kong, UAE, Jordan, Lebanon and Malaysia) through August 12 2025 highlight sustained financial credential theft and long-term C2 persistence.
hits.title: Gh0st RAT-based GodRAT attacks financial organizations

hits.text: Since early 2025, a sophisticated threat actor has deployed PS1Bot, a multi-stage PowerShell/C# malware framework distributed via malvertising and SEO-poisoned archives named to resemble legitimate documents (e.g., “chapter 8 medicare benefit policy manual.zip”), which drops an obfuscated VBScript downloader (“FULL DOCUMENT.js”) that retrieves a JScript scriptlet to write and execute a PowerShell loader (e.g., ntu.ps1) from C:\ProgramData\; this loader polls a C2—deriving unique URLs from the C-drive serial number—and uses Invoke-Expression to run in-memory modules with minimal disk footprints. PS1Bot’s modular toolkit includes a WMI-based antivirus reconnaissance module, a dynamic C# screen-capture module exfiltrating Base64‐encoded bitmaps, a “grabber” that harvests browser and 40+ crypto wallet credentials (including MetaMask, Ledger, Exodus, Electrum) using embedded multilingual seed-phrase wordlists, a SetWindowsHookEx keylogger, and a WMIComputerCSHARP system survey. Persistence is achieved via randomized %PROGRAMDATA% directories, LNK startup shortcuts, and mutex checks. Cisco Talos notes overlaps with AHK Bot and Skitnet infrastructures and reports rapid evolution with undisclosed modules poised for espionage, financial theft, and lateral movement. Organizations should monitor anomalous PowerShell execution, unexpected WMI queries, and malvertising indicators to detect and disrupt this ongoing campaign.
hits.title: PS1Bot: Multi-Stage Malware Framework Targeting Windows Systems

canonical_entities: registered variables in the Windows Registry
hits.text: In June 2024, HP’s Threat Research team led by Patrick Schlapfer intercepted a low-grade phishing campaign leveraging HTML smuggling via an AES-encrypted HTML attachment containing JavaScript-embedded decryption logic—a novel twist on typical encrypted archives—which, when decrypted, mimicked a legitimate website but dropped a fully commented, French-language VBScript that registered variables in the Windows Registry, staged a JavaScript payload as a scheduled task, and invoked a PowerShell script to deploy the freely available AsyncRAT infostealer. Schlapfer and co-lead Alex Holland’s analysis, including comparison with generative-AI–produced code, concluded the well-structured, human-readable script was likely authored by gen-AI by a low-skill newcomer benefitting from reduced entry barriers, with no obfuscation or complex infrastructure beyond a single C2 server. This first definitive proof of AI-generated malware in the wild underscores the need for defenders to adapt detection strategies to AI-crafted droppers, monitor anomalous AES-in-JavaScript decryption patterns, and anticipate more sophisticated AI-generated payloads poised to emerge within the next two years, thereby heightening the risk to network and endpoint security.
hits.title: AI-Generated Malware Found in the Wild - SecurityWeek

hits.text: New research reveals that over 80,000 Hikvision cameras worldwide remain unpatched against the critical CVE-2021-36260 command-injection flaw (NIST score 9.8/10) disclosed last fall, allowing remote code execution and potential espionage by state-linked groups such as MISSION2025/APT41, APT10 and unknown Russian actors trading stolen credentials on dark-web forums; systemic deficiencies—default or hardcoded passwords, no auto-update mechanism, poor forensics and lack of security-by-design—have left devices in 100+ countries (including the U.S., despite an FCC “unacceptable risk” designation) continuously discoverable via Shodan or Censys and ripe for exploitation, underscoring the urgent need for organizations to inventory IoT assets, change default credentials, deploy available patches and improve visibility and update processes to mitigate geopolitical and operational impact.

hits.text: Operation Triangulation, a sophisticated iOS-targeting advanced persistent threat (APT) platform documented by Kaspersky researchers Georgy Kucherin, Leonid Bezvershenko, and Valentin Pashkov, exploited zero-day kernel vulnerabilities CVE-2023-32434 and CVE-2023-32435 via iMessage to deliver the TriangleDB backdoor implant; the attack chain utilized JavaScript Validator and Binary Validator stages performing canvas fingerprinting and device reconnaissance before deployment, with the validators collecting fingerprint data to identify research environments and subsequently exfiltrating crash logs, iMessage evidence, process lists, jailbreak status, device identifiers (username, phone number, IMEI, Apple ID), and installed applications via C2 servers; TriangleDB comprised microphone-recording, iCloud Keychain extraction, SQLite database theft, and location-triangulation modules using GSM data (MCC, MNC, LAC) when GPS unavailable, with recording suspended during screen-on states and below 10% battery; the backdoor employed private undocumented APIs and periodically exfiltrated data from /private/var/tmp while establishing heartbeat C2 communication and receiving commands to delete forensic artifacts; Kaspersky became a target in early 2023, prompting investigation; Apple patched CVE-2023-32434 in iOS 15.8 and iPadOS 15.8 as of October 25, 2023.
hits.title: iOS Zero-Day Attacks: Experts Uncover Deeper Insights into Operation Triangulation

canonical_entities: dual-pronged cyberespionage campaign against the Tibetan diaspora
hits.text: Since at least September 2023, the China-aligned Evasive Panda APT (aka BRONZE HIGHLAND/Daggerfly) has conducted a dual-pronged cyberespionage campaign against the Tibetan diaspora by compromising both the Kagyu International Monlam Trust’s website and the official Monlam translation-software supply chain—first implanting obfuscated JavaScript into jquery.js on the festival site that verifies victims’ first three IP octets via an MD5 hash salted with “1qaz0okm!@#,” serves a faux “Aw, Snap!” error page to users in India, Taiwan, Hong Kong, Australia and the U.S., and lures them to download a malicious “certificate.exe” or “.pkg” downloader; that loader side-loads memmgrset.dll (http_dy.dll) to fetch a JSON config from update.devicebug[.]com and ultimately deploys the undocumented Nightdoor backdoor alongside the group’s modular MgBot implant, while a trojanized Monlam software installer (Windows autorun.exe abusing MonlamUpdate.exe for DLL side-loading of RPHost.dll, and macOS Mach-O downloaders) has delivered further downloaders and payloads—retrieved from tibetpost[.]net and a direct IP—to %TEMP%\default_ico.exe for additional Nightdoor and MgBot installation.
hits.title: Evasive Panda leverages Monlam Festival to target Tibetans

hits.text: Operation Triangulation, an advanced persistent threat zero-click iMessage campaign active since 2019 and targeting Russian diplomats, Kaspersky employees and other high-value assets, exploits a previously undocumented Apple SoC feature (ADJUST TrueType font instruction) and four zero-day flaws—CVE-2023-41990 (iMessage RCE), CVE-2023-32434 (XNU integer overflow), CVE-2023-38606 (hardware PPL bypass via MMIO registers) and CVE-2023-32435 (Safari shellcode)—in a multistage chain. Attackers initiate a malicious iMessage attachment to trigger RCE, then use return-oriented programming, NSExpression/NSPredicate payloads and an 11,000-line obfuscated JavaScriptCore exploit leveraging the $vm debugging feature to execute native APIs. Next, they map physical memory for read/write access, bypass hardware memory protections, launch the IMAgent process to clear traces, and spin up an invisible Safari instance for victim verification and shellcode delivery. A Mach-object kernel exploit reuses CVE-2023-32434 and CVE-2023-38606 for root privileges, culminating in deployment of the TriangleDB spyware implant. Kaspersky GReAT deems this the most sophisticated iOS attack chain observed, underscoring the difficulty of detecting hardware-level exploits on closed systems and recommending prompt iOS patching, disabling iMessage/FaceTime, EDR deployment, and network/forensic backup analysis.
hits.title: 'Operation Triangulation' Spyware Attackers Bypass iPhone Memory Protections

hits.text: Since mid-November 2024, Russian nation-state actor Star Blizzard has significantly escalated its evasion tradecraft following public exposure by Microsoft Threat Intelligence: shifting from a single registrar (NameCheap) to multiple registrars (Hostinger, RealTime Register, GMO Internet) and implementing multi-stage redirection chains—embedding Microsoft 365 Safe Links in PDF lures that pass through Bitly and Cuttly shortened URLs and legitimate open-redirect sites (e.g., mechengsys[.]net) before landing on an Evilginx-equipped VPS (vidmemax[.]com)—to mount AiTM spear-phishing campaigns that harvest email credentials, including MFA tokens. Between July and August 2024 they also experimented with altered OneDrive file-share notifications—using ProtonMail accounts to spoof trusted senders and rewire the “Open” button URL to their Evilginx infrastructure—targeting individuals in politics, diplomacy, NGOs and think tanks. In October 2024, Microsoft’s Digital Crimes Unit disrupted core infrastructure, and ongoing collaboration with UK NCSC, NSA and FBI ensures rapid customer notification and defenses. Historically, since 2022 Star Blizzard has iteratively refined detection evasion—employing server-side fingerprinting scripts, HubSpot and MailerLite email platforms to mask domains, DNS obfuscation, password-protected PDFs and randomized DGAs—with each ephemeral TTP swiftly modified, underscoring the need for continuous updates to email security controls, link inspection and behavioral detection.
hits.title: Star Blizzard increases sophistication and evasion in ongoing attacks | Microsoft Security Blog

canonical_entities: regional organizations in Vietnam and South Korea
hits.text: In early 2018 McAfee Advanced Threat Research uncovered Operation Honeybee, a North Korean–linked campaign—tracked to the persona snoopykiller@mail.ru and control domains navermail.byethost3.com/nihon.byethost11.com—targeting humanitarian aid groups and regional organizations in Vietnam and South Korea with malicious Microsoft Word documents named “Honeybee” that exploited politically themed and generic “not compatible” lures to execute VBA macros embedding a custom‐alphabet Base64 payload. Beginning January 15, these macros dropped CAB archives to %TEMP%, used wusa.exe or expand.exe for UAC bypass, then hijacked cliconfg.exe via a malicious NTWDBLIB.dll to install a persistent COMSysApp service loading ipnet.dll from %SystemRoot%\System32. The implant gathers systeminfo and tasklist outputs, packages them into Base64‐encoded ZIPs, and exfiltrates data to FTP servers (e.g., 1113427185.ifastnet.org), while also supporting remote commands (pull, chip, put, user execution). A related Win32 dropper, MaoCheng—signed with a stolen Adobe certificate—demonstrated a tactical shift with Xero lures and test-phase bugs. This operation’s technical sophistication and evolving decoy tactics underscore a sustained threat to critical NGO networks, resulting in persistent backdoors and unauthorized data extraction.
hits.title: McAfee Uncovers Operation Honeybee, a Malicious Campaign Targeting Humanitarian Aid Groups | McAfee Blog

hits.text: In October 2023, a spearphishing campaign against a major Ukrainian defense company and an EU agency leveraged a spoofed Gmail sender (it.[redacted]@gmail.com) and look-alike OAuth URLs on login.microsoftidonline[.]com and choicelive149200[.]com to harvest Office 365 credentials, and forensic pivots revealed the same network infrastructure powering Operation Texonto’s two PSYOP waves in November and December 2023, which eschewed common channels like Telegram in favor of six attacker-owned domains (e.g., ua-minagro[.]com, minuaregionbecareful[.]com, uamtu[.]com) to disseminate PDF attachments misusing Ukrainian ministry logos to spread Russian propaganda themes of heating failures, energy blackouts, food scarcity and drug shortages; further pivots uncovered Navalny-themed domains targeting Russian dissidents and the reuse of the PSYOP mail server for Canadian pharmacy spam, a tactic long favored by Russia‐aligned threat actors, and although no direct code overlaps tie Texonto to known groups such as Callisto, the blend of credential phishing, disinformation, domain masquerading and infrastructure reuse supports a high-confidence attribution to a Russia-aligned operator conducting hybrid warfare against Ukrainian speakers and related targets.
hits.title: Operation Texonto: Information operation targeting Ukrainian speakers in the context of the war

canonical_entities: BMW 5 for sale in Kyiv flyer campaign
BMW 5 for sale in Kyiv flyer
Turkish MFA earthquake relief guidance lure
hits.text: Between April and May 2023, Russia’s SVR-linked Cloaked Ursa (aka APT29, Cozy Bear, Midnight Blizzard/Nobelium) repurposed a legitimate “BMW 5 for sale in Kyiv” flyer—initially circulated by a Polish diplomat and likely harvested via a compromised mail server—into malicious Word documents that leverage URL‐shortening services (t[.]ly/tinyurl[.]com) to redirect victims to a co-opted landing page (hxxps://resetlocations[.]com/bmw.htm) where Windows shortcut files masquerading as PNG images deploy a silent payload; this campaign targeted at least 22 of 80+ foreign missions in Kyiv (80 percent via publicly listed embassy addresses, 20 percent via unpublished contacts) and follows a February–March lure impersonating Turkish MFA earthquake relief guidance, both demonstrating Cloaked Ursa’s hallmark TTPs—phishing lures themed to individual diplomat needs, code overlap with known malware, exploitation of benign attachments requiring a web browser to trigger—and highlights that one payload SHA256 (311e9c8cf6d0b295074ffefaa9f277cb1f806343be262c59f88fbdf6fe242517) is vendor-detected while the other (8902bd7d085397745e05883f05c08de87623cc15fe630b36ad3d208f01ef0596) remains undetected, underscoring the need for region-specific APT training, vigilant URL redirection checks, cautious handling of web‐based attachments (.hta, .svg, .html), scrutiny of archive contents (.zip, .rar, .iso), JavaScript disablement where feasible, and deployment of protections such as Cortex XDR, WildFire and DNS Security to mitigate espionage risk.
hits.title: Diplomats Beware: Cloaked Ursa Phishing With a Twist

canonical_entities: Deliver maliciously crafted PDFs into iMessage sandbox
hits.text: In late 2021 Apple patched a zero-click iMessage vulnerability (CVE-2021-30860, “FORCEDENTRY”) exploited since February by NSO Group’s Pegasus spyware—sold to nation-states yet repeatedly abused against journalists and activists—to silently deliver maliciously crafted PDFs into iMessage’s sandbox, enabling arbitrary code execution to harvest messages, calls, location, passwords, microphone and camera data. Citizen Lab and Amnesty International identified infection URLs that Symantec WebPulse flagged in 1 of every 150,000 iOS devices, demonstrating that WebPulse–backed Symantec Endpoint Protection Mobile can intercept hidden iMessage fields, block command-and-control traffic, and quarantine zero-day payloads. Organizations are urged to deploy iOS 14.8+ patches and enforce layered mobile endpoint protection leveraging global URL intelligence to mitigate current and future Pegasus-style threats.
hits.title: Pegasus Spyware Takes Flight Again | Symantec Enterprise Blogs

hits.text: In early April, Palo Alto Networks’ Advanced WildFire and Cortex XDR uncovered SnipBot—a new v5.0 iteration of the RomCom RAT family—employing advanced window message–based control-flow obfuscation and anti-sandbox checks (filename hash and HKCU\…\RecentDocs entries) in a multi-stage chain beginning with a PDF-labeled EXE downloader signed using a likely stolen certificate; the downloader contacts xeontime[.]com for config-pdf.dll, which uses registry-based COM hijacking to load keyprov.dll from drvmcprotect[.]com into explorer.exe, decrypts payloads stored in HKCU\Software\AppDataSoft\Software, and opens a TCP listener on port 1342 for commands to update, delete, or execute modules. The main backdoor single.dll (mutex “SnipMutex”) supports 27 encrypted commands for drive and process enumeration, file upload/download, and remote module execution, facilitating network pivoting and targeted file exfiltration. Active since December 2023 (RomCom activity since 2022), SnipBot’s tactics, stolen certificates, unique obfuscation, and sophisticated loader underscore a high-risk threat actor likely focused on intelligence gathering; Palo Alto products classify its samples, URLs, and domains as malicious to prevent compromise.
hits.title: Inside SnipBot: The Latest RomCom Malware Variant

retrieved_context.text: Operation Triangulation, a sophisticated iOS-targeting advanced persistent threat (APT) platform documented by Kaspersky researchers Georgy Kucherin, Leonid Bezvershenko, and Valentin Pashkov, exploited zero-day kernel vulnerabilities CVE-2023-32434 and CVE-2023-32435 via iMessage to deliver the TriangleDB backdoor implant; the attack chain utilized JavaScript Validator and Binary Validator stages performing canvas fingerprinting and device reconnaissance before deployment, with the validators collecting fingerprint data to identify research environments and subsequently exfiltrating crash logs, iMessage evidence, process lists, jailbreak status, device identifiers (username, phone number, IMEI, Apple ID), and installed applications via C2 servers; TriangleDB comprised microphone-recording, iCloud Keychain extraction, SQLite database theft, and location-triangulation modules using GSM data (MCC, MNC, LAC) when GPS unavailable, with recording suspended during screen-on states and below 10% battery; the backdoor employed private undocumented APIs and periodically exfiltrated data from /private/var/tmp while establishing heartbeat C2 communication and receiving commands to delete forensic artifacts; Kaspersky became a target in early 2023, prompting investigation; Apple patched CVE-2023-32434 in iOS 15.8 and iPadOS 15.8 as of October 25, 2023.

retrieved_context.text: Operation Triangulation, an advanced persistent threat zero-click iMessage campaign active since 2019 and targeting Russian diplomats, Kaspersky employees and other high-value assets, exploits a previously undocumented Apple SoC feature (ADJUST TrueType font instruction) and four zero-day flaws—CVE-2023-41990 (iMessage RCE), CVE-2023-32434 (XNU integer overflow), CVE-2023-38606 (hardware PPL bypass via MMIO registers) and CVE-2023-32435 (Safari shellcode)—in a multistage chain. Attackers initiate a malicious iMessage attachment to trigger RCE, then use return-oriented programming, NSExpression/NSPredicate payloads and an 11,000-line obfuscated JavaScriptCore exploit leveraging the $vm debugging feature to execute native APIs. Next, they map physical memory for read/write access, bypass hardware memory protections, launch the IMAgent process to clear traces, and spin up an invisible Safari instance for victim verification and shellcode delivery. A Mach-object kernel exploit reuses CVE-2023-32434 and CVE-2023-38606 for root privileges, culminating in deployment of the TriangleDB spyware implant. Kaspersky GReAT deems this the most sophisticated iOS attack chain observed, underscoring the difficulty of detecting hardware-level exploits on closed systems and recommending prompt iOS patching, disabling iMessage/FaceTime, EDR deployment, and network/forensic backup analysis.
retrieved_context.title: 'Operation Triangulation' Spyware Attackers Bypass iPhone Memory Protections

retrieved_context.text: In early 2018 McAfee Advanced Threat Research uncovered Operation Honeybee, a North Korean–linked campaign—tracked to the persona snoopykiller@mail.ru and control domains navermail.byethost3.com/nihon.byethost11.com—targeting humanitarian aid groups and regional organizations in Vietnam and South Korea with malicious Microsoft Word documents named “Honeybee” that exploited politically themed and generic “not compatible” lures to execute VBA macros embedding a custom‐alphabet Base64 payload. Beginning January 15, these macros dropped CAB archives to %TEMP%, used wusa.exe or expand.exe for UAC bypass, then hijacked cliconfg.exe via a malicious NTWDBLIB.dll to install a persistent COMSysApp service loading ipnet.dll from %SystemRoot%\System32. The implant gathers systeminfo and tasklist outputs, packages them into Base64‐encoded ZIPs, and exfiltrates data to FTP servers (e.g., 1113427185.ifastnet.org), while also supporting remote commands (pull, chip, put, user execution). A related Win32 dropper, MaoCheng—signed with a stolen Adobe certificate—demonstrated a tactical shift with Xero lures and test-phase bugs. This operation’s technical sophistication and evolving decoy tactics underscore a sustained threat to critical NGO networks, resulting in persistent backdoors and unauthorized data extraction.

AridSpy’s capabilities center on remote data espionage—collecting contacts, messages, device metadata and location—and its modular architecture and third-party distribution model pose ongoing risks to Android users in high-value geopolitical regions.

hits.text: Between April and May 2023, Russia’s SVR-linked Cloaked Ursa (aka APT29, Cozy Bear, Midnight Blizzard/Nobelium) repurposed a legitimate “BMW 5 for sale in Kyiv” flyer—initially circulated by a Polish diplomat and likely harvested via a compromised mail server—into malicious Word documents that leverage URL‐shortening services (t[.]ly/tinyurl[.]com) to redirect victims to a co-opted landing page (hxxps://resetlocations[.]com/bmw.htm) where Windows shortcut files masquerading as PNG images deploy a silent payload; this campaign targeted at least 22 of 80+ foreign missions in Kyiv (80 percent via publicly listed embassy addresses, 20 percent via unpublished contacts) and follows a February–March lure impersonating Turkish MFA earthquake relief guidance, both demonstrating Cloaked Ursa’s hallmark TTPs—phishing lures themed to individual diplomat needs, code overlap with known malware, exploitation of benign attachments requiring a web browser to trigger—and highlights that one payload SHA256 (311e9c8cf6d0b295074ffefaa9f277cb1f806343be262c59f88fbdf6fe242517) is vendor-detected while the other (8902bd7d085397745e05883f05c08de87623cc15fe630b36ad3d208f01ef0596) remains undetected, underscoring the need for region-specific APT training, vigilant URL redirection checks, cautious handling of web‐based attachments (.hta, .svg, .html), scrutiny of archive contents (.zip, .rar, .iso), JavaScript disablement where feasible, and deployment of protections such as Cortex XDR, WildFire and DNS Security to mitigate espionage risk.

canonical_entities: regional organizations in Vietnam and South Korea
hits.text: In early 2018 McAfee Advanced Threat Research uncovered Operation Honeybee, a North Korean–linked campaign—tracked to the persona snoopykiller@mail.ru and control domains navermail.byethost3.com/nihon.byethost11.com—targeting humanitarian aid groups and regional organizations in Vietnam and South Korea with malicious Microsoft Word documents named “Honeybee” that exploited politically themed and generic “not compatible” lures to execute VBA macros embedding a custom‐alphabet Base64 payload. Beginning January 15, these macros dropped CAB archives to %TEMP%, used wusa.exe or expand.exe for UAC bypass, then hijacked cliconfg.exe via a malicious NTWDBLIB.dll to install a persistent COMSysApp service loading ipnet.dll from %SystemRoot%\System32. The implant gathers systeminfo and tasklist outputs, packages them into Base64‐encoded ZIPs, and exfiltrates data to FTP servers (e.g., 1113427185.ifastnet.org), while also supporting remote commands (pull, chip, put, user execution). A related Win32 dropper, MaoCheng—signed with a stolen Adobe certificate—demonstrated a tactical shift with Xero lures and test-phase bugs. This operation’s technical sophistication and evolving decoy tactics underscore a sustained threat to critical NGO networks, resulting in persistent backdoors and unauthorized data extraction.

Kaspersky GReAT deems this the most sophisticated iOS attack chain observed, underscoring the difficulty of detecting hardware-level exploits on closed systems and recommending prompt iOS patching, disabling iMessage/FaceTime, EDR deployment, and network/forensic backup analysis.
retrieved_context.title: 'Operation Triangulation' Spyware Attackers Bypass iPhone Memory Protections

canonical_entities: dual-pronged cyberespionage campaign against the Tibetan diaspora
retrieved_context.text: Since at least September 2023, the China-aligned Evasive Panda APT (aka BRONZE HIGHLAND/Daggerfly) has conducted a dual-pronged cyberespionage campaign against the Tibetan diaspora by compromising both the Kagyu International Monlam Trust’s website and the official Monlam translation-software supply chain—first implanting obfuscated JavaScript into jquery.js on the festival site that verifies victims’ first three IP octets via an MD5 hash salted with “1qaz0okm!@#,” serves a faux “Aw, Snap!” error page to users in India, Taiwan, Hong Kong, Australia and the U.S., and lures them to download a malicious “certificate.exe” or “.pkg” downloader; that loader side-loads memmgrset.dll (http_dy.dll) to fetch a JSON config from update.devicebug[.]com and ultimately deploys the undocumented Nightdoor backdoor alongside the group’s modular MgBot implant, while a trojanized Monlam software installer (Windows autorun.exe abusing MonlamUpdate.exe for DLL side-loading of RPHost.dll, and macOS Mach-O downloaders) has delivered further downloaders and payloads—retrieved from tibetpost[.]net and a direct IP—to %TEMP%\default_ico.exe for additional Nightdoor and MgBot installation.
retrieved_context.title: Evasive Panda leverages Monlam Festival to target Tibetans

retrieved_context.text: In October 2023, a spearphishing campaign against a major Ukrainian defense company and an EU agency leveraged a spoofed Gmail sender (it.[redacted]@gmail.com) and look-alike OAuth URLs on login.microsoftidonline[.]com and choicelive149200[.]com to harvest Office 365 credentials, and forensic pivots revealed the same network infrastructure powering Operation Texonto’s two PSYOP waves in November and December 2023, which eschewed common channels like Telegram in favor of six attacker-owned domains (e.g., ua-minagro[.]com, minuaregionbecareful[.]com, uamtu[.]com) to disseminate PDF attachments misusing Ukrainian ministry logos to spread Russian propaganda themes of heating failures, energy blackouts, food scarcity and drug shortages; further pivots uncovered Navalny-themed domains targeting Russian dissidents and the reuse of the PSYOP mail server for Canadian pharmacy spam, a tactic long favored by Russia‐aligned threat actors, and although no direct code overlaps tie Texonto to known groups such as Callisto, the blend of credential phishing, disinformation, domain masquerading and infrastructure reuse supports a high-confidence attribution to a Russia-aligned operator conducting hybrid warfare against Ukrainian speakers and related targets.
retrieved_context.title: Operation Texonto: Information operation targeting Ukrainian speakers in the context of the war

canonical_entities: BMW 5 for sale in Kyiv flyer campaign
BMW 5 for sale in Kyiv flyer
Turkish MFA earthquake relief guidance lure
retrieved_context.text: Between April and May 2023, Russia’s SVR-linked Cloaked Ursa (aka APT29, Cozy Bear, Midnight Blizzard/Nobelium) repurposed a legitimate “BMW 5 for sale in Kyiv” flyer—initially circulated by a Polish diplomat and likely harvested via a compromised mail server—into malicious Word documents that leverage URL‐shortening services (t[.]ly/tinyurl[.]com) to redirect victims to a co-opted landing page (hxxps://resetlocations[.]com/bmw.htm) where Windows shortcut files masquerading as PNG images deploy a silent payload; this campaign targeted at least 22 of 80+ foreign missions in Kyiv (80 percent via publicly listed embassy addresses, 20 percent via unpublished contacts) and follows a February–March lure impersonating Turkish MFA earthquake relief guidance, both demonstrating Cloaked Ursa’s hallmark TTPs—phishing lures themed to individual diplomat needs, code overlap with known malware, exploitation of benign attachments requiring a web browser to trigger—and highlights that one payload SHA256 (311e9c8cf6d0b295074ffefaa9f277cb1f806343be262c59f88fbdf6fe242517) is vendor-detected while the other (8902bd7d085397745e05883f05c08de87623cc15fe630b36ad3d208f01ef0596) remains undetected, underscoring the need for region-specific APT training, vigilant URL redirection checks, cautious handling of web‐based attachments (.hta, .svg, .html), scrutiny of archive contents (.zip, .rar, .iso), JavaScript disablement where feasible, and deployment of protections such as Cortex XDR, WildFire and DNS Security to mitigate espionage risk.
retrieved_context.title: Diplomats Beware: Cloaked Ursa Phishing With a Twist

retrieved_context.text: Since mid-November 2024, Russian nation-state actor Star Blizzard has significantly escalated its evasion tradecraft following public exposure by Microsoft Threat Intelligence: shifting from a single registrar (NameCheap) to multiple registrars (Hostinger, RealTime Register, GMO Internet) and implementing multi-stage redirection chains—embedding Microsoft 365 Safe Links in PDF lures that pass through Bitly and Cuttly shortened URLs and legitimate open-redirect sites (e.g., mechengsys[.]net) before landing on an Evilginx-equipped VPS (vidmemax[.]com)—to mount AiTM spear-phishing campaigns that harvest email credentials, including MFA tokens. Between July and August 2024 they also experimented with altered OneDrive file-share notifications—using ProtonMail accounts to spoof trusted senders and rewire the “Open” button URL to their Evilginx infrastructure—targeting individuals in politics, diplomacy, NGOs and think tanks. In October 2024, Microsoft’s Digital Crimes Unit disrupted core infrastructure, and ongoing collaboration with UK NCSC, NSA and FBI ensures rapid customer notification and defenses. Historically, since 2022 Star Blizzard has iteratively refined detection evasion—employing server-side fingerprinting scripts, HubSpot and MailerLite email platforms to mask domains, DNS obfuscation, password-protected PDFs and randomized DGAs—with each ephemeral TTP swiftly modified, underscoring the need for continuous updates to email security controls, link inspection and behavioral detection.
retrieved_context.title: Star Blizzard increases sophistication and evasion in ongoing attacks | Microsoft Security Blog

canonical_entities: regional organizations in Vietnam and South Korea
retrieved_context.text: In early 2018 McAfee Advanced Threat Research uncovered Operation Honeybee, a North Korean–linked campaign—tracked to the persona snoopykiller@mail.ru and control domains navermail.byethost3.com/nihon.byethost11.com—targeting humanitarian aid groups and regional organizations in Vietnam and South Korea with malicious Microsoft Word documents named “Honeybee” that exploited politically themed and generic “not compatible” lures to execute VBA macros embedding a custom‐alphabet Base64 payload. Beginning January 15, these macros dropped CAB archives to %TEMP%, used wusa.exe or expand.exe for UAC bypass, then hijacked cliconfg.exe via a malicious NTWDBLIB.dll to install a persistent COMSysApp service loading ipnet.dll from %SystemRoot%\System32. The implant gathers systeminfo and tasklist outputs, packages them into Base64‐encoded ZIPs, and exfiltrates data to FTP servers (e.g., 1113427185.ifastnet.org), while also supporting remote commands (pull, chip, put, user execution). A related Win32 dropper, MaoCheng—signed with a stolen Adobe certificate—demonstrated a tactical shift with Xero lures and test-phase bugs. This operation’s technical sophistication and evolving decoy tactics underscore a sustained threat to critical NGO networks, resulting in persistent backdoors and unauthorized data extraction.
retrieved_context.title: McAfee Uncovers Operation Honeybee, a Malicious Campaign Targeting Humanitarian Aid Groups | McAfee Blog

canonical_entities: Deliver maliciously crafted PDFs into iMessage sandbox
retrieved_context.text: In late 2021 Apple patched a zero-click iMessage vulnerability (CVE-2021-30860, “FORCEDENTRY”) exploited since February by NSO Group’s Pegasus spyware—sold to nation-states yet repeatedly abused against journalists and activists—to silently deliver maliciously crafted PDFs into iMessage’s sandbox, enabling arbitrary code execution to harvest messages, calls, location, passwords, microphone and camera data. Citizen Lab and Amnesty International identified infection URLs that Symantec WebPulse flagged in 1 of every 150,000 iOS devices, demonstrating that WebPulse–backed Symantec Endpoint Protection Mobile can intercept hidden iMessage fields, block command-and-control traffic, and quarantine zero-day payloads. Organizations are urged to deploy iOS 14.8+ patches and enforce layered mobile endpoint protection leveraging global URL intelligence to mitigate current and future Pegasus-style threats.
retrieved_context.title: Pegasus Spyware Takes Flight Again | Symantec Enterprise Blogs

retrieved_context.text: ESET Research has uncovered five overlapping campaigns, active since 2022 and three still live, in which the Arid Viper APT (aka APT-C-23, Desert Falcons, Two-tailed Scorpion) has been distributing a three-stage Android spyware suite dubbed AridSpy via dedicated phishing sites (lapizachat[.]com, nortirchats[.]com, reblychat[.]com, plus inactive pariberychat[.]com and renatchat[.]com) impersonating messaging apps (LapizaChat, NortirChat, ReblyChat), a job-opportunities app and a Palestinian Civil Registry app; these trojanized versions of legitimate apps (StealthChat, Session, Voxer) require manual install from unknown sources and leverage a custom myScript.js downloader to fetch successive payloads from C2 servers, enabling dynamic code loading and evasion. The first-stage loader—documented by Zimperium in 2021—evolved in 2022 during a Qatar World Cup campaign (Kora442) into multistage AridSpy, with ESET detecting six infections in Palestine and Egypt beginning August 2023. Medium-confidence attribution to Arid Viper is based on targeting in its historic Middle East focus, reuse and obfuscation of the myScript.js indicator (first tied to the group by 360 Beacon Labs and FOFA), and telemetry pivoting. AridSpy’s capabilities center on remote data espionage—collecting contacts, messages, device metadata and location—and its modular architecture and third-party distribution model pose ongoing risks to Android users in high-value geopolitical regions.
retrieved_context.title: Arid Viper poisons Android apps with AridSpy

technology organizations in and around Saudi Arabia
hits.text: Since mid-2016, an Iran-linked espionage operation dubbed “Magic Hound” has targeted energy, government and technology organizations in and around Saudi Arabia using macro-enabled Word and Excel documents masquerading as holiday cards, job offers and official Ministry of Health and Commerce files to launch PowerShell-based downloaders and custom droppers, executable and document loaders and IRC bots that ultimately deploy a Python-based Pupy RAT; Palo Alto Networks analysts—citing overlaps in domains and initial breach methods with the recent Shamoon 2 campaign—have linked Magic Hound to the Iran-aligned Rocket Kitten group, while SecureWorks attributes it to COBALT GYPSY and IBM X-Force has observed shared infrastructure, and additional code similarities tie an IRC bot to Charming Kitten/Newscaster activity and to MacDownloader tools used by other Iranian actors, underscoring the need to block malicious macros, monitor PowerShell and IRC traffic for known C2 signatures, and flag Pupy-related domains and custom loader behaviors to disrupt long-running cross-platform intrusion operations.
hits.title: Iranian Spies Target Saudi Arabia in "Magic Hound" Attacks

canonical_entities: diplomatic and defense networks in Ukraine
hits.text: Secret Blizzard, the Russian FSB’s Center 16, has escalated global espionage by co-opting C2 infrastructures of at least six threat actors—including Pakistan-based Storm-0156, Hazel Sandstorm and Storm-0473—to install backdoors (CrimsonRAT, Wainscot), deploy custom payloads (TwoDash downloader, MiniPocket fetcher), a TinyTurla variant disguised as a Windows service, and the Statuezy clipboard-monitoring trojan via DLL sideloading and batch files; this cross-actor compromise secured persistent access to diplomatic and defense networks in Ukraine, Afghanistan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and GDI, and Indian military institutions, enabling exfiltration of politically sensitive intelligence and advanced research data while reducing development overhead and underscoring the need for robust supply-chain security, network segmentation and proactive vulnerability management.
hits.title: Hackers with Russian Blizzard Steal Data from Rival Networks

hits.text: ESET researchers uncovered the Iran-aligned APT35 (aka Ballistic Bobcat, Charming Kitten, TA453/PHOSPHORUS) deploying a novel Sponsor backdoor across at least 34 opportunistic victims—primarily Israeli organizations in sectors from automotive to telecommunications, plus medical targets in Brazil and the UAE—by scanning for and exploiting Exchange CVE-2021-26855 vulnerabilities since September 2021, wrapping up their CISA AA21-321A/PowerLess campaign before dropping Sponsor via innocuously named batch files that deploy configuration files (config.txt, node.txt) to disk, install a persistent Windows service (“SystemNetwork”/“Update”) when run with an “install” argument, then periodically RC4-decrypt and call back to embedded C2 relays, all while leveraging open-source tooling (Mimikatz, Chisel, GO Simple Tunnel, Plink, RevSocks and Merlin) for lateral movement and data exfiltration; ESET has catalogued five Sponsor versions through June 2022, underscoring Ballistic Bobcat’s modular, short-duration, narrowly targeted “Sponsoring Access” campaign and highlighting the need for Exchange patching, service and file monitoring for batch deployments, and detection of RC4-encrypted config lookups to disrupt ongoing espionage operations.
hits.title: Sponsor with batch-filed whiskers: Ballistic Bobcat’s scan and strike backdoor

hits.text: Last week Google’s Threat Analysis Group, in partnership with The Citizen Lab, exposed an in-the-wild exploit chain developed by the commercial surveillance vendor Intellexa in Egypt that leverages a man-in-the-middle injection on HTTP traffic to silently redirect targets first to c.betly[.]me and then to sec-flare[.]com, delivering Predator spyware without any user interaction; on iOS this chain combined Safari RCE (CVE-2023-41993), certificate validation bypass (CVE-2023-41991) and XNU kernel local privilege escalation (CVE-2023-41992) and was patched in iOS 16.7/17.0.1, while on Android initial Chrome renderer RCE (CVE-2023-4762), delivered via MITM or one-time links, was patched on September 5; this campaign highlights the serious risk posed by proliferating commercial spyware, underscores the urgency of enforcing universal HTTPS and enabling Chrome’s HTTPS-First Mode, and demonstrates the critical need for organizations and users to apply the latest OS and browser updates, deploy encrypted-traffic protections, and monitor for anomalous network redirects to mitigate future attacks.
hits.title: 0-days exploited by commercial surveillance vendor in Egypt

hits.text: In 2024, ESET researchers uncovered a sustained cyberespionage campaign by the Iran-aligned APT group BladedFeline—active since at least 2017 against Kurdish Regional Government (KRG) and Iraqi government officials—that leverages an evolving toolset including the Shahmaran 64-bit backdoor, two reverse tunnels (Laret and Pinar), Whisper (an Exchange-based backdoor communicating via email attachments), a malicious IIS module dubbed PrimeCache bearing code similarities to OilRig’s RDAT backdoor, and supplementary implants such as the Flog webshell and Hawking Listener. Forensic analysis revealed early indicators on KRG systems—VideoSRV reverse shell (Sept 2017) and RDAT (Jan 2018)—consistent with OilRig’s operational patterns, leading to a medium-confidence assessment that BladedFeline operates as a subgroup of OilRig alongside Lyceum. The timeline spans initial KRG compromises in 2017–2018, Shahmaran deployment against diplomatic officials in early 2023, expansion to a telecommunications provider in Uzbekistan in March 2023, and the 2024 discovery of Whisper, Laret, Pinar, and PrimeCache across KRG, GOI, and Uzbek networks. BladedFeline’s tactics—native IIS module implantation, email-based C&C, reverse tunnels, and webshell exploitation—underscore the need to monitor Exchange mailbox activity for anomalous attachments, IIS module registrations (e.g., HttpModule.pdb), port listeners, and VirusTotal submitter IDs to detect and disrupt this persistent threat targeting strategic communications, oil-related infrastructure, and diplomatic data in the Middle East.
hits.title: BladedFeline: Whispering in the dark

hits.text: Storm-842 (Void Manticore), an Iranian MOIS-linked APT also operating as Homeland Justice in Albania and Karma in Israel, first emerged in July 2022 by crippling Albania’s e-government and border systems ahead of an MEK conference—an attack detailed in a Sept. 2022 FBI/CISA advisory—and by December 2023 had extended its destructive campaigns to Israeli infrastructure; it executes a two-stage kill chain in partnership with Scarred Manticore (OilRig/APT34), which gains initial access via web shells (reGeorge, Karma Shell), RDP and SSH-based SOCKS C2 channels, credential harvesting and environment mapping, then hands off to Void Manticore to deploy custom Windows/Linux wipers (Cl Wiper using ElRawDisk, Partition Wiper, BiBi Wiper with .BiBi extension variants) that delete files, corrupt partitions, disable recovery mechanisms and erase shadow copies, all while concurrent influence operations leak stolen data under various personas to sow distrust—mitigation requires enforcing MFA and role-based access, rigorous patch and vulnerability management, network segmentation with IDS/IPS monitoring, phishing-resistant email/web filtering, offline backups with tested recovery drills and integration of real-time threat intelligence to detect and disrupt this sophisticated blend of destructive malware and psychological warfare.
hits.title: Dark Web Profile: Storm-842 (Void Manticore) - SOCRadar® Cyber Intelligence Inc.

canonical_entities: Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of the Interior
hits.text: Moses Staff, also dubbed Cobalt Sapling, is an Iran-linked APT active since November 2020 and publicly identified in September 2021, originally posting 16 leak events of Israeli corporate data and personal information of IDF intelligence personnel by December 2022 using a toolkit comprising the PyDCrypt custom loader, DCSrv cryptographic wiper, StrifeWater RAT and its DriveGuard monitoring utility; in November 2022, Secureworks attributed a new hacktivist persona, Abraham’s Ax—featuring similar biblical branding, Tor-hosted leak sites on adjacent subnets and recycled “Hollywood-style” hacking videos—to the same operators, who have since shifted toward exfiltrating and leaking data from Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of the Interior (including a purported intercepted ministerial phone conversation) rather than directly attacking Israel, likely in response to Saudi-Israeli rapprochement, while Moses Staff continues operations (claiming a CCTV system hack at an Israeli terror site); these insights highlight the urgency for Saudi and Israeli government entities to strengthen network segmentation, deploy advanced endpoint detection for known Iranian toolsets, monitor darknet leak platforms and prepare incident response plans tailored to politically motivated exfiltration campaigns.
hits.title: Iranian APT Leaks Data From Saudi Arabia Government Under New Persona

hits.text: A state-sponsored APT42 (formerly UNC788), attributed to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, conducted over 30 confirmed espionage attacks since 2015 targeting activists, dissidents, and strategic organizations across non-profits, education, governments, healthcare, legal, manufacturing, media, and pharmaceuticals in 14+ countries including Australia, Europe, Middle East, and U.S. The group shares partial overlaps with APT35 (Charming Kitten, Cobalt Illusion, ITG18, Phosphorus, TA453, Yellow Garuda) and uses highly targeted spear-phishing and social engineering to build trust, distributing Android malware VINETHORN and PINEFLOWER via text messages capable of recording audio, extracting multimedia/SMS, and tracking geolocation, with a SaferVPN masqueraded payload observed April-October 2021. Windows malware includes TAMECAT (PowerShell backdoor), TABBYCAT (VBA macro dropper), and VBREVSHELL (reverse shell macro). APT42's link to UNC2448/DEV-0270/Cobalt Mirage (ransomware operators using BitLocker) operates through front company Najee Technology Hooshmand with aliases Secnerd and Lifeweb, though missions differ—APT42 focuses on domestic politics and regime stability while APT35 targets long-term resource-intensive operations, with pharmaceutical intrusions commencing March 2020 during COVID-19 pandemic onset.
hits.title: Iranian APT42 Launched Over 30 Espionage Attacks Against Activists and Dissidents

hits.text: ESET’s analysis of the Iranian APT “BladedFeline,” assessed with medium confidence as a subgroup of APT34/OilRig, reveals the actor infiltrated Kurdish and Iraqi government networks as early as September 2017 and remained undetected until 2023–2024, maintaining strategic espionage access to high-ranking officials tied to Western diplomatic relations and regional oil reserves. The group deployed a suite of proprietary and modified implants—most notably the simple, uncompressed 64-bit Shahmaran backdoor, the Whisper backdoor, the PrimeCache IIS module, the VideoSRV reverse shell, PowerShell executors and multiple reverse tunnels—via unknown initial vectors and a likely internet-facing web server exploit, using unencrypted C2 channels over normal traffic to execute commands, manipulate files and exfiltrate data. ESET identified code overlaps between PrimeCache and OilRig’s RDAT and common usage of VideoSRV, expects continued implant development, and advises defenders to maintain detailed inventories of VIP-used applications, establish network baselines to detect stealthy exfiltration paths and anomalies, and audit internet-facing servers to thwart initial compromise.
hits.title: Iranian APT 'BladedFeline' Hides in Network for 8 Years

hits.text: Iran-linked APT Hexane (aka Lyceum/SiameseKitten), active since at least 2018 and previously focused on oil & gas and telecommunications in the Middle East and Africa, has shifted in 2021 to target Israeli IT and communications firms via sophisticated supply-chain phishing operations, ClearSky reports. Leveraging a newly expanded infrastructure to impersonate legitimate companies and HR personnel on LinkedIn, Hexane conducted a May 2021 attack on an Israeli IT provider followed by a July wave against additional organizations by luring candidates with fake job offers for roles in France, Israel and the UK. Victims are directed to a phishing site where tailored lure files deploy a dual-stage infection—first the Milan implant to establish C2 connectivity, then the DanBot RAT—to harvest data, perform espionage and move laterally, presumably to breach client networks downstream. This upgrade mirrors North Korea’s “dream job” campaigns and OilRig (APT34) activity, underscoring Hexane’s evolving tactics, renewed toolset and continued focus on supply-chain compromise to facilitate deep network infiltration.
hits.title: Report: Iranian APT Hexane Targets Israeli Companies

hits.text: In 2024, ESET researchers uncovered a sustained cyberespionage campaign by the Iran-aligned APT group BladedFeline—active since at least 2017 against Kurdish Regional Government (KRG) and Iraqi government officials—that leverages an evolving toolset including the Shahmaran 64-bit backdoor, two reverse tunnels (Laret and Pinar), Whisper (an Exchange-based backdoor communicating via email attachments), a malicious IIS module dubbed PrimeCache bearing code similarities to OilRig’s RDAT backdoor, and supplementary implants such as the Flog webshell and Hawking Listener. Forensic analysis revealed early indicators on KRG systems—VideoSRV reverse shell (Sept 2017) and RDAT (Jan 2018)—consistent with OilRig’s operational patterns, leading to a medium-confidence assessment that BladedFeline operates as a subgroup of OilRig alongside Lyceum. The timeline spans initial KRG compromises in 2017–2018, Shahmaran deployment against diplomatic officials in early 2023, expansion to a telecommunications provider in Uzbekistan in March 2023, and the 2024 discovery of Whisper, Laret, Pinar, and PrimeCache across KRG, GOI, and Uzbek networks. BladedFeline’s tactics—native IIS module implantation, email-based C&C, reverse tunnels, and webshell exploitation—underscore the need to monitor Exchange mailbox activity for anomalous attachments, IIS module registrations (e.g., HttpModule.pdb), port listeners, and VirusTotal submitter IDs to detect and disrupt this persistent threat targeting strategic communications, oil-related infrastructure, and diplomatic data in the Middle East.
hits.title: BladedFeline: Whispering in the dark

hits.text: Last week Google’s Threat Analysis Group, in partnership with The Citizen Lab, exposed an in-the-wild exploit chain developed by the commercial surveillance vendor Intellexa in Egypt that leverages a man-in-the-middle injection on HTTP traffic to silently redirect targets first to c.betly[.]me and then to sec-flare[.]com, delivering Predator spyware without any user interaction; on iOS this chain combined Safari RCE (CVE-2023-41993), certificate validation bypass (CVE-2023-41991) and XNU kernel local privilege escalation (CVE-2023-41992) and was patched in iOS 16.7/17.0.1, while on Android initial Chrome renderer RCE (CVE-2023-4762), delivered via MITM or one-time links, was patched on September 5; this campaign highlights the serious risk posed by proliferating commercial spyware, underscores the urgency of enforcing universal HTTPS and enabling Chrome’s HTTPS-First Mode, and demonstrates the critical need for organizations and users to apply the latest OS and browser updates, deploy encrypted-traffic protections, and monitor for anomalous network redirects to mitigate future attacks.
hits.title: 0-days exploited by commercial surveillance vendor in Egypt

hits.text: Microsoft has traced a stealthy espionage campaign by Flax Typhoon (aka Ethereal Panda), a China-based nation-state actor active since mid-2021, targeting dozens of Taiwanese organizations (with spill-over in Southeast Asia, North America, and Africa) by exploiting known vulnerabilities in public-facing VPN, web, Java, and SQL services to deploy the China Chopper web shell for initial access; the group escalates privileges via open-source exploits like Juicy Potato and BadPotato, then establishes persistence by disabling RDP network-level authentication, hijacking the Sticky Keys (sethc.exe) binary to launch Task Manager as SYSTEM, and installing a renamed SoftEther VPN-over-HTTPS bridge (conhost.exe/dllhost.exe) as a service to maintain covert C2 over port 443; leveraging LOLBins such as PowerShell Invoke-WebRequest, certutil, bitsadmin, WinRM, and WMIC for lateral movement, vulnerability scanning, and remote execution, it harvests credentials from LSASS memory and the SAM registry hive using Mimikatz for pass-the-hash attacks; although no exfiltration or final objectives have been observed, organizations are urged to enforce rigorous patch and vulnerability management on internet-exposed systems, monitor registry and file-integrity changes, deploy web application firewalls, reset compromised credentials, isolate and forensically examine affected hosts, and leverage detections in Microsoft 365 Defender to disrupt living-off-the-land tactics.

hits.text: Since early 2025, a sophisticated threat actor has deployed PS1Bot, a multi-stage PowerShell/C# malware framework distributed via malvertising and SEO-poisoned archives named to resemble legitimate documents (e.g., “chapter 8 medicare benefit policy manual.zip”), which drops an obfuscated VBScript downloader (“FULL DOCUMENT.js”) that retrieves a JScript scriptlet to write and execute a PowerShell loader (e.g., ntu.ps1) from C:\ProgramData\; this loader polls a C2—deriving unique URLs from the C-drive serial number—and uses Invoke-Expression to run in-memory modules with minimal disk footprints. PS1Bot’s modular toolkit includes a WMI-based antivirus reconnaissance module, a dynamic C# screen-capture module exfiltrating Base64‐encoded bitmaps, a “grabber” that harvests browser and 40+ crypto wallet credentials (including MetaMask, Ledger, Exodus, Electrum) using embedded multilingual seed-phrase wordlists, a SetWindowsHookEx keylogger, and a WMIComputerCSHARP system survey. Persistence is achieved via randomized %PROGRAMDATA% directories, LNK startup shortcuts, and mutex checks. hits.text: A state-sponsored APT42 (formerly UNC788), attributed to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, conducted over 30 confirmed espionage attacks since 2015 targeting activists, dissidents, and strategic organizations across non-profits, education, governments, healthcare, legal, manufacturing, media, and pharmaceuticals in 14+ countries including Australia, Europe, Middle East, and U.S. The group shares partial overlaps with APT35 (Charming Kitten, Cobalt Illusion, ITG18, Phosphorus, TA453, Yellow Garuda) and uses highly targeted spear-phishing and social engineering to build trust, distributing Android malware VINETHORN and PINEFLOWER via text messages capable of recording audio, extracting multimedia/SMS, and tracking geolocation, with a SaferVPN masqueraded payload observed April-October 2021. APT42's link to UNC2448/DEV-0270/Cobalt Mirage (ransomware operators using BitLocker) operates through front company Najee Technology Hooshmand with aliases Secnerd and Lifeweb, though missions differ—APT42 focuses on domestic politics and regime stability while APT35 targets long-term resource-intensive operations, with pharmaceutical intrusions commencing March 2020 during COVID-19 pandemic onset.
hits.title: Iranian APT42 Launched Over 30 Espionage Attacks Against Activists and Dissidents

hits.text: Since at least 2015, Mandiant has identified APT42—an IRGC-linked Iranian state-sponsored threat actor also known as APT35—conducting over 30 spear-phishing operations across 14 countries against government officials, policymakers, journalists, academics and dissidents, evolving tactics from 2020 Oxford vaccinologist-themed pharmaceutical lures to 2021 fake interview requests using compromised U.S. media accounts for 37-day MFA-intercepting credential harvesting, and February 2022 phishes posing as a British news agency targeting political science professors; beyond credential theft via shortened URLs and PDF attachments directing victims to spoofed login portals, APT42 deploys custom Android spyware—spread via SMS links to messaging/VPN apps—to exfiltrate calls, SMS, audio recordings, images and GPS data in real time, while on Windows it employs lightweight custom malware for initial access, privilege escalation, reconnaissance, lateral movement through follow-on phishing, and persistence via scheduled tasks and registry keys; Mandiant further correlates APT42’s TTPs with November 2021 PHOSPHORUS BitLocker ransomware attempts against Fortinet FortiOS SSL VPN and unpatched Exchange servers, highlighting the group’s multi-platform espionage-to-ransom capabilities and real-world threat to high-value targets.

retrieved_context.text: Since mid-2016, an Iran-linked espionage operation dubbed “Magic Hound” has targeted energy, government and technology organizations in and around Saudi Arabia using macro-enabled Word and Excel documents masquerading as holiday cards, job offers and official Ministry of Health and Commerce files to launch PowerShell-based downloaders and custom droppers, executable and document loaders and IRC bots that ultimately deploy a Python-based Pupy RAT; Palo Alto Networks analysts—citing overlaps in domains and initial breach methods with the recent Shamoon 2 campaign—have linked Magic Hound to the Iran-aligned Rocket Kitten group, while SecureWorks attributes it to COBALT GYPSY and IBM X-Force has observed shared infrastructure, and additional code similarities tie an IRC bot to Charming Kitten/Newscaster activity and to MacDownloader tools used by other Iranian actors, underscoring the need to block malicious macros, monitor PowerShell and IRC traffic for known C2 signatures, and flag Pupy-related domains and custom loader behaviors to disrupt long-running cross-platform intrusion operations.

retrieved_context.text: ESET researchers uncovered the Iran-aligned APT35 (aka Ballistic Bobcat, Charming Kitten, TA453/PHOSPHORUS) deploying a novel Sponsor backdoor across at least 34 opportunistic victims—primarily Israeli organizations in sectors from automotive to telecommunications, plus medical targets in Brazil and the UAE—by scanning for and exploiting Exchange CVE-2021-26855 vulnerabilities since September 2021, wrapping up their CISA AA21-321A/PowerLess campaign before dropping Sponsor via innocuously named batch files that deploy configuration files (config.txt, node.txt) to disk, install a persistent Windows service (“SystemNetwork”/“Update”) when run with an “install” argument, then periodically RC4-decrypt and call back to embedded C2 relays, all while leveraging open-source tooling (Mimikatz, Chisel, GO Simple Tunnel, Plink, RevSocks and Merlin) for lateral movement and data exfiltration; ESET has catalogued five Sponsor versions through June 2022, underscoring Ballistic Bobcat’s modular, short-duration, narrowly targeted “Sponsoring Access” campaign and highlighting the need for Exchange patching, service and file monitoring for batch deployments, and detection of RC4-encrypted config lookups to disrupt ongoing espionage operations.

retrieved_context.text: In 2024, ESET researchers uncovered a sustained cyberespionage campaign by the Iran-aligned APT group BladedFeline—active since at least 2017 against Kurdish Regional Government (KRG) and Iraqi government officials—that leverages an evolving toolset including the Shahmaran 64-bit backdoor, two reverse tunnels (Laret and Pinar), Whisper (an Exchange-based backdoor communicating via email attachments), a malicious IIS module dubbed PrimeCache bearing code similarities to OilRig’s RDAT backdoor, and supplementary implants such as the Flog webshell and Hawking Listener. Forensic analysis revealed early indicators on KRG systems—VideoSRV reverse shell (Sept 2017) and RDAT (Jan 2018)—consistent with OilRig’s operational patterns, leading to a medium-confidence assessment that BladedFeline operates as a subgroup of OilRig alongside Lyceum. The timeline spans initial KRG compromises in 2017–2018, Shahmaran deployment against diplomatic officials in early 2023, expansion to a telecommunications provider in Uzbekistan in March 2023, and the 2024 discovery of Whisper, Laret, Pinar, and PrimeCache across KRG, GOI, and Uzbek networks. BladedFeline’s tactics—native IIS module implantation, email-based C&C, reverse tunnels, and webshell exploitation—underscore the need to monitor Exchange mailbox activity for anomalous attachments, IIS module registrations (e.g., HttpModule.pdb), port listeners, and VirusTotal submitter IDs to detect and disrupt this persistent threat targeting strategic communications, oil-related infrastructure, and diplomatic data in the Middle East.
retrieved_context.title: BladedFeline: Whispering in the dark

retrieved_context.text: Last week Google’s Threat Analysis Group, in partnership with The Citizen Lab, exposed an in-the-wild exploit chain developed by the commercial surveillance vendor Intellexa in Egypt that leverages a man-in-the-middle injection on HTTP traffic to silently redirect targets first to c.betly[.]me and then to sec-flare[.]com, delivering Predator spyware without any user interaction; on iOS this chain combined Safari RCE (CVE-2023-41993), certificate validation bypass (CVE-2023-41991) and XNU kernel local privilege escalation (CVE-2023-41992) and was patched in iOS 16.7/17.0.1, while on Android initial Chrome renderer RCE (CVE-2023-4762), delivered via MITM or one-time links, was patched on September 5; this campaign highlights the serious risk posed by proliferating commercial spyware, underscores the urgency of enforcing universal HTTPS and enabling Chrome’s HTTPS-First Mode, and demonstrates the critical need for organizations and users to apply the latest OS and browser updates, deploy encrypted-traffic protections, and monitor for anomalous network redirects to mitigate future attacks.

retrieved_context.text: Microsoft has traced a stealthy espionage campaign by Flax Typhoon (aka Ethereal Panda), a China-based nation-state actor active since mid-2021, targeting dozens of Taiwanese organizations (with spill-over in Southeast Asia, North America, and Africa) by exploiting known vulnerabilities in public-facing VPN, web, Java, and SQL services to deploy the China Chopper web shell for initial access; the group escalates privileges via open-source exploits like Juicy Potato and BadPotato, then establishes persistence by disabling RDP network-level authentication, hijacking the Sticky Keys (sethc.exe) binary to launch Task Manager as SYSTEM, and installing a renamed SoftEther VPN-over-HTTPS bridge (conhost.exe/dllhost.exe) as a service to maintain covert C2 over port 443; leveraging LOLBins such as PowerShell Invoke-WebRequest, certutil, bitsadmin, WinRM, and WMIC for lateral movement, vulnerability scanning, and remote execution, it harvests credentials from LSASS memory and the SAM registry hive using Mimikatz for pass-the-hash attacks; although no exfiltration or final objectives have been observed, organizations are urged to enforce rigorous patch and vulnerability management on internet-exposed systems, monitor registry and file-integrity changes, deploy web application firewalls, reset compromised credentials, isolate and forensically examine affected hosts, and leverage detections in Microsoft 365 Defender to disrupt living-off-the-land tactics.

hits.text: Security researchers at McAfee first observed Operation Sharpshooter in October–November 2018, a sophisticated phishing campaign targeting 87 critical‐infrastructure organizations—predominantly in the United States—including nuclear, defense, energy and financial firms, via recruitment‐style Microsoft Word attachments containing weaponized macros that load an in‐memory downloader to fetch a second‐stage implant dubbed Rising Sun; this implant, which exfiltrates host data to a command server, incorporates publicly available Lazarus Group source code as a likely false flag rather than evidence of Lazarus involvement. McAfee analysts Ryan Sherstobitoff and Asheer Malhotra note that Rising Sun’s multi‐step execution—weaponized document, in‐memory downloader, intelligence‐gathering implant—highlights the continued efficacy of social‐engineering vectors, while experts from CipherCloud, Positive Technologies and Lucy Security emphasize that defenses must go beyond spam filters to include ongoing user awareness training, holistic people-and-technology security models, robust data protection, network visibility and rapid incident response to detect and halt such advanced, evolving threats.

hits.text: McAfee’s Advanced Threat Research team uncovered “Operation Sharpshooter,” a global cyber-espionage campaign targeting nuclear, defense, energy and financial organizations via weaponized Office documents masquerading as recruitment materials; an initial macro‐enabled loader drops an in‐memory implant that retrieves a second‐stage backdoor dubbed “Rising Sun,” which leverages source code from Lazarus Group’s 2015 Duuzer Trojan to perform account, file/directory, process and system/network discovery, process injection and automated encrypted exfiltration over C2 channels (e.g., 34.214.99.20/view_style.php); from October to November 2018 McAfee telemetry identified at least 87 predominantly English-speaking targets, with key IOCs including hashes such as 8106a30bd35526bded384627d8eebce15da35d17 and document URLs like hxxp://208.117.44.112/Strategic Planning Manager.doc, detectable by McAfee signatures RDN/Generic Downloader.x and Rising-Sun, and mitigated by monitoring macro executions, anomalous process injections and outbound C2 traffic while the broader community assesses attribution and monitors for follow-on exploitation.
hits.title: ‘Operation Sharpshooter’ Targets Global Defense, Critical Infrastructure | McAfee Blog

hits.text: ESET researchers have traced the China-aligned hacker group FishMonger, aka Aquatic Panda, and its global espionage campaign “FishMedley” back to the iSoon APT contractor (Axun Information Technology) operating under the Ministry of Public Security, Ministry of State Security and PLA, following the U.S. DOJ’s addition of key members to the FBI’s Most Wanted list; FishMonger’s modus operandi relies on compromising high-privilege user accounts—likely harvested via phishing or credential theft—to gain domain administrator access, then deploying publicly available modular backdoors and loaders (ShadowPad, Spyder loader, SodaMaster) and the RPipeCommander reverse shell rather than zero-day exploits, enabling sustained infiltration of governmental bodies, Catholic charities, NGOs and think tanks across Taiwan, Hungary, Turkey, Thailand, the U.S. and France; while technically unsophisticated, the group’s efficient use of known tools has yielded consistent exfiltration of confidential data, underscoring the need for potential targets to hunt for these specific indicators of compromise and strengthen monitoring of privileged accounts.
hits.title: Chinese Hacker Group Tracked Back to iSoon APT Operation

hits.text: Moses Staff, an Iran-linked APT active since September 2021, has conducted politically motivated sabotage campaigns—initially against Israeli organizations and later targets in India, Germany, the U.S., Italy, Chile, Turkey and the UAE—by exploiting known public-facing server vulnerabilities (e.g., Microsoft Exchange), moving laterally with PsExec, WMIC and PowerShell, and deploying a two-stage destructive toolkit: a Python-based loader (PyDCrypt) that installs a custom DiskCryptor variant (DCSrv) to encrypt files and disrupt operations without ransom demands, and, as newly documented by Cybereason, the StrifeWater RAT masquerading as calc.exe to establish early footholds, harvest system metadata (machine name, OS version, CPU architecture, user privileges, time zone), execute commands, capture screens, maintain persistence via scheduled tasks, and download auxiliary modules before self-removal—all while communicating with hard-coded C2 IPs, URLs and domain names—to evade detection; organizations should urgently patch exposed servers, monitor anomalous calc.exe and scheduled-task activity, and enhance EDR rules to detect PyDCrypt, DCSrv and StrifeWater behaviors to thwart data exfiltration and infrastructure damage.
hits.title: Iranian APT group uses previously undocumented Trojan for destructive access to organizations

hits.text: In August, the DPRK–linked APT TA444 (aka APT38, BlueNoroff, BlackAlicanto, Coperenicum, Sapphire Sleet and Stardust Chollima) deployed SpectralBlur, a custom post-exploitation macOS backdoor that leverages command-and-control instructions to upload/download files, spawn a shell, update its configuration, delete files or enter hibernation/sleep mode; Proofpoint researcher Greg Lesnewich identified code overlaps with the KandyKorn macOS data stealer—earlier tied to Lazarus Group phishing campaigns against blockchain engineers—linking both tools through shared strings and infrastructure. This rapid iteration of proprietary macOS malware underscores TA444’s dedicated development capability and signals an intensified DPRK espionage focus on Apple users, particularly within the cryptocurrency sector, demonstrating persistent operational tempo and advanced post-exploitation tactics.
hits.title: North Korea Debuts 'SpectralBlur' Malware Amid macOS Onslaught
