retrieved_context.text: A state-sponsored APT42 (formerly UNC788), attributed to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, conducted over 30 confirmed espionage attacks since 2015 targeting activists, dissidents, and strategic organizations across non-profits, education, governments, healthcare, legal, manufacturing, media, and pharmaceuticals in 14+ countries including Australia, Europe, Middle East, and U.S. The group shares partial overlaps with APT35 (Charming Kitten, Cobalt Illusion, ITG18, Phosphorus, TA453, Yellow Garuda) and uses highly targeted spear-phishing and social engineering to build trust, distributing Android malware VINETHORN and PINEFLOWER via text messages capable of recording audio, extracting multimedia/SMS, and tracking geolocation, with a SaferVPN masqueraded payload observed April-October 2021. Windows malware includes TAMECAT (PowerShell backdoor), TABBYCAT (VBA macro dropper), and VBREVSHELL (reverse shell macro). APT42's link to UNC2448/DEV-0270/Cobalt Mirage (ransomware operators using BitLocker) operates through front company Najee Technology Hooshmand with aliases Secnerd and Lifeweb, though missions differ—APT42 focuses on domestic politics and regime stability while APT35 targets long-term resource-intensive operations, with pharmaceutical intrusions commencing March 2020 during COVID-19 pandemic onset.

retrieved_context.text: In February 2022, CISA, the FBI, US Cyber Command CNMF, NCSC-UK and NSA issued a joint advisory on Iranian Ministry of Intelligence–linked APT MuddyWater (aka MERCURY, Earth Vetala, Static Kitten, Seedworm, TEMP.Zagros), active since 2018 and focused on cyber espionage, intellectual property theft and ransomware against defense, oil & gas, government and telecom sectors across Asia, Africa, Europe and North America. retrieved_context.text: Dragos researchers, in collaboration with Ukraine’s CSSC, unearthed FrostyGoop—an ICS-specific malware first spotted in April and used in January to disrupt central heating in over 600 Lviv apartment buildings—marking the first known malware to leverage Modbus TCP for read/write operations on operational technology. Attackers gained initial access in April 2023 by exploiting a MikroTik router vulnerability, deployed a webshell on the router’s web server, and maintained persistence via Tor and L2TP tunnels to Moscow-based IPs. After spending months conducting reconnaissance, they extracted credentials by dumping the SAM registry hive in December, then directly issued scripted Modbus commands—read from a JSON configuration file—to publicly exposed ENCO heating controllers, even downgrading firmware to disable monitoring and force inaccurate measurements that halted heating services for nearly two days amid subzero temperatures. This incident underscores the threat posed by internet-exposed ICS devices—over 46,000 globally using Modbus—and highlights poor network segmentation, unpatched ICS CVEs, and the ease with which FrostyGoop’s protocol-agnostic payload can be repurposed against diverse industrial controllers, necessitating immediate network segmentation, firmware monitoring, and patch management in OT environments.
retrieved_context.title: ICS malware FrostyGoop disrupted heating in Ukraine, remains threat to OT worldwide

canonical_entities: installing Sagerunex variants in the Windows Registry
retrieved_context.text: The Lotus Blossom APT (aka Lotus Panda, Billbug, Spring Dragon) has stepped up cyberespionage against APAC government targets by deploying new Sagerunex backdoor variants and abusing Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) for stealthy post-exploitation and lateral movement, enabling remote command execution without additional malware. Initial access methods include spear-phishing, watering-hole attacks and exploiting public-facing application flaws; once inside, operators run reconnaissance commands (tasklist, ipconfig, netstat), harvest credentials with Chrome cookie stealers, compress data via RAR and relay traffic through custom Venom proxies or proxy configurations when direct internet access is blocked. Persistence is achieved by installing Sagerunex variants in the Windows Registry under hijacked service names (tapisrv, swprv) to auto-launch at startup, while command-and-control blends encrypted traffic into legitimate platforms—stolen data uploaded as .rar on Dropbox, commands hidden in Twitter status updates and Zimbra draft emails—evading detection. Organizations are advised to deploy behavior-based EDR for registry and encrypted cloud-service anomalies, implement zero-trust network segmentation, validate defenses with breach-and-attack simulation and maintain robust, regularly tested incident response plans.
retrieved_context.title: Lotus Blossom APT Exploits WMI for Post-Exploitation Activities

hits.text: Since its emergence in 2021 and first detection on Trend Micro telemetry in March 2022, the TargetCompany ransomware group has launched 269 attempted attacks against 250 disclosed Trend customers—predominantly in Asia (notably India and Saudi Arabia)—while avoiding Kazakhstan, Russia, Qatar, and Ukraine, and focusing on manufacturing, retail, and telecommunications; their November 2022–May 2023 leak site lists 20 confirmed victims (mostly small businesses) across the Asia-Pacific, Europe, and Middle East in IT, manufacturing, apparel, and automotive sectors. Initial access vectors include exploitation of CVE-2019-1069 and CVE-2020-0618 RCE flaws, SQL Server xp_cmdshell abuse, and OneNote-based spam campaigns. Execution relies on WMIC-invoked PowerShell scripts to retrieve various payloads (TargetComp ransomware, Remcos backdoor, Negasteal, Snake Keylogger) and, since January 2022, reflective loading of a .NET downloader that decrypts and runs payloads in memory via XOR or inversion. For defense evasion, operators deploy GMER, PCHunter64 (YDArk.exe), Advance Process Termination, KILLAV, and killer.bat to disable AV and security services; discovery is achieved through network scans and Mimikatz credential dumping; lateral movement via RDP-based RCE; C2 evolved from an open Mallox directory to an Nginx-protected server. Impact involves ChaCha20 file encryption with keys generated by Curve25519 and AES-128, file extensions such as .mallox/.exploit/.avast and ransom notes titled “HOW TO RECOVER!!.TXT,” and potential data exfiltration. Their tactics span MITRE techniques T1190, T1059.001, T1047, T1562.001, T1003.001, T1071.001, T1486, and more. The group’s maturation—evidenced by reflective loading and possible RaaS adoption—underscores the urgency for organizations to enforce asset inventories, least-privilege access, prompt patching (or virtual patching), multifactor authentication, sandboxed email defenses, AI/ML-driven detection, regular backups, and continuous red-team testing to thwart this active threat.
hits.title: Ransomware Spotlight: TargetCompany | Trend Micro (US)

hits.text: Since at least 2021, the Chinese state-linked APT group FishMonger—operating under the I-SOON umbrella—has waged sophisticated espionage against government institutions and NGOs in Southeast Asia and Europe, initiating attacks via spear-phishing emails that deliver template-injected Microsoft Office documents to exploit vulnerabilities or employ social engineering and deploy a Spyder loader, then install the custom “SilentBreeze” backdoor. SilentBreeze establishes persistence through a scheduled PowerShell task using a Mozilla-style User-Agent header to download additional payloads from hxxps://cdn-storage.cloud-service.site/updates.php, communicates with command-and-control servers over encrypted channels via compromised third-party proxies, and remains undetected for months while harvesting credentials and exfiltrating sensitive diplomatic and policy-related data aligned with Chinese strategic interests in the South China Sea and human rights monitoring. ESET researchers note FishMonger’s continual toolset modifications and counter-detection tactics, distinctive network traffic patterns, and reliance on third-party proxies to mask true C2 infrastructure, underscoring the urgent need for organizations to harden phishing defenses, monitor for template injection in Office files, audit scheduled PowerShell tasks, and scrutinize outbound connections to anomalous cloud-service URLs to disrupt this persistent threat.

hits.text: In late 2023, researchers uncovered a sophisticated Taiwan-focused espionage operation in which a China-linked APT actor (likely APT27) hijacked an abandoned Sogou Zhuyin Windows update server—vacated when Sogou ceased Zhuyin support in mid-2022—and weaponized it to distribute a trojanized updater (SHA-256: 3f5c…) that deployed a custom backdoor and Cobalt Strike beacon via HTTP(S) (MITRE T1195.002, T1071.001). Initial access was achieved by swapping the legitimate SogouZhuyinUpdater.exe with the malicious variant, which installed a loader employing code-injection and obfuscation to evade AV detection; post-deployment techniques included Mimikatz for credential harvesting (T1003.001) and encrypted exfiltration of 2 GB of sensitive defense and policy documents from at least five Taiwanese government and research organizations (T1041). This incident underscores the risk of unmaintained update infrastructure in software supply-chain compromises and highlights the need for regular decommissioning audits, code signing validation, and network segmentation to mitigate such persistent threats.

hits.text: Google’s Threat Analysis Group (TAG) has observed a 33% year-over-year increase in government-backed phishing warnings—over 50,000 sent to users so far in 2021—driven in part by a large APT28 (Fancy Bear) campaign and sustained by ongoing operations from Iran-aligned APT35. Since early 2021, APT35 has compromised a UK university website to host a phishing kit targeting Gmail, Yahoo and Hotmail credentials—including second-factor codes—and continues its credential harvesting campaigns against government, academia, journalism and NGOs using hijacked sites and link-shortening redirects. In May 2020 it attempted to distribute spyware disguised as a VPN on Google Play Store (blocked before installation) and has pursued similar Android C2 apps on other platforms. The group also impersonates conference officials (e.g., Munich Security, T20 Italy) to initiate phishing, embedding JavaScript to relay visitor IP, user-agent and locale via Telegram bots—a tactic TAG disrupted by reporting the bots. TAG’s layered defenses include batch-sent warnings, Workspace admin alerts, Safe Browsing domain blocks and urging high-risk users to enable two-factor authentication or enroll in Advanced Protection.

ESET researchers note FishMonger’s continual toolset modifications and counter-detection tactics, distinctive network traffic patterns, and reliance on third-party proxies to mask true C2 infrastructure, underscoring the urgent need for organizations to harden phishing defenses, monitor for template injection in Office files, audit scheduled PowerShell tasks, and scrutinize outbound connections to anomalous cloud-service URLs to disrupt this persistent threat.
retrieved_context.title: Chinese FishMonger APT Operated by I‑SOON Attacking Government Entities & NGOs

canonical_entities: Supply Chain Compromise: Compromise Software Supply Chain
retrieved_context.text: In late 2023, researchers uncovered a sophisticated Taiwan-focused espionage operation in which a China-linked APT actor (likely APT27) hijacked an abandoned Sogou Zhuyin Windows update server—vacated when Sogou ceased Zhuyin support in mid-2022—and weaponized it to distribute a trojanized updater (SHA-256: 3f5c…) that deployed a custom backdoor and Cobalt Strike beacon via HTTP(S) (MITRE T1195.002, T1071.001). Initial access was achieved by swapping the legitimate SogouZhuyinUpdater.exe with the malicious variant, which installed a loader employing code-injection and obfuscation to evade AV detection; post-deployment techniques included Mimikatz for credential harvesting (T1003.001) and encrypted exfiltration of 2 GB of sensitive defense and policy documents from at least five Taiwanese government and research organizations (T1041). This incident underscores the risk of unmaintained update infrastructure in software supply-chain compromises and highlights the need for regular decommissioning audits, code signing validation, and network segmentation to mitigate such persistent threats.
retrieved_context.title: Abandoned Sogou Zhuyin Update Server Hijacked, Weaponized in Taiwan Espionage Campaign

retrieved_context.text: A state-sponsored APT42 (formerly UNC788), attributed to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, conducted over 30 confirmed espionage attacks since 2015 targeting activists, dissidents, and strategic organizations across non-profits, education, governments, healthcare, legal, manufacturing, media, and pharmaceuticals in 14+ countries including Australia, Europe, Middle East, and U.S. The group shares partial overlaps with APT35 (Charming Kitten, Cobalt Illusion, ITG18, Phosphorus, TA453, Yellow Garuda) and uses highly targeted spear-phishing and social engineering to build trust, distributing Android malware VINETHORN and PINEFLOWER via text messages capable of recording audio, extracting multimedia/SMS, and tracking geolocation, with a SaferVPN masqueraded payload observed April-October 2021. Windows malware includes TAMECAT (PowerShell backdoor), TABBYCAT (VBA macro dropper), and VBREVSHELL (reverse shell macro). APT42's link to UNC2448/DEV-0270/Cobalt Mirage (ransomware operators using BitLocker) operates through front company Najee Technology Hooshmand with aliases Secnerd and Lifeweb, though missions differ—APT42 focuses on domestic politics and regime stability while APT35 targets long-term resource-intensive operations, with pharmaceutical intrusions commencing March 2020 during COVID-19 pandemic onset.
retrieved_context.title: Iranian APT42 Launched Over 30 Espionage Attacks Against Activists and Dissidents

retrieved_context.text: In February 2022, CISA, the FBI, US Cyber Command CNMF, NCSC-UK and NSA issued a joint advisory on Iranian Ministry of Intelligence–linked APT MuddyWater (aka MERCURY, Earth Vetala, Static Kitten, Seedworm, TEMP.Zagros), active since 2018 and focused on cyber espionage, intellectual property theft and ransomware against defense, oil & gas, government and telecom sectors across Asia, Africa, Europe and North America. Exploiting publicly disclosed vulnerabilities and open-source tools, MuddyWater delivers malicious PDFs with embedded links that display error messages prompting users to download Excel maldocs or Windows executables; these files host VBA macros that drop WSF scripts to execute PowerShell and VB payloads, leverage LoLBins, and stage RATs and malware families including PowGoop, Canopy, Small Sieve, POWERSTATS and Mori while communicating with C2 over HTTP and DNS and persisting via Registry Run keys. Cisco Talos observed regional campaigns in Turkey (Nov 2021), Pakistan (Aug 2021) and Armenia (Jun 2021) using decoy documents, signaling tokens and a consistent TTP set, suggesting a conglomerate of subgroups migrating techniques across regions. The resultant network access and data exfiltration underscore the imperative for proactive DFIR readiness, deployment of XDR/MDR platforms, rigorous vulnerability management, macro execution restrictions, PowerShell/LoLBin monitoring and ongoing user awareness training reinforced by incident response tabletop exercises.
retrieved_context.title: An In-Depth Look at Iranian APT "MuddyWater"

retrieved_context.text: Google’s Threat Analysis Group (TAG) has observed a 33% year-over-year increase in government-backed phishing warnings—over 50,000 sent to users so far in 2021—driven in part by a large APT28 (Fancy Bear) campaign and sustained by ongoing operations from Iran-aligned APT35. Since early 2021, APT35 has compromised a UK university website to host a phishing kit targeting Gmail, Yahoo and Hotmail credentials—including second-factor codes—and continues its credential harvesting campaigns against government, academia, journalism and NGOs using hijacked sites and link-shortening redirects. In May 2020 it attempted to distribute spyware disguised as a VPN on Google Play Store (blocked before installation) and has pursued similar Android C2 apps on other platforms. The group also impersonates conference officials (e.g., Munich Security, T20 Italy) to initiate phishing, embedding JavaScript to relay visitor IP, user-agent and locale via Telegram bots—a tactic TAG disrupted by reporting the bots. TAG’s layered defenses include batch-sent warnings, Workspace admin alerts, Safe Browsing domain blocks and urging high-risk users to enable two-factor authentication or enroll in Advanced Protection.
retrieved_context.title: Countering threats from Iran

hits.text: Evil Corp–linked operators began by abusing the open-source Responder tool to poison LLMNR and NBT-NS name-resolution queries on Windows hosts, harvesting NTLMv2 hashes and cleartext credentials, then used pass-the-hash techniques alongside PSExec and WMI for rapid lateral movement and privilege escalation to domain admin; once established, they deployed WastedLocker ransomware via scheduled tasks, encrypting over 95% of critical servers and workstations with AES-256, causing 72 hours of operational downtime and a $10 million ransom demand. Cynet’s automated threat detection flagged abnormal name-resolution traffic and excessive SMB authentication failures, enabling immediate host isolation, credential resets, and network segmentation. Key mitigations include disabling LLMNR/NBT-NS, enforcing SMB signing, monitoring NTLM authentication events, and strictly enforcing least-privilege service accounts to prevent similar intrusions.
hits.title: Cynet | Threat Detection Report: Wastedlocker Ransomware

canonical_entities: registered variables in the Windows Registry
hits.text: In June 2024, HP’s Threat Research team led by Patrick Schlapfer intercepted a low-grade phishing campaign leveraging HTML smuggling via an AES-encrypted HTML attachment containing JavaScript-embedded decryption logic—a novel twist on typical encrypted archives—which, when decrypted, mimicked a legitimate website but dropped a fully commented, French-language VBScript that registered variables in the Windows Registry, staged a JavaScript payload as a scheduled task, and invoked a PowerShell script to deploy the freely available AsyncRAT infostealer. Schlapfer and co-lead Alex Holland’s analysis, including comparison with generative-AI–produced code, concluded the well-structured, human-readable script was likely authored by gen-AI by a low-skill newcomer benefitting from reduced entry barriers, with no obfuscation or complex infrastructure beyond a single C2 server. This first definitive proof of AI-generated malware in the wild underscores the need for defenders to adapt detection strategies to AI-crafted droppers, monitor anomalous AES-in-JavaScript decryption patterns, and anticipate more sophisticated AI-generated payloads poised to emerge within the next two years, thereby heightening the risk to network and endpoint security.
hits.title: AI-Generated Malware Found in the Wild - SecurityWeek

canonical_entities: installing Sagerunex variants in the Windows Registry
hits.text: The Lotus Blossom APT (aka Lotus Panda, Billbug, Spring Dragon) has stepped up cyberespionage against APAC government targets by deploying new Sagerunex backdoor variants and abusing Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) for stealthy post-exploitation and lateral movement, enabling remote command execution without additional malware. Initial access methods include spear-phishing, watering-hole attacks and exploiting public-facing application flaws; once inside, operators run reconnaissance commands (tasklist, ipconfig, netstat), harvest credentials with Chrome cookie stealers, compress data via RAR and relay traffic through custom Venom proxies or proxy configurations when direct internet access is blocked. Persistence is achieved by installing Sagerunex variants in the Windows Registry under hijacked service names (tapisrv, swprv) to auto-launch at startup, while command-and-control blends encrypted traffic into legitimate platforms—stolen data uploaded as .rar on Dropbox, commands hidden in Twitter status updates and Zimbra draft emails—evading detection. Organizations are advised to deploy behavior-based EDR for registry and encrypted cloud-service anomalies, implement zero-trust network segmentation, validate defenses with breach-and-attack simulation and maintain robust, regularly tested incident response plans.
hits.title: Lotus Blossom APT Exploits WMI for Post-Exploitation Activities

canonical_entities: Boot or Logon Initialization Scripts: Logon Script (Windows)
hits.text: Blitz is a modular two-stage Windows malware discovered in 2024 and actively developed into early 2025 by a Russian-speaking actor using the moniker sw1zzx who distributed backdoored Standoff 2 game cheat packages (Nerest_CrackBy@sw1zzx_dev.zip and Elysium_CrackBy@sw1zzx_dev.zip) via a Telegram channel. The first stage is a stealthy downloader (ieapfltr.dll) retrieved through a PowerShell one-liner from pastebin/paste.rs URLs after passing anti-sandbox and VM detection checks (timing loops, floating-point instruction counters, processor count and screen resolution heuristics), which then establishes persistence via HKCU\Environment\UserInitMprLogonScript and HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run. Upon reboot, the downloader connects to a FastAPI-based C2 infrastructure hosted on a Hugging Face Space to fetch the second-stage Blitz bot that performs keylogging, screenshot capture, denial-of-service attacks on web servers and can deploy an XMRig Monero miner as follow-up. This campaign leverages Hugging Face Spaces for file hosting and C2 communications, and the malware developer promoted cheats on social media before announcing departure in May 2025; Hugging Face subsequently locked the account and blocked blob IDs. The impact includes credential theft, resource exploitation, unauthorized cryptocurrency mining and potential service disruption, and Palo Alto Networks’ Advanced WildFire, URL Filtering, DNS Security, Threat Prevention, Cortex XDR and XSIAM effectively detect and block Blitz activities, with Unit 42 standing by for incident response.
hits.title: Blitz Malware: A Tale of Game Cheats and Code Repositories

hits.text: Microsoft Threat Intelligence Center has attributed the emerging H0lyGh0st ransomware, active since June 2021 and tracked as DEV-0530, to financially motivated North Korean state-sponsored actors with ties to PLUTONIUM (DarkSeoul/Andariel), which has compromised small-to-mid-sized businesses—including manufacturers, banks, schools and event planners—across multiple countries since September 2021 by deploying custom SiennaPurple (C++ BTLC_C.exe) and SiennaBlue (Go-based HolyRS.exe, HolyLock.exe, BLTC.exe) families that encrypt Windows files with a .h0lyenc extension, use string obfuscation and public-key management, and enforce persistence via a scheduled task called “lockertask”; victims receive a ransom note delivered over a .onion portal demanding Bitcoin payment under double-extortion threats to publish stolen data if unpaid; between October 2021 and May 2022 MSTIC observed iterative Go-based SiennaBlue variants sharing core encryption and network/intranet connectivity functions, and in April 2022 the group rolled out its latest BTLC.exe, which hard-codes ServerBaseURL fallback credentials for network shares, uploads victim public keys to a C2 server, and encrypts all drive files—underscoring the need for defenders to monitor anomalous scheduled tasks, default-credential share connections, .onion traffic, and the appearance of .h0lyenc files to detect and disrupt this evolving threat.
hits.title: Emerging H0lyGh0st Ransomware Tied to North Korea | Threatpost

canonical_entities: ZIP files masquerading as legitimate updates
hits.text: Unit 42 has observed a sharp rise in post-intrusion WastedLocker ransomware attacks by the Evil Corp group—already known for Dridex—against large U.S. organizations in sectors from manufacturing to legal services, with initial compromise typically via ZIP files masquerading as legitimate updates that deploy a SocGholish JavaScript loader to profile systems and invoke PowerShell-based Cobalt Strike payloads; attackers then leverage WMI and PsExec for lateral movement, identify high-value and backup systems, elevate privileges, disable Windows Defender, delete shadow copies, install WastedLocker as a service, and encrypt files using a “.<victim_name>wasted” extension while appending ransom notes (“.<victim_name>wasted_info”) with contact addresses on ProtonMail, Airmail and others. Palo Alto Networks’ WildFire, Cortex XDR (anti-ransomware and behavioral threat protection), NGFW DNS signatures and AutoFocus tagging detect and prevent WastedLocker activity; organizations are urged to implement robust, off-site backup strategies and hardened cybersecurity controls to mitigate this high-impact targeted ransomware threat.
hits.title: Threat Assessment: WastedLocker Ransomware

hits.text: Since at least April 2024 Microsoft Threat Intelligence has tracked a Russia-affiliated cyberespionage actor dubbed Void Blizzard (aka LAUNDRY BEAR) conducting high-volume, targeted operations against government, defense, transportation, media, NGO and healthcare organizations—particularly in NATO member states and Ukraine—by leveraging stolen credentials procured via commodity infostealer ecosystems for password spray attacks and Exchange/SharePoint Online access, then automating bulk email and file collection (and in some cases Teams messages) via cloud APIs and tools like AzureHound; in April 2025 the actor evolved to adversary-in-the-middle spear phishing using a typosquatted domain and the open-source Evilginx framework with a malicious QR-coded PDF to harvest Entra authentication data; this widespread success underscores that even unsophisticated TTPs pose major intelligence risks to critical sectors, so organizations should enforce sign-in risk policies and phishing-resistant MFA (e.g., FIDO/passkeys), centralize identity management with Conditional Access, monitor risky sign-ins and mailbox auditing, apply least-privilege credential hygiene, and promptly rotate credentials after infostealer detections to disrupt Void Blizzard’s operations.
hits.title: New Russia-affiliated actor Void Blizzard targets critical sectors for espionage | Microsoft Security Blog

canonical_entities: Launch EC2 instances across regions via VPN
hits.text: Unit42’s “EleKtra-Leak” campaign, active since December 2020, uses automated scripts to clone public GitHub repos every few minutes, extract exposed AWS IAM keys within five minutes, then—if not blocked by GitHub-AWS quarantine policies—execute rapid AWS reconnaissance (DescribeRegions), create security groups, and launch hundreds of EC2 instances across regions via VPN for Monero cryptojacking, generating over 400 API calls in seven minutes. Between Aug. 30 and Oct. 6, 2023, researchers tracked 474 actor-controlled miners. The actor employs custom mining software and blocklists high-profile AWS account IDs to avoid honey traps. Leveraging the Prisma Cloud HoneyCloud project’s ephemeral key leaks and policy overrides, Unit42 obtained full visibility, informing Prisma Cloud Secrets Security, CI/CD IaC scanning, Cortex XDR, and recommendations for independent repo scanning, strict IAM policies, and continuous monitoring.
hits.title: CloudKeys in the Air: Tracking Malicious Operations of Exposed IAM Keys

hits.text: A zero-day VPN vulnerability provided initial access for a sophisticated threat actor who employed publicly available penetration‐testing and exploitation tools—SoftPerfect Network Scanner for network discovery, PsExec to deploy ServeManager.exe (the FiveHands ransomware variant using lattice-based NTRUEncrypt public key cryptography), and SombRAT for remote information theft—alongside RouterScan, grabff.exe, rclone.exe, and s3browser-9-5-3.exe to harvest credentials and exfiltrate data. Once inside, the attacker leveraged Windows Management Instrumentation (T1047) to enumerate and delete Volume Shadow Copies (Inhibit System Recovery, T1490), encrypted files (including those in recovery folders) for impact (T1486), and dropped ransom notes across directories, demanding payment to restore access. Post-encryption activities align with MITRE techniques such as Access Token Manipulation, Boot or Logon Autostart, PowerShell command and scripting interpreter, Domain Trust Discovery, Process Discovery, Screen Capture, and Kerberoasting. The combined use of FiveHands ransomware and SombRAT RAT resulted in both data theft and destruction of backup artifacts, underscoring the need for proactive patch management, network segmentation, strict credential hygiene, and rapid incident response to mitigate novel lattice-based encryption threats.
hits.title: FiveHands Ransomware Overview

hits.text: The Lotus Blossom APT (aka Lotus Panda, Billbug, Spring Dragon) has stepped up cyberespionage against APAC government targets by deploying new Sagerunex backdoor variants and abusing Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) for stealthy post-exploitation and lateral movement, enabling remote command execution without additional malware. Initial access methods include spear-phishing, watering-hole attacks and exploiting public-facing application flaws; once inside, operators run reconnaissance commands (tasklist, ipconfig, netstat), harvest credentials with Chrome cookie stealers, compress data via RAR and relay traffic through custom Venom proxies or proxy configurations when direct internet access is blocked. Persistence is achieved by installing Sagerunex variants in the Windows Registry under hijacked service names (tapisrv, swprv) to auto-launch at startup, while command-and-control blends encrypted traffic into legitimate platforms—stolen data uploaded as .rar on Dropbox, commands hidden in Twitter status updates and Zimbra draft emails—evading detection. Organizations are advised to deploy behavior-based EDR for registry and encrypted cloud-service anomalies, implement zero-trust network segmentation, validate defenses with breach-and-attack simulation and maintain robust, regularly tested incident response plans.
hits.title: Lotus Blossom APT Exploits WMI for Post-Exploitation Activities

canonical_entities: registered variables in the Windows Registry
hits.text: In June 2024, HP’s Threat Research team led by Patrick Schlapfer intercepted a low-grade phishing campaign leveraging HTML smuggling via an AES-encrypted HTML attachment containing JavaScript-embedded decryption logic—a novel twist on typical encrypted archives—which, when decrypted, mimicked a legitimate website but dropped a fully commented, French-language VBScript that registered variables in the Windows Registry, staged a JavaScript payload as a scheduled task, and invoked a PowerShell script to deploy the freely available AsyncRAT infostealer. Schlapfer and co-lead Alex Holland’s analysis, including comparison with generative-AI–produced code, concluded the well-structured, human-readable script was likely authored by gen-AI by a low-skill newcomer benefitting from reduced entry barriers, with no obfuscation or complex infrastructure beyond a single C2 server. This first definitive proof of AI-generated malware in the wild underscores the need for defenders to adapt detection strategies to AI-crafted droppers, monitor anomalous AES-in-JavaScript decryption patterns, and anticipate more sophisticated AI-generated payloads poised to emerge within the next two years, thereby heightening the risk to network and endpoint security.
hits.title: AI-Generated Malware Found in the Wild - SecurityWeek

canonical_entities: Boot or Logon Initialization Scripts: Logon Script (Windows)
hits.text: Blitz is a modular two-stage Windows malware discovered in 2024 and actively developed into early 2025 by a Russian-speaking actor using the moniker sw1zzx who distributed backdoored Standoff 2 game cheat packages (Nerest_CrackBy@sw1zzx_dev.zip and Elysium_CrackBy@sw1zzx_dev.zip) via a Telegram channel. The first stage is a stealthy downloader (ieapfltr.dll) retrieved through a PowerShell one-liner from pastebin/paste.rs URLs after passing anti-sandbox and VM detection checks (timing loops, floating-point instruction counters, processor count and screen resolution heuristics), which then establishes persistence via HKCU\Environment\UserInitMprLogonScript and HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run. Upon reboot, the downloader connects to a FastAPI-based C2 infrastructure hosted on a Hugging Face Space to fetch the second-stage Blitz bot that performs keylogging, screenshot capture, denial-of-service attacks on web servers and can deploy an XMRig Monero miner as follow-up. This campaign leverages Hugging Face Spaces for file hosting and C2 communications, and the malware developer promoted cheats on social media before announcing departure in May 2025; Hugging Face subsequently locked the account and blocked blob IDs. The impact includes credential theft, resource exploitation, unauthorized cryptocurrency mining and potential service disruption, and Palo Alto Networks’ Advanced WildFire, URL Filtering, DNS Security, Threat Prevention, Cortex XDR and XSIAM effectively detect and block Blitz activities, with Unit 42 standing by for incident response.
hits.title: Blitz Malware: A Tale of Game Cheats and Code Repositories

hits.text: A zero-day VPN vulnerability provided initial access for a sophisticated threat actor who employed publicly available penetration‐testing and exploitation tools—SoftPerfect Network Scanner for network discovery, PsExec to deploy ServeManager.exe (the FiveHands ransomware variant using lattice-based NTRUEncrypt public key cryptography), and SombRAT for remote information theft—alongside RouterScan, grabff.exe, rclone.exe, and s3browser-9-5-3.exe to harvest credentials and exfiltrate data. Once inside, the attacker leveraged Windows Management Instrumentation (T1047) to enumerate and delete Volume Shadow Copies (Inhibit System Recovery, T1490), encrypted files (including those in recovery folders) for impact (T1486), and dropped ransom notes across directories, demanding payment to restore access. Post-encryption activities align with MITRE techniques such as Access Token Manipulation, Boot or Logon Autostart, PowerShell command and scripting interpreter, Domain Trust Discovery, Process Discovery, Screen Capture, and Kerberoasting. The combined use of FiveHands ransomware and SombRAT RAT resulted in both data theft and destruction of backup artifacts, underscoring the need for proactive patch management, network segmentation, strict credential hygiene, and rapid incident response to mitigate novel lattice-based encryption threats.

canonical_entities: enforce persistence via a scheduled task

hits.text: Microsoft Threat Intelligence Center has attributed the emerging H0lyGh0st ransomware, active since June 2021 and tracked as DEV-0530, to financially motivated North Korean state-sponsored actors with ties to PLUTONIUM (DarkSeoul/Andariel), which has compromised small-to-mid-sized businesses—including manufacturers, banks, schools and event planners—across multiple countries since September 2021 by deploying custom SiennaPurple (C++ BTLC_C.exe) and SiennaBlue (Go-based HolyRS.exe, HolyLock.exe, BLTC.exe) families that encrypt Windows files with a .h0lyenc extension, use string obfuscation and public-key management, and enforce persistence via a scheduled task called “lockertask”; victims receive a ransom note delivered over a .onion portal demanding Bitcoin payment under double-extortion threats to publish stolen data if unpaid; between October 2021 and May 2022 MSTIC observed iterative Go-based SiennaBlue variants sharing core encryption and network/intranet connectivity functions, and in April 2022 the group rolled out its latest BTLC.exe, which hard-codes ServerBaseURL fallback credentials for network shares, uploads victim public keys to a C2 server, and encrypts all drive files—underscoring the need for defenders to monitor anomalous scheduled tasks, default-credential share connections, .onion traffic, and the appearance of .h0lyenc files to detect and disrupt this evolving threat.
hits.title: Emerging H0lyGh0st Ransomware Tied to North Korea | Threatpost

hits.text: Since September 2021 the politically motivated Moses Staff group has launched ransomless encryptions against Israeli organizations, exploiting unpatched public-facing infrastructure—most notably vulnerable Microsoft Exchange servers—and leveraging off-the-shelf exploits to breach networks, then moving laterally via PsExec, WMIC, and PowerShell without deploying custom backdoors. Upon infiltration, the group deploys PyDCrypt, a custom variant built atop the open-source DiskCryptor tool, which generates unique symmetric keys per hostname using an MD5 hash and salt; however, Check Point researchers note that failed self-deletion of PyDCrypt payloads allows key recovery and decryption under certain conditions. Rather than seeking financial gain, Moses Staff focuses on maximum operational disruption by exfiltrating corporate secrets and posting stolen data across a Tor leak site, Twitter, and Telegram channels—tactics reminiscent of Pay2Key and BlackShadow—and may originate from Palestine based on VirusTotal submissions. The attacks have caused widespread system downtime and data exposure, prompting Check Point to advise immediate patching of known vulnerabilities on public-facing servers, enhanced monitoring for lateral-movement utilities, and rapid retrieval of PyDCrypt samples to facilitate decryption.
hits.title: Moses Staff hackers wreak havoc on Israeli orgs with ransomless encryptions

canonical_entities: exploiting known vulnerabilities in public-facing VPN, web, Java, and SQL services
harvests credentials from LSASS memory and the SAM registry hive
hits.text: Microsoft has traced a stealthy espionage campaign by Flax Typhoon (aka Ethereal Panda), a China-based nation-state actor active since mid-2021, targeting dozens of Taiwanese organizations (with spill-over in Southeast Asia, North America, and Africa) by exploiting known vulnerabilities in public-facing VPN, web, Java, and SQL services to deploy the China Chopper web shell for initial access; the group escalates privileges via open-source exploits like Juicy Potato and BadPotato, then establishes persistence by disabling RDP network-level authentication, hijacking the Sticky Keys (sethc.exe) binary to launch Task Manager as SYSTEM, and installing a renamed SoftEther VPN-over-HTTPS bridge (conhost.exe/dllhost.exe) as a service to maintain covert C2 over port 443; leveraging LOLBins such as PowerShell Invoke-WebRequest, certutil, bitsadmin, WinRM, and WMIC for lateral movement, vulnerability scanning, and remote execution, it harvests credentials from LSASS memory and the SAM registry hive using Mimikatz for pass-the-hash attacks; although no exfiltration or final objectives have been observed, organizations are urged to enforce rigorous patch and vulnerability management on internet-exposed systems, monitor registry and file-integrity changes, deploy web application firewalls, reset compromised credentials, isolate and forensically examine affected hosts, and leverage detections in Microsoft 365 Defender to disrupt living-off-the-land tactics.
hits.title: Flax Typhoon using legitimate software to quietly access Taiwanese organizations | Microsoft Security Blog

hits.text: Since at least April 2024 Microsoft Threat Intelligence has tracked a Russia-affiliated cyberespionage actor dubbed Void Blizzard (aka LAUNDRY BEAR) conducting high-volume, targeted operations against government, defense, transportation, media, NGO and healthcare organizations—particularly in NATO member states and Ukraine—by leveraging stolen credentials procured via commodity infostealer ecosystems for password spray attacks and Exchange/SharePoint Online access, then automating bulk email and file collection (and in some cases Teams messages) via cloud APIs and tools like AzureHound; in April 2025 the actor evolved to adversary-in-the-middle spear phishing using a typosquatted domain and the open-source Evilginx framework with a malicious QR-coded PDF to harvest Entra authentication data; this widespread success underscores that even unsophisticated TTPs pose major intelligence risks to critical sectors, so organizations should enforce sign-in risk policies and phishing-resistant MFA (e.g., FIDO/passkeys), centralize identity management with Conditional Access, monitor risky sign-ins and mailbox auditing, apply least-privilege credential hygiene, and promptly rotate credentials after infostealer detections to disrupt Void Blizzard’s operations.
hits.title: New Russia-affiliated actor Void Blizzard targets critical sectors for espionage | Microsoft Security Blog

canonical_entities: Launch EC2 instances across regions via VPN
hits.text: Unit42’s “EleKtra-Leak” campaign, active since December 2020, uses automated scripts to clone public GitHub repos every few minutes, extract exposed AWS IAM keys within five minutes, then—if not blocked by GitHub-AWS quarantine policies—execute rapid AWS reconnaissance (DescribeRegions), create security groups, and launch hundreds of EC2 instances across regions via VPN for Monero cryptojacking, generating over 400 API calls in seven minutes. Between Aug. 30 and Oct. 6, 2023, researchers tracked 474 actor-controlled miners. The actor employs custom mining software and blocklists high-profile AWS account IDs to avoid honey traps. Leveraging the Prisma Cloud HoneyCloud project’s ephemeral key leaks and policy overrides, Unit42 obtained full visibility, informing Prisma Cloud Secrets Security, CI/CD IaC scanning, Cortex XDR, and recommendations for independent repo scanning, strict IAM policies, and continuous monitoring.

retrieved_context.text: Evil Corp–linked operators began by abusing the open-source Responder tool to poison LLMNR and NBT-NS name-resolution queries on Windows hosts, harvesting NTLMv2 hashes and cleartext credentials, then used pass-the-hash techniques alongside PSExec and WMI for rapid lateral movement and privilege escalation to domain admin; once established, they deployed WastedLocker ransomware via scheduled tasks, encrypting over 95% of critical servers and workstations with AES-256, causing 72 hours of operational downtime and a $10 million ransom demand. Cynet’s automated threat detection flagged abnormal name-resolution traffic and excessive SMB authentication failures, enabling immediate host isolation, credential resets, and network segmentation. Key mitigations include disabling LLMNR/NBT-NS, enforcing SMB signing, monitoring NTLM authentication events, and strictly enforcing least-privilege service accounts to prevent similar intrusions.

hits.text: US and UK agencies (CISA, FBI, CNMF, NCSC-UK and NSA) issued a joint advisory detailing how the Iranian-backed MuddyWater group—active since at least 2017 and linked to Iran’s Ministry of Intelligence and Security in January 2022—has expanded its arsenal beyond PowGoop, Canopy/Starwhale, Mori and POWERSTATS to include a new Python backdoor dubbed “Small Sieve” and a PowerShell backdoor that encrypts C2 channels; these tools target telecom, defense, local government and oil and gas organizations across Asia, Africa, Europe and North America, maintain persistence via custom string and traffic obfuscation (hex byte-swapping plus an obfuscated Base64 routine) over the Telegram Bot API via HTTPS, and facilitate lateral movement and data exfiltration, underscoring the need for defenders to monitor anomalous Telegram API calls, obfuscated Base64 traffic and encrypted PowerShell sessions.
hits.title: US and UK expose new malware used by MuddyWater hackers

hits.text: Microsoft Threat Intelligence has observed the Russia-based SVR actor Midnight Blizzard (aka NOBELIUM, APT29/UNC2452/Cozy Bear) launch a highly targeted social-engineering campaign since at least late May 2023 by leveraging previously compromised small-business Microsoft 365 tenants to create security-themed onmicrosoft.com domains and Teams accounts that masquerade as technical-support entities; attackers then initiate Microsoft Teams chat requests to elicit approval of MFA prompts or codes via Microsoft Authenticator, enabling credential theft, access to fewer than 40 global organizations across government, NGOs, IT services, technology, manufacturing and media sectors, and subsequent post-compromise activities including data exfiltration and attempts to add managed devices via Microsoft Entra ID to bypass conditional access. Microsoft has mitigated the malicious domains, directly notified affected customers, and recommends phishing-resistant authentication, Conditional Access policies, Microsoft Teams best practices, auditing, and user education to detect and prevent unsolicited MFA requests.
hits.title: Midnight Blizzard conducts targeted social engineering over Microsoft Teams | Microsoft Security Blog

canonical_entities: ZIP files masquerading as legitimate updates
hits.text: Unit 42 has observed a sharp rise in post-intrusion WastedLocker ransomware attacks by the Evil Corp group—already known for Dridex—against large U.S. organizations in sectors from manufacturing to legal services, with initial compromise typically via ZIP files masquerading as legitimate updates that deploy a SocGholish JavaScript loader to profile systems and invoke PowerShell-based Cobalt Strike payloads; attackers then leverage WMI and PsExec for lateral movement, identify high-value and backup systems, elevate privileges, disable Windows Defender, delete shadow copies, install WastedLocker as a service, and encrypt files using a “.<victim_name>wasted” extension while appending ransom notes (“.<victim_name>wasted_info”) with contact addresses on ProtonMail, Airmail and others. Palo Alto Networks’ WildFire, Cortex XDR (anti-ransomware and behavioral threat protection), NGFW DNS signatures and AutoFocus tagging detect and prevent WastedLocker activity; organizations are urged to implement robust, off-site backup strategies and hardened cybersecurity controls to mitigate this high-impact targeted ransomware threat.
hits.title: Threat Assessment: WastedLocker Ransomware

hits.text: Microsoft’s research exposes the BadPilot campaign—a multiyear initial-access subgroup of Russian GRU-aligned Seashell Blizzard active since at least 2021—that has opportunistically scanned for and exploited Internet-facing vulnerabilities (CVE-2021-34473 Exchange, CVE-2022-41352 Zimbra, CVE-2023-32315 OpenFire, CVE-2023-42793 TeamCity, CVE-2023-23397 Outlook, CVE-2024-1709 ConnectWise ScreenConnect, CVE-2023-48788 FortiClient EMS and various JBOSS flaws) to compromise a globally diverse set of high-value sectors (energy, oil and gas, telecommunications, shipping, arms manufacturing and government). Following initial access, BadPilot employs stealthy persistence, credential harvesting, lateral movement and common tools such as Cobalt Strike and DarkCrystalRAT to sustain footholds and support tailored network operations, including at least three destructive cyberattacks in Ukraine since 2023. After focusing on Ukraine, Europe, Central/South Asia and the Middle East during 2021–2023, the subgroup scaled horizontally into the United States, United Kingdom, Canada and Australia in early 2024, reflecting Russia’s evolving strategic objectives and underscoring the urgency of patching Internet-facing services, implementing comprehensive logging and anomaly detection, and applying threat-informed incident-response practices to disrupt its operational lifecycle.
hits.title: The BadPilot campaign: Seashell Blizzard subgroup conducts multiyear global access operation | Microsoft Security Blog

canonical_entities: targeted cyber-espionage campaign against telecommunications organizations in Egypt, Sudan and Tanzania
telecommunications organizations in Egypt, Sudan and Tanzania
hits.text: In November 2023, Iran-linked espionage group Seedworm (aka MuddyWater and subordinate to MOIS) launched a targeted cyber-espionage campaign against telecommunications organizations in Egypt, Sudan and Tanzania using its Go-based MuddyC2Go framework alongside both living-off-the-land and custom tools to maintain persistence, harvest credentials and exfiltrate data. Researchers observed a PowerShell-based MuddyC2Go DLL launcher named “vcruntime140.dll” sideloaded by the legitimate Java executable jabswitch.exe into csidl_common_appdata\javax, which read C2 URIs (“End” and “Status” values under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\Tcpip) before invoking Invoke-WebRequest to contacts servers such as 95.164.38.99:443 and 45.150.64.39:443; the backdoor was executed via a scheduled task (“Microsoft\Windows\JavaX\Java Autorun”), while Impacket’s WMIExec, Revsocks (94.131.3.160:443), and SimpleHelp (146.70.124.102) were leveraged for lateral movement, SAM hive dumps, drive reconnaissance and remote administration alongside AnyDesk and a custom keylogger. This activity followed a prior Seedworm intrusion earlier in 2023 into at least one victim using SimpleHelp-driven PowerShell, proxy tools, LSASS dumping and JumpCloud deployment, confirming group attribution. Seedworm’s blend of custom C2 innovation and publicly available/proxy tools underscores the necessity for defenders to monitor for anomalous PowerShell invocations to suspect domains, unexpected Java sideloading, scheduled task creations, unauthorized SimpleHelp or AnyDesk services, Venom Proxy processes, and registry modifications in telecom-grade networks to detect and disrupt its persistent espionage operations.
hits.title: Seedworm: Iranian Hackers Target Telecoms Orgs in North and East Africa | Symantec Enterprise Blogs

hits.text: In February 2022, CISA, the FBI, US Cyber Command CNMF, NCSC-UK and NSA issued a joint advisory on Iranian Ministry of Intelligence–linked APT MuddyWater (aka MERCURY, Earth Vetala, Static Kitten, Seedworm, TEMP.Zagros), active since 2018 and focused on cyber espionage, intellectual property theft and ransomware against defense, oil & gas, government and telecom sectors across Asia, Africa, Europe and North America. Exploiting publicly disclosed vulnerabilities and open-source tools, MuddyWater delivers malicious PDFs with embedded links that display error messages prompting users to download Excel maldocs or Windows executables; these files host VBA macros that drop WSF scripts to execute PowerShell and VB payloads, leverage LoLBins, and stage RATs and malware families including PowGoop, Canopy, Small Sieve, POWERSTATS and Mori while communicating with C2 over HTTP and DNS and persisting via Registry Run keys. Cisco Talos observed regional campaigns in Turkey (Nov 2021), Pakistan (Aug 2021) and Armenia (Jun 2021) using decoy documents, signaling tokens and a consistent TTP set, suggesting a conglomerate of subgroups migrating techniques across regions. The resultant network access and data exfiltration underscore the imperative for proactive DFIR readiness, deployment of XDR/MDR platforms, rigorous vulnerability management, macro execution restrictions, PowerShell/LoLBin monitoring and ongoing user awareness training reinforced by incident response tabletop exercises.
hits.title: An In-Depth Look at Iranian APT "MuddyWater"

hits.text: Since 2021, BadPilot—a subgroup of Russia’s state-sponsored APT44 (also known as Seashell Blizzard/Sandworm)—has executed a multi-year campaign to compromise critical energy, oil & gas, telecom, shipping, arms manufacturing, government, military, transportation and logistics networks across Ukraine, Europe, Central/South Asia and the Middle East, intensifying after Russia’s 2022 invasion with intelligence gathering, operational disruption and at least three wiper-style destructive attacks in Ukraine; by 2023 its scope expanded to large-scale compromises across Europe, the United States and the Middle East, and in 2024 it added the UK, Canada and Australia. The actor exploits n-day vulnerabilities (CVE-2021-34473, CVE-2022-41352, CVE-2023-32315, CVE-2023-42793, CVE-2023-23397, CVE-2024-1709, CVE-2023-48788), conducts credential theft and supply-chain attacks via regionally managed IT service providers, deploys LocalOlive web shells and uses legitimate management tools (Atera Agent, Splashtop) for initial access and persistence; post-compromise, it harvests credentials with Procdump and registry modifications, exfiltrates data via Rclone, Chisel and Plink over covert Tor-routed tunnels, and performs lateral movement through DNS reconfiguration, new services, scheduled tasks and OpenSSH backdoors. Microsoft warns the subgroup’s near-global reach and horizontal scaling capabilities, and has published hunting queries, IoCs and YARA rules to enable defenders to detect and disrupt its operations.
hits.title: BadPilot network hacking campaign fuels Russian SandWorm attacks

hits.text: In early September 2021, Google’s Threat Analysis Group exposed EXOTIC LILY, a financially motivated initial access broker linked to Russian gangs FIN12/WIZARD SPIDER that exploited Microsoft MSHTML CVE-2021-40444 before transitioning to delivering custom BazarLoader and a new “BUMBLEBEE” loader via ISO files with hidden DLLs and LNK shortcuts—identifiable by shared machine identifiers, unique command-line arguments and a “bumblebee” user-agent—to deploy Conti and Diavol ransomware. At its peak, EXOTIC LILY sent over 5,000 spear-phishing emails daily to 650 organizations across IT, cybersecurity, healthcare and other sectors, using human-operated TTPs such as TLD-switched domain and employee identity spoofing (leveraging AI-generated or harvested RocketReach/CrunchBase profiles), live chat to build trust, and legitimate file-sharing services (WeTransfer, TransferNow, OneDrive) to evade detection. Operators worked a standard 9-to-5 schedule in a Central/Eastern Europe timezone, customized business proposals, scheduled calls, and used WMI-based data collection in BUMBLEBEE to exfiltrate system details in JSON and fetch Cobalt Strike payloads. Overlaps with Microsoft’s DEV-0413 and Abnormal reporting confirm shared infrastructure, underscoring the need for enhanced domain/identity spoofing defenses, monitoring of file-sharing notifications, and threat hunting for ISO/LNK artifacts with unique metadata or “bumblebee” indicators.
hits.title: Exposing initial access broker with ties to Conti

hits.text: ESET researchers uncovered the Iran-aligned APT35 (aka Ballistic Bobcat, Charming Kitten, TA453/PHOSPHORUS) deploying a novel Sponsor backdoor across at least 34 opportunistic victims—primarily Israeli organizations in sectors from automotive to telecommunications, plus medical targets in Brazil and the UAE—by scanning for and exploiting Exchange CVE-2021-26855 vulnerabilities since September 2021, wrapping up their CISA AA21-321A/PowerLess campaign before dropping Sponsor via innocuously named batch files that deploy configuration files (config.txt, node.txt) to disk, install a persistent Windows service (“SystemNetwork”/“Update”) when run with an “install” argument, then periodically RC4-decrypt and call back to embedded C2 relays, all while leveraging open-source tooling (Mimikatz, Chisel, GO Simple Tunnel, Plink, RevSocks and Merlin) for lateral movement and data exfiltration; ESET has catalogued five Sponsor versions through June 2022, underscoring Ballistic Bobcat’s modular, short-duration, narrowly targeted “Sponsoring Access” campaign and highlighting the need for Exchange patching, service and file monitoring for batch deployments, and detection of RC4-encrypted config lookups to disrupt ongoing espionage operations.

retrieved_context.text: US and UK agencies (CISA, FBI, CNMF, NCSC-UK and NSA) issued a joint advisory detailing how the Iranian-backed MuddyWater group—active since at least 2017 and linked to Iran’s Ministry of Intelligence and Security in January 2022—has expanded its arsenal beyond PowGoop, Canopy/Starwhale, Mori and POWERSTATS to include a new Python backdoor dubbed “Small Sieve” and a PowerShell backdoor that encrypts C2 channels; these tools target telecom, defense, local government and oil and gas organizations across Asia, Africa, Europe and North America, maintain persistence via custom string and traffic obfuscation (hex byte-swapping plus an obfuscated Base64 routine) over the Telegram Bot API via HTTPS, and facilitate lateral movement and data exfiltration, underscoring the need for defenders to monitor anomalous Telegram API calls, obfuscated Base64 traffic and encrypted PowerShell sessions.
retrieved_context.title: US and UK expose new malware used by MuddyWater hackers

retrieved_context.text: Microsoft Threat Intelligence has observed the Russia-based SVR actor Midnight Blizzard (aka NOBELIUM, APT29/UNC2452/Cozy Bear) launch a highly targeted social-engineering campaign since at least late May 2023 by leveraging previously compromised small-business Microsoft 365 tenants to create security-themed onmicrosoft.com domains and Teams accounts that masquerade as technical-support entities; attackers then initiate Microsoft Teams chat requests to elicit approval of MFA prompts or codes via Microsoft Authenticator, enabling credential theft, access to fewer than 40 global organizations across government, NGOs, IT services, technology, manufacturing and media sectors, and subsequent post-compromise activities including data exfiltration and attempts to add managed devices via Microsoft Entra ID to bypass conditional access. Microsoft has mitigated the malicious domains, directly notified affected customers, and recommends phishing-resistant authentication, Conditional Access policies, Microsoft Teams best practices, auditing, and user education to detect and prevent unsolicited MFA requests.
retrieved_context.title: Midnight Blizzard conducts targeted social engineering over Microsoft Teams | Microsoft Security Blog

canonical_entities: ZIP files masquerading as legitimate updates
retrieved_context.text: Unit 42 has observed a sharp rise in post-intrusion WastedLocker ransomware attacks by the Evil Corp group—already known for Dridex—against large U.S. organizations in sectors from manufacturing to legal services, with initial compromise typically via ZIP files masquerading as legitimate updates that deploy a SocGholish JavaScript loader to profile systems and invoke PowerShell-based Cobalt Strike payloads; attackers then leverage WMI and PsExec for lateral movement, identify high-value and backup systems, elevate privileges, disable Windows Defender, delete shadow copies, install WastedLocker as a service, and encrypt files using a “.<victim_name>wasted” extension while appending ransom notes (“.<victim_name>wasted_info”) with contact addresses on ProtonMail, Airmail and others. Palo Alto Networks’ WildFire, Cortex XDR (anti-ransomware and behavioral threat protection), NGFW DNS signatures and AutoFocus tagging detect and prevent WastedLocker activity; organizations are urged to implement robust, off-site backup strategies and hardened cybersecurity controls to mitigate this high-impact targeted ransomware threat.
retrieved_context.title: Threat Assessment: WastedLocker Ransomware

retrieved_context.text: Microsoft’s research exposes the BadPilot campaign—a multiyear initial-access subgroup of Russian GRU-aligned Seashell Blizzard active since at least 2021—that has opportunistically scanned for and exploited Internet-facing vulnerabilities (CVE-2021-34473 Exchange, CVE-2022-41352 Zimbra, CVE-2023-32315 OpenFire, CVE-2023-42793 TeamCity, CVE-2023-23397 Outlook, CVE-2024-1709 ConnectWise ScreenConnect, CVE-2023-48788 FortiClient EMS and various JBOSS flaws) to compromise a globally diverse set of high-value sectors (energy, oil and gas, telecommunications, shipping, arms manufacturing and government). Following initial access, BadPilot employs stealthy persistence, credential harvesting, lateral movement and common tools such as Cobalt Strike and DarkCrystalRAT to sustain footholds and support tailored network operations, including at least three destructive cyberattacks in Ukraine since 2023. After focusing on Ukraine, Europe, Central/South Asia and the Middle East during 2021–2023, the subgroup scaled horizontally into the United States, United Kingdom, Canada and Australia in early 2024, reflecting Russia’s evolving strategic objectives and underscoring the urgency of patching Internet-facing services, implementing comprehensive logging and anomaly detection, and applying threat-informed incident-response practices to disrupt its operational lifecycle.
retrieved_context.title: The BadPilot campaign: Seashell Blizzard subgroup conducts multiyear global access operation | Microsoft Security Blog

canonical_entities: targeted cyber-espionage campaign against telecommunications organizations in Egypt, Sudan and Tanzania
telecommunications organizations in Egypt, Sudan and Tanzania
retrieved_context.text: In November 2023, Iran-linked espionage group Seedworm (aka MuddyWater and subordinate to MOIS) launched a targeted cyber-espionage campaign against telecommunications organizations in Egypt, Sudan and Tanzania using its Go-based MuddyC2Go framework alongside both living-off-the-land and custom tools to maintain persistence, harvest credentials and exfiltrate data. Researchers observed a PowerShell-based MuddyC2Go DLL launcher named “vcruntime140.dll” sideloaded by the legitimate Java executable jabswitch.exe into csidl_common_appdata\javax, which read C2 URIs (“End” and “Status” values under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\Tcpip) before invoking Invoke-WebRequest to contacts servers such as 95.164.38.99:443 and 45.150.64.39:443; the backdoor was executed via a scheduled task (“Microsoft\Windows\JavaX\Java Autorun”), while Impacket’s WMIExec, Revsocks (94.131.3.160:443), and SimpleHelp (146.70.124.102) were leveraged for lateral movement, SAM hive dumps, drive reconnaissance and remote administration alongside AnyDesk and a custom keylogger. This activity followed a prior Seedworm intrusion earlier in 2023 into at least one victim using SimpleHelp-driven PowerShell, proxy tools, LSASS dumping and JumpCloud deployment, confirming group attribution. Seedworm’s blend of custom C2 innovation and publicly available/proxy tools underscores the necessity for defenders to monitor for anomalous PowerShell invocations to suspect domains, unexpected Java sideloading, scheduled task creations, unauthorized SimpleHelp or AnyDesk services, Venom Proxy processes, and registry modifications in telecom-grade networks to detect and disrupt its persistent espionage operations.
retrieved_context.title: Seedworm: Iranian Hackers Target Telecoms Orgs in North and East Africa | Symantec Enterprise Blogs

canonical_entities: Launch EC2 instances across regions via VPN
retrieved_context.text: Unit42’s “EleKtra-Leak” campaign, active since December 2020, uses automated scripts to clone public GitHub repos every few minutes, extract exposed AWS IAM keys within five minutes, then—if not blocked by GitHub-AWS quarantine policies—execute rapid AWS reconnaissance (DescribeRegions), create security groups, and launch hundreds of EC2 instances across regions via VPN for Monero cryptojacking, generating over 400 API calls in seven minutes. Between Aug. 30 and Oct. 6, 2023, researchers tracked 474 actor-controlled miners. The actor employs custom mining software and blocklists high-profile AWS account IDs to avoid honey traps. Leveraging the Prisma Cloud HoneyCloud project’s ephemeral key leaks and policy overrides, Unit42 obtained full visibility, informing Prisma Cloud Secrets Security, CI/CD IaC scanning, Cortex XDR, and recommendations for independent repo scanning, strict IAM policies, and continuous monitoring.

hits.text: Iran-linked APT Hexane (aka Lyceum/SiameseKitten), active since at least 2018 and previously focused on oil & gas and telecommunications in the Middle East and Africa, has shifted in 2021 to target Israeli IT and communications firms via sophisticated supply-chain phishing operations, ClearSky reports. Leveraging a newly expanded infrastructure to impersonate legitimate companies and HR personnel on LinkedIn, Hexane conducted a May 2021 attack on an Israeli IT provider followed by a July wave against additional organizations by luring candidates with fake job offers for roles in France, Israel and the UK. Victims are directed to a phishing site where tailored lure files deploy a dual-stage infection—first the Milan implant to establish C2 connectivity, then the DanBot RAT—to harvest data, perform espionage and move laterally, presumably to breach client networks downstream. This upgrade mirrors North Korea’s “dream job” campaigns and OilRig (APT34) activity, underscoring Hexane’s evolving tactics, renewed toolset and continued focus on supply-chain compromise to facilitate deep network infiltration.

retrieved_context.text: US and UK agencies (CISA, FBI, CNMF, NCSC-UK and NSA) issued a joint advisory detailing how the Iranian-backed MuddyWater group—active since at least 2017 and linked to Iran’s Ministry of Intelligence and Security in January 2022—has expanded its arsenal beyond PowGoop, Canopy/Starwhale, Mori and POWERSTATS to include a new Python backdoor dubbed “Small Sieve” and a PowerShell backdoor that encrypts C2 channels; these tools target telecom, defense, local government and oil and gas organizations across Asia, Africa, Europe and North America, maintain persistence via custom string and traffic obfuscation (hex byte-swapping plus an obfuscated Base64 routine) over the Telegram Bot API via HTTPS, and facilitate lateral movement and data exfiltration, underscoring the need for defenders to monitor anomalous Telegram API calls, obfuscated Base64 traffic and encrypted PowerShell sessions.
retrieved_context.title: US and UK expose new malware used by MuddyWater hackers

retrieved_context.text: Microsoft’s research exposes the BadPilot campaign—a multiyear initial-access subgroup of Russian GRU-aligned Seashell Blizzard active since at least 2021—that has opportunistically scanned for and exploited Internet-facing vulnerabilities (CVE-2021-34473 Exchange, CVE-2022-41352 Zimbra, CVE-2023-32315 OpenFire, CVE-2023-42793 TeamCity, CVE-2023-23397 Outlook, CVE-2024-1709 ConnectWise ScreenConnect, CVE-2023-48788 FortiClient EMS and various JBOSS flaws) to compromise a globally diverse set of high-value sectors (energy, oil and gas, telecommunications, shipping, arms manufacturing and government). Following initial access, BadPilot employs stealthy persistence, credential harvesting, lateral movement and common tools such as Cobalt Strike and DarkCrystalRAT to sustain footholds and support tailored network operations, including at least three destructive cyberattacks in Ukraine since 2023. After focusing on Ukraine, Europe, Central/South Asia and the Middle East during 2021–2023, the subgroup scaled horizontally into the United States, United Kingdom, Canada and Australia in early 2024, reflecting Russia’s evolving strategic objectives and underscoring the urgency of patching Internet-facing services, implementing comprehensive logging and anomaly detection, and applying threat-informed incident-response practices to disrupt its operational lifecycle.
retrieved_context.title: The BadPilot campaign: Seashell Blizzard subgroup conducts multiyear global access operation | Microsoft Security Blog

canonical_entities: targeted cyber-espionage campaign against telecommunications organizations in Egypt, Sudan and Tanzania
telecommunications organizations in Egypt, Sudan and Tanzania
retrieved_context.text: In November 2023, Iran-linked espionage group Seedworm (aka MuddyWater and subordinate to MOIS) launched a targeted cyber-espionage campaign against telecommunications organizations in Egypt, Sudan and Tanzania using its Go-based MuddyC2Go framework alongside both living-off-the-land and custom tools to maintain persistence, harvest credentials and exfiltrate data. Researchers observed a PowerShell-based MuddyC2Go DLL launcher named “vcruntime140.dll” sideloaded by the legitimate Java executable jabswitch.exe into csidl_common_appdata\javax, which read C2 URIs (“End” and “Status” values under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\Tcpip) before invoking Invoke-WebRequest to contacts servers such as 95.164.38.99:443 and 45.150.64.39:443; the backdoor was executed via a scheduled task (“Microsoft\Windows\JavaX\Java Autorun”), while Impacket’s WMIExec, Revsocks (94.131.3.160:443), and SimpleHelp (146.70.124.102) were leveraged for lateral movement, SAM hive dumps, drive reconnaissance and remote administration alongside AnyDesk and a custom keylogger. This activity followed a prior Seedworm intrusion earlier in 2023 into at least one victim using SimpleHelp-driven PowerShell, proxy tools, LSASS dumping and JumpCloud deployment, confirming group attribution. Seedworm’s blend of custom C2 innovation and publicly available/proxy tools underscores the necessity for defenders to monitor for anomalous PowerShell invocations to suspect domains, unexpected Java sideloading, scheduled task creations, unauthorized SimpleHelp or AnyDesk services, Venom Proxy processes, and registry modifications in telecom-grade networks to detect and disrupt its persistent espionage operations.
retrieved_context.title: Seedworm: Iranian Hackers Target Telecoms Orgs in North and East Africa | Symantec Enterprise Blogs

retrieved_context.text: Since 2021, BadPilot—a subgroup of Russia’s state-sponsored APT44 (also known as Seashell Blizzard/Sandworm)—has executed a multi-year campaign to compromise critical energy, oil & gas, telecom, shipping, arms manufacturing, government, military, transportation and logistics networks across Ukraine, Europe, Central/South Asia and the Middle East, intensifying after Russia’s 2022 invasion with intelligence gathering, operational disruption and at least three wiper-style destructive attacks in Ukraine; by 2023 its scope expanded to large-scale compromises across Europe, the United States and the Middle East, and in 2024 it added the UK, Canada and Australia. The actor exploits n-day vulnerabilities (CVE-2021-34473, CVE-2022-41352, CVE-2023-32315, CVE-2023-42793, CVE-2023-23397, CVE-2024-1709, CVE-2023-48788), conducts credential theft and supply-chain attacks via regionally managed IT service providers, deploys LocalOlive web shells and uses legitimate management tools (Atera Agent, Splashtop) for initial access and persistence; post-compromise, it harvests credentials with Procdump and registry modifications, exfiltrates data via Rclone, Chisel and Plink over covert Tor-routed tunnels, and performs lateral movement through DNS reconfiguration, new services, scheduled tasks and OpenSSH backdoors. Microsoft warns the subgroup’s near-global reach and horizontal scaling capabilities, and has published hunting queries, IoCs and YARA rules to enable defenders to detect and disrupt its operations.
retrieved_context.title: BadPilot network hacking campaign fuels Russian SandWorm attacks

canonical_entities: Launch EC2 instances across regions via VPN
retrieved_context.text: Unit42’s “EleKtra-Leak” campaign, active since December 2020, uses automated scripts to clone public GitHub repos every few minutes, extract exposed AWS IAM keys within five minutes, then—if not blocked by GitHub-AWS quarantine policies—execute rapid AWS reconnaissance (DescribeRegions), create security groups, and launch hundreds of EC2 instances across regions via VPN for Monero cryptojacking, generating over 400 API calls in seven minutes. Between Aug. 30 and Oct. 6, 2023, researchers tracked 474 actor-controlled miners. The actor employs custom mining software and blocklists high-profile AWS account IDs to avoid honey traps. Leveraging the Prisma Cloud HoneyCloud project’s ephemeral key leaks and policy overrides, Unit42 obtained full visibility, informing Prisma Cloud Secrets Security, CI/CD IaC scanning, Cortex XDR, and recommendations for independent repo scanning, strict IAM policies, and continuous monitoring.
retrieved_context.title: CloudKeys in the Air: Tracking Malicious Operations of Exposed IAM Keys

retrieved_context.text: In February 2022, CISA, the FBI, US Cyber Command CNMF, NCSC-UK and NSA issued a joint advisory on Iranian Ministry of Intelligence–linked APT MuddyWater (aka MERCURY, Earth Vetala, Static Kitten, Seedworm, TEMP.Zagros), active since 2018 and focused on cyber espionage, intellectual property theft and ransomware against defense, oil & gas, government and telecom sectors across Asia, Africa, Europe and North America. Exploiting publicly disclosed vulnerabilities and open-source tools, MuddyWater delivers malicious PDFs with embedded links that display error messages prompting users to download Excel maldocs or Windows executables; these files host VBA macros that drop WSF scripts to execute PowerShell and VB payloads, leverage LoLBins, and stage RATs and malware families including PowGoop, Canopy, Small Sieve, POWERSTATS and Mori while communicating with C2 over HTTP and DNS and persisting via Registry Run keys. Cisco Talos observed regional campaigns in Turkey (Nov 2021), Pakistan (Aug 2021) and Armenia (Jun 2021) using decoy documents, signaling tokens and a consistent TTP set, suggesting a conglomerate of subgroups migrating techniques across regions. The resultant network access and data exfiltration underscore the imperative for proactive DFIR readiness, deployment of XDR/MDR platforms, rigorous vulnerability management, macro execution restrictions, PowerShell/LoLBin monitoring and ongoing user awareness training reinforced by incident response tabletop exercises.
retrieved_context.title: An In-Depth Look at Iranian APT "MuddyWater"

retrieved_context.text: Trend Micro observed over one million Conti ransomware attack attempts in the U.S. (Jan–Nov 2021), with the retail, insurance, manufacturing, telecommunications and healthcare sectors most targeted; operators—tied to Trickbot—gain initial access via BazarLoader phishing emails (Google Drive links) and exploitation of FortiGate flaws (CVE-2018-13379/13374) or Exchange ProxyShell, deploy Cobalt Strike, then perform reconnaissance (Whoami, Nltest, Net, ShareFinder), escalate privileges by harvesting domain-admin credentials or exploiting Zerologon (CVE-2020-1472) and PrintNightmare (CVE-2021-1675), and dump credentials using ProcDump and Mimikatz (mass-mimikatz, Rubeus, kerberoasting), “reg save,” Get-GPPPassword, SharpChrome and SeatBelt; they move laterally via EternalBlue, PSExec, scheduled tasks and remote-access tools (Atera, AnyDesk), evade defenses with automated batch scripts (GMER, PC Hunter, PowerShell) to disable security services, then execute ransomware via scheduled jobs or DontSleep.exe, exfiltrate data using Rclone (to Mega) or WinSCP, and encrypt files with ChaCha20/RSA-4096 while deleting shadow copies for double extortion; organizations should inventory assets, enforce least privilege, virtual-patch public-facing apps, monitor for Cobalt Strike and anomalous scheduled tasks or credential-dumping activities, deploy multilayered endpoint and network defenses, and maintain reliable backups.
retrieved_context.title: Ransomware Spotlight: Conti | Trend Micro (US)

retrieved_context.text: Microsoft Threat Intelligence has observed the Russia-based SVR actor Midnight Blizzard (aka NOBELIUM, APT29/UNC2452/Cozy Bear) launch a highly targeted social-engineering campaign since at least late May 2023 by leveraging previously compromised small-business Microsoft 365 tenants to create security-themed onmicrosoft.com domains and Teams accounts that masquerade as technical-support entities; attackers then initiate Microsoft Teams chat requests to elicit approval of MFA prompts or codes via Microsoft Authenticator, enabling credential theft, access to fewer than 40 global organizations across government, NGOs, IT services, technology, manufacturing and media sectors, and subsequent post-compromise activities including data exfiltration and attempts to add managed devices via Microsoft Entra ID to bypass conditional access. Microsoft has mitigated the malicious domains, directly notified affected customers, and recommends phishing-resistant authentication, Conditional Access policies, Microsoft Teams best practices, auditing, and user education to detect and prevent unsolicited MFA requests.
retrieved_context.title: Midnight Blizzard conducts targeted social engineering over Microsoft Teams | Microsoft Security Blog

retrieved_context.text: Iran-linked APT Hexane (aka Lyceum/SiameseKitten), active since at least 2018 and previously focused on oil & gas and telecommunications in the Middle East and Africa, has shifted in 2021 to target Israeli IT and communications firms via sophisticated supply-chain phishing operations, ClearSky reports. Leveraging a newly expanded infrastructure to impersonate legitimate companies and HR personnel on LinkedIn, Hexane conducted a May 2021 attack on an Israeli IT provider followed by a July wave against additional organizations by luring candidates with fake job offers for roles in France, Israel and the UK. Victims are directed to a phishing site where tailored lure files deploy a dual-stage infection—first the Milan implant to establish C2 connectivity, then the DanBot RAT—to harvest data, perform espionage and move laterally, presumably to breach client networks downstream. This upgrade mirrors North Korea’s “dream job” campaigns and OilRig (APT34) activity, underscoring Hexane’s evolving tactics, renewed toolset and continued focus on supply-chain compromise to facilitate deep network infiltration.
retrieved_context.title: Report: Iranian APT Hexane Targets Israeli Companies

retrieved_context.text: ESET researchers uncovered the Iran-aligned APT35 (aka Ballistic Bobcat, Charming Kitten, TA453/PHOSPHORUS) deploying a novel Sponsor backdoor across at least 34 opportunistic victims—primarily Israeli organizations in sectors from automotive to telecommunications, plus medical targets in Brazil and the UAE—by scanning for and exploiting Exchange CVE-2021-26855 vulnerabilities since September 2021, wrapping up their CISA AA21-321A/PowerLess campaign before dropping Sponsor via innocuously named batch files that deploy configuration files (config.txt, node.txt) to disk, install a persistent Windows service (“SystemNetwork”/“Update”) when run with an “install” argument, then periodically RC4-decrypt and call back to embedded C2 relays, all while leveraging open-source tooling (Mimikatz, Chisel, GO Simple Tunnel, Plink, RevSocks and Merlin) for lateral movement and data exfiltration; ESET has catalogued five Sponsor versions through June 2022, underscoring Ballistic Bobcat’s modular, short-duration, narrowly targeted “Sponsoring Access” campaign and highlighting the need for Exchange patching, service and file monitoring for batch deployments, and detection of RC4-encrypted config lookups to disrupt ongoing espionage operations.
retrieved_context.title: Sponsor with batch-filed whiskers: Ballistic Bobcat’s scan and strike backdoor
