hits.text: In 2024, ESET researchers uncovered a sustained cyberespionage campaign by the Iran-aligned APT group BladedFeline—active since at least 2017 against Kurdish Regional Government (KRG) and Iraqi government officials—that leverages an evolving toolset including the Shahmaran 64-bit backdoor, two reverse tunnels (Laret and Pinar), Whisper (an Exchange-based backdoor communicating via email attachments), a malicious IIS module dubbed PrimeCache bearing code similarities to OilRig’s RDAT backdoor, and supplementary implants such as the Flog webshell and Hawking Listener. Forensic analysis revealed early indicators on KRG systems—VideoSRV reverse shell (Sept 2017) and RDAT (Jan 2018)—consistent with OilRig’s operational patterns, leading to a medium-confidence assessment that BladedFeline operates as a subgroup of OilRig alongside Lyceum. The timeline spans initial KRG compromises in 2017–2018, Shahmaran deployment against diplomatic officials in early 2023, expansion to a telecommunications provider in Uzbekistan in March 2023, and the 2024 discovery of Whisper, Laret, Pinar, and PrimeCache across KRG, GOI, and Uzbek networks. BladedFeline’s tactics—native IIS module implantation, email-based C&C, reverse tunnels, and webshell exploitation—underscore the need to monitor Exchange mailbox activity for anomalous attachments, IIS module registrations (e.g., HttpModule.pdb), port listeners, and VirusTotal submitter IDs to detect and disrupt this persistent threat targeting strategic communications, oil-related infrastructure, and diplomatic data in the Middle East.
hits.title: BladedFeline: Whispering in the dark

hits.text: Since September 2017, the Iran-aligned BladedFeline subcluster of the OilRig APT has executed persistent cyber espionage against Kurdish and Iraqi government entities, initially compromising KRG systems and a regional Uzbekistan telecom provider via an internet-facing application vulnerability and social engineering to deploy the Flog web shell. ESET’s Q4 2023–Q1 2024 report documents the group’s evolving malware arsenal: the Shahmaran backdoor for remote file manipulation, the C#/.NET Whisper (aka Veaty) email-based implant, the DNS-tunneling Spearal and its optimized variant, Optimizer, the Slippery Snakelet Python implant for command execution and data exfiltration, and tunneling tools Laret and Pinar. BladedFeline leverages a malicious IIS module, PrimeCache—akin to OilRig’s RDAT—and the Hawking Listener early-stage implant to maintain stealthy access, systematically harvesting diplomatic and financial intelligence tied to KRG oil reserves and Western relations to further Iranian strategic objectives.
hits.title: Iran-Linked BladedFeline Hits Iraqi and Kurdish Targets with Whisper and Spearal Malware

hits.text: CISA has released a detailed analysis of the FiveHands ransomware, a C++-based DeathRansom successor with HelloKitty ties, deployed by financially motivated UNC2447 in recent European and North American intrusions; leveraging a VPN product zero-day for initial access, the adversary used open-source exploitation tools and SombRAT to map the network, exfiltrate data, and execute the NTRUEncrypt-powered ransomware stage, which enumerates and erases Volume Shadow Copies to thwart recovery, before demanding payment. CISA’s malware analysis (MAR) and accompanying report (AR) catalog 18 submitted artifacts—eight pen-test utilities, the ransomware binary, and nine SombRAT components—and provide mitigation guidance including timely VPN patching, network segmentation, multi-factor authentication, robust backup strategies, and behavior-based detection tuned to NTRUEncrypt operations and shadow copy deletion. These findings align with IST’s 48 anti-ransomware recommendations and the NCIJTF’s tactics-focused fact sheet, underscoring the need for proactive vulnerability management, continuous monitoring, and rapid response frameworks to neutralize UNC2447’s evolving capabilities.
hits.title: CISA Analyzes FiveHands Ransomware

canonical_entities: Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Tools
hits.text: Since its emergence in 2021 and first detection on Trend Micro telemetry in March 2022, the TargetCompany ransomware group has launched 269 attempted attacks against 250 disclosed Trend customers—predominantly in Asia (notably India and Saudi Arabia)—while avoiding Kazakhstan, Russia, Qatar, and Ukraine, and focusing on manufacturing, retail, and telecommunications; their November 2022–May 2023 leak site lists 20 confirmed victims (mostly small businesses) across the Asia-Pacific, Europe, and Middle East in IT, manufacturing, apparel, and automotive sectors. Initial access vectors include exploitation of CVE-2019-1069 and CVE-2020-0618 RCE flaws, SQL Server xp_cmdshell abuse, and OneNote-based spam campaigns. Execution relies on WMIC-invoked PowerShell scripts to retrieve various payloads (TargetComp ransomware, Remcos backdoor, Negasteal, Snake Keylogger) and, since January 2022, reflective loading of a .NET downloader that decrypts and runs payloads in memory via XOR or inversion. For defense evasion, operators deploy GMER, PCHunter64 (YDArk.exe), Advance Process Termination, KILLAV, and killer.bat to disable AV and security services; discovery is achieved through network scans and Mimikatz credential dumping; lateral movement via RDP-based RCE; C2 evolved from an open Mallox directory to an Nginx-protected server. Impact involves ChaCha20 file encryption with keys generated by Curve25519 and AES-128, file extensions such as .mallox/.exploit/.avast and ransom notes titled “HOW TO RECOVER!!.TXT,” and potential data exfiltration. Their tactics span MITRE techniques T1190, T1059.001, T1047, T1562.001, T1003.001, T1071.001, T1486, and more. The group’s maturation—evidenced by reflective loading and possible RaaS adoption—underscores the urgency for organizations to enforce asset inventories, least-privilege access, prompt patching (or virtual patching), multifactor authentication, sandboxed email defenses, AI/ML-driven detection, regular backups, and continuous red-team testing to thwart this active threat.
hits.title: Ransomware Spotlight: TargetCompany | Trend Micro (US)

canonical_entities: diplomatic and defense networks in Ukraine
hits.text: Secret Blizzard, the Russian FSB’s Center 16, has escalated global espionage by co-opting C2 infrastructures of at least six threat actors—including Pakistan-based Storm-0156, Hazel Sandstorm and Storm-0473—to install backdoors (CrimsonRAT, Wainscot), deploy custom payloads (TwoDash downloader, MiniPocket fetcher), a TinyTurla variant disguised as a Windows service, and the Statuezy clipboard-monitoring trojan via DLL sideloading and batch files; this cross-actor compromise secured persistent access to diplomatic and defense networks in Ukraine, Afghanistan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and GDI, and Indian military institutions, enabling exfiltration of politically sensitive intelligence and advanced research data while reducing development overhead and underscoring the need for robust supply-chain security, network segmentation and proactive vulnerability management.
hits.title: Hackers with Russian Blizzard Steal Data from Rival Networks

canonical_entities: Launch EC2 instances across regions via VPN
hits.text: Unit42’s “EleKtra-Leak” campaign, active since December 2020, uses automated scripts to clone public GitHub repos every few minutes, extract exposed AWS IAM keys within five minutes, then—if not blocked by GitHub-AWS quarantine policies—execute rapid AWS reconnaissance (DescribeRegions), create security groups, and launch hundreds of EC2 instances across regions via VPN for Monero cryptojacking, generating over 400 API calls in seven minutes. Between Aug. 30 and Oct. 6, 2023, researchers tracked 474 actor-controlled miners. The actor employs custom mining software and blocklists high-profile AWS account IDs to avoid honey traps. Leveraging the Prisma Cloud HoneyCloud project’s ephemeral key leaks and policy overrides, Unit42 obtained full visibility, informing Prisma Cloud Secrets Security, CI/CD IaC scanning, Cortex XDR, and recommendations for independent repo scanning, strict IAM policies, and continuous monitoring.
hits.title: CloudKeys in the Air: Tracking Malicious Operations of Exposed IAM Keys

hits.text: Storm-842 (Void Manticore), an Iranian MOIS-linked APT also operating as Homeland Justice in Albania and Karma in Israel, first emerged in July 2022 by crippling Albania’s e-government and border systems ahead of an MEK conference—an attack detailed in a Sept. 2022 FBI/CISA advisory—and by December 2023 had extended its destructive campaigns to Israeli infrastructure; it executes a two-stage kill chain in partnership with Scarred Manticore (OilRig/APT34), which gains initial access via web shells (reGeorge, Karma Shell), RDP and SSH-based SOCKS C2 channels, credential harvesting and environment mapping, then hands off to Void Manticore to deploy custom Windows/Linux wipers (Cl Wiper using ElRawDisk, Partition Wiper, BiBi Wiper with .BiBi extension variants) that delete files, corrupt partitions, disable recovery mechanisms and erase shadow copies, all while concurrent influence operations leak stolen data under various personas to sow distrust—mitigation requires enforcing MFA and role-based access, rigorous patch and vulnerability management, network segmentation with IDS/IPS monitoring, phishing-resistant email/web filtering, offline backups with tested recovery drills and integration of real-time threat intelligence to detect and disrupt this sophisticated blend of destructive malware and psychological warfare.
hits.title: Dark Web Profile: Storm-842 (Void Manticore) - SOCRadar® Cyber Intelligence Inc.

hits.text: McAfee researchers at RSA Conference 2019 revealed that Operation Sharpshooter—a previously disclosed December 2018 espionage campaign first observed via October 25 weaponized macro-laden Dropbox documents—actually began as early as September 2017, using embedded shellcode in Microsoft Word to deploy a modular, in-memory second-stage implant dubbed “Rising Sun.” Rising Sun, which reuses source code from the Lazarus Group’s Duuzer backdoor, performs reconnaissance, encrypts and exfiltrates system data (computer names, IP addresses, native OS details) and communicates with multiple newly identified command-and-control servers. Initially detected in 87 global organizations—50 percent in U.S. defense, nuclear, energy and financial sectors—the ongoing campaign has expanded to target financial services, government and critical infrastructure in Germany, Turkey, the U.K. and the U.S., exhibiting TTP overlaps and code reuse linking it to Lazarus operations. These findings underscore the need for strengthened macro and memory-resident malware defenses, proactive C2 infrastructure takedown efforts and enhanced attribution methodologies.
hits.title: RSAC 2019: New Operation Sharpshooter Data Reveals Higher Complexity, Scope | Threatpost

hits.text: Since its emergence in 2013, Iran-linked APT35 (aka Charming Kitten/Phosphorus) has executed a series of high-value espionage campaigns—beginning with a 2014 social-media spying operation—and continued in 2019 with spear-phishing against U.S., French and Middle East academic institutions before Microsoft’s Digital Crimes Unit seized control of 99 APT35 domains; in late 2020 the group targeted oncology, genetics and neurology researchers in Israel and the U.S. via its “BadBlood” PDF-based spear-phishing campaign, while in 2021 it chained Exchange Server flaws (ProxyShell) for network intrusion and demonstrated TTP overlaps with Momento ransomware (CVE-2021-21972 exploiter); in January 2022 it performed mass Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228) scans—over 80 percent of attempts originated in the U.S.—and later deployed a stealthy .NET-based PowerShell backdoor (“PowerLess”) that runs in-process to avoid detection, followed by Hyperscrape, a Windows .NET mailbox exfiltration tool for Outlook, Gmail and Yahoo! that quietly harvests emails once the actor possesses valid credentials or session cookies, and a companion Telegram dump utility; APT35 maintains persistence for intelligence collection or monetizes access when systems lack strategic value, underscoring the need for timely patching, multi-factor authentication and continuous monitoring.
hits.title: An In-Depth Look at APT35 aka Charming Kitten

hits.text: Since mid-2016, a cyber espionage operation dubbed Magic Hound, attributed to Iranian government–linked actors including COBALT GYPSY and showing overlaps with Rocket Kitten (Operation Saffron Rose/Ajax Security Team/Operation Woolen-Goldfish) and Newscasters (Charming Kitten/NewsBeef), has targeted energy, government and technology organizations in and tied to Saudi Arabia by distributing Word and Excel documents embedding malicious macros that launch PowerShell downloaders and droppers to deploy a custom toolkit—comprising executable and document loaders, IRC bots and the multi-platform Python-based PupyRAT—for full system access and data exfiltration; analysis by Palo Alto Networks and SecureWorks revealed domain and tool reuse with the Shamoon 2 wiper campaign, and bait lures mimicking holiday greetings, job offers and official Ministry of Health and Commerce communications, underscoring the need for enhanced macro-enablement policies, network segmentation and proactive IOC monitoring of associated domains and IRC traffic.
hits.title: Iranian hackers behind the Magic Hound campaign linked to Shamoon

retrieval_events.query: How has BladedFeline's operational approach evolved across the report timeline?

retrieved_context.text: In 2024, ESET researchers uncovered a sustained cyberespionage campaign by the Iran-aligned APT group BladedFeline—active since at least 2017 against Kurdish Regional Government (KRG) and Iraqi government officials—that leverages an evolving toolset including the Shahmaran 64-bit backdoor, two reverse tunnels (Laret and Pinar), Whisper (an Exchange-based backdoor communicating via email attachments), a malicious IIS module dubbed PrimeCache bearing code similarities to OilRig’s RDAT backdoor, and supplementary implants such as the Flog webshell and Hawking Listener. Forensic analysis revealed early indicators on KRG systems—VideoSRV reverse shell (Sept 2017) and RDAT (Jan 2018)—consistent with OilRig’s operational patterns, leading to a medium-confidence assessment that BladedFeline operates as a subgroup of OilRig alongside Lyceum. The timeline spans initial KRG compromises in 2017–2018, Shahmaran deployment against diplomatic officials in early 2023, expansion to a telecommunications provider in Uzbekistan in March 2023, and the 2024 discovery of Whisper, Laret, Pinar, and PrimeCache across KRG, GOI, and Uzbek networks. BladedFeline’s tactics—native IIS module implantation, email-based C&C, reverse tunnels, and webshell exploitation—underscore the need to monitor Exchange mailbox activity for anomalous attachments, IIS module registrations (e.g., HttpModule.pdb), port listeners, and VirusTotal submitter IDs to detect and disrupt this persistent threat targeting strategic communications, oil-related infrastructure, and diplomatic data in the Middle East.
retrieved_context.title: BladedFeline: Whispering in the dark

canonical_entities: ZIP files masquerading as legitimate updates
hits.text: Unit 42 has observed a sharp rise in post-intrusion WastedLocker ransomware attacks by the Evil Corp group—already known for Dridex—against large U.S. organizations in sectors from manufacturing to legal services, with initial compromise typically via ZIP files masquerading as legitimate updates that deploy a SocGholish JavaScript loader to profile systems and invoke PowerShell-based Cobalt Strike payloads; attackers then leverage WMI and PsExec for lateral movement, identify high-value and backup systems, elevate privileges, disable Windows Defender, delete shadow copies, install WastedLocker as a service, and encrypt files using a “.<victim_name>wasted” extension while appending ransom notes (“.<victim_name>wasted_info”) with contact addresses on ProtonMail, Airmail and others. Palo Alto Networks’ WildFire, Cortex XDR (anti-ransomware and behavioral threat protection), NGFW DNS signatures and AutoFocus tagging detect and prevent WastedLocker activity; organizations are urged to implement robust, off-site backup strategies and hardened cybersecurity controls to mitigate this high-impact targeted ransomware threat.
hits.title: Threat Assessment: WastedLocker Ransomware

canonical_entities: Remote Code Execution via ms-msdt URI in Word/RTF documents
ms-msdt URI-based RCE in Word/RTF documents
hits.text: In late May 2022, Symantec identified multiple threat actors exploiting the MSDT Follina bug (CVE-2022-30190) through ms-msdt URI-based RCE in Word/RTF documents that load a malicious HTML via Word’s remote template feature to launch msdt.exe, sdiagnhost.exe and ultimately PowerShell—bypassing the need for macros—to install a digitally signed AsyncRAT remote access Trojan that performs anti-analysis checks, collects hardware IDs, user names, execution paths and OS details, and maintains C&C communications, alongside parallel deployments of a browser infostealer targeting cookies and saved credentials in Firefox, Chrome and Edge. Symantec customers should apply Microsoft’s advisories or disable the ms-msdt handler, update Symantec Endpoint definitions (File-based-Downloader-Backdoor:Async, InfoStealer) and monitor for related IOCs to thwart these rapid, damaging campaigns.
hits.title: Attackers Exploit MSDT Follina Bug to Drop RAT, Infostealer | Symantec Enterprise Blogs

hits.text: Microsoft Threat Intelligence has observed the Russia-based SVR actor Midnight Blizzard (aka NOBELIUM, APT29/UNC2452/Cozy Bear) launch a highly targeted social-engineering campaign since at least late May 2023 by leveraging previously compromised small-business Microsoft 365 tenants to create security-themed onmicrosoft.com domains and Teams accounts that masquerade as technical-support entities; attackers then initiate Microsoft Teams chat requests to elicit approval of MFA prompts or codes via Microsoft Authenticator, enabling credential theft, access to fewer than 40 global organizations across government, NGOs, IT services, technology, manufacturing and media sectors, and subsequent post-compromise activities including data exfiltration and attempts to add managed devices via Microsoft Entra ID to bypass conditional access. Microsoft has mitigated the malicious domains, directly notified affected customers, and recommends phishing-resistant authentication, Conditional Access policies, Microsoft Teams best practices, auditing, and user education to detect and prevent unsolicited MFA requests.
hits.title: Midnight Blizzard conducts targeted social engineering over Microsoft Teams | Microsoft Security Blog

canonical_entities: enumerates SSH directories to harvest credentials
Persistence is achieved through multiple cronjobs
hits.text: Aqua Security’s Nautilus team has uncovered Hadooken, a new Linux malware targeting Oracle WebLogic servers via weak passwords. Post-compromise, attackers deploy redundant shell and Python scripts to ensure download and execution of Hadooken, which enumerates SSH directories to harvest credentials, moves laterally, and clears logs. Hadooken then drops a three-path cryptominer and a Tsunami backdoor with a randomized name, the latter reserved for potential later-stage attacks. Persistence is achieved through multiple cronjobs under varied names and frequencies stored across cron directories. The malware is hosted on two IPs—one German address linked to TeamTNT and Gang 8220, the other inactive in Russia—where researchers also identified a Mallox ransomware PowerShell loader targeting Windows. Static analysis links Hadooken to Rhombus and NoEscape families. With over 230,000 internet-connected WebLogic instances—hundreds of which expose vulnerable admin consoles—this campaign underscores the dual risk of cryptojacking and ransomware across Linux and Windows environments.
hits.title: New 'Hadooken' Linux Malware Targets WebLogic Servers - SecurityWeek

hits.text: In early April, Palo Alto Networks’ Advanced WildFire and Cortex XDR uncovered SnipBot—a new v5.0 iteration of the RomCom RAT family—employing advanced window message–based control-flow obfuscation and anti-sandbox checks (filename hash and HKCU\…\RecentDocs entries) in a multi-stage chain beginning with a PDF-labeled EXE downloader signed using a likely stolen certificate; the downloader contacts xeontime[.]com for config-pdf.dll, which uses registry-based COM hijacking to load keyprov.dll from drvmcprotect[.]com into explorer.exe, decrypts payloads stored in HKCU\Software\AppDataSoft\Software, and opens a TCP listener on port 1342 for commands to update, delete, or execute modules. The main backdoor single.dll (mutex “SnipMutex”) supports 27 encrypted commands for drive and process enumeration, file upload/download, and remote module execution, facilitating network pivoting and targeted file exfiltration. retrieved_context.text: In 2024, ESET researchers uncovered a sustained cyberespionage campaign by the Iran-aligned APT group BladedFeline—active since at least 2017 against Kurdish Regional Government (KRG) and Iraqi government officials—that leverages an evolving toolset including the Shahmaran 64-bit backdoor, two reverse tunnels (Laret and Pinar), Whisper (an Exchange-based backdoor communicating via email attachments), a malicious IIS module dubbed PrimeCache bearing code similarities to OilRig’s RDAT backdoor, and supplementary implants such as the Flog webshell and Hawking Listener. Forensic analysis revealed early indicators on KRG systems—VideoSRV reverse shell (Sept 2017) and RDAT (Jan 2018)—consistent with OilRig’s operational patterns, leading to a medium-confidence assessment that BladedFeline operates as a subgroup of OilRig alongside Lyceum. The timeline spans initial KRG compromises in 2017–2018, Shahmaran deployment against diplomatic officials in early 2023, expansion to a telecommunications provider in Uzbekistan in March 2023, and the 2024 discovery of Whisper, Laret, Pinar, and PrimeCache across KRG, GOI, and Uzbek networks. BladedFeline’s tactics—native IIS module implantation, email-based C&C, reverse tunnels, and webshell exploitation—underscore the need to monitor Exchange mailbox activity for anomalous attachments, IIS module registrations (e.g., HttpModule.pdb), port listeners, and VirusTotal submitter IDs to detect and disrupt this persistent threat targeting strategic communications, oil-related infrastructure, and diplomatic data in the Middle East.
retrieved_context.title: BladedFeline: Whispering in the dark

retrieved_context.text: Since September 2017, the Iran-aligned BladedFeline subcluster of the OilRig APT has executed persistent cyber espionage against Kurdish and Iraqi government entities, initially compromising KRG systems and a regional Uzbekistan telecom provider via an internet-facing application vulnerability and social engineering to deploy the Flog web shell. ESET’s Q4 2023–Q1 2024 report documents the group’s evolving malware arsenal: the Shahmaran backdoor for remote file manipulation, the C#/.NET Whisper (aka Veaty) email-based implant, the DNS-tunneling Spearal and its optimized variant, Optimizer, the Slippery Snakelet Python implant for command execution and data exfiltration, and tunneling tools Laret and Pinar. BladedFeline leverages a malicious IIS module, PrimeCache—akin to OilRig’s RDAT—and the Hawking Listener early-stage implant to maintain stealthy access, systematically harvesting diplomatic and financial intelligence tied to KRG oil reserves and Western relations to further Iranian strategic objectives.
retrieved_context.title: Iran-Linked BladedFeline Hits Iraqi and Kurdish Targets with Whisper and Spearal Malware

canonical_entities: Launch EC2 instances across regions via VPN
retrieved_context.text: Unit42’s “EleKtra-Leak” campaign, active since December 2020, uses automated scripts to clone public GitHub repos every few minutes, extract exposed AWS IAM keys within five minutes, then—if not blocked by GitHub-AWS quarantine policies—execute rapid AWS reconnaissance (DescribeRegions), create security groups, and launch hundreds of EC2 instances across regions via VPN for Monero cryptojacking, generating over 400 API calls in seven minutes. Between Aug. 30 and Oct. 6, 2023, researchers tracked 474 actor-controlled miners. The actor employs custom mining software and blocklists high-profile AWS account IDs to avoid honey traps. Leveraging the Prisma Cloud HoneyCloud project’s ephemeral key leaks and policy overrides, Unit42 obtained full visibility, informing Prisma Cloud Secrets Security, CI/CD IaC scanning, Cortex XDR, and recommendations for independent repo scanning, strict IAM policies, and continuous monitoring.
retrieved_context.title: CloudKeys in the Air: Tracking Malicious Operations of Exposed IAM Keys

canonical_entities: ZIP files masquerading as legitimate updates
retrieved_context.text: Unit 42 has observed a sharp rise in post-intrusion WastedLocker ransomware attacks by the Evil Corp group—already known for Dridex—against large U.S. organizations in sectors from manufacturing to legal services, with initial compromise typically via ZIP files masquerading as legitimate updates that deploy a SocGholish JavaScript loader to profile systems and invoke PowerShell-based Cobalt Strike payloads; attackers then leverage WMI and PsExec for lateral movement, identify high-value and backup systems, elevate privileges, disable Windows Defender, delete shadow copies, install WastedLocker as a service, and encrypt files using a “.<victim_name>wasted” extension while appending ransom notes (“.<victim_name>wasted_info”) with contact addresses on ProtonMail, Airmail and others. Palo Alto Networks’ WildFire, Cortex XDR (anti-ransomware and behavioral threat protection), NGFW DNS signatures and AutoFocus tagging detect and prevent WastedLocker activity; organizations are urged to implement robust, off-site backup strategies and hardened cybersecurity controls to mitigate this high-impact targeted ransomware threat.
retrieved_context.title: Threat Assessment: WastedLocker Ransomware

canonical_entities: Remote Code Execution via ms-msdt URI in Word/RTF documents
ms-msdt URI-based RCE in Word/RTF documents
retrieved_context.text: In late May 2022, Symantec identified multiple threat actors exploiting the MSDT Follina bug (CVE-2022-30190) through ms-msdt URI-based RCE in Word/RTF documents that load a malicious HTML via Word’s remote template feature to launch msdt.exe, sdiagnhost.exe and ultimately PowerShell—bypassing the need for macros—to install a digitally signed AsyncRAT remote access Trojan that performs anti-analysis checks, collects hardware IDs, user names, execution paths and OS details, and maintains C&C communications, alongside parallel deployments of a browser infostealer targeting cookies and saved credentials in Firefox, Chrome and Edge. Symantec customers should apply Microsoft’s advisories or disable the ms-msdt handler, update Symantec Endpoint definitions (File-based-Downloader-Backdoor:Async, InfoStealer) and monitor for related IOCs to thwart these rapid, damaging campaigns.
retrieved_context.title: Attackers Exploit MSDT Follina Bug to Drop RAT, Infostealer | Symantec Enterprise Blogs

retrieved_context.text: Microsoft Threat Intelligence has observed the Russia-based SVR actor Midnight Blizzard (aka NOBELIUM, APT29/UNC2452/Cozy Bear) launch a highly targeted social-engineering campaign since at least late May 2023 by leveraging previously compromised small-business Microsoft 365 tenants to create security-themed onmicrosoft.com domains and Teams accounts that masquerade as technical-support entities; attackers then initiate Microsoft Teams chat requests to elicit approval of MFA prompts or codes via Microsoft Authenticator, enabling credential theft, access to fewer than 40 global organizations across government, NGOs, IT services, technology, manufacturing and media sectors, and subsequent post-compromise activities including data exfiltration and attempts to add managed devices via Microsoft Entra ID to bypass conditional access. Microsoft has mitigated the malicious domains, directly notified affected customers, and recommends phishing-resistant authentication, Conditional Access policies, Microsoft Teams best practices, auditing, and user education to detect and prevent unsolicited MFA requests.
retrieved_context.title: Midnight Blizzard conducts targeted social engineering over Microsoft Teams | Microsoft Security Blog

canonical_entities: enumerates SSH directories to harvest credentials
Persistence is achieved through multiple cronjobs
retrieved_context.text: Aqua Security’s Nautilus team has uncovered Hadooken, a new Linux malware targeting Oracle WebLogic servers via weak passwords. Post-compromise, attackers deploy redundant shell and Python scripts to ensure download and execution of Hadooken, which enumerates SSH directories to harvest credentials, moves laterally, and clears logs. Hadooken then drops a three-path cryptominer and a Tsunami backdoor with a randomized name, the latter reserved for potential later-stage attacks. Persistence is achieved through multiple cronjobs under varied names and frequencies stored across cron directories. The malware is hosted on two IPs—one German address linked to TeamTNT and Gang 8220, the other inactive in Russia—where researchers also identified a Mallox ransomware PowerShell loader targeting Windows. Static analysis links Hadooken to Rhombus and NoEscape families. With over 230,000 internet-connected WebLogic instances—hundreds of which expose vulnerable admin consoles—this campaign underscores the dual risk of cryptojacking and ransomware across Linux and Windows environments.
retrieved_context.title: New 'Hadooken' Linux Malware Targets WebLogic Servers - SecurityWeek

hits.text: Moses Staff, also dubbed Cobalt Sapling, is an Iran-linked APT active since November 2020 and publicly identified in September 2021, originally posting 16 leak events of Israeli corporate data and personal information of IDF intelligence personnel by December 2022 using a toolkit comprising the PyDCrypt custom loader, DCSrv cryptographic wiper, StrifeWater RAT and its DriveGuard monitoring utility; in November 2022, Secureworks attributed a new hacktivist persona, Abraham’s Ax—featuring similar biblical branding, Tor-hosted leak sites on adjacent subnets and recycled “Hollywood-style” hacking videos—to the same operators, who have since shifted toward exfiltrating and leaking data from Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of the Interior (including a purported intercepted ministerial phone conversation) rather than directly attacking Israel, likely in response to Saudi-Israeli rapprochement, while Moses Staff continues operations (claiming a CCTV system hack at an Israeli terror site); these insights highlight the urgency for Saudi and Israeli government entities to strengthen network segmentation, deploy advanced endpoint detection for known Iranian toolsets, monitor darknet leak platforms and prepare incident response plans tailored to politically motivated exfiltration campaigns.

hits.text: Microsoft has traced a stealthy espionage campaign by Flax Typhoon (aka Ethereal Panda), a China-based nation-state actor active since mid-2021, targeting dozens of Taiwanese organizations (with spill-over in Southeast Asia, North America, and Africa) by exploiting known vulnerabilities in public-facing VPN, web, Java, and SQL services to deploy the China Chopper web shell for initial access; the group escalates privileges via open-source exploits like Juicy Potato and BadPotato, then establishes persistence by disabling RDP network-level authentication, hijacking the Sticky Keys (sethc.exe) binary to launch Task Manager as SYSTEM, and installing a renamed SoftEther VPN-over-HTTPS bridge (conhost.exe/dllhost.exe) as a service to maintain covert C2 over port 443; leveraging LOLBins such as PowerShell Invoke-WebRequest, certutil, bitsadmin, WinRM, and WMIC for lateral movement, vulnerability scanning, and remote execution, it harvests credentials from LSASS memory and the SAM registry hive using Mimikatz for pass-the-hash attacks; although no exfiltration or final objectives have been observed, organizations are urged to enforce rigorous patch and vulnerability management on internet-exposed systems, monitor registry and file-integrity changes, deploy web application firewalls, reset compromised credentials, isolate and forensically examine affected hosts, and leverage detections in Microsoft 365 Defender to disrupt living-off-the-land tactics.
hits.title: Flax Typhoon using legitimate software to quietly access Taiwanese organizations | Microsoft Security Blog

hits.text: ESET researchers have identified SwiftSlicer, a new Go-written destructive wiper attributed to the Sandworm APT, on a Ukrainian organization’s network on January 25 via malicious Group Policy, indicating full Active Directory compromise; detected as WinGo/KillFiles, SwiftSlicer deletes shadow copies and recursively overwrites files in %CSIDL_SYSTEM%\drivers, %CSIDL_SYSTEM_DRIVE%\Windows\NTDS and other drives with 4,096-byte random blocks before forcing a reboot. This deployment method mirrors earlier HermeticWiper and CaddyWiper attacks—CaddyWiper was used against Ukrinform—and follows a wave of RansomBoggs ransomware linked to Sandworm two months prior. Sandworm’s near-decade track record of disruptive campaigns against Ukrainian critical infrastructure includes BlackEnergy, GreyEnergy, the original Industroyer, and a thwarted Industroyer2 in April, underscoring the imperative to harden Active Directory, monitor Group Policy changes, and maintain secure, offline backups.
hits.title: SwiftSlicer: New destructive wiper malware strikes Ukraine

hits.text: Since mid-2016, an Iran-linked espionage operation dubbed “Magic Hound” has targeted energy, government and technology organizations in and around Saudi Arabia using macro-enabled Word and Excel documents masquerading as holiday cards, job offers and official Ministry of Health and Commerce files to launch PowerShell-based downloaders and custom droppers, executable and document loaders and IRC bots that ultimately deploy a Python-based Pupy RAT; Palo Alto Networks analysts—citing overlaps in domains and initial breach methods with the recent Shamoon 2 campaign—have linked Magic Hound to the Iran-aligned Rocket Kitten group, while SecureWorks attributes it to COBALT GYPSY and IBM X-Force has observed shared infrastructure, and additional code similarities tie an IRC bot to Charming Kitten/Newscaster activity and to MacDownloader tools used by other Iranian actors, underscoring the need to block malicious macros, monitor PowerShell and IRC traffic for known C2 signatures, and flag Pupy-related domains and custom loader behaviors to disrupt long-running cross-platform intrusion operations.
hits.title: Iranian Spies Target Saudi Arabia in "Magic Hound" Attacks

canonical_entities: diplomatic and defense networks in Ukraine
hits.text: Secret Blizzard, the Russian FSB’s Center 16, has escalated global espionage by co-opting C2 infrastructures of at least six threat actors—including Pakistan-based Storm-0156, Hazel Sandstorm and Storm-0473—to install backdoors (CrimsonRAT, Wainscot), deploy custom payloads (TwoDash downloader, MiniPocket fetcher), a TinyTurla variant disguised as a Windows service, and the Statuezy clipboard-monitoring trojan via DLL sideloading and batch files; this cross-actor compromise secured persistent access to diplomatic and defense networks in Ukraine, Afghanistan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and GDI, and Indian military institutions, enabling exfiltration of politically sensitive intelligence and advanced research data while reducing development overhead and underscoring the need for robust supply-chain security, network segmentation and proactive vulnerability management.
hits.title: Hackers with Russian Blizzard Steal Data from Rival Networks

hits.text: Since at least April 2024 Microsoft Threat Intelligence has tracked a Russia-affiliated cyberespionage actor dubbed Void Blizzard (aka LAUNDRY BEAR) conducting high-volume, targeted operations against government, defense, transportation, media, NGO and healthcare organizations—particularly in NATO member states and Ukraine—by leveraging stolen credentials procured via commodity infostealer ecosystems for password spray attacks and Exchange/SharePoint Online access, then automating bulk email and file collection (and in some cases Teams messages) via cloud APIs and tools like AzureHound; in April 2025 the actor evolved to adversary-in-the-middle spear phishing using a typosquatted domain and the open-source Evilginx framework with a malicious QR-coded PDF to harvest Entra authentication data; this widespread success underscores that even unsophisticated TTPs pose major intelligence risks to critical sectors, so organizations should enforce sign-in risk policies and phishing-resistant MFA (e.g., FIDO/passkeys), centralize identity management with Conditional Access, monitor risky sign-ins and mailbox auditing, apply least-privilege credential hygiene, and promptly rotate credentials after infostealer detections to disrupt Void Blizzard’s operations.
hits.title: New Russia-affiliated actor Void Blizzard targets critical sectors for espionage | Microsoft Security Blog

hits.text: In August 2025 Microsoft Threat Intelligence revealed that Storm-2460, associated with the Play ransomware group, has resumed exploiting CVE-2025-29824—a zero-day elevation-of-privilege flaw in the Windows Common Log File System patched in April—to gain SYSTEM privileges on unpatched hosts across IT, financial and real estate organizations in the US, Europe, South America and the Middle East. The campaign begins with an in-memory dropper masquerading as the open-source ChatGPT Desktop app that decrypts and launches PipeMagic, a modular backdoor first observed in December 2022 and now updated with persistence and lateral-movement enhancements targeting Saudi Arabian and Brazilian manufacturing entities. PipeMagic communicates with its TCP C2 over a named pipe, self-updates by storing distinct payload modules in memory via doubly linked lists for staging, execution and communication (plus an additional dynamic list), then leverages the CLFS exploit to escalate privileges before deploying Play ransomware. Although the campaign’s footprint remains limited, the combination of a zero-day exploit and a sophisticated modular backdoor underscores a heightened risk; organizations are urged to immediately apply the April patch for CVE-2025-29824, enable tamper and network protection in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, run EDR in block mode, enforce full automated investigation and remediation, and leverage cloud-delivered machine-learning protections to block novel variants.
hits.title: PipeMagic Backdoor Resurfaces as Part of Play Ransomware Attack Chain

retrieved_context.text: Microsoft has traced a stealthy espionage campaign by Flax Typhoon (aka Ethereal Panda), a China-based nation-state actor active since mid-2021, targeting dozens of Taiwanese organizations (with spill-over in Southeast Asia, North America, and Africa) by exploiting known vulnerabilities in public-facing VPN, web, Java, and SQL services to deploy the China Chopper web shell for initial access; the group escalates privileges via open-source exploits like Juicy Potato and BadPotato, then establishes persistence by disabling RDP network-level authentication, hijacking the Sticky Keys (sethc.exe) binary to launch Task Manager as SYSTEM, and installing a renamed SoftEther VPN-over-HTTPS bridge (conhost.exe/dllhost.exe) as a service to maintain covert C2 over port 443; leveraging LOLBins such as PowerShell Invoke-WebRequest, certutil, bitsadmin, WinRM, and WMIC for lateral movement, vulnerability scanning, and remote execution, it harvests credentials from LSASS memory and the SAM registry hive using Mimikatz for pass-the-hash attacks; although no exfiltration or final objectives have been observed, organizations are urged to enforce rigorous patch and vulnerability management on internet-exposed systems, monitor registry and file-integrity changes, deploy web application firewalls, reset compromised credentials, isolate and forensically examine affected hosts, and leverage detections in Microsoft 365 Defender to disrupt living-off-the-land tactics.
retrieved_context.title: Flax Typhoon using legitimate software to quietly access Taiwanese organizations | Microsoft Security Blog

retrieved_context.text: ESET researchers have identified SwiftSlicer, a new Go-written destructive wiper attributed to the Sandworm APT, on a Ukrainian organization’s network on January 25 via malicious Group Policy, indicating full Active Directory compromise; detected as WinGo/KillFiles, SwiftSlicer deletes shadow copies and recursively overwrites files in %CSIDL_SYSTEM%\drivers, %CSIDL_SYSTEM_DRIVE%\Windows\NTDS and other drives with 4,096-byte random blocks before forcing a reboot. This deployment method mirrors earlier HermeticWiper and CaddyWiper attacks—CaddyWiper was used against Ukrinform—and follows a wave of RansomBoggs ransomware linked to Sandworm two months prior. Sandworm’s near-decade track record of disruptive campaigns against Ukrainian critical infrastructure includes BlackEnergy, GreyEnergy, the original Industroyer, and a thwarted Industroyer2 in April, underscoring the imperative to harden Active Directory, monitor Group Policy changes, and maintain secure, offline backups.
retrieved_context.title: SwiftSlicer: New destructive wiper malware strikes Ukraine

retrieved_context.text: Since mid-2016, an Iran-linked espionage operation dubbed “Magic Hound” has targeted energy, government and technology organizations in and around Saudi Arabia using macro-enabled Word and Excel documents masquerading as holiday cards, job offers and official Ministry of Health and Commerce files to launch PowerShell-based downloaders and custom droppers, executable and document loaders and IRC bots that ultimately deploy a Python-based Pupy RAT; Palo Alto Networks analysts—citing overlaps in domains and initial breach methods with the recent Shamoon 2 campaign—have linked Magic Hound to the Iran-aligned Rocket Kitten group, while SecureWorks attributes it to COBALT GYPSY and IBM X-Force has observed shared infrastructure, and additional code similarities tie an IRC bot to Charming Kitten/Newscaster activity and to MacDownloader tools used by other Iranian actors, underscoring the need to block malicious macros, monitor PowerShell and IRC traffic for known C2 signatures, and flag Pupy-related domains and custom loader behaviors to disrupt long-running cross-platform intrusion operations.
retrieved_context.title: Iranian Spies Target Saudi Arabia in "Magic Hound" Attacks

canonical_entities: diplomatic and defense networks in Ukraine
retrieved_context.text: Secret Blizzard, the Russian FSB’s Center 16, has escalated global espionage by co-opting C2 infrastructures of at least six threat actors—including Pakistan-based Storm-0156, Hazel Sandstorm and Storm-0473—to install backdoors (CrimsonRAT, Wainscot), deploy custom payloads (TwoDash downloader, MiniPocket fetcher), a TinyTurla variant disguised as a Windows service, and the Statuezy clipboard-monitoring trojan via DLL sideloading and batch files; this cross-actor compromise secured persistent access to diplomatic and defense networks in Ukraine, Afghanistan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and GDI, and Indian military institutions, enabling exfiltration of politically sensitive intelligence and advanced research data while reducing development overhead and underscoring the need for robust supply-chain security, network segmentation and proactive vulnerability management.
retrieved_context.title: Hackers with Russian Blizzard Steal Data from Rival Networks

retrieved_context.text: Since at least April 2024 Microsoft Threat Intelligence has tracked a Russia-affiliated cyberespionage actor dubbed Void Blizzard (aka LAUNDRY BEAR) conducting high-volume, targeted operations against government, defense, transportation, media, NGO and healthcare organizations—particularly in NATO member states and Ukraine—by leveraging stolen credentials procured via commodity infostealer ecosystems for password spray attacks and Exchange/SharePoint Online access, then automating bulk email and file collection (and in some cases Teams messages) via cloud APIs and tools like AzureHound; in April 2025 the actor evolved to adversary-in-the-middle spear phishing using a typosquatted domain and the open-source Evilginx framework with a malicious QR-coded PDF to harvest Entra authentication data; this widespread success underscores that even unsophisticated TTPs pose major intelligence risks to critical sectors, so organizations should enforce sign-in risk policies and phishing-resistant MFA (e.g., FIDO/passkeys), centralize identity management with Conditional Access, monitor risky sign-ins and mailbox auditing, apply least-privilege credential hygiene, and promptly rotate credentials after infostealer detections to disrupt Void Blizzard’s operations.
retrieved_context.title: New Russia-affiliated actor Void Blizzard targets critical sectors for espionage | Microsoft Security Blog

retrieved_context.text: In August 2025 Microsoft Threat Intelligence revealed that Storm-2460, associated with the Play ransomware group, has resumed exploiting CVE-2025-29824—a zero-day elevation-of-privilege flaw in the Windows Common Log File System patched in April—to gain SYSTEM privileges on unpatched hosts across IT, financial and real estate organizations in the US, Europe, South America and the Middle East. The campaign begins with an in-memory dropper masquerading as the open-source ChatGPT Desktop app that decrypts and launches PipeMagic, a modular backdoor first observed in December 2022 and now updated with persistence and lateral-movement enhancements targeting Saudi Arabian and Brazilian manufacturing entities. PipeMagic communicates with its TCP C2 over a named pipe, self-updates by storing distinct payload modules in memory via doubly linked lists for staging, execution and communication (plus an additional dynamic list), then leverages the CLFS exploit to escalate privileges before deploying Play ransomware. Although the campaign’s footprint remains limited, the combination of a zero-day exploit and a sophisticated modular backdoor underscores a heightened risk; organizations are urged to immediately apply the April patch for CVE-2025-29824, enable tamper and network protection in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, run EDR in block mode, enforce full automated investigation and remediation, and leverage cloud-delivered machine-learning protections to block novel variants.
retrieved_context.title: PipeMagic Backdoor Resurfaces as Part of Play Ransomware Attack Chain

hits.text: In 2024, ESET researchers uncovered a sustained cyberespionage campaign by the Iran-aligned APT group BladedFeline—active since at least 2017 against Kurdish Regional Government (KRG) and Iraqi government officials—that leverages an evolving toolset including the Shahmaran 64-bit backdoor, two reverse tunnels (Laret and Pinar), Whisper (an Exchange-based backdoor communicating via email attachments), a malicious IIS module dubbed PrimeCache bearing code similarities to OilRig’s RDAT backdoor, and supplementary implants such as the Flog webshell and Hawking Listener. Forensic analysis revealed early indicators on KRG systems—VideoSRV reverse shell (Sept 2017) and RDAT (Jan 2018)—consistent with OilRig’s operational patterns, leading to a medium-confidence assessment that BladedFeline operates as a subgroup of OilRig alongside Lyceum. The timeline spans initial KRG compromises in 2017–2018, Shahmaran deployment against diplomatic officials in early 2023, expansion to a telecommunications provider in Uzbekistan in March 2023, and the 2024 discovery of Whisper, Laret, Pinar, and PrimeCache across KRG, GOI, and Uzbek networks. BladedFeline’s tactics—native IIS module implantation, email-based C&C, reverse tunnels, and webshell exploitation—underscore the need to monitor Exchange mailbox activity for anomalous attachments, IIS module registrations (e.g., HttpModule.pdb), port listeners, and VirusTotal submitter IDs to detect and disrupt this persistent threat targeting strategic communications, oil-related infrastructure, and diplomatic data in the Middle East.
hits.title: BladedFeline: Whispering in the dark

hits.text: Since September 2017, the Iran-aligned BladedFeline subcluster of the OilRig APT has executed persistent cyber espionage against Kurdish and Iraqi government entities, initially compromising KRG systems and a regional Uzbekistan telecom provider via an internet-facing application vulnerability and social engineering to deploy the Flog web shell. ESET’s Q4 2023–Q1 2024 report documents the group’s evolving malware arsenal: the Shahmaran backdoor for remote file manipulation, the C#/.NET Whisper (aka Veaty) email-based implant, the DNS-tunneling Spearal and its optimized variant, Optimizer, the Slippery Snakelet Python implant for command execution and data exfiltration, and tunneling tools Laret and Pinar. BladedFeline leverages a malicious IIS module, PrimeCache—akin to OilRig’s RDAT—and the Hawking Listener early-stage implant to maintain stealthy access, systematically harvesting diplomatic and financial intelligence tied to KRG oil reserves and Western relations to further Iranian strategic objectives.
hits.title: Iran-Linked BladedFeline Hits Iraqi and Kurdish Targets with Whisper and Spearal Malware

canonical_entities: Bypass authentication by sending empty or invalid USERNAME and PASSWORD parameters with requirePasswordChange=Y
hits.text: A critical zero-day flaw (CVE-2023-51467) has been identified in Apache OfBiz’s login functionality—stemming from an incomplete patch for a prior high-severity RCE vulnerability (CVE-2023-49070, CVSS 9.8) tied to a deprecated XML-RPC component—that allows attackers to bypass authentication by sending empty or invalid USERNAME and PASSWORD parameters alongside “requirePasswordChange=Y,” effectively granting unauthorized access and enabling simple SSRF attacks against internal resources; discovered by SonicWall Capture Labs, the bug follows observations by The Shadowserver Foundation of active exploitation attempts against CVE-2023-49070, and SonicWall reports exploit traffic for CVE-2023-51467 spiking from 235 attempts on December 27, 2023, to 26,928 on December 29 and 3,129 on January 1, 2024, underscoring urgent need for organizations using OfBiz versions prior to 18.12.11 to upgrade immediately to mitigate further data exfiltration and system takeover risks.
hits.title: Critical Zero-Day in Apache OfBiz ERP System Exposes Businesses to Attack

hits.text: Storm-842 (Void Manticore), an Iranian MOIS-linked APT also operating as Homeland Justice in Albania and Karma in Israel, first emerged in July 2022 by crippling Albania’s e-government and border systems ahead of an MEK conference—an attack detailed in a Sept. 2022 FBI/CISA advisory—and by December 2023 had extended its destructive campaigns to Israeli infrastructure; it executes a two-stage kill chain in partnership with Scarred Manticore (OilRig/APT34), which gains initial access via web shells (reGeorge, Karma Shell), RDP and SSH-based SOCKS C2 channels, credential harvesting and environment mapping, then hands off to Void Manticore to deploy custom Windows/Linux wipers (Cl Wiper using ElRawDisk, Partition Wiper, BiBi Wiper with .BiBi extension variants) that delete files, corrupt partitions, disable recovery mechanisms and erase shadow copies, all while concurrent influence operations leak stolen data under various personas to sow distrust—mitigation requires enforcing MFA and role-based access, rigorous patch and vulnerability management, network segmentation with IDS/IPS monitoring, phishing-resistant email/web filtering, offline backups with tested recovery drills and integration of real-time threat intelligence to detect and disrupt this sophisticated blend of destructive malware and psychological warfare.
hits.title: Dark Web Profile: Storm-842 (Void Manticore) - SOCRadar® Cyber Intelligence Inc.

canonical_entities: Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Tools
OS Credential Dumping: Security Account Manager
hits.text: Water Ouroboros is a Ransomware-as-a-Service operation that exploits public-facing Oracle WebLogic vulnerabilities (CVE-2019-2725, CVE-2017-10271, CVE-2019-2729) or drive-by installers for initial access (T1190, T1189), then executes remote Windows commands (wmic.exe, bcdedit.exe, wbadmin.exe, vssadmin.exe) to delete backups and disable recovery (T1490, T1562.001) before encrypting fixed, removable and network drives via a Go-based custom routine that uses RTLGenRandom to generate a symmetric key, protects it with embedded RSA public keys (App_ExportKey), appends “.locked” (unless suppressed with –E), excludes over 60 file extensions, and accepts credentials (c {user}:{pass}), logging (–a), non-aggressive (–A) and size filters (–m). Victims find Contact Us.txt ransom notes pointing to a TOR payment site and Hive Leaks data-dump threat. Post-infection, actors maintain access via compromised admin accounts (T1078), disable security tools (PCHunter, ProcessHacker), dump credentials from registry hives (T1003.002), move laterally over RDP/SMB (T1021.001/002), discover assets via AdFind (T1595.002) and exfiltrate data over C&C (SharpRhino RAT/T1071.001, T1041). With 136 incidents in the US and notable impacts on construction, IT, manufacturing and healthcare SMBs, the campaign underscores the need for timely patching, hardened public-facing apps, least-privilege access, MFA, robust backups and advanced threat detection.
hits.title: Ransomware Spotlight: Water Ouroboros | Trend Micro (US)

canonical_entities: Scanning the Internet for IoT devices with open Telnet/SSH ports
Use of default or weak credentials
Encrypted SOCKS5 tunneling to proxy infrastructure
hits.text: Researchers have uncovered that since early 2024 a previously undocumented botnet, dubbed Ngioweb, has been systematically scanning the Internet for IoT devices—primarily DVRs, IP cameras and home routers—with open Telnet/SSH ports and default or weak credentials, exploiting known firmware vulnerabilities to deploy a lightweight Go-based loader that establishes encrypted SOCKS5 tunnels back to a resilient NSOCKS residential proxy network of over 150,000 infected nodes. Once a device is compromised, Ngioweb drops a persistent agent that connects to fast-flux C2 domains via HTTPS, retrieves updated encryption keys and proxy configuration, and registers the node for NSOCKS’ tiered subscription service (starting at $25/month), which reportedly generates upwards of $500K in monthly revenue by fueling large-scale credential-stuffing campaigns, ad fraud and DDoS-for-hire operations. The actors behind Ngioweb continually rotate fallback C2 domains, employ encryption and obfuscation to evade signature-based detection, and monitor infection success rates in real time, enabling rapid retooling and expansion. Defenders are urged to enforce strong, unique credentials on all IoT assets, disable unused management interfaces, apply timely firmware updates, implement network segmentation and deploy behavioral analytics or honeypots to detect anomalous outbound proxy traffic.
hits.title: Ngioweb Botnet Fuels NSOCKS Residential Proxy Network Exploiting IoT Devices

hits.text: Microsoft Threat Intelligence has observed the Russia-based SVR actor Midnight Blizzard (aka NOBELIUM, APT29/UNC2452/Cozy Bear) launch a highly targeted social-engineering campaign since at least late May 2023 by leveraging previously compromised small-business Microsoft 365 tenants to create security-themed onmicrosoft.com domains and Teams accounts that masquerade as technical-support entities; attackers then initiate Microsoft Teams chat requests to elicit approval of MFA prompts or codes via Microsoft Authenticator, enabling credential theft, access to fewer than 40 global organizations across government, NGOs, IT services, technology, manufacturing and media sectors, and subsequent post-compromise activities including data exfiltration and attempts to add managed devices via Microsoft Entra ID to bypass conditional access. Microsoft has mitigated the malicious domains, directly notified affected customers, and recommends phishing-resistant authentication, Conditional Access policies, Microsoft Teams best practices, auditing, and user education to detect and prevent unsolicited MFA requests.
hits.title: Midnight Blizzard conducts targeted social engineering over Microsoft Teams | Microsoft Security Blog

hits.text: In August 2025 the FBI issued a public service announcement that FSB-linked Berserk Bear (aka Blue Kraken, Crouching Yeti, Dragonfly, Koala Team) has been exploiting the seven-year-old Cisco IOS/IOS XE Smart Install remote code execution/DoS vulnerability (CVE-2018-0171) to compromise critical infrastructure worldwide. Since Cisco first detected opportunistic attacks in November 2021, the group has collected configuration files from thousands of unpatched devices associated with U.S. critical infrastructure sectors, covertly modified those configs to maintain persistent unauthorized access, and conducted network reconnaissance targeting ICS-related protocols and applications. Cisco Talos reports that the campaign, referred to as Static Tundra, has aggressively hit telecommunications, higher education, and manufacturing networks across North America, Asia, Africa, and Europe, deploying custom SNMP tools and the SYNful Knock firmware implant—originally identified by FireEye in 2015—to evade detection and embed for years. The FBI’s warning underscores the urgent need for organizations to patch CVE-2018-0171, disable Smart Install, and implement comprehensive hardening, as other state-sponsored actors are likely conducting similar network device compromise campaigns.
hits.title: FBI warns of Russian hackers exploiting 7-year-old Cisco flaw

hits.text: McAfee researchers at RSA Conference 2019 revealed that Operation Sharpshooter—a previously disclosed December 2018 espionage campaign first observed via October 25 weaponized macro-laden Dropbox documents—actually began as early as September 2017, using embedded shellcode in Microsoft Word to deploy a modular, in-memory second-stage implant dubbed “Rising Sun.” Rising Sun, which reuses source code from the Lazarus Group’s Duuzer backdoor, performs reconnaissance, encrypts and exfiltrates system data (computer names, IP addresses, native OS details) and communicates with multiple newly identified command-and-control servers. Initially detected in 87 global organizations—50 percent in U.S. defense, nuclear, energy and financial sectors—the ongoing campaign has expanded to target financial services, government and critical infrastructure in Germany, Turkey, the U.K. and the U.S., exhibiting TTP overlaps and code reuse linking it to Lazarus operations. These findings underscore the need for strengthened macro and memory-resident malware defenses, proactive C2 infrastructure takedown efforts and enhanced attribution methodologies.
hits.title: RSAC 2019: New Operation Sharpshooter Data Reveals Higher Complexity, Scope | Threatpost

retrieved_context.text: McAfee researchers at RSA Conference 2019 revealed that Operation Sharpshooter—a previously disclosed December 2018 espionage campaign first observed via October 25 weaponized macro-laden Dropbox documents—actually began as early as September 2017, using embedded shellcode in Microsoft Word to deploy a modular, in-memory second-stage implant dubbed “Rising Sun.” Rising Sun, which reuses source code from the Lazarus Group’s Duuzer backdoor, performs reconnaissance, encrypts and exfiltrates system data (computer names, IP addresses, native OS details) and communicates with multiple newly identified command-and-control servers. These findings underscore the need for strengthened macro and memory-resident malware defenses, proactive C2 infrastructure takedown efforts and enhanced attribution methodologies.
retrieved_context.title: RSAC 2019: New Operation Sharpshooter Data Reveals Higher Complexity, Scope | Threatpost

hits.text: RansomHub, first reported in February 2024 and linked to the Knight ransomware family, gains initial access through spear-phishing voice scams with convincing American-accent callers and compromised VPN credentials, then leverages PsExec, PowerShell and Python scripts to harvest credentials (Mimikatz, LaZagne, SecretServerSecretStealer), discover remote systems, establish SSH sessions and exploit CVE-2023-27532 in Veeam Backup & Replication to dump database credentials. hits.text: Trend Micro analysts uncovered in December 2023 a new ransomware strain dubbed Kasseika—likely developed by former BlackMatter affiliates or buyers of its source code—that employs a Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver (BYOVD) attack by abusing TG Soft’s Martini driver (Martini.sys/viragt64.sys) to disable antivirus and security tools before encryption. hits.text: Avast researchers uncovered that North Korea’s Lazarus group leveraged a Windows zero-day privilege escalation flaw in Microsoft’s AppLocker “appid.sys” driver (CVE-2024-21338) to execute a truly fileless kernel attack during 2023 intrusions, sending a proof-of-concept exploit to Microsoft in August and prompting a February 2024 patch and subsequent advisory update once active exploitation was confirmed; by abusing a ubiquitous signed driver rather than importing custom code (BYOVD), Lazarus gained kernel read/write primitives, manipulated kernel objects to deploy an enhanced FudModule rootkit—now capable of evading AhnLab V3, Defender, CrowdStrike Falcon and HitmanPro—and bypassed driver allowlisting, then deployed a new remote access trojan for persistent access, underscoring the need for immediate patching, vigilant driver integrity monitoring and behavior-based detection to thwart stealthy, living-off-the-land attacks.

hits.text: Russia’s APT29 (aka Cozy Bear/Nobelium) has been exploiting a critical unauthenticated remote-code-execution flaw in JetBrains TeamCity (CVE-2023-42793, CVSS 9.8) since September—shortly after JetBrains issued a patch and Rapid7 published a proof-of-concept—to gain initial access to SDLC management servers, escalate privileges, move laterally, deploy stealthy backdoors that persist through updates, and potentially manipulate build pipelines or insert malicious updates in SolarWinds-style supply-chain attacks; CISA, FBI, NSA and international partners warn that around 800 internet-exposed instances remain vulnerable (with uncounted internally reachable servers also at risk), and that North Korea’s Lazarus and Andariel groups have similarly weaponized the same flaw, prompting Fortinet to report multi-actor post-exploit techniques in live incidents; mitigation guidance urges immediate upgrading to TeamCity 2023.05.4, removal of public exposure, comprehensive IoC-based threat hunting across servers and build agents, and full compromise assessments to eradicate entrenched backdoors.

hits.text: A zero-day VPN vulnerability provided initial access for a sophisticated threat actor who employed publicly available penetration‐testing and exploitation tools—SoftPerfect Network Scanner for network discovery, PsExec to deploy ServeManager.exe (the FiveHands ransomware variant using lattice-based NTRUEncrypt public key cryptography), and SombRAT for remote information theft—alongside RouterScan, grabff.exe, rclone.exe, and s3browser-9-5-3.exe to harvest credentials and exfiltrate data. The combined use of FiveHands ransomware and SombRAT RAT resulted in both data theft and destruction of backup artifacts, underscoring the need for proactive patch management, network segmentation, strict credential hygiene, and rapid incident response to mitigate novel lattice-based encryption threats.

hits.text: Unit42’s “EleKtra-Leak” campaign, active since December 2020, uses automated scripts to clone public GitHub repos every few minutes, extract exposed AWS IAM keys within five minutes, then—if not blocked by GitHub-AWS quarantine policies—execute rapid AWS reconnaissance (DescribeRegions), create security groups, and launch hundreds of EC2 instances across regions via VPN for Monero cryptojacking, generating over 400 API calls in seven minutes. Between Aug. 30 and Oct. 6, 2023, researchers tracked 474 actor-controlled miners. The actor employs custom mining software and blocklists high-profile AWS account IDs to avoid honey traps. Leveraging the Prisma Cloud HoneyCloud project’s ephemeral key leaks and policy overrides, Unit42 obtained full visibility, informing Prisma Cloud Secrets Security, CI/CD IaC scanning, Cortex XDR, and recommendations for independent repo scanning, strict IAM policies, and continuous monitoring.
hits.title: CloudKeys in the Air: Tracking Malicious Operations of Exposed IAM Keys

hits.text: Avast researchers uncovered that North Korea’s Lazarus group leveraged a Windows zero-day privilege escalation flaw in Microsoft’s AppLocker “appid.sys” driver (CVE-2024-21338) to execute a truly fileless kernel attack during 2023 intrusions, sending a proof-of-concept exploit to Microsoft in August and prompting a February 2024 patch and subsequent advisory update once active exploitation was confirmed; by abusing a ubiquitous signed driver rather than importing custom code (BYOVD), Lazarus gained kernel read/write primitives, manipulated kernel objects to deploy an enhanced FudModule rootkit—now capable of evading AhnLab V3, Defender, CrowdStrike Falcon and HitmanPro—and bypassed driver allowlisting, then deployed a new remote access trojan for persistent access, underscoring the need for immediate patching, vigilant driver integrity monitoring and behavior-based detection to thwart stealthy, living-off-the-land attacks.
hits.title: Windows Zero-Day Exploited by North Korean Hackers in Rootkit Attack - SecurityWeek

canonical_entities: ZIP files masquerading as legitimate updates
hits.text: Unit 42 has observed a sharp rise in post-intrusion WastedLocker ransomware attacks by the Evil Corp group—already known for Dridex—against large U.S. organizations in sectors from manufacturing to legal services, with initial compromise typically via ZIP files masquerading as legitimate updates that deploy a SocGholish JavaScript loader to profile systems and invoke PowerShell-based Cobalt Strike payloads; attackers then leverage WMI and PsExec for lateral movement, identify high-value and backup systems, elevate privileges, disable Windows Defender, delete shadow copies, install WastedLocker as a service, and encrypt files using a “.<victim_name>wasted” extension while appending ransom notes (“.<victim_name>wasted_info”) with contact addresses on ProtonMail, Airmail and others. Palo Alto Networks’ WildFire, Cortex XDR (anti-ransomware and behavioral threat protection), NGFW DNS signatures and AutoFocus tagging detect and prevent WastedLocker activity; organizations are urged to implement robust, off-site backup strategies and hardened cybersecurity controls to mitigate this high-impact targeted ransomware threat.
hits.title: Threat Assessment: WastedLocker Ransomware

hits.text: Security researcher Marc Newlin of SkySafe disclosed CVE-2023-45866, a critical, decade-old keystroke-injection flaw in the Bluetooth host state-machine that exploits an unauthenticated pairing mechanism in the Bluetooth specification to trick macOS (13.3.3), iOS (16.6, even in Lockdown Mode), Android (from 4.2.2 through 14 on devices including Pixel 7/6/4a, Pixel 2, Nexus 5, BLU DASH), and Linux BlueZ stacks (Ubuntu 18.04–23.10) into pairing with a malicious emulated keyboard, enabling remote attackers within Bluetooth range to run a Python-based script, inject arbitrary keystrokes, install apps, forward emails or texts, and execute commands without user confirmation or biometric/password authentication. After informing Apple, Google, Canonical, and the Bluetooth SIG between August and September, patches have been released for Android 11–14 and BlueZ (via GitHub) but Apple has yet to announce a timeline for CVE-2023-42929, proof-of-concept exploit scripts will be published in January, and no active in-the-wild exploitation has been observed to date.
hits.title: Critical Bluetooth Flaw Exposes Android, Apple & Linux Devices to Takeover

hits.text: Microsoft Threat Intelligence has observed the Russia-based SVR actor Midnight Blizzard (aka NOBELIUM, APT29/UNC2452/Cozy Bear) launch a highly targeted social-engineering campaign since at least late May 2023 by leveraging previously compromised small-business Microsoft 365 tenants to create security-themed onmicrosoft.com domains and Teams accounts that masquerade as technical-support entities; attackers then initiate Microsoft Teams chat requests to elicit approval of MFA prompts or codes via Microsoft Authenticator, enabling credential theft, access to fewer than 40 global organizations across government, NGOs, IT services, technology, manufacturing and media sectors, and subsequent post-compromise activities including data exfiltration and attempts to add managed devices via Microsoft Entra ID to bypass conditional access. Microsoft has mitigated the malicious domains, directly notified affected customers, and recommends phishing-resistant authentication, Conditional Access policies, Microsoft Teams best practices, auditing, and user education to detect and prevent unsolicited MFA requests.
hits.title: Midnight Blizzard conducts targeted social engineering over Microsoft Teams | Microsoft Security Blog

canonical_entities: enumerates SSH directories to harvest credentials
Persistence is achieved through multiple cronjobs
hits.text: Aqua Security’s Nautilus team has uncovered Hadooken, a new Linux malware targeting Oracle WebLogic servers via weak passwords. Post-compromise, attackers deploy redundant shell and Python scripts to ensure download and execution of Hadooken, which enumerates SSH directories to harvest credentials, moves laterally, and clears logs. Hadooken then drops a three-path cryptominer and a Tsunami backdoor with a randomized name, the latter reserved for potential later-stage attacks. Persistence is achieved through multiple cronjobs under varied names and frequencies stored across cron directories. The malware is hosted on two IPs—one German address linked to TeamTNT and Gang 8220, the other inactive in Russia—where researchers also identified a Mallox ransomware PowerShell loader targeting Windows. Static analysis links Hadooken to Rhombus and NoEscape families. With over 230,000 internet-connected WebLogic instances—hundreds of which expose vulnerable admin consoles—this campaign underscores the dual risk of cryptojacking and ransomware across Linux and Windows environments.
hits.title: New 'Hadooken' Linux Malware Targets WebLogic Servers - SecurityWeek

hits.text: Symantec’s Threat Hunter Team has linked the newly discovered Sidewalk loader backdoor—an evolution of the Crosswalk/Backdoor.Motnug family—to Grayfly (aka GREF/Wicked Panda), a China-linked espionage group active since March 2017 that employs custom backdoors, Trojan.Chattak, Cobalt Strike, web shells and credential-dumpers against telecom, IT, media and finance targets in Taiwan, Vietnam, the US and Mexico; in a recent campaign they exploited public-facing Microsoft Exchange and MySQL servers via commodity and zero-day flaws to execute Base64-encoded PowerShell commands through certutil, install an ASPX web shell in the ClientAccess\ecp directory, deploy Sidewalk via installutil.exe, create persistence with WMIC-launched scheduled tasks, then run a custom Mimikatz variant (SHA256 b3eb783b017da32e33d19670b39eae0b11de8e983891dd4feb873d6e9333608d) to harvest credentials—all within about an hour before ceasing observable activity; three Chengdu 404 executives were indicted in 2020 for attacks on over 100 organizations, highlighting Grayfly’s persistence and underscoring the need to promptly patch Exchange and MySQL servers, monitor anomalous PowerShell and scheduled-task activity, and deploy IOC-based detection to block Sidewalk and related tools.
hits.title: Grayfly: Chinese Threat Actor Uses Newly-discovered Sidewalk Malware | Symantec Enterprise Blogs

retrieved_context.text: RansomHub, first reported in February 2024 and linked to the Knight ransomware family, gains initial access through spear-phishing voice scams with convincing American-accent callers and compromised VPN credentials, then leverages PsExec, PowerShell and Python scripts to harvest credentials (Mimikatz, LaZagne, SecretServerSecretStealer), discover remote systems, establish SSH sessions and exploit CVE-2023-27532 in Veeam Backup & Replication to dump database credentials. Operators maintain persistence by creating local administrative accounts and registry run keys, evade defenses with disableAV.bat (BAT.KAPROCHANDLER.A), the STONESTOP binary using the signed POORTRY driver, batch scripts that disable Windows Defender and purge AV registry entries, TDSSKiller, EDR Kill Shifter via BYOVD and IOBit Unlocker, then transfer encryptors via SFTP or an Impacket-based SMB spreader. They also automate vCenter interactions to enable and exploit ESXi SSH, reset host passwords and move laterally, while command and control is managed through Atera, Splashtop, AnyDesk, Ngrok, Screen Connect and Remmina, and data exfiltration is conducted using RClone. The ransomware employs ECDH and AES to encrypt files—appending a 32-byte master public key and requiring a 32-byte passphrase to decrypt its embedded configuration that specifies targeted file types, exclusions and service terminations. Since April 2024, Trend Micro observed at least 338 RansomHub victims across 58 countries—predominantly small educational enterprises in the U.S. and Malaysia—underscoring the need for hardened email defenses, credential monitoring, timely Veeam patching, isolated backups and robust EDR solutions.
retrieved_context.title: Ransomware Spotlight: Ransomhub | Trend Micro (US)

retrieved_context.text: Trend Micro analysts uncovered in December 2023 a new ransomware strain dubbed Kasseika—likely developed by former BlackMatter affiliates or buyers of its source code—that employs a Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver (BYOVD) attack by abusing TG Soft’s Martini driver (Martini.sys/viragt64.sys) to disable antivirus and security tools before encryption. Kasseika’s chain begins with credential-harvesting phishing emails for initial access, followed by PsExec-driven execution of malicious .bat scripts that terminate any running Martini.exe, deploy the vulnerable Martini.sys driver (without which the attack halts), and leverage its flaws to kill 991 hard-coded processes. The threat then runs Martini.exe to neutralize defenses, launches its main ransomware binary (smartscreen_protected.exe), encrypts files with ChaCha20 and RSA—appending pseudo-random strings to filenames—drops ransom notes and wallpaper warnings, and erases event logs via wevutil.exe. Victims face a 72-hour deadline to pay 50 BTC (~$2 million) with $500,000 added every 24 hours of delay and must post proof to a private Telegram group within five days; Trend Micro has separately published related IoCs.
retrieved_context.title: Kasseika ransomware uses antivirus driver to kill other antiviruses

canonical_entities: Remote Code Execution via ms-msdt URI in Word/RTF documents
ms-msdt URI-based RCE in Word/RTF documents
retrieved_context.text: In late May 2022, Symantec identified multiple threat actors exploiting the MSDT Follina bug (CVE-2022-30190) through ms-msdt URI-based RCE in Word/RTF documents that load a malicious HTML via Word’s remote template feature to launch msdt.exe, sdiagnhost.exe and ultimately PowerShell—bypassing the need for macros—to install a digitally signed AsyncRAT remote access Trojan that performs anti-analysis checks, collects hardware IDs, user names, execution paths and OS details, and maintains C&C communications, alongside parallel deployments of a browser infostealer targeting cookies and saved credentials in Firefox, Chrome and Edge. Symantec customers should apply Microsoft’s advisories or disable the ms-msdt handler, update Symantec Endpoint definitions (File-based-Downloader-Backdoor:Async, InfoStealer) and monitor for related IOCs to thwart these rapid, damaging campaigns.
retrieved_context.title: Attackers Exploit MSDT Follina Bug to Drop RAT, Infostealer | Symantec Enterprise Blogs

canonical_entities: Scanning the Internet for IoT devices with open Telnet/SSH ports
Use of default or weak credentials
Encrypted SOCKS5 tunneling to proxy infrastructure
hits.text: Researchers have uncovered that since early 2024 a previously undocumented botnet, dubbed Ngioweb, has been systematically scanning the Internet for IoT devices—primarily DVRs, IP cameras and home routers—with open Telnet/SSH ports and default or weak credentials, exploiting known firmware vulnerabilities to deploy a lightweight Go-based loader that establishes encrypted SOCKS5 tunnels back to a resilient NSOCKS residential proxy network of over 150,000 infected nodes. Once a device is compromised, Ngioweb drops a persistent agent that connects to fast-flux C2 domains via HTTPS, retrieves updated encryption keys and proxy configuration, and registers the node for NSOCKS’ tiered subscription service (starting at $25/month), which reportedly generates upwards of $500K in monthly revenue by fueling large-scale credential-stuffing campaigns, ad fraud and DDoS-for-hire operations. The actors behind Ngioweb continually rotate fallback C2 domains, employ encryption and obfuscation to evade signature-based detection, and monitor infection success rates in real time, enabling rapid retooling and expansion. Defenders are urged to enforce strong, unique credentials on all IoT assets, disable unused management interfaces, apply timely firmware updates, implement network segmentation and deploy behavioral analytics or honeypots to detect anomalous outbound proxy traffic.
hits.title: Ngioweb Botnet Fuels NSOCKS Residential Proxy Network Exploiting IoT Devices
