Although attribution remains unconfirmed, the breach shares hallmarks of the Scattered Spider threat group (aka 0ktapus, UNC3944, Scatter Swine, Starfraud, Muddled Libra), known for social-engineering and identity-based attacks—including phishing, SIM swapping, MFA bombing and help-desk phone calls—and recent pivots to aviation targets such as Hawaiian Airlines and WestJet (which was breached via a self-service password reset exploit). To defend against these tactics, organizations should gain complete visibility across infrastructure and identity systems and harden self-service password reset portals, help desks and third-party identity vendors, leveraging hardening guides published by Google Threat Intelligence Group and Palo Alto Networks.
hits.title: Qantas discloses cyberattack amid Scattered Spider aviation breaches

hits.text: In a joint advisory, US, Australian and Canadian agencies warn that financially motivated group Scattered Spider (UNC3944, aka Muddled Libra/Scatter Swine/Starfraud) has leveraged advanced social engineering against help-desk personnel to harvest compromised credentials from hacking forums, deploy RMM tools, create fake social-media personas, and target VMware ESXi servers and Snowflake environments—running thousands of concurrent queries to exfiltrate data to MEGA.nz and Amazon S3—before encrypting systems with DragonForce ransomware and deploying RattyRAT; although recent UK arrests have paused UNC3944 operations, other actors including UNC6040, UNC2165 (RansomHub), UNC4393 (Basta) and UNC2465 (DarkSide/LockBit) are now replicating these TTPs, extending attacks to backup platforms by deleting routines and tampering with permissions to thwart recovery, often exploiting weak credentials, misconfigurations, API/UI flaws and RCE vulnerabilities; defenders are urged to adopt identity-centric security, layered MFA, Zero Trust principles, robust patching, segmentation and proactive disruption of human-driven intrusion paths.
hits.title: Scattered Spider Activity Drops Following Arrests, but Others Adopting Group's Tactics

hits.text: On June 30, 2025, Qantas Airlines discovered that hackers had exploited a vulnerability in a third-party call-center platform to access personally identifiable information (PII) for approximately six million customers—names, email addresses, phone numbers, birth dates and frequent-flyer numbers—but not passports or payment data—before the breach was contained shortly thereafter; in response, Qantas has launched a dedicated support line and webpage, tightened IT monitoring and access controls, and is investigating alongside federal authorities.  Cybersecurity experts from CyberCX attribute “all the hallmarks” of the attack to the advanced persistent threat group Scattered Spider (aka UNC3944, 0ktapus/Roasted Oktapus, Scatter Swine, Octo Tempest, Muddled Libra), which the FBI recently warned is increasingly targeting aviation, while government minister Tony Burke cautioned Australians to resist cold calls or unsolicited emails and to verify Qantas communications via published contact channels to thwart follow-on phishing campaigns.  Apollo Information Systems CISO Andy Bennett highlights attackers’ use of AI to amalgamate PII from multiple breaches for highly personalized social‐engineering, underscoring the need for rigorous vendor security assessments, proactive threat hunting and cross-sector collaboration under Australia’s $1.67 billion cybersecurity strategy and new critical-infrastructure legislation.
hits.title: Qantas Airlines Breached, Impacting 6M Customers

hits.text: Since mid-2022, Unit 42 has attributed over 100 high-value cryptocurrency and BPO incidents to Muddled Libra—a fluid subset of the Scattered Spider collective—initially executing structured smishing and 0ktapus phishing campaigns (leveraging over 200 realistic mobile-auth portals) against large business process outsourcers, then evolving in 2023 into an ALPHV/BlackCat affiliate with multi-million-dollar extortion demands, later resuming high-profile attacks in late 2024 and expanding through May 2025 into software automation, telecom, hospitality, finance and retail verticals; their adaptable tradecraft blends social engineering of IT helpdesks to reset passwords and MFA, inside BPO access, legitimate remote management tools for CRM exfiltration, NSOCKS/TrueSocks anonymizing proxies, custom virtual machines, the open-source “bedevil” rootkit on VMware vCenter, email-forwarding rules to hijack incident response communications, and AI-driven voice spoofing for vishing, with members cycling via Discord and Telegram to refresh niche skills and spawn offshoots such as Scatter Swine and Octo Tempest, while leveraging deep incident response framework knowledge to persist in environments and repeatedly reclaim stolen data before affiliating with DragonForce for ransomware; defenders should deploy interwoven modern security architectures (Cortex XSIAM/XDR, Advanced URL Filtering, DNS Security, App-ID), enforce strict access controls, conduct rigorous awareness training, and maintain vigilant MITRE-mapped monitoring (T1566, T1556, T1215, T1562) to thwart these multifaceted, evolving extortion campaigns.
hits.title: Threat Group Assessment: Muddled Libra (Updated May 16, 2025)

hits.text: Last week Google’s Threat Analysis Group, in partnership with The Citizen Lab, exposed an in-the-wild exploit chain developed by the commercial surveillance vendor Intellexa in Egypt that leverages a man-in-the-middle injection on HTTP traffic to silently redirect targets first to c.betly[.]me and then to sec-flare[.]com, delivering Predator spyware without any user interaction; on iOS this chain combined Safari RCE (CVE-2023-41993), certificate validation bypass (CVE-2023-41991) and XNU kernel local privilege escalation (CVE-2023-41992) and was patched in iOS 16.7/17.0.1, while on Android initial Chrome renderer RCE (CVE-2023-4762), delivered via MITM or one-time links, was patched on September 5; this campaign highlights the serious risk posed by proliferating commercial spyware, underscores the urgency of enforcing universal HTTPS and enabling Chrome’s HTTPS-First Mode, and demonstrates the critical need for organizations and users to apply the latest OS and browser updates, deploy encrypted-traffic protections, and monitor for anomalous network redirects to mitigate future attacks.
hits.title: 0-days exploited by commercial surveillance vendor in Egypt

canonical_entities: trading and brokerage firms in Hong Kong, the UAE, Jordan, Lebanon and Malaysia
hits.text: First observed in September 2024 and active through at least August 12, 2025, the GodRAT campaign—attributed to an APT likely linked to Winnti—targets financial institutions, particularly trading and brokerage firms in Hong Kong, the UAE, Jordan, Lebanon and Malaysia, by distributing malicious .scr and .pif files via Skype messenger disguised as legitimate financial documents. Evolving from the AwesomePuppet RAT on a Gh0st RAT codebase, GodRAT employs a two-stage loader architecture: an initial stub invokes SDL2.dll to allocate memory and extract XOR-decoded (key 0x63) shellcode hidden via steganography in image files named to mimic authentic financial reports, then searches for the “godinfo” marker and uses the authentication string “GETGOD” to contact C2 servers, download UPX-packed GodRAT DLL modules and launch browser credential-stealing and remote-access payloads. This advanced steganographic delivery evades signature-based defenses and underscores the need to inspect .scr/.pif attachments, monitor Skype channels, and deploy detection rules for “godinfo,” “GETGOD” and related shellcode patterns.
hits.title: New GodRAT Weaponizing Screen Saver and Program Files to Attack Organizations

hits.text: Microsoft Threat Intelligence has observed the Russia-based SVR actor Midnight Blizzard (aka NOBELIUM, APT29/UNC2452/Cozy Bear) launch a highly targeted social-engineering campaign since at least late May 2023 by leveraging previously compromised small-business Microsoft 365 tenants to create security-themed onmicrosoft.com domains and Teams accounts that masquerade as technical-support entities; attackers then initiate Microsoft Teams chat requests to elicit approval of MFA prompts or codes via Microsoft Authenticator, enabling credential theft, access to fewer than 40 global organizations across government, NGOs, IT services, technology, manufacturing and media sectors, and subsequent post-compromise activities including data exfiltration and attempts to add managed devices via Microsoft Entra ID to bypass conditional access. Microsoft has mitigated the malicious domains, directly notified affected customers, and recommends phishing-resistant authentication, Conditional Access policies, Microsoft Teams best practices, auditing, and user education to detect and prevent unsolicited MFA requests.
hits.title: Midnight Blizzard conducts targeted social engineering over Microsoft Teams | Microsoft Security Blog

hits.text: Since January 2021, Google’s Threat Analysis Group (TAG) has tracked a government-backed North Korean campaign that leverages social engineering via X (formerly Twitter) and encrypted messaging apps to befriend security researchers and deliver malicious files containing at least one unpatched 0-day in a popular software package; upon exploitation the custom shellcode performs anti-virtual-machine checks, captures system data and screenshots, and exfiltrates them to C2 infrastructure (e.g., 23.106.215[.]105, www.blgbeach[.]com), with the latest vulnerability reported and patched on September 12, 2023 (see TAG’s published RCA). In parallel, the actors published a seemingly benign Windows tool called GetSymbol on GitHub (https://github.com/dbgsymbol/) that quietly downloads debugging symbols—and arbitrary code—from attacker domains, requiring full OS reinstalls for compromised hosts. TAG has added malicious sites to Safe Browsing, issued government-backed attacker alerts to targeted Gmail and Workspace users, and urges researchers to enable Enhanced Safe Browsing, keep software up to date, and verify system integrity after using third-party tools.
hits.title: Active North Korean campaign targeting security researchers

hits.text: In early April, Palo Alto Networks’ Advanced WildFire and Cortex XDR uncovered SnipBot—a new v5.0 iteration of the RomCom RAT family—employing advanced window message–based control-flow obfuscation and anti-sandbox checks (filename hash and HKCU\…\RecentDocs entries) in a multi-stage chain beginning with a PDF-labeled EXE downloader signed using a likely stolen certificate; the downloader contacts xeontime[.]com for config-pdf.dll, which uses registry-based COM hijacking to load keyprov.dll from drvmcprotect[.]com into explorer.exe, decrypts payloads stored in HKCU\Software\AppDataSoft\Software, and opens a TCP listener on port 1342 for commands to update, delete, or execute modules. The main backdoor single.dll (mutex “SnipMutex”) supports 27 encrypted commands for drive and process enumeration, file upload/download, and remote module execution, facilitating network pivoting and targeted file exfiltration. Active since December 2023 (RomCom activity since 2022), SnipBot’s tactics, stolen certificates, unique obfuscation, and sophisticated loader underscore a high-risk threat actor likely focused on intelligence gathering; Palo Alto products classify its samples, URLs, and domains as malicious to prevent compromise.
hits.title: Inside SnipBot: The Latest RomCom Malware Variant

canonical_entities: Launch EC2 instances across regions via VPN
hits.text: Unit42’s “EleKtra-Leak” campaign, active since December 2020, uses automated scripts to clone public GitHub repos every few minutes, extract exposed AWS IAM keys within five minutes, then—if not blocked by GitHub-AWS quarantine policies—execute rapid AWS reconnaissance (DescribeRegions), create security groups, and launch hundreds of EC2 instances across regions via VPN for Monero cryptojacking, generating over 400 API calls in seven minutes. Between Aug. 30 and Oct. 6, 2023, researchers tracked 474 actor-controlled miners. The actor employs custom mining software and blocklists high-profile AWS account IDs to avoid honey traps. Leveraging the Prisma Cloud HoneyCloud project’s ephemeral key leaks and policy overrides, Unit42 obtained full visibility, informing Prisma Cloud Secrets Security, CI/CD IaC scanning, Cortex XDR, and recommendations for independent repo scanning, strict IAM policies, and continuous monitoring.
hits.title: CloudKeys in the Air: Tracking Malicious Operations of Exposed IAM Keys

canonical_entities: ZIP files masquerading as legitimate updates
hits.text: Unit 42 has observed a sharp rise in post-intrusion WastedLocker ransomware attacks by the Evil Corp group—already known for Dridex—against large U.S. organizations in sectors from manufacturing to legal services, with initial compromise typically via ZIP files masquerading as legitimate updates that deploy a SocGholish JavaScript loader to profile systems and invoke PowerShell-based Cobalt Strike payloads; attackers then leverage WMI and PsExec for lateral movement, identify high-value and backup systems, elevate privileges, disable Windows Defender, delete shadow copies, install WastedLocker as a service, and encrypt files using a “.<victim_name>wasted” extension while appending ransom notes (“.<victim_name>wasted_info”) with contact addresses on ProtonMail, Airmail and others. Palo Alto Networks’ WildFire, Cortex XDR (anti-ransomware and behavioral threat protection), NGFW DNS signatures and AutoFocus tagging detect and prevent WastedLocker activity; organizations are urged to implement robust, off-site backup strategies and hardened cybersecurity controls to mitigate this high-impact targeted ransomware threat.
hits.title: Threat Assessment: WastedLocker Ransomware

canonical_entities: Remote Code Execution via ms-msdt URI in Word/RTF documents
ms-msdt URI-based RCE in Word/RTF documents
hits.text: In late May 2022, Symantec identified multiple threat actors exploiting the MSDT Follina bug (CVE-2022-30190) through ms-msdt URI-based RCE in Word/RTF documents that load a malicious HTML via Word’s remote template feature to launch msdt.exe, sdiagnhost.exe and ultimately PowerShell—bypassing the need for macros—to install a digitally signed AsyncRAT remote access Trojan that performs anti-analysis checks, collects hardware IDs, user names, execution paths and OS details, and maintains C&C communications, alongside parallel deployments of a browser infostealer targeting cookies and saved credentials in Firefox, Chrome and Edge. Symantec customers should apply Microsoft’s advisories or disable the ms-msdt handler, update Symantec Endpoint definitions (File-based-Downloader-Backdoor:Async, InfoStealer) and monitor for related IOCs to thwart these rapid, damaging campaigns.
hits.title: Attackers Exploit MSDT Follina Bug to Drop RAT, Infostealer | Symantec Enterprise Blogs

hits.text: In early April, Palo Alto Networks’ Advanced WildFire and Cortex XDR uncovered SnipBot—a new v5.0 iteration of the RomCom RAT family—employing advanced window message–based control-flow obfuscation and anti-sandbox checks (filename hash and HKCU\…\RecentDocs entries) in a multi-stage chain beginning with a PDF-labeled EXE downloader signed using a likely stolen certificate; the downloader contacts xeontime[.]com for config-pdf.dll, which uses registry-based COM hijacking to load keyprov.dll from drvmcprotect[.]com into explorer.exe, decrypts payloads stored in HKCU\Software\AppDataSoft\Software, and opens a TCP listener on port 1342 for commands to update, delete, or execute modules. The main backdoor single.dll (mutex “SnipMutex”) supports 27 encrypted commands for drive and process enumeration, file upload/download, and remote module execution, facilitating network pivoting and targeted file exfiltration. Active since December 2023 (RomCom activity since 2022), SnipBot’s tactics, stolen certificates, unique obfuscation, and sophisticated loader underscore a high-risk threat actor likely focused on intelligence gathering; Palo Alto products classify its samples, URLs, and domains as malicious to prevent compromise.
hits.title: Inside SnipBot: The Latest RomCom Malware Variant

retrieval_events.query: What is the canonical threat actor name, resolving any aliases mentioned across these reports?

retrieved_context.text: Scattered Spider, active since May 2022, has evolved from SIM-swapping and typosquatted credential harvesting to sophisticated social-engineering-driven cloud intrusions, most recently impersonating a CFO via public personal data to trick help-desk staff into resetting their Oracle Cloud device, then mapping Entra ID (Azure AD) privileges and SharePoint data, breaching Horizon VDI, VPN, and on-premise environments, reactivating a decommissioned VM, extracting NTDS.dit and over 1,400 secrets from CyberArk vaults using scripts and tools like ngrok, abusing AWS Systems Manager Session Manager, EC2 Serial Console, IAM role enumeration and Teleport for persistence, assigning Exchange Administrator roles to monitor senior employee inboxes, and deleting Azure Firewall policy rules in a tug-of-war over tenant control that required Microsoft intervention, inflicting millions in operational disruption (e.g., MGM Resorts, Marks & Spencer, Hawaiian Airlines) and exposing critical lapses in help-desk verification and privileged access management; organizations should deploy phishing-resistant MFA, enforce least-privilege and strict identity proofing for help-desks, monitor cloud and endpoint activity, and conduct regular social-engineering training to mitigate Scattered Spider’s fast, multi-vector ransomware preparation tactics.
retrieved_context.title: Anatomy of a Scattered Spider attack: A growing ransomware threat evolves

canonical_entities: Office of the Australian Information Commissioner
retrieved_context.text: On Monday Qantas detected unusual activity on a third-party call-centre customer-service platform used by six million customers and immediately contained the system, confirming that a “significant” volume of data—names, email addresses, phone numbers, birth dates and frequent flyer numbers—was likely stolen while credit card and personal financial data, as well as passwords, PINs and login details, remained secure; the airline, which operates globally across six continents, has notified the Australian Cyber Security Centre, the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner and the Australian Federal Police and reports all Qantas systems are currently secure. Although attribution remains unconfirmed, the breach shares hallmarks of the Scattered Spider threat group (aka 0ktapus, UNC3944, Scatter Swine, Starfraud, Muddled Libra), known for social-engineering and identity-based attacks—including phishing, SIM swapping, MFA bombing and help-desk phone calls—and recent pivots to aviation targets such as Hawaiian Airlines and WestJet (which was breached via a self-service password reset exploit). To defend against these tactics, organizations should gain complete visibility across infrastructure and identity systems and harden self-service password reset portals, help desks and third-party identity vendors, leveraging hardening guides published by Google Threat Intelligence Group and Palo Alto Networks.
retrieved_context.title: Qantas discloses cyberattack amid Scattered Spider aviation breaches

retrieved_context.text: In a joint advisory, US, Australian and Canadian agencies warn that financially motivated group Scattered Spider (UNC3944, aka Muddled Libra/Scatter Swine/Starfraud) has leveraged advanced social engineering against help-desk personnel to harvest compromised credentials from hacking forums, deploy RMM tools, create fake social-media personas, and target VMware ESXi servers and Snowflake environments—running thousands of concurrent queries to exfiltrate data to MEGA.nz and Amazon S3—before encrypting systems with DragonForce ransomware and deploying RattyRAT; although recent UK arrests have paused UNC3944 operations, other actors including UNC6040, UNC2165 (RansomHub), UNC4393 (Basta) and UNC2465 (DarkSide/LockBit) are now replicating these TTPs, extending attacks to backup platforms by deleting routines and tampering with permissions to thwart recovery, often exploiting weak credentials, misconfigurations, API/UI flaws and RCE vulnerabilities; defenders are urged to adopt identity-centric security, layered MFA, Zero Trust principles, robust patching, segmentation and proactive disruption of human-driven intrusion paths.
retrieved_context.title: Scattered Spider Activity Drops Following Arrests, but Others Adopting Group's Tactics

retrieved_context.text: On June 30, 2025, Qantas Airlines discovered that hackers had exploited a vulnerability in a third-party call-center platform to access personally identifiable information (PII) for approximately six million customers—names, email addresses, phone numbers, birth dates and frequent-flyer numbers—but not passports or payment data—before the breach was contained shortly thereafter; in response, Qantas has launched a dedicated support line and webpage, tightened IT monitoring and access controls, and is investigating alongside federal authorities.  Cybersecurity experts from CyberCX attribute “all the hallmarks” of the attack to the advanced persistent threat group Scattered Spider (aka UNC3944, 0ktapus/Roasted Oktapus, Scatter Swine, Octo Tempest, Muddled Libra), which the FBI recently warned is increasingly targeting aviation, while government minister Tony Burke cautioned Australians to resist cold calls or unsolicited emails and to verify Qantas communications via published contact channels to thwart follow-on phishing campaigns.  Apollo Information Systems CISO Andy Bennett highlights attackers’ use of AI to amalgamate PII from multiple breaches for highly personalized social‐engineering, underscoring the need for rigorous vendor security assessments, proactive threat hunting and cross-sector collaboration under Australia’s $1.67 billion cybersecurity strategy and new critical-infrastructure legislation.
retrieved_context.title: Qantas Airlines Breached, Impacting 6M Customers

retrieved_context.text: Since mid-2022, Unit 42 has attributed over 100 high-value cryptocurrency and BPO incidents to Muddled Libra—a fluid subset of the Scattered Spider collective—initially executing structured smishing and 0ktapus phishing campaigns (leveraging over 200 realistic mobile-auth portals) against large business process outsourcers, then evolving in 2023 into an ALPHV/BlackCat affiliate with multi-million-dollar extortion demands, later resuming high-profile attacks in late 2024 and expanding through May 2025 into software automation, telecom, hospitality, finance and retail verticals; their adaptable tradecraft blends social engineering of IT helpdesks to reset passwords and MFA, inside BPO access, legitimate remote management tools for CRM exfiltration, NSOCKS/TrueSocks anonymizing proxies, custom virtual machines, the open-source “bedevil” rootkit on VMware vCenter, email-forwarding rules to hijack incident response communications, and AI-driven voice spoofing for vishing, with members cycling via Discord and Telegram to refresh niche skills and spawn offshoots such as Scatter Swine and Octo Tempest, while leveraging deep incident response framework knowledge to persist in environments and repeatedly reclaim stolen data before affiliating with DragonForce for ransomware; defenders should deploy interwoven modern security architectures (Cortex XSIAM/XDR, Advanced URL Filtering, DNS Security, App-ID), enforce strict access controls, conduct rigorous awareness training, and maintain vigilant MITRE-mapped monitoring (T1566, T1556, T1215, T1562) to thwart these multifaceted, evolving extortion campaigns.
retrieved_context.title: Threat Group Assessment: Muddled Libra (Updated May 16, 2025)

canonical_entities: Launch EC2 instances across regions via VPN
retrieved_context.text: Unit42’s “EleKtra-Leak” campaign, active since December 2020, uses automated scripts to clone public GitHub repos every few minutes, extract exposed AWS IAM keys within five minutes, then—if not blocked by GitHub-AWS quarantine policies—execute rapid AWS reconnaissance (DescribeRegions), create security groups, and launch hundreds of EC2 instances across regions via VPN for Monero cryptojacking, generating over 400 API calls in seven minutes. Between Aug. 30 and Oct. 6, 2023, researchers tracked 474 actor-controlled miners. The actor employs custom mining software and blocklists high-profile AWS account IDs to avoid honey traps. Leveraging the Prisma Cloud HoneyCloud project’s ephemeral key leaks and policy overrides, Unit42 obtained full visibility, informing Prisma Cloud Secrets Security, CI/CD IaC scanning, Cortex XDR, and recommendations for independent repo scanning, strict IAM policies, and continuous monitoring.
retrieved_context.title: CloudKeys in the Air: Tracking Malicious Operations of Exposed IAM Keys

retrieved_context.text: Microsoft Threat Intelligence has observed the Russia-based SVR actor Midnight Blizzard (aka NOBELIUM, APT29/UNC2452/Cozy Bear) launch a highly targeted social-engineering campaign since at least late May 2023 by leveraging previously compromised small-business Microsoft 365 tenants to create security-themed onmicrosoft.com domains and Teams accounts that masquerade as technical-support entities; attackers then initiate Microsoft Teams chat requests to elicit approval of MFA prompts or codes via Microsoft Authenticator, enabling credential theft, access to fewer than 40 global organizations across government, NGOs, IT services, technology, manufacturing and media sectors, and subsequent post-compromise activities including data exfiltration and attempts to add managed devices via Microsoft Entra ID to bypass conditional access. Microsoft has mitigated the malicious domains, directly notified affected customers, and recommends phishing-resistant authentication, Conditional Access policies, Microsoft Teams best practices, auditing, and user education to detect and prevent unsolicited MFA requests.
retrieved_context.title: Midnight Blizzard conducts targeted social engineering over Microsoft Teams | Microsoft Security Blog

hits.text: Since mid-November 2024, Russian nation-state actor Star Blizzard has significantly escalated its evasion tradecraft following public exposure by Microsoft Threat Intelligence: shifting from a single registrar (NameCheap) to multiple registrars (Hostinger, RealTime Register, GMO Internet) and implementing multi-stage redirection chains—embedding Microsoft 365 Safe Links in PDF lures that pass through Bitly and Cuttly shortened URLs and legitimate open-redirect sites (e.g., mechengsys[.]net) before landing on an Evilginx-equipped VPS (vidmemax[.]com)—to mount AiTM spear-phishing campaigns that harvest email credentials, including MFA tokens. Between July and August 2024 they also experimented with altered OneDrive file-share notifications—using ProtonMail accounts to spoof trusted senders and rewire the “Open” button URL to their Evilginx infrastructure—targeting individuals in politics, diplomacy, NGOs and think tanks. In October 2024, Microsoft’s Digital Crimes Unit disrupted core infrastructure, and ongoing collaboration with UK NCSC, NSA and FBI ensures rapid customer notification and defenses. Historically, since 2022 Star Blizzard has iteratively refined detection evasion—employing server-side fingerprinting scripts, HubSpot and MailerLite email platforms to mask domains, DNS obfuscation, password-protected PDFs and randomized DGAs—with each ephemeral TTP swiftly modified, underscoring the need for continuous updates to email security controls, link inspection and behavioral detection.
hits.title: Star Blizzard increases sophistication and evasion in ongoing attacks | Microsoft Security Blog

hits.text: ESET researchers uncovered a novel crimeware campaign, active in Czechia since November 2023 and paused only by the arrest of a suspect in March 2024, in which attackers combined social engineering, phishing and Android malware to target clients of three Czech banks via deceptive SMS links to malicious progressive web apps (PWAs) and WebAPKs; after harvesting credentials, the attackers lured victims into installing NGate, a custom Android malware named for its incorporation of the open-source NFCGate tool, which relays NFC data from victims’ unrooted smartphones to an attacker’s rooted device, enabling the emulation of cloned payment cards and unauthorized ATM withdrawals (over 160,000 CZK recovered from just three recent victims, with likely higher overall losses), with a fallback tactic of illicit bank-to-bank transfers when the relay method fails.
hits.title: NGate Android malware relays NFC traffic to steal cash

Apollo Information Systems CISO Andy Bennett highlights attackers’ use of AI to amalgamate PII from multiple breaches for highly personalized social‐engineering, underscoring the need for rigorous vendor security assessments, proactive threat hunting and cross-sector collaboration under Australia’s $1.67 billion cybersecurity strategy and new critical-infrastructure legislation.
retrieved_context.title: Qantas Airlines Breached, Impacting 6M Customers

retrieved_context.text: Since mid-2022, Unit 42 has attributed over 100 high-value cryptocurrency and BPO incidents to Muddled Libra—a fluid subset of the Scattered Spider collective—initially executing structured smishing and 0ktapus phishing campaigns (leveraging over 200 realistic mobile-auth portals) against large business process outsourcers, then evolving in 2023 into an ALPHV/BlackCat affiliate with multi-million-dollar extortion demands, later resuming high-profile attacks in late 2024 and expanding through May 2025 into software automation, telecom, hospitality, finance and retail verticals; their adaptable tradecraft blends social engineering of IT helpdesks to reset passwords and MFA, inside BPO access, legitimate remote management tools for CRM exfiltration, NSOCKS/TrueSocks anonymizing proxies, custom virtual machines, the open-source “bedevil” rootkit on VMware vCenter, email-forwarding rules to hijack incident response communications, and AI-driven voice spoofing for vishing, with members cycling via Discord and Telegram to refresh niche skills and spawn offshoots such as Scatter Swine and Octo Tempest, while leveraging deep incident response framework knowledge to persist in environments and repeatedly reclaim stolen data before affiliating with DragonForce for ransomware; defenders should deploy interwoven modern security architectures (Cortex XSIAM/XDR, Advanced URL Filtering, DNS Security, App-ID), enforce strict access controls, conduct rigorous awareness training, and maintain vigilant MITRE-mapped monitoring (T1566, T1556, T1215, T1562) to thwart these multifaceted, evolving extortion campaigns.
retrieved_context.title: Threat Group Assessment: Muddled Libra (Updated May 16, 2025)

retrieved_context.text: Microsoft Threat Intelligence has observed the Russia-based SVR actor Midnight Blizzard (aka NOBELIUM, APT29/UNC2452/Cozy Bear) launch a highly targeted social-engineering campaign since at least late May 2023 by leveraging previously compromised small-business Microsoft 365 tenants to create security-themed onmicrosoft.com domains and Teams accounts that masquerade as technical-support entities; attackers then initiate Microsoft Teams chat requests to elicit approval of MFA prompts or codes via Microsoft Authenticator, enabling credential theft, access to fewer than 40 global organizations across government, NGOs, IT services, technology, manufacturing and media sectors, and subsequent post-compromise activities including data exfiltration and attempts to add managed devices via Microsoft Entra ID to bypass conditional access. Microsoft has mitigated the malicious domains, directly notified affected customers, and recommends phishing-resistant authentication, Conditional Access policies, Microsoft Teams best practices, auditing, and user education to detect and prevent unsolicited MFA requests.
retrieved_context.title: Midnight Blizzard conducts targeted social engineering over Microsoft Teams | Microsoft Security Blog

retrieved_context.text: Since mid-November 2024, Russian nation-state actor Star Blizzard has significantly escalated its evasion tradecraft following public exposure by Microsoft Threat Intelligence: shifting from a single registrar (NameCheap) to multiple registrars (Hostinger, RealTime Register, GMO Internet) and implementing multi-stage redirection chains—embedding Microsoft 365 Safe Links in PDF lures that pass through Bitly and Cuttly shortened URLs and legitimate open-redirect sites (e.g., mechengsys[.]net) before landing on an Evilginx-equipped VPS (vidmemax[.]com)—to mount AiTM spear-phishing campaigns that harvest email credentials, including MFA tokens. Between July and August 2024 they also experimented with altered OneDrive file-share notifications—using ProtonMail accounts to spoof trusted senders and rewire the “Open” button URL to their Evilginx infrastructure—targeting individuals in politics, diplomacy, NGOs and think tanks. In October 2024, Microsoft’s Digital Crimes Unit disrupted core infrastructure, and ongoing collaboration with UK NCSC, NSA and FBI ensures rapid customer notification and defenses. Historically, since 2022 Star Blizzard has iteratively refined detection evasion—employing server-side fingerprinting scripts, HubSpot and MailerLite email platforms to mask domains, DNS obfuscation, password-protected PDFs and randomized DGAs—with each ephemeral TTP swiftly modified, underscoring the need for continuous updates to email security controls, link inspection and behavioral detection.
retrieved_context.title: Star Blizzard increases sophistication and evasion in ongoing attacks | Microsoft Security Blog

canonical_entities: Remote Code Execution via ms-msdt URI in Word/RTF documents
ms-msdt URI-based RCE in Word/RTF documents
retrieved_context.text: In late May 2022, Symantec identified multiple threat actors exploiting the MSDT Follina bug (CVE-2022-30190) through ms-msdt URI-based RCE in Word/RTF documents that load a malicious HTML via Word’s remote template feature to launch msdt.exe, sdiagnhost.exe and ultimately PowerShell—bypassing the need for macros—to install a digitally signed AsyncRAT remote access Trojan that performs anti-analysis checks, collects hardware IDs, user names, execution paths and OS details, and maintains C&C communications, alongside parallel deployments of a browser infostealer targeting cookies and saved credentials in Firefox, Chrome and Edge. Symantec customers should apply Microsoft’s advisories or disable the ms-msdt handler, update Symantec Endpoint definitions (File-based-Downloader-Backdoor:Async, InfoStealer) and monitor for related IOCs to thwart these rapid, damaging campaigns.
retrieved_context.title: Attackers Exploit MSDT Follina Bug to Drop RAT, Infostealer | Symantec Enterprise Blogs

retrieved_context.text: ESET researchers uncovered a novel crimeware campaign, active in Czechia since November 2023 and paused only by the arrest of a suspect in March 2024, in which attackers combined social engineering, phishing and Android malware to target clients of three Czech banks via deceptive SMS links to malicious progressive web apps (PWAs) and WebAPKs; after harvesting credentials, the attackers lured victims into installing NGate, a custom Android malware named for its incorporation of the open-source NFCGate tool, which relays NFC data from victims’ unrooted smartphones to an attacker’s rooted device, enabling the emulation of cloned payment cards and unauthorized ATM withdrawals (over 160,000 CZK recovered from just three recent victims, with likely higher overall losses), with a fallback tactic of illicit bank-to-bank transfers when the relay method fails.
retrieved_context.title: NGate Android malware relays NFC traffic to steal cash

retrieved_context.text: In early April, Palo Alto Networks’ Advanced WildFire and Cortex XDR uncovered SnipBot—a new v5.0 iteration of the RomCom RAT family—employing advanced window message–based control-flow obfuscation and anti-sandbox checks (filename hash and HKCU\…\RecentDocs entries) in a multi-stage chain beginning with a PDF-labeled EXE downloader signed using a likely stolen certificate; the downloader contacts xeontime[.]com for config-pdf.dll, which uses registry-based COM hijacking to load keyprov.dll from drvmcprotect[.]com into explorer.exe, decrypts payloads stored in HKCU\Software\AppDataSoft\Software, and opens a TCP listener on port 1342 for commands to update, delete, or execute modules. The main backdoor single.dll (mutex “SnipMutex”) supports 27 encrypted commands for drive and process enumeration, file upload/download, and remote module execution, facilitating network pivoting and targeted file exfiltration. Active since December 2023 (RomCom activity since 2022), SnipBot’s tactics, stolen certificates, unique obfuscation, and sophisticated loader underscore a high-risk threat actor likely focused on intelligence gathering; Palo Alto products classify its samples, URLs, and domains as malicious to prevent compromise.
retrieved_context.title: Inside SnipBot: The Latest RomCom Malware Variant

canonical_entities: Palo Alto Networks NGFW Advanced Threat Prevention
hits.text: Since its debut in 2017 as an advanced .NET second-stage backdoor, Kazuar—attributed to Russian FSB–linked Pensive Ursa (Turla)—reemerged in July 2023 targeting Ukraine’s defense sector alongside a new Capibar first-stage loader, marking its first wild appearance since late 2020. This upgraded variant features extensive stealth and anti-analysis countermeasures—fake 2008 compilation timestamps, custom multi-layer string encryption, assembly-location checks and GUID-based pseudorandom directory and mutex generation—and boasts 45 C2-driven commands for comprehensive system profiling, data collection and credential theft from cloud platforms, source control and Signal. It supports six injection modes (inject, zombify, combined, remote, single and non-interactive), a multithreaded architecture for asynchronous task execution, and a hybrid AES–RSA encryption scheme for task/result files, complicating forensic recovery. Organizations can detect and block Kazuar with Palo Alto Networks NGFW Advanced Threat Prevention, Cortex XDR/XSIAM and WildFire, and engage Unit 42 Incident Response teams for targeted hunting and mitigation guidance.
hits.title: Over the Kazuar’s Nest: Cracking Down on a Freshly Hatched Backdoor Used by Pensive Ursa (Aka Turla)

canonical_entities: Palo Alto Networks NGFW Advanced Threat Prevention
hits.text: Unit 42 researchers have uncovered a new, substantially upgraded variant of the Kazuar .NET backdoor—previously observed in 2017 as a second-stage payload by Russian Federal Security Service–linked Pensive Ursa (Turla/Uroburos)—that re-emerged in July 2023 targeting Ukrainian defense organizations via a multi-stage Capibar loader to steal Signal messages, cloud and source-control credentials and other high-value data. This variant adds robust anti-analysis checks (Assembly.Location byte-array loader validation, faked 2008 compilation timestamps), extensive string encryption (multiple custom and ConfuserEx ciphers), hybrid AES payload encryption with RSA-encrypted IV/key plus HMAC-MD5 integrity, and obfuscation of IOCs. It supports 45 discrete commands for system profiling, credential theft and automated task workflows in a multithreaded solver component that writes AES- and RSA-protected result files. Kazuar also implements multiple injection modes (inject, browser- and svchost.exe-centric zombify, combined fallback, remote proxy, single and headless) and uses GUID-derived pseudorandom directories and mutexes to evade detection, while hard-coded agent and build identifiers enable variant tracking. Code overlap with Sunburst underscores its sophistication. Unit 42 has released detailed IOCs, artifacts and a GitHub appendix, and recommends Palo Alto Networks NGFW Advanced Threat Prevention, Cortex XDR, XSIAM, Advanced WildFire and Unit 42 incident response engagement to detect, hunt and mitigate this persistent threat.
hits.title: Over the Kazuar’s Nest: Cracking Down on a Freshly Hatched Backdoor Used by Pensive Ursa (Aka Turla)

canonical_entities: diplomatic and defense networks in Ukraine
hits.text: Secret Blizzard, the Russian FSB’s Center 16, has escalated global espionage by co-opting C2 infrastructures of at least six threat actors—including Pakistan-based Storm-0156, Hazel Sandstorm and Storm-0473—to install backdoors (CrimsonRAT, Wainscot), deploy custom payloads (TwoDash downloader, MiniPocket fetcher), a TinyTurla variant disguised as a Windows service, and the Statuezy clipboard-monitoring trojan via DLL sideloading and batch files; this cross-actor compromise secured persistent access to diplomatic and defense networks in Ukraine, Afghanistan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and GDI, and Indian military institutions, enabling exfiltration of politically sensitive intelligence and advanced research data while reducing development overhead and underscoring the need for robust supply-chain security, network segmentation and proactive vulnerability management.
hits.title: Hackers with Russian Blizzard Steal Data from Rival Networks

hits.text: Since April 2024, the Russia-affiliated threat actor Void Blizzard (aka Laundry Bear) has targeted over 20 NGOs and multiple government, defense, transportation, media and healthcare organizations across NATO member states, Western Europe, North America and Ukraine, initially leveraging password spraying and stolen credentials—likely purchased from cybercrime marketplaces—to access Exchange and SharePoint Online, enumerate Microsoft Entra ID via AzureHound, and exfiltrate large volumes of emails and files. More recently, the group shifted to adversary-in-the-middle spear-phishing using a typosquatted “micsrosoftonline[.]com” domain and an Evilginx-based phishing page delivered through malicious QR codes in forged European Defense and Security Summit PDF invitations, automating bulk data collection via Exchange, Microsoft Graph and Teams web client. Overlaps with Forest Blizzard, Midnight Blizzard and Secret Blizzard indicate coordinated Russian strategic espionage, and a September 2024 pass-the-cookie breach of a Dutch police account underscores their evolving cookie-theft capabilities—highlighting urgent needs for phishing-resistant MFA and hardened Entra ID configurations.
hits.title: Russian Hackers Breach 20+ NGOs Using Evilginx Phishing via Fake Microsoft Entra Pages

canonical_entities: military and government organizations in Hong Kong, Taiwan, Vietnam, the Philippines and Indonesia
hits.text: In their June 16, 2015 report, Unit 42 unveiled Operation Lotus Blossom, a three-year, state-sponsored cyber-espionage campaign against military and government organizations in Hong Kong, Taiwan, Vietnam, the Philippines and Indonesia, in which over 50 spearphishing attacks exploited enticing subject lines and decoy personnel-roster documents to deploy the custom “Elise” Trojan backdoor in three variants capable of evading virtual-machine analysis, contacting C2 servers for instructions and exfiltrating data; Unit 42’s use of Palo Alto Networks’ AutoFocus and WildFire platforms enabled the rapid correlation of samples and the deployment of IPS signature 14358 to block Elise, and they recommend that defenders review the published indicators of compromise in the full report and GitHub repo, bolster email security controls and ensure WildFire and Threat Prevention signatures are properly implemented to thwart future Lotus Blossom intrusions.
hits.title: Operation Lotus Blossom: A New Nation-State Cyberthreat?

hits.text: Secret Blizzard, attributed to Russia’s FSB and active for over seven years, has escalated state-level espionage by hijacking the infrastructure and tools of at least six threat actors—most notably Pakistan’s Storm-0156 (aka SideCopy/APT36)—to target Windows environments in ministries of foreign affairs, embassies and defense departments worldwide. Since November 2022, it has abused Storm-0156’s CrimsonRAT and Arsenal toolsets via DLL-sideloading to deploy its own backdoors TwoDash, MiniPocket, TinyTurla variant and Statuezy clipboard monitor, redirecting C2 traffic to its infrastructure. In October 2023 it added the Golang-based Wainscot backdoor alongside a Linux variant, enabling command execution, file transfer, screenshots and keylogging. The campaign has successfully exfiltrated politically sensitive data from Afghan and Indian government networks, highlighting the need for vigilant C2 traffic analysis, DLL integrity checks and behavioral detection of novel payloads.
hits.title: Secret Blizzard Hackers Attack Windows Infrastructure Using Multiple Hacking Tools

hits.text: McAfee researchers at RSA Conference 2019 revealed that Operation Sharpshooter—a previously disclosed December 2018 espionage campaign first observed via October 25 weaponized macro-laden Dropbox documents—actually began as early as September 2017, using embedded shellcode in Microsoft Word to deploy a modular, in-memory second-stage implant dubbed “Rising Sun.” Rising Sun, which reuses source code from the Lazarus Group’s Duuzer backdoor, performs reconnaissance, encrypts and exfiltrates system data (computer names, IP addresses, native OS details) and communicates with multiple newly identified command-and-control servers. Initially detected in 87 global organizations—50 percent in U.S. defense, nuclear, energy and financial sectors—the ongoing campaign has expanded to target financial services, government and critical infrastructure in Germany, Turkey, the U.K. and the U.S., exhibiting TTP overlaps and code reuse linking it to Lazarus operations. These findings underscore the need for strengthened macro and memory-resident malware defenses, proactive C2 infrastructure takedown efforts and enhanced attribution methodologies.
hits.title: RSAC 2019: New Operation Sharpshooter Data Reveals Higher Complexity, Scope | Threatpost

hits.text: Last week Google’s Threat Analysis Group, in partnership with The Citizen Lab, exposed an in-the-wild exploit chain developed by the commercial surveillance vendor Intellexa in Egypt that leverages a man-in-the-middle injection on HTTP traffic to silently redirect targets first to c.betly[.]me and then to sec-flare[.]com, delivering Predator spyware without any user interaction; on iOS this chain combined Safari RCE (CVE-2023-41993), certificate validation bypass (CVE-2023-41991) and XNU kernel local privilege escalation (CVE-2023-41992) and was patched in iOS 16.7/17.0.1, while on Android initial Chrome renderer RCE (CVE-2023-4762), delivered via MITM or one-time links, was patched on September 5; this campaign highlights the serious risk posed by proliferating commercial spyware, underscores the urgency of enforcing universal HTTPS and enabling Chrome’s HTTPS-First Mode, and demonstrates the critical need for organizations and users to apply the latest OS and browser updates, deploy encrypted-traffic protections, and monitor for anomalous network redirects to mitigate future attacks.

hits.text: Unit 42 researchers have uncovered a new, substantially upgraded variant of the Kazuar .NET backdoor—previously observed in 2017 as a second-stage payload by Russian Federal Security Service–linked Pensive Ursa (Turla/Uroburos)—that re-emerged in July 2023 targeting Ukrainian defense organizations via a multi-stage Capibar loader to steal Signal messages, cloud and source-control credentials and other high-value data. This variant adds robust anti-analysis checks (Assembly.Location byte-array loader validation, faked 2008 compilation timestamps), extensive string encryption (multiple custom and ConfuserEx ciphers), hybrid AES payload encryption with RSA-encrypted IV/key plus HMAC-MD5 integrity, and obfuscation of IOCs. It supports 45 discrete commands for system profiling, credential theft and automated task workflows in a multithreaded solver component that writes AES- and RSA-protected result files. Kazuar also implements multiple injection modes (inject, browser- and svchost.exe-centric zombify, combined fallback, remote proxy, single and headless) and uses GUID-derived pseudorandom directories and mutexes to evade detection, while hard-coded agent and build identifiers enable variant tracking. Code overlap with Sunburst underscores its sophistication. Unit 42 has released detailed IOCs, artifacts and a GitHub appendix, and recommends Palo Alto Networks NGFW Advanced Threat Prevention, Cortex XDR, XSIAM, Advanced WildFire and Unit 42 incident response engagement to detect, hunt and mitigate this persistent threat.
hits.title: Over the Kazuar’s Nest: Cracking Down on a Freshly Hatched Backdoor Used by Pensive Ursa (Aka Turla)

canonical_entities: diplomatic and defense networks in Ukraine
hits.text: Secret Blizzard, the Russian FSB’s Center 16, has escalated global espionage by co-opting C2 infrastructures of at least six threat actors—including Pakistan-based Storm-0156, Hazel Sandstorm and Storm-0473—to install backdoors (CrimsonRAT, Wainscot), deploy custom payloads (TwoDash downloader, MiniPocket fetcher), a TinyTurla variant disguised as a Windows service, and the Statuezy clipboard-monitoring trojan via DLL sideloading and batch files; this cross-actor compromise secured persistent access to diplomatic and defense networks in Ukraine, Afghanistan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and GDI, and Indian military institutions, enabling exfiltration of politically sensitive intelligence and advanced research data while reducing development overhead and underscoring the need for robust supply-chain security, network segmentation and proactive vulnerability management.
hits.title: Hackers with Russian Blizzard Steal Data from Rival Networks

canonical_entities: Launch EC2 instances across regions via VPN
hits.text: Unit42’s “EleKtra-Leak” campaign, active since December 2020, uses automated scripts to clone public GitHub repos every few minutes, extract exposed AWS IAM keys within five minutes, then—if not blocked by GitHub-AWS quarantine policies—execute rapid AWS reconnaissance (DescribeRegions), create security groups, and launch hundreds of EC2 instances across regions via VPN for Monero cryptojacking, generating over 400 API calls in seven minutes. Between Aug. 30 and Oct. 6, 2023, researchers tracked 474 actor-controlled miners. The actor employs custom mining software and blocklists high-profile AWS account IDs to avoid honey traps. Leveraging the Prisma Cloud HoneyCloud project’s ephemeral key leaks and policy overrides, Unit42 obtained full visibility, informing Prisma Cloud Secrets Security, CI/CD IaC scanning, Cortex XDR, and recommendations for independent repo scanning, strict IAM policies, and continuous monitoring.
hits.title: CloudKeys in the Air: Tracking Malicious Operations of Exposed IAM Keys

hits.text: In early April, Palo Alto Networks’ Advanced WildFire and Cortex XDR uncovered SnipBot—a new v5.0 iteration of the RomCom RAT family—employing advanced window message–based control-flow obfuscation and anti-sandbox checks (filename hash and HKCU\…\RecentDocs entries) in a multi-stage chain beginning with a PDF-labeled EXE downloader signed using a likely stolen certificate; the downloader contacts xeontime[.]com for config-pdf.dll, which uses registry-based COM hijacking to load keyprov.dll from drvmcprotect[.]com into explorer.exe, decrypts payloads stored in HKCU\Software\AppDataSoft\Software, and opens a TCP listener on port 1342 for commands to update, delete, or execute modules. The main backdoor single.dll (mutex “SnipMutex”) supports 27 encrypted commands for drive and process enumeration, file upload/download, and remote module execution, facilitating network pivoting and targeted file exfiltration. Active since December 2023 (RomCom activity since 2022), SnipBot’s tactics, stolen certificates, unique obfuscation, and sophisticated loader underscore a high-risk threat actor likely focused on intelligence gathering; Palo Alto products classify its samples, URLs, and domains as malicious to prevent compromise.
hits.title: Inside SnipBot: The Latest RomCom Malware Variant

canonical_entities: ZIP files masquerading as legitimate updates
hits.text: Unit 42 has observed a sharp rise in post-intrusion WastedLocker ransomware attacks by the Evil Corp group—already known for Dridex—against large U.S. organizations in sectors from manufacturing to legal services, with initial compromise typically via ZIP files masquerading as legitimate updates that deploy a SocGholish JavaScript loader to profile systems and invoke PowerShell-based Cobalt Strike payloads; attackers then leverage WMI and PsExec for lateral movement, identify high-value and backup systems, elevate privileges, disable Windows Defender, delete shadow copies, install WastedLocker as a service, and encrypt files using a “.<victim_name>wasted” extension while appending ransom notes (“.<victim_name>wasted_info”) with contact addresses on ProtonMail, Airmail and others. Palo Alto Networks’ WildFire, Cortex XDR (anti-ransomware and behavioral threat protection), NGFW DNS signatures and AutoFocus tagging detect and prevent WastedLocker activity; organizations are urged to implement robust, off-site backup strategies and hardened cybersecurity controls to mitigate this high-impact targeted ransomware threat.
hits.title: Threat Assessment: WastedLocker Ransomware

hits.text: Since April 2024, the Russia-affiliated threat actor Void Blizzard (aka Laundry Bear) has targeted over 20 NGOs and multiple government, defense, transportation, media and healthcare organizations across NATO member states, Western Europe, North America and Ukraine, initially leveraging password spraying and stolen credentials—likely purchased from cybercrime marketplaces—to access Exchange and SharePoint Online, enumerate Microsoft Entra ID via AzureHound, and exfiltrate large volumes of emails and files. More recently, the group shifted to adversary-in-the-middle spear-phishing using a typosquatted “micsrosoftonline[.]com” domain and an Evilginx-based phishing page delivered through malicious QR codes in forged European Defense and Security Summit PDF invitations, automating bulk data collection via Exchange, Microsoft Graph and Teams web client. Overlaps with Forest Blizzard, Midnight Blizzard and Secret Blizzard indicate coordinated Russian strategic espionage, and a September 2024 pass-the-cookie breach of a Dutch police account underscores their evolving cookie-theft capabilities—highlighting urgent needs for phishing-resistant MFA and hardened Entra ID configurations.
hits.title: Russian Hackers Breach 20+ NGOs Using Evilginx Phishing via Fake Microsoft Entra Pages

hits.text: Microsoft Threat Intelligence has observed the Russia-based SVR actor Midnight Blizzard (aka NOBELIUM, APT29/UNC2452/Cozy Bear) launch a highly targeted social-engineering campaign since at least late May 2023 by leveraging previously compromised small-business Microsoft 365 tenants to create security-themed onmicrosoft.com domains and Teams accounts that masquerade as technical-support entities; attackers then initiate Microsoft Teams chat requests to elicit approval of MFA prompts or codes via Microsoft Authenticator, enabling credential theft, access to fewer than 40 global organizations across government, NGOs, IT services, technology, manufacturing and media sectors, and subsequent post-compromise activities including data exfiltration and attempts to add managed devices via Microsoft Entra ID to bypass conditional access. Microsoft has mitigated the malicious domains, directly notified affected customers, and recommends phishing-resistant authentication, Conditional Access policies, Microsoft Teams best practices, auditing, and user education to detect and prevent unsolicited MFA requests.
hits.title: Midnight Blizzard conducts targeted social engineering over Microsoft Teams | Microsoft Security Blog

hits.text: Secret Blizzard, attributed to Russia’s FSB and active for over seven years, has escalated state-level espionage by hijacking the infrastructure and tools of at least six threat actors—most notably Pakistan’s Storm-0156 (aka SideCopy/APT36)—to target Windows environments in ministries of foreign affairs, embassies and defense departments worldwide. Since November 2022, it has abused Storm-0156’s CrimsonRAT and Arsenal toolsets via DLL-sideloading to deploy its own backdoors TwoDash, MiniPocket, TinyTurla variant and Statuezy clipboard monitor, redirecting C2 traffic to its infrastructure. In October 2023 it added the Golang-based Wainscot backdoor alongside a Linux variant, enabling command execution, file transfer, screenshots and keylogging. The campaign has successfully exfiltrated politically sensitive data from Afghan and Indian government networks, highlighting the need for vigilant C2 traffic analysis, DLL integrity checks and behavioral detection of novel payloads.
hits.title: Secret Blizzard Hackers Attack Windows Infrastructure Using Multiple Hacking Tools

canonical_entities: Remote Code Execution via ms-msdt URI in Word/RTF documents
ms-msdt URI-based RCE in Word/RTF documents
hits.text: In late May 2022, Symantec identified multiple threat actors exploiting the MSDT Follina bug (CVE-2022-30190) through ms-msdt URI-based RCE in Word/RTF documents that load a malicious HTML via Word’s remote template feature to launch msdt.exe, sdiagnhost.exe and ultimately PowerShell—bypassing the need for macros—to install a digitally signed AsyncRAT remote access Trojan that performs anti-analysis checks, collects hardware IDs, user names, execution paths and OS details, and maintains C&C communications, alongside parallel deployments of a browser infostealer targeting cookies and saved credentials in Firefox, Chrome and Edge. Symantec customers should apply Microsoft’s advisories or disable the ms-msdt handler, update Symantec Endpoint definitions (File-based-Downloader-Backdoor:Async, InfoStealer) and monitor for related IOCs to thwart these rapid, damaging campaigns.
hits.title: Attackers Exploit MSDT Follina Bug to Drop RAT, Infostealer | Symantec Enterprise Blogs

hits.text: In August 2025 the FBI issued a public service announcement that FSB-linked Berserk Bear (aka Blue Kraken, Crouching Yeti, Dragonfly, Koala Team) has been exploiting the seven-year-old Cisco IOS/IOS XE Smart Install remote code execution/DoS vulnerability (CVE-2018-0171) to compromise critical infrastructure worldwide. Since Cisco first detected opportunistic attacks in November 2021, the group has collected configuration files from thousands of unpatched devices associated with U.S. critical infrastructure sectors, covertly modified those configs to maintain persistent unauthorized access, and conducted network reconnaissance targeting ICS-related protocols and applications. Cisco Talos reports that the campaign, referred to as Static Tundra, has aggressively hit telecommunications, higher education, and manufacturing networks across North America, Asia, Africa, and Europe, deploying custom SNMP tools and the SYNful Knock firmware implant—originally identified by FireEye in 2015—to evade detection and embed for years. The FBI’s warning underscores the urgent need for organizations to patch CVE-2018-0171, disable Smart Install, and implement comprehensive hardening, as other state-sponsored actors are likely conducting similar network device compromise campaigns.
hits.title: FBI warns of Russian hackers exploiting 7-year-old Cisco flaw

hits.text: McAfee researchers at RSA Conference 2019 revealed that Operation Sharpshooter—a previously disclosed December 2018 espionage campaign first observed via October 25 weaponized macro-laden Dropbox documents—actually began as early as September 2017, using embedded shellcode in Microsoft Word to deploy a modular, in-memory second-stage implant dubbed “Rising Sun.” Rising Sun, which reuses source code from the Lazarus Group’s Duuzer backdoor, performs reconnaissance, encrypts and exfiltrates system data (computer names, IP addresses, native OS details) and communicates with multiple newly identified command-and-control servers. Initially detected in 87 global organizations—50 percent in U.S. defense, nuclear, energy and financial sectors—the ongoing campaign has expanded to target financial services, government and critical infrastructure in Germany, Turkey, the U.K. and the U.S., exhibiting TTP overlaps and code reuse linking it to Lazarus operations. These findings underscore the need for strengthened macro and memory-resident malware defenses, proactive C2 infrastructure takedown efforts and enhanced attribution methodologies.
hits.title: RSAC 2019: New Operation Sharpshooter Data Reveals Higher Complexity, Scope | Threatpost

hits.text: Last week Google’s Threat Analysis Group, in partnership with The Citizen Lab, exposed an in-the-wild exploit chain developed by the commercial surveillance vendor Intellexa in Egypt that leverages a man-in-the-middle injection on HTTP traffic to silently redirect targets first to c.betly[.]me and then to sec-flare[.]com, delivering Predator spyware without any user interaction; on iOS this chain combined Safari RCE (CVE-2023-41993), certificate validation bypass (CVE-2023-41991) and XNU kernel local privilege escalation (CVE-2023-41992) and was patched in iOS 16.7/17.0.1, while on Android initial Chrome renderer RCE (CVE-2023-4762), delivered via MITM or one-time links, was patched on September 5; this campaign highlights the serious risk posed by proliferating commercial spyware, underscores the urgency of enforcing universal HTTPS and enabling Chrome’s HTTPS-First Mode, and demonstrates the critical need for organizations and users to apply the latest OS and browser updates, deploy encrypted-traffic protections, and monitor for anomalous network redirects to mitigate future attacks.
hits.title: 0-days exploited by commercial surveillance vendor in Egypt

canonical_entities: Palo Alto Networks NGFW Advanced Threat Prevention
retrieved_context.text: Unit 42 researchers have uncovered a new, substantially upgraded variant of the Kazuar .NET backdoor—previously observed in 2017 as a second-stage payload by Russian Federal Security Service–linked Pensive Ursa (Turla/Uroburos)—that re-emerged in July 2023 targeting Ukrainian defense organizations via a multi-stage Capibar loader to steal Signal messages, cloud and source-control credentials and other high-value data. This variant adds robust anti-analysis checks (Assembly.Location byte-array loader validation, faked 2008 compilation timestamps), extensive string encryption (multiple custom and ConfuserEx ciphers), hybrid AES payload encryption with RSA-encrypted IV/key plus HMAC-MD5 integrity, and obfuscation of IOCs. It supports 45 discrete commands for system profiling, credential theft and automated task workflows in a multithreaded solver component that writes AES- and RSA-protected result files. Kazuar also implements multiple injection modes (inject, browser- and svchost.exe-centric zombify, combined fallback, remote proxy, single and headless) and uses GUID-derived pseudorandom directories and mutexes to evade detection, while hard-coded agent and build identifiers enable variant tracking. Code overlap with Sunburst underscores its sophistication. Unit 42 has released detailed IOCs, artifacts and a GitHub appendix, and recommends Palo Alto Networks NGFW Advanced Threat Prevention, Cortex XDR, XSIAM, Advanced WildFire and Unit 42 incident response engagement to detect, hunt and mitigate this persistent threat.
retrieved_context.title: Over the Kazuar’s Nest: Cracking Down on a Freshly Hatched Backdoor Used by Pensive Ursa (Aka Turla)

retrieved_context.text: In August 2025 the FBI issued a public service announcement that FSB-linked Berserk Bear (aka Blue Kraken, Crouching Yeti, Dragonfly, Koala Team) has been exploiting the seven-year-old Cisco IOS/IOS XE Smart Install remote code execution/DoS vulnerability (CVE-2018-0171) to compromise critical infrastructure worldwide. Since Cisco first detected opportunistic attacks in November 2021, the group has collected configuration files from thousands of unpatched devices associated with U.S. critical infrastructure sectors, covertly modified those configs to maintain persistent unauthorized access, and conducted network reconnaissance targeting ICS-related protocols and applications. Cisco Talos reports that the campaign, referred to as Static Tundra, has aggressively hit telecommunications, higher education, and manufacturing networks across North America, Asia, Africa, and Europe, deploying custom SNMP tools and the SYNful Knock firmware implant—originally identified by FireEye in 2015—to evade detection and embed for years. The FBI’s warning underscores the urgent need for organizations to patch CVE-2018-0171, disable Smart Install, and implement comprehensive hardening, as other state-sponsored actors are likely conducting similar network device compromise campaigns.
retrieved_context.title: FBI warns of Russian hackers exploiting 7-year-old Cisco flaw

retrieved_context.text: In early April, Palo Alto Networks’ Advanced WildFire and Cortex XDR uncovered SnipBot—a new v5.0 iteration of the RomCom RAT family—employing advanced window message–based control-flow obfuscation and anti-sandbox checks (filename hash and HKCU\…\RecentDocs entries) in a multi-stage chain beginning with a PDF-labeled EXE downloader signed using a likely stolen certificate; the downloader contacts xeontime[.]com for config-pdf.dll, which uses registry-based COM hijacking to load keyprov.dll from drvmcprotect[.]com into explorer.exe, decrypts payloads stored in HKCU\Software\AppDataSoft\Software, and opens a TCP listener on port 1342 for commands to update, delete, or execute modules. The main backdoor single.dll (mutex “SnipMutex”) supports 27 encrypted commands for drive and process enumeration, file upload/download, and remote module execution, facilitating network pivoting and targeted file exfiltration. Active since December 2023 (RomCom activity since 2022), SnipBot’s tactics, stolen certificates, unique obfuscation, and sophisticated loader underscore a high-risk threat actor likely focused on intelligence gathering; Palo Alto products classify its samples, URLs, and domains as malicious to prevent compromise.
retrieved_context.title: Inside SnipBot: The Latest RomCom Malware Variant

retrieved_context.text: McAfee researchers at RSA Conference 2019 revealed that Operation Sharpshooter—a previously disclosed December 2018 espionage campaign first observed via October 25 weaponized macro-laden Dropbox documents—actually began as early as September 2017, using embedded shellcode in Microsoft Word to deploy a modular, in-memory second-stage implant dubbed “Rising Sun.” Rising Sun, which reuses source code from the Lazarus Group’s Duuzer backdoor, performs reconnaissance, encrypts and exfiltrates system data (computer names, IP addresses, native OS details) and communicates with multiple newly identified command-and-control servers. Initially detected in 87 global organizations—50 percent in U.S. defense, nuclear, energy and financial sectors—the ongoing campaign has expanded to target financial services, government and critical infrastructure in Germany, Turkey, the U.K. and the U.S., exhibiting TTP overlaps and code reuse linking it to Lazarus operations. These findings underscore the need for strengthened macro and memory-resident malware defenses, proactive C2 infrastructure takedown efforts and enhanced attribution methodologies.
retrieved_context.title: RSAC 2019: New Operation Sharpshooter Data Reveals Higher Complexity, Scope | Threatpost

retrieved_context.text: Last week Google’s Threat Analysis Group, in partnership with The Citizen Lab, exposed an in-the-wild exploit chain developed by the commercial surveillance vendor Intellexa in Egypt that leverages a man-in-the-middle injection on HTTP traffic to silently redirect targets first to c.betly[.]me and then to sec-flare[.]com, delivering Predator spyware without any user interaction; on iOS this chain combined Safari RCE (CVE-2023-41993), certificate validation bypass (CVE-2023-41991) and XNU kernel local privilege escalation (CVE-2023-41992) and was patched in iOS 16.7/17.0.1, while on Android initial Chrome renderer RCE (CVE-2023-4762), delivered via MITM or one-time links, was patched on September 5; this campaign highlights the serious risk posed by proliferating commercial spyware, underscores the urgency of enforcing universal HTTPS and enabling Chrome’s HTTPS-First Mode, and demonstrates the critical need for organizations and users to apply the latest OS and browser updates, deploy encrypted-traffic protections, and monitor for anomalous network redirects to mitigate future attacks.
retrieved_context.title: 0-days exploited by commercial surveillance vendor in Egypt

retrieved_context.text: Microsoft Threat Intelligence has observed the Russia-based SVR actor Midnight Blizzard (aka NOBELIUM, APT29/UNC2452/Cozy Bear) launch a highly targeted social-engineering campaign since at least late May 2023 by leveraging previously compromised small-business Microsoft 365 tenants to create security-themed onmicrosoft.com domains and Teams accounts that masquerade as technical-support entities; attackers then initiate Microsoft Teams chat requests to elicit approval of MFA prompts or codes via Microsoft Authenticator, enabling credential theft, access to fewer than 40 global organizations across government, NGOs, IT services, technology, manufacturing and media sectors, and subsequent post-compromise activities including data exfiltration and attempts to add managed devices via Microsoft Entra ID to bypass conditional access. Microsoft has mitigated the malicious domains, directly notified affected customers, and recommends phishing-resistant authentication, Conditional Access policies, Microsoft Teams best practices, auditing, and user education to detect and prevent unsolicited MFA requests.
retrieved_context.title: Midnight Blizzard conducts targeted social engineering over Microsoft Teams | Microsoft Security Blog

retrieved_context.text: Since April 2024, the Russia-affiliated threat actor Void Blizzard (aka Laundry Bear) has targeted over 20 NGOs and multiple government, defense, transportation, media and healthcare organizations across NATO member states, Western Europe, North America and Ukraine, initially leveraging password spraying and stolen credentials—likely purchased from cybercrime marketplaces—to access Exchange and SharePoint Online, enumerate Microsoft Entra ID via AzureHound, and exfiltrate large volumes of emails and files. More recently, the group shifted to adversary-in-the-middle spear-phishing using a typosquatted “micsrosoftonline[.]com” domain and an Evilginx-based phishing page delivered through malicious QR codes in forged European Defense and Security Summit PDF invitations, automating bulk data collection via Exchange, Microsoft Graph and Teams web client. hits.text: At least four distinct campaigns exploited CVE-2023-37580, a reflected XSS zero-day in Zimbra Collaboration Suite, to siphon emails, attachments, user credentials and authentication tokens from government organizations worldwide before the July 5 hotfix and July 25 official patch; in chronological order, unidentified actors targeted Greece on June 29 via malicious URLs that, when clicked during active Zimbra sessions, deployed a data-theft framework and auto-forward rules, Winter Vivern’s APT leveraged unique exploit links to hit Moldova and Tunisia between July 11 and 25, another group used a phishing-style XSS link in Vietnam to harvest webmail credentials and exfiltrate them to a compromised government domain, and on August 25 unknown attackers employed an N-day variant to steal tokens from Pakistan’s mail servers; Google’s Threat Analysis Group warns these campaigns underscore the urgency of promptly applying open-source fixes, hardening mail-server code to prevent XSS, and maintaining vigilant patch management as attackers continuously monitor public repositories for unpatched vulnerabilities.
hits.title: APTs Swarm Zimbra Zero-Day to Steal Government Info Worldwide

hits.text: ESET researchers uncovered a novel crimeware campaign, active in Czechia since November 2023 and paused only by the arrest of a suspect in March 2024, in which attackers combined social engineering, phishing and Android malware to target clients of three Czech banks via deceptive SMS links to malicious progressive web apps (PWAs) and WebAPKs; after harvesting credentials, the attackers lured victims into installing NGate, a custom Android malware named for its incorporation of the open-source NFCGate tool, which relays NFC data from victims’ unrooted smartphones to an attacker’s rooted device, enabling the emulation of cloned payment cards and unauthorized ATM withdrawals (over 160,000 CZK recovered from just three recent victims, with likely higher overall losses), with a fallback tactic of illicit bank-to-bank transfers when the relay method fails.
hits.title: NGate Android malware relays NFC traffic to steal cash

retrieved_context.text: At least four distinct campaigns exploited CVE-2023-37580, a reflected XSS zero-day in Zimbra Collaboration Suite, to siphon emails, attachments, user credentials and authentication tokens from government organizations worldwide before the July 5 hotfix and July 25 official patch; in chronological order, unidentified actors targeted Greece on June 29 via malicious URLs that, when clicked during active Zimbra sessions, deployed a data-theft framework and auto-forward rules, Winter Vivern’s APT leveraged unique exploit links to hit Moldova and Tunisia between July 11 and 25, another group used a phishing-style XSS link in Vietnam to harvest webmail credentials and exfiltrate them to a compromised government domain, and on August 25 unknown attackers employed an N-day variant to steal tokens from Pakistan’s mail servers; Google’s Threat Analysis Group warns these campaigns underscore the urgency of promptly applying open-source fixes, hardening mail-server code to prevent XSS, and maintaining vigilant patch management as attackers continuously monitor public repositories for unpatched vulnerabilities.
retrieved_context.title: APTs Swarm Zimbra Zero-Day to Steal Government Info Worldwide

retrieved_context.text: Secret Blizzard, attributed to Russia’s FSB and active for over seven years, has escalated state-level espionage by hijacking the infrastructure and tools of at least six threat actors—most notably Pakistan’s Storm-0156 (aka SideCopy/APT36)—to target Windows environments in ministries of foreign affairs, embassies and defense departments worldwide. Since November 2022, it has abused Storm-0156’s CrimsonRAT and Arsenal toolsets via DLL-sideloading to deploy its own backdoors TwoDash, MiniPocket, TinyTurla variant and Statuezy clipboard monitor, redirecting C2 traffic to its infrastructure. In October 2023 it added the Golang-based Wainscot backdoor alongside a Linux variant, enabling command execution, file transfer, screenshots and keylogging. The campaign has successfully exfiltrated politically sensitive data from Afghan and Indian government networks, highlighting the need for vigilant C2 traffic analysis, DLL integrity checks and behavioral detection of novel payloads.
retrieved_context.title: Secret Blizzard Hackers Attack Windows Infrastructure Using Multiple Hacking Tools

retrieved_context.text: ESET researchers uncovered a novel crimeware campaign, active in Czechia since November 2023 and paused only by the arrest of a suspect in March 2024, in which attackers combined social engineering, phishing and Android malware to target clients of three Czech banks via deceptive SMS links to malicious progressive web apps (PWAs) and WebAPKs; after harvesting credentials, the attackers lured victims into installing NGate, a custom Android malware named for its incorporation of the open-source NFCGate tool, which relays NFC data from victims’ unrooted smartphones to an attacker’s rooted device, enabling the emulation of cloned payment cards and unauthorized ATM withdrawals (over 160,000 CZK recovered from just three recent victims, with likely higher overall losses), with a fallback tactic of illicit bank-to-bank transfers when the relay method fails.
retrieved_context.title: NGate Android malware relays NFC traffic to steal cash

hits.text: Espionage actor Lotus Blossom (aka Spring Dragon, Billbug, Thrip), active since 2012 and of unconfirmed origin, has been targeting governments, manufacturing, media, and telecommunications organizations in Hong Kong, the Philippines, Taiwan, and Vietnam using a proprietary in-memory backdoor called Sagerunex (evolved from Evora). According to Cisco Talos, the group initiates Windows Management Instrumentation reconnaissance to enumerate user accounts, network configurations, processes, and directory structures, then either installs Sagerunex and ancillary tools when Internet connectivity is available or establishes a proxy via local settings or the “Venom” penetration-testing tool when it is not. Once injected as a DLL, Sagerunex conducts self-checks, beacons to its C2 server, and deploys modules for Chrome cookie theft, privilege escalation, proxy relaying, and file archiving for exfiltration. Notably, two newly discovered Sagerunex variants abuse Dropbox and Twitter APIs or the Zimbra mail API as unconventional C2 channels to evade detection and sustain long-term persistence with command-shell implants. This evolving toolkit underscores a significant threat to regional critical infrastructure and highlights the need for enhanced WMI command logging, in-memory attack detection, and network monitoring for anomalous third-party cloud service traffic to disrupt Lotus Blossom’s espionage operations.
hits.title: Espionage Actor 'Lotus Blossom' Targets Southeast Asia
