canonical_entities: ZIP files masquerading as legitimate updates
hits.text: Unit 42 has observed a sharp rise in post-intrusion WastedLocker ransomware attacks by the Evil Corp group—already known for Dridex—against large U.S. organizations in sectors from manufacturing to legal services, with initial compromise typically via ZIP files masquerading as legitimate updates that deploy a SocGholish JavaScript loader to profile systems and invoke PowerShell-based Cobalt Strike payloads; attackers then leverage WMI and PsExec for lateral movement, identify high-value and backup systems, elevate privileges, disable Windows Defender, delete shadow copies, install WastedLocker as a service, and encrypt files using a “.<victim_name>wasted” extension while appending ransom notes (“.<victim_name>wasted_info”) with contact addresses on ProtonMail, Airmail and others. Palo Alto Networks’ WildFire, Cortex XDR (anti-ransomware and behavioral threat protection), NGFW DNS signatures and AutoFocus tagging detect and prevent WastedLocker activity; organizations are urged to implement robust, off-site backup strategies and hardened cybersecurity controls to mitigate this high-impact targeted ransomware threat.
hits.title: Threat Assessment: WastedLocker Ransomware

canonical_entities: Remote Code Execution via ms-msdt URI in Word/RTF documents
ms-msdt URI-based RCE in Word/RTF documents
hits.text: In late May 2022, Symantec identified multiple threat actors exploiting the MSDT Follina bug (CVE-2022-30190) through ms-msdt URI-based RCE in Word/RTF documents that load a malicious HTML via Word’s remote template feature to launch msdt.exe, sdiagnhost.exe and ultimately PowerShell—bypassing the need for macros—to install a digitally signed AsyncRAT remote access Trojan that performs anti-analysis checks, collects hardware IDs, user names, execution paths and OS details, and maintains C&C communications, alongside parallel deployments of a browser infostealer targeting cookies and saved credentials in Firefox, Chrome and Edge. Symantec customers should apply Microsoft’s advisories or disable the ms-msdt handler, update Symantec Endpoint definitions (File-based-Downloader-Backdoor:Async, InfoStealer) and monitor for related IOCs to thwart these rapid, damaging campaigns.
hits.title: Attackers Exploit MSDT Follina Bug to Drop RAT, Infostealer | Symantec Enterprise Blogs

hits.text: Sea Turtle, also known as Cosmic Wolf, Marbled Dust, Teal Kurma and UNC1326, has been conducting a stealthy, Türkiye-linked cyber espionage campaign since at least January 2017, recently targeting Dutch ISPs, telecom, IT-service and media providers as well as Kurdish websites via supply-chain and island-hopping attacks to harvest politically sensitive personal data and potential dissident communications. First detailed by Cisco Talos in April 2019 for state-sponsored DNS hijacking to redirect legitimate domain queries to attacker-controlled servers, the group elevated its upstream foothold tactics in late 2021 by exploiting known telecom and IT vulnerabilities across Armenia, Cyprus, Greece, Iraq and Syria, per Microsoft. Between 2021 and 2023 PwC observed deployment of “SnappyTCP,” a simple Linux/Unix reverse-TCP web shell (with and without OpenSSL/TLS) for persistence and C2, and Hunt & Hackett’s 2023 incident revealed credential-theft via a compromised cPanel account used to deploy SnappyTCP, tar and expose email archives publicly for direct exfiltration. Organizations should enforce strong password policies, 2FA, login-rate limiting, SSH monitoring and timely patching to mitigate this ongoing espionage threat.
hits.title: Sea Turtle Cyber Espionage Campaign Targets Dutch IT and Telecom Companies

hits.text: Security researcher Marc Newlin of SkySafe disclosed CVE-2023-45866, a critical, decade-old keystroke-injection flaw in the Bluetooth host state-machine that exploits an unauthenticated pairing mechanism in the Bluetooth specification to trick macOS (13.3.3), iOS (16.6, even in Lockdown Mode), Android (from 4.2.2 through 14 on devices including Pixel 7/6/4a, Pixel 2, Nexus 5, BLU DASH), and Linux BlueZ stacks (Ubuntu 18.04–23.10) into pairing with a malicious emulated keyboard, enabling remote attackers within Bluetooth range to run a Python-based script, inject arbitrary keystrokes, install apps, forward emails or texts, and execute commands without user confirmation or biometric/password authentication. After informing Apple, Google, Canonical, and the Bluetooth SIG between August and September, patches have been released for Android 11–14 and BlueZ (via GitHub) but Apple has yet to announce a timeline for CVE-2023-42929, proof-of-concept exploit scripts will be published in January, and no active in-the-wild exploitation has been observed to date.
hits.title: Critical Bluetooth Flaw Exposes Android, Apple & Linux Devices to Takeover

canonical_entities: enumerates SSH directories to harvest credentials
Persistence is achieved through multiple cronjobs
hits.text: Aqua Security’s Nautilus team has uncovered Hadooken, a new Linux malware targeting Oracle WebLogic servers via weak passwords. Post-compromise, attackers deploy redundant shell and Python scripts to ensure download and execution of Hadooken, which enumerates SSH directories to harvest credentials, moves laterally, and clears logs. Hadooken then drops a three-path cryptominer and a Tsunami backdoor with a randomized name, the latter reserved for potential later-stage attacks. Persistence is achieved through multiple cronjobs under varied names and frequencies stored across cron directories. The malware is hosted on two IPs—one German address linked to TeamTNT and Gang 8220, the other inactive in Russia—where researchers also identified a Mallox ransomware PowerShell loader targeting Windows. Static analysis links Hadooken to Rhombus and NoEscape families. With over 230,000 internet-connected WebLogic instances—hundreds of which expose vulnerable admin consoles—this campaign underscores the dual risk of cryptojacking and ransomware across Linux and Windows environments.
hits.title: New 'Hadooken' Linux Malware Targets WebLogic Servers - SecurityWeek

hits.text: In early April, Palo Alto Networks’ Advanced WildFire and Cortex XDR uncovered SnipBot—a new v5.0 iteration of the RomCom RAT family—employing advanced window message–based control-flow obfuscation and anti-sandbox checks (filename hash and HKCU\…\RecentDocs entries) in a multi-stage chain beginning with a PDF-labeled EXE downloader signed using a likely stolen certificate; the downloader contacts xeontime[.]com for config-pdf.dll, which uses registry-based COM hijacking to load keyprov.dll from drvmcprotect[.]com into explorer.exe, decrypts payloads stored in HKCU\Software\AppDataSoft\Software, and opens a TCP listener on port 1342 for commands to update, delete, or execute modules. The main backdoor single.dll (mutex “SnipMutex”) supports 27 encrypted commands for drive and process enumeration, file upload/download, and remote module execution, facilitating network pivoting and targeted file exfiltration. Active since December 2023 (RomCom activity since 2022), SnipBot’s tactics, stolen certificates, unique obfuscation, and sophisticated loader underscore a high-risk threat actor likely focused on intelligence gathering; Palo Alto products classify its samples, URLs, and domains as malicious to prevent compromise.
hits.title: Inside SnipBot: The Latest RomCom Malware Variant

Post-compromise, attackers deploy redundant shell and Python scripts to ensure download and execution of Hadooken, which enumerates SSH directories to harvest credentials, moves laterally, and clears logs. Hadooken then drops a three-path cryptominer and a Tsunami backdoor with a randomized name, the latter reserved for potential later-stage attacks. Persistence is achieved through multiple cronjobs under varied names and frequencies stored across cron directories. The malware is hosted on two IPs—one German address linked to TeamTNT and Gang 8220, the other inactive in Russia—where researchers also identified a Mallox ransomware PowerShell loader targeting Windows. Static analysis links Hadooken to Rhombus and NoEscape families. With over 230,000 internet-connected WebLogic instances—hundreds of which expose vulnerable admin consoles—this campaign underscores the dual risk of cryptojacking and ransomware across Linux and Windows environments.
retrieved_context.title: New 'Hadooken' Linux Malware Targets WebLogic Servers - SecurityWeek

retrieved_context.text: In early April, Palo Alto Networks’ Advanced WildFire and Cortex XDR uncovered SnipBot—a new v5.0 iteration of the RomCom RAT family—employing advanced window message–based control-flow obfuscation and anti-sandbox checks (filename hash and HKCU\…\RecentDocs entries) in a multi-stage chain beginning with a PDF-labeled EXE downloader signed using a likely stolen certificate; the downloader contacts xeontime[.]com for config-pdf.dll, which uses registry-based COM hijacking to load keyprov.dll from drvmcprotect[.]com into explorer.exe, decrypts payloads stored in HKCU\Software\AppDataSoft\Software, and opens a TCP listener on port 1342 for commands to update, delete, or execute modules. The main backdoor single.dll (mutex “SnipMutex”) supports 27 encrypted commands for drive and process enumeration, file upload/download, and remote module execution, facilitating network pivoting and targeted file exfiltration. Active since December 2023 (RomCom activity since 2022), SnipBot’s tactics, stolen certificates, unique obfuscation, and sophisticated loader underscore a high-risk threat actor likely focused on intelligence gathering; Palo Alto products classify its samples, URLs, and domains as malicious to prevent compromise.
retrieved_context.title: Inside SnipBot: The Latest RomCom Malware Variant

hits.text: The North Korea-linked threat actor Slow Pisces (also tracked as Jade Sleet, PUKCHONG, TraderTraitor, and UNC4899) has been conducting a multi-stage malware campaign targeting cryptocurrency developers via LinkedIn job opportunity lures since at least June 2024, leveraging trojanized Python and JavaScript projects hosted on GitHub that employ YAML deserialization and EJS templating to execute gated payloads only to validated targets meeting specific criteria (IP address, geolocation, time, HTTP headers); the campaign delivers RN Loader and RN Stealer malware on macOS systems capable of harvesting system metadata, installed applications, SSH keys, AWS/Kubernetes/Google Cloud configuration files, and iCloud Keychain data, with payloads remaining memory-resident and deployed selectively to prevent analysis; Slow Pisces is assessed to be responsible for the February 2025 Bybit cryptocurrency exchange breach and operates alongside other North Korean clusters including Operation Dream Job, Contagious Interview, Alluring Pisces, and Moonstone Sleet, though with notably superior operational security practices involving heavily guarded payload delivery across infection stages.

hits.text: Microsoft Threat Intelligence has observed the Russia-based SVR actor Midnight Blizzard (aka NOBELIUM, APT29/UNC2452/Cozy Bear) launch a highly targeted social-engineering campaign since at least late May 2023 by leveraging previously compromised small-business Microsoft 365 tenants to create security-themed onmicrosoft.com domains and Teams accounts that masquerade as technical-support entities; attackers then initiate Microsoft Teams chat requests to elicit approval of MFA prompts or codes via Microsoft Authenticator, enabling credential theft, access to fewer than 40 global organizations across government, NGOs, IT services, technology, manufacturing and media sectors, and subsequent post-compromise activities including data exfiltration and attempts to add managed devices via Microsoft Entra ID to bypass conditional access. Microsoft has mitigated the malicious domains, directly notified affected customers, and recommends phishing-resistant authentication, Conditional Access policies, Microsoft Teams best practices, auditing, and user education to detect and prevent unsolicited MFA requests.
hits.title: Midnight Blizzard conducts targeted social engineering over Microsoft Teams | Microsoft Security Blog

hits.text: ESET researchers uncovered a novel crimeware campaign, active in Czechia since November 2023 and paused only by the arrest of a suspect in March 2024, in which attackers combined social engineering, phishing and Android malware to target clients of three Czech banks via deceptive SMS links to malicious progressive web apps (PWAs) and WebAPKs; after harvesting credentials, the attackers lured victims into installing NGate, a custom Android malware named for its incorporation of the open-source NFCGate tool, which relays NFC data from victims’ unrooted smartphones to an attacker’s rooted device, enabling the emulation of cloned payment cards and unauthorized ATM withdrawals (over 160,000 CZK recovered from just three recent victims, with likely higher overall losses), with a fallback tactic of illicit bank-to-bank transfers when the relay method fails.

hits.text: At least four distinct campaigns exploited CVE-2023-37580, a reflected XSS zero-day in Zimbra Collaboration Suite, to siphon emails, attachments, user credentials and authentication tokens from government organizations worldwide before the July 5 hotfix and July 25 official patch; in chronological order, unidentified actors targeted Greece on June 29 via malicious URLs that, when clicked during active Zimbra sessions, deployed a data-theft framework and auto-forward rules, Winter Vivern’s APT leveraged unique exploit links to hit Moldova and Tunisia between July 11 and 25, another group used a phishing-style XSS link in Vietnam to harvest webmail credentials and exfiltrate them to a compromised government domain, and on August 25 unknown attackers employed an N-day variant to steal tokens from Pakistan’s mail servers; Google’s Threat Analysis Group warns these campaigns underscore the urgency of promptly applying open-source fixes, hardening mail-server code to prevent XSS, and maintaining vigilant patch management as attackers continuously monitor public repositories for unpatched vulnerabilities.

hits.text: Since mid-November 2024, Russian nation-state actor Star Blizzard has significantly escalated its evasion tradecraft following public exposure by Microsoft Threat Intelligence: shifting from a single registrar (NameCheap) to multiple registrars (Hostinger, RealTime Register, GMO Internet) and implementing multi-stage redirection chains—embedding Microsoft 365 Safe Links in PDF lures that pass through Bitly and Cuttly shortened URLs and legitimate open-redirect sites (e.g., mechengsys[.]net) before landing on an Evilginx-equipped VPS (vidmemax[.]com)—to mount AiTM spear-phishing campaigns that harvest email credentials, including MFA tokens. Between July and August 2024 they also experimented with altered OneDrive file-share notifications—using ProtonMail accounts to spoof trusted senders and rewire the “Open” button URL to their Evilginx infrastructure—targeting individuals in politics, diplomacy, NGOs and think tanks. Historically, since 2022 Star Blizzard has iteratively refined detection evasion—employing server-side fingerprinting scripts, HubSpot and MailerLite email platforms to mask domains, DNS obfuscation, password-protected PDFs and randomized DGAs—with each ephemeral TTP swiftly modified, underscoring the need for continuous updates to email security controls, link inspection and behavioral detection.
hits.title: Star Blizzard increases sophistication and evasion in ongoing attacks | Microsoft Security Blog

hits.text: Since January 2021, Google’s Threat Analysis Group (TAG) has tracked a government-backed North Korean campaign that leverages social engineering via X (formerly Twitter) and encrypted messaging apps to befriend security researchers and deliver malicious files containing at least one unpatched 0-day in a popular software package; upon exploitation the custom shellcode performs anti-virtual-machine checks, captures system data and screenshots, and exfiltrates them to C2 infrastructure (e.g., 23.106.215[.]105, www.blgbeach[.]com), with the latest vulnerability reported and patched on September 12, 2023 (see TAG’s published RCA). hits.text: Microsoft Threat Intelligence Center has attributed the emerging H0lyGh0st ransomware, active since June 2021 and tracked as DEV-0530, to financially motivated North Korean state-sponsored actors with ties to PLUTONIUM (DarkSeoul/Andariel), which has compromised small-to-mid-sized businesses—including manufacturers, banks, schools and event planners—across multiple countries since September 2021 by deploying custom SiennaPurple (C++ BTLC_C.exe) and SiennaBlue (Go-based HolyRS.exe, HolyLock.exe, BLTC.exe) families that encrypt Windows files with a .h0lyenc extension, use string obfuscation and public-key management, and enforce persistence via a scheduled task called “lockertask”; victims receive a ransom note delivered over a .onion portal demanding Bitcoin payment under double-extortion threats to publish stolen data if unpaid; between October 2021 and May 2022 MSTIC observed iterative Go-based SiennaBlue variants sharing core encryption and network/intranet connectivity functions, and in April 2022 the group rolled out its latest BTLC.exe, which hard-codes ServerBaseURL fallback credentials for network shares, uploads victim public keys to a C2 server, and encrypts all drive files—underscoring the need for defenders to monitor anomalous scheduled tasks, default-credential share connections, .onion traffic, and the appearance of .h0lyenc files to detect and disrupt this evolving threat.

hits.text: Last week Google’s Threat Analysis Group, in partnership with The Citizen Lab, exposed an in-the-wild exploit chain developed by the commercial surveillance vendor Intellexa in Egypt that leverages a man-in-the-middle injection on HTTP traffic to silently redirect targets first to c.betly[.]me and then to sec-flare[.]com, delivering Predator spyware without any user interaction; on iOS this chain combined Safari RCE (CVE-2023-41993), certificate validation bypass (CVE-2023-41991) and XNU kernel local privilege escalation (CVE-2023-41992) and was patched in iOS 16.7/17.0.1, while on Android initial Chrome renderer RCE (CVE-2023-4762), delivered via MITM or one-time links, was patched on September 5; this campaign highlights the serious risk posed by proliferating commercial spyware, underscores the urgency of enforcing universal HTTPS and enabling Chrome’s HTTPS-First Mode, and demonstrates the critical need for organizations and users to apply the latest OS and browser updates, deploy encrypted-traffic protections, and monitor for anomalous network redirects to mitigate future attacks.
hits.title: 0-days exploited by commercial surveillance vendor in Egypt

canonical_entities: Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Tools
hits.text: Since its emergence in 2021 and first detection on Trend Micro telemetry in March 2022, the TargetCompany ransomware group has launched 269 attempted attacks against 250 disclosed Trend customers—predominantly in Asia (notably India and Saudi Arabia)—while avoiding Kazakhstan, Russia, Qatar, and Ukraine, and focusing on manufacturing, retail, and telecommunications; their November 2022–May 2023 leak site lists 20 confirmed victims (mostly small businesses) across the Asia-Pacific, Europe, and Middle East in IT, manufacturing, apparel, and automotive sectors. Initial access vectors include exploitation of CVE-2019-1069 and CVE-2020-0618 RCE flaws, SQL Server xp_cmdshell abuse, and OneNote-based spam campaigns. Execution relies on WMIC-invoked PowerShell scripts to retrieve various payloads (TargetComp ransomware, Remcos backdoor, Negasteal, Snake Keylogger) and, since January 2022, reflective loading of a .NET downloader that decrypts and runs payloads in memory via XOR or inversion. For defense evasion, operators deploy GMER, PCHunter64 (YDArk.exe), Advance Process Termination, KILLAV, and killer.bat to disable AV and security services; discovery is achieved through network scans and Mimikatz credential dumping; lateral movement via RDP-based RCE; C2 evolved from an open Mallox directory to an Nginx-protected server. Impact involves ChaCha20 file encryption with keys generated by Curve25519 and AES-128, file extensions such as .mallox/.exploit/.avast and ransom notes titled “HOW TO RECOVER!!.TXT,” and potential data exfiltration. Their tactics span MITRE techniques T1190, T1059.001, T1047, T1562.001, T1003.001, T1071.001, T1486, and more. The group’s maturation—evidenced by reflective loading and possible RaaS adoption—underscores the urgency for organizations to enforce asset inventories, least-privilege access, prompt patching (or virtual patching), multifactor authentication, sandboxed email defenses, AI/ML-driven detection, regular backups, and continuous red-team testing to thwart this active threat.
hits.title: Ransomware Spotlight: TargetCompany | Trend Micro (US)

canonical_entities: bypasses the Mark of the Web

hits.text: Microsoft’s August 2023 Patch Tuesday addressed two actively exploited zero-days—CVE-2023-36884, a remote code execution flaw in Microsoft Office that bypasses the Mark of the Web, and CVE-2023-38180, a .NET/Visual Studio vulnerability enabling DDoS attacks without requiring user privileges—after one was publicly disclosed pre-patch. The Russian actor Storm-0978 (aka RomCom/Underground), noted for Industrial Spy ransomware, leveraged crafted Office documents to execute payloads and extort victims, while CVE-2023-38180 attacks demand only network proximity. To mitigate these threats, Microsoft released an Office Defense-in-Depth update and a .NET/Visual Studio patch and recommends deploying both Office and Windows August updates, enabling cloud-delivered protection in Defender Antivirus, activating EDR block mode, enforcing attack surface reduction rules to block Office-spawned child processes, and applying the advisory’s update for CVE-2023-38180. retrieved_context.text: Since its emergence in 2021 and first detection on Trend Micro telemetry in March 2022, the TargetCompany ransomware group has launched 269 attempted attacks against 250 disclosed Trend customers—predominantly in Asia (notably India and Saudi Arabia)—while avoiding Kazakhstan, Russia, Qatar, and Ukraine, and focusing on manufacturing, retail, and telecommunications; their November 2022–May 2023 leak site lists 20 confirmed victims (mostly small businesses) across the Asia-Pacific, Europe, and Middle East in IT, manufacturing, apparel, and automotive sectors. Initial access vectors include exploitation of CVE-2019-1069 and CVE-2020-0618 RCE flaws, SQL Server xp_cmdshell abuse, and OneNote-based spam campaigns. Execution relies on WMIC-invoked PowerShell scripts to retrieve various payloads (TargetComp ransomware, Remcos backdoor, Negasteal, Snake Keylogger) and, since January 2022, reflective loading of a .NET downloader that decrypts and runs payloads in memory via XOR or inversion. For defense evasion, operators deploy GMER, PCHunter64 (YDArk.exe), Advance Process Termination, KILLAV, and killer.bat to disable AV and security services; discovery is achieved through network scans and Mimikatz credential dumping; lateral movement via RDP-based RCE; C2 evolved from an open Mallox directory to an Nginx-protected server. Impact involves ChaCha20 file encryption with keys generated by Curve25519 and AES-128, file extensions such as .mallox/.exploit/.avast and ransom notes titled “HOW TO RECOVER!!.TXT,” and potential data exfiltration. Their tactics span MITRE techniques T1190, T1059.001, T1047, T1562.001, T1003.001, T1071.001, T1486, and more. The group’s maturation—evidenced by reflective loading and possible RaaS adoption—underscores the urgency for organizations to enforce asset inventories, least-privilege access, prompt patching (or virtual patching), multifactor authentication, sandboxed email defenses, AI/ML-driven detection, regular backups, and continuous red-team testing to thwart this active threat.

hits.text: Unit42’s “EleKtra-Leak” campaign, active since December 2020, uses automated scripts to clone public GitHub repos every few minutes, extract exposed AWS IAM keys within five minutes, then—if not blocked by GitHub-AWS quarantine policies—execute rapid AWS reconnaissance (DescribeRegions), create security groups, and launch hundreds of EC2 instances across regions via VPN for Monero cryptojacking, generating over 400 API calls in seven minutes. Between Aug. 30 and Oct. 6, 2023, researchers tracked 474 actor-controlled miners. The actor employs custom mining software and blocklists high-profile AWS account IDs to avoid honey traps. Leveraging the Prisma Cloud HoneyCloud project’s ephemeral key leaks and policy overrides, Unit42 obtained full visibility, informing Prisma Cloud Secrets Security, CI/CD IaC scanning, Cortex XDR, and recommendations for independent repo scanning, strict IAM policies, and continuous monitoring.

hits.text: CISA has added CVE-2022-22047—a high-severity (CVSS 7.8) elevation-of-privilege flaw in the Windows Client Server Runtime Subsystem used since Windows 7 through Windows 11 and Server 2008–2022—to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog and is urging federal agencies to install Microsoft’s July 5 Patch Tuesday update by August 2 after evidence emerged of in-the-wild exploitation; initially disclosed as a zero-day by Microsoft’s security team, the CSRSS bug enables adversaries who already hold local or physical access—or who gain remote code execution via malware or specially crafted Office/Adobe documents and macros—to escalate to SYSTEM privileges for lateral movement, although FortiGuard Labs rates the overall business threat as “medium” given the prerequisite foothold and available patch, while Trend Micro’s ZDI notes such elevation flaws are typically paired with a separate RCE vector and Microsoft has signaled future default blocking of VBA macros to mitigate this attack chain.

hits.text: Since at least April 2024 Microsoft Threat Intelligence has tracked a Russia-affiliated cyberespionage actor dubbed Void Blizzard (aka LAUNDRY BEAR) conducting high-volume, targeted operations against government, defense, transportation, media, NGO and healthcare organizations—particularly in NATO member states and Ukraine—by leveraging stolen credentials procured via commodity infostealer ecosystems for password spray attacks and Exchange/SharePoint Online access, then automating bulk email and file collection (and in some cases Teams messages) via cloud APIs and tools like AzureHound; in April 2025 the actor evolved to adversary-in-the-middle spear phishing using a typosquatted domain and the open-source Evilginx framework with a malicious QR-coded PDF to harvest Entra authentication data; this widespread success underscores that even unsophisticated TTPs pose major intelligence risks to critical sectors, so organizations should enforce sign-in risk policies and phishing-resistant MFA (e.g., FIDO/passkeys), centralize identity management with Conditional Access, monitor risky sign-ins and mailbox auditing, apply least-privilege credential hygiene, and promptly rotate credentials after infostealer detections to disrupt Void Blizzard’s operations.

hits.text: Since mid-September, unknown cybercriminals have been conducting large-scale brute-force attacks against internet-exposed instances of Foundation Accounting Software—widely used by construction sub-industries such as plumbing, HVAC and concrete—by targeting the default “sa” administrator and a second high-privilege account within the MSSQL database accessible via TCP port 4243 (opened for Foundation’s mobile app). After an observed peak of roughly 35,000 rapid login attempts to obtain valid credentials, the attackers enable an extended stored procedure (e.g., xp_cmdshell) to execute OS-level commands and scripts, automating lateral movement and data theft across multiple unrelated victims. Huntress has identified just 33 hosts left with unchanged default passwords, alerted all impacted and at-risk customers, and urges organizations to rotate all Foundation credentials, remove direct internet exposure, and disable the exploited stored procedure to mitigate further compromise.
hits.title: Threat Actors Target Accounting Software Used by Construction Contractors - SecurityWeek

hits.text: Originally released by the Chinese C.Rufus Security Team in March 2008, the open-source Gh0st RAT has reemerged in late August 2023 as SugarGh0st RAT, deployed by a China-linked actor against South Korean targets and Uzbekistan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs via phishing-delivered archives containing Windows .LNK shortcuts that execute embedded JavaScript, display customized decoy documents, and install the 32-bit C++ DLL. The backdoor collects system data, grants full remote control—including process and file manipulation, log removal, keylogging, screenshot and camera access, and arbitrary command execution—and now evades legacy detection by altering its C2 protocol packet header from 5 to 8 magic bytes. Cisco Talos highlights these cosmetic yet effective modifications as a blind spot in signature-based defenses, underscoring the urgent need for updated heuristics and layered monitoring.
hits.title: A New, Spookier Gh0st RAT Malware Haunts Global Cyber Targets

hits.text: In August 2025 Microsoft Threat Intelligence revealed that Storm-2460, associated with the Play ransomware group, has resumed exploiting CVE-2025-29824—a zero-day elevation-of-privilege flaw in the Windows Common Log File System patched in April—to gain SYSTEM privileges on unpatched hosts across IT, financial and real estate organizations in the US, Europe, South America and the Middle East. The campaign begins with an in-memory dropper masquerading as the open-source ChatGPT Desktop app that decrypts and launches PipeMagic, a modular backdoor first observed in December 2022 and now updated with persistence and lateral-movement enhancements targeting Saudi Arabian and Brazilian manufacturing entities. PipeMagic communicates with its TCP C2 over a named pipe, self-updates by storing distinct payload modules in memory via doubly linked lists for staging, execution and communication (plus an additional dynamic list), then leverages the CLFS exploit to escalate privileges before deploying Play ransomware. Although the campaign’s footprint remains limited, the combination of a zero-day exploit and a sophisticated modular backdoor underscores a heightened risk; organizations are urged to immediately apply the April patch for CVE-2025-29824, enable tamper and network protection in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, run EDR in block mode, enforce full automated investigation and remediation, and leverage cloud-delivered machine-learning protections to block novel variants.

retrieved_context.text: The North Korea-linked threat actor Slow Pisces (also tracked as Jade Sleet, PUKCHONG, TraderTraitor, and UNC4899) has been conducting a multi-stage malware campaign targeting cryptocurrency developers via LinkedIn job opportunity lures since at least June 2024, leveraging trojanized Python and JavaScript projects hosted on GitHub that employ YAML deserialization and EJS templating to execute gated payloads only to validated targets meeting specific criteria (IP address, geolocation, time, HTTP headers); the campaign delivers RN Loader and RN Stealer malware on macOS systems capable of harvesting system metadata, installed applications, SSH keys, AWS/Kubernetes/Google Cloud configuration files, and iCloud Keychain data, with payloads remaining memory-resident and deployed selectively to prevent analysis; Slow Pisces is assessed to be responsible for the February 2025 Bybit cryptocurrency exchange breach and operates alongside other North Korean clusters including Operation Dream Job, Contagious Interview, Alluring Pisces, and Moonstone Sleet, though with notably superior operational security practices involving heavily guarded payload delivery across infection stages.
retrieved_context.title: Crypto Developers Targeted by Python Malware Disguised as Coding Challenges

canonical_entities: Launch EC2 instances across regions via VPN
retrieved_context.text: Unit42’s “EleKtra-Leak” campaign, active since December 2020, uses automated scripts to clone public GitHub repos every few minutes, extract exposed AWS IAM keys within five minutes, then—if not blocked by GitHub-AWS quarantine policies—execute rapid AWS reconnaissance (DescribeRegions), create security groups, and launch hundreds of EC2 instances across regions via VPN for Monero cryptojacking, generating over 400 API calls in seven minutes. Between Aug. 30 and Oct. 6, 2023, researchers tracked 474 actor-controlled miners. The actor employs custom mining software and blocklists high-profile AWS account IDs to avoid honey traps. Leveraging the Prisma Cloud HoneyCloud project’s ephemeral key leaks and policy overrides, Unit42 obtained full visibility, informing Prisma Cloud Secrets Security, CI/CD IaC scanning, Cortex XDR, and recommendations for independent repo scanning, strict IAM policies, and continuous monitoring.
retrieved_context.title: CloudKeys in the Air: Tracking Malicious Operations of Exposed IAM Keys

retrieved_context.text: Last week Google’s Threat Analysis Group, in partnership with The Citizen Lab, exposed an in-the-wild exploit chain developed by the commercial surveillance vendor Intellexa in Egypt that leverages a man-in-the-middle injection on HTTP traffic to silently redirect targets first to c.betly[.]me and then to sec-flare[.]com, delivering Predator spyware without any user interaction; on iOS this chain combined Safari RCE (CVE-2023-41993), certificate validation bypass (CVE-2023-41991) and XNU kernel local privilege escalation (CVE-2023-41992) and was patched in iOS 16.7/17.0.1, while on Android initial Chrome renderer RCE (CVE-2023-4762), delivered via MITM or one-time links, was patched on September 5; this campaign highlights the serious risk posed by proliferating commercial spyware, underscores the urgency of enforcing universal HTTPS and enabling Chrome’s HTTPS-First Mode, and demonstrates the critical need for organizations and users to apply the latest OS and browser updates, deploy encrypted-traffic protections, and monitor for anomalous network redirects to mitigate future attacks.
retrieved_context.title: 0-days exploited by commercial surveillance vendor in Egypt

retrieved_context.text: CISA has added CVE-2022-22047—a high-severity (CVSS 7.8) elevation-of-privilege flaw in the Windows Client Server Runtime Subsystem used since Windows 7 through Windows 11 and Server 2008–2022—to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog and is urging federal agencies to install Microsoft’s July 5 Patch Tuesday update by August 2 after evidence emerged of in-the-wild exploitation; initially disclosed as a zero-day by Microsoft’s security team, the CSRSS bug enables adversaries who already hold local or physical access—or who gain remote code execution via malware or specially crafted Office/Adobe documents and macros—to escalate to SYSTEM privileges for lateral movement, although FortiGuard Labs rates the overall business threat as “medium” given the prerequisite foothold and available patch, while Trend Micro’s ZDI notes such elevation flaws are typically paired with a separate RCE vector and Microsoft has signaled future default blocking of VBA macros to mitigate this attack chain.
retrieved_context.title: CISA Urges Patch of Exploited Windows 11 Bug by Aug. 2 | Threatpost

retrieved_context.text: Since at least April 2024 Microsoft Threat Intelligence has tracked a Russia-affiliated cyberespionage actor dubbed Void Blizzard (aka LAUNDRY BEAR) conducting high-volume, targeted operations against government, defense, transportation, media, NGO and healthcare organizations—particularly in NATO member states and Ukraine—by leveraging stolen credentials procured via commodity infostealer ecosystems for password spray attacks and Exchange/SharePoint Online access, then automating bulk email and file collection (and in some cases Teams messages) via cloud APIs and tools like AzureHound; in April 2025 the actor evolved to adversary-in-the-middle spear phishing using a typosquatted domain and the open-source Evilginx framework with a malicious QR-coded PDF to harvest Entra authentication data; this widespread success underscores that even unsophisticated TTPs pose major intelligence risks to critical sectors, so organizations should enforce sign-in risk policies and phishing-resistant MFA (e.g., FIDO/passkeys), centralize identity management with Conditional Access, monitor risky sign-ins and mailbox auditing, apply least-privilege credential hygiene, and promptly rotate credentials after infostealer detections to disrupt Void Blizzard’s operations.
retrieved_context.title: New Russia-affiliated actor Void Blizzard targets critical sectors for espionage | Microsoft Security Blog

retrieved_context.text: Since mid-September, unknown cybercriminals have been conducting large-scale brute-force attacks against internet-exposed instances of Foundation Accounting Software—widely used by construction sub-industries such as plumbing, HVAC and concrete—by targeting the default “sa” administrator and a second high-privilege account within the MSSQL database accessible via TCP port 4243 (opened for Foundation’s mobile app). After an observed peak of roughly 35,000 rapid login attempts to obtain valid credentials, the attackers enable an extended stored procedure (e.g., xp_cmdshell) to execute OS-level commands and scripts, automating lateral movement and data theft across multiple unrelated victims. Huntress has identified just 33 hosts left with unchanged default passwords, alerted all impacted and at-risk customers, and urges organizations to rotate all Foundation credentials, remove direct internet exposure, and disable the exploited stored procedure to mitigate further compromise.
retrieved_context.title: Threat Actors Target Accounting Software Used by Construction Contractors - SecurityWeek

retrieved_context.text: Originally released by the Chinese C.Rufus Security Team in March 2008, the open-source Gh0st RAT has reemerged in late August 2023 as SugarGh0st RAT, deployed by a China-linked actor against South Korean targets and Uzbekistan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs via phishing-delivered archives containing Windows .LNK shortcuts that execute embedded JavaScript, display customized decoy documents, and install the 32-bit C++ DLL. The backdoor collects system data, grants full remote control—including process and file manipulation, log removal, keylogging, screenshot and camera access, and arbitrary command execution—and now evades legacy detection by altering its C2 protocol packet header from 5 to 8 magic bytes. Cisco Talos highlights these cosmetic yet effective modifications as a blind spot in signature-based defenses, underscoring the urgent need for updated heuristics and layered monitoring.
retrieved_context.title: A New, Spookier Gh0st RAT Malware Haunts Global Cyber Targets

retrieved_context.text: In August 2025 Microsoft Threat Intelligence revealed that Storm-2460, associated with the Play ransomware group, has resumed exploiting CVE-2025-29824—a zero-day elevation-of-privilege flaw in the Windows Common Log File System patched in April—to gain SYSTEM privileges on unpatched hosts across IT, financial and real estate organizations in the US, Europe, South America and the Middle East. The campaign begins with an in-memory dropper masquerading as the open-source ChatGPT Desktop app that decrypts and launches PipeMagic, a modular backdoor first observed in December 2022 and now updated with persistence and lateral-movement enhancements targeting Saudi Arabian and Brazilian manufacturing entities. PipeMagic communicates with its TCP C2 over a named pipe, self-updates by storing distinct payload modules in memory via doubly linked lists for staging, execution and communication (plus an additional dynamic list), then leverages the CLFS exploit to escalate privileges before deploying Play ransomware. Although the campaign’s footprint remains limited, the combination of a zero-day exploit and a sophisticated modular backdoor underscores a heightened risk; organizations are urged to immediately apply the April patch for CVE-2025-29824, enable tamper and network protection in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, run EDR in block mode, enforce full automated investigation and remediation, and leverage cloud-delivered machine-learning protections to block novel variants.
retrieved_context.title: PipeMagic Backdoor Resurfaces as Part of Play Ransomware Attack Chain

retrieved_context.text: Microsoft Threat Intelligence has observed the Russia-based SVR actor Midnight Blizzard (aka NOBELIUM, APT29/UNC2452/Cozy Bear) launch a highly targeted social-engineering campaign since at least late May 2023 by leveraging previously compromised small-business Microsoft 365 tenants to create security-themed onmicrosoft.com domains and Teams accounts that masquerade as technical-support entities; attackers then initiate Microsoft Teams chat requests to elicit approval of MFA prompts or codes via Microsoft Authenticator, enabling credential theft, access to fewer than 40 global organizations across government, NGOs, IT services, technology, manufacturing and media sectors, and subsequent post-compromise activities including data exfiltration and attempts to add managed devices via Microsoft Entra ID to bypass conditional access. Microsoft has mitigated the malicious domains, directly notified affected customers, and recommends phishing-resistant authentication, Conditional Access policies, Microsoft Teams best practices, auditing, and user education to detect and prevent unsolicited MFA requests.
retrieved_context.title: Midnight Blizzard conducts targeted social engineering over Microsoft Teams | Microsoft Security Blog

hits.text: New research reveals that over 80,000 Hikvision cameras worldwide remain unpatched against the critical CVE-2021-36260 command-injection flaw (NIST score 9.8/10) disclosed last fall, allowing remote code execution and potential espionage by state-linked groups such as MISSION2025/APT41, APT10 and unknown Russian actors trading stolen credentials on dark-web forums; systemic deficiencies—default or hardcoded passwords, no auto-update mechanism, poor forensics and lack of security-by-design—have left devices in 100+ countries (including the U.S., despite an FCC “unacceptable risk” designation) continuously discoverable via Shodan or Censys and ripe for exploitation, underscoring the urgent need for organizations to inventory IoT assets, change default credentials, deploy available patches and improve visibility and update processes to mitigate geopolitical and operational impact.
hits.title: Cybercriminals Are Selling Access to Chinese Surveillance Cameras | Threatpost

hits.text: Since mid-2021, Microsoft has tracked Volt Typhoon, a China-linked state-sponsored actor, conducting stealthy living-off-the-land campaigns against U.S. critical infrastructure—spanning communications, utilities, transportation, manufacturing, government and education—aimed at post-compromise credential access, network discovery and long-term espionage with an eye toward potential disruption of Asia-U.S. communications in future crises. Initial access is achieved via internet-exposed Fortinet FortiGuard devices, whose AD credentials are harvested to move laterally; all traffic is proxied through compromised SOHO routers, firewalls and VPN hardware (ASUS, Cisco, D-Link, NETGEAR, Zyxel) to blend with legitimate activity. Post-compromise hands-on-keyboard operations rely almost exclusively on LOLBins and valid credentials to dump LSASS memory and use Ntdsutil.exe to create domain controller installation media for offline hash cracking, enumerate systems via PowerShell, WMIC and ping, collect browser and system data into staged archives, then exfiltrate via password-protected files. In rare cases, Volt Typhoon deploys custom Impacket or FRP-based C2 over portproxy, observable as unusual successful sign-ins and command-line activity from anomalous IPs. Detection is challenging due to use of built-in binaries and normal sign-in channels; Microsoft 365 Defender and cloud-delivered Microsoft Defender Antivirus yield behavioral alerts (e.g., SuspPowershellExec, SuspNtdsUtilUsage), while Defender for Endpoint flags suspicious LSASS dumps, wmic.exe executions and domain-controller media creation. Mitigation hinges on closing or rotating compromised accounts, enforcing strong MFA or passwordless authentication, disabling internet-facing device management interfaces, enabling LSASS Protective Process Light and Credential Guard on Windows 11, applying attack surface reduction rules to block LSASS and PSExec/WMI abuse, and running EDR in block mode to thwart post-compromise artifacts.
hits.title: Volt Typhoon targets US critical infrastructure with living-off-the-land techniques | Microsoft Security Blog

hits.text: Since at least 2019, China-linked Winnti APT (aka APT41/BARIUM/Blackfly) has run the stealthy CuckooBees campaign against technology and manufacturing firms in North America, Europe, and Asia to support Beijing’s Made in China 2025 initiative, exploiting ERP platform vulnerabilities for initial access and deploying a “house of cards” kill chain—including an undocumented Deploylog backdoor and updated Winnti malware concealed via rare Windows CLFS abuse—to maintain persistence through a VBScript WebShell (up_win32.jsp variant), modified WinRM HTTP(S) listeners, a signed kernel rootkit, and side-loaded DLLs via IKEEXT and PrintNotify services; after reconnaissance with built-in Windows commands, attackers stole credentials using reg save to dump SYSTEM/SAM/SECURITY hives and a custom MFSDLL.exe loader of mktzx64.dll, leveraged stolen domain admin rights and scheduled tasks for lateral movement, then exfiltrated hundreds of gigabytes of proprietary data in password-protected WinRAR archives renamed as rundll32.exe; Cybereason’s discovery underscores the need to patch ERP systems, monitor unusual CLFS writes and service modifications, detect script-based web shells, scrutinize registry hive exports, review scheduled-task anomalies, and flag renamed archival tools to thwart similar state-sponsored espionage.
hits.title: China-Linked Winnti APT Group Silently Stole Trade Secrets for Years: Report

hits.text: Symantec’s Threat Hunter Team has linked the newly discovered Sidewalk loader backdoor—an evolution of the Crosswalk/Backdoor.Motnug family—to Grayfly (aka GREF/Wicked Panda), a China-linked espionage group active since March 2017 that employs custom backdoors, Trojan.Chattak, Cobalt Strike, web shells and credential-dumpers against telecom, IT, media and finance targets in Taiwan, Vietnam, the US and Mexico; in a recent campaign they exploited public-facing Microsoft Exchange and MySQL servers via commodity and zero-day flaws to execute Base64-encoded PowerShell commands through certutil, install an ASPX web shell in the ClientAccess\ecp directory, deploy Sidewalk via installutil.exe, create persistence with WMIC-launched scheduled tasks, then run a custom Mimikatz variant (SHA256 b3eb783b017da32e33d19670b39eae0b11de8e983891dd4feb873d6e9333608d) to harvest credentials—all within about an hour before ceasing observable activity; three Chengdu 404 executives were indicted in 2020 for attacks on over 100 organizations, highlighting Grayfly’s persistence and underscoring the need to promptly patch Exchange and MySQL servers, monitor anomalous PowerShell and scheduled-task activity, and deploy IOC-based detection to block Sidewalk and related tools.
hits.title: Grayfly: Chinese Threat Actor Uses Newly-discovered Sidewalk Malware | Symantec Enterprise Blogs

canonical_entities: trading and brokerage firms in Hong Kong, the UAE, Jordan, Lebanon and Malaysia
hits.text: First observed in September 2024 and active through at least August 12, 2025, the GodRAT campaign—attributed to an APT likely linked to Winnti—targets financial institutions, particularly trading and brokerage firms in Hong Kong, the UAE, Jordan, Lebanon and Malaysia, by distributing malicious .scr and .pif files via Skype messenger disguised as legitimate financial documents. Evolving from the AwesomePuppet RAT on a Gh0st RAT codebase, GodRAT employs a two-stage loader architecture: an initial stub invokes SDL2.dll to allocate memory and extract XOR-decoded (key 0x63) shellcode hidden via steganography in image files named to mimic authentic financial reports, then searches for the “godinfo” marker and uses the authentication string “GETGOD” to contact C2 servers, download UPX-packed GodRAT DLL modules and launch browser credential-stealing and remote-access payloads. This advanced steganographic delivery evades signature-based defenses and underscores the need to inspect .scr/.pif attachments, monitor Skype channels, and deploy detection rules for “godinfo,” “GETGOD” and related shellcode patterns.
hits.title: New GodRAT Weaponizing Screen Saver and Program Files to Attack Organizations

canonical_entities: inject the decoded first-stage shellcode into legitimate processes
hits.text: In September 2024, a Winnti-linked APT began targeting trading and brokerage firms by distributing malicious .scr/.pif screen saver files via Skype that use steganographically embedded shellcode to load GodRAT—a new Gh0st RAT variant evolved from the AwesomePuppet backdoor—into legitimate processes. Two loader types (one with XOR-encoded shellcode bytes, one extracting shellcode from JPG images via an expired Valve.exe/SDL2.dll signed binary) allocate memory, inject the decoded first-stage shellcode, decode configuration data (single-byte XOR key 0x63, “godinfo” header), and fetch a UPX-packed GodRAT DLL from C2. GodRAT launches under a “-Puppet” flag in curl.exe or cmd.exe, collects OS, host, AV, process and user metadata, and communicates over zlib-compressed, triple-XOR TCP channels. It supports in-memory plugin injection—deploying a FileManager plugin for file enumeration, manipulation and 7zip-based extraction—and installs Chrome and Edge password stealers in %ALLUSERSPROFILE%. AsyncRAT serves as a secondary fallback implant. Ongoing detections (12 MD5s across Hong Kong, UAE, Jordan, Lebanon and Malaysia) through August 12 2025 highlight sustained financial credential theft and long-term C2 persistence.
hits.title: Gh0st RAT-based GodRAT attacks financial organizations

hits.text: Security researchers at Cybereason uncovered that since at least 2019 a Chinese state-sponsored APT group known as Winnti (also tracked as APT41, Barium, Wicked Panda, Axiom) has been running “Operation CuckooBees,” a multi-year, multi-stage espionage campaign targeting technology and manufacturing firms across Asia, Europe and North America to steal hundreds of gigabytes of trade secrets. The attackers exploited both known and zero-day RCE flaws in a popular ERP platform to deploy JSP web shells, enabled WinRM for persistence, dumped registry-stored credentials to move laterally via scheduled tasks, and used a sophisticated loader chain—Spyder Loader (disguised as SQLite3 DLL), STASHLOG (which hides payloads in Windows’ proprietary CLFS logs), SPARKLOG (which extracts and side-loads PRIVATELOG via DLL hijacking for SYSTEM privileges), and DEPLOYLOG (which abuses Transactional NTFS to overwrite dbghelp.dll and hijack the AMD K8 kernel driver)—to install WINNKIT, a kernel-level rootkit signed with a stolen BenQ certificate that hooks TCP/IP at the NIC to receive commands for shell execution, file enumeration, SOCKS5 proxy, RDP and process control, all while evading detection for years.
hits.title: Chinese APT group Winnti stole trade secrets in years-long undetected campaign

hits.text: The Chinese state-backed APT41 group Winnti has since at least 2019 conducted Operation CuckooBees against technology and manufacturing firms across East Asia, Western Europe and North America, stealthily exfiltrating hundreds of gigabytes of intellectual property—including patents, blueprints and proprietary manufacturing data—via an infection chain that begins with exploiting known and zero-day ERP vulnerabilities and establishes persistence through an encoded WebShell, WinRM abuse, DLL side-loading (via IKEEXT and PrintNotify services) or a signed kernel rootkit. After recon with native commands run as scheduled tasks (‘systeminfo’, ‘net start’, ‘dir C:\’), Winnti performs credential dumping with ‘reg save’ and the MFSDLL.exe tool, moves laterally via scheduled task-launched batch files, and exfiltrates archives using a digitally-signed WinRAR wrapped in rundll32.exe. Cybereason’s discovery of the novel DEPLOYLOG 64-bit DLL, which hides payloads in Windows CLFS logs and deploys the reflective-loading WINNKIT rootkit (leveraging an expired BenQ signature to bypass DSE) with dual C2 channels, underscores the campaign’s sophistication and antivirus evasion. Given the group’s enduring activity despite DOJ indictments, defenders should ensure all software is patched, monitor network traffic for anomalous scheduled tasks and CLFS usage, and implement strict network segmentation to mitigate similar espionage operations.
hits.title: Hackers stole data undetected from US, European orgs since 2019

hits.text: Salt Typhoon—also known as GhostEmperor, Operator Panda, RedMike and UNC5807—has, since at least 2021, compromised backbone and edge routers across telecom, government, transportation, lodging and military networks in the US, Canada, UK, Australia and New Zealand by exploiting known vulnerabilities in Cisco (CVE-2018-0171, CVE-2023-20198, CVE-2023-20273), Ivanti (CVE-2024-21887) and Palo Alto Networks (CVE-2024-3400) products to gain initial access, then modified routing, mirrored traffic and pivoted laterally via ACL tampering, custom tunnels, BGP route hijacks and open-source multi-hop tools; for persistence and evasion it has created privileged accounts, opened non-standard ports, deleted logs, disabled logging and abused peering connections for exfiltration, ultimately enabling Chinese intelligence services—including contractor affiliates such as Sichuan Juxinhe, Beijing Huanyu Tianqiong and Sichuan Zhixin Ruijie—to track target communications and movements, with intrusions blamed for breaches at telecom firms and a US National Guard unit and affecting hundreds of organizations in 80 countries in 2024 alone; organizations are urged to patch vulnerable devices, deploy the joint advisory’s IOCs for proactive hunting, secure mail and administrator accounts against monitoring by APT actors and fully understand attacker access before visible incident response to maximize chances of full eviction.
hits.title: China’s Salt Typhoon Hacked Critical Infrastructure Globally for Years

hits.text: In May 2025, Fog ransomware operators stealthily compromised a financial institution in Asia two weeks before detonating their payload, first infecting two Exchange servers and initiating their chain with GC2—a Google Sheets/SharePoint command-and-control and exfiltration tool linked to APT41 in 2023—then using Stowaway as a proxy to deploy Syteca (formerly Ekran) employee-monitoring software loaded with libraries for screen capture and keystroke logging. For lateral movement they invoked PsExec, SMBExec, Syteca and GC2, while Freefilesync and MegaSync exfiltrated data; the Adaptix C2 Agent Beacon, an open-source post-exploitation framework akin to Cobalt Strike, established command-and-control, a custom Windows service ensured persistence, and Impacket likely executed the Fog payload. Symantec notes this unusual fusion of legitimate monitoring tools, open-source pentesting utilities and ransomware indicates a primary espionage objective—with ransomware serving as a decoy or revenue stream—mirroring evolving TTPs that leverage compromised VPN credentials, vulnerable Veeam Backup & Replication servers (CVE-2024-40711) and phishing for initial access, and marking Fog’s shift since its 2024 emergence targeting the U.S. education sector.
hits.title: Fog Ransomware Attack Employs Unusual Tools - SecurityWeek

retrieved_context.text: In May 2025, Fog ransomware operators stealthily compromised a financial institution in Asia two weeks before detonating their payload, first infecting two Exchange servers and initiating their chain with GC2—a Google Sheets/SharePoint command-and-control and exfiltration tool linked to APT41 in 2023—then using Stowaway as a proxy to deploy Syteca (formerly Ekran) employee-monitoring software loaded with libraries for screen capture and keystroke logging. hits.text: Since mid-2021, Microsoft has tracked Volt Typhoon, a China-linked state-sponsored actor, conducting stealthy living-off-the-land campaigns against U.S. critical infrastructure—spanning communications, utilities, transportation, manufacturing, government and education—aimed at post-compromise credential access, network discovery and long-term espionage with an eye toward potential disruption of Asia-U.S. communications in future crises. In rare cases, Volt Typhoon deploys custom Impacket or FRP-based C2 over portproxy, observable as unusual successful sign-ins and command-line activity from anomalous IPs. GodRAT launches under a “-Puppet” flag in curl.exe or cmd.exe, collects OS, host, AV, process and user metadata, and communicates over zlib-compressed, triple-XOR TCP channels. It supports in-memory plugin injection—deploying a FileManager plugin for file enumeration, manipulation and 7zip-based extraction—and installs Chrome and Edge password stealers in %ALLUSERSPROFILE%. AsyncRAT serves as a secondary fallback implant. Ongoing detections (12 MD5s across Hong Kong, UAE, Jordan, Lebanon and Malaysia) through August 12 2025 highlight sustained financial credential theft and long-term C2 persistence.
hits.title: Gh0st RAT-based GodRAT attacks financial organizations

hits.text: Since at least 2019, China-linked Winnti APT (aka APT41/BARIUM/Blackfly) has run the stealthy CuckooBees campaign against technology and manufacturing firms in North America, Europe, and Asia to support Beijing’s Made in China 2025 initiative, exploiting ERP platform vulnerabilities for initial access and deploying a “house of cards” kill chain—including an undocumented Deploylog backdoor and updated Winnti malware concealed via rare Windows CLFS abuse—to maintain persistence through a VBScript WebShell (up_win32.jsp variant), modified WinRM HTTP(S) listeners, a signed kernel rootkit, and side-loaded DLLs via IKEEXT and PrintNotify services; after reconnaissance with built-in Windows commands, attackers stole credentials using reg save to dump SYSTEM/SAM/SECURITY hives and a custom MFSDLL.exe loader of mktzx64.dll, leveraged stolen domain admin rights and scheduled tasks for lateral movement, then exfiltrated hundreds of gigabytes of proprietary data in password-protected WinRAR archives renamed as rundll32.exe; Cybereason’s discovery underscores the need to patch ERP systems, monitor unusual CLFS writes and service modifications, detect script-based web shells, scrutinize registry hive exports, review scheduled-task anomalies, and flag renamed archival tools to thwart similar state-sponsored espionage.
hits.title: China-Linked Winnti APT Group Silently Stole Trade Secrets for Years: Report

hits.text: Symantec’s Threat Hunter Team has linked the newly discovered Sidewalk loader backdoor—an evolution of the Crosswalk/Backdoor.Motnug family—to Grayfly (aka GREF/Wicked Panda), a China-linked espionage group active since March 2017 that employs custom backdoors, Trojan.Chattak, Cobalt Strike, web shells and credential-dumpers against telecom, IT, media and finance targets in Taiwan, Vietnam, the US and Mexico; in a recent campaign they exploited public-facing Microsoft Exchange and MySQL servers via commodity and zero-day flaws to execute Base64-encoded PowerShell commands through certutil, install an ASPX web shell in the ClientAccess\ecp directory, deploy Sidewalk via installutil.exe, create persistence with WMIC-launched scheduled tasks, then run a custom Mimikatz variant (SHA256 b3eb783b017da32e33d19670b39eae0b11de8e983891dd4feb873d6e9333608d) to harvest credentials—all within about an hour before ceasing observable activity; three Chengdu 404 executives were indicted in 2020 for attacks on over 100 organizations, highlighting Grayfly’s persistence and underscoring the need to promptly patch Exchange and MySQL servers, monitor anomalous PowerShell and scheduled-task activity, and deploy IOC-based detection to block Sidewalk and related tools.
hits.title: Grayfly: Chinese Threat Actor Uses Newly-discovered Sidewalk Malware | Symantec Enterprise Blogs

hits.text: Security researchers at Cybereason uncovered that since at least 2019 a Chinese state-sponsored APT group known as Winnti (also tracked as APT41, Barium, Wicked Panda, Axiom) has been running “Operation CuckooBees,” a multi-year, multi-stage espionage campaign targeting technology and manufacturing firms across Asia, Europe and North America to steal hundreds of gigabytes of trade secrets. The attackers exploited both known and zero-day RCE flaws in a popular ERP platform to deploy JSP web shells, enabled WinRM for persistence, dumped registry-stored credentials to move laterally via scheduled tasks, and used a sophisticated loader chain—Spyder Loader (disguised as SQLite3 DLL), STASHLOG (which hides payloads in Windows’ proprietary CLFS logs), SPARKLOG (which extracts and side-loads PRIVATELOG via DLL hijacking for SYSTEM privileges), and DEPLOYLOG (which abuses Transactional NTFS to overwrite dbghelp.dll and hijack the AMD K8 kernel driver)—to install WINNKIT, a kernel-level rootkit signed with a stolen BenQ certificate that hooks TCP/IP at the NIC to receive commands for shell execution, file enumeration, SOCKS5 proxy, RDP and process control, all while evading detection for years.
hits.title: Chinese APT group Winnti stole trade secrets in years-long undetected campaign

hits.text: Microsoft has identified a China-based nation-state threat actor tracked as Flax Typhoon (aka Ethereal Panda) conducting espionage against dozens of Taiwanese organizations since mid-2021 by exploiting known vulnerabilities in public-facing VPN, web, Java and SQL servers to deploy the China Chopper web shell, escalate privileges with Juicy Potato and BadPotato, and establish persistence by disabling RDP network-level authentication, hijacking the Sticky Keys binary to launch Task Manager as SYSTEM, and installing a renamed SoftEther VPN bridge over HTTPS on port 443 for stealthy command-and-control. Once inside, the actor leverages WinRM and WMIC for lateral movement and deploys Mimikatz to dump LSASS and SAM for pass-the-hash attacks, yet conducts minimal post-persistence activity, suggesting long-term credential harvesting rather than immediate data exfiltration. To mitigate, organizations must enforce rigorous patch management, monitor registry changes and RDP configurations, deploy file integrity and behavioral monitoring on public-facing servers, isolate and forensically examine compromised systems, and rotate or disable exposed credentials.
hits.title: Flax Typhoon using legitimate software to quietly access Taiwanese organizations | Microsoft Security Blog

hits.text: The Chinese state-backed APT41 group Winnti has since at least 2019 conducted Operation CuckooBees against technology and manufacturing firms across East Asia, Western Europe and North America, stealthily exfiltrating hundreds of gigabytes of intellectual property—including patents, blueprints and proprietary manufacturing data—via an infection chain that begins with exploiting known and zero-day ERP vulnerabilities and establishes persistence through an encoded WebShell, WinRM abuse, DLL side-loading (via IKEEXT and PrintNotify services) or a signed kernel rootkit. After recon with native commands run as scheduled tasks (‘systeminfo’, ‘net start’, ‘dir C:\’), Winnti performs credential dumping with ‘reg save’ and the MFSDLL.exe tool, moves laterally via scheduled task-launched batch files, and exfiltrates archives using a digitally-signed WinRAR wrapped in rundll32.exe. Cybereason’s discovery of the novel DEPLOYLOG 64-bit DLL, which hides payloads in Windows CLFS logs and deploys the reflective-loading WINNKIT rootkit (leveraging an expired BenQ signature to bypass DSE) with dual C2 channels, underscores the campaign’s sophistication and antivirus evasion. Given the group’s enduring activity despite DOJ indictments, defenders should ensure all software is patched, monitor network traffic for anomalous scheduled tasks and CLFS usage, and implement strict network segmentation to mitigate similar espionage operations.
hits.title: Hackers stole data undetected from US, European orgs since 2019

hits.text: Salt Typhoon—also known as GhostEmperor, Operator Panda, RedMike and UNC5807—has, since at least 2021, compromised backbone and edge routers across telecom, government, transportation, lodging and military networks in the US, Canada, UK, Australia and New Zealand by exploiting known vulnerabilities in Cisco (CVE-2018-0171, CVE-2023-20198, CVE-2023-20273), Ivanti (CVE-2024-21887) and Palo Alto Networks (CVE-2024-3400) products to gain initial access, then modified routing, mirrored traffic and pivoted laterally via ACL tampering, custom tunnels, BGP route hijacks and open-source multi-hop tools; for persistence and evasion it has created privileged accounts, opened non-standard ports, deleted logs, disabled logging and abused peering connections for exfiltration, ultimately enabling Chinese intelligence services—including contractor affiliates such as Sichuan Juxinhe, Beijing Huanyu Tianqiong and Sichuan Zhixin Ruijie—to track target communications and movements, with intrusions blamed for breaches at telecom firms and a US National Guard unit and affecting hundreds of organizations in 80 countries in 2024 alone; organizations are urged to patch vulnerable devices, deploy the joint advisory’s IOCs for proactive hunting, secure mail and administrator accounts against monitoring by APT actors and fully understand attacker access before visible incident response to maximize chances of full eviction.
hits.title: China’s Salt Typhoon Hacked Critical Infrastructure Globally for Years

retrieval_events.query: What attribution evidence links BLOG-247, BLOG-228, and BLOG-266 to the same threat actor?

retrieved_context.text: New research reveals that over 80,000 Hikvision cameras worldwide remain unpatched against the critical CVE-2021-36260 command-injection flaw (NIST score 9.8/10) disclosed last fall, allowing remote code execution and potential espionage by state-linked groups such as MISSION2025/APT41, APT10 and unknown Russian actors trading stolen credentials on dark-web forums; systemic deficiencies—default or hardcoded passwords, no auto-update mechanism, poor forensics and lack of security-by-design—have left devices in 100+ countries (including the U.S., despite an FCC “unacceptable risk” designation) continuously discoverable via Shodan or Censys and ripe for exploitation, underscoring the urgent need for organizations to inventory IoT assets, change default credentials, deploy available patches and improve visibility and update processes to mitigate geopolitical and operational impact.
retrieved_context.title: Cybercriminals Are Selling Access to Chinese Surveillance Cameras | Threatpost

canonical_entities: trading and brokerage firms in Hong Kong, the UAE, Jordan, Lebanon and Malaysia
retrieved_context.text: First observed in September 2024 and active through at least August 12, 2025, the GodRAT campaign—attributed to an APT likely linked to Winnti—targets financial institutions, particularly trading and brokerage firms in Hong Kong, the UAE, Jordan, Lebanon and Malaysia, by distributing malicious .scr and .pif files via Skype messenger disguised as legitimate financial documents. Evolving from the AwesomePuppet RAT on a Gh0st RAT codebase, GodRAT employs a two-stage loader architecture: an initial stub invokes SDL2.dll to allocate memory and extract XOR-decoded (key 0x63) shellcode hidden via steganography in image files named to mimic authentic financial reports, then searches for the “godinfo” marker and uses the authentication string “GETGOD” to contact C2 servers, download UPX-packed GodRAT DLL modules and launch browser credential-stealing and remote-access payloads. This advanced steganographic delivery evades signature-based defenses and underscores the need to inspect .scr/.pif attachments, monitor Skype channels, and deploy detection rules for “godinfo,” “GETGOD” and related shellcode patterns.
retrieved_context.title: New GodRAT Weaponizing Screen Saver and Program Files to Attack Organizations

retrieved_context.text: Since mid-2021, Microsoft has tracked Volt Typhoon, a China-linked state-sponsored actor, conducting stealthy living-off-the-land campaigns against U.S. critical infrastructure—spanning communications, utilities, transportation, manufacturing, government and education—aimed at post-compromise credential access, network discovery and long-term espionage with an eye toward potential disruption of Asia-U.S. communications in future crises. Initial access is achieved via internet-exposed Fortinet FortiGuard devices, whose AD credentials are harvested to move laterally; all traffic is proxied through compromised SOHO routers, firewalls and VPN hardware (ASUS, Cisco, D-Link, NETGEAR, Zyxel) to blend with legitimate activity. Post-compromise hands-on-keyboard operations rely almost exclusively on LOLBins and valid credentials to dump LSASS memory and use Ntdsutil.exe to create domain controller installation media for offline hash cracking, enumerate systems via PowerShell, WMIC and ping, collect browser and system data into staged archives, then exfiltrate via password-protected files. In rare cases, Volt Typhoon deploys custom Impacket or FRP-based C2 over portproxy, observable as unusual successful sign-ins and command-line activity from anomalous IPs. Detection is challenging due to use of built-in binaries and normal sign-in channels; Microsoft 365 Defender and cloud-delivered Microsoft Defender Antivirus yield behavioral alerts (e.g., SuspPowershellExec, SuspNtdsUtilUsage), while Defender for Endpoint flags suspicious LSASS dumps, wmic.exe executions and domain-controller media creation. Mitigation hinges on closing or rotating compromised accounts, enforcing strong MFA or passwordless authentication, disabling internet-facing device management interfaces, enabling LSASS Protective Process Light and Credential Guard on Windows 11, applying attack surface reduction rules to block LSASS and PSExec/WMI abuse, and running EDR in block mode to thwart post-compromise artifacts.
retrieved_context.title: Volt Typhoon targets US critical infrastructure with living-off-the-land techniques | Microsoft Security Blog
