retrieved_context.text: BlackBerry researchers have identified “Silent Skimming,” a year-long, financially motivated campaign by a Chinese-language proficient threat actor that exploits a .NET deserialization flaw (CVE-2019-18935) in Progress Telerik UI for ASP.NET AJAX to remotely deploy malicious DLLs on internet-facing payment and POS servers across APAC, North America and Latin America. Following initial access, the actor leverages a suite of post-exploitation tools—BadPotato, Godzilla Webshell, Juicy Potato, SweetPotato, PowerShell RATs (server.ps1), HTML HTA downloaders and Cobalt Strike beacons—hosted on attacker-controlled HTTP file servers to escalate privileges, execute code, establish C2 via Cloudflare and exfiltrate billing and credit-card data. Attribution is supported by Simplified Chinese code, C2 infrastructure in Japan and region-specific VPS deployments, while intelligence links similar tactics to BlackSuit and Zeon groups. To mitigate risk, organizations should urgently patch Telerik components, monitor for anomalous DLL or webshell activity, enforce PCI DSS Requirement 6.5 for third-party applications, implement rigorous Governance, Risk and Compliance frameworks, and continuously assess payment-processing systems for insecure deserialization and unauthorized data flows.
retrieved_context.title: Everything You Need to Know About Silent Skimming

canonical_entities: lateral movement to additional cloud resources
retrieved_context.text: Attackers exploited an unpatched SQL injection vulnerability in an application to gain elevated permissions on a Microsoft SQL Server instance running in an Azure VM, then enumerated databases, schemas, network settings and enabled xp_cmdshell via “sp_configure” commands to execute OS-level commands, deploy encoded PowerShell scripts, establish persistence via scheduled tasks, dump SAM and SECURITY hives, and exfiltrate data discreetly using webhook[.]site. In a novel twist on known techniques, they attempted lateral movement to additional cloud resources by querying the Azure Instance Metadata Service (169.254.169.254) to obtain the managed identity’s OAuth2 token and abuse its privileges, but the move failed due to an error. Microsoft Defender for SQL triggered alerts for potential SQL injection, abnormal shell spawning, and IMDS calls from SQL Server, while Defender for Cloud and Defender for Endpoint provide further visibility into anomalous cloud-identity and xp_cmdshell activity. Although no breach of downstream cloud services was confirmed, this case underscores the critical need to enforce least privilege on managed identities, disable or tightly control xp_cmdshell, patch applications, monitor metadata endpoint access, and leverage Defender XDR’s detection capabilities to thwart SQL Server–to-cloud lateral movement.
retrieved_context.title: Defending new vectors: Threat actors attempt SQL Server to cloud lateral movement | Microsoft Security Blog

canonical_entities: FIN11’s and FIN7’s twin zero-day campaigns
retrieved_context.text: Clop ransomware, a TA505-sponsored RaaS strain appending the “.ClOP” extension, infects entire networks by compromising Active Directory servers and manipulating Group Policy for persistence, then uses phishing-delivered HTML attachments to drop the Get2 loader, which in turn pulls SDBOT, FlawedAmmyy RATs, Cobalt Strike beacons and TinyMet reverse shells for reconnaissance, lateral movement (via SMB exploits), and exfiltration (often using the DEWMODE web shell). Operators employ double and quadruple extortion—threatening to publish or auction stolen data on their Cl0p^_-Leaks site and targeting executives/customers—to coerce ransoms, driving average payments up 43% to $220,298 (median $78,398) in Q1 2021 after FIN11’s and FIN7’s twin zero-day campaigns against Kiteworks FTA (CVE-2021-27101/02/03/04) and Fortra GoAnywhere MFT, while in 2023 they exploited PaperCut CVE-2023-27350 to deploy Truebot and LockBit/Clop, then MOVEit CVE-2023-24362/CVE-2023-35036 and an unpatched SQL injection flaw to steal data without payloads. Trend Micro detections reveal a May 2023 surge (245 attempts), with top targets in banking, retail and healthcare across Türkiye, Canada, the US and large enterprises worldwide.
retrieved_context.title: Ransomware Spotlight: Clop | Trend Micro (US)

canonical_entities: trading and brokerage firms in Hong Kong, the UAE, Jordan, Lebanon and Malaysia
retrieved_context.text: First observed in September 2024 and active through at least August 12, 2025, the GodRAT campaign—attributed to an APT likely linked to Winnti—targets financial institutions, particularly trading and brokerage firms in Hong Kong, the UAE, Jordan, Lebanon and Malaysia, by distributing malicious .scr and .pif files via Skype messenger disguised as legitimate financial documents. Evolving from the AwesomePuppet RAT on a Gh0st RAT codebase, GodRAT employs a two-stage loader architecture: an initial stub invokes SDL2.dll to allocate memory and extract XOR-decoded (key 0x63) shellcode hidden via steganography in image files named to mimic authentic financial reports, then searches for the “godinfo” marker and uses the authentication string “GETGOD” to contact C2 servers, download UPX-packed GodRAT DLL modules and launch browser credential-stealing and remote-access payloads. This advanced steganographic delivery evades signature-based defenses and underscores the need to inspect .scr/.pif attachments, monitor Skype channels, and deploy detection rules for “godinfo,” “GETGOD” and related shellcode patterns.
retrieved_context.title: New GodRAT Weaponizing Screen Saver and Program Files to Attack Organizations

canonical_entities: inject the decoded first-stage shellcode into legitimate processes
retrieved_context.text: In September 2024, a Winnti-linked APT began targeting trading and brokerage firms by distributing malicious .scr/.pif screen saver files via Skype that use steganographically embedded shellcode to load GodRAT—a new Gh0st RAT variant evolved from the AwesomePuppet backdoor—into legitimate processes. Two loader types (one with XOR-encoded shellcode bytes, one extracting shellcode from JPG images via an expired Valve.exe/SDL2.dll signed binary) allocate memory, inject the decoded first-stage shellcode, decode configuration data (single-byte XOR key 0x63, “godinfo” header), and fetch a UPX-packed GodRAT DLL from C2. GodRAT launches under a “-Puppet” flag in curl.exe or cmd.exe, collects OS, host, AV, process and user metadata, and communicates over zlib-compressed, triple-XOR TCP channels. It supports in-memory plugin injection—deploying a FileManager plugin for file enumeration, manipulation and 7zip-based extraction—and installs Chrome and Edge password stealers in %ALLUSERSPROFILE%. AsyncRAT serves as a secondary fallback implant. Ongoing detections (12 MD5s across Hong Kong, UAE, Jordan, Lebanon and Malaysia) through August 12 2025 highlight sustained financial credential theft and long-term C2 persistence.
retrieved_context.title: Gh0st RAT-based GodRAT attacks financial organizations

canonical_entities: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Windows Command Shell
retrieved_context.text: NCC Group’s RIFT team uncovered a sophisticated new FiveHands ransomware variant deployed by an affiliate linked to UNC2447, who gained initial access in June 2021 by exploiting a SonicWall VPN appliance—evidenced by a “command0/Commando” login from source port 4444 (Metasploit default)—then moved laterally via RDP (T1021.001) using the weak password “Remark123!” and PsExec (T1059.003). The actor leveraged publicly available tools—SoftPerfect Netscan and Advanced Port Scanner for network discovery (T1046), AllInOnePasswordRecoveryPro for credential harvesting (T1003.001), Remote Utilities (“Hostclean.exe”) for persistent C2 (T1219), and pCloud (“pCloud.exe”) for exfiltration (T1567.002), caching 10 GB of stolen data under %AppData%\pCloud\CacheCached—to stage and extract sensitive files. The Go-written loader (“Encryptor.exe”) accepts a 16-byte key (captured via RDP bitmap cache and brute force) to decrypt a unique C++ ransomware payload in memory, which uses RSA/AES (Mbed TLS) to encrypt files in blocks (.crypt/.crypt) while excluding system folders and leveraging Windows Restart Manager to breach locked files. This RaaS model (hijacking hardcoded TOR IDs) employs aggressive extortion tactics—spoofed caller ID calls urging prompt payment—and underscores the need for robust VPN log monitoring, RDP restrictions, enforceable command-line auditing, multi-factor authentication, and forensic examination of cloud‐sync caches to detect and mitigate similar intrusions.
retrieved_context.title: Handy guide to a new Fivehands ransomware variant

hits.text: NCC Group’s RIFT team has tracked a previously unknown extortion actor, SnapMC, which conducts sub-30-minute data breach attacks—eschewing ransomware to steal and threaten to publicly leak data unless victims pay—by scanning for and exploiting public-facing vulnerabilities (notably CVE-2019-18935 in Telerik UI and SQL injection) to deploy a reverse shell, executing reconnaissance via PowerShell (whoami, wmic, net users), occasionally leveraging privilege-escalation scripts such as Invoke-Nightmare and JuicyPotato, then collecting data with 7zip and Invoke-SQLcmd before exfiltrating compressed CSVs to cloud storage via the MinIO client (mc.exe) configured through config.json in C:\Windows\Temp; extortion emails grant a 24-hour contact window and 72-hour negotiation period, with SnapMC raising pressure early and notifying customers and media upon non-response, illustrating a low-skill, high-impact modus operandi poised to grow as data-only extortion demands less time and expertise than ransomware—mitigations include prompt patching, rigorous vulnerability scanning (including third-party components), properly configured WAFs, and robust detection and incident response processes to counter T1190, T1560.001 and T1567.002 techniques.
hits.title: SnapMC skips ransomware, steals data | NCC Group

hits.text: Researchers at NCC Group have identified SnapMC as a new rapid-strike extortion group that eschews file encryption in favor of pure data theft, leveraging the Acunetix vulnerability scanner to pinpoint and exploit unpatched PrintNightmare LPE, Telerik UI for ASPX.NET RCE and SQL-injection flaws in VPN and web-server applications, then running SQL export scripts, compressing stolen CSVs with 7zip and exfiltrating them via the MinIO client—all within 30 minutes—before delivering standard extortion emails. By making data theft the primary leverage, SnapMC renders backup-based recovery moot and heightens the risk that victims who pay ransoms will face repeated extortion or public data sale, as seen with Sodinokibi, Netwalker, Mespinoza and Conti, and echoed by Coveware’s advice never to pay. Effective defenses include prompt patching of known CVEs, deploying well-configured web application firewalls around vulnerable services like Telerik and maintaining rigorous vulnerability management to thwart this growing threat.
hits.title: SnapMC hackers skip file encryption and just steal your files

hits.text: During a recent incident, a LockBit affiliate conducted initial intrusions using gpresult for policy dumping, Cobalt Strike loaders and PsExec for privilege escalation, followed by reconnaissance (whoami, netstat, quser, net view), lateral movement, persistence via a new user account, and data exfiltration over FTP with Wput; when deployment of LockBit (SHA256 079b99f6…) was blocked on the target network, the attacker pivoted to a newly observed Rust-written ransomware family dubbed 3AM (SHA256 307a1217…), which appends “.threeamtime” to encrypted files, stops over 100 security and backup services via net stop and wbadmin/bcdedit/wmic commands, deletes Volume Shadow copies with vssadmin.exe delete shadows /all /quiet, and drops a Tor‐accessible ransom note requiring a 32-character “-k” access key and offering decryption/mystical-themed extortion; although 3AM encryption succeeded on only one of three attempted hosts, its Conti-style “-m” (local/net) and “-h” parameters, heavy service-termination payload, and aggressive VSS wipe underscore its potential as a fallback vector—defenders should update Symantec/Broadcom signatures, monitor for the .threeamtime extension, suspicious Rust binaries, command-line flags “-k” and “-m”, and mass service stoppage activity, and block associated IOCs (185.202.0[.]111, 212.18.104[.]6, 85.159.229[.]62) to mitigate future 3AM use.
hits.title: 3AM: New Ransomware Family Used As Fallback in Failed LockBit Attack | Symantec Enterprise Blogs

hits.text: Microsoft Threat Intelligence has observed the Russia-based SVR actor Midnight Blizzard (aka NOBELIUM, APT29/UNC2452/Cozy Bear) launch a highly targeted social-engineering campaign since at least late May 2023 by leveraging previously compromised small-business Microsoft 365 tenants to create security-themed onmicrosoft.com domains and Teams accounts that masquerade as technical-support entities; attackers then initiate Microsoft Teams chat requests to elicit approval of MFA prompts or codes via Microsoft Authenticator, enabling credential theft, access to fewer than 40 global organizations across government, NGOs, IT services, technology, manufacturing and media sectors, and subsequent post-compromise activities including data exfiltration and attempts to add managed devices via Microsoft Entra ID to bypass conditional access. Microsoft has mitigated the malicious domains, directly notified affected customers, and recommends phishing-resistant authentication, Conditional Access policies, Microsoft Teams best practices, auditing, and user education to detect and prevent unsolicited MFA requests.
hits.title: Midnight Blizzard conducts targeted social engineering over Microsoft Teams | Microsoft Security Blog

hits.text: At least four distinct campaigns exploited CVE-2023-37580, a reflected XSS zero-day in Zimbra Collaboration Suite, to siphon emails, attachments, user credentials and authentication tokens from government organizations worldwide before the July 5 hotfix and July 25 official patch; in chronological order, unidentified actors targeted Greece on June 29 via malicious URLs that, when clicked during active Zimbra sessions, deployed a data-theft framework and auto-forward rules, Winter Vivern’s APT leveraged unique exploit links to hit Moldova and Tunisia between July 11 and 25, another group used a phishing-style XSS link in Vietnam to harvest webmail credentials and exfiltrate them to a compromised government domain, and on August 25 unknown attackers employed an N-day variant to steal tokens from Pakistan’s mail servers; Google’s Threat Analysis Group warns these campaigns underscore the urgency of promptly applying open-source fixes, hardening mail-server code to prevent XSS, and maintaining vigilant patch management as attackers continuously monitor public repositories for unpatched vulnerabilities.
hits.title: APTs Swarm Zimbra Zero-Day to Steal Government Info Worldwide

hits.text: Since January 2021, Google’s Threat Analysis Group (TAG) has tracked a government-backed North Korean campaign that leverages social engineering via X (formerly Twitter) and encrypted messaging apps to befriend security researchers and deliver malicious files containing at least one unpatched 0-day in a popular software package; upon exploitation the custom shellcode performs anti-virtual-machine checks, captures system data and screenshots, and exfiltrates them to C2 infrastructure (e.g., 23.106.215[.]105, www.blgbeach[.]com), with the latest vulnerability reported and patched on September 12, 2023 (see TAG’s published RCA). In parallel, the actors published a seemingly benign Windows tool called GetSymbol on GitHub (https://github.com/dbgsymbol/) that quietly downloads debugging symbols—and arbitrary code—from attacker domains, requiring full OS reinstalls for compromised hosts. TAG has added malicious sites to Safe Browsing, issued government-backed attacker alerts to targeted Gmail and Workspace users, and urges researchers to enable Enhanced Safe Browsing, keep software up to date, and verify system integrity after using third-party tools.
hits.title: Active North Korean campaign targeting security researchers

hits.text: Since mid-November 2024, Russian nation-state actor Star Blizzard has significantly escalated its evasion tradecraft following public exposure by Microsoft Threat Intelligence: shifting from a single registrar (NameCheap) to multiple registrars (Hostinger, RealTime Register, GMO Internet) and implementing multi-stage redirection chains—embedding Microsoft 365 Safe Links in PDF lures that pass through Bitly and Cuttly shortened URLs and legitimate open-redirect sites (e.g., mechengsys[.]net) before landing on an Evilginx-equipped VPS (vidmemax[.]com)—to mount AiTM spear-phishing campaigns that harvest email credentials, including MFA tokens. Between July and August 2024 they also experimented with altered OneDrive file-share notifications—using ProtonMail accounts to spoof trusted senders and rewire the “Open” button URL to their Evilginx infrastructure—targeting individuals in politics, diplomacy, NGOs and think tanks. In October 2024, Microsoft’s Digital Crimes Unit disrupted core infrastructure, and ongoing collaboration with UK NCSC, NSA and FBI ensures rapid customer notification and defenses. Historically, since 2022 Star Blizzard has iteratively refined detection evasion—employing server-side fingerprinting scripts, HubSpot and MailerLite email platforms to mask domains, DNS obfuscation, password-protected PDFs and randomized DGAs—with each ephemeral TTP swiftly modified, underscoring the need for continuous updates to email security controls, link inspection and behavioral detection.
hits.title: Star Blizzard increases sophistication and evasion in ongoing attacks | Microsoft Security Blog

hits.text: ESET researchers uncovered a novel crimeware campaign, active in Czechia since November 2023 and paused only by the arrest of a suspect in March 2024, in which attackers combined social engineering, phishing and Android malware to target clients of three Czech banks via deceptive SMS links to malicious progressive web apps (PWAs) and WebAPKs; after harvesting credentials, the attackers lured victims into installing NGate, a custom Android malware named for its incorporation of the open-source NFCGate tool, which relays NFC data from victims’ unrooted smartphones to an attacker’s rooted device, enabling the emulation of cloned payment cards and unauthorized ATM withdrawals (over 160,000 CZK recovered from just three recent victims, with likely higher overall losses), with a fallback tactic of illicit bank-to-bank transfers when the relay method fails.
hits.title: NGate Android malware relays NFC traffic to steal cash

hits.text: Since November 2024, Iran-linked APT42 (aka TA453/Mint Sandstorm) has executed multi-stage intrusions against government ministries and critical infrastructure across Europe and the Middle East, initially using spear-phishing lures with malicious RTF attachments to deploy its custom ChainDoor RAT and establish HTTPS-based C2 channels; in December 2024 it leveraged a zero-day SQL injection against public-facing web portals to plant a secondary backdoor, then used Mimikatz for credential harvesting and lateral movement, exfiltrating over 3.5 TB of sensitive PII and policy documents—hiding stolen data via steganography in JPEGs—and deploying coin-miner payloads on select hosts; this campaign has compromised at least 150 systems, caused an estimated $2 million in operational disruption, and underscores the need for immediate patching of web applications, enforcement of MFA, network segmentation, and enhanced monitoring for anomalous HTTPS traffic to known C2 domains.

canonical_entities: Scanning the Internet for IoT devices with open Telnet/SSH ports
Use of default or weak credentials
Encrypted SOCKS5 tunneling to proxy infrastructure
hits.text: Researchers have uncovered that since early 2024 a previously undocumented botnet, dubbed Ngioweb, has been systematically scanning the Internet for IoT devices—primarily DVRs, IP cameras and home routers—with open Telnet/SSH ports and default or weak credentials, exploiting known firmware vulnerabilities to deploy a lightweight Go-based loader that establishes encrypted SOCKS5 tunnels back to a resilient NSOCKS residential proxy network of over 150,000 infected nodes. Once a device is compromised, Ngioweb drops a persistent agent that connects to fast-flux C2 domains via HTTPS, retrieves updated encryption keys and proxy configuration, and registers the node for NSOCKS’ tiered subscription service (starting at $25/month), which reportedly generates upwards of $500K in monthly revenue by fueling large-scale credential-stuffing campaigns, ad fraud and DDoS-for-hire operations. The actors behind Ngioweb continually rotate fallback C2 domains, employ encryption and obfuscation to evade signature-based detection, and monitor infection success rates in real time, enabling rapid retooling and expansion. Defenders are urged to enforce strong, unique credentials on all IoT assets, disable unused management interfaces, apply timely firmware updates, implement network segmentation and deploy behavioral analytics or honeypots to detect anomalous outbound proxy traffic.
hits.title: Ngioweb Botnet Fuels NSOCKS Residential Proxy Network Exploiting IoT Devices

hits.text: McAfee researchers at RSA Conference 2019 revealed that Operation Sharpshooter—a previously disclosed December 2018 espionage campaign first observed via October 25 weaponized macro-laden Dropbox documents—actually began as early as September 2017, using embedded shellcode in Microsoft Word to deploy a modular, in-memory second-stage implant dubbed “Rising Sun.” Rising Sun, which reuses source code from the Lazarus Group’s Duuzer backdoor, performs reconnaissance, encrypts and exfiltrates system data (computer names, IP addresses, native OS details) and communicates with multiple newly identified command-and-control servers. Initially detected in 87 global organizations—50 percent in U.S. defense, nuclear, energy and financial sectors—the ongoing campaign has expanded to target financial services, government and critical infrastructure in Germany, Turkey, the U.K. and the U.S., exhibiting TTP overlaps and code reuse linking it to Lazarus operations. These findings underscore the need for strengthened macro and memory-resident malware defenses, proactive C2 infrastructure takedown efforts and enhanced attribution methodologies.
hits.title: RSAC 2019: New Operation Sharpshooter Data Reveals Higher Complexity, Scope | Threatpost

hits.text: In November 2023, Russian state-sponsored group Nobelium (aka Midnight Blizzard/APT29) executed a month-long breach of Microsoft’s corporate email environment by conducting a password-spray brute-force attack against a legacy non-production test tenant lacking multi-factor authentication, enabling pivoting to a small subset of high-value accounts—including leadership, cybersecurity and legal team mailboxes—from which they exfiltrated emails and attachments; discovered on January 12, 2024, the campaign underscores the risk of poorly secured account configurations rather than software vulnerabilities, prompting Microsoft to notify impacted employees, reaffirm its MFA mandate, and reinforce zero-trust controls. This incident, following Nobelium’s SolarWinds and 2021 support-tool intrusions, highlights the necessity of enforcing MFA, minimizing default permissions, and hardening non-prod assets to mitigate advanced persistent threats.

hits.text: Clop ransomware, a TA505-sponsored RaaS strain appending the “.ClOP” extension, infects entire networks by compromising Active Directory servers and manipulating Group Policy for persistence, then uses phishing-delivered HTML attachments to drop the Get2 loader, which in turn pulls SDBOT, FlawedAmmyy RATs, Cobalt Strike beacons and TinyMet reverse shells for reconnaissance, lateral movement (via SMB exploits), and exfiltration (often using the DEWMODE web shell). Operators employ double and quadruple extortion—threatening to publish or auction stolen data on their Cl0p^_-Leaks site and targeting executives/customers—to coerce ransoms, driving average payments up 43% to $220,298 (median $78,398) in Q1 2021 after FIN11’s and FIN7’s twin zero-day campaigns against Kiteworks FTA (CVE-2021-27101/02/03/04) and Fortra GoAnywhere MFT, while in 2023 they exploited PaperCut CVE-2023-27350 to deploy Truebot and LockBit/Clop, then MOVEit CVE-2023-24362/CVE-2023-35036 and an unpatched SQL injection flaw to steal data without payloads. Trend Micro detections reveal a May 2023 surge (245 attempts), with top targets in banking, retail and healthcare across Türkiye, Canada, the US and large enterprises worldwide.

hits.text: ESET’s 2024 analysis shows that in the wake of law-enforcement-led Operation Cronos and the collapse of LockBit and BlackCat, RansomHub emerged in February as the dominant RaaS operator—driving a 15 percent rise in leak-site victims even as overall ransomware payments fell 35 percent—and by November had eclipsed LockBit in cumulative victim postings. By tracing unique victim IDs and builder tool fingerprints, researchers linked RansomHub to established gangs Play, Medusa and BianLian and revealed that its multiplatform encryptor (Windows, Linux, ESXi) repurposes Knight source code and is protected by a unique 64-character password per sample. In May, operators added “EDRKillShifter,” a custom EDR killer that abuses at least two publicly known vulnerable drivers and uses password-encrypted shellcode to disable security products, all delivered via RansomHub’s web panel under the same affiliate-specific password model. Affiliates—who keep 90 percent of ransoms and enroll via recommendation, reputation proof or a refundable US $5 000 deposit—negotiate exclusively over Tor, post detailed ransom notes to victims, and benefit from free trial decryptions. Key mitigations include strict driver allow-listing, monitoring for anomalous driver loads, hardening EDR self-protection, blocking known Tor endpoints, and correlating builder requests and password probes to detect emerging RansomHub activity.
hits.title: Shifting the sands of RansomHub’s EDRKillShifter

hits.text: BlackCat ransomware operators have introduced “Munchkin,” a new VM-based utility—delivered as an Alpine ISO loaded in VirtualBox—that automates propagation of the Rust-based BlackCat payload to remote machines and SMB/CIFS shares to evade host-level defenses. At boot, Munchkin’s ISO resets the VM root password, spawns a tmux “controller” session to run the /app/controller binary, decrypts strings via single-byte XOR, validates and deserializes a serialized /app/config file containing access tokens, victim credentials, target hosts/shares and block-lists, then mounts a /payloads directory to generate customized BlackCat samples from a template before iterating through configured tasks to encrypt network shares. The VM also houses numerous Python scripts for lateral movement and credential harvesting. This evolution in BlackCat’s RaaS toolkit reflects a broader trend of leveraging embedded VMs to thwart security solutions, expands the group’s global targeting footprint and underscores the need for defenses tuned to detect ISO-based VM deployments and tmux-launched malware.
hits.title: BlackCat Climbs the Summit With a New Tactic

hits.text: Emerging January 2022 and initially attributed to Microsoft’s DEV-0569, the Royal ransomware gang—comprising vetted operators rather than affiliates—has rebranded itself in Tor-hosted README.TXT notes and leaked exfiltrated data via victim-specific negotiation pages, employing malvertising (including Google Ads through the Keitaro TDS), phishing (callback lures impersonating software or food delivery), malicious attachments, and forum/blog links to deliver signed BATLOADER payloads that leverage MSI Custom Actions, Nsudo and PowerShell/batch scripts to disable security controls and install remote-access tools (notably Zoho), then deploy either BlackCat’s encryptor or their own Zeon encryptor with a .Royal extension; since intensifying operations in September 2022, they’ve struck high-profile victims such as Silverstone Circuit and Travis Central Appraisal District, exfiltrating data and demanding $250K–$2M, prompting HC3, CISA and FBI alerts—particularly for healthcare—while continuously innovating defense-evasion and post-compromise techniques; organizations should proactively monitor IOCs, enforce MFA, patch systems, segment networks, restrict macros, audit remote-access deployments and maintain offline backups to mitigate this financially driven threat.
hits.title: Everything You Need to Know About Royal Ransomware

hits.text: Since mid-2022, Unit 42 has attributed over 100 high-value cryptocurrency and BPO incidents to Muddled Libra—a fluid subset of the Scattered Spider collective—initially executing structured smishing and 0ktapus phishing campaigns (leveraging over 200 realistic mobile-auth portals) against large business process outsourcers, then evolving in 2023 into an ALPHV/BlackCat affiliate with multi-million-dollar extortion demands, later resuming high-profile attacks in late 2024 and expanding through May 2025 into software automation, telecom, hospitality, finance and retail verticals; their adaptable tradecraft blends social engineering of IT helpdesks to reset passwords and MFA, inside BPO access, legitimate remote management tools for CRM exfiltration, NSOCKS/TrueSocks anonymizing proxies, custom virtual machines, the open-source “bedevil” rootkit on VMware vCenter, email-forwarding rules to hijack incident response communications, and AI-driven voice spoofing for vishing, with members cycling via Discord and Telegram to refresh niche skills and spawn offshoots such as Scatter Swine and Octo Tempest, while leveraging deep incident response framework knowledge to persist in environments and repeatedly reclaim stolen data before affiliating with DragonForce for ransomware; defenders should deploy interwoven modern security architectures (Cortex XSIAM/XDR, Advanced URL Filtering, DNS Security, App-ID), enforce strict access controls, conduct rigorous awareness training, and maintain vigilant MITRE-mapped monitoring (T1566, T1556, T1215, T1562) to thwart these multifaceted, evolving extortion campaigns.
hits.title: Threat Group Assessment: Muddled Libra (Updated May 16, 2025)

canonical_entities: installing Sagerunex variants in the Windows Registry
hits.text: The Lotus Blossom APT (aka Lotus Panda, Billbug, Spring Dragon) has stepped up cyberespionage against APAC government targets by deploying new Sagerunex backdoor variants and abusing Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) for stealthy post-exploitation and lateral movement, enabling remote command execution without additional malware. Initial access methods include spear-phishing, watering-hole attacks and exploiting public-facing application flaws; once inside, operators run reconnaissance commands (tasklist, ipconfig, netstat), harvest credentials with Chrome cookie stealers, compress data via RAR and relay traffic through custom Venom proxies or proxy configurations when direct internet access is blocked. Persistence is achieved by installing Sagerunex variants in the Windows Registry under hijacked service names (tapisrv, swprv) to auto-launch at startup, while command-and-control blends encrypted traffic into legitimate platforms—stolen data uploaded as .rar on Dropbox, commands hidden in Twitter status updates and Zimbra draft emails—evading detection. Organizations are advised to deploy behavior-based EDR for registry and encrypted cloud-service anomalies, implement zero-trust network segmentation, validate defenses with breach-and-attack simulation and maintain robust, regularly tested incident response plans.
hits.title: Lotus Blossom APT Exploits WMI for Post-Exploitation Activities

canonical_entities: enumerates SSH directories to harvest credentials
Persistence is achieved through multiple cronjobs
hits.text: Aqua Security’s Nautilus team has uncovered Hadooken, a new Linux malware targeting Oracle WebLogic servers via weak passwords. Post-compromise, attackers deploy redundant shell and Python scripts to ensure download and execution of Hadooken, which enumerates SSH directories to harvest credentials, moves laterally, and clears logs. Hadooken then drops a three-path cryptominer and a Tsunami backdoor with a randomized name, the latter reserved for potential later-stage attacks. Persistence is achieved through multiple cronjobs under varied names and frequencies stored across cron directories. The malware is hosted on two IPs—one German address linked to TeamTNT and Gang 8220, the other inactive in Russia—where researchers also identified a Mallox ransomware PowerShell loader targeting Windows. Static analysis links Hadooken to Rhombus and NoEscape families. With over 230,000 internet-connected WebLogic instances—hundreds of which expose vulnerable admin consoles—this campaign underscores the dual risk of cryptojacking and ransomware across Linux and Windows environments.
hits.title: New 'Hadooken' Linux Malware Targets WebLogic Servers - SecurityWeek

hits.text: McAfee researchers at RSA Conference 2019 revealed that Operation Sharpshooter—a previously disclosed December 2018 espionage campaign first observed via October 25 weaponized macro-laden Dropbox documents—actually began as early as September 2017, using embedded shellcode in Microsoft Word to deploy a modular, in-memory second-stage implant dubbed “Rising Sun.” Rising Sun, which reuses source code from the Lazarus Group’s Duuzer backdoor, performs reconnaissance, encrypts and exfiltrates system data (computer names, IP addresses, native OS details) and communicates with multiple newly identified command-and-control servers. Initially detected in 87 global organizations—50 percent in U.S. defense, nuclear, energy and financial sectors—the ongoing campaign has expanded to target financial services, government and critical infrastructure in Germany, Turkey, the U.K. and the U.S., exhibiting TTP overlaps and code reuse linking it to Lazarus operations. These findings underscore the need for strengthened macro and memory-resident malware defenses, proactive C2 infrastructure takedown efforts and enhanced attribution methodologies.
hits.title: RSAC 2019: New Operation Sharpshooter Data Reveals Higher Complexity, Scope | Threatpost

hits.text: Security researchers at McAfee first observed Operation Sharpshooter in October–November 2018, a sophisticated phishing campaign targeting 87 critical‐infrastructure organizations—predominantly in the United States—including nuclear, defense, energy and financial firms, via recruitment‐style Microsoft Word attachments containing weaponized macros that load an in‐memory downloader to fetch a second‐stage implant dubbed Rising Sun; this implant, which exfiltrates host data to a command server, incorporates publicly available Lazarus Group source code as a likely false flag rather than evidence of Lazarus involvement. McAfee analysts Ryan Sherstobitoff and Asheer Malhotra note that Rising Sun’s multi‐step execution—weaponized document, in‐memory downloader, intelligence‐gathering implant—highlights the continued efficacy of social‐engineering vectors, while experts from CipherCloud, Positive Technologies and Lucy Security emphasize that defenses must go beyond spam filters to include ongoing user awareness training, holistic people-and-technology security models, robust data protection, network visibility and rapid incident response to detect and halt such advanced, evolving threats.
hits.title: Operation Sharpshooter targets infrastructure around the world | TechTarget

canonical_entities: Palo Alto Networks Cortex XDR Anti-Ransomware
hits.text: Following the sale of INC ransomware source code in March 2024 and its initial appearance in August 2023, researchers in July 2024 uncovered Lynx ransomware, a Windows-only, C++-based RaaS variant that shares ~48% of INC’s functions (70.8% among common routines) and has been deployed against U.S. and U.K. retail, real estate, architecture, financial and environmental service firms via phishing, malicious downloads and underground forums; employing AES-128-CTR and Curve25519 Donna for encryption with a .lynx extension, it conducts double-extortion by exfiltrating victims’ data (published on lynxblog[.]net under a policy excluding governments, hospitals and non-profits) before encrypting all files by default—killing processes, encrypting network shares and hidden disks, deleting shadow copies and backups, leveraging the Restart Manager API to target in-use files, and printing a OneNote report—then dropping a README.txt ransom note; this evolution of RaaS underscores the need for organizations to adopt robust cybersecurity measures, including anti-phishing training, backup hardening, dynamic and behavioral detections via Palo Alto Networks’ Cortex XDR Anti-Ransomware and Advanced WildFire, and vigilant monitoring of Indicators of Compromise such as published SHA256 hashes to mitigate high-profile, code-reused ransomware campaigns.
hits.title: Lynx Ransomware: A Rebranding of INC Ransomware

hits.text: Since its emergence in 2013, Iran-linked APT35 (aka Charming Kitten/Phosphorus) has executed a series of high-value espionage campaigns—beginning with a 2014 social-media spying operation—and continued in 2019 with spear-phishing against U.S., French and Middle East academic institutions before Microsoft’s Digital Crimes Unit seized control of 99 APT35 domains; in late 2020 the group targeted oncology, genetics and neurology researchers in Israel and the U.S. via its “BadBlood” PDF-based spear-phishing campaign, while in 2021 it chained Exchange Server flaws (ProxyShell) for network intrusion and demonstrated TTP overlaps with Momento ransomware (CVE-2021-21972 exploiter); in January 2022 it performed mass Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228) scans—over 80 percent of attempts originated in the U.S.—and later deployed a stealthy .NET-based PowerShell backdoor (“PowerLess”) that runs in-process to avoid detection, followed by Hyperscrape, a Windows .NET mailbox exfiltration tool for Outlook, Gmail and Yahoo! that quietly harvests emails once the actor possesses valid credentials or session cookies, and a companion Telegram dump utility; APT35 maintains persistence for intelligence collection or monetizes access when systems lack strategic value, underscoring the need for timely patching, multi-factor authentication and continuous monitoring.
hits.title: An In-Depth Look at APT35 aka Charming Kitten

retrieval_events.query: What is the most notable new capability that appeared in later variants compared to earlier ones?

retrieved_context.text: ESET’s 2024 analysis shows that in the wake of law-enforcement-led Operation Cronos and the collapse of LockBit and BlackCat, RansomHub emerged in February as the dominant RaaS operator—driving a 15 percent rise in leak-site victims even as overall ransomware payments fell 35 percent—and by November had eclipsed LockBit in cumulative victim postings. By tracing unique victim IDs and builder tool fingerprints, researchers linked RansomHub to established gangs Play, Medusa and BianLian and revealed that its multiplatform encryptor (Windows, Linux, ESXi) repurposes Knight source code and is protected by a unique 64-character password per sample. In May, operators added “EDRKillShifter,” a custom EDR killer that abuses at least two publicly known vulnerable drivers and uses password-encrypted shellcode to disable security products, all delivered via RansomHub’s web panel under the same affiliate-specific password model. Affiliates—who keep 90 percent of ransoms and enroll via recommendation, reputation proof or a refundable US $5 000 deposit—negotiate exclusively over Tor, post detailed ransom notes to victims, and benefit from free trial decryptions. Key mitigations include strict driver allow-listing, monitoring for anomalous driver loads, hardening EDR self-protection, blocking known Tor endpoints, and correlating builder requests and password probes to detect emerging RansomHub activity.
retrieved_context.title: Shifting the sands of RansomHub’s EDRKillShifter

retrieved_context.text: BlackCat ransomware operators have introduced “Munchkin,” a new VM-based utility—delivered as an Alpine ISO loaded in VirtualBox—that automates propagation of the Rust-based BlackCat payload to remote machines and SMB/CIFS shares to evade host-level defenses. At boot, Munchkin’s ISO resets the VM root password, spawns a tmux “controller” session to run the /app/controller binary, decrypts strings via single-byte XOR, validates and deserializes a serialized /app/config file containing access tokens, victim credentials, target hosts/shares and block-lists, then mounts a /payloads directory to generate customized BlackCat samples from a template before iterating through configured tasks to encrypt network shares. The VM also houses numerous Python scripts for lateral movement and credential harvesting. This evolution in BlackCat’s RaaS toolkit reflects a broader trend of leveraging embedded VMs to thwart security solutions, expands the group’s global targeting footprint and underscores the need for defenses tuned to detect ISO-based VM deployments and tmux-launched malware.
retrieved_context.title: BlackCat Climbs the Summit With a New Tactic

retrieved_context.text: Emerging January 2022 and initially attributed to Microsoft’s DEV-0569, the Royal ransomware gang—comprising vetted operators rather than affiliates—has rebranded itself in Tor-hosted README.TXT notes and leaked exfiltrated data via victim-specific negotiation pages, employing malvertising (including Google Ads through the Keitaro TDS), phishing (callback lures impersonating software or food delivery), malicious attachments, and forum/blog links to deliver signed BATLOADER payloads that leverage MSI Custom Actions, Nsudo and PowerShell/batch scripts to disable security controls and install remote-access tools (notably Zoho), then deploy either BlackCat’s encryptor or their own Zeon encryptor with a .Royal extension; since intensifying operations in September 2022, they’ve struck high-profile victims such as Silverstone Circuit and Travis Central Appraisal District, exfiltrating data and demanding $250K–$2M, prompting HC3, CISA and FBI alerts—particularly for healthcare—while continuously innovating defense-evasion and post-compromise techniques; organizations should proactively monitor IOCs, enforce MFA, patch systems, segment networks, restrict macros, audit remote-access deployments and maintain offline backups to mitigate this financially driven threat.
retrieved_context.title: Everything You Need to Know About Royal Ransomware

retrieved_context.text: Since mid-2022, Unit 42 has attributed over 100 high-value cryptocurrency and BPO incidents to Muddled Libra—a fluid subset of the Scattered Spider collective—initially executing structured smishing and 0ktapus phishing campaigns (leveraging over 200 realistic mobile-auth portals) against large business process outsourcers, then evolving in 2023 into an ALPHV/BlackCat affiliate with multi-million-dollar extortion demands, later resuming high-profile attacks in late 2024 and expanding through May 2025 into software automation, telecom, hospitality, finance and retail verticals; their adaptable tradecraft blends social engineering of IT helpdesks to reset passwords and MFA, inside BPO access, legitimate remote management tools for CRM exfiltration, NSOCKS/TrueSocks anonymizing proxies, custom virtual machines, the open-source “bedevil” rootkit on VMware vCenter, email-forwarding rules to hijack incident response communications, and AI-driven voice spoofing for vishing, with members cycling via Discord and Telegram to refresh niche skills and spawn offshoots such as Scatter Swine and Octo Tempest, while leveraging deep incident response framework knowledge to persist in environments and repeatedly reclaim stolen data before affiliating with DragonForce for ransomware; defenders should deploy interwoven modern security architectures (Cortex XSIAM/XDR, Advanced URL Filtering, DNS Security, App-ID), enforce strict access controls, conduct rigorous awareness training, and maintain vigilant MITRE-mapped monitoring (T1566, T1556, T1215, T1562) to thwart these multifaceted, evolving extortion campaigns.
retrieved_context.title: Threat Group Assessment: Muddled Libra (Updated May 16, 2025)

canonical_entities: installing Sagerunex variants in the Windows Registry
retrieved_context.text: The Lotus Blossom APT (aka Lotus Panda, Billbug, Spring Dragon) has stepped up cyberespionage against APAC government targets by deploying new Sagerunex backdoor variants and abusing Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) for stealthy post-exploitation and lateral movement, enabling remote command execution without additional malware. Initial access methods include spear-phishing, watering-hole attacks and exploiting public-facing application flaws; once inside, operators run reconnaissance commands (tasklist, ipconfig, netstat), harvest credentials with Chrome cookie stealers, compress data via RAR and relay traffic through custom Venom proxies or proxy configurations when direct internet access is blocked. Persistence is achieved by installing Sagerunex variants in the Windows Registry under hijacked service names (tapisrv, swprv) to auto-launch at startup, while command-and-control blends encrypted traffic into legitimate platforms—stolen data uploaded as .rar on Dropbox, commands hidden in Twitter status updates and Zimbra draft emails—evading detection. Organizations are advised to deploy behavior-based EDR for registry and encrypted cloud-service anomalies, implement zero-trust network segmentation, validate defenses with breach-and-attack simulation and maintain robust, regularly tested incident response plans.
retrieved_context.title: Lotus Blossom APT Exploits WMI for Post-Exploitation Activities

canonical_entities: bypasses the Mark of the Web
attack surface reduction rules to block Office-spawned child processes
hits.text: Microsoft’s August 2023 Patch Tuesday addressed two actively exploited zero-days—CVE-2023-36884, a remote code execution flaw in Microsoft Office that bypasses the Mark of the Web, and CVE-2023-38180, a .NET/Visual Studio vulnerability enabling DDoS attacks without requiring user privileges—after one was publicly disclosed pre-patch. The Russian actor Storm-0978 (aka RomCom/Underground), noted for Industrial Spy ransomware, leveraged crafted Office documents to execute payloads and extort victims, while CVE-2023-38180 attacks demand only network proximity. To mitigate these threats, Microsoft released an Office Defense-in-Depth update and a .NET/Visual Studio patch and recommends deploying both Office and Windows August updates, enabling cloud-delivered protection in Defender Antivirus, activating EDR block mode, enforcing attack surface reduction rules to block Office-spawned child processes, and applying the advisory’s update for CVE-2023-38180. Avertium validates these controls, provides IoCs for RomCom campaigns, and advocates continuous vulnerability management and its Fusion MXDR for Microsoft service to detect suspicious Office-to-script execution chains and remediate artifacts proactively.
hits.title: Flash Notice: Two Microsoft Zero-Day Vulnerabilities Exploited by Attackers

canonical_entities: exploiting known vulnerabilities in public-facing VPN, web, Java, and SQL services
harvests credentials from LSASS memory and the SAM registry hive
hits.text: Microsoft has traced a stealthy espionage campaign by Flax Typhoon (aka Ethereal Panda), a China-based nation-state actor active since mid-2021, targeting dozens of Taiwanese organizations (with spill-over in Southeast Asia, North America, and Africa) by exploiting known vulnerabilities in public-facing VPN, web, Java, and SQL services to deploy the China Chopper web shell for initial access; the group escalates privileges via open-source exploits like Juicy Potato and BadPotato, then establishes persistence by disabling RDP network-level authentication, hijacking the Sticky Keys (sethc.exe) binary to launch Task Manager as SYSTEM, and installing a renamed SoftEther VPN-over-HTTPS bridge (conhost.exe/dllhost.exe) as a service to maintain covert C2 over port 443; leveraging LOLBins such as PowerShell Invoke-WebRequest, certutil, bitsadmin, WinRM, and WMIC for lateral movement, vulnerability scanning, and remote execution, it harvests credentials from LSASS memory and the SAM registry hive using Mimikatz for pass-the-hash attacks; although no exfiltration or final objectives have been observed, organizations are urged to enforce rigorous patch and vulnerability management on internet-exposed systems, monitor registry and file-integrity changes, deploy web application firewalls, reset compromised credentials, isolate and forensically examine affected hosts, and leverage detections in Microsoft 365 Defender to disrupt living-off-the-land tactics.
hits.title: Flax Typhoon using legitimate software to quietly access Taiwanese organizations | Microsoft Security Blog

retrieved_context.text: Emerging January 2022 and initially attributed to Microsoft’s DEV-0569, the Royal ransomware gang—comprising vetted operators rather than affiliates—has rebranded itself in Tor-hosted README.TXT notes and leaked exfiltrated data via victim-specific negotiation pages, employing malvertising (including Google Ads through the Keitaro TDS), phishing (callback lures impersonating software or food delivery), malicious attachments, and forum/blog links to deliver signed BATLOADER payloads that leverage MSI Custom Actions, Nsudo and PowerShell/batch scripts to disable security controls and install remote-access tools (notably Zoho), then deploy either BlackCat’s encryptor or their own Zeon encryptor with a .Royal extension; since intensifying operations in September 2022, they’ve struck high-profile victims such as Silverstone Circuit and Travis Central Appraisal District, exfiltrating data and demanding $250K–$2M, prompting HC3, CISA and FBI alerts—particularly for healthcare—while continuously innovating defense-evasion and post-compromise techniques; organizations should proactively monitor IOCs, enforce MFA, patch systems, segment networks, restrict macros, audit remote-access deployments and maintain offline backups to mitigate this financially driven threat.

retrieved_context.text: Since mid-2022, Unit 42 has attributed over 100 high-value cryptocurrency and BPO incidents to Muddled Libra—a fluid subset of the Scattered Spider collective—initially executing structured smishing and 0ktapus phishing campaigns (leveraging over 200 realistic mobile-auth portals) against large business process outsourcers, then evolving in 2023 into an ALPHV/BlackCat affiliate with multi-million-dollar extortion demands, later resuming high-profile attacks in late 2024 and expanding through May 2025 into software automation, telecom, hospitality, finance and retail verticals; their adaptable tradecraft blends social engineering of IT helpdesks to reset passwords and MFA, inside BPO access, legitimate remote management tools for CRM exfiltration, NSOCKS/TrueSocks anonymizing proxies, custom virtual machines, the open-source “bedevil” rootkit on VMware vCenter, email-forwarding rules to hijack incident response communications, and AI-driven voice spoofing for vishing, with members cycling via Discord and Telegram to refresh niche skills and spawn offshoots such as Scatter Swine and Octo Tempest, while leveraging deep incident response framework knowledge to persist in environments and repeatedly reclaim stolen data before affiliating with DragonForce for ransomware; defenders should deploy interwoven modern security architectures (Cortex XSIAM/XDR, Advanced URL Filtering, DNS Security, App-ID), enforce strict access controls, conduct rigorous awareness training, and maintain vigilant MITRE-mapped monitoring (T1566, T1556, T1215, T1562) to thwart these multifaceted, evolving extortion campaigns.

retrieved_context.text: McAfee researchers at RSA Conference 2019 revealed that Operation Sharpshooter—a previously disclosed December 2018 espionage campaign first observed via October 25 weaponized macro-laden Dropbox documents—actually began as early as September 2017, using embedded shellcode in Microsoft Word to deploy a modular, in-memory second-stage implant dubbed “Rising Sun.” Rising Sun, which reuses source code from the Lazarus Group’s Duuzer backdoor, performs reconnaissance, encrypts and exfiltrates system data (computer names, IP addresses, native OS details) and communicates with multiple newly identified command-and-control servers. Initially detected in 87 global organizations—50 percent in U.S. defense, nuclear, energy and financial sectors—the ongoing campaign has expanded to target financial services, government and critical infrastructure in Germany, Turkey, the U.K. and the U.S., exhibiting TTP overlaps and code reuse linking it to Lazarus operations. These findings underscore the need for strengthened macro and memory-resident malware defenses, proactive C2 infrastructure takedown efforts and enhanced attribution methodologies.
retrieved_context.title: RSAC 2019: New Operation Sharpshooter Data Reveals Higher Complexity, Scope | Threatpost

retrieved_context.text: Since its emergence in 2013, Iran-linked APT35 (aka Charming Kitten/Phosphorus) has executed a series of high-value espionage campaigns—beginning with a 2014 social-media spying operation—and continued in 2019 with spear-phishing against U.S., French and Middle East academic institutions before Microsoft’s Digital Crimes Unit seized control of 99 APT35 domains; in late 2020 the group targeted oncology, genetics and neurology researchers in Israel and the U.S. via its “BadBlood” PDF-based spear-phishing campaign, while in 2021 it chained Exchange Server flaws (ProxyShell) for network intrusion and demonstrated TTP overlaps with Momento ransomware (CVE-2021-21972 exploiter); in January 2022 it performed mass Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228) scans—over 80 percent of attempts originated in the U.S.—and later deployed a stealthy .NET-based PowerShell backdoor (“PowerLess”) that runs in-process to avoid detection, followed by Hyperscrape, a Windows .NET mailbox exfiltration tool for Outlook, Gmail and Yahoo! that quietly harvests emails once the actor possesses valid credentials or session cookies, and a companion Telegram dump utility; APT35 maintains persistence for intelligence collection or monetizes access when systems lack strategic value, underscoring the need for timely patching, multi-factor authentication and continuous monitoring.
retrieved_context.title: An In-Depth Look at APT35 aka Charming Kitten

canonical_entities: bypasses the Mark of the Web
attack surface reduction rules to block Office-spawned child processes
retrieved_context.text: Microsoft’s August 2023 Patch Tuesday addressed two actively exploited zero-days—CVE-2023-36884, a remote code execution flaw in Microsoft Office that bypasses the Mark of the Web, and CVE-2023-38180, a .NET/Visual Studio vulnerability enabling DDoS attacks without requiring user privileges—after one was publicly disclosed pre-patch. The Russian actor Storm-0978 (aka RomCom/Underground), noted for Industrial Spy ransomware, leveraged crafted Office documents to execute payloads and extort victims, while CVE-2023-38180 attacks demand only network proximity. To mitigate these threats, Microsoft released an Office Defense-in-Depth update and a .NET/Visual Studio patch and recommends deploying both Office and Windows August updates, enabling cloud-delivered protection in Defender Antivirus, activating EDR block mode, enforcing attack surface reduction rules to block Office-spawned child processes, and applying the advisory’s update for CVE-2023-38180. Avertium validates these controls, provides IoCs for RomCom campaigns, and advocates continuous vulnerability management and its Fusion MXDR for Microsoft service to detect suspicious Office-to-script execution chains and remediate artifacts proactively.
retrieved_context.title: Flash Notice: Two Microsoft Zero-Day Vulnerabilities Exploited by Attackers

canonical_entities: exploiting known vulnerabilities in public-facing VPN, web, Java, and SQL services
harvests credentials from LSASS memory and the SAM registry hive
retrieved_context.text: Microsoft has traced a stealthy espionage campaign by Flax Typhoon (aka Ethereal Panda), a China-based nation-state actor active since mid-2021, targeting dozens of Taiwanese organizations (with spill-over in Southeast Asia, North America, and Africa) by exploiting known vulnerabilities in public-facing VPN, web, Java, and SQL services to deploy the China Chopper web shell for initial access; the group escalates privileges via open-source exploits like Juicy Potato and BadPotato, then establishes persistence by disabling RDP network-level authentication, hijacking the Sticky Keys (sethc.exe) binary to launch Task Manager as SYSTEM, and installing a renamed SoftEther VPN-over-HTTPS bridge (conhost.exe/dllhost.exe) as a service to maintain covert C2 over port 443; leveraging LOLBins such as PowerShell Invoke-WebRequest, certutil, bitsadmin, WinRM, and WMIC for lateral movement, vulnerability scanning, and remote execution, it harvests credentials from LSASS memory and the SAM registry hive using Mimikatz for pass-the-hash attacks; although no exfiltration or final objectives have been observed, organizations are urged to enforce rigorous patch and vulnerability management on internet-exposed systems, monitor registry and file-integrity changes, deploy web application firewalls, reset compromised credentials, isolate and forensically examine affected hosts, and leverage detections in Microsoft 365 Defender to disrupt living-off-the-land tactics.
retrieved_context.title: Flax Typhoon using legitimate software to quietly access Taiwanese organizations | Microsoft Security Blog

retrieved_context.text: Security researchers at McAfee first observed Operation Sharpshooter in October–November 2018, a sophisticated phishing campaign targeting 87 critical‐infrastructure organizations—predominantly in the United States—including nuclear, defense, energy and financial firms, via recruitment‐style Microsoft Word attachments containing weaponized macros that load an in‐memory downloader to fetch a second‐stage implant dubbed Rising Sun; this implant, which exfiltrates host data to a command server, incorporates publicly available Lazarus Group source code as a likely false flag rather than evidence of Lazarus involvement. McAfee analysts Ryan Sherstobitoff and Asheer Malhotra note that Rising Sun’s multi‐step execution—weaponized document, in‐memory downloader, intelligence‐gathering implant—highlights the continued efficacy of social‐engineering vectors, while experts from CipherCloud, Positive Technologies and Lucy Security emphasize that defenses must go beyond spam filters to include ongoing user awareness training, holistic people-and-technology security models, robust data protection, network visibility and rapid incident response to detect and halt such advanced, evolving threats.
retrieved_context.title: Operation Sharpshooter targets infrastructure around the world | TechTarget

canonical_entities: enumerates SSH directories to harvest credentials
Persistence is achieved through multiple cronjobs
retrieved_context.text: Aqua Security’s Nautilus team has uncovered Hadooken, a new Linux malware targeting Oracle WebLogic servers via weak passwords. Post-compromise, attackers deploy redundant shell and Python scripts to ensure download and execution of Hadooken, which enumerates SSH directories to harvest credentials, moves laterally, and clears logs. Hadooken then drops a three-path cryptominer and a Tsunami backdoor with a randomized name, the latter reserved for potential later-stage attacks. Persistence is achieved through multiple cronjobs under varied names and frequencies stored across cron directories. The malware is hosted on two IPs—one German address linked to TeamTNT and Gang 8220, the other inactive in Russia—where researchers also identified a Mallox ransomware PowerShell loader targeting Windows. Static analysis links Hadooken to Rhombus and NoEscape families. With over 230,000 internet-connected WebLogic instances—hundreds of which expose vulnerable admin consoles—this campaign underscores the dual risk of cryptojacking and ransomware across Linux and Windows environments.
retrieved_context.title: New 'Hadooken' Linux Malware Targets WebLogic Servers - SecurityWeek

hits.text: During a recent incident, a LockBit affiliate conducted initial intrusions using gpresult for policy dumping, Cobalt Strike loaders and PsExec for privilege escalation, followed by reconnaissance (whoami, netstat, quser, net view), lateral movement, persistence via a new user account, and data exfiltration over FTP with Wput; when deployment of LockBit (SHA256 079b99f6…) was blocked on the target network, the attacker pivoted to a newly observed Rust-written ransomware family dubbed 3AM (SHA256 307a1217…), which appends “.threeamtime” to encrypted files, stops over 100 security and backup services via net stop and wbadmin/bcdedit/wmic commands, deletes Volume Shadow copies with vssadmin.exe delete shadows /all /quiet, and drops a Tor‐accessible ransom note requiring a 32-character “-k” access key and offering decryption/mystical-themed extortion; although 3AM encryption succeeded on only one of three attempted hosts, its Conti-style “-m” (local/net) and “-h” parameters, heavy service-termination payload, and aggressive VSS wipe underscore its potential as a fallback vector—defenders should update Symantec/Broadcom signatures, monitor for the .threeamtime extension, suspicious Rust binaries, command-line flags “-k” and “-m”, and mass service stoppage activity, and block associated IOCs (185.202.0[.]111, 212.18.104[.]6, 85.159.229[.]62) to mitigate future 3AM use.
hits.title: 3AM: New Ransomware Family Used As Fallback in Failed LockBit Attack | Symantec Enterprise Blogs

canonical_entities: Launch EC2 instances across regions via VPN
hits.text: Unit42’s “EleKtra-Leak” campaign, active since December 2020, uses automated scripts to clone public GitHub repos every few minutes, extract exposed AWS IAM keys within five minutes, then—if not blocked by GitHub-AWS quarantine policies—execute rapid AWS reconnaissance (DescribeRegions), create security groups, and launch hundreds of EC2 instances across regions via VPN for Monero cryptojacking, generating over 400 API calls in seven minutes. Between Aug. 30 and Oct. 6, 2023, researchers tracked 474 actor-controlled miners. The actor employs custom mining software and blocklists high-profile AWS account IDs to avoid honey traps. Leveraging the Prisma Cloud HoneyCloud project’s ephemeral key leaks and policy overrides, Unit42 obtained full visibility, informing Prisma Cloud Secrets Security, CI/CD IaC scanning, Cortex XDR, and recommendations for independent repo scanning, strict IAM policies, and continuous monitoring.
hits.title: CloudKeys in the Air: Tracking Malicious Operations of Exposed IAM Keys

hits.text: Proofpoint researchers led by Sherrod DeGrippo have uncovered state-sponsored actors exploiting CVE-2022-30190 (Follina), a Microsoft Office remote code execution flaw in the Windows Support Diagnostic Tool (MSDT) invoked via URL protocol, in phishing campaigns since mid-April targeting U.S. and E.U. government workers; following Shadow Chaser Group’s April 12 discovery and Microsoft’s May patch, adversaries dispatched over 1,000 recruitment-themed emails promising a “20% increase” and urging recipients to open a Word attachment that launches a PowerShell script to detect virtualized environments, perform extensive reconnaissance across browsers, mail clients and file shares, zip collected data for exfiltration, and enable arbitrary code execution with user-level privileges to install malware, manipulate or delete data, and create accounts—activities indicative of a state-aligned nexus that underscore the urgency of rapid patch deployment, user training and network-level MSDT exploit mitigations.
hits.title: Follina Exploited by State-Sponsored Hackers | Threatpost

canonical_entities: Remote Code Execution via ms-msdt URI in Word/RTF documents
ms-msdt URI-based RCE in Word/RTF documents
hits.text: In late May 2022, Symantec identified multiple threat actors exploiting the MSDT Follina bug (CVE-2022-30190) through ms-msdt URI-based RCE in Word/RTF documents that load a malicious HTML via Word’s remote template feature to launch msdt.exe, sdiagnhost.exe and ultimately PowerShell—bypassing the need for macros—to install a digitally signed AsyncRAT remote access Trojan that performs anti-analysis checks, collects hardware IDs, user names, execution paths and OS details, and maintains C&C communications, alongside parallel deployments of a browser infostealer targeting cookies and saved credentials in Firefox, Chrome and Edge. Symantec customers should apply Microsoft’s advisories or disable the ms-msdt handler, update Symantec Endpoint definitions (File-based-Downloader-Backdoor:Async, InfoStealer) and monitor for related IOCs to thwart these rapid, damaging campaigns.
hits.title: Attackers Exploit MSDT Follina Bug to Drop RAT, Infostealer | Symantec Enterprise Blogs

retrieved_context.text: Proofpoint researchers led by Sherrod DeGrippo have uncovered state-sponsored actors exploiting CVE-2022-30190 (Follina), a Microsoft Office remote code execution flaw in the Windows Support Diagnostic Tool (MSDT) invoked via URL protocol, in phishing campaigns since mid-April targeting U.S. and E.U. government workers; following Shadow Chaser Group’s April 12 discovery and Microsoft’s May patch, adversaries dispatched over 1,000 recruitment-themed emails promising a “20% increase” and urging recipients to open a Word attachment that launches a PowerShell script to detect virtualized environments, perform extensive reconnaissance across browsers, mail clients and file shares, zip collected data for exfiltration, and enable arbitrary code execution with user-level privileges to install malware, manipulate or delete data, and create accounts—activities indicative of a state-aligned nexus that underscore the urgency of rapid patch deployment, user training and network-level MSDT exploit mitigations.

hits.text: In May 2025, a financially motivated group deployed Fog ransomware against an Asian financial institution after a roughly two-week dwell, leveraging a highly atypical toolset that blended legitimate and dual-use utilities with open-source pentesting frameworks to conduct discovery, exfiltration, lateral movement and persistence.  After gaining initial access—possibly via compromised Exchange Servers—the attackers installed GC2 implants that polled Google Sheets or SharePoint for commands (“whoami,” “ipconfig,” netstat, “upload,” “download,” “load,” “exit”), then used Stowaway to proxy and deliver the Syteca (formerly Ekran) employee-monitoring client to capture keystrokes and screen data.  They further spread laterally with PsExec and SMBExec, exfiltrated data using FreeFileSync, MegaSync and 7-Zip, and stealthily removed Syteca binaries and config files via PsExec.  On the day of encryption, Fog ransomware was deployed—continuing a trend since May 2024 of targeting VPN credentials and Veeam CVE-2024-40711—yet, unusually, a custom “SecurityHealthIron” service was created days later to maintain long-term access, suggesting espionage under the guise of ransomware.
hits.title: Fog Ransomware: Unusual Toolset Used in Recent Attack | Symantec Enterprise Blogs

hits.text: Symantec’s Threat Hunter Team has linked the newly discovered Sidewalk loader backdoor—an evolution of the Crosswalk/Backdoor.Motnug family—to Grayfly (aka GREF/Wicked Panda), a China-linked espionage group active since March 2017 that employs custom backdoors, Trojan.Chattak, Cobalt Strike, web shells and credential-dumpers against telecom, IT, media and finance targets in Taiwan, Vietnam, the US and Mexico; in a recent campaign they exploited public-facing Microsoft Exchange and MySQL servers via commodity and zero-day flaws to execute Base64-encoded PowerShell commands through certutil, install an ASPX web shell in the ClientAccess\ecp directory, deploy Sidewalk via installutil.exe, create persistence with WMIC-launched scheduled tasks, then run a custom Mimikatz variant (SHA256 b3eb783b017da32e33d19670b39eae0b11de8e983891dd4feb873d6e9333608d) to harvest credentials—all within about an hour before ceasing observable activity; three Chengdu 404 executives were indicted in 2020 for attacks on over 100 organizations, highlighting Grayfly’s persistence and underscoring the need to promptly patch Exchange and MySQL servers, monitor anomalous PowerShell and scheduled-task activity, and deploy IOC-based detection to block Sidewalk and related tools.
hits.title: Grayfly: Chinese Threat Actor Uses Newly-discovered Sidewalk Malware | Symantec Enterprise Blogs

hits.text: After a year-long investigation researchers at Lumen’s Black Lotus Labs dissected the Ngioweb botnet—first observed in 2017—which uses a loader network and roughly 15 n-day exploits to deploy malware that contacts C2 domains generated via a domain generation algorithm (augmented by DNS TXT records to resist sinkholing), evaluates device traffic capacity, and links compromised Zyxel, Reolink, Alpha Technologies and, increasingly, Netgear routers (now 10 % of bots) to over 180 “backconnect” C2 nodes that provide at least 80 % of the 35,000 residential proxies in the NSOCKS[.]net service across 180 countries; NSOCKS’s lack of authentication and appearance on free proxy lists has enabled cybercriminals to carry out DDoS amplification, credential stuffing, phishing and malware proxying (e.g., Agent Tesla), while APT28 state-sponsored actors have mixed espionage with criminal traffic on the same infrastructure. To disrupt both operations, Lumen, alongside The ShadowServer Foundation and other partners, is actively blocking traffic to known C2 nodes and publishing indicators of compromise to help organizations identify and remediate infected devices.

hits.text: In September 2024, a Winnti-linked APT began targeting trading and brokerage firms by distributing malicious .scr/.pif screen saver files via Skype that use steganographically embedded shellcode to load GodRAT—a new Gh0st RAT variant evolved from the AwesomePuppet backdoor—into legitimate processes. Two loader types (one with XOR-encoded shellcode bytes, one extracting shellcode from JPG images via an expired Valve.exe/SDL2.dll signed binary) allocate memory, inject the decoded first-stage shellcode, decode configuration data (single-byte XOR key 0x63, “godinfo” header), and fetch a UPX-packed GodRAT DLL from C2. GodRAT launches under a “-Puppet” flag in curl.exe or cmd.exe, collects OS, host, AV, process and user metadata, and communicates over zlib-compressed, triple-XOR TCP channels. It supports in-memory plugin injection—deploying a FileManager plugin for file enumeration, manipulation and 7zip-based extraction—and installs Chrome and Edge password stealers in %ALLUSERSPROFILE%. AsyncRAT serves as a secondary fallback implant. Ongoing detections (12 MD5s across Hong Kong, UAE, Jordan, Lebanon and Malaysia) through August 12 2025 highlight sustained financial credential theft and long-term C2 persistence.

hits.text: ESET’s 2024 analysis shows that in the wake of law-enforcement-led Operation Cronos and the collapse of LockBit and BlackCat, RansomHub emerged in February as the dominant RaaS operator—driving a 15 percent rise in leak-site victims even as overall ransomware payments fell 35 percent—and by November had eclipsed LockBit in cumulative victim postings. By tracing unique victim IDs and builder tool fingerprints, researchers linked RansomHub to established gangs Play, Medusa and BianLian and revealed that its multiplatform encryptor (Windows, Linux, ESXi) repurposes Knight source code and is protected by a unique 64-character password per sample. In May, operators added “EDRKillShifter,” a custom EDR killer that abuses at least two publicly known vulnerable drivers and uses password-encrypted shellcode to disable security products, all delivered via RansomHub’s web panel under the same affiliate-specific password model. Affiliates—who keep 90 percent of ransoms and enroll via recommendation, reputation proof or a refundable US $5 000 deposit—negotiate exclusively over Tor, post detailed ransom notes to victims, and benefit from free trial decryptions. Key mitigations include strict driver allow-listing, monitoring for anomalous driver loads, hardening EDR self-protection, blocking known Tor endpoints, and correlating builder requests and password probes to detect emerging RansomHub activity.
hits.title: Shifting the sands of RansomHub’s EDRKillShifter

canonical_entities: FIN11’s and FIN7’s twin zero-day campaigns
hits.text: Clop ransomware, a TA505-sponsored RaaS strain appending the “.ClOP” extension, infects entire networks by compromising Active Directory servers and manipulating Group Policy for persistence, then uses phishing-delivered HTML attachments to drop the Get2 loader, which in turn pulls SDBOT, FlawedAmmyy RATs, Cobalt Strike beacons and TinyMet reverse shells for reconnaissance, lateral movement (via SMB exploits), and exfiltration (often using the DEWMODE web shell). Operators employ double and quadruple extortion—threatening to publish or auction stolen data on their Cl0p^_-Leaks site and targeting executives/customers—to coerce ransoms, driving average payments up 43% to $220,298 (median $78,398) in Q1 2021 after FIN11’s and FIN7’s twin zero-day campaigns against Kiteworks FTA (CVE-2021-27101/02/03/04) and Fortra GoAnywhere MFT, while in 2023 they exploited PaperCut CVE-2023-27350 to deploy Truebot and LockBit/Clop, then MOVEit CVE-2023-24362/CVE-2023-35036 and an unpatched SQL injection flaw to steal data without payloads. Trend Micro detections reveal a May 2023 surge (245 attempts), with top targets in banking, retail and healthcare across Türkiye, Canada, the US and large enterprises worldwide.

hits.title: 3AM: New Ransomware Family Used As Fallback in Failed LockBit Attack | Symantec Enterprise Blogs

hits.text: Conti ransomware, a profit-driven RaaS syndicate linked by the FBI to over 400 global attacks (75% in the U.S.) with demands up to $25 million, has spent more than a year targeting high-stakes environments—hospitals, 911 dispatch centers, EMS and law enforcement—where IT outages can be life-threatening, exemplified by Ireland’s mid-May healthcare system shutdown that halted X-ray services and COVID testing; it gains initial access through Spearphishing Attachment (T1566.001), Exploit Public-Facing Application (T1190) and lacking MFA, then uses Cobalt Strike and PowerShell for discovery (T1083, T1135), lateral movement (SMB Shares T1021.002), privilege escalation (DLL Injection T1055.001) and defense evasion (Obfuscated Files T1027, Deobfuscate/Decode T1140), before executing “double extortion” (Data Encrypted for Impact T1486, Inhibit System Recovery T1490) and often reneging on decryption promises; actionable defenses include enforcing MFA, applying NGFW Threat Prevention with secure Vulnerability Protection Profiles, WildFire file analysis, Cortex XDR’s anti-malware/exploit modules, regular WildFire updates, Cortex XSOAR playbooks, and tracking IoCs via Unit 42’s GitHub and TAXII feeds.

canonical_entities: installing Sagerunex variants in the Windows Registry
hits.text: The Lotus Blossom APT (aka Lotus Panda, Billbug, Spring Dragon) has stepped up cyberespionage against APAC government targets by deploying new Sagerunex backdoor variants and abusing Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) for stealthy post-exploitation and lateral movement, enabling remote command execution without additional malware. Initial access methods include spear-phishing, watering-hole attacks and exploiting public-facing application flaws; once inside, operators run reconnaissance commands (tasklist, ipconfig, netstat), harvest credentials with Chrome cookie stealers, compress data via RAR and relay traffic through custom Venom proxies or proxy configurations when direct internet access is blocked. Persistence is achieved by installing Sagerunex variants in the Windows Registry under hijacked service names (tapisrv, swprv) to auto-launch at startup, while command-and-control blends encrypted traffic into legitimate platforms—stolen data uploaded as .rar on Dropbox, commands hidden in Twitter status updates and Zimbra draft emails—evading detection. Organizations are advised to deploy behavior-based EDR for registry and encrypted cloud-service anomalies, implement zero-trust network segmentation, validate defenses with breach-and-attack simulation and maintain robust, regularly tested incident response plans.
hits.title: Lotus Blossom APT Exploits WMI for Post-Exploitation Activities

hits.text: Microsoft has traced a stealthy espionage campaign by Flax Typhoon (aka Ethereal Panda), a China-based nation-state actor active since mid-2021, targeting dozens of Taiwanese organizations (with spill-over in Southeast Asia, North America, and Africa) by exploiting known vulnerabilities in public-facing VPN, web, Java, and SQL services to deploy the China Chopper web shell for initial access; the group escalates privileges via open-source exploits like Juicy Potato and BadPotato, then establishes persistence by disabling RDP network-level authentication, hijacking the Sticky Keys (sethc.exe) binary to launch Task Manager as SYSTEM, and installing a renamed SoftEther VPN-over-HTTPS bridge (conhost.exe/dllhost.exe) as a service to maintain covert C2 over port 443; leveraging LOLBins such as PowerShell Invoke-WebRequest, certutil, bitsadmin, WinRM, and WMIC for lateral movement, vulnerability scanning, and remote execution, it harvests credentials from LSASS memory and the SAM registry hive using Mimikatz for pass-the-hash attacks; although no exfiltration or final objectives have been observed, organizations are urged to enforce rigorous patch and vulnerability management on internet-exposed systems, monitor registry and file-integrity changes, deploy web application firewalls, reset compromised credentials, isolate and forensically examine affected hosts, and leverage detections in Microsoft 365 Defender to disrupt living-off-the-land tactics.
