retrieval_events.query: In the evolution of the LockBit ransomware described in these reports, what is the most notable new capability seen in later variants?

canonical_entities: FIN11’s and FIN7’s twin zero-day campaigns
retrieved_context.text: Clop ransomware, a TA505-sponsored RaaS strain appending the “.ClOP” extension, infects entire networks by compromising Active Directory servers and manipulating Group Policy for persistence, then uses phishing-delivered HTML attachments to drop the Get2 loader, which in turn pulls SDBOT, FlawedAmmyy RATs, Cobalt Strike beacons and TinyMet reverse shells for reconnaissance, lateral movement (via SMB exploits), and exfiltration (often using the DEWMODE web shell). Operators employ double and quadruple extortion—threatening to publish or auction stolen data on their Cl0p^_-Leaks site and targeting executives/customers—to coerce ransoms, driving average payments up 43% to $220,298 (median $78,398) in Q1 2021 after FIN11’s and FIN7’s twin zero-day campaigns against Kiteworks FTA (CVE-2021-27101/02/03/04) and Fortra GoAnywhere MFT, while in 2023 they exploited PaperCut CVE-2023-27350 to deploy Truebot and LockBit/Clop, then MOVEit CVE-2023-24362/CVE-2023-35036 and an unpatched SQL injection flaw to steal data without payloads. Trend Micro detections reveal a May 2023 surge (245 attempts), with top targets in banking, retail and healthcare across Türkiye, Canada, the US and large enterprises worldwide.
retrieved_context.title: Ransomware Spotlight: Clop | Trend Micro (US)

retrieved_context.text: Following ConnectWise’s February 19 disclosure of two critical ScreenConnect flaws—CVE-2024-1709 (CVSS 10.0 authentication bypass) and CVE-2024-1708 (CVSS 8.4 path traversal)—an updated advisory two days later warned of active exploitation, and by week’s end a public SlashAndGrab PoC enabled threat actors to mimic admin roles, delete users and seize control. Trend Micro reports Black Basta leveraging these bugs for reconnaissance, AD discovery, privilege escalation, creation of new admin accounts, deployment of Cobalt Strike beacons and scripts to trace recent AD connections before dropping ransomware. Bl00dy similarly abused leaked Conti and LockBit builders to plant ransom notes, while other groups installed XWorm RAT, disabled Windows Defender real-time protection and deployed alternate RMM tools (Atera, Syncro). Immediate patching to ScreenConnect 23.9.8 is critical to halt ongoing remote-access intrusions, ransomware deployment and potential data theft.
retrieved_context.title: Black Basta, Bl00dy Ransomware Exploiting Recent ScreenConnect Flaws - SecurityWeek

retrieved_context.text: Researchers at Mandiant Intelligence have identified UNC2165—the latest evolution of the U.S.-sanctioned Evil Corp—as leveraging the FakeUpdates infection chain to gain initial access, followed by deployment of LockBit ransomware to obscure attribution and monetize extortion efforts. After OFAC sanctions in December 2019 crippled Evil Corp’s ability to profit from Dridex and its WastedLocker strain, the group briefly resurfaced under PayloadBin (likely a WastedLocker rebrand) and used HTML redirectors in malicious Excel files, then adopted Hades ransomware with code overlaps to distance itself further. By aligning with LockBit’s RaaS model—already proven effective against high-profile victims such as Accenture and Bangkok Air—UNC2165 can blend in with legitimate affiliates, reduce development overhead, and bypass sanctions enforcement that deters U.S. entities from negotiating ransoms with known Evil Corp actors. This shift underscores the need for defenders to monitor FakeUpdates chains and LockBit activity for potential Evil Corp–linked intrusions and to enhance detection of rebranded ransomware variants despite attribution obfuscation tactics.
retrieved_context.title: Evil Corp Pivots LockBit to Dodge U.S. Sanctions | Threatpost

retrieved_context.text: In early 2023, ransomware postings dropped 41% month-on-month yet LockBit stayed dominant, and despite predictions of waning ROI, Q3 saw a surge—driven by CL0P’s mass exploits of file-transfer flaws—that surpassed the combined victim counts of 2021–22 and hit law firms, government, manufacturing, oil & gas, and logistics hardest. In Q4 two new strains surfaced: CACTUS, first observed by Kroll in March 2023, leverages critical Qlik Sense vulnerabilities (CVE-2023-41266, ‑41265, ‑48365) or VPN appliance flaws for initial access; embeds a decryption key in ntuser.dat via scheduled tasks; uses SoftPerfect Network Scanner, PowerShell, Cobalt Strike, Splashtop, AnyDesk and Chisel for reconnaissance, persistence and lateral movement; exfiltrates data over Tox and Rclone; and encrypts files with AES/OpenSSL (.cts1 extension) accompanied by cAcTuS.readme.txt demands. When a LockBit affiliate’s deployment failed, they defaulted to 3AM, a new Rust-based backup encryptor that halts services, deletes VSS snapshots, appends .threeamtime and a “0x666” marker, exfiltrates via Wput to FTP, and issues Tor-based ransom negotiations. To counter these evolving threats, organizations must patch VPN and Qlik Sense flaws, enforce least-privilege RDP with MFA, restrict unauthorized remote access tools, monitor for anomalous scheduled tasks, scanner and Tox/Rclone traffic, deploy EDR to flag Cobalt Strike and script-based execution, and maintain secure, offline backups.
retrieved_context.title: New Ransomware Strains - CACTUS and 3AM

retrieved_context.text: ESET’s 2024 analysis shows that in the wake of law-enforcement-led Operation Cronos and the collapse of LockBit and BlackCat, RansomHub emerged in February as the dominant RaaS operator—driving a 15 percent rise in leak-site victims even as overall ransomware payments fell 35 percent—and by November had eclipsed LockBit in cumulative victim postings. By tracing unique victim IDs and builder tool fingerprints, researchers linked RansomHub to established gangs Play, Medusa and BianLian and revealed that its multiplatform encryptor (Windows, Linux, ESXi) repurposes Knight source code and is protected by a unique 64-character password per sample. In May, operators added “EDRKillShifter,” a custom EDR killer that abuses at least two publicly known vulnerable drivers and uses password-encrypted shellcode to disable security products, all delivered via RansomHub’s web panel under the same affiliate-specific password model. Affiliates—who keep 90 percent of ransoms and enroll via recommendation, reputation proof or a refundable US $5 000 deposit—negotiate exclusively over Tor, post detailed ransom notes to victims, and benefit from free trial decryptions. Key mitigations include strict driver allow-listing, monitoring for anomalous driver loads, hardening EDR self-protection, blocking known Tor endpoints, and correlating builder requests and password probes to detect emerging RansomHub activity.
retrieved_context.title: Shifting the sands of RansomHub’s EDRKillShifter

canonical_entities: Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Tools
hits.text: Since its emergence in 2021 and first detection on Trend Micro telemetry in March 2022, the TargetCompany ransomware group has launched 269 attempted attacks against 250 disclosed Trend customers—predominantly in Asia (notably India and Saudi Arabia)—while avoiding Kazakhstan, Russia, Qatar, and Ukraine, and focusing on manufacturing, retail, and telecommunications; their November 2022–May 2023 leak site lists 20 confirmed victims (mostly small businesses) across the Asia-Pacific, Europe, and Middle East in IT, manufacturing, apparel, and automotive sectors. Initial access vectors include exploitation of CVE-2019-1069 and CVE-2020-0618 RCE flaws, SQL Server xp_cmdshell abuse, and OneNote-based spam campaigns. Execution relies on WMIC-invoked PowerShell scripts to retrieve various payloads (TargetComp ransomware, Remcos backdoor, Negasteal, Snake Keylogger) and, since January 2022, reflective loading of a .NET downloader that decrypts and runs payloads in memory via XOR or inversion. For defense evasion, operators deploy GMER, PCHunter64 (YDArk.exe), Advance Process Termination, KILLAV, and killer.bat to disable AV and security services; discovery is achieved through network scans and Mimikatz credential dumping; lateral movement via RDP-based RCE; C2 evolved from an open Mallox directory to an Nginx-protected server. Impact involves ChaCha20 file encryption with keys generated by Curve25519 and AES-128, file extensions such as .mallox/.exploit/.avast and ransom notes titled “HOW TO RECOVER!!.TXT,” and potential data exfiltration. Their tactics span MITRE techniques T1190, T1059.001, T1047, T1562.001, T1003.001, T1071.001, T1486, and more. The group’s maturation—evidenced by reflective loading and possible RaaS adoption—underscores the urgency for organizations to enforce asset inventories, least-privilege access, prompt patching (or virtual patching), multifactor authentication, sandboxed email defenses, AI/ML-driven detection, regular backups, and continuous red-team testing to thwart this active threat.

Operators employ double and quadruple extortion—threatening to publish or auction stolen data on their Cl0p^_-Leaks site and targeting executives/customers—to coerce ransoms, driving average payments up 43% to $220,298 (median $78,398) in Q1 2021 after FIN11’s and FIN7’s twin zero-day campaigns against Kiteworks FTA (CVE-2021-27101/02/03/04) and Fortra GoAnywhere MFT, while in 2023 they exploited PaperCut CVE-2023-27350 to deploy Truebot and LockBit/Clop, then MOVEit CVE-2023-24362/CVE-2023-35036 and an unpatched SQL injection flaw to steal data without payloads. Trend Micro detections reveal a May 2023 surge (245 attempts), with top targets in banking, retail and healthcare across Türkiye, Canada, the US and large enterprises worldwide.

retrieved_context.text: Researchers at Mandiant Intelligence have identified UNC2165—the latest evolution of the U.S.-sanctioned Evil Corp—as leveraging the FakeUpdates infection chain to gain initial access, followed by deployment of LockBit ransomware to obscure attribution and monetize extortion efforts. retrieved_context.text: In early 2023, ransomware postings dropped 41% month-on-month yet LockBit stayed dominant, and despite predictions of waning ROI, Q3 saw a surge—driven by CL0P’s mass exploits of file-transfer flaws—that surpassed the combined victim counts of 2021–22 and hit law firms, government, manufacturing, oil & gas, and logistics hardest. retrieved_context.text: Since its emergence in 2021 and first detection on Trend Micro telemetry in March 2022, the TargetCompany ransomware group has launched 269 attempted attacks against 250 disclosed Trend customers—predominantly in Asia (notably India and Saudi Arabia)—while avoiding Kazakhstan, Russia, Qatar, and Ukraine, and focusing on manufacturing, retail, and telecommunications; their November 2022–May 2023 leak site lists 20 confirmed victims (mostly small businesses) across the Asia-Pacific, Europe, and Middle East in IT, manufacturing, apparel, and automotive sectors. Initial access vectors include exploitation of CVE-2019-1069 and CVE-2020-0618 RCE flaws, SQL Server xp_cmdshell abuse, and OneNote-based spam campaigns. Execution relies on WMIC-invoked PowerShell scripts to retrieve various payloads (TargetComp ransomware, Remcos backdoor, Negasteal, Snake Keylogger) and, since January 2022, reflective loading of a .NET downloader that decrypts and runs payloads in memory via XOR or inversion. For defense evasion, operators deploy GMER, PCHunter64 (YDArk.exe), Advance Process Termination, KILLAV, and killer.bat to disable AV and security services; discovery is achieved through network scans and Mimikatz credential dumping; lateral movement via RDP-based RCE; C2 evolved from an open Mallox directory to an Nginx-protected server. Impact involves ChaCha20 file encryption with keys generated by Curve25519 and AES-128, file extensions such as .mallox/.exploit/.avast and ransom notes titled “HOW TO RECOVER!!.TXT,” and potential data exfiltration. Their tactics span MITRE techniques T1190, T1059.001, T1047, T1562.001, T1003.001, T1071.001, T1486, and more. The group’s maturation—evidenced by reflective loading and possible RaaS adoption—underscores the urgency for organizations to enforce asset inventories, least-privilege access, prompt patching (or virtual patching), multifactor authentication, sandboxed email defenses, AI/ML-driven detection, regular backups, and continuous red-team testing to thwart this active threat.

retrieved_context.text: Conti ransomware, a profit-driven RaaS syndicate linked by the FBI to over 400 global attacks (75% in the U.S.) with demands up to $25 million, has spent more than a year targeting high-stakes environments—hospitals, 911 dispatch centers, EMS and law enforcement—where IT outages can be life-threatening, exemplified by Ireland’s mid-May healthcare system shutdown that halted X-ray services and COVID testing; it gains initial access through Spearphishing Attachment (T1566.001), Exploit Public-Facing Application (T1190) and lacking MFA, then uses Cobalt Strike and PowerShell for discovery (T1083, T1135), lateral movement (SMB Shares T1021.002), privilege escalation (DLL Injection T1055.001) and defense evasion (Obfuscated Files T1027, Deobfuscate/Decode T1140), before executing “double extortion” (Data Encrypted for Impact T1486, Inhibit System Recovery T1490) and often reneging on decryption promises; actionable defenses include enforcing MFA, applying NGFW Threat Prevention with secure Vulnerability Protection Profiles, WildFire file analysis, Cortex XDR’s anti-malware/exploit modules, regular WildFire updates, Cortex XSOAR playbooks, and tracking IoCs via Unit 42’s GitHub and TAXII feeds.
retrieved_context.title: Conti Ransomware Gang: An Overview

retrieved_context.text: ESET’s 2024 analysis shows that in the wake of law-enforcement-led Operation Cronos and the collapse of LockBit and BlackCat, RansomHub emerged in February as the dominant RaaS operator—driving a 15 percent rise in leak-site victims even as overall ransomware payments fell 35 percent—and by November had eclipsed LockBit in cumulative victim postings. By tracing unique victim IDs and builder tool fingerprints, researchers linked RansomHub to established gangs Play, Medusa and BianLian and revealed that its multiplatform encryptor (Windows, Linux, ESXi) repurposes Knight source code and is protected by a unique 64-character password per sample. In May, operators added “EDRKillShifter,” a custom EDR killer that abuses at least two publicly known vulnerable drivers and uses password-encrypted shellcode to disable security products, all delivered via RansomHub’s web panel under the same affiliate-specific password model. Affiliates—who keep 90 percent of ransoms and enroll via recommendation, reputation proof or a refundable US $5 000 deposit—negotiate exclusively over Tor, post detailed ransom notes to victims, and benefit from free trial decryptions. Key mitigations include strict driver allow-listing, monitoring for anomalous driver loads, hardening EDR self-protection, blocking known Tor endpoints, and correlating builder requests and password probes to detect emerging RansomHub activity.

hits.text: Microsoft has identified a China-based nation-state threat actor tracked as Flax Typhoon (aka Ethereal Panda) conducting espionage against dozens of Taiwanese organizations since mid-2021 by exploiting known vulnerabilities in public-facing VPN, web, Java and SQL servers to deploy the China Chopper web shell, escalate privileges with Juicy Potato and BadPotato, and establish persistence by disabling RDP network-level authentication, hijacking the Sticky Keys binary to launch Task Manager as SYSTEM, and installing a renamed SoftEther VPN bridge over HTTPS on port 443 for stealthy command-and-control. Once inside, the actor leverages WinRM and WMIC for lateral movement and deploys Mimikatz to dump LSASS and SAM for pass-the-hash attacks, yet conducts minimal post-persistence activity, suggesting long-term credential harvesting rather than immediate data exfiltration. To mitigate, organizations must enforce rigorous patch management, monitor registry changes and RDP configurations, deploy file integrity and behavioral monitoring on public-facing servers, isolate and forensically examine compromised systems, and rotate or disable exposed credentials.

hits.text: Unit 42 has observed a sharp rise in post-intrusion WastedLocker ransomware attacks by the Evil Corp group—already known for Dridex—against large U.S. organizations in sectors from manufacturing to legal services, with initial compromise typically via ZIP files masquerading as legitimate updates that deploy a SocGholish JavaScript loader to profile systems and invoke PowerShell-based Cobalt Strike payloads; attackers then leverage WMI and PsExec for lateral movement, identify high-value and backup systems, elevate privileges, disable Windows Defender, delete shadow copies, install WastedLocker as a service, and encrypt files using a “.<victim_name>wasted” extension while appending ransom notes (“.<victim_name>wasted_info”) with contact addresses on ProtonMail, Airmail and others. Palo Alto Networks’ WildFire, Cortex XDR (anti-ransomware and behavioral threat protection), NGFW DNS signatures and AutoFocus tagging detect and prevent WastedLocker activity; organizations are urged to implement robust, off-site backup strategies and hardened cybersecurity controls to mitigate this high-impact targeted ransomware threat.

hits.text: Evil Corp, the decade-old cybercrime group behind the Dridex/Cridex banking Trojan and botnet indicted by the US DOJ in December 2019, resurfaced in May 2020 with WastedLocker, a novel, manually deployed ransomware that extorts $500 000–$10 million from predominantly US organizations by delivering a custom, per-target binary via SocGholish JavaScript fake-update kits on compromised news sites and a tailored Cobalt Strike loader; following reconnaissance, credential theft, privilege escalation (DLL hijacking) and lateral movement with living-off-the-land tools, WastedLocker prioritizes and encrypts critical directories using per-file AES-256 keys sealed with unique RSA-4096 public keys while deleting Windows shadow copies and network-stored backups, appending victim-specific “.wasted” extensions and thousands of ransom-note files to cripple operations—as seen in Garmin’s $10 million demand—and analysts warn that Evil Corp’s rapid malware iteration and exploitation skillset necessitate offline or immutable backups, rollback capabilities, robust privilege-escalation controls, network segmentation and continuous monitoring for post-exploitation frameworks to defend against this highly evasive threat.
hits.title: WastedLocker explained: How this targeted ransomware extorts millions from victims

hits.text: On March 2, 2025, CyberMaterial’s report on Void Manticore (aka Storm-0842, linked to the cybercriminal Storm-1811 cluster) details a coordinated espionage campaign that began in late 2024 against aerospace, defense and government organizations in Europe and North America: operators initiated intrusions via spear-phishing emails embedding weaponized RTFs exploiting CVE-2024-4113 to drop a custom loader (“VoidLoader”), which in turn deployed the “ManticoreShell” backdoor; post-compromise activities included credential harvesting (Mimikatz), lateral movement via PSExec and WMI, privilege escalation through a signed kernel-mode driver exploit, and persistence using registry Run keys and scheduled tasks; C2 communications leveraged HTTPS with a domain generation algorithm (DGA) and fallback to TOR. Over a three-month window they compromised at least 15 organizations, exfiltrated more than 20 GB of intellectual property, and triggered system outages exceeding 48 hours in critical environments. Key mitigation measures include immediate patching of CVE-2024-4113, deployment of EDR solutions to detect anomalous IOCTL and PowerShell activity, network segmentation to contain lateral movement, strict monitoring of DGA-style DNS queries, and implementation of multi-factor authentication to thwart credential abuse.
hits.title: Void Manticore (Storm-0842) – Threat Actor - CyberMaterial

hits.text: Moses Staff, an Iran-linked APT active since September 2021, has conducted politically motivated sabotage campaigns—initially against Israeli organizations and later targets in India, Germany, the U.S., Italy, Chile, Turkey and the UAE—by exploiting known public-facing server vulnerabilities (e.g., Microsoft Exchange), moving laterally with PsExec, WMIC and PowerShell, and deploying a two-stage destructive toolkit: a Python-based loader (PyDCrypt) that installs a custom DiskCryptor variant (DCSrv) to encrypt files and disrupt operations without ransom demands, and, as newly documented by Cybereason, the StrifeWater RAT masquerading as calc.exe to establish early footholds, harvest system metadata (machine name, OS version, CPU architecture, user privileges, time zone), execute commands, capture screens, maintain persistence via scheduled tasks, and download auxiliary modules before self-removal—all while communicating with hard-coded C2 IPs, URLs and domain names—to evade detection; organizations should urgently patch exposed servers, monitor anomalous calc.exe and scheduled-task activity, and enhance EDR rules to detect PyDCrypt, DCSrv and StrifeWater behaviors to thwart data exfiltration and infrastructure damage.
hits.title: Iranian APT group uses previously undocumented Trojan for destructive access to organizations

hits.text: Between March and July 2025, DPRK-linked Kimsuky operators executed at least 19 highly tailored spear-phishing attacks against Western, Central, Eastern and Southern European embassies in Seoul, spoofing real diplomats and embedding password-protected ZIPs delivered via Dropbox, Daum or Google Drive. Victims unwittingly launched malicious .LNK shortcuts that triggered obfuscated PowerShell scripts to decode and in-memory execute a Confuser-Core-obfuscated XenoRAT (MoonPeak) payload—identified by GUID 12DE1212-167D-45BA-1284-780DA98CF901 and mutex “Dansweit_Hk65-PSAccerdle”—leveraging scheduled tasks for persistence. Reconnaissance data (OS build, IP, process list) was exfiltrated as base64-encoded text files over HTTPS to the attackers’ private GitHub repo via the Contents API, while C2 instructions (e.g., onf.txt) directed dynamic payload rotations hosted on Dropbox with rapid header-fix GZIP routines. This ongoing campaign provided full system control—including keystroke logging, screenshots and remote shells—and underscores the need to monitor abnormal GitHub API usage, cloud-based archive downloads and anomalous PowerShell invocations.
hits.title: The Coordinated Embassy Hunt: Unmasking the DPRK-linked GitHub C2 Espionage Campaign

canonical_entities: registered variables in the Windows Registry
hits.text: In June 2024, HP’s Threat Research team led by Patrick Schlapfer intercepted a low-grade phishing campaign leveraging HTML smuggling via an AES-encrypted HTML attachment containing JavaScript-embedded decryption logic—a novel twist on typical encrypted archives—which, when decrypted, mimicked a legitimate website but dropped a fully commented, French-language VBScript that registered variables in the Windows Registry, staged a JavaScript payload as a scheduled task, and invoked a PowerShell script to deploy the freely available AsyncRAT infostealer. Schlapfer and co-lead Alex Holland’s analysis, including comparison with generative-AI–produced code, concluded the well-structured, human-readable script was likely authored by gen-AI by a low-skill newcomer benefitting from reduced entry barriers, with no obfuscation or complex infrastructure beyond a single C2 server. This first definitive proof of AI-generated malware in the wild underscores the need for defenders to adapt detection strategies to AI-crafted droppers, monitor anomalous AES-in-JavaScript decryption patterns, and anticipate more sophisticated AI-generated payloads poised to emerge within the next two years, thereby heightening the risk to network and endpoint security.
hits.title: AI-Generated Malware Found in the Wild - SecurityWeek

retrieved_context.text: Microsoft has identified a China-based nation-state threat actor tracked as Flax Typhoon (aka Ethereal Panda) conducting espionage against dozens of Taiwanese organizations since mid-2021 by exploiting known vulnerabilities in public-facing VPN, web, Java and SQL servers to deploy the China Chopper web shell, escalate privileges with Juicy Potato and BadPotato, and establish persistence by disabling RDP network-level authentication, hijacking the Sticky Keys binary to launch Task Manager as SYSTEM, and installing a renamed SoftEther VPN bridge over HTTPS on port 443 for stealthy command-and-control. Once inside, the actor leverages WinRM and WMIC for lateral movement and deploys Mimikatz to dump LSASS and SAM for pass-the-hash attacks, yet conducts minimal post-persistence activity, suggesting long-term credential harvesting rather than immediate data exfiltration. To mitigate, organizations must enforce rigorous patch management, monitor registry changes and RDP configurations, deploy file integrity and behavioral monitoring on public-facing servers, isolate and forensically examine compromised systems, and rotate or disable exposed credentials.

retrieved_context.text: Researchers at Mandiant Intelligence have identified UNC2165—the latest evolution of the U.S.-sanctioned Evil Corp—as leveraging the FakeUpdates infection chain to gain initial access, followed by deployment of LockBit ransomware to obscure attribution and monetize extortion efforts. After OFAC sanctions in December 2019 crippled Evil Corp’s ability to profit from Dridex and its WastedLocker strain, the group briefly resurfaced under PayloadBin (likely a WastedLocker rebrand) and used HTML redirectors in malicious Excel files, then adopted Hades ransomware with code overlaps to distance itself further. By aligning with LockBit’s RaaS model—already proven effective against high-profile victims such as Accenture and Bangkok Air—UNC2165 can blend in with legitimate affiliates, reduce development overhead, and bypass sanctions enforcement that deters U.S. entities from negotiating ransoms with known Evil Corp actors. This shift underscores the need for defenders to monitor FakeUpdates chains and LockBit activity for potential Evil Corp–linked intrusions and to enhance detection of rebranded ransomware variants despite attribution obfuscation tactics.
retrieved_context.title: Evil Corp Pivots LockBit to Dodge U.S. Sanctions | Threatpost

retrieved_context.text: Evil Corp, the decade-old cybercrime group behind the Dridex/Cridex banking Trojan and botnet indicted by the US DOJ in December 2019, resurfaced in May 2020 with WastedLocker, a novel, manually deployed ransomware that extorts $500 000–$10 million from predominantly US organizations by delivering a custom, per-target binary via SocGholish JavaScript fake-update kits on compromised news sites and a tailored Cobalt Strike loader; following reconnaissance, credential theft, privilege escalation (DLL hijacking) and lateral movement with living-off-the-land tools, WastedLocker prioritizes and encrypts critical directories using per-file AES-256 keys sealed with unique RSA-4096 public keys while deleting Windows shadow copies and network-stored backups, appending victim-specific “.wasted” extensions and thousands of ransom-note files to cripple operations—as seen in Garmin’s $10 million demand—and analysts warn that Evil Corp’s rapid malware iteration and exploitation skillset necessitate offline or immutable backups, rollback capabilities, robust privilege-escalation controls, network segmentation and continuous monitoring for post-exploitation frameworks to defend against this highly evasive threat.
retrieved_context.title: WastedLocker explained: How this targeted ransomware extorts millions from victims

retrieved_context.text: On March 2, 2025, CyberMaterial’s report on Void Manticore (aka Storm-0842, linked to the cybercriminal Storm-1811 cluster) details a coordinated espionage campaign that began in late 2024 against aerospace, defense and government organizations in Europe and North America: operators initiated intrusions via spear-phishing emails embedding weaponized RTFs exploiting CVE-2024-4113 to drop a custom loader (“VoidLoader”), which in turn deployed the “ManticoreShell” backdoor; post-compromise activities included credential harvesting (Mimikatz), lateral movement via PSExec and WMI, privilege escalation through a signed kernel-mode driver exploit, and persistence using registry Run keys and scheduled tasks; C2 communications leveraged HTTPS with a domain generation algorithm (DGA) and fallback to TOR. Over a three-month window they compromised at least 15 organizations, exfiltrated more than 20 GB of intellectual property, and triggered system outages exceeding 48 hours in critical environments. Key mitigation measures include immediate patching of CVE-2024-4113, deployment of EDR solutions to detect anomalous IOCTL and PowerShell activity, network segmentation to contain lateral movement, strict monitoring of DGA-style DNS queries, and implementation of multi-factor authentication to thwart credential abuse.
retrieved_context.title: Void Manticore (Storm-0842) – Threat Actor - CyberMaterial

retrieved_context.text: Moses Staff, an Iran-linked APT active since September 2021, has conducted politically motivated sabotage campaigns—initially against Israeli organizations and later targets in India, Germany, the U.S., Italy, Chile, Turkey and the UAE—by exploiting known public-facing server vulnerabilities (e.g., Microsoft Exchange), moving laterally with PsExec, WMIC and PowerShell, and deploying a two-stage destructive toolkit: a Python-based loader (PyDCrypt) that installs a custom DiskCryptor variant (DCSrv) to encrypt files and disrupt operations without ransom demands, and, as newly documented by Cybereason, the StrifeWater RAT masquerading as calc.exe to establish early footholds, harvest system metadata (machine name, OS version, CPU architecture, user privileges, time zone), execute commands, capture screens, maintain persistence via scheduled tasks, and download auxiliary modules before self-removal—all while communicating with hard-coded C2 IPs, URLs and domain names—to evade detection; organizations should urgently patch exposed servers, monitor anomalous calc.exe and scheduled-task activity, and enhance EDR rules to detect PyDCrypt, DCSrv and StrifeWater behaviors to thwart data exfiltration and infrastructure damage.
retrieved_context.title: Iranian APT group uses previously undocumented Trojan for destructive access to organizations

retrieved_context.text: Between March and July 2025, DPRK-linked Kimsuky operators executed at least 19 highly tailored spear-phishing attacks against Western, Central, Eastern and Southern European embassies in Seoul, spoofing real diplomats and embedding password-protected ZIPs delivered via Dropbox, Daum or Google Drive. Victims unwittingly launched malicious .LNK shortcuts that triggered obfuscated PowerShell scripts to decode and in-memory execute a Confuser-Core-obfuscated XenoRAT (MoonPeak) payload—identified by GUID 12DE1212-167D-45BA-1284-780DA98CF901 and mutex “Dansweit_Hk65-PSAccerdle”—leveraging scheduled tasks for persistence. Reconnaissance data (OS build, IP, process list) was exfiltrated as base64-encoded text files over HTTPS to the attackers’ private GitHub repo via the Contents API, while C2 instructions (e.g., onf.txt) directed dynamic payload rotations hosted on Dropbox with rapid header-fix GZIP routines. This ongoing campaign provided full system control—including keystroke logging, screenshots and remote shells—and underscores the need to monitor abnormal GitHub API usage, cloud-based archive downloads and anomalous PowerShell invocations.
retrieved_context.title: The Coordinated Embassy Hunt: Unmasking the DPRK-linked GitHub C2 Espionage Campaign

retrieved_context.text: In June 2024, HP’s Threat Research team led by Patrick Schlapfer intercepted a low-grade phishing campaign leveraging HTML smuggling via an AES-encrypted HTML attachment containing JavaScript-embedded decryption logic—a novel twist on typical encrypted archives—which, when decrypted, mimicked a legitimate website but dropped a fully commented, French-language VBScript that registered variables in the Windows Registry, staged a JavaScript payload as a scheduled task, and invoked a PowerShell script to deploy the freely available AsyncRAT infostealer. Schlapfer and co-lead Alex Holland’s analysis, including comparison with generative-AI–produced code, concluded the well-structured, human-readable script was likely authored by gen-AI by a low-skill newcomer benefitting from reduced entry barriers, with no obfuscation or complex infrastructure beyond a single C2 server. This first definitive proof of AI-generated malware in the wild underscores the need for defenders to adapt detection strategies to AI-crafted droppers, monitor anomalous AES-in-JavaScript decryption patterns, and anticipate more sophisticated AI-generated payloads poised to emerge within the next two years, thereby heightening the risk to network and endpoint security.
retrieved_context.title: AI-Generated Malware Found in the Wild - SecurityWeek

hits.text: During a recent incident, a LockBit affiliate conducted initial intrusions using gpresult for policy dumping, Cobalt Strike loaders and PsExec for privilege escalation, followed by reconnaissance (whoami, netstat, quser, net view), lateral movement, persistence via a new user account, and data exfiltration over FTP with Wput; when deployment of LockBit (SHA256 079b99f6…) was blocked on the target network, the attacker pivoted to a newly observed Rust-written ransomware family dubbed 3AM (SHA256 307a1217…), which appends “.threeamtime” to encrypted files, stops over 100 security and backup services via net stop and wbadmin/bcdedit/wmic commands, deletes Volume Shadow copies with vssadmin.exe delete shadows /all /quiet, and drops a Tor‐accessible ransom note requiring a 32-character “-k” access key and offering decryption/mystical-themed extortion; although 3AM encryption succeeded on only one of three attempted hosts, its Conti-style “-m” (local/net) and “-h” parameters, heavy service-termination payload, and aggressive VSS wipe underscore its potential as a fallback vector—defenders should update Symantec/Broadcom signatures, monitor for the .threeamtime extension, suspicious Rust binaries, command-line flags “-k” and “-m”, and mass service stoppage activity, and block associated IOCs (185.202.0[.]111, 212.18.104[.]6, 85.159.229[.]62) to mitigate future 3AM use.
hits.title: 3AM: New Ransomware Family Used As Fallback in Failed LockBit Attack | Symantec Enterprise Blogs

hits.text: A zero-day VPN vulnerability provided initial access for a sophisticated threat actor who employed publicly available penetration‐testing and exploitation tools—SoftPerfect Network Scanner for network discovery, PsExec to deploy ServeManager.exe (the FiveHands ransomware variant using lattice-based NTRUEncrypt public key cryptography), and SombRAT for remote information theft—alongside RouterScan, grabff.exe, rclone.exe, and s3browser-9-5-3.exe to harvest credentials and exfiltrate data. Once inside, the attacker leveraged Windows Management Instrumentation (T1047) to enumerate and delete Volume Shadow Copies (Inhibit System Recovery, T1490), encrypted files (including those in recovery folders) for impact (T1486), and dropped ransom notes across directories, demanding payment to restore access. Post-encryption activities align with MITRE techniques such as Access Token Manipulation, Boot or Logon Autostart, PowerShell command and scripting interpreter, Domain Trust Discovery, Process Discovery, Screen Capture, and Kerberoasting. The combined use of FiveHands ransomware and SombRAT RAT resulted in both data theft and destruction of backup artifacts, underscoring the need for proactive patch management, network segmentation, strict credential hygiene, and rapid incident response to mitigate novel lattice-based encryption threats.
hits.title: FiveHands Ransomware Overview

hits.text: Since mid-2021, Microsoft has tracked Volt Typhoon, a China-linked state-sponsored actor, conducting stealthy living-off-the-land campaigns against U.S. critical infrastructure—spanning communications, utilities, transportation, manufacturing, government and education—aimed at post-compromise credential access, network discovery and long-term espionage with an eye toward potential disruption of Asia-U.S. communications in future crises. Initial access is achieved via internet-exposed Fortinet FortiGuard devices, whose AD credentials are harvested to move laterally; all traffic is proxied through compromised SOHO routers, firewalls and VPN hardware (ASUS, Cisco, D-Link, NETGEAR, Zyxel) to blend with legitimate activity. Post-compromise hands-on-keyboard operations rely almost exclusively on LOLBins and valid credentials to dump LSASS memory and use Ntdsutil.exe to create domain controller installation media for offline hash cracking, enumerate systems via PowerShell, WMIC and ping, collect browser and system data into staged archives, then exfiltrate via password-protected files. In rare cases, Volt Typhoon deploys custom Impacket or FRP-based C2 over portproxy, observable as unusual successful sign-ins and command-line activity from anomalous IPs. Detection is challenging due to use of built-in binaries and normal sign-in channels; Microsoft 365 Defender and cloud-delivered Microsoft Defender Antivirus yield behavioral alerts (e.g., SuspPowershellExec, SuspNtdsUtilUsage), while Defender for Endpoint flags suspicious LSASS dumps, wmic.exe executions and domain-controller media creation. Mitigation hinges on closing or rotating compromised accounts, enforcing strong MFA or passwordless authentication, disabling internet-facing device management interfaces, enabling LSASS Protective Process Light and Credential Guard on Windows 11, applying attack surface reduction rules to block LSASS and PSExec/WMI abuse, and running EDR in block mode to thwart post-compromise artifacts.
hits.title: Volt Typhoon targets US critical infrastructure with living-off-the-land techniques | Microsoft Security Blog

retrieved_context.text: Unit 42 has observed a sharp rise in post-intrusion WastedLocker ransomware attacks by the Evil Corp group—already known for Dridex—against large U.S. organizations in sectors from manufacturing to legal services, with initial compromise typically via ZIP files masquerading as legitimate updates that deploy a SocGholish JavaScript loader to profile systems and invoke PowerShell-based Cobalt Strike payloads; attackers then leverage WMI and PsExec for lateral movement, identify high-value and backup systems, elevate privileges, disable Windows Defender, delete shadow copies, install WastedLocker as a service, and encrypt files using a “.<victim_name>wasted” extension while appending ransom notes (“.<victim_name>wasted_info”) with contact addresses on ProtonMail, Airmail and others. Palo Alto Networks’ WildFire, Cortex XDR (anti-ransomware and behavioral threat protection), NGFW DNS signatures and AutoFocus tagging detect and prevent WastedLocker activity; organizations are urged to implement robust, off-site backup strategies and hardened cybersecurity controls to mitigate this high-impact targeted ransomware threat.
retrieved_context.title: Threat Assessment: WastedLocker Ransomware

retrieved_context.text: Moses Staff, an Iran-linked APT active since September 2021, has conducted politically motivated sabotage campaigns—initially against Israeli organizations and later targets in India, Germany, the U.S., Italy, Chile, Turkey and the UAE—by exploiting known public-facing server vulnerabilities (e.g., Microsoft Exchange), moving laterally with PsExec, WMIC and PowerShell, and deploying a two-stage destructive toolkit: a Python-based loader (PyDCrypt) that installs a custom DiskCryptor variant (DCSrv) to encrypt files and disrupt operations without ransom demands, and, as newly documented by Cybereason, the StrifeWater RAT masquerading as calc.exe to establish early footholds, harvest system metadata (machine name, OS version, CPU architecture, user privileges, time zone), execute commands, capture screens, maintain persistence via scheduled tasks, and download auxiliary modules before self-removal—all while communicating with hard-coded C2 IPs, URLs and domain names—to evade detection; organizations should urgently patch exposed servers, monitor anomalous calc.exe and scheduled-task activity, and enhance EDR rules to detect PyDCrypt, DCSrv and StrifeWater behaviors to thwart data exfiltration and infrastructure damage.
retrieved_context.title: Iranian APT group uses previously undocumented Trojan for destructive access to organizations

retrieved_context.text: During a recent incident, a LockBit affiliate conducted initial intrusions using gpresult for policy dumping, Cobalt Strike loaders and PsExec for privilege escalation, followed by reconnaissance (whoami, netstat, quser, net view), lateral movement, persistence via a new user account, and data exfiltration over FTP with Wput; when deployment of LockBit (SHA256 079b99f6…) was blocked on the target network, the attacker pivoted to a newly observed Rust-written ransomware family dubbed 3AM (SHA256 307a1217…), which appends “.threeamtime” to encrypted files, stops over 100 security and backup services via net stop and wbadmin/bcdedit/wmic commands, deletes Volume Shadow copies with vssadmin.exe delete shadows /all /quiet, and drops a Tor‐accessible ransom note requiring a 32-character “-k” access key and offering decryption/mystical-themed extortion; although 3AM encryption succeeded on only one of three attempted hosts, its Conti-style “-m” (local/net) and “-h” parameters, heavy service-termination payload, and aggressive VSS wipe underscore its potential as a fallback vector—defenders should update Symantec/Broadcom signatures, monitor for the .threeamtime extension, suspicious Rust binaries, command-line flags “-k” and “-m”, and mass service stoppage activity, and block associated IOCs (185.202.0[.]111, 212.18.104[.]6, 85.159.229[.]62) to mitigate future 3AM use.
retrieved_context.title: 3AM: New Ransomware Family Used As Fallback in Failed LockBit Attack | Symantec Enterprise Blogs

retrieved_context.text: A zero-day VPN vulnerability provided initial access for a sophisticated threat actor who employed publicly available penetration‐testing and exploitation tools—SoftPerfect Network Scanner for network discovery, PsExec to deploy ServeManager.exe (the FiveHands ransomware variant using lattice-based NTRUEncrypt public key cryptography), and SombRAT for remote information theft—alongside RouterScan, grabff.exe, rclone.exe, and s3browser-9-5-3.exe to harvest credentials and exfiltrate data. Once inside, the attacker leveraged Windows Management Instrumentation (T1047) to enumerate and delete Volume Shadow Copies (Inhibit System Recovery, T1490), encrypted files (including those in recovery folders) for impact (T1486), and dropped ransom notes across directories, demanding payment to restore access. Post-encryption activities align with MITRE techniques such as Access Token Manipulation, Boot or Logon Autostart, PowerShell command and scripting interpreter, Domain Trust Discovery, Process Discovery, Screen Capture, and Kerberoasting. The combined use of FiveHands ransomware and SombRAT RAT resulted in both data theft and destruction of backup artifacts, underscoring the need for proactive patch management, network segmentation, strict credential hygiene, and rapid incident response to mitigate novel lattice-based encryption threats.
retrieved_context.title: FiveHands Ransomware Overview

canonical_entities: registered variables in the Windows Registry
retrieved_context.text: In June 2024, HP’s Threat Research team led by Patrick Schlapfer intercepted a low-grade phishing campaign leveraging HTML smuggling via an AES-encrypted HTML attachment containing JavaScript-embedded decryption logic—a novel twist on typical encrypted archives—which, when decrypted, mimicked a legitimate website but dropped a fully commented, French-language VBScript that registered variables in the Windows Registry, staged a JavaScript payload as a scheduled task, and invoked a PowerShell script to deploy the freely available AsyncRAT infostealer. Schlapfer and co-lead Alex Holland’s analysis, including comparison with generative-AI–produced code, concluded the well-structured, human-readable script was likely authored by gen-AI by a low-skill newcomer benefitting from reduced entry barriers, with no obfuscation or complex infrastructure beyond a single C2 server. This first definitive proof of AI-generated malware in the wild underscores the need for defenders to adapt detection strategies to AI-crafted droppers, monitor anomalous AES-in-JavaScript decryption patterns, and anticipate more sophisticated AI-generated payloads poised to emerge within the next two years, thereby heightening the risk to network and endpoint security.
retrieved_context.title: AI-Generated Malware Found in the Wild - SecurityWeek

retrieved_context.text: Researchers at Mandiant Intelligence have identified UNC2165—the latest evolution of the U.S.-sanctioned Evil Corp—as leveraging the FakeUpdates infection chain to gain initial access, followed by deployment of LockBit ransomware to obscure attribution and monetize extortion efforts. After OFAC sanctions in December 2019 crippled Evil Corp’s ability to profit from Dridex and its WastedLocker strain, the group briefly resurfaced under PayloadBin (likely a WastedLocker rebrand) and used HTML redirectors in malicious Excel files, then adopted Hades ransomware with code overlaps to distance itself further. By aligning with LockBit’s RaaS model—already proven effective against high-profile victims such as Accenture and Bangkok Air—UNC2165 can blend in with legitimate affiliates, reduce development overhead, and bypass sanctions enforcement that deters U.S. entities from negotiating ransoms with known Evil Corp actors. This shift underscores the need for defenders to monitor FakeUpdates chains and LockBit activity for potential Evil Corp–linked intrusions and to enhance detection of rebranded ransomware variants despite attribution obfuscation tactics.
retrieved_context.title: Evil Corp Pivots LockBit to Dodge U.S. Sanctions | Threatpost

retrieved_context.text: Since mid-2021, Microsoft has tracked Volt Typhoon, a China-linked state-sponsored actor, conducting stealthy living-off-the-land campaigns against U.S. critical infrastructure—spanning communications, utilities, transportation, manufacturing, government and education—aimed at post-compromise credential access, network discovery and long-term espionage with an eye toward potential disruption of Asia-U.S. communications in future crises. Initial access is achieved via internet-exposed Fortinet FortiGuard devices, whose AD credentials are harvested to move laterally; all traffic is proxied through compromised SOHO routers, firewalls and VPN hardware (ASUS, Cisco, D-Link, NETGEAR, Zyxel) to blend with legitimate activity. Post-compromise hands-on-keyboard operations rely almost exclusively on LOLBins and valid credentials to dump LSASS memory and use Ntdsutil.exe to create domain controller installation media for offline hash cracking, enumerate systems via PowerShell, WMIC and ping, collect browser and system data into staged archives, then exfiltrate via password-protected files. In rare cases, Volt Typhoon deploys custom Impacket or FRP-based C2 over portproxy, observable as unusual successful sign-ins and command-line activity from anomalous IPs. Detection is challenging due to use of built-in binaries and normal sign-in channels; Microsoft 365 Defender and cloud-delivered Microsoft Defender Antivirus yield behavioral alerts (e.g., SuspPowershellExec, SuspNtdsUtilUsage), while Defender for Endpoint flags suspicious LSASS dumps, wmic.exe executions and domain-controller media creation. Mitigation hinges on closing or rotating compromised accounts, enforcing strong MFA or passwordless authentication, disabling internet-facing device management interfaces, enabling LSASS Protective Process Light and Credential Guard on Windows 11, applying attack surface reduction rules to block LSASS and PSExec/WMI abuse, and running EDR in block mode to thwart post-compromise artifacts.
retrieved_context.title: Volt Typhoon targets US critical infrastructure with living-off-the-land techniques | Microsoft Security Blog

canonical_entities: injected commands via a malicious URL
hits.text: CrowdStrike researchers in April 2022 uncovered that ransomware actors exploited a critical remote code execution flaw (CVE-2022-29499) in unpatched Linux-based Mitel MiVoice appliances (SA 100, SA 400 and Virtual SA) to gain initial access, plant malware and pivot laterally: the exploit chain began with an external HTTP GET to a “get_url” parameter in a PHP file (to bypass IP restrictions) followed by a device-originated GET that injected commands via a malicious URL, enabling an SSL-enabled reverse shell (using mkfifo and openssl_client) and deployment of a “pdf_import.php” web shell and the Chisel tunneling tool. Although the threat actors deleted evidence from the VoIP filesystem, CrowdStrike recovered the undocumented exploit, downloaded tools and anti-forensic measures. With some 21,000 MITEL devices worldwide still exposed (per Kevin Beaumont’s Shodan string “http.html_hash:-1971546278”), organizations are urged to apply Mitel’s April advisory patches for MiVoice Connect 19.2 SP3 and earlier, enforce strict network segmentation around perimeter devices, conduct threat modeling to detect anomalous GET requests, and prioritize timely firmware updates to thwart zero-day exploitation.
hits.title: Mitel VoIP Bug Exploited in Ransomware Attacks | Threatpost

hits.text: Lorenz ransomware, emerging in 2021 and likely a rebranding of the .sZ40/ThunderCrypt family, has preyed on over 20 mostly small-to-mid-sized organizations in the US, China and Mexico—demanding $500K–$700K via a double-extortion scheme and posting stolen data on a Tor leak site—most notably compromising Germany’s defense contractor Hensoldt in January 2022 (exfiltrating 95% of files) before exploiting a Mitel MiVoice Connect VoIP RCE (CVE-2022-29499, CVSS 9.8) in September to gain a perimeter foothold; CrowdStrike observed operators deploying a reverse shell via “pdf_import.php,” renaming binaries to “memdump” for anti-forensics, then using Chisel over SSH-secured HTTP to tunnel into the environment. Arctic Wolf analysis indicates either an initial-access broker or in-house exploit capability, a month-long dwell before invoking cURL to download and execute the “wc2_deploy” script for SSL pipes (mkfifo/OpenSSL), followed by CrackMapExec dumping credentials via comsvcs and Out-Minidump LSASS memory, installation of FileZilla under compromised admin accounts, and encryption via BitLocker triggered by a “worm.txt” script on the domain controller—with all event logs wiped and encryption progress beaconed via HTTP POSTs. These TTPs underscore the critical need to monitor IoT devices in real time, maintain up-to-date inventories with device-role tagging, enforce robust patch management, and deploy zero-trust, SIEM, whitelisting and vulnerability-management controls; Avertium specifically advocates applying Mitel’s remediation script for CVE-2022-29499 to mitigate further exploitation.
hits.title: An In-Depth Look at Lorenz Ransomware

hits.text: HC3’s November 2022 alert warns of human-operated Lorenz ransomware, first observed in February 2021 and linked to earlier sZ40 and ThunderCrypt activity, which specifically targets large healthcare organizations by customizing its executable code and following a kill chain of initial access, extended reconnaissance, lateral movement to Windows domain controllers for administrator credential theft, then encryption and extortion. Operators demand $500,000–$700,000 and employ a non-typical leak site where stolen data is first offered for sale to other threat actors, then distributed in password-protected archives or, if sales fail, released publicly. With relatively limited public intelligence on Lorenz, HC3 emphasizes that victims should address common ransomware vectors—phishing, exploitation of known vulnerabilities, remote-access compromise and distributed attacks—by reinforcing patch management, intrusion detection, access controls and incident-response planning, especially in light of concurrent Hive ransomware warnings issued by HHS, FBI and CISA.
hits.title: Lorenz Ransomware Targets Large Healthcare Orgs, HC3 Warns | TechTarget

canonical_entities: enumerates SSH directories to harvest credentials
Persistence is achieved through multiple cronjobs
hits.text: Aqua Security’s Nautilus team has uncovered Hadooken, a new Linux malware targeting Oracle WebLogic servers via weak passwords. Post-compromise, attackers deploy redundant shell and Python scripts to ensure download and execution of Hadooken, which enumerates SSH directories to harvest credentials, moves laterally, and clears logs. Hadooken then drops a three-path cryptominer and a Tsunami backdoor with a randomized name, the latter reserved for potential later-stage attacks. Persistence is achieved through multiple cronjobs under varied names and frequencies stored across cron directories. The malware is hosted on two IPs—one German address linked to TeamTNT and Gang 8220, the other inactive in Russia—where researchers also identified a Mallox ransomware PowerShell loader targeting Windows. Static analysis links Hadooken to Rhombus and NoEscape families. With over 230,000 internet-connected WebLogic instances—hundreds of which expose vulnerable admin consoles—this campaign underscores the dual risk of cryptojacking and ransomware across Linux and Windows environments.
hits.title: New 'Hadooken' Linux Malware Targets WebLogic Servers - SecurityWeek

initial access via compromised VPN credentials
Create new domain accounts for persistence
establish persistence by creating new domain accounts
hits.text: Between April and August 2023, the newly emerged Akira ransomware group targeted 107 organizations—predominantly SMBs in North America (85.9%) and France (53.1% of detections), with additional impacts in the United States and Turkey—surging from just three recorded attempts in May to 508 in June; operators gain initial access via compromised VPN credentials (including exploitation of CVE-2023-20269 on Cisco ASA/FTD), employ third-party tools such as PCHunter, PowerTool, AdFind, Advanced IP Scanner and MASSCAN for defense evasion and discovery, dump credentials with Mimikatz and LaZagne, and establish persistence by creating new domain accounts, then move laterally via RDP, exfiltrate data through RClone, FTP clients (FileZilla, WinSCP), AnyDesk, Radmin, Cloudflare Tunnel, MobaXterm, RustDesk or Ngrok, and encrypt data using a hybrid ChaCha20/RSA scheme—avoiding system directories and common extensions, deleting shadow copies, and appending .akira to files before dropping akira_readme.txt—and to mitigate this threat organizations should prioritize patching and virtual patching of vulnerable VPN appliances, enforce multifactor authentication and least-privilege access, monitor anomalous use of administration and reconnaissance tools, implement comprehensive backup and recovery procedures, and deploy layered endpoint, network and email defenses with behavior-based detection.
hits.title: Ransomware Spotlight: Akira | Trend Micro (US)

canonical_entities: installing Sagerunex variants in the Windows Registry
hits.text: The Lotus Blossom APT (aka Lotus Panda, Billbug, Spring Dragon) has stepped up cyberespionage against APAC government targets by deploying new Sagerunex backdoor variants and abusing Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) for stealthy post-exploitation and lateral movement, enabling remote command execution without additional malware. Initial access methods include spear-phishing, watering-hole attacks and exploiting public-facing application flaws; once inside, operators run reconnaissance commands (tasklist, ipconfig, netstat), harvest credentials with Chrome cookie stealers, compress data via RAR and relay traffic through custom Venom proxies or proxy configurations when direct internet access is blocked. Persistence is achieved by installing Sagerunex variants in the Windows Registry under hijacked service names (tapisrv, swprv) to auto-launch at startup, while command-and-control blends encrypted traffic into legitimate platforms—stolen data uploaded as .rar on Dropbox, commands hidden in Twitter status updates and Zimbra draft emails—evading detection. Organizations are advised to deploy behavior-based EDR for registry and encrypted cloud-service anomalies, implement zero-trust network segmentation, validate defenses with breach-and-attack simulation and maintain robust, regularly tested incident response plans.
hits.title: Lotus Blossom APT Exploits WMI for Post-Exploitation Activities

canonical_entities: exploiting known vulnerabilities in public-facing VPN, web, Java, and SQL services
harvests credentials from LSASS memory and the SAM registry hive
hits.text: Microsoft has traced a stealthy espionage campaign by Flax Typhoon (aka Ethereal Panda), a China-based nation-state actor active since mid-2021, targeting dozens of Taiwanese organizations (with spill-over in Southeast Asia, North America, and Africa) by exploiting known vulnerabilities in public-facing VPN, web, Java, and SQL services to deploy the China Chopper web shell for initial access; the group escalates privileges via open-source exploits like Juicy Potato and BadPotato, then establishes persistence by disabling RDP network-level authentication, hijacking the Sticky Keys (sethc.exe) binary to launch Task Manager as SYSTEM, and installing a renamed SoftEther VPN-over-HTTPS bridge (conhost.exe/dllhost.exe) as a service to maintain covert C2 over port 443; leveraging LOLBins such as PowerShell Invoke-WebRequest, certutil, bitsadmin, WinRM, and WMIC for lateral movement, vulnerability scanning, and remote execution, it harvests credentials from LSASS memory and the SAM registry hive using Mimikatz for pass-the-hash attacks; although no exfiltration or final objectives have been observed, organizations are urged to enforce rigorous patch and vulnerability management on internet-exposed systems, monitor registry and file-integrity changes, deploy web application firewalls, reset compromised credentials, isolate and forensically examine affected hosts, and leverage detections in Microsoft 365 Defender to disrupt living-off-the-land tactics.
hits.title: Flax Typhoon using legitimate software to quietly access Taiwanese organizations | Microsoft Security Blog

hits.text: In mid-2022 Sophos reported that 66% of healthcare organizations were hit by ransomware—a 94% year-over-year increase—underscoring the continued success of the RaaS model and the emergence of Quantum ransomware, a splinter group from Conti (originally Quantum Locker, AstroLocker, MountLocker and XingLocker) officially taken over by Conti Team Two in April 2022; since June 2022 Quantum has deployed its BazarCall variant “Jormungandr,” leveraging OSINT, spamming, design and call-center specialists to execute callback phishing that tricks victims into installing legitimate remote-access tools, while DFIR reports show initial access via IcedID payloads embedded in mountable ISO files and malicious LNK shortcuts, leading to hands-on-keyboard activity within two hours, rapid Cobalt Strike and RDP lateral movement, WMI and PsExec to push the ttsel.exe ransomware payload, encryption and exfiltration, and the dropping of README_TO_DECRYPT.html notes with demands ranging from $150K to $500K; Quantum’s brand-impersonation phishing campaigns (masquerading as Oracle, CrowdStrike and others) have compromised a New Jersey behavioral‐health system, Interim Healthcare, a biopharmaceutical research firm and an IVF clinic in Delhi, exposing high-value patient data and demonstrating the urgent need for proactive defenses—including call-back phishing awareness, tight remote-access policies, IcedID and Cobalt Strike detection, LSASS memory monitoring and rapid incident response—to thwart these fast, socially engineered RaaS attacks.
hits.title: An In-Depth Look at Quantum Ransomware

canonical_entities: Session token extraction from device memory
extract session tokens from device memory
exposed 35,879,455 customers’ usernames, hashed passwords, names, contact details, last four SSN digits, dates of birth and security Q&A
hits.text: Since at least August 2023, threat actors have exploited CVE-2023-4966 (CitrixBleed), a 7.5-rated flaw in Citrix NetScaler ADC and Gateway, culminating in an October 16–19 breach at Comcast Xfinity that exposed 35,879,455 customers’ usernames, hashed passwords, names, contact details, last four SSN digits, dates of birth and security Q&A; despite Citrix’s October 10 patch and Comcast’s claim of prompt mitigation, attackers used publicly available proofs-of-concept and rumored Python automation scripts to extract session tokens from device memory, hijack active sessions and bypass authentication, a tactic linked by ReliaQuest to at least five threat groups including LockBit; this incident highlights the necessity not only of timely patching and reboots but also of invalidating all active and persistent session tokens, enforcing multi-factor authentication, resetting credentials and maintaining continuous 24x7 monitoring to prevent further data exfiltration and ransomware deployment.
hits.title: Comcast Xfinity Breached via CitrixBleed; 35M Customers Affected

canonical_entities: Scanning the Internet for IoT devices with open Telnet/SSH ports
Use of default or weak credentials
Encrypted SOCKS5 tunneling to proxy infrastructure
hits.text: Researchers have uncovered that since early 2024 a previously undocumented botnet, dubbed Ngioweb, has been systematically scanning the Internet for IoT devices—primarily DVRs, IP cameras and home routers—with open Telnet/SSH ports and default or weak credentials, exploiting known firmware vulnerabilities to deploy a lightweight Go-based loader that establishes encrypted SOCKS5 tunnels back to a resilient NSOCKS residential proxy network of over 150,000 infected nodes. Once a device is compromised, Ngioweb drops a persistent agent that connects to fast-flux C2 domains via HTTPS, retrieves updated encryption keys and proxy configuration, and registers the node for NSOCKS’ tiered subscription service (starting at $25/month), which reportedly generates upwards of $500K in monthly revenue by fueling large-scale credential-stuffing campaigns, ad fraud and DDoS-for-hire operations. The actors behind Ngioweb continually rotate fallback C2 domains, employ encryption and obfuscation to evade signature-based detection, and monitor infection success rates in real time, enabling rapid retooling and expansion. Defenders are urged to enforce strong, unique credentials on all IoT assets, disable unused management interfaces, apply timely firmware updates, implement network segmentation and deploy behavioral analytics or honeypots to detect anomalous outbound proxy traffic.
hits.title: Ngioweb Botnet Fuels NSOCKS Residential Proxy Network Exploiting IoT Devices

retrieved_context.text: Researchers have uncovered that since early 2024 a previously undocumented botnet, dubbed Ngioweb, has been systematically scanning the Internet for IoT devices—primarily DVRs, IP cameras and home routers—with open Telnet/SSH ports and default or weak credentials, exploiting known firmware vulnerabilities to deploy a lightweight Go-based loader that establishes encrypted SOCKS5 tunnels back to a resilient NSOCKS residential proxy network of over 150,000 infected nodes. Defenders are urged to enforce strong, unique credentials on all IoT assets, disable unused management interfaces, apply timely firmware updates, implement network segmentation and deploy behavioral analytics or honeypots to detect anomalous outbound proxy traffic.

hits.text: CrowdStrike researchers in April 2022 uncovered that ransomware actors exploited a critical remote code execution flaw (CVE-2022-29499) in unpatched Linux-based Mitel MiVoice appliances (SA 100, SA 400 and Virtual SA) to gain initial access, plant malware and pivot laterally: the exploit chain began with an external HTTP GET to a “get_url” parameter in a PHP file (to bypass IP restrictions) followed by a device-originated GET that injected commands via a malicious URL, enabling an SSL-enabled reverse shell (using mkfifo and openssl_client) and deployment of a “pdf_import.php” web shell and the Chisel tunneling tool. Although the threat actors deleted evidence from the VoIP filesystem, CrowdStrike recovered the undocumented exploit, downloaded tools and anti-forensic measures. With some 21,000 MITEL devices worldwide still exposed (per Kevin Beaumont’s Shodan string “http.html_hash:-1971546278”), organizations are urged to apply Mitel’s April advisory patches for MiVoice Connect 19.2 SP3 and earlier, enforce strict network segmentation around perimeter devices, conduct threat modeling to detect anomalous GET requests, and prioritize timely firmware updates to thwart zero-day exploitation.

hits.text: Lorenz ransomware, emerging in 2021 and likely a rebranding of the .sZ40/ThunderCrypt family, has preyed on over 20 mostly small-to-mid-sized organizations in the US, China and Mexico—demanding $500K–$700K via a double-extortion scheme and posting stolen data on a Tor leak site—most notably compromising Germany’s defense contractor Hensoldt in January 2022 (exfiltrating 95% of files) before exploiting a Mitel MiVoice Connect VoIP RCE (CVE-2022-29499, CVSS 9.8) in September to gain a perimeter foothold; CrowdStrike observed operators deploying a reverse shell via “pdf_import.php,” renaming binaries to “memdump” for anti-forensics, then using Chisel over SSH-secured HTTP to tunnel into the environment. hits.text: BlackBerry’s Research and Intelligence Team has uncovered “Silent Skimmer,” a year-long, financially motivated campaign by a Chinese-fluent actor exploiting Internet Information Services (IIS) vulnerabilities to breach online payment and PoS web applications across Asia-Pacific, North America and Latin America, achieving initial foothold before leveraging open-source and living-off-the-land tools for privilege escalation and executing a PowerShell-based RAT (server.ps1); this malware connects to geolocated VPS C2 servers to download additional utilities, deploy web shells and inject scrapers into checkout pages, stealthily harvesting payment data via reverse proxies and Cobalt Strike beacons. In parallel, Sophos detailed a “pig butchering” crypto scam using dating-app social engineering and liquidity-mining lures—no malware required—to trick victims into connecting wallets to malicious Ethereum contracts, netting actors millions; these findings highlight the urgent need for patching IIS, monitoring PowerShell and Cobalt Strike activity, enforcing least-privilege controls, detecting web shells, and training users against DeFi phishing.
hits.title: Silent Skimmer: A Year-Long Web Skimming Campaign Targeting Online Payment Businesses

Credentials from Password Stores: Security Account Manager
hits.text: Dragos researchers, in collaboration with Ukraine’s CSSC, unearthed FrostyGoop—an ICS-specific malware first spotted in April and used in January to disrupt central heating in over 600 Lviv apartment buildings—marking the first known malware to leverage Modbus TCP for read/write operations on operational technology. Attackers gained initial access in April 2023 by exploiting a MikroTik router vulnerability, deployed a webshell on the router’s web server, and maintained persistence via Tor and L2TP tunnels to Moscow-based IPs. After spending months conducting reconnaissance, they extracted credentials by dumping the SAM registry hive in December, then directly issued scripted Modbus commands—read from a JSON configuration file—to publicly exposed ENCO heating controllers, even downgrading firmware to disable monitoring and force inaccurate measurements that halted heating services for nearly two days amid subzero temperatures. This incident underscores the threat posed by internet-exposed ICS devices—over 46,000 globally using Modbus—and highlights poor network segmentation, unpatched ICS CVEs, and the ease with which FrostyGoop’s protocol-agnostic payload can be repurposed against diverse industrial controllers, necessitating immediate network segmentation, firmware monitoring, and patch management in OT environments.
hits.title: ICS malware FrostyGoop disrupted heating in Ukraine, remains threat to OT worldwide

hits.text: The Lotus Blossom APT (aka Lotus Panda, Billbug, Spring Dragon) has stepped up cyberespionage against APAC government targets by deploying new Sagerunex backdoor variants and abusing Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) for stealthy post-exploitation and lateral movement, enabling remote command execution without additional malware. Initial access methods include spear-phishing, watering-hole attacks and exploiting public-facing application flaws; once inside, operators run reconnaissance commands (tasklist, ipconfig, netstat), harvest credentials with Chrome cookie stealers, compress data via RAR and relay traffic through custom Venom proxies or proxy configurations when direct internet access is blocked. Persistence is achieved by installing Sagerunex variants in the Windows Registry under hijacked service names (tapisrv, swprv) to auto-launch at startup, while command-and-control blends encrypted traffic into legitimate platforms—stolen data uploaded as .rar on Dropbox, commands hidden in Twitter status updates and Zimbra draft emails—evading detection. Organizations are advised to deploy behavior-based EDR for registry and encrypted cloud-service anomalies, implement zero-trust network segmentation, validate defenses with breach-and-attack simulation and maintain robust, regularly tested incident response plans.
hits.title: Lotus Blossom APT Exploits WMI for Post-Exploitation Activities

hits.text: Symantec has warned that extortion actors, notably the Clop ransomware operation (aka Snakefly/TA505/FIN11), have been exploiting a zero-day SQL injection vulnerability in the MOVEit Transfer web application (CVE-2023-34362) since May 27, 2023, enabling supply-chain attacks across multiple organizations; although first patched on May 31, additional vulnerabilities (CVEs pending) were disclosed on June 9. Attackers deploy a bespoke web shell, Lemurloot (detected as JS.Malscript!g1, Trojan.Gen.2, WS.Malware), to authenticate via hard-coded credentials, execute SQL statements to alter or delete database elements, exfiltrate records and Azure settings, and manipulate user accounts. hits.text: Palo Alto Networks’ Unit 42 has identified a first-of-its-kind collaboration between North Korea’s state-sponsored Jumpy Pisces (linked to the Reconnaissance General Bureau) and the Play ransomware gang, revealing a blurring of nation-state and criminal operations: Jumpy Pisces gained initial access in May via a compromised user account, spent months conducting lateral movement and persistence using Sliver C2, custom DTrack info-stealer, a bespoke Mimikatz variant, RDP privileged-account creation tools and a trojanized binary that exfiltrates browser history, autofill data and credit-card details from Chrome, Edge and Brave, then in early September Play deployed its ransomware payload using the same account; Unit 42 attributed the joint operation with moderate confidence based on shared access credentials, continuous Sliver communications until deployment and Play’s known TTPs, though it remains unclear whether Jumpy Pisces acted as a Play affiliate or initial-access broker—this nexus not only underscores the need for defenders to monitor Sliver C2 indicators, credential-theft and RDP hardening but also signals a potential trend of North Korean actors increasingly leveraging underground ransomware networks to fund operations, raising the stakes for global cyber defenses.
hits.title: Play ransomware attack tied to North Korean nation-state actor | TechTarget

hits.text: Silent Push researchers uncovered FIN7’s largest-ever infrastructure, identifying over 4,000 malicious IOFA domains and associated IP addresses used to fuel a global phishing and malware campaign that hit high-profile targets such as the Louvre, Meta and Reuters. Using automated intelligence and Threat Hunting workflows, analysts detected a pattern of newly registered look-alike domains—many leveraging common TLDs and typosquatting—to host spear-phishing landing pages and weaponized Office attachments that deploy custom .NET droppers and Cobalt Strike beacons. Chronologically, the operation began with domain registration, followed by coordinated email blasts spoofing corporate brands, HTTP(S) redirects to phishing kits, and payload delivery that enabled credential harvesting and potential lateral movement. Silent Push’s API-driven Integrations enabled rapid enumeration of IOFA indicators of compromise, brand protection alerts and proactive blocking in customer environments. Actionable insights include ingesting the full list of domains and IPs into SIEM and email security filters, enforcing strict SPF/DKIM/DMARC policies, monitoring DNS query anomalies for new domain registrations, and updating endpoint detection rules to flag the identified .NET loader behaviors.

hits.text: Lynx ransomware, emerging in July 2024 as the INC ransomware successor under a Ransomware-as-a-Service model, employs a sophisticated double-extortion strategy—exfiltrating data prior to encryption and threatening publication on a leak site—and reuses significant INC source code. Between July and November 2024, it disrupted U.S. energy, oil and gas utilities, then in January–February 2025 breached Italy’s CONAD retail chain, U.S. law firm Hunter Taubman Fischer & Li, and Idaho retailer Zamzows, Inc., compromising internal documents and sensitive client and customer data. Initial access leverages phishing (T1566.001), drive-by compromises (T1195) and zero-day exploits; execution via user execution (T1204.002) and scripting interpreters (T1059.001); persistence through autostart mechanisms (T1070.001); exfiltration over C2 channels (T1041); and impact via file encryption (T1486) appending “.LYNX.” Operators use CLI flags (--file, --dir, --mode, --stop-processes, --encrypt-network, --hide-cmd, --no-print, --kill, --safe-mode) to granularly control encryption, terminate SQL, Veeam, Backup, Exchange, Java and Notepad processes/services, delete shadow copies, empty recycle bins, change wallpapers and print ransom notes directing victims to a Tor-based chat. Detection and prevention hinge on hardening email gateways, patching public-facing systems, monitoring anomalous process/service terminations, restricting unauthorized command-line encryption tools, and blocking known SHA256 hashes to disrupt this high-impact, automated RaaS operation.

hits.text: Water Ouroboros is a Ransomware-as-a-Service operation that exploits public-facing Oracle WebLogic vulnerabilities (CVE-2019-2725, CVE-2017-10271, CVE-2019-2729) or drive-by installers for initial access (T1190, T1189), then executes remote Windows commands (wmic.exe, bcdedit.exe, wbadmin.exe, vssadmin.exe) to delete backups and disable recovery (T1490, T1562.001) before encrypting fixed, removable and network drives via a Go-based custom routine that uses RTLGenRandom to generate a symmetric key, protects it with embedded RSA public keys (App_ExportKey), appends “.locked” (unless suppressed with –E), excludes over 60 file extensions, and accepts credentials (c {user}:{pass}), logging (–a), non-aggressive (–A) and size filters (–m). Victims find Contact Us.txt ransom notes pointing to a TOR payment site and Hive Leaks data-dump threat. Post-infection, actors maintain access via compromised admin accounts (T1078), disable security tools (PCHunter, ProcessHacker), dump credentials from registry hives (T1003.002), move laterally over RDP/SMB (T1021.001/002), discover assets via AdFind (T1595.002) and exfiltrate data over C&C (SharpRhino RAT/T1071.001, T1041). With 136 incidents in the US and notable impacts on construction, IT, manufacturing and healthcare SMBs, the campaign underscores the need for timely patching, hardened public-facing apps, least-privilege access, MFA, robust backups and advanced threat detection.

hits.text: Trend Micro data shows BlackCat executed 39.3% of its 176 manufacturing detections against US targets and confirmed 173 leak-site compromises from December 2021 to September 2022—58.7% US-based—favoring finance, professional, legal, technology, energy, utilities, construction, and manufacturing sectors, with small (52%) and midsize (26%) businesses most targeted. Initial access was achieved via Exchange CVE-2021-26855/26857/26858/27065 exploits, ConnectWise RCE, and SSH key abuse. Execution leverages COBEACON to inject the Rust-based ransomware into ntoskrnl.exe, evading detection; defense evasion includes disabling AV, using AdFind/ADRecon/SoftPerfect, Process Hacker, Mimikatz, WMIC, Netstat, and LSASS credential dumping. Lateral movement exploits embedded PsExec, RDP, MobaXterm, and BITSAdmin transfers of zzz.exe/xxx.exe/yyy.exe/sv.exe. C2 communication uses Base64-encoded PowerShell with a Cobalt Strike SMB beacon over named pipes. Exfiltration employs ExMatter (upgraded September 2022), 7-Zip, Rclone, MEGASync, WinSCP, and FreeFileSync for double extortion. The payload defaces backgrounds, terminates backup/AV/DB/Internet/VM services, disables recovery (shadow copy deletion, safe-mode variant), and appends variable Sphynx extensions while avoiding critical directories and file types. BlackCat maps to MITRE ATT&CK T1190, T1078, T1562.001/009, T1003.001, T1021.002, T1486, T1490, T1489, T1048/T1567. Security teams should patch Exchange CVEs, secure MSP tools, enforce least privilege, segment networks, monitor PowerShell injections, and vet outbound file transfers to disrupt this evolving affiliate-driven operation.
