hits.text: Between November 2023 and February 2024, operators of the StrelaStealer infostealer—first documented in November 2022—conducted three large-scale phishing campaigns that leveraged localized spam to target over 100 US and EU organizations across high-tech, finance, legal, manufacturing, government, utilities, energy, insurance and construction sectors. In place of earlier ISO-based LNK/HTML chains, these campaigns delivered ZIP attachments containing JScript droppers that deploy a malicious DLL configured to harvest credentials from popular email clients and exfiltrate them to attacker-controlled C&C servers. The actors enhanced obfuscation, removed debugging symbols and changed attachment types to evade signature-based detection and frustrate forensic analysis. To defend against StrelaStealer’s evolving tactics, security teams should monitor for ZIP-delivered script droppers, anomalous DLL loads and suspicious external connections, and bolster email gateway filtering, endpoint behavior analytics and credential-monitoring controls.

hits.text: HC3’s November 2022 alert warns of human-operated Lorenz ransomware, first observed in February 2021 and linked to earlier sZ40 and ThunderCrypt activity, which specifically targets large healthcare organizations by customizing its executable code and following a kill chain of initial access, extended reconnaissance, lateral movement to Windows domain controllers for administrator credential theft, then encryption and extortion. Operators demand $500,000–$700,000 and employ a non-typical leak site where stolen data is first offered for sale to other threat actors, then distributed in password-protected archives or, if sales fail, released publicly. With relatively limited public intelligence on Lorenz, HC3 emphasizes that victims should address common ransomware vectors—phishing, exploitation of known vulnerabilities, remote-access compromise and distributed attacks—by reinforcing patch management, intrusion detection, access controls and incident-response planning, especially in light of concurrent Hive ransomware warnings issued by HHS, FBI and CISA.

hits.text: Attackers have been exploiting an unpatched Windows and Office zero-day vulnerability (CVE-2023-36884), disclosed by Microsoft on July 11, in highly targeted campaigns against government and defense organizations in Europe and North America; initial exploitation was documented by BlackBerry on July 8 when Storm-0978 (aka RomCom), a Russia-linked actor using the RomCom RAT with ties to the Hawker group and Cuba ransomware developers (and potentially to Industrial Spy ransomware operators), delivered malicious Word documents masquerading as Ukrainian World Congress materials to NATO Summit attendees, enabling remote code execution once opened. hits.text: Trend Micro’s investigation into the LockBit ransomware-as-a-service operation, tracked as intrusion set Water Selkie, reveals the group’s marketing of its lightning-fast AES-128 head-only file encryption (first 4 KB) with RSA-wrapped keys, deployed via versatile affiliate-driven campaigns that source initial access through phishing (T1566), CVE-2018-13379 Fortinet VPN exploits (T1190) and compromised RDP/VPN accounts (T1078), then execute payloads via PowerShell Empire, Meterpreter, scheduled tasks or signed binaries (T1059, T1218), evade defenses with Mimikatz, GMER, Process Hacker or disabled Windows Defender (T1562), discover network shares and AD servers (T1083, T1135), laterally propagate via SMB or Cobalt Strike (T1570), exfiltrate data using StealBit or cloud storage (T1567) and encrypt data for impact (T1486), often on weekdays (~78%). Between July 2021 and January 2022 LockBit attempts surged globally—chiefly the US, India and Brazil—targeting healthcare and education yet boasting 41 leak-site victims (Dec 2021–Jan 2022) primarily SMBs (65.9%) across North America, Europe and APAC. With a professional affiliate program fueling continuous innovation and predicted upticks in supply-chain attacks in 2022, organizations should implement comprehensive asset inventory, least-privilege access, regular patching (including Fortinet CVE-2018-13379), RDP/VPN lockdown, application allow-listing, multifactor authentication, offline backups and MITRE TTP monitoring to detect and disrupt LockBit activity.

retrieved_context.text: Lynx ransomware, emerging in July 2024 as the INC ransomware successor under a Ransomware-as-a-Service model, employs a sophisticated double-extortion strategy—exfiltrating data prior to encryption and threatening publication on a leak site—and reuses significant INC source code. Between July and November 2024, it disrupted U.S. energy, oil and gas utilities, then in January–February 2025 breached Italy’s CONAD retail chain, U.S. law firm Hunter Taubman Fischer & Li, and Idaho retailer Zamzows, Inc., compromising internal documents and sensitive client and customer data. Initial access leverages phishing (T1566.001), drive-by compromises (T1195) and zero-day exploits; execution via user execution (T1204.002) and scripting interpreters (T1059.001); persistence through autostart mechanisms (T1070.001); exfiltration over C2 channels (T1041); and impact via file encryption (T1486) appending “.LYNX.” Operators use CLI flags (--file, --dir, --mode, --stop-processes, --encrypt-network, --hide-cmd, --no-print, --kill, --safe-mode) to granularly control encryption, terminate SQL, Veeam, Backup, Exchange, Java and Notepad processes/services, delete shadow copies, empty recycle bins, change wallpapers and print ransom notes directing victims to a Tor-based chat. Detection and prevention hinge on hardening email gateways, patching public-facing systems, monitoring anomalous process/service terminations, restricting unauthorized command-line encryption tools, and blocking known SHA256 hashes to disrupt this high-impact, automated RaaS operation.
retrieved_context.title: Lynx Ransomware: INC Ransomware Reincarnated - Threat Actors

retrieved_context.text: Water Ouroboros is a Ransomware-as-a-Service operation that exploits public-facing Oracle WebLogic vulnerabilities (CVE-2019-2725, CVE-2017-10271, CVE-2019-2729) or drive-by installers for initial access (T1190, T1189), then executes remote Windows commands (wmic.exe, bcdedit.exe, wbadmin.exe, vssadmin.exe) to delete backups and disable recovery (T1490, T1562.001) before encrypting fixed, removable and network drives via a Go-based custom routine that uses RTLGenRandom to generate a symmetric key, protects it with embedded RSA public keys (App_ExportKey), appends “.locked” (unless suppressed with –E), excludes over 60 file extensions, and accepts credentials (c {user}:{pass}), logging (–a), non-aggressive (–A) and size filters (–m). Victims find Contact Us.txt ransom notes pointing to a TOR payment site and Hive Leaks data-dump threat. Post-infection, actors maintain access via compromised admin accounts (T1078), disable security tools (PCHunter, ProcessHacker), dump credentials from registry hives (T1003.002), move laterally over RDP/SMB (T1021.001/002), discover assets via AdFind (T1595.002) and exfiltrate data over C&C (SharpRhino RAT/T1071.001, T1041). With 136 incidents in the US and notable impacts on construction, IT, manufacturing and healthcare SMBs, the campaign underscores the need for timely patching, hardened public-facing apps, least-privilege access, MFA, robust backups and advanced threat detection.

retrieved_context.text: Trend Micro data shows BlackCat executed 39.3% of its 176 manufacturing detections against US targets and confirmed 173 leak-site compromises from December 2021 to September 2022—58.7% US-based—favoring finance, professional, legal, technology, energy, utilities, construction, and manufacturing sectors, with small (52%) and midsize (26%) businesses most targeted. Initial access was achieved via Exchange CVE-2021-26855/26857/26858/27065 exploits, ConnectWise RCE, and SSH key abuse. Execution leverages COBEACON to inject the Rust-based ransomware into ntoskrnl.exe, evading detection; defense evasion includes disabling AV, using AdFind/ADRecon/SoftPerfect, Process Hacker, Mimikatz, WMIC, Netstat, and LSASS credential dumping. Lateral movement exploits embedded PsExec, RDP, MobaXterm, and BITSAdmin transfers of zzz.exe/xxx.exe/yyy.exe/sv.exe. C2 communication uses Base64-encoded PowerShell with a Cobalt Strike SMB beacon over named pipes. Exfiltration employs ExMatter (upgraded September 2022), 7-Zip, Rclone, MEGASync, WinSCP, and FreeFileSync for double extortion. The payload defaces backgrounds, terminates backup/AV/DB/Internet/VM services, disables recovery (shadow copy deletion, safe-mode variant), and appends variable Sphynx extensions while avoiding critical directories and file types. BlackCat maps to MITRE ATT&CK T1190, T1078, T1562.001/009, T1003.001, T1021.002, T1486, T1490, T1489, T1048/T1567. Security teams should patch Exchange CVEs, secure MSP tools, enforce least privilege, segment networks, monitor PowerShell injections, and vet outbound file transfers to disrupt this evolving affiliate-driven operation.
retrieved_context.title: Ransomware Spotlight: BlackCat | Trend Micro (US)

retrieved_context.text: Between November 2023 and February 2024, operators of the StrelaStealer infostealer—first documented in November 2022—conducted three large-scale phishing campaigns that leveraged localized spam to target over 100 US and EU organizations across high-tech, finance, legal, manufacturing, government, utilities, energy, insurance and construction sectors. In place of earlier ISO-based LNK/HTML chains, these campaigns delivered ZIP attachments containing JScript droppers that deploy a malicious DLL configured to harvest credentials from popular email clients and exfiltrate them to attacker-controlled C&C servers. The actors enhanced obfuscation, removed debugging symbols and changed attachment types to evade signature-based detection and frustrate forensic analysis. To defend against StrelaStealer’s evolving tactics, security teams should monitor for ZIP-delivered script droppers, anomalous DLL loads and suspicious external connections, and bolster email gateway filtering, endpoint behavior analytics and credential-monitoring controls.

hits.text: Dragos researchers, in collaboration with Ukraine’s CSSC, unearthed FrostyGoop—an ICS-specific malware first spotted in April and used in January to disrupt central heating in over 600 Lviv apartment buildings—marking the first known malware to leverage Modbus TCP for read/write operations on operational technology. Attackers gained initial access in April 2023 by exploiting a MikroTik router vulnerability, deployed a webshell on the router’s web server, and maintained persistence via Tor and L2TP tunnels to Moscow-based IPs. After spending months conducting reconnaissance, they extracted credentials by dumping the SAM registry hive in December, then directly issued scripted Modbus commands—read from a JSON configuration file—to publicly exposed ENCO heating controllers, even downgrading firmware to disable monitoring and force inaccurate measurements that halted heating services for nearly two days amid subzero temperatures. This incident underscores the threat posed by internet-exposed ICS devices—over 46,000 globally using Modbus—and highlights poor network segmentation, unpatched ICS CVEs, and the ease with which FrostyGoop’s protocol-agnostic payload can be repurposed against diverse industrial controllers, necessitating immediate network segmentation, firmware monitoring, and patch management in OT environments.
hits.title: ICS malware FrostyGoop disrupted heating in Ukraine, remains threat to OT worldwide

canonical_entities: installing Sagerunex variants in the Windows Registry
hits.text: The Lotus Blossom APT (aka Lotus Panda, Billbug, Spring Dragon) has stepped up cyberespionage against APAC government targets by deploying new Sagerunex backdoor variants and abusing Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) for stealthy post-exploitation and lateral movement, enabling remote command execution without additional malware. Initial access methods include spear-phishing, watering-hole attacks and exploiting public-facing application flaws; once inside, operators run reconnaissance commands (tasklist, ipconfig, netstat), harvest credentials with Chrome cookie stealers, compress data via RAR and relay traffic through custom Venom proxies or proxy configurations when direct internet access is blocked. Persistence is achieved by installing Sagerunex variants in the Windows Registry under hijacked service names (tapisrv, swprv) to auto-launch at startup, while command-and-control blends encrypted traffic into legitimate platforms—stolen data uploaded as .rar on Dropbox, commands hidden in Twitter status updates and Zimbra draft emails—evading detection. Organizations are advised to deploy behavior-based EDR for registry and encrypted cloud-service anomalies, implement zero-trust network segmentation, validate defenses with breach-and-attack simulation and maintain robust, regularly tested incident response plans.
hits.title: Lotus Blossom APT Exploits WMI for Post-Exploitation Activities

hits.text: In August 2019 Dragos and SecureWorks detailed a protracted (since April 2018) campaign by the Lyceum/Hexane threat group targeting Middle East critical infrastructure with straightforward but effective tactics: initial password‐spraying and brute‐force attacks on corporate email accounts, followed by spear-phishing from compromised internal accounts to executives, HR and IT staff using malicious Excel macros that deploy the DanBot RAT; once inside, operators run PoshC2-sourced PowerShell scripts—Decrypt-RDCMan.ps1 to extract RDCMan-stored passwords and Get-LAPSP.ps1 to harvest Active Directory credentials via LDAP—enabling environment reconnaissance and lateral movement. Despite its reliance on common techniques rather than novel malware or zero-days, Lyceum’s persistence highlights the urgency of enforcing multi-factor authentication, disabling macros, monitoring for unauthorized PowerShell/PoshC2 activity and training high-value users to detect spear-phishing, thereby mitigating the group’s primary objective of information collection before any potential pivot into OT/ICS environments.
hits.title: Lyceum/Hexane Threat Group Uses Common Hacking Tactics

canonical_entities: enumerates SSH directories to harvest credentials
Persistence is achieved through multiple cronjobs
hits.text: Aqua Security’s Nautilus team has uncovered Hadooken, a new Linux malware targeting Oracle WebLogic servers via weak passwords. Post-compromise, attackers deploy redundant shell and Python scripts to ensure download and execution of Hadooken, which enumerates SSH directories to harvest credentials, moves laterally, and clears logs. Hadooken then drops a three-path cryptominer and a Tsunami backdoor with a randomized name, the latter reserved for potential later-stage attacks. Persistence is achieved through multiple cronjobs under varied names and frequencies stored across cron directories. The malware is hosted on two IPs—one German address linked to TeamTNT and Gang 8220, the other inactive in Russia—where researchers also identified a Mallox ransomware PowerShell loader targeting Windows. Static analysis links Hadooken to Rhombus and NoEscape families. With over 230,000 internet-connected WebLogic instances—hundreds of which expose vulnerable admin consoles—this campaign underscores the dual risk of cryptojacking and ransomware across Linux and Windows environments.
hits.title: New 'Hadooken' Linux Malware Targets WebLogic Servers - SecurityWeek

hits.text: In February 2022, CISA, the FBI, US Cyber Command CNMF, NCSC-UK and NSA issued a joint advisory on Iranian Ministry of Intelligence–linked APT MuddyWater (aka MERCURY, Earth Vetala, Static Kitten, Seedworm, TEMP.Zagros), active since 2018 and focused on cyber espionage, intellectual property theft and ransomware against defense, oil & gas, government and telecom sectors across Asia, Africa, Europe and North America. Exploiting publicly disclosed vulnerabilities and open-source tools, MuddyWater delivers malicious PDFs with embedded links that display error messages prompting users to download Excel maldocs or Windows executables; these files host VBA macros that drop WSF scripts to execute PowerShell and VB payloads, leverage LoLBins, and stage RATs and malware families including PowGoop, Canopy, Small Sieve, POWERSTATS and Mori while communicating with C2 over HTTP and DNS and persisting via Registry Run keys. Cisco Talos observed regional campaigns in Turkey (Nov 2021), Pakistan (Aug 2021) and Armenia (Jun 2021) using decoy documents, signaling tokens and a consistent TTP set, suggesting a conglomerate of subgroups migrating techniques across regions. The resultant network access and data exfiltration underscore the imperative for proactive DFIR readiness, deployment of XDR/MDR platforms, rigorous vulnerability management, macro execution restrictions, PowerShell/LoLBin monitoring and ongoing user awareness training reinforced by incident response tabletop exercises.
hits.title: An In-Depth Look at Iranian APT "MuddyWater"

canonical_entities: Scanning the Internet for IoT devices with open Telnet/SSH ports
Use of default or weak credentials
Encrypted SOCKS5 tunneling to proxy infrastructure
hits.text: Researchers have uncovered that since early 2024 a previously undocumented botnet, dubbed Ngioweb, has been systematically scanning the Internet for IoT devices—primarily DVRs, IP cameras and home routers—with open Telnet/SSH ports and default or weak credentials, exploiting known firmware vulnerabilities to deploy a lightweight Go-based loader that establishes encrypted SOCKS5 tunnels back to a resilient NSOCKS residential proxy network of over 150,000 infected nodes. Once a device is compromised, Ngioweb drops a persistent agent that connects to fast-flux C2 domains via HTTPS, retrieves updated encryption keys and proxy configuration, and registers the node for NSOCKS’ tiered subscription service (starting at $25/month), which reportedly generates upwards of $500K in monthly revenue by fueling large-scale credential-stuffing campaigns, ad fraud and DDoS-for-hire operations. The actors behind Ngioweb continually rotate fallback C2 domains, employ encryption and obfuscation to evade signature-based detection, and monitor infection success rates in real time, enabling rapid retooling and expansion. Defenders are urged to enforce strong, unique credentials on all IoT assets, disable unused management interfaces, apply timely firmware updates, implement network segmentation and deploy behavioral analytics or honeypots to detect anomalous outbound proxy traffic.
hits.title: Ngioweb Botnet Fuels NSOCKS Residential Proxy Network Exploiting IoT Devices

hits.text: In July 2024, evolving from an early-year attack on a Ukrainian municipal energy provider disclosed by Ukraine’s CSSC, the Russian-linked OT malware FrostyGoop (aka BUSTLEBERM) exploited an obscure Go-based Modbus TCP library, goccy’s go-json encoder/decoder and an open-source ‘queues’ execution controller—delivered via compromised MikroTik routers or internet-exposed OT devices—to issue bespoke Modbus read/write commands that disrupted heating services to over 600 apartment buildings for two days in sub-zero conditions. FrostyGoop accepts JSON or command-line arguments to configure operation codes, addresses, counts, values and timing, includes a PEB BeingDebugged flag check for anti-analysis, and our telemetry reveals 1,088,175 Modbus TCP devices exposed from Sept. 2–Oct. 2, 2024 (6,211,623 total), including 32 ENCO control devices with Telnet-accessible TCP/23 in Romania and Ukraine. Concurrently, we identified a co-occurring Golang sample, go-encrypt.exe, using AES-CFB to encrypt/decrypt JSON files—likely for concealing FrostyGoop configs—that first appeared with task_test.json on Oct. 10, 2023. These insights highlight the need for ICS-centric detection—signatures for the unique Modbus library and JSON schema, monitoring for PEB debug checks and encrypted JSON usage—and rigorous network segmentation to mitigate the growing OT threat.

retrieved_context.text: The Lotus Blossom APT (aka Lotus Panda, Billbug, Spring Dragon) has stepped up cyberespionage against APAC government targets by deploying new Sagerunex backdoor variants and abusing Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) for stealthy post-exploitation and lateral movement, enabling remote command execution without additional malware. Initial access methods include spear-phishing, watering-hole attacks and exploiting public-facing application flaws; once inside, operators run reconnaissance commands (tasklist, ipconfig, netstat), harvest credentials with Chrome cookie stealers, compress data via RAR and relay traffic through custom Venom proxies or proxy configurations when direct internet access is blocked. Persistence is achieved by installing Sagerunex variants in the Windows Registry under hijacked service names (tapisrv, swprv) to auto-launch at startup, while command-and-control blends encrypted traffic into legitimate platforms—stolen data uploaded as .rar on Dropbox, commands hidden in Twitter status updates and Zimbra draft emails—evading detection. Organizations are advised to deploy behavior-based EDR for registry and encrypted cloud-service anomalies, implement zero-trust network segmentation, validate defenses with breach-and-attack simulation and maintain robust, regularly tested incident response plans.

retrieved_context.text: In August 2019 Dragos and SecureWorks detailed a protracted (since April 2018) campaign by the Lyceum/Hexane threat group targeting Middle East critical infrastructure with straightforward but effective tactics: initial password‐spraying and brute‐force attacks on corporate email accounts, followed by spear-phishing from compromised internal accounts to executives, HR and IT staff using malicious Excel macros that deploy the DanBot RAT; once inside, operators run PoshC2-sourced PowerShell scripts—Decrypt-RDCMan.ps1 to extract RDCMan-stored passwords and Get-LAPSP.ps1 to harvest Active Directory credentials via LDAP—enabling environment reconnaissance and lateral movement. retrieved_context.text: Aqua Security’s Nautilus team has uncovered Hadooken, a new Linux malware targeting Oracle WebLogic servers via weak passwords. Post-compromise, attackers deploy redundant shell and Python scripts to ensure download and execution of Hadooken, which enumerates SSH directories to harvest credentials, moves laterally, and clears logs. Hadooken then drops a three-path cryptominer and a Tsunami backdoor with a randomized name, the latter reserved for potential later-stage attacks. Persistence is achieved through multiple cronjobs under varied names and frequencies stored across cron directories. The malware is hosted on two IPs—one German address linked to TeamTNT and Gang 8220, the other inactive in Russia—where researchers also identified a Mallox ransomware PowerShell loader targeting Windows. retrieved_context.text: In February 2022, CISA, the FBI, US Cyber Command CNMF, NCSC-UK and NSA issued a joint advisory on Iranian Ministry of Intelligence–linked APT MuddyWater (aka MERCURY, Earth Vetala, Static Kitten, Seedworm, TEMP.Zagros), active since 2018 and focused on cyber espionage, intellectual property theft and ransomware against defense, oil & gas, government and telecom sectors across Asia, Africa, Europe and North America. retrieved_context.text: Researchers have uncovered that since early 2024 a previously undocumented botnet, dubbed Ngioweb, has been systematically scanning the Internet for IoT devices—primarily DVRs, IP cameras and home routers—with open Telnet/SSH ports and default or weak credentials, exploiting known firmware vulnerabilities to deploy a lightweight Go-based loader that establishes encrypted SOCKS5 tunnels back to a resilient NSOCKS residential proxy network of over 150,000 infected nodes. Once a device is compromised, Ngioweb drops a persistent agent that connects to fast-flux C2 domains via HTTPS, retrieves updated encryption keys and proxy configuration, and registers the node for NSOCKS’ tiered subscription service (starting at $25/month), which reportedly generates upwards of $500K in monthly revenue by fueling large-scale credential-stuffing campaigns, ad fraud and DDoS-for-hire operations. The actors behind Ngioweb continually rotate fallback C2 domains, employ encryption and obfuscation to evade signature-based detection, and monitor infection success rates in real time, enabling rapid retooling and expansion. Defenders are urged to enforce strong, unique credentials on all IoT assets, disable unused management interfaces, apply timely firmware updates, implement network segmentation and deploy behavioral analytics or honeypots to detect anomalous outbound proxy traffic.

retrieved_context.text: In July 2024, evolving from an early-year attack on a Ukrainian municipal energy provider disclosed by Ukraine’s CSSC, the Russian-linked OT malware FrostyGoop (aka BUSTLEBERM) exploited an obscure Go-based Modbus TCP library, goccy’s go-json encoder/decoder and an open-source ‘queues’ execution controller—delivered via compromised MikroTik routers or internet-exposed OT devices—to issue bespoke Modbus read/write commands that disrupted heating services to over 600 apartment buildings for two days in sub-zero conditions. FrostyGoop accepts JSON or command-line arguments to configure operation codes, addresses, counts, values and timing, includes a PEB BeingDebugged flag check for anti-analysis, and our telemetry reveals 1,088,175 Modbus TCP devices exposed from Sept. 2–Oct. 2, 2024 (6,211,623 total), including 32 ENCO control devices with Telnet-accessible TCP/23 in Romania and Ukraine. Concurrently, we identified a co-occurring Golang sample, go-encrypt.exe, using AES-CFB to encrypt/decrypt JSON files—likely for concealing FrostyGoop configs—that first appeared with task_test.json on Oct. 10, 2023. These insights highlight the need for ICS-centric detection—signatures for the unique Modbus library and JSON schema, monitoring for PEB debug checks and encrypted JSON usage—and rigorous network segmentation to mitigate the growing OT threat.

hits.text: Unit42’s “EleKtra-Leak” campaign, active since December 2020, uses automated scripts to clone public GitHub repos every few minutes, extract exposed AWS IAM keys within five minutes, then—if not blocked by GitHub-AWS quarantine policies—execute rapid AWS reconnaissance (DescribeRegions), create security groups, and launch hundreds of EC2 instances across regions via VPN for Monero cryptojacking, generating over 400 API calls in seven minutes. Between Aug. 30 and Oct. 6, 2023, researchers tracked 474 actor-controlled miners. The actor employs custom mining software and blocklists high-profile AWS account IDs to avoid honey traps. Leveraging the Prisma Cloud HoneyCloud project’s ephemeral key leaks and policy overrides, Unit42 obtained full visibility, informing Prisma Cloud Secrets Security, CI/CD IaC scanning, Cortex XDR, and recommendations for independent repo scanning, strict IAM policies, and continuous monitoring.

hits.text: Secret Blizzard, the Russian FSB’s Center 16, has escalated global espionage by co-opting C2 infrastructures of at least six threat actors—including Pakistan-based Storm-0156, Hazel Sandstorm and Storm-0473—to install backdoors (CrimsonRAT, Wainscot), deploy custom payloads (TwoDash downloader, MiniPocket fetcher), a TinyTurla variant disguised as a Windows service, and the Statuezy clipboard-monitoring trojan via DLL sideloading and batch files; this cross-actor compromise secured persistent access to diplomatic and defense networks in Ukraine, Afghanistan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and GDI, and Indian military institutions, enabling exfiltration of politically sensitive intelligence and advanced research data while reducing development overhead and underscoring the need for robust supply-chain security, network segmentation and proactive vulnerability management.

hits.text: Since at least August 2023, threat actors have exploited CVE-2023-4966 (CitrixBleed), a 7.5-rated flaw in Citrix NetScaler ADC and Gateway, culminating in an October 16–19 breach at Comcast Xfinity that exposed 35,879,455 customers’ usernames, hashed passwords, names, contact details, last four SSN digits, dates of birth and security Q&A; despite Citrix’s October 10 patch and Comcast’s claim of prompt mitigation, attackers used publicly available proofs-of-concept and rumored Python automation scripts to extract session tokens from device memory, hijack active sessions and bypass authentication, a tactic linked by ReliaQuest to at least five threat groups including LockBit; this incident highlights the necessity not only of timely patching and reboots but also of invalidating all active and persistent session tokens, enforcing multi-factor authentication, resetting credentials and maintaining continuous 24x7 monitoring to prevent further data exfiltration and ransomware deployment.

hits.text: The North Korea-linked threat actor Slow Pisces (also tracked as Jade Sleet, PUKCHONG, TraderTraitor, and UNC4899) has been conducting a multi-stage malware campaign targeting cryptocurrency developers via LinkedIn job opportunity lures since at least June 2024, leveraging trojanized Python and JavaScript projects hosted on GitHub that employ YAML deserialization and EJS templating to execute gated payloads only to validated targets meeting specific criteria (IP address, geolocation, time, HTTP headers); the campaign delivers RN Loader and RN Stealer malware on macOS systems capable of harvesting system metadata, installed applications, SSH keys, AWS/Kubernetes/Google Cloud configuration files, and iCloud Keychain data, with payloads remaining memory-resident and deployed selectively to prevent analysis; Slow Pisces is assessed to be responsible for the February 2025 Bybit cryptocurrency exchange breach and operates alongside other North Korean clusters including Operation Dream Job, Contagious Interview, Alluring Pisces, and Moonstone Sleet, though with notably superior operational security practices involving heavily guarded payload delivery across infection stages.
hits.title: Crypto Developers Targeted by Python Malware Disguised as Coding Challenges

hits.text: Symantec’s Threat Hunter Team has linked the newly discovered Sidewalk loader backdoor—an evolution of the Crosswalk/Backdoor.Motnug family—to Grayfly (aka GREF/Wicked Panda), a China-linked espionage group active since March 2017 that employs custom backdoors, Trojan.Chattak, Cobalt Strike, web shells and credential-dumpers against telecom, IT, media and finance targets in Taiwan, Vietnam, the US and Mexico; in a recent campaign they exploited public-facing Microsoft Exchange and MySQL servers via commodity and zero-day flaws to execute Base64-encoded PowerShell commands through certutil, install an ASPX web shell in the ClientAccess\ecp directory, deploy Sidewalk via installutil.exe, create persistence with WMIC-launched scheduled tasks, then run a custom Mimikatz variant (SHA256 b3eb783b017da32e33d19670b39eae0b11de8e983891dd4feb873d6e9333608d) to harvest credentials—all within about an hour before ceasing observable activity; three Chengdu 404 executives were indicted in 2020 for attacks on over 100 organizations, highlighting Grayfly’s persistence and underscoring the need to promptly patch Exchange and MySQL servers, monitor anomalous PowerShell and scheduled-task activity, and deploy IOC-based detection to block Sidewalk and related tools.
hits.title: Grayfly: Chinese Threat Actor Uses Newly-discovered Sidewalk Malware | Symantec Enterprise Blogs

hits.text: During a recent incident, a LockBit affiliate conducted initial intrusions using gpresult for policy dumping, Cobalt Strike loaders and PsExec for privilege escalation, followed by reconnaissance (whoami, netstat, quser, net view), lateral movement, persistence via a new user account, and data exfiltration over FTP with Wput; when deployment of LockBit (SHA256 079b99f6…) was blocked on the target network, the attacker pivoted to a newly observed Rust-written ransomware family dubbed 3AM (SHA256 307a1217…), which appends “.threeamtime” to encrypted files, stops over 100 security and backup services via net stop and wbadmin/bcdedit/wmic commands, deletes Volume Shadow copies with vssadmin.exe delete shadows /all /quiet, and drops a Tor‐accessible ransom note requiring a 32-character “-k” access key and offering decryption/mystical-themed extortion; although 3AM encryption succeeded on only one of three attempted hosts, its Conti-style “-m” (local/net) and “-h” parameters, heavy service-termination payload, and aggressive VSS wipe underscore its potential as a fallback vector—defenders should update Symantec/Broadcom signatures, monitor for the .threeamtime extension, suspicious Rust binaries, command-line flags “-k” and “-m”, and mass service stoppage activity, and block associated IOCs (185.202.0[.]111, 212.18.104[.]6, 85.159.229[.]62) to mitigate future 3AM use.
hits.title: 3AM: New Ransomware Family Used As Fallback in Failed LockBit Attack | Symantec Enterprise Blogs

retrieved_context.title: CloudKeys in the Air: Tracking Malicious Operations of Exposed IAM Keys

canonical_entities: diplomatic and defense networks in Ukraine
retrieved_context.text: Secret Blizzard, the Russian FSB’s Center 16, has escalated global espionage by co-opting C2 infrastructures of at least six threat actors—including Pakistan-based Storm-0156, Hazel Sandstorm and Storm-0473—to install backdoors (CrimsonRAT, Wainscot), deploy custom payloads (TwoDash downloader, MiniPocket fetcher), a TinyTurla variant disguised as a Windows service, and the Statuezy clipboard-monitoring trojan via DLL sideloading and batch files; this cross-actor compromise secured persistent access to diplomatic and defense networks in Ukraine, Afghanistan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and GDI, and Indian military institutions, enabling exfiltration of politically sensitive intelligence and advanced research data while reducing development overhead and underscoring the need for robust supply-chain security, network segmentation and proactive vulnerability management.
retrieved_context.title: Hackers with Russian Blizzard Steal Data from Rival Networks

canonical_entities: Remote Code Execution via ms-msdt URI in Word/RTF documents
ms-msdt URI-based RCE in Word/RTF documents
retrieved_context.text: In late May 2022, Symantec identified multiple threat actors exploiting the MSDT Follina bug (CVE-2022-30190) through ms-msdt URI-based RCE in Word/RTF documents that load a malicious HTML via Word’s remote template feature to launch msdt.exe, sdiagnhost.exe and ultimately PowerShell—bypassing the need for macros—to install a digitally signed AsyncRAT remote access Trojan that performs anti-analysis checks, collects hardware IDs, user names, execution paths and OS details, and maintains C&C communications, alongside parallel deployments of a browser infostealer targeting cookies and saved credentials in Firefox, Chrome and Edge. Symantec customers should apply Microsoft’s advisories or disable the ms-msdt handler, update Symantec Endpoint definitions (File-based-Downloader-Backdoor:Async, InfoStealer) and monitor for related IOCs to thwart these rapid, damaging campaigns.
retrieved_context.title: Attackers Exploit MSDT Follina Bug to Drop RAT, Infostealer | Symantec Enterprise Blogs

retrieved_context.text: In August 2019 Dragos and SecureWorks detailed a protracted (since April 2018) campaign by the Lyceum/Hexane threat group targeting Middle East critical infrastructure with straightforward but effective tactics: initial password‐spraying and brute‐force attacks on corporate email accounts, followed by spear-phishing from compromised internal accounts to executives, HR and IT staff using malicious Excel macros that deploy the DanBot RAT; once inside, operators run PoshC2-sourced PowerShell scripts—Decrypt-RDCMan.ps1 to extract RDCMan-stored passwords and Get-LAPSP.ps1 to harvest Active Directory credentials via LDAP—enabling environment reconnaissance and lateral movement. Despite its reliance on common techniques rather than novel malware or zero-days, Lyceum’s persistence highlights the urgency of enforcing multi-factor authentication, disabling macros, monitoring for unauthorized PowerShell/PoshC2 activity and training high-value users to detect spear-phishing, thereby mitigating the group’s primary objective of information collection before any potential pivot into OT/ICS environments.
retrieved_context.title: Lyceum/Hexane Threat Group Uses Common Hacking Tactics

canonical_entities: Session token extraction from device memory
extract session tokens from device memory
exposed 35,879,455 customers’ usernames, hashed passwords, names, contact details, last four SSN digits, dates of birth and security Q&A
retrieved_context.text: Since at least August 2023, threat actors have exploited CVE-2023-4966 (CitrixBleed), a 7.5-rated flaw in Citrix NetScaler ADC and Gateway, culminating in an October 16–19 breach at Comcast Xfinity that exposed 35,879,455 customers’ usernames, hashed passwords, names, contact details, last four SSN digits, dates of birth and security Q&A; despite Citrix’s October 10 patch and Comcast’s claim of prompt mitigation, attackers used publicly available proofs-of-concept and rumored Python automation scripts to extract session tokens from device memory, hijack active sessions and bypass authentication, a tactic linked by ReliaQuest to at least five threat groups including LockBit; this incident highlights the necessity not only of timely patching and reboots but also of invalidating all active and persistent session tokens, enforcing multi-factor authentication, resetting credentials and maintaining continuous 24x7 monitoring to prevent further data exfiltration and ransomware deployment.
retrieved_context.title: Comcast Xfinity Breached via CitrixBleed; 35M Customers Affected

retrieved_context.text: The North Korea-linked threat actor Slow Pisces (also tracked as Jade Sleet, PUKCHONG, TraderTraitor, and UNC4899) has been conducting a multi-stage malware campaign targeting cryptocurrency developers via LinkedIn job opportunity lures since at least June 2024, leveraging trojanized Python and JavaScript projects hosted on GitHub that employ YAML deserialization and EJS templating to execute gated payloads only to validated targets meeting specific criteria (IP address, geolocation, time, HTTP headers); the campaign delivers RN Loader and RN Stealer malware on macOS systems capable of harvesting system metadata, installed applications, SSH keys, AWS/Kubernetes/Google Cloud configuration files, and iCloud Keychain data, with payloads remaining memory-resident and deployed selectively to prevent analysis; Slow Pisces is assessed to be responsible for the February 2025 Bybit cryptocurrency exchange breach and operates alongside other North Korean clusters including Operation Dream Job, Contagious Interview, Alluring Pisces, and Moonstone Sleet, though with notably superior operational security practices involving heavily guarded payload delivery across infection stages.
retrieved_context.title: Crypto Developers Targeted by Python Malware Disguised as Coding Challenges

retrieved_context.text: Symantec’s Threat Hunter Team has linked the newly discovered Sidewalk loader backdoor—an evolution of the Crosswalk/Backdoor.Motnug family—to Grayfly (aka GREF/Wicked Panda), a China-linked espionage group active since March 2017 that employs custom backdoors, Trojan.Chattak, Cobalt Strike, web shells and credential-dumpers against telecom, IT, media and finance targets in Taiwan, Vietnam, the US and Mexico; in a recent campaign they exploited public-facing Microsoft Exchange and MySQL servers via commodity and zero-day flaws to execute Base64-encoded PowerShell commands through certutil, install an ASPX web shell in the ClientAccess\ecp directory, deploy Sidewalk via installutil.exe, create persistence with WMIC-launched scheduled tasks, then run a custom Mimikatz variant (SHA256 b3eb783b017da32e33d19670b39eae0b11de8e983891dd4feb873d6e9333608d) to harvest credentials—all within about an hour before ceasing observable activity; three Chengdu 404 executives were indicted in 2020 for attacks on over 100 organizations, highlighting Grayfly’s persistence and underscoring the need to promptly patch Exchange and MySQL servers, monitor anomalous PowerShell and scheduled-task activity, and deploy IOC-based detection to block Sidewalk and related tools.
retrieved_context.title: Grayfly: Chinese Threat Actor Uses Newly-discovered Sidewalk Malware | Symantec Enterprise Blogs

retrieved_context.text: During a recent incident, a LockBit affiliate conducted initial intrusions using gpresult for policy dumping, Cobalt Strike loaders and PsExec for privilege escalation, followed by reconnaissance (whoami, netstat, quser, net view), lateral movement, persistence via a new user account, and data exfiltration over FTP with Wput; when deployment of LockBit (SHA256 079b99f6…) was blocked on the target network, the attacker pivoted to a newly observed Rust-written ransomware family dubbed 3AM (SHA256 307a1217…), which appends “.threeamtime” to encrypted files, stops over 100 security and backup services via net stop and wbadmin/bcdedit/wmic commands, deletes Volume Shadow copies with vssadmin.exe delete shadows /all /quiet, and drops a Tor‐accessible ransom note requiring a 32-character “-k” access key and offering decryption/mystical-themed extortion; although 3AM encryption succeeded on only one of three attempted hosts, its Conti-style “-m” (local/net) and “-h” parameters, heavy service-termination payload, and aggressive VSS wipe underscore its potential as a fallback vector—defenders should update Symantec/Broadcom signatures, monitor for the .threeamtime extension, suspicious Rust binaries, command-line flags “-k” and “-m”, and mass service stoppage activity, and block associated IOCs (185.202.0[.]111, 212.18.104[.]6, 85.159.229[.]62) to mitigate future 3AM use.
retrieved_context.title: 3AM: New Ransomware Family Used As Fallback in Failed LockBit Attack | Symantec Enterprise Blogs

hits.text: A zero-day VPN vulnerability provided initial access for a sophisticated threat actor who employed publicly available penetration‐testing and exploitation tools—SoftPerfect Network Scanner for network discovery, PsExec to deploy ServeManager.exe (the FiveHands ransomware variant using lattice-based NTRUEncrypt public key cryptography), and SombRAT for remote information theft—alongside RouterScan, grabff.exe, rclone.exe, and s3browser-9-5-3.exe to harvest credentials and exfiltrate data. Once inside, the attacker leveraged Windows Management Instrumentation (T1047) to enumerate and delete Volume Shadow Copies (Inhibit System Recovery, T1490), encrypted files (including those in recovery folders) for impact (T1486), and dropped ransom notes across directories, demanding payment to restore access. Post-encryption activities align with MITRE techniques such as Access Token Manipulation, Boot or Logon Autostart, PowerShell command and scripting interpreter, Domain Trust Discovery, Process Discovery, Screen Capture, and Kerberoasting. The combined use of FiveHands ransomware and SombRAT RAT resulted in both data theft and destruction of backup artifacts, underscoring the need for proactive patch management, network segmentation, strict credential hygiene, and rapid incident response to mitigate novel lattice-based encryption threats.
hits.title: FiveHands Ransomware Overview

hits.text: On May 6, 2021, CISA disclosed that FiveHands ransomware actors exploited a zero-day VPN vulnerability for initial access, then used SoftPerfect Network Scanner for host discovery and PsExec to deploy ServeManager.exe (the NTRUEncrypt-based FiveHands payload) alongside SombRAT RAT, leveraging publicly available tools (RouterScan, grabff, rclone, s3browser) and PowerSploit modules for credential access, persistence, token manipulation, Kerberoasting, and exfiltration; once in place, FiveHands enumerated and deleted Volume Shadow Copies via WMI (T1490, T1047), encrypted recovery folders and user data (T1486), and dropped ransom notes across directories. The campaign caused direct financial losses (ransoms, legal fees, incident response, downtime, reputational harm) and exposed third-party partners. Mitigation hinges on patching/decommissioning unused VPN servers, enforcing MFA on remote and privileged accounts, maintaining up-to-date AV/OS, implementing robust backup and recovery routines, hunting for IoCs, and reinforcing employee training against phishing and malicious attachments.
hits.title: FiveHands Ransomware Overview

canonical_entities: Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Tools
hits.text: Trend Micro data shows BlackCat executed 39.3% of its 176 manufacturing detections against US targets and confirmed 173 leak-site compromises from December 2021 to September 2022—58.7% US-based—favoring finance, professional, legal, technology, energy, utilities, construction, and manufacturing sectors, with small (52%) and midsize (26%) businesses most targeted. Initial access was achieved via Exchange CVE-2021-26855/26857/26858/27065 exploits, ConnectWise RCE, and SSH key abuse. Execution leverages COBEACON to inject the Rust-based ransomware into ntoskrnl.exe, evading detection; defense evasion includes disabling AV, using AdFind/ADRecon/SoftPerfect, Process Hacker, Mimikatz, WMIC, Netstat, and LSASS credential dumping. Lateral movement exploits embedded PsExec, RDP, MobaXterm, and BITSAdmin transfers of zzz.exe/xxx.exe/yyy.exe/sv.exe. C2 communication uses Base64-encoded PowerShell with a Cobalt Strike SMB beacon over named pipes. Exfiltration employs ExMatter (upgraded September 2022), 7-Zip, Rclone, MEGASync, WinSCP, and FreeFileSync for double extortion. The payload defaces backgrounds, terminates backup/AV/DB/Internet/VM services, disables recovery (shadow copy deletion, safe-mode variant), and appends variable Sphynx extensions while avoiding critical directories and file types. BlackCat maps to MITRE ATT&CK T1190, T1078, T1562.001/009, T1003.001, T1021.002, T1486, T1490, T1489, T1048/T1567. Security teams should patch Exchange CVEs, secure MSP tools, enforce least privilege, segment networks, monitor PowerShell injections, and vet outbound file transfers to disrupt this evolving affiliate-driven operation.
hits.title: Ransomware Spotlight: BlackCat | Trend Micro (US)

canonical_entities: installing Sagerunex variants in the Windows Registry
hits.text: The Lotus Blossom APT (aka Lotus Panda, Billbug, Spring Dragon) has stepped up cyberespionage against APAC government targets by deploying new Sagerunex backdoor variants and abusing Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) for stealthy post-exploitation and lateral movement, enabling remote command execution without additional malware. Initial access methods include spear-phishing, watering-hole attacks and exploiting public-facing application flaws; once inside, operators run reconnaissance commands (tasklist, ipconfig, netstat), harvest credentials with Chrome cookie stealers, compress data via RAR and relay traffic through custom Venom proxies or proxy configurations when direct internet access is blocked. Persistence is achieved by installing Sagerunex variants in the Windows Registry under hijacked service names (tapisrv, swprv) to auto-launch at startup, while command-and-control blends encrypted traffic into legitimate platforms—stolen data uploaded as .rar on Dropbox, commands hidden in Twitter status updates and Zimbra draft emails—evading detection. Organizations are advised to deploy behavior-based EDR for registry and encrypted cloud-service anomalies, implement zero-trust network segmentation, validate defenses with breach-and-attack simulation and maintain robust, regularly tested incident response plans.
hits.title: Lotus Blossom APT Exploits WMI for Post-Exploitation Activities

hits.text: Water Ouroboros is a Ransomware-as-a-Service operation that exploits public-facing Oracle WebLogic vulnerabilities (CVE-2019-2725, CVE-2017-10271, CVE-2019-2729) or drive-by installers for initial access (T1190, T1189), then executes remote Windows commands (wmic.exe, bcdedit.exe, wbadmin.exe, vssadmin.exe) to delete backups and disable recovery (T1490, T1562.001) before encrypting fixed, removable and network drives via a Go-based custom routine that uses RTLGenRandom to generate a symmetric key, protects it with embedded RSA public keys (App_ExportKey), appends “.locked” (unless suppressed with –E), excludes over 60 file extensions, and accepts credentials (c {user}:{pass}), logging (–a), non-aggressive (–A) and size filters (–m). Victims find Contact Us.txt ransom notes pointing to a TOR payment site and Hive Leaks data-dump threat. Post-infection, actors maintain access via compromised admin accounts (T1078), disable security tools (PCHunter, ProcessHacker), dump credentials from registry hives (T1003.002), move laterally over RDP/SMB (T1021.001/002), discover assets via AdFind (T1595.002) and exfiltrate data over C&C (SharpRhino RAT/T1071.001, T1041). With 136 incidents in the US and notable impacts on construction, IT, manufacturing and healthcare SMBs, the campaign underscores the need for timely patching, hardened public-facing apps, least-privilege access, MFA, robust backups and advanced threat detection.
hits.title: Ransomware Spotlight: Water Ouroboros | Trend Micro (US)

hits.text: In mid-2022 Sophos reported that 66% of healthcare organizations were hit by ransomware—a 94% year-over-year increase—underscoring the continued success of the RaaS model and the emergence of Quantum ransomware, a splinter group from Conti (originally Quantum Locker, AstroLocker, MountLocker and XingLocker) officially taken over by Conti Team Two in April 2022; since June 2022 Quantum has deployed its BazarCall variant “Jormungandr,” leveraging OSINT, spamming, design and call-center specialists to execute callback phishing that tricks victims into installing legitimate remote-access tools, while DFIR reports show initial access via IcedID payloads embedded in mountable ISO files and malicious LNK shortcuts, leading to hands-on-keyboard activity within two hours, rapid Cobalt Strike and RDP lateral movement, WMI and PsExec to push the ttsel.exe ransomware payload, encryption and exfiltration, and the dropping of README_TO_DECRYPT.html notes with demands ranging from $150K to $500K; Quantum’s brand-impersonation phishing campaigns (masquerading as Oracle, CrowdStrike and others) have compromised a New Jersey behavioral‐health system, Interim Healthcare, a biopharmaceutical research firm and an IVF clinic in Delhi, exposing high-value patient data and demonstrating the urgent need for proactive defenses—including call-back phishing awareness, tight remote-access policies, IcedID and Cobalt Strike detection, LSASS memory monitoring and rapid incident response—to thwart these fast, socially engineered RaaS attacks.
hits.title: An In-Depth Look at Quantum Ransomware

hits.text: Between April and August 2023, the newly emerged Akira ransomware group targeted 107 organizations—predominantly SMBs in North America (85.9%) and France (53.1% of detections), with additional impacts in the United States and Turkey—surging from just three recorded attempts in May to 508 in June; operators gain initial access via compromised VPN credentials (including exploitation of CVE-2023-20269 on Cisco ASA/FTD), employ third-party tools such as PCHunter, PowerTool, AdFind, Advanced IP Scanner and MASSCAN for defense evasion and discovery, dump credentials with Mimikatz and LaZagne, and establish persistence by creating new domain accounts, then move laterally via RDP, exfiltrate data through RClone, FTP clients (FileZilla, WinSCP), AnyDesk, Radmin, Cloudflare Tunnel, MobaXterm, RustDesk or Ngrok, and encrypt data using a hybrid ChaCha20/RSA scheme—avoiding system directories and common extensions, deleting shadow copies, and appending .akira to files before dropping akira_readme.txt—and to mitigate this threat organizations should prioritize patching and virtual patching of vulnerable VPN appliances, enforce multifactor authentication and least-privilege access, monitor anomalous use of administration and reconnaissance tools, implement comprehensive backup and recovery procedures, and deploy layered endpoint, network and email defenses with behavior-based detection.
hits.title: Ransomware Spotlight: Akira | Trend Micro (US)

hits.text: NCC Group’s RIFT team has tracked a previously unknown extortion actor, SnapMC, which conducts sub-30-minute data breach attacks—eschewing ransomware to steal and threaten to publicly leak data unless victims pay—by scanning for and exploiting public-facing vulnerabilities (notably CVE-2019-18935 in Telerik UI and SQL injection) to deploy a reverse shell, executing reconnaissance via PowerShell (whoami, wmic, net users), occasionally leveraging privilege-escalation scripts such as Invoke-Nightmare and JuicyPotato, then collecting data with 7zip and Invoke-SQLcmd before exfiltrating compressed CSVs to cloud storage via the MinIO client (mc.exe) configured through config.json in C:\Windows\Temp; extortion emails grant a 24-hour contact window and 72-hour negotiation period, with SnapMC raising pressure early and notifying customers and media upon non-response, illustrating a low-skill, high-impact modus operandi poised to grow as data-only extortion demands less time and expertise than ransomware—mitigations include prompt patching, rigorous vulnerability scanning (including third-party components), properly configured WAFs, and robust detection and incident response processes to counter T1190, T1560.001 and T1567.002 techniques.
hits.title: SnapMC skips ransomware, steals data | NCC Group

hits.text: Since at least August 2021, the Yanluowang ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) operation has targeted U.S. financial firms and other sectors—including manufacturing, IT services, consultancy, and engineering—using a toolkit and playbook that mirror veteran groups Thieflock and Fivehands and suggesting possible affiliate ties; Symantec’s Threat Hunter Team first observed an underdeveloped October 2021 deployment in which attackers used AdFind for Active Directory reconnaissance, then refined their approach with PowerShell-driven BazarLoader implants, registry-based RDP enablement, ConnectWise for persistent access, and SoftPerfect Network Scanner for lateral movement, followed by credential theft via KeeThief, custom secretdump.exe, and deployment of Cobalt Strike Beacon, culminating in file encryption and double-extortion ransom notes threatening DDoS, employee calls, repeated attacks, and data deletion if law enforcement or negotiation firms are engaged; this operation contributes to the $590 million in ransomware payments recorded in 2021 and 314 global double-extortion incidents in October alone, underscoring the need for hardened Active Directory security, RDP restrictions, EDR with credential-dump detection, network monitoring for AdFind and BazarLoader activity, and adherence to FBI/CISA incident response recommendations.
hits.title: An In-Depth Look at Yanluowang Ransomware

canonical_entities: Supply Chain Compromise: Compromise Software Supply Chain
hits.text: In late 2023, researchers uncovered a sophisticated Taiwan-focused espionage operation in which a China-linked APT actor (likely APT27) hijacked an abandoned Sogou Zhuyin Windows update server—vacated when Sogou ceased Zhuyin support in mid-2022—and weaponized it to distribute a trojanized updater (SHA-256: 3f5c…) that deployed a custom backdoor and Cobalt Strike beacon via HTTP(S) (MITRE T1195.002, T1071.001). Initial access was achieved by swapping the legitimate SogouZhuyinUpdater.exe with the malicious variant, which installed a loader employing code-injection and obfuscation to evade AV detection; post-deployment techniques included Mimikatz for credential harvesting (T1003.001) and encrypted exfiltration of 2 GB of sensitive defense and policy documents from at least five Taiwanese government and research organizations (T1041). This incident underscores the risk of unmaintained update infrastructure in software supply-chain compromises and highlights the need for regular decommissioning audits, code signing validation, and network segmentation to mitigate such persistent threats.
hits.title: Abandoned Sogou Zhuyin Update Server Hijacked, Weaponized in Taiwan Espionage Campaign

retrieved_context.text: In late 2023, researchers uncovered a sophisticated Taiwan-focused espionage operation in which a China-linked APT actor (likely APT27) hijacked an abandoned Sogou Zhuyin Windows update server—vacated when Sogou ceased Zhuyin support in mid-2022—and weaponized it to distribute a trojanized updater (SHA-256: 3f5c…) that deployed a custom backdoor and Cobalt Strike beacon via HTTP(S) (MITRE T1195.002, T1071.001). hits.text: NCC Group’s CIRT has tracked Karakurt as an extortion-focused threat actor exploiting single-factor FortiGate VPNs via legitimate Active Directory credentials to achieve initial access, with an average dwell time of just over one month due to living-off-the-land techniques and lack of malware. Although the exact privilege escalation method remains unclear, Karakurt has attempted CVE-2020-1472 (Zerologon) and attained domain-admin rights, then used PsExec and RDP for lateral movement to the primary domain controller. Early in the breach they execute an encoded PowerShell DNS zone export—generating Microsoft-Windows-DNS-Server-Service Event ID 3150—and extract NTDS.dit via Volume Shadow Copy for further credential harvesting. After a brief exit, they re-enter to deploy AnyDesk for persistence, archive sensitive files with 7-Zip, and likely exfiltrate data via Rclone to cloud hosts. NCC Group recommends immediate FortiGate VPN MFA implementation, critical patching of domain controllers, and monitoring for Event ID 3150, unauthorized AnyDesk or PsExec usage, and VPN pool host authentications (e.g., DESKTOP-XXXXXX) to detect potential Karakurt intrusions.

hits.text: Since early October 2023 Microsoft has tracked two North Korean nation-state actors, Diamond Sleet (ZINC) and Onyx Sleet (PLUTONIUM), exploiting CVE-2023-42793, a remote-code execution flaw in JetBrains TeamCity CI/CD servers, to opportunistically breach build environments and deploy tailored post-exploitation tooling for persistent access and credential theft. Diamond Sleet leveraged two distinct attack paths: first, PowerShell scripts to download Forest64.exe and an encrypted payload (using static key “uTYNkfKxHiZrx3KJ”) which, when decrypted, installs the ForestTiger backdoor via a scheduled task and dumps LSASS memory; second, DLL search-order hijacking with malicious DSROLE.dll loaded by wsmprovhost.exe (RollSling) to deobfuscate and launch PE payloads in memory (e.g., wksprt.exe for C2) and Version.dll loaded by clip.exe (FeedLoad) which uses a readme.md XOR key to deploy a remote access trojan and spawns iexpress.exe, followed by additional LSASS dumps. Onyx Sleet, after exploiting the same flaw, creates a fake “krtbgt” admin account, executes system discovery commands, stops the TeamCity service, and deploys a PowerShell-downloaded proxy tool (HazyLoad) via temp.exe and ADFSbginetmgr.exe to maintain C2, uses RDP for lateral movement, and harvests credentials from LSASS and browsers. JetBrains has released patches and mitigations, and Microsoft urges organizations to apply updates, use provided IOCs and Defender Antivirus (detecting ForestTiger, RollSling, FeedLoad, HazyLoad), enable cloud-delivered protection, Safe DLL Search Mode and attack surface reduction rules, block identified IPs, isolate and credential-reset compromised hosts, and hunt for related activity with Microsoft 365 Defender, Defender Vulnerability Management, Defender for Endpoint alerts, and Sentinel TI mapping.
hits.title: Multiple North Korean threat actors exploiting the TeamCity CVE-2023-42793 vulnerability | Microsoft Security Blog

hits.text: Dragos researchers, in collaboration with Ukraine’s CSSC, unearthed FrostyGoop—an ICS-specific malware first spotted in April and used in January to disrupt central heating in over 600 Lviv apartment buildings—marking the first known malware to leverage Modbus TCP for read/write operations on operational technology. Attackers gained initial access in April 2023 by exploiting a MikroTik router vulnerability, deployed a webshell on the router’s web server, and maintained persistence via Tor and L2TP tunnels to Moscow-based IPs. After spending months conducting reconnaissance, they extracted credentials by dumping the SAM registry hive in December, then directly issued scripted Modbus commands—read from a JSON configuration file—to publicly exposed ENCO heating controllers, even downgrading firmware to disable monitoring and force inaccurate measurements that halted heating services for nearly two days amid subzero temperatures. This incident underscores the threat posed by internet-exposed ICS devices—over 46,000 globally using Modbus—and highlights poor network segmentation, unpatched ICS CVEs, and the ease with which FrostyGoop’s protocol-agnostic payload can be repurposed against diverse industrial controllers, necessitating immediate network segmentation, firmware monitoring, and patch management in OT environments.
hits.title: ICS malware FrostyGoop disrupted heating in Ukraine, remains threat to OT worldwide

hits.text: The SnapMC group, newly identified by NCC Group, uses its mc.exe exfiltration tool to rapidly compromise unpatched VPNs and webserver apps—exploiting CVE-2019-18935 in Telerik UI for ASPX.NET and SQL injection flaws—to steal sensitive data and demand extortion within a 24-hour contact window and 72-hour negotiation deadline, often escalating pressure before expiration. Without deploying ransomware, SnapMC publishes a list of exfiltrated records and threatens breach disclosures to customers and media if victims fail to comply, exemplifying a streamlined “smash-and-grab” model that requires minimal technical effort. Observations of related exploits—such as CVE-2019-7418 against SonicWall and CVE-2021-1609 on Cisco VPN routers—underscore the critical need for timely patching, zero-trust network access (ZTNA) policies, cloud access security broker (CASB) controls, and a ready incident response plan to detect and mitigate these accelerated data-extortion attacks.

Attackers gained initial access in April 2023 by exploiting a MikroTik router vulnerability, deployed a webshell on the router’s web server, and maintained persistence via Tor and L2TP tunnels to Moscow-based IPs. After spending months conducting reconnaissance, they extracted credentials by dumping the SAM registry hive in December, then directly issued scripted Modbus commands—read from a JSON configuration file—to publicly exposed ENCO heating controllers, even downgrading firmware to disable monitoring and force inaccurate measurements that halted heating services for nearly two days amid subzero temperatures. retrieved_context.text: The SnapMC group, newly identified by NCC Group, uses its mc.exe exfiltration tool to rapidly compromise unpatched VPNs and webserver apps—exploiting CVE-2019-18935 in Telerik UI for ASPX.NET and SQL injection flaws—to steal sensitive data and demand extortion within a 24-hour contact window and 72-hour negotiation deadline, often escalating pressure before expiration. hits.text: Microsoft has traced a stealthy espionage campaign by Flax Typhoon (aka Ethereal Panda), a China-based nation-state actor active since mid-2021, targeting dozens of Taiwanese organizations (with spill-over in Southeast Asia, North America, and Africa) by exploiting known vulnerabilities in public-facing VPN, web, Java, and SQL services to deploy the China Chopper web shell for initial access; the group escalates privileges via open-source exploits like Juicy Potato and BadPotato, then establishes persistence by disabling RDP network-level authentication, hijacking the Sticky Keys (sethc.exe) binary to launch Task Manager as SYSTEM, and installing a renamed SoftEther VPN-over-HTTPS bridge (conhost.exe/dllhost.exe) as a service to maintain covert C2 over port 443; leveraging LOLBins such as PowerShell Invoke-WebRequest, certutil, bitsadmin, WinRM, and WMIC for lateral movement, vulnerability scanning, and remote execution, it harvests credentials from LSASS memory and the SAM registry hive using Mimikatz for pass-the-hash attacks; although no exfiltration or final objectives have been observed, organizations are urged to enforce rigorous patch and vulnerability management on internet-exposed systems, monitor registry and file-integrity changes, deploy web application firewalls, reset compromised credentials, isolate and forensically examine affected hosts, and leverage detections in Microsoft 365 Defender to disrupt living-off-the-land tactics.

hits.text: In late 2023, researchers uncovered a sophisticated Taiwan-focused espionage operation in which a China-linked APT actor (likely APT27) hijacked an abandoned Sogou Zhuyin Windows update server—vacated when Sogou ceased Zhuyin support in mid-2022—and weaponized it to distribute a trojanized updater (SHA-256: 3f5c…) that deployed a custom backdoor and Cobalt Strike beacon via HTTP(S) (MITRE T1195.002, T1071.001). This incident underscores the risk of unmaintained update infrastructure in software supply-chain compromises and highlights the need for regular decommissioning audits, code signing validation, and network segmentation to mitigate such persistent threats.

hits.text: After a year-long investigation researchers at Lumen’s Black Lotus Labs dissected the Ngioweb botnet—first observed in 2017—which uses a loader network and roughly 15 n-day exploits to deploy malware that contacts C2 domains generated via a domain generation algorithm (augmented by DNS TXT records to resist sinkholing), evaluates device traffic capacity, and links compromised Zyxel, Reolink, Alpha Technologies and, increasingly, Netgear routers (now 10 % of bots) to over 180 “backconnect” C2 nodes that provide at least 80 % of the 35,000 residential proxies in the NSOCKS[.]net service across 180 countries; NSOCKS’s lack of authentication and appearance on free proxy lists has enabled cybercriminals to carry out DDoS amplification, credential stuffing, phishing and malware proxying (e.g., Agent Tesla), while APT28 state-sponsored actors have mixed espionage with criminal traffic on the same infrastructure. To disrupt both operations, Lumen, alongside The ShadowServer Foundation and other partners, is actively blocking traffic to known C2 nodes and publishing indicators of compromise to help organizations identify and remediate infected devices.

hits.text: Following the sale of INC ransomware source code in March 2024 and its initial appearance in August 2023, researchers in July 2024 uncovered Lynx ransomware, a Windows-only, C++-based RaaS variant that shares ~48% of INC’s functions (70.8% among common routines) and has been deployed against U.S. and U.K. retail, real estate, architecture, financial and environmental service firms via phishing, malicious downloads and underground forums; employing AES-128-CTR and Curve25519 Donna for encryption with a .lynx extension, it conducts double-extortion by exfiltrating victims’ data (published on lynxblog[.]net under a policy excluding governments, hospitals and non-profits) before encrypting all files by default—killing processes, encrypting network shares and hidden disks, deleting shadow copies and backups, leveraging the Restart Manager API to target in-use files, and printing a OneNote report—then dropping a README.txt ransom note; this evolution of RaaS underscores the need for organizations to adopt robust cybersecurity measures, including anti-phishing training, backup hardening, dynamic and behavioral detections via Palo Alto Networks’ Cortex XDR Anti-Ransomware and Advanced WildFire, and vigilant monitoring of Indicators of Compromise such as published SHA256 hashes to mitigate high-profile, code-reused ransomware campaigns.
hits.title: Lynx Ransomware: A Rebranding of INC Ransomware

canonical_entities: Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Tools
OS Credential Dumping: Security Account Manager
hits.text: Water Ouroboros is a Ransomware-as-a-Service operation that exploits public-facing Oracle WebLogic vulnerabilities (CVE-2019-2725, CVE-2017-10271, CVE-2019-2729) or drive-by installers for initial access (T1190, T1189), then executes remote Windows commands (wmic.exe, bcdedit.exe, wbadmin.exe, vssadmin.exe) to delete backups and disable recovery (T1490, T1562.001) before encrypting fixed, removable and network drives via a Go-based custom routine that uses RTLGenRandom to generate a symmetric key, protects it with embedded RSA public keys (App_ExportKey), appends “.locked” (unless suppressed with –E), excludes over 60 file extensions, and accepts credentials (c {user}:{pass}), logging (–a), non-aggressive (–A) and size filters (–m). Victims find Contact Us.txt ransom notes pointing to a TOR payment site and Hive Leaks data-dump threat. Post-infection, actors maintain access via compromised admin accounts (T1078), disable security tools (PCHunter, ProcessHacker), dump credentials from registry hives (T1003.002), move laterally over RDP/SMB (T1021.001/002), discover assets via AdFind (T1595.002) and exfiltrate data over C&C (SharpRhino RAT/T1071.001, T1041). With 136 incidents in the US and notable impacts on construction, IT, manufacturing and healthcare SMBs, the campaign underscores the need for timely patching, hardened public-facing apps, least-privilege access, MFA, robust backups and advanced threat detection.
hits.title: Ransomware Spotlight: Water Ouroboros | Trend Micro (US)

hits.text: Russia’s APT29 (aka Cozy Bear/Nobelium) has been exploiting a critical unauthenticated remote-code-execution flaw in JetBrains TeamCity (CVE-2023-42793, CVSS 9.8) since September—shortly after JetBrains issued a patch and Rapid7 published a proof-of-concept—to gain initial access to SDLC management servers, escalate privileges, move laterally, deploy stealthy backdoors that persist through updates, and potentially manipulate build pipelines or insert malicious updates in SolarWinds-style supply-chain attacks; CISA, FBI, NSA and international partners warn that around 800 internet-exposed instances remain vulnerable (with uncounted internally reachable servers also at risk), and that North Korea’s Lazarus and Andariel groups have similarly weaponized the same flaw, prompting Fortinet to report multi-actor post-exploit techniques in live incidents; mitigation guidance urges immediate upgrading to TeamCity 2023.05.4, removal of public exposure, comprehensive IoC-based threat hunting across servers and build agents, and full compromise assessments to eradicate entrenched backdoors.
hits.title: Global TeamCity Exploitation Opens Door to SolarWinds-Style Nightmare

canonical_entities: installing Sagerunex variants in the Windows Registry
hits.text: The Lotus Blossom APT (aka Lotus Panda, Billbug, Spring Dragon) has stepped up cyberespionage against APAC government targets by deploying new Sagerunex backdoor variants and abusing Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) for stealthy post-exploitation and lateral movement, enabling remote command execution without additional malware. Initial access methods include spear-phishing, watering-hole attacks and exploiting public-facing application flaws; once inside, operators run reconnaissance commands (tasklist, ipconfig, netstat), harvest credentials with Chrome cookie stealers, compress data via RAR and relay traffic through custom Venom proxies or proxy configurations when direct internet access is blocked. Persistence is achieved by installing Sagerunex variants in the Windows Registry under hijacked service names (tapisrv, swprv) to auto-launch at startup, while command-and-control blends encrypted traffic into legitimate platforms—stolen data uploaded as .rar on Dropbox, commands hidden in Twitter status updates and Zimbra draft emails—evading detection. Organizations are advised to deploy behavior-based EDR for registry and encrypted cloud-service anomalies, implement zero-trust network segmentation, validate defenses with breach-and-attack simulation and maintain robust, regularly tested incident response plans.
hits.title: Lotus Blossom APT Exploits WMI for Post-Exploitation Activities

canonical_entities: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Windows Command Shell
hits.text: NCC Group’s RIFT team uncovered a sophisticated new FiveHands ransomware variant deployed by an affiliate linked to UNC2447, who gained initial access in June 2021 by exploiting a SonicWall VPN appliance—evidenced by a “command0/Commando” login from source port 4444 (Metasploit default)—then moved laterally via RDP (T1021.001) using the weak password “Remark123!” and PsExec (T1059.003). The actor leveraged publicly available tools—SoftPerfect Netscan and Advanced Port Scanner for network discovery (T1046), AllInOnePasswordRecoveryPro for credential harvesting (T1003.001), Remote Utilities (“Hostclean.exe”) for persistent C2 (T1219), and pCloud (“pCloud.exe”) for exfiltration (T1567.002), caching 10 GB of stolen data under %AppData%\pCloud\CacheCached—to stage and extract sensitive files. The Go-written loader (“Encryptor.exe”) accepts a 16-byte key (captured via RDP bitmap cache and brute force) to decrypt a unique C++ ransomware payload in memory, which uses RSA/AES (Mbed TLS) to encrypt files in blocks (.crypt/.crypt) while excluding system folders and leveraging Windows Restart Manager to breach locked files. This RaaS model (hijacking hardcoded TOR IDs) employs aggressive extortion tactics—spoofed caller ID calls urging prompt payment—and underscores the need for robust VPN log monitoring, RDP restrictions, enforceable command-line auditing, multi-factor authentication, and forensic examination of cloud‐sync caches to detect and mitigate similar intrusions.
hits.title: Handy guide to a new Fivehands ransomware variant

canonical_entities: enumerates SSH directories to harvest credentials
Persistence is achieved through multiple cronjobs
hits.text: Aqua Security’s Nautilus team has uncovered Hadooken, a new Linux malware targeting Oracle WebLogic servers via weak passwords. Post-compromise, attackers deploy redundant shell and Python scripts to ensure download and execution of Hadooken, which enumerates SSH directories to harvest credentials, moves laterally, and clears logs. Hadooken then drops a three-path cryptominer and a Tsunami backdoor with a randomized name, the latter reserved for potential later-stage attacks. Persistence is achieved through multiple cronjobs under varied names and frequencies stored across cron directories. The malware is hosted on two IPs—one German address linked to TeamTNT and Gang 8220, the other inactive in Russia—where researchers also identified a Mallox ransomware PowerShell loader targeting Windows. Static analysis links Hadooken to Rhombus and NoEscape families. With over 230,000 internet-connected WebLogic instances—hundreds of which expose vulnerable admin consoles—this campaign underscores the dual risk of cryptojacking and ransomware across Linux and Windows environments.
hits.title: New 'Hadooken' Linux Malware Targets WebLogic Servers - SecurityWeek

hits.text: ESET researchers have retrospectively identified WinorDLL64.dll—a backdoor payload for the Wslink loader (WinorLoaderDLL64.dll) first uncovered in 2021—that operates as an in-memory server using MemoryModule and is protected by Oreans Code Virtualizer; although the initial compromise vector remains unknown, sparse detections in Central Europe, North America and the Middle East and a South Korean VirusTotal submission triggered YARA alerts based on its unique filename. Communicating over the loader’s established AES-256-CBC encrypted TCP channel, WinorDLL64 implements at least 16 commands—including comprehensive system profiling, secure file exfiltration, overwrite and deletion, process and RDP session management, unrestricted PowerShell execution, directory compression for data theft, and connection latency measurement—facilitating reconnaissance, persistence and lateral movement. Low-confidence attribution to North Korea–aligned Lazarus (HIDDEN COBRA) derives from targeting of South Korean victims, shared VS2010 LTCG build signatures and code/behavior overlap with 2018 GhostSecret (FE887FCAB66D7D7F79F05E0266C0649F0114BA7C) and Bankshot implants; this underscores Lazarus’s organized, modular arsenal and highlights the need to detect anomalous in-memory loaders and encrypted session anomalies.
hits.title: WinorDLL64: A backdoor from the vast Lazarus arsenal?

hits.text: A zero-day VPN vulnerability provided initial access for a sophisticated threat actor who employed publicly available penetration‐testing and exploitation tools—SoftPerfect Network Scanner for network discovery, PsExec to deploy ServeManager.exe (the FiveHands ransomware variant using lattice-based NTRUEncrypt public key cryptography), and SombRAT for remote information theft—alongside RouterScan, grabff.exe, rclone.exe, and s3browser-9-5-3.exe to harvest credentials and exfiltrate data. Once inside, the attacker leveraged Windows Management Instrumentation (T1047) to enumerate and delete Volume Shadow Copies (Inhibit System Recovery, T1490), encrypted files (including those in recovery folders) for impact (T1486), and dropped ransom notes across directories, demanding payment to restore access. Post-encryption activities align with MITRE techniques such as Access Token Manipulation, Boot or Logon Autostart, PowerShell command and scripting interpreter, Domain Trust Discovery, Process Discovery, Screen Capture, and Kerberoasting. The combined use of FiveHands ransomware and SombRAT RAT resulted in both data theft and destruction of backup artifacts, underscoring the need for proactive patch management, network segmentation, strict credential hygiene, and rapid incident response to mitigate novel lattice-based encryption threats.
hits.title: FiveHands Ransomware Overview

canonical_entities: harvest subscriber location, billing and communications metadata
hits.text: On Sept. 25, 2024, the Wall Street Journal disclosed that the Chinese state-sponsored APT Salt Typhoon has stealthily infiltrated multiple U.S. cable and broadband ISPs—likely via firmware and supply-chain compromises in core networking gear—to establish long-term persistence, harvest subscriber location, billing and communications metadata for espionage, and pre-position disruptive capabilities against federal, military and Fortune 100 users; this campaign, echoing Volt Typhoon’s telecom backdoors, Flax Typhoon’s 200,000-device IoT botnet, Brass Typhoon’s cross-domain implants and Mustang Panda’s telco intrusions, signals a shift from surveillance to offensive “blink-the-lights” or infrastructure-crippling attacks in a Taiwan contingency, driving urgent recommendations for carriers to enforce threat-intelligence sharing, secure firmware, tighten supply-chain controls and bolster routing security.
hits.title: China's 'Salt Typhoon' Cooks Up Cyberattacks on US ISPs
