hits.text: After a year-long investigation researchers at Lumen’s Black Lotus Labs dissected the Ngioweb botnet—first observed in 2017—which uses a loader network and roughly 15 n-day exploits to deploy malware that contacts C2 domains generated via a domain generation algorithm (augmented by DNS TXT records to resist sinkholing), evaluates device traffic capacity, and links compromised Zyxel, Reolink, Alpha Technologies and, increasingly, Netgear routers (now 10 % of bots) to over 180 “backconnect” C2 nodes that provide at least 80 % of the 35,000 residential proxies in the NSOCKS[.]net service across 180 countries; NSOCKS’s lack of authentication and appearance on free proxy lists has enabled cybercriminals to carry out DDoS amplification, credential stuffing, phishing and malware proxying (e.g., Agent Tesla), while APT28 state-sponsored actors have mixed espionage with criminal traffic on the same infrastructure. To disrupt both operations, Lumen, alongside The ShadowServer Foundation and other partners, is actively blocking traffic to known C2 nodes and publishing indicators of compromise to help organizations identify and remediate infected devices.
hits.title: Botnet fueling residential proxies disrupted in cybercrime crackdown

hits.text: Symantec’s Threat Hunter Team has linked the newly discovered Sidewalk loader backdoor—an evolution of the Crosswalk/Backdoor.Motnug family—to Grayfly (aka GREF/Wicked Panda), a China-linked espionage group active since March 2017 that employs custom backdoors, Trojan.Chattak, Cobalt Strike, web shells and credential-dumpers against telecom, IT, media and finance targets in Taiwan, Vietnam, the US and Mexico; in a recent campaign they exploited public-facing Microsoft Exchange and MySQL servers via commodity and zero-day flaws to execute Base64-encoded PowerShell commands through certutil, install an ASPX web shell in the ClientAccess\ecp directory, deploy Sidewalk via installutil.exe, create persistence with WMIC-launched scheduled tasks, then run a custom Mimikatz variant (SHA256 b3eb783b017da32e33d19670b39eae0b11de8e983891dd4feb873d6e9333608d) to harvest credentials—all within about an hour before ceasing observable activity; three Chengdu 404 executives were indicted in 2020 for attacks on over 100 organizations, highlighting Grayfly’s persistence and underscoring the need to promptly patch Exchange and MySQL servers, monitor anomalous PowerShell and scheduled-task activity, and deploy IOC-based detection to block Sidewalk and related tools.
hits.title: Grayfly: Chinese Threat Actor Uses Newly-discovered Sidewalk Malware | Symantec Enterprise Blogs

hits.text: Since its emergence in 2013, Iran-linked APT35 (aka Charming Kitten/Phosphorus) has executed a series of high-value espionage campaigns—beginning with a 2014 social-media spying operation—and continued in 2019 with spear-phishing against U.S., French and Middle East academic institutions before Microsoft’s Digital Crimes Unit seized control of 99 APT35 domains; in late 2020 the group targeted oncology, genetics and neurology researchers in Israel and the U.S. via its “BadBlood” PDF-based spear-phishing campaign, while in 2021 it chained Exchange Server flaws (ProxyShell) for network intrusion and demonstrated TTP overlaps with Momento ransomware (CVE-2021-21972 exploiter); in January 2022 it performed mass Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228) scans—over 80 percent of attempts originated in the U.S.—and later deployed a stealthy .NET-based PowerShell backdoor (“PowerLess”) that runs in-process to avoid detection, followed by Hyperscrape, a Windows .NET mailbox exfiltration tool for Outlook, Gmail and Yahoo! that quietly harvests emails once the actor possesses valid credentials or session cookies, and a companion Telegram dump utility; APT35 maintains persistence for intelligence collection or monetizes access when systems lack strategic value, underscoring the need for timely patching, multi-factor authentication and continuous monitoring.
hits.title: An In-Depth Look at APT35 aka Charming Kitten

hits.text: Microsoft’s research exposes the BadPilot campaign—a multiyear initial-access subgroup of Russian GRU-aligned Seashell Blizzard active since at least 2021—that has opportunistically scanned for and exploited Internet-facing vulnerabilities (CVE-2021-34473 Exchange, CVE-2022-41352 Zimbra, CVE-2023-32315 OpenFire, CVE-2023-42793 TeamCity, CVE-2023-23397 Outlook, CVE-2024-1709 ConnectWise ScreenConnect, CVE-2023-48788 FortiClient EMS and various JBOSS flaws) to compromise a globally diverse set of high-value sectors (energy, oil and gas, telecommunications, shipping, arms manufacturing and government). Following initial access, BadPilot employs stealthy persistence, credential harvesting, lateral movement and common tools such as Cobalt Strike and DarkCrystalRAT to sustain footholds and support tailored network operations, including at least three destructive cyberattacks in Ukraine since 2023. After focusing on Ukraine, Europe, Central/South Asia and the Middle East during 2021–2023, the subgroup scaled horizontally into the United States, United Kingdom, Canada and Australia in early 2024, reflecting Russia’s evolving strategic objectives and underscoring the urgency of patching Internet-facing services, implementing comprehensive logging and anomaly detection, and applying threat-informed incident-response practices to disrupt its operational lifecycle.
hits.title: The BadPilot campaign: Seashell Blizzard subgroup conducts multiyear global access operation | Microsoft Security Blog

canonical_entities: Remote Code Execution via ms-msdt URI in Word/RTF documents
ms-msdt URI-based RCE in Word/RTF documents
hits.text: In late May 2022, Symantec identified multiple threat actors exploiting the MSDT Follina bug (CVE-2022-30190) through ms-msdt URI-based RCE in Word/RTF documents that load a malicious HTML via Word’s remote template feature to launch msdt.exe, sdiagnhost.exe and ultimately PowerShell—bypassing the need for macros—to install a digitally signed AsyncRAT remote access Trojan that performs anti-analysis checks, collects hardware IDs, user names, execution paths and OS details, and maintains C&C communications, alongside parallel deployments of a browser infostealer targeting cookies and saved credentials in Firefox, Chrome and Edge. Symantec customers should apply Microsoft’s advisories or disable the ms-msdt handler, update Symantec Endpoint definitions (File-based-Downloader-Backdoor:Async, InfoStealer) and monitor for related IOCs to thwart these rapid, damaging campaigns.
hits.title: Attackers Exploit MSDT Follina Bug to Drop RAT, Infostealer | Symantec Enterprise Blogs

canonical_entities: Launch EC2 instances across regions via VPN
hits.text: Unit42’s “EleKtra-Leak” campaign, active since December 2020, uses automated scripts to clone public GitHub repos every few minutes, extract exposed AWS IAM keys within five minutes, then—if not blocked by GitHub-AWS quarantine policies—execute rapid AWS reconnaissance (DescribeRegions), create security groups, and launch hundreds of EC2 instances across regions via VPN for Monero cryptojacking, generating over 400 API calls in seven minutes. Between Aug. 30 and Oct. 6, 2023, researchers tracked 474 actor-controlled miners. The actor employs custom mining software and blocklists high-profile AWS account IDs to avoid honey traps. Leveraging the Prisma Cloud HoneyCloud project’s ephemeral key leaks and policy overrides, Unit42 obtained full visibility, informing Prisma Cloud Secrets Security, CI/CD IaC scanning, Cortex XDR, and recommendations for independent repo scanning, strict IAM policies, and continuous monitoring.
hits.title: CloudKeys in the Air: Tracking Malicious Operations of Exposed IAM Keys

hits.text: Our GReAT team uncovered Operation ForumTroll—a state-sponsored APT campaign targeting Russian media, academic and government personnel—delivering previously unknown malware via phishing emails masquerading as Primakov Readings invitations containing two malicious links; clicking either on a Windows PC using Chrome or any Chromium-based browser silently triggers a zero-day exploit (CVE-2025-2783), exploiting a logic flaw at the Chrome-Windows interface to bypass the browser’s sandbox and deploy the payload without further user interaction. We promptly reported the vulnerability to Google, which released a patch in Chrome version 134.0.6998.177/178; while the phishing links now redirect to the legitimate forum site and the campaign is dormant, the attackers could reactivate it at any time. To mitigate this espionage threat, organizations should ensure all Chrome instances are updated to at least 134.0.6998.177/.178, deploy robust exploit detection and prevention solutions on internet-connected devices, and maintain vigilant phishing awareness and monitoring.
hits.title: CVE-2025-2783 in Operation ForumTroll APT

canonical_entities: diplomatic and defense networks in Ukraine
hits.text: Secret Blizzard, the Russian FSB’s Center 16, has escalated global espionage by co-opting C2 infrastructures of at least six threat actors—including Pakistan-based Storm-0156, Hazel Sandstorm and Storm-0473—to install backdoors (CrimsonRAT, Wainscot), deploy custom payloads (TwoDash downloader, MiniPocket fetcher), a TinyTurla variant disguised as a Windows service, and the Statuezy clipboard-monitoring trojan via DLL sideloading and batch files; this cross-actor compromise secured persistent access to diplomatic and defense networks in Ukraine, Afghanistan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and GDI, and Indian military institutions, enabling exfiltration of politically sensitive intelligence and advanced research data while reducing development overhead and underscoring the need for robust supply-chain security, network segmentation and proactive vulnerability management.
hits.title: Hackers with Russian Blizzard Steal Data from Rival Networks

retrieved_context.text: In August 2025 Microsoft Threat Intelligence revealed that Storm-2460, associated with the Play ransomware group, has resumed exploiting CVE-2025-29824—a zero-day elevation-of-privilege flaw in the Windows Common Log File System patched in April—to gain SYSTEM privileges on unpatched hosts across IT, financial and real estate organizations in the US, Europe, South America and the Middle East. The campaign begins with an in-memory dropper masquerading as the open-source ChatGPT Desktop app that decrypts and launches PipeMagic, a modular backdoor first observed in December 2022 and now updated with persistence and lateral-movement enhancements targeting Saudi Arabian and Brazilian manufacturing entities. PipeMagic communicates with its TCP C2 over a named pipe, self-updates by storing distinct payload modules in memory via doubly linked lists for staging, execution and communication (plus an additional dynamic list), then leverages the CLFS exploit to escalate privileges before deploying Play ransomware. Although the campaign’s footprint remains limited, the combination of a zero-day exploit and a sophisticated modular backdoor underscores a heightened risk; organizations are urged to immediately apply the April patch for CVE-2025-29824, enable tamper and network protection in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, run EDR in block mode, enforce full automated investigation and remediation, and leverage cloud-delivered machine-learning protections to block novel variants.
retrieved_context.title: PipeMagic Backdoor Resurfaces as Part of Play Ransomware Attack Chain

retrieved_context.text: In April 2025, Microsoft patched 121 vulnerabilities—including CVE-2025-29824, the sole flaw exploited by PipeMagic—an evolution of a backdoor first spotted in December 2022 during a RansomExx campaign against Southeast Asian industrial firms via CVE-2017-0144 and resurfaced in September 2024 in the Middle East using a Rust-based fake ChatGPT loader (Tauri/Tokio) that decrypts AES-encrypted shellcode, resolves APIs via FNV-1a hashing, relocates imports and invokes its entry point. PipeMagic generates random 16-byte named pipes (“\\.\\pipe\\1.<hex>”) alongside a 127.0.0.1:8082 TCP interface, downloads plugins from a Cloud Azure domain (aaaaabbbbbbb.eastus.cloudapp.azure[.]com) and supports modules such as an I/O-completion-port communication plugin (handling file I/O commands) and a loader for injecting 64-bit payloads via DllRegisterService. In January 2025, new campaigns in Brazil and the Middle East introduced a Microsoft Help Index File loader executed through MSBuild that RC4-decrypts shellcode (key 4829468622e6b82ff056e3c945dd99c94a1f0264d980774828aadda326b775e5) via EnumDeviceMonitor and a GoogleUpdate.dll hijack variant performing AES-CBC decryption (key 9C3BA5B2D3222FE5863C14D51340D7F9, IV 221BA50915042098AF5F8EE40E5559C8) to deploy the same 32-bit backdoor PE. Joint analysis with BI.ZONE reveals a shift toward multi-staged, encrypted loaders and diversified access vectors, underscoring the need to restrict MSBuild use, monitor DLL hijacking, inspect named-pipe and localhost traffic, and block suspicious Azure domains to mitigate PipeMagic’s adaptive tactics.
retrieved_context.title: PipeMagic in 2025: How the backdoor operators’ tactics have changed

retrieved_context.text: After a year-long investigation researchers at Lumen’s Black Lotus Labs dissected the Ngioweb botnet—first observed in 2017—which uses a loader network and roughly 15 n-day exploits to deploy malware that contacts C2 domains generated via a domain generation algorithm (augmented by DNS TXT records to resist sinkholing), evaluates device traffic capacity, and links compromised Zyxel, Reolink, Alpha Technologies and, increasingly, Netgear routers (now 10 % of bots) to over 180 “backconnect” C2 nodes that provide at least 80 % of the 35,000 residential proxies in the NSOCKS[.]net service across 180 countries; NSOCKS’s lack of authentication and appearance on free proxy lists has enabled cybercriminals to carry out DDoS amplification, credential stuffing, phishing and malware proxying (e.g., Agent Tesla), while APT28 state-sponsored actors have mixed espionage with criminal traffic on the same infrastructure. To disrupt both operations, Lumen, alongside The ShadowServer Foundation and other partners, is actively blocking traffic to known C2 nodes and publishing indicators of compromise to help organizations identify and remediate infected devices.
retrieved_context.title: Botnet fueling residential proxies disrupted in cybercrime crackdown

canonical_entities: exploiting known vulnerabilities in public-facing VPN, web, Java, and SQL services
harvests credentials from LSASS memory and the SAM registry hive
hits.text: Microsoft has traced a stealthy espionage campaign by Flax Typhoon (aka Ethereal Panda), a China-based nation-state actor active since mid-2021, targeting dozens of Taiwanese organizations (with spill-over in Southeast Asia, North America, and Africa) by exploiting known vulnerabilities in public-facing VPN, web, Java, and SQL services to deploy the China Chopper web shell for initial access; the group escalates privileges via open-source exploits like Juicy Potato and BadPotato, then establishes persistence by disabling RDP network-level authentication, hijacking the Sticky Keys (sethc.exe) binary to launch Task Manager as SYSTEM, and installing a renamed SoftEther VPN-over-HTTPS bridge (conhost.exe/dllhost.exe) as a service to maintain covert C2 over port 443; leveraging LOLBins such as PowerShell Invoke-WebRequest, certutil, bitsadmin, WinRM, and WMIC for lateral movement, vulnerability scanning, and remote execution, it harvests credentials from LSASS memory and the SAM registry hive using Mimikatz for pass-the-hash attacks; although no exfiltration or final objectives have been observed, organizations are urged to enforce rigorous patch and vulnerability management on internet-exposed systems, monitor registry and file-integrity changes, deploy web application firewalls, reset compromised credentials, isolate and forensically examine affected hosts, and leverage detections in Microsoft 365 Defender to disrupt living-off-the-land tactics.
hits.title: Flax Typhoon using legitimate software to quietly access Taiwanese organizations | Microsoft Security Blog

hits.text: A zero-day VPN vulnerability provided initial access for a sophisticated threat actor who employed publicly available penetration‐testing and exploitation tools—SoftPerfect Network Scanner for network discovery, PsExec to deploy ServeManager.exe (the FiveHands ransomware variant using lattice-based NTRUEncrypt public key cryptography), and SombRAT for remote information theft—alongside RouterScan, grabff.exe, rclone.exe, and s3browser-9-5-3.exe to harvest credentials and exfiltrate data. Once inside, the attacker leveraged Windows Management Instrumentation (T1047) to enumerate and delete Volume Shadow Copies (Inhibit System Recovery, T1490), encrypted files (including those in recovery folders) for impact (T1486), and dropped ransom notes across directories, demanding payment to restore access. Post-encryption activities align with MITRE techniques such as Access Token Manipulation, Boot or Logon Autostart, PowerShell command and scripting interpreter, Domain Trust Discovery, Process Discovery, Screen Capture, and Kerberoasting. The combined use of FiveHands ransomware and SombRAT RAT resulted in both data theft and destruction of backup artifacts, underscoring the need for proactive patch management, network segmentation, strict credential hygiene, and rapid incident response to mitigate novel lattice-based encryption threats.
hits.title: FiveHands Ransomware Overview

canonical_entities: bypasses the Mark of the Web
attack surface reduction rules to block Office-spawned child processes
hits.text: Microsoft’s August 2023 Patch Tuesday addressed two actively exploited zero-days—CVE-2023-36884, a remote code execution flaw in Microsoft Office that bypasses the Mark of the Web, and CVE-2023-38180, a .NET/Visual Studio vulnerability enabling DDoS attacks without requiring user privileges—after one was publicly disclosed pre-patch. The Russian actor Storm-0978 (aka RomCom/Underground), noted for Industrial Spy ransomware, leveraged crafted Office documents to execute payloads and extort victims, while CVE-2023-38180 attacks demand only network proximity. To mitigate these threats, Microsoft released an Office Defense-in-Depth update and a .NET/Visual Studio patch and recommends deploying both Office and Windows August updates, enabling cloud-delivered protection in Defender Antivirus, activating EDR block mode, enforcing attack surface reduction rules to block Office-spawned child processes, and applying the advisory’s update for CVE-2023-38180. Avertium validates these controls, provides IoCs for RomCom campaigns, and advocates continuous vulnerability management and its Fusion MXDR for Microsoft service to detect suspicious Office-to-script execution chains and remediate artifacts proactively.
hits.title: Flash Notice: Two Microsoft Zero-Day Vulnerabilities Exploited by Attackers

canonical_entities: Lorenz ransomware group exploiting CVE-2022-29499 against Mitel MiVoice Connect
harvested local and domain admin credentials
hits.text: In mid-2022, Arctic Wolf researchers discovered the Lorenz ransomware group exploiting CVE-2022-29499, a remote code execution flaw in Mitel MiVoice Connect VoIP appliances disclosed in April and patched in July, to gain an initial reverse shell. Once inside, the attackers used the compromised Mitel Service Appliance’s CLI to create a hidden directory, download and rename the Golang-based Chisel tunneling tool via Wget, and establish a fast TCP/UDP SOCKS proxy over HTTP (skipping TLS verification) to evade firewalls. After lying dormant for nearly a month and deploying a “pdf_import_export.php” web shell for persistence, they harvested local and domain admin credentials, moved laterally via RDP to a domain controller, exfiltrated data via FileZilla for double-extortion, and encrypted ESXi hosts using BitLocker and Lorenz ransomware. Targeting primarily US SMBs (with outliers in China and Mexico), this campaign underscores the critical need for timely patching of IoT/VoIP devices, comprehensive asset discovery and hardening, network segmentation, and robust PowerShell and module logging with centralized log management.
hits.title: Lorenz Ransomware Goes After SMBs via Mitel VoIP Phone Systems

canonical_entities: Session token extraction from device memory
extract session tokens from device memory
exposed 35,879,455 customers’ usernames, hashed passwords, names, contact details, last four SSN digits, dates of birth and security Q&A
hits.text: Since at least August 2023, threat actors have exploited CVE-2023-4966 (CitrixBleed), a 7.5-rated flaw in Citrix NetScaler ADC and Gateway, culminating in an October 16–19 breach at Comcast Xfinity that exposed 35,879,455 customers’ usernames, hashed passwords, names, contact details, last four SSN digits, dates of birth and security Q&A; despite Citrix’s October 10 patch and Comcast’s claim of prompt mitigation, attackers used publicly available proofs-of-concept and rumored Python automation scripts to extract session tokens from device memory, hijack active sessions and bypass authentication, a tactic linked by ReliaQuest to at least five threat groups including LockBit; this incident highlights the necessity not only of timely patching and reboots but also of invalidating all active and persistent session tokens, enforcing multi-factor authentication, resetting credentials and maintaining continuous 24x7 monitoring to prevent further data exfiltration and ransomware deployment.
hits.title: Comcast Xfinity Breached via CitrixBleed; 35M Customers Affected

hits.text: Since at least 2015, Mandiant has identified APT42—an IRGC-linked Iranian state-sponsored threat actor also known as APT35—conducting over 30 spear-phishing operations across 14 countries against government officials, policymakers, journalists, academics and dissidents, evolving tactics from 2020 Oxford vaccinologist-themed pharmaceutical lures to 2021 fake interview requests using compromised U.S. media accounts for 37-day MFA-intercepting credential harvesting, and February 2022 phishes posing as a British news agency targeting political science professors; beyond credential theft via shortened URLs and PDF attachments directing victims to spoofed login portals, APT42 deploys custom Android spyware—spread via SMS links to messaging/VPN apps—to exfiltrate calls, SMS, audio recordings, images and GPS data in real time, while on Windows it employs lightweight custom malware for initial access, privilege escalation, reconnaissance, lateral movement through follow-on phishing, and persistence via scheduled tasks and registry keys; Mandiant further correlates APT42’s TTPs with November 2021 PHOSPHORUS BitLocker ransomware attempts against Fortinet FortiOS SSL VPN and unpatched Exchange servers, highlighting the group’s multi-platform espionage-to-ransom capabilities and real-world threat to high-value targets.
hits.title: New Iranian hacking group APT42 deploys custom Android spyware

canonical_entities: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Windows Command Shell
hits.text: NCC Group’s RIFT team uncovered a sophisticated new FiveHands ransomware variant deployed by an affiliate linked to UNC2447, who gained initial access in June 2021 by exploiting a SonicWall VPN appliance—evidenced by a “command0/Commando” login from source port 4444 (Metasploit default)—then moved laterally via RDP (T1021.001) using the weak password “Remark123!” and PsExec (T1059.003). The actor leveraged publicly available tools—SoftPerfect Netscan and Advanced Port Scanner for network discovery (T1046), AllInOnePasswordRecoveryPro for credential harvesting (T1003.001), Remote Utilities (“Hostclean.exe”) for persistent C2 (T1219), and pCloud (“pCloud.exe”) for exfiltration (T1567.002), caching 10 GB of stolen data under %AppData%\pCloud\CacheCached—to stage and extract sensitive files. The Go-written loader (“Encryptor.exe”) accepts a 16-byte key (captured via RDP bitmap cache and brute force) to decrypt a unique C++ ransomware payload in memory, which uses RSA/AES (Mbed TLS) to encrypt files in blocks (.crypt/.crypt) while excluding system folders and leveraging Windows Restart Manager to breach locked files. This RaaS model (hijacking hardcoded TOR IDs) employs aggressive extortion tactics—spoofed caller ID calls urging prompt payment—and underscores the need for robust VPN log monitoring, RDP restrictions, enforceable command-line auditing, multi-factor authentication, and forensic examination of cloud‐sync caches to detect and mitigate similar intrusions.

retrieved_context.text: After a year-long investigation researchers at Lumen’s Black Lotus Labs dissected the Ngioweb botnet—first observed in 2017—which uses a loader network and roughly 15 n-day exploits to deploy malware that contacts C2 domains generated via a domain generation algorithm (augmented by DNS TXT records to resist sinkholing), evaluates device traffic capacity, and links compromised Zyxel, Reolink, Alpha Technologies and, increasingly, Netgear routers (now 10 % of bots) to over 180 “backconnect” C2 nodes that provide at least 80 % of the 35,000 residential proxies in the NSOCKS[.]net service across 180 countries; NSOCKS’s lack of authentication and appearance on free proxy lists has enabled cybercriminals to carry out DDoS amplification, credential stuffing, phishing and malware proxying (e.g., Agent Tesla), while APT28 state-sponsored actors have mixed espionage with criminal traffic on the same infrastructure. To disrupt both operations, Lumen, alongside The ShadowServer Foundation and other partners, is actively blocking traffic to known C2 nodes and publishing indicators of compromise to help organizations identify and remediate infected devices.
retrieved_context.title: Botnet fueling residential proxies disrupted in cybercrime crackdown

canonical_entities: exploiting known vulnerabilities in public-facing VPN, web, Java, and SQL services
harvests credentials from LSASS memory and the SAM registry hive
retrieved_context.text: Microsoft has traced a stealthy espionage campaign by Flax Typhoon (aka Ethereal Panda), a China-based nation-state actor active since mid-2021, targeting dozens of Taiwanese organizations (with spill-over in Southeast Asia, North America, and Africa) by exploiting known vulnerabilities in public-facing VPN, web, Java, and SQL services to deploy the China Chopper web shell for initial access; the group escalates privileges via open-source exploits like Juicy Potato and BadPotato, then establishes persistence by disabling RDP network-level authentication, hijacking the Sticky Keys (sethc.exe) binary to launch Task Manager as SYSTEM, and installing a renamed SoftEther VPN-over-HTTPS bridge (conhost.exe/dllhost.exe) as a service to maintain covert C2 over port 443; leveraging LOLBins such as PowerShell Invoke-WebRequest, certutil, bitsadmin, WinRM, and WMIC for lateral movement, vulnerability scanning, and remote execution, it harvests credentials from LSASS memory and the SAM registry hive using Mimikatz for pass-the-hash attacks; although no exfiltration or final objectives have been observed, organizations are urged to enforce rigorous patch and vulnerability management on internet-exposed systems, monitor registry and file-integrity changes, deploy web application firewalls, reset compromised credentials, isolate and forensically examine affected hosts, and leverage detections in Microsoft 365 Defender to disrupt living-off-the-land tactics.
retrieved_context.title: Flax Typhoon using legitimate software to quietly access Taiwanese organizations | Microsoft Security Blog

retrieved_context.text: A zero-day VPN vulnerability provided initial access for a sophisticated threat actor who employed publicly available penetration‐testing and exploitation tools—SoftPerfect Network Scanner for network discovery, PsExec to deploy ServeManager.exe (the FiveHands ransomware variant using lattice-based NTRUEncrypt public key cryptography), and SombRAT for remote information theft—alongside RouterScan, grabff.exe, rclone.exe, and s3browser-9-5-3.exe to harvest credentials and exfiltrate data. Once inside, the attacker leveraged Windows Management Instrumentation (T1047) to enumerate and delete Volume Shadow Copies (Inhibit System Recovery, T1490), encrypted files (including those in recovery folders) for impact (T1486), and dropped ransom notes across directories, demanding payment to restore access. Post-encryption activities align with MITRE techniques such as Access Token Manipulation, Boot or Logon Autostart, PowerShell command and scripting interpreter, Domain Trust Discovery, Process Discovery, Screen Capture, and Kerberoasting. The combined use of FiveHands ransomware and SombRAT RAT resulted in both data theft and destruction of backup artifacts, underscoring the need for proactive patch management, network segmentation, strict credential hygiene, and rapid incident response to mitigate novel lattice-based encryption threats.
retrieved_context.title: FiveHands Ransomware Overview

canonical_entities: bypasses the Mark of the Web
attack surface reduction rules to block Office-spawned child processes
retrieved_context.text: Microsoft’s August 2023 Patch Tuesday addressed two actively exploited zero-days—CVE-2023-36884, a remote code execution flaw in Microsoft Office that bypasses the Mark of the Web, and CVE-2023-38180, a .NET/Visual Studio vulnerability enabling DDoS attacks without requiring user privileges—after one was publicly disclosed pre-patch. The Russian actor Storm-0978 (aka RomCom/Underground), noted for Industrial Spy ransomware, leveraged crafted Office documents to execute payloads and extort victims, while CVE-2023-38180 attacks demand only network proximity. To mitigate these threats, Microsoft released an Office Defense-in-Depth update and a .NET/Visual Studio patch and recommends deploying both Office and Windows August updates, enabling cloud-delivered protection in Defender Antivirus, activating EDR block mode, enforcing attack surface reduction rules to block Office-spawned child processes, and applying the advisory’s update for CVE-2023-38180. Avertium validates these controls, provides IoCs for RomCom campaigns, and advocates continuous vulnerability management and its Fusion MXDR for Microsoft service to detect suspicious Office-to-script execution chains and remediate artifacts proactively.
retrieved_context.title: Flash Notice: Two Microsoft Zero-Day Vulnerabilities Exploited by Attackers

canonical_entities: Lorenz ransomware group exploiting CVE-2022-29499 against Mitel MiVoice Connect
harvested local and domain admin credentials
retrieved_context.text: In mid-2022, Arctic Wolf researchers discovered the Lorenz ransomware group exploiting CVE-2022-29499, a remote code execution flaw in Mitel MiVoice Connect VoIP appliances disclosed in April and patched in July, to gain an initial reverse shell. Once inside, the attackers used the compromised Mitel Service Appliance’s CLI to create a hidden directory, download and rename the Golang-based Chisel tunneling tool via Wget, and establish a fast TCP/UDP SOCKS proxy over HTTP (skipping TLS verification) to evade firewalls. After lying dormant for nearly a month and deploying a “pdf_import_export.php” web shell for persistence, they harvested local and domain admin credentials, moved laterally via RDP to a domain controller, exfiltrated data via FileZilla for double-extortion, and encrypted ESXi hosts using BitLocker and Lorenz ransomware. Targeting primarily US SMBs (with outliers in China and Mexico), this campaign underscores the critical need for timely patching of IoT/VoIP devices, comprehensive asset discovery and hardening, network segmentation, and robust PowerShell and module logging with centralized log management.
retrieved_context.title: Lorenz Ransomware Goes After SMBs via Mitel VoIP Phone Systems

canonical_entities: Launch EC2 instances across regions via VPN
retrieved_context.text: Unit42’s “EleKtra-Leak” campaign, active since December 2020, uses automated scripts to clone public GitHub repos every few minutes, extract exposed AWS IAM keys within five minutes, then—if not blocked by GitHub-AWS quarantine policies—execute rapid AWS reconnaissance (DescribeRegions), create security groups, and launch hundreds of EC2 instances across regions via VPN for Monero cryptojacking, generating over 400 API calls in seven minutes. Between Aug. 30 and Oct. 6, 2023, researchers tracked 474 actor-controlled miners. The actor employs custom mining software and blocklists high-profile AWS account IDs to avoid honey traps. Leveraging the Prisma Cloud HoneyCloud project’s ephemeral key leaks and policy overrides, Unit42 obtained full visibility, informing Prisma Cloud Secrets Security, CI/CD IaC scanning, Cortex XDR, and recommendations for independent repo scanning, strict IAM policies, and continuous monitoring.
retrieved_context.title: CloudKeys in the Air: Tracking Malicious Operations of Exposed IAM Keys

canonical_entities: Session token extraction from device memory
extract session tokens from device memory
exposed 35,879,455 customers’ usernames, hashed passwords, names, contact details, last four SSN digits, dates of birth and security Q&A
retrieved_context.text: Since at least August 2023, threat actors have exploited CVE-2023-4966 (CitrixBleed), a 7.5-rated flaw in Citrix NetScaler ADC and Gateway, culminating in an October 16–19 breach at Comcast Xfinity that exposed 35,879,455 customers’ usernames, hashed passwords, names, contact details, last four SSN digits, dates of birth and security Q&A; despite Citrix’s October 10 patch and Comcast’s claim of prompt mitigation, attackers used publicly available proofs-of-concept and rumored Python automation scripts to extract session tokens from device memory, hijack active sessions and bypass authentication, a tactic linked by ReliaQuest to at least five threat groups including LockBit; this incident highlights the necessity not only of timely patching and reboots but also of invalidating all active and persistent session tokens, enforcing multi-factor authentication, resetting credentials and maintaining continuous 24x7 monitoring to prevent further data exfiltration and ransomware deployment.
retrieved_context.title: Comcast Xfinity Breached via CitrixBleed; 35M Customers Affected

retrieved_context.text: Since at least 2015, Mandiant has identified APT42—an IRGC-linked Iranian state-sponsored threat actor also known as APT35—conducting over 30 spear-phishing operations across 14 countries against government officials, policymakers, journalists, academics and dissidents, evolving tactics from 2020 Oxford vaccinologist-themed pharmaceutical lures to 2021 fake interview requests using compromised U.S. media accounts for 37-day MFA-intercepting credential harvesting, and February 2022 phishes posing as a British news agency targeting political science professors; beyond credential theft via shortened URLs and PDF attachments directing victims to spoofed login portals, APT42 deploys custom Android spyware—spread via SMS links to messaging/VPN apps—to exfiltrate calls, SMS, audio recordings, images and GPS data in real time, while on Windows it employs lightweight custom malware for initial access, privilege escalation, reconnaissance, lateral movement through follow-on phishing, and persistence via scheduled tasks and registry keys; Mandiant further correlates APT42’s TTPs with November 2021 PHOSPHORUS BitLocker ransomware attempts against Fortinet FortiOS SSL VPN and unpatched Exchange servers, highlighting the group’s multi-platform espionage-to-ransom capabilities and real-world threat to high-value targets.
retrieved_context.title: New Iranian hacking group APT42 deploys custom Android spyware

canonical_entities: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Windows Command Shell
retrieved_context.text: NCC Group’s RIFT team uncovered a sophisticated new FiveHands ransomware variant deployed by an affiliate linked to UNC2447, who gained initial access in June 2021 by exploiting a SonicWall VPN appliance—evidenced by a “command0/Commando” login from source port 4444 (Metasploit default)—then moved laterally via RDP (T1021.001) using the weak password “Remark123!” and PsExec (T1059.003). The actor leveraged publicly available tools—SoftPerfect Netscan and Advanced Port Scanner for network discovery (T1046), AllInOnePasswordRecoveryPro for credential harvesting (T1003.001), Remote Utilities (“Hostclean.exe”) for persistent C2 (T1219), and pCloud (“pCloud.exe”) for exfiltration (T1567.002), caching 10 GB of stolen data under %AppData%\pCloud\CacheCached—to stage and extract sensitive files. The Go-written loader (“Encryptor.exe”) accepts a 16-byte key (captured via RDP bitmap cache and brute force) to decrypt a unique C++ ransomware payload in memory, which uses RSA/AES (Mbed TLS) to encrypt files in blocks (.crypt/.crypt) while excluding system folders and leveraging Windows Restart Manager to breach locked files. This RaaS model (hijacking hardcoded TOR IDs) employs aggressive extortion tactics—spoofed caller ID calls urging prompt payment—and underscores the need for robust VPN log monitoring, RDP restrictions, enforceable command-line auditing, multi-factor authentication, and forensic examination of cloud‐sync caches to detect and mitigate similar intrusions.

hits.text: In 2022 Magniber ransomware attacks accelerated from fewer than 20 monthly attempts in Q1 to a peak of 1,482 detections in September and 508 in December, with Trend Micro data showing Taiwan as the hardest-hit nation (204 attempts, ~76.1% of total), followed by South Korea (15), Australia (9), Turkey and Japan (6) and emerging targets beyond Asia; industry-wise education, government and manufacturing bore the brunt (987 detections), then healthcare and technology, with energy, transportation and real estate also affected. Attackers gain initial access via exploit kits and public-facing flaws—CVE-2016-0189, CVE-2018-8174, CVE-2019-1367, CVE-2020-0968, CVE-2021-26411, CVE-2021-40444, PrintNightmare (CVE-2021-34527) and CVE-2022-44698—delivering payloads through fake MSI and CPL installers, MSHTML/Regsvr32 proxy execution and Mark-of-the-Web bypass. They employ NtQuerySystemInformation for discovery, thread execution hijacking and process injection for defense evasion, UAC bypass via Fodhelper scripts that delete shadow copies, then encrypt files using AES per 1 MiB block and RSA-wrapped keys, inhibit recovery and append mutex-based extensions. Security teams should prioritize patching these CVEs, monitor anomalous Msiexec/Regsvr32 activity, script-based installers and registry modifications, and detect shadow-copy deletion or process injection to mitigate this streamlined yet potent ransomware chain.
hits.title: Ransomware Spotlight: Magniber | Trend Micro (US)

hits.text: Researchers have identified a new ransomware strain dubbed Magniber—an affiliate of both the Magnitude exploit kit and Cerber ransomware—exclusively targeting users in South Korea and the Asia-Pacific region following Magnitude’s reemergence on October 15, 2017, after a brief hiatus during which its Cerber distribution waned. FireEye and Trend Micro findings reveal that Magniber leverages malvertising and IE memory corruption vulnerability CVE-2016-0189 to deliver a binary payload encrypted in reverse RC4 with 30-byte keys, unpacks it in memory, then executes an AES-128 encryption routine that renames files with a “.ihsdj” extension before self-deletion. It employs a GetSystemDefaultUILanguage check to exit on non-Korean systems and generates four callback URLs via a 19-character pseudorandom string to evade virtual machines. Organizations should prioritize patching IE CVE-2016-0189, deploy ad blockers and updated exploit kit defenses, and monitor for Magnitude EK activity in APAC environments.
hits.title: New Magniber Ransomware Targets South Korea, Asia Pacific | Threatpost

hits.text: In late October 2022, Google’s Threat Analysis Group (TAG) discovered that North Korean government-backed actor APT37 was exploiting a never-before-seen Internet Explorer JScript engine vulnerability (CVE-2022-41128) via malicious Microsoft Office documents themed on the Itaewon Halloween tragedy to achieve arbitrary code execution on Windows hosts; the attack chain began when a user disabled Protected View on a Word document that fetched a remote RTF template hosting HTML rendered through IE, triggering a JIT optimization–induced type-confusion bug in jscript9.dll, which checked for a unique cookie to evade sandboxing, reported to its C2 infrastructure both pre- and post-exploit, and deployed a custom-hashed shellcode that cleared IE cache/history before downloading follow-on payloads; TAG reported the flaw to Microsoft on October 31 and a patch shipped on November 8, and defenders should ensure CVE-2022-41128 is remediated, monitor related IOCs (e.g., word-template[.]net, openxmlformat[.]org) and document hashes, and harden Office macro and remote-template protections against similar APT37 tactics.
hits.title: Internet Explorer 0-day exploited by North Korean actor APT37

hits.text: At least four distinct campaigns exploited CVE-2023-37580, a reflected XSS zero-day in Zimbra Collaboration Suite, to siphon emails, attachments, user credentials and authentication tokens from government organizations worldwide before the July 5 hotfix and July 25 official patch; in chronological order, unidentified actors targeted Greece on June 29 via malicious URLs that, when clicked during active Zimbra sessions, deployed a data-theft framework and auto-forward rules, Winter Vivern’s APT leveraged unique exploit links to hit Moldova and Tunisia between July 11 and 25, another group used a phishing-style XSS link in Vietnam to harvest webmail credentials and exfiltrate them to a compromised government domain, and on August 25 unknown attackers employed an N-day variant to steal tokens from Pakistan’s mail servers; Google’s Threat Analysis Group warns these campaigns underscore the urgency of promptly applying open-source fixes, hardening mail-server code to prevent XSS, and maintaining vigilant patch management as attackers continuously monitor public repositories for unpatched vulnerabilities.
hits.title: APTs Swarm Zimbra Zero-Day to Steal Government Info Worldwide

hits.text: Since January 2021, Google’s Threat Analysis Group (TAG) has tracked a government-backed North Korean campaign that leverages social engineering via X (formerly Twitter) and encrypted messaging apps to befriend security researchers and deliver malicious files containing at least one unpatched 0-day in a popular software package; upon exploitation the custom shellcode performs anti-virtual-machine checks, captures system data and screenshots, and exfiltrates them to C2 infrastructure (e.g., 23.106.215[.]105, www.blgbeach[.]com), with the latest vulnerability reported and patched on September 12, 2023 (see TAG’s published RCA). In parallel, the actors published a seemingly benign Windows tool called GetSymbol on GitHub (https://github.com/dbgsymbol/) that quietly downloads debugging symbols—and arbitrary code—from attacker domains, requiring full OS reinstalls for compromised hosts. TAG has added malicious sites to Safe Browsing, issued government-backed attacker alerts to targeted Gmail and Workspace users, and urges researchers to enable Enhanced Safe Browsing, keep software up to date, and verify system integrity after using third-party tools.
hits.title: Active North Korean campaign targeting security researchers

hits.text: Since late 2019, a hack-for-hire group recruited via Russian-language forums has conducted coordinated phishing campaigns against YouTube creators by posing as legitimate companies (e.g., VPNs, antivirus, photo editors, “Covid19 news” software) to deliver non-persistent cookie-theft malware (RedLine, Vidar, Predator The Thief, Nexus Stealer, Azorult, Raccoon, Grand Stealer, Vikro Stealer, Masad, Kantal, Sorano, AdamantiumThief) via fake landing pages on over 1,011 domains and forged social-media pages; upon infection they exfiltrate session cookies for channel hijack and resale ($3–$4,000 USD) or crypto-scam livestreams. In partnership with YouTube, Gmail, Trust & Safety, Cybercrime Investigation and Safe Browsing teams, Google’s Threat Analysis Group reduced related Gmail phishing by 99.6% since May 2021—blocking 1.6 M messages, warning 62 K users, blocking 2.4 K files and restoring ~4 K accounts—while observing a shift to email.cz, seznam.cz, post.cz and aol.com and messaging apps. Protections include heuristic email filters, Safe Browsing blocks, hardened authentication and channel recovery workflows; users are urged to heed Safe Browsing warnings, scan files via antivirus or VirusTotal, enable Enhanced Safe Browsing and enforce 2-Step Verification.
hits.title: Phishing campaign targets YouTube creators with cookie theft malware

hits.text: Last week Google’s Threat Analysis Group, in partnership with The Citizen Lab, exposed an in-the-wild exploit chain developed by the commercial surveillance vendor Intellexa in Egypt that leverages a man-in-the-middle injection on HTTP traffic to silently redirect targets first to c.betly[.]me and then to sec-flare[.]com, delivering Predator spyware without any user interaction; on iOS this chain combined Safari RCE (CVE-2023-41993), certificate validation bypass (CVE-2023-41991) and XNU kernel local privilege escalation (CVE-2023-41992) and was patched in iOS 16.7/17.0.1, while on Android initial Chrome renderer RCE (CVE-2023-4762), delivered via MITM or one-time links, was patched on September 5; this campaign highlights the serious risk posed by proliferating commercial spyware, underscores the urgency of enforcing universal HTTPS and enabling Chrome’s HTTPS-First Mode, and demonstrates the critical need for organizations and users to apply the latest OS and browser updates, deploy encrypted-traffic protections, and monitor for anomalous network redirects to mitigate future attacks.
hits.title: 0-days exploited by commercial surveillance vendor in Egypt

hits.text: In early September 2021, Google’s Threat Analysis Group exposed EXOTIC LILY, a financially motivated initial access broker linked to Russian gangs FIN12/WIZARD SPIDER that exploited Microsoft MSHTML CVE-2021-40444 before transitioning to delivering custom BazarLoader and a new “BUMBLEBEE” loader via ISO files with hidden DLLs and LNK shortcuts—identifiable by shared machine identifiers, unique command-line arguments and a “bumblebee” user-agent—to deploy Conti and Diavol ransomware. At its peak, EXOTIC LILY sent over 5,000 spear-phishing emails daily to 650 organizations across IT, cybersecurity, healthcare and other sectors, using human-operated TTPs such as TLD-switched domain and employee identity spoofing (leveraging AI-generated or harvested RocketReach/CrunchBase profiles), live chat to build trust, and legitimate file-sharing services (WeTransfer, TransferNow, OneDrive) to evade detection. Operators worked a standard 9-to-5 schedule in a Central/Eastern Europe timezone, customized business proposals, scheduled calls, and used WMI-based data collection in BUMBLEBEE to exfiltrate system details in JSON and fetch Cobalt Strike payloads. Overlaps with Microsoft’s DEV-0413 and Abnormal reporting confirm shared infrastructure, underscoring the need for enhanced domain/identity spoofing defenses, monitoring of file-sharing notifications, and threat hunting for ISO/LNK artifacts with unique metadata or “bumblebee” indicators.
hits.title: Exposing initial access broker with ties to Conti

hits.text: Google’s TAG disclosed that Charming Kitten (Iranian APT35) has been using a custom .NET Windows tool called HYPERSCRAPE—active since 2020—to siphon inbox data from fewer than two dozen Gmail, Yahoo! and Outlook accounts in Iran by leveraging hijacked or pre-obtained credentials; the tool validates connectivity via hardcoded/Base64-obfuscated C2s (e.g. 136.243.108.14, 173.209.51.54), spoofs an outdated browser UA to force basic HTML view, switches the account language to English, iteratively downloads emails as .eml files while preserving unread status, reverts language settings, deletes Google security alerts, and reports system metadata via HTTP POST without exfiltrating content, with early builds also offering an automated Google Takeout option using pipe communication; TAG re-secured compromised accounts, issued Government-Backed Attacker Warnings and published detection data—including numerous SHA-256 hashes for HYPERSCRAPE binaries and a related Live DLL—to aid defenders, and urges high-risk users to enroll in Google’s Advanced Protection Program and enable Enhanced Safe Browsing.
hits.title: New Iranian APT data extraction tool

hits.text: Google’s Threat Analysis Group (TAG) has observed a 33% year-over-year increase in government-backed phishing warnings—over 50,000 sent to users so far in 2021—driven in part by a large APT28 (Fancy Bear) campaign and sustained by ongoing operations from Iran-aligned APT35. Since early 2021, APT35 has compromised a UK university website to host a phishing kit targeting Gmail, Yahoo and Hotmail credentials—including second-factor codes—and continues its credential harvesting campaigns against government, academia, journalism and NGOs using hijacked sites and link-shortening redirects. In May 2020 it attempted to distribute spyware disguised as a VPN on Google Play Store (blocked before installation) and has pursued similar Android C2 apps on other platforms. The group also impersonates conference officials (e.g., Munich Security, T20 Italy) to initiate phishing, embedding JavaScript to relay visitor IP, user-agent and locale via Telegram bots—a tactic TAG disrupted by reporting the bots. TAG’s layered defenses include batch-sent warnings, Workspace admin alerts, Safe Browsing domain blocks and urging high-risk users to enable two-factor authentication or enroll in Advanced Protection.
hits.title: Countering threats from Iran

In partnership with YouTube, Gmail, Trust & Safety, Cybercrime Investigation and Safe Browsing teams, Google’s Threat Analysis Group reduced related Gmail phishing by 99.6% since May 2021—blocking 1.6 M messages, warning 62 K users, blocking 2.4 K files and restoring ~4 K accounts—while observing a shift to email.cz, seznam.cz, post.cz and aol.com and messaging apps. Protections include heuristic email filters, Safe Browsing blocks, hardened authentication and channel recovery workflows; users are urged to heed Safe Browsing warnings, scan files via antivirus or VirusTotal, enable Enhanced Safe Browsing and enforce 2-Step Verification.
retrieved_context.title: Phishing campaign targets YouTube creators with cookie theft malware

retrieved_context.text: Last week Google’s Threat Analysis Group, in partnership with The Citizen Lab, exposed an in-the-wild exploit chain developed by the commercial surveillance vendor Intellexa in Egypt that leverages a man-in-the-middle injection on HTTP traffic to silently redirect targets first to c.betly[.]me and then to sec-flare[.]com, delivering Predator spyware without any user interaction; on iOS this chain combined Safari RCE (CVE-2023-41993), certificate validation bypass (CVE-2023-41991) and XNU kernel local privilege escalation (CVE-2023-41992) and was patched in iOS 16.7/17.0.1, while on Android initial Chrome renderer RCE (CVE-2023-4762), delivered via MITM or one-time links, was patched on September 5; this campaign highlights the serious risk posed by proliferating commercial spyware, underscores the urgency of enforcing universal HTTPS and enabling Chrome’s HTTPS-First Mode, and demonstrates the critical need for organizations and users to apply the latest OS and browser updates, deploy encrypted-traffic protections, and monitor for anomalous network redirects to mitigate future attacks.
retrieved_context.title: 0-days exploited by commercial surveillance vendor in Egypt

retrieved_context.text: In early September 2021, Google’s Threat Analysis Group exposed EXOTIC LILY, a financially motivated initial access broker linked to Russian gangs FIN12/WIZARD SPIDER that exploited Microsoft MSHTML CVE-2021-40444 before transitioning to delivering custom BazarLoader and a new “BUMBLEBEE” loader via ISO files with hidden DLLs and LNK shortcuts—identifiable by shared machine identifiers, unique command-line arguments and a “bumblebee” user-agent—to deploy Conti and Diavol ransomware. At its peak, EXOTIC LILY sent over 5,000 spear-phishing emails daily to 650 organizations across IT, cybersecurity, healthcare and other sectors, using human-operated TTPs such as TLD-switched domain and employee identity spoofing (leveraging AI-generated or harvested RocketReach/CrunchBase profiles), live chat to build trust, and legitimate file-sharing services (WeTransfer, TransferNow, OneDrive) to evade detection. Operators worked a standard 9-to-5 schedule in a Central/Eastern Europe timezone, customized business proposals, scheduled calls, and used WMI-based data collection in BUMBLEBEE to exfiltrate system details in JSON and fetch Cobalt Strike payloads. Overlaps with Microsoft’s DEV-0413 and Abnormal reporting confirm shared infrastructure, underscoring the need for enhanced domain/identity spoofing defenses, monitoring of file-sharing notifications, and threat hunting for ISO/LNK artifacts with unique metadata or “bumblebee” indicators.
retrieved_context.title: Exposing initial access broker with ties to Conti

retrieved_context.text: Google’s TAG disclosed that Charming Kitten (Iranian APT35) has been using a custom .NET Windows tool called HYPERSCRAPE—active since 2020—to siphon inbox data from fewer than two dozen Gmail, Yahoo! and Outlook accounts in Iran by leveraging hijacked or pre-obtained credentials; the tool validates connectivity via hardcoded/Base64-obfuscated C2s (e.g. 136.243.108.14, 173.209.51.54), spoofs an outdated browser UA to force basic HTML view, switches the account language to English, iteratively downloads emails as .eml files while preserving unread status, reverts language settings, deletes Google security alerts, and reports system metadata via HTTP POST without exfiltrating content, with early builds also offering an automated Google Takeout option using pipe communication; TAG re-secured compromised accounts, issued Government-Backed Attacker Warnings and published detection data—including numerous SHA-256 hashes for HYPERSCRAPE binaries and a related Live DLL—to aid defenders, and urges high-risk users to enroll in Google’s Advanced Protection Program and enable Enhanced Safe Browsing.
retrieved_context.title: New Iranian APT data extraction tool

retrieved_context.text: Google’s Threat Analysis Group (TAG) has observed a 33% year-over-year increase in government-backed phishing warnings—over 50,000 sent to users so far in 2021—driven in part by a large APT28 (Fancy Bear) campaign and sustained by ongoing operations from Iran-aligned APT35. Since early 2021, APT35 has compromised a UK university website to host a phishing kit targeting Gmail, Yahoo and Hotmail credentials—including second-factor codes—and continues its credential harvesting campaigns against government, academia, journalism and NGOs using hijacked sites and link-shortening redirects. In May 2020 it attempted to distribute spyware disguised as a VPN on Google Play Store (blocked before installation) and has pursued similar Android C2 apps on other platforms. The group also impersonates conference officials (e.g., Munich Security, T20 Italy) to initiate phishing, embedding JavaScript to relay visitor IP, user-agent and locale via Telegram bots—a tactic TAG disrupted by reporting the bots. TAG’s layered defenses include batch-sent warnings, Workspace admin alerts, Safe Browsing domain blocks and urging high-risk users to enable two-factor authentication or enroll in Advanced Protection.
retrieved_context.title: Countering threats from Iran

hits.text: In 2022 Magniber ransomware attacks accelerated from fewer than 20 monthly attempts in Q1 to a peak of 1,482 detections in September and 508 in December, with Trend Micro data showing Taiwan as the hardest-hit nation (204 attempts, ~76.1% of total), followed by South Korea (15), Australia (9), Turkey and Japan (6) and emerging targets beyond Asia; industry-wise education, government and manufacturing bore the brunt (987 detections), then healthcare and technology, with energy, transportation and real estate also affected. Attackers gain initial access via exploit kits and public-facing flaws—CVE-2016-0189, CVE-2018-8174, CVE-2019-1367, CVE-2020-0968, CVE-2021-26411, CVE-2021-40444, PrintNightmare (CVE-2021-34527) and CVE-2022-44698—delivering payloads through fake MSI and CPL installers, MSHTML/Regsvr32 proxy execution and Mark-of-the-Web bypass. They employ NtQuerySystemInformation for discovery, thread execution hijacking and process injection for defense evasion, UAC bypass via Fodhelper scripts that delete shadow copies, then encrypt files using AES per 1 MiB block and RSA-wrapped keys, inhibit recovery and append mutex-based extensions. Security teams should prioritize patching these CVEs, monitor anomalous Msiexec/Regsvr32 activity, script-based installers and registry modifications, and detect shadow-copy deletion or process injection to mitigate this streamlined yet potent ransomware chain.
hits.title: Ransomware Spotlight: Magniber | Trend Micro (US)

hits.text: Researchers have identified a new ransomware strain dubbed Magniber—an affiliate of both the Magnitude exploit kit and Cerber ransomware—exclusively targeting users in South Korea and the Asia-Pacific region following Magnitude’s reemergence on October 15, 2017, after a brief hiatus during which its Cerber distribution waned. FireEye and Trend Micro findings reveal that Magniber leverages malvertising and IE memory corruption vulnerability CVE-2016-0189 to deliver a binary payload encrypted in reverse RC4 with 30-byte keys, unpacks it in memory, then executes an AES-128 encryption routine that renames files with a “.ihsdj” extension before self-deletion. It employs a GetSystemDefaultUILanguage check to exit on non-Korean systems and generates four callback URLs via a 19-character pseudorandom string to evade virtual machines. Organizations should prioritize patching IE CVE-2016-0189, deploy ad blockers and updated exploit kit defenses, and monitor for Magnitude EK activity in APAC environments.
hits.title: New Magniber Ransomware Targets South Korea, Asia Pacific | Threatpost

hits.text: In late October 2022, Google’s Threat Analysis Group (TAG) discovered that North Korean government-backed actor APT37 was exploiting a never-before-seen Internet Explorer JScript engine vulnerability (CVE-2022-41128) via malicious Microsoft Office documents themed on the Itaewon Halloween tragedy to achieve arbitrary code execution on Windows hosts; the attack chain began when a user disabled Protected View on a Word document that fetched a remote RTF template hosting HTML rendered through IE, triggering a JIT optimization–induced type-confusion bug in jscript9.dll, which checked for a unique cookie to evade sandboxing, reported to its C2 infrastructure both pre- and post-exploit, and deployed a custom-hashed shellcode that cleared IE cache/history before downloading follow-on payloads; TAG reported the flaw to Microsoft on October 31 and a patch shipped on November 8, and defenders should ensure CVE-2022-41128 is remediated, monitor related IOCs (e.g., word-template[.]net, openxmlformat[.]org) and document hashes, and harden Office macro and remote-template protections against similar APT37 tactics.
hits.title: Internet Explorer 0-day exploited by North Korean actor APT37

hits.text: Google’s Threat Analysis Group (TAG) has documented how over 30 commercial spyware vendors are selling 0-day and n-day exploits to government-backed actors, enabling targeted campaigns against dissidents, journalists and human rights workers on Android, iOS and Samsung Internet Browser; in November 2022, TAG observed a smishing campaign using bit.ly links to deliver two parallel exploit chains—on iOS (CVE-2022-42856 WebKit RCE with a PAC bypass technique also seen in Cytrox’s Predator, and CVE-2021-30900 AGXAccelerator sandbox escape) that installed a GPS-pinging IPA stager, and on Android (CVE-2022-3723 Chrome type confusion, CVE-2022-4135 GPU sandbox bypass analyzed by Sergei Glazunov, and CVE-2022-38181 ARM privilege escalation) with Intent redirection to Chrome—both remaining effective until patched in Chrome 107/108 and Pixel January 2023 updates; in December 2022, TAG uncovered a one-time SMS link campaign targeting UAE users via a Heliconia-style landing page delivering a C++-based Android spyware suite after chaining four faults—CVE-2022-4262 Chrome type confusion, CVE-2022-3038 Chrome sandbox escape, CVE-2022-22706 Mali GPU kernel exploit and CVE-2023-0266 Linux kernel race (with auxiliary info-leak 0-days)—against unpatched Samsung Internet Browser (Chromium 102), underscoring that smaller surveillance vendors now stockpile and share advanced exploits historically limited to nation-state developers, highlighting the critical need for immediate patch deployment, comprehensive mitigations (PAC, V8 sandbox, MiraclePTR) and continuous IOC monitoring to disrupt these highly targeted intrusion operations.

hits.text: Microsoft’s research exposes the BadPilot campaign—a multiyear initial-access subgroup of Russian GRU-aligned Seashell Blizzard active since at least 2021—that has opportunistically scanned for and exploited Internet-facing vulnerabilities (CVE-2021-34473 Exchange, CVE-2022-41352 Zimbra, CVE-2023-32315 OpenFire, CVE-2023-42793 TeamCity, CVE-2023-23397 Outlook, CVE-2024-1709 ConnectWise ScreenConnect, CVE-2023-48788 FortiClient EMS and various JBOSS flaws) to compromise a globally diverse set of high-value sectors (energy, oil and gas, telecommunications, shipping, arms manufacturing and government). After focusing on Ukraine, Europe, Central/South Asia and the Middle East during 2021–2023, the subgroup scaled horizontally into the United States, United Kingdom, Canada and Australia in early 2024, reflecting Russia’s evolving strategic objectives and underscoring the urgency of patching Internet-facing services, implementing comprehensive logging and anomaly detection, and applying threat-informed incident-response practices to disrupt its operational lifecycle.

hits.text: In 2022 Magniber ransomware attacks accelerated from fewer than 20 monthly attempts in Q1 to a peak of 1,482 detections in September and 508 in December, with Trend Micro data showing Taiwan as the hardest-hit nation (204 attempts, ~76.1% of total), followed by South Korea (15), Australia (9), Turkey and Japan (6) and emerging targets beyond Asia; industry-wise education, government and manufacturing bore the brunt (987 detections), then healthcare and technology, with energy, transportation and real estate also affected. Attackers gain initial access via exploit kits and public-facing flaws—CVE-2016-0189, CVE-2018-8174, CVE-2019-1367, CVE-2020-0968, CVE-2021-26411, CVE-2021-40444, PrintNightmare (CVE-2021-34527) and CVE-2022-44698—delivering payloads through fake MSI and CPL installers, MSHTML/Regsvr32 proxy execution and Mark-of-the-Web bypass. They employ NtQuerySystemInformation for discovery, thread execution hijacking and process injection for defense evasion, UAC bypass via Fodhelper scripts that delete shadow copies, then encrypt files using AES per 1 MiB block and RSA-wrapped keys, inhibit recovery and append mutex-based extensions. Security teams should prioritize patching these CVEs, monitor anomalous Msiexec/Regsvr32 activity, script-based installers and registry modifications, and detect shadow-copy deletion or process injection to mitigate this streamlined yet potent ransomware chain.

hits.text: Researchers have identified a new ransomware strain dubbed Magniber—an affiliate of both the Magnitude exploit kit and Cerber ransomware—exclusively targeting users in South Korea and the Asia-Pacific region following Magnitude’s reemergence on October 15, 2017, after a brief hiatus during which its Cerber distribution waned. FireEye and Trend Micro findings reveal that Magniber leverages malvertising and IE memory corruption vulnerability CVE-2016-0189 to deliver a binary payload encrypted in reverse RC4 with 30-byte keys, unpacks it in memory, then executes an AES-128 encryption routine that renames files with a “.ihsdj” extension before self-deletion. It employs a GetSystemDefaultUILanguage check to exit on non-Korean systems and generates four callback URLs via a 19-character pseudorandom string to evade virtual machines. Organizations should prioritize patching IE CVE-2016-0189, deploy ad blockers and updated exploit kit defenses, and monitor for Magnitude EK activity in APAC environments.
hits.title: New Magniber Ransomware Targets South Korea, Asia Pacific | Threatpost

hits.text: In late October 2022, Google’s Threat Analysis Group (TAG) discovered that North Korean government-backed actor APT37 was exploiting a never-before-seen Internet Explorer JScript engine vulnerability (CVE-2022-41128) via malicious Microsoft Office documents themed on the Itaewon Halloween tragedy to achieve arbitrary code execution on Windows hosts; the attack chain began when a user disabled Protected View on a Word document that fetched a remote RTF template hosting HTML rendered through IE, triggering a JIT optimization–induced type-confusion bug in jscript9.dll, which checked for a unique cookie to evade sandboxing, reported to its C2 infrastructure both pre- and post-exploit, and deployed a custom-hashed shellcode that cleared IE cache/history before downloading follow-on payloads; TAG reported the flaw to Microsoft on October 31 and a patch shipped on November 8, and defenders should ensure CVE-2022-41128 is remediated, monitor related IOCs (e.g., word-template[.]net, openxmlformat[.]org) and document hashes, and harden Office macro and remote-template protections against similar APT37 tactics.
hits.title: Internet Explorer 0-day exploited by North Korean actor APT37

hits.text: Since late 2019, a hack-for-hire group recruited via Russian-language forums has conducted coordinated phishing campaigns against YouTube creators by posing as legitimate companies (e.g., VPNs, antivirus, photo editors, “Covid19 news” software) to deliver non-persistent cookie-theft malware (RedLine, Vidar, Predator The Thief, Nexus Stealer, Azorult, Raccoon, Grand Stealer, Vikro Stealer, Masad, Kantal, Sorano, AdamantiumThief) via fake landing pages on over 1,011 domains and forged social-media pages; upon infection they exfiltrate session cookies for channel hijack and resale ($3–$4,000 USD) or crypto-scam livestreams. In partnership with YouTube, Gmail, Trust & Safety, Cybercrime Investigation and Safe Browsing teams, Google’s Threat Analysis Group reduced related Gmail phishing by 99.6% since May 2021—blocking 1.6 M messages, warning 62 K users, blocking 2.4 K files and restoring ~4 K accounts—while observing a shift to email.cz, seznam.cz, post.cz and aol.com and messaging apps. Protections include heuristic email filters, Safe Browsing blocks, hardened authentication and channel recovery workflows; users are urged to heed Safe Browsing warnings, scan files via antivirus or VirusTotal, enable Enhanced Safe Browsing and enforce 2-Step Verification.

hits.text: In late May 2022, Symantec identified multiple threat actors exploiting the MSDT Follina bug (CVE-2022-30190) through ms-msdt URI-based RCE in Word/RTF documents that load a malicious HTML via Word’s remote template feature to launch msdt.exe, sdiagnhost.exe and ultimately PowerShell—bypassing the need for macros—to install a digitally signed AsyncRAT remote access Trojan that performs anti-analysis checks, collects hardware IDs, user names, execution paths and OS details, and maintains C&C communications, alongside parallel deployments of a browser infostealer targeting cookies and saved credentials in Firefox, Chrome and Edge. Symantec customers should apply Microsoft’s advisories or disable the ms-msdt handler, update Symantec Endpoint definitions (File-based-Downloader-Backdoor:Async, InfoStealer) and monitor for related IOCs to thwart these rapid, damaging campaigns.
hits.title: Attackers Exploit MSDT Follina Bug to Drop RAT, Infostealer | Symantec Enterprise Blogs

hits.text: In Q1 2023, Google’s Threat Analysis Group (TAG) found that over 60 percent of Russian state-backed phishing campaigns were aimed at Ukraine, led by FROZENBARENTS (aka Sandworm, GRU Unit 74455), which abused globally compromised EXIM mail servers, SMS-delivered phishing links and fake Windows update payloads deploying the Rhadamanthys stealer, then maintained persistence via webshells and Adminer to exfiltrate data to the CyberArmyofRussia_Reborn Telegram channel across government, defense, energy (notably the Caspian Pipeline Consortium), transport, education and humanitarian sectors while conducting information operations. Simultaneously, FROZENLAKE (APT28) leveraged reflected XSS on Ukrainian government sites to redirect users to phishing domains hosted on free services, with harvested credentials sent to compromised Ubiquiti devices; Belarusian PUSHCHA continued targeted low-volume campaigns against regional webmail providers; and IRA-linked actors deployed coordinated YouTube Shorts and Blogger posts to amplify pro-Wagner, anti-Ukrainian narratives. Financially motivated Cuba ransomware affiliates pivoted to intelligence collection using RomCom malware via ChatGPT/OpenAI-spoofed domains against conference attendees. TAG’s takedowns and Safe Browsing protections, coupled with targeted Gmail alerts, underscore the need for organizations to enable Enhanced Safe Browsing, patch mail servers, monitor for unauthorized EXIM access, and guard against reflected XSS and SMS phishing.
hits.title: Ukraine remains Russia’s biggest cyber focus in 2023

hits.text: Since January 2021, Google’s Threat Analysis Group (TAG) has tracked a government-backed North Korean campaign that leverages social engineering via X (formerly Twitter) and encrypted messaging apps to befriend security researchers and deliver malicious files containing at least one unpatched 0-day in a popular software package; upon exploitation the custom shellcode performs anti-virtual-machine checks, captures system data and screenshots, and exfiltrates them to C2 infrastructure (e.g., 23.106.215[.]105, www.blgbeach[.]com), with the latest vulnerability reported and patched on September 12, 2023 (see TAG’s published RCA). In parallel, the actors published a seemingly benign Windows tool called GetSymbol on GitHub (https://github.com/dbgsymbol/) that quietly downloads debugging symbols—and arbitrary code—from attacker domains, requiring full OS reinstalls for compromised hosts. TAG has added malicious sites to Safe Browsing, issued government-backed attacker alerts to targeted Gmail and Workspace users, and urges researchers to enable Enhanced Safe Browsing, keep software up to date, and verify system integrity after using third-party tools.
hits.title: Active North Korean campaign targeting security researchers

hits.text: At least four distinct campaigns exploited CVE-2023-37580, a reflected XSS zero-day in Zimbra Collaboration Suite, to siphon emails, attachments, user credentials and authentication tokens from government organizations worldwide before the July 5 hotfix and July 25 official patch; in chronological order, unidentified actors targeted Greece on June 29 via malicious URLs that, when clicked during active Zimbra sessions, deployed a data-theft framework and auto-forward rules, Winter Vivern’s APT leveraged unique exploit links to hit Moldova and Tunisia between July 11 and 25, another group used a phishing-style XSS link in Vietnam to harvest webmail credentials and exfiltrate them to a compromised government domain, and on August 25 unknown attackers employed an N-day variant to steal tokens from Pakistan’s mail servers; Google’s Threat Analysis Group warns these campaigns underscore the urgency of promptly applying open-source fixes, hardening mail-server code to prevent XSS, and maintaining vigilant patch management as attackers continuously monitor public repositories for unpatched vulnerabilities.
hits.title: APTs Swarm Zimbra Zero-Day to Steal Government Info Worldwide

hits.text: Google’s TAG disclosed that Charming Kitten (Iranian APT35) has been using a custom .NET Windows tool called HYPERSCRAPE—active since 2020—to siphon inbox data from fewer than two dozen Gmail, Yahoo! and Outlook accounts in Iran by leveraging hijacked or pre-obtained credentials; the tool validates connectivity via hardcoded/Base64-obfuscated C2s (e.g. 136.243.108.14, 173.209.51.54), spoofs an outdated browser UA to force basic HTML view, switches the account language to English, iteratively downloads emails as .eml files while preserving unread status, reverts language settings, deletes Google security alerts, and reports system metadata via HTTP POST without exfiltrating content, with early builds also offering an automated Google Takeout option using pipe communication; TAG re-secured compromised accounts, issued Government-Backed Attacker Warnings and published detection data—including numerous SHA-256 hashes for HYPERSCRAPE binaries and a related Live DLL—to aid defenders, and urges high-risk users to enroll in Google’s Advanced Protection Program and enable Enhanced Safe Browsing.
hits.title: New Iranian APT data extraction tool

hits.text: Last week Google’s Threat Analysis Group, in partnership with The Citizen Lab, exposed an in-the-wild exploit chain developed by the commercial surveillance vendor Intellexa in Egypt that leverages a man-in-the-middle injection on HTTP traffic to silently redirect targets first to c.betly[.]me and then to sec-flare[.]com, delivering Predator spyware without any user interaction; on iOS this chain combined Safari RCE (CVE-2023-41993), certificate validation bypass (CVE-2023-41991) and XNU kernel local privilege escalation (CVE-2023-41992) and was patched in iOS 16.7/17.0.1, while on Android initial Chrome renderer RCE (CVE-2023-4762), delivered via MITM or one-time links, was patched on September 5; this campaign highlights the serious risk posed by proliferating commercial spyware, underscores the urgency of enforcing universal HTTPS and enabling Chrome’s HTTPS-First Mode, and demonstrates the critical need for organizations and users to apply the latest OS and browser updates, deploy encrypted-traffic protections, and monitor for anomalous network redirects to mitigate future attacks.
hits.title: 0-days exploited by commercial surveillance vendor in Egypt
