hits.text: Since at least August 2023, threat actors have exploited CVE-2023-4966 (CitrixBleed), a 7.5-rated flaw in Citrix NetScaler ADC and Gateway, culminating in an October 16–19 breach at Comcast Xfinity that exposed 35,879,455 customers’ usernames, hashed passwords, names, contact details, last four SSN digits, dates of birth and security Q&A; despite Citrix’s October 10 patch and Comcast’s claim of prompt mitigation, attackers used publicly available proofs-of-concept and rumored Python automation scripts to extract session tokens from device memory, hijack active sessions and bypass authentication, a tactic linked by ReliaQuest to at least five threat groups including LockBit; this incident highlights the necessity not only of timely patching and reboots but also of invalidating all active and persistent session tokens, enforcing multi-factor authentication, resetting credentials and maintaining continuous 24x7 monitoring to prevent further data exfiltration and ransomware deployment.
hits.title: Comcast Xfinity Breached via CitrixBleed; 35M Customers Affected

canonical_entities: Launch EC2 instances across regions via VPN
hits.text: Unit42’s “EleKtra-Leak” campaign, active since December 2020, uses automated scripts to clone public GitHub repos every few minutes, extract exposed AWS IAM keys within five minutes, then—if not blocked by GitHub-AWS quarantine policies—execute rapid AWS reconnaissance (DescribeRegions), create security groups, and launch hundreds of EC2 instances across regions via VPN for Monero cryptojacking, generating over 400 API calls in seven minutes. Between Aug. 30 and Oct. 6, 2023, researchers tracked 474 actor-controlled miners. The actor employs custom mining software and blocklists high-profile AWS account IDs to avoid honey traps. Leveraging the Prisma Cloud HoneyCloud project’s ephemeral key leaks and policy overrides, Unit42 obtained full visibility, informing Prisma Cloud Secrets Security, CI/CD IaC scanning, Cortex XDR, and recommendations for independent repo scanning, strict IAM policies, and continuous monitoring.
hits.title: CloudKeys in the Air: Tracking Malicious Operations of Exposed IAM Keys

canonical_entities: Remote Code Execution via ms-msdt URI in Word/RTF documents
ms-msdt URI-based RCE in Word/RTF documents
hits.text: In late May 2022, Symantec identified multiple threat actors exploiting the MSDT Follina bug (CVE-2022-30190) through ms-msdt URI-based RCE in Word/RTF documents that load a malicious HTML via Word’s remote template feature to launch msdt.exe, sdiagnhost.exe and ultimately PowerShell—bypassing the need for macros—to install a digitally signed AsyncRAT remote access Trojan that performs anti-analysis checks, collects hardware IDs, user names, execution paths and OS details, and maintains C&C communications, alongside parallel deployments of a browser infostealer targeting cookies and saved credentials in Firefox, Chrome and Edge. Symantec customers should apply Microsoft’s advisories or disable the ms-msdt handler, update Symantec Endpoint definitions (File-based-Downloader-Backdoor:Async, InfoStealer) and monitor for related IOCs to thwart these rapid, damaging campaigns.
hits.title: Attackers Exploit MSDT Follina Bug to Drop RAT, Infostealer | Symantec Enterprise Blogs

hits.text: The North Korea-linked threat actor Slow Pisces (also tracked as Jade Sleet, PUKCHONG, TraderTraitor, and UNC4899) has been conducting a multi-stage malware campaign targeting cryptocurrency developers via LinkedIn job opportunity lures since at least June 2024, leveraging trojanized Python and JavaScript projects hosted on GitHub that employ YAML deserialization and EJS templating to execute gated payloads only to validated targets meeting specific criteria (IP address, geolocation, time, HTTP headers); the campaign delivers RN Loader and RN Stealer malware on macOS systems capable of harvesting system metadata, installed applications, SSH keys, AWS/Kubernetes/Google Cloud configuration files, and iCloud Keychain data, with payloads remaining memory-resident and deployed selectively to prevent analysis; Slow Pisces is assessed to be responsible for the February 2025 Bybit cryptocurrency exchange breach and operates alongside other North Korean clusters including Operation Dream Job, Contagious Interview, Alluring Pisces, and Moonstone Sleet, though with notably superior operational security practices involving heavily guarded payload delivery across infection stages.
hits.title: Crypto Developers Targeted by Python Malware Disguised as Coding Challenges

hits.text: Since at least 2019, China-linked Winnti APT (aka APT41/BARIUM/Blackfly) has run the stealthy CuckooBees campaign against technology and manufacturing firms in North America, Europe, and Asia to support Beijing’s Made in China 2025 initiative, exploiting ERP platform vulnerabilities for initial access and deploying a “house of cards” kill chain—including an undocumented Deploylog backdoor and updated Winnti malware concealed via rare Windows CLFS abuse—to maintain persistence through a VBScript WebShell (up_win32.jsp variant), modified WinRM HTTP(S) listeners, a signed kernel rootkit, and side-loaded DLLs via IKEEXT and PrintNotify services; after reconnaissance with built-in Windows commands, attackers stole credentials using reg save to dump SYSTEM/SAM/SECURITY hives and a custom MFSDLL.exe loader of mktzx64.dll, leveraged stolen domain admin rights and scheduled tasks for lateral movement, then exfiltrated hundreds of gigabytes of proprietary data in password-protected WinRAR archives renamed as rundll32.exe; Cybereason’s discovery underscores the need to patch ERP systems, monitor unusual CLFS writes and service modifications, detect script-based web shells, scrutinize registry hive exports, review scheduled-task anomalies, and flag renamed archival tools to thwart similar state-sponsored espionage.
hits.title: China-Linked Winnti APT Group Silently Stole Trade Secrets for Years: Report

canonical_entities: Korean American National Coordinating Council domain
hits.text: Trend Micro’s “Operation Earth Kitsune” report reveals that the SLUB threat actor recently pivoted from abusing Slack and GitHub to using an on-premise Mattermost instance—complete with five C&C servers and 15 user accounts—to coordinate a sophisticated watering-hole campaign against GNUBoard CMS sites (notably the Korean American National Coordinating Council domain), redirecting visitors to a weaponized proof-of-concept for CVE-2019-5782 (Chrome) that loads shellcode to fetch three backdoors (“1.jpg,” “2.jpg,” “3.jpg”) and exploiting CVE-2020-0674 (Internet Explorer) via a PowerShell loader (with optional LPE via CVE-2019-1458), alongside prior flaws CVE-2016-0189 and CVE-2019-1458; two new malware variants (dneSpy and agfSpy) extend system-information exfiltration and remote-control capabilities, underscoring the need for organizations to patch affected browsers, CMS platforms, audit Mattermost usage for unauthorized channels, and monitor for anomalous shellcode or PowerShell activity to disrupt SLUB’s evolving toolkit.
hits.title: Operation Earth Kitsune: Tracking SLUB’s Current Operations | Trend Micro (US)

hits.text: Our GReAT team uncovered Operation ForumTroll—a state-sponsored APT campaign targeting Russian media, academic and government personnel—delivering previously unknown malware via phishing emails masquerading as Primakov Readings invitations containing two malicious links; clicking either on a Windows PC using Chrome or any Chromium-based browser silently triggers a zero-day exploit (CVE-2025-2783), exploiting a logic flaw at the Chrome-Windows interface to bypass the browser’s sandbox and deploy the payload without further user interaction. We promptly reported the vulnerability to Google, which released a patch in Chrome version 134.0.6998.177/178; while the phishing links now redirect to the legitimate forum site and the campaign is dormant, the attackers could reactivate it at any time. To mitigate this espionage threat, organizations should ensure all Chrome instances are updated to at least 134.0.6998.177/.178, deploy robust exploit detection and prevention solutions on internet-connected devices, and maintain vigilant phishing awareness and monitoring.

retrieved_context.text: In 2022 Magniber ransomware attacks accelerated from fewer than 20 monthly attempts in Q1 to a peak of 1,482 detections in September and 508 in December, with Trend Micro data showing Taiwan as the hardest-hit nation (204 attempts, ~76.1% of total), followed by South Korea (15), Australia (9), Turkey and Japan (6) and emerging targets beyond Asia; industry-wise education, government and manufacturing bore the brunt (987 detections), then healthcare and technology, with energy, transportation and real estate also affected. Attackers gain initial access via exploit kits and public-facing flaws—CVE-2016-0189, CVE-2018-8174, CVE-2019-1367, CVE-2020-0968, CVE-2021-26411, CVE-2021-40444, PrintNightmare (CVE-2021-34527) and CVE-2022-44698—delivering payloads through fake MSI and CPL installers, MSHTML/Regsvr32 proxy execution and Mark-of-the-Web bypass. They employ NtQuerySystemInformation for discovery, thread execution hijacking and process injection for defense evasion, UAC bypass via Fodhelper scripts that delete shadow copies, then encrypt files using AES per 1 MiB block and RSA-wrapped keys, inhibit recovery and append mutex-based extensions. Security teams should prioritize patching these CVEs, monitor anomalous Msiexec/Regsvr32 activity, script-based installers and registry modifications, and detect shadow-copy deletion or process injection to mitigate this streamlined yet potent ransomware chain.
retrieved_context.title: Ransomware Spotlight: Magniber | Trend Micro (US)

retrieved_context.text: Google’s Threat Analysis Group uncovered that Magniber ransomware operators exploited a previously unpatched SmartScreen bypass (CVE-2023-24880) to deliver MSI installers signed with malformed Authenticode certificates that trigger a parsing error in smartscreen.exe, causing shdocvw.dll’s DoSafeOpenPromptForShellExec to proceed without displaying warnings—resulting in over 100,000 downloads since January 2023 (80 percent in Europe) before Microsoft issued a Patch Tuesday fix; this mirrors a prior bypass (CVE-2022-44698) used in late 2022 to spread Magniber via JScript and later adopted by Qakbot, with virtually identical signatures suggesting shared tooling, and highlights a systemic root-cause in SmartScreen’s error-handling logic—specifically NULL cert_context or NULL psIndirectData paths—that attackers now exploit by corrupting the SPC_INDIRECT_DATA_OBJID ASN.1 identifier, demonstrating the urgent need for holistic SmartScreen hardening and end-to-end certificate validation.
retrieved_context.title: Magniber ransomware actors used a variant of Microsoft SmartScreen bypass

retrieved_context.text: After a year-long investigation researchers at Lumen’s Black Lotus Labs dissected the Ngioweb botnet—first observed in 2017—which uses a loader network and roughly 15 n-day exploits to deploy malware that contacts C2 domains generated via a domain generation algorithm (augmented by DNS TXT records to resist sinkholing), evaluates device traffic capacity, and links compromised Zyxel, Reolink, Alpha Technologies and, increasingly, Netgear routers (now 10 % of bots) to over 180 “backconnect” C2 nodes that provide at least 80 % of the 35,000 residential proxies in the NSOCKS[.]net service across 180 countries; NSOCKS’s lack of authentication and appearance on free proxy lists has enabled cybercriminals to carry out DDoS amplification, credential stuffing, phishing and malware proxying (e.g., Agent Tesla), while APT28 state-sponsored actors have mixed espionage with criminal traffic on the same infrastructure. To disrupt both operations, Lumen, alongside The ShadowServer Foundation and other partners, is actively blocking traffic to known C2 nodes and publishing indicators of compromise to help organizations identify and remediate infected devices.
retrieved_context.title: Botnet fueling residential proxies disrupted in cybercrime crackdown

canonical_entities: Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Tools
hits.text: Since its emergence in 2021 and first detection on Trend Micro telemetry in March 2022, the TargetCompany ransomware group has launched 269 attempted attacks against 250 disclosed Trend customers—predominantly in Asia (notably India and Saudi Arabia)—while avoiding Kazakhstan, Russia, Qatar, and Ukraine, and focusing on manufacturing, retail, and telecommunications; their November 2022–May 2023 leak site lists 20 confirmed victims (mostly small businesses) across the Asia-Pacific, Europe, and Middle East in IT, manufacturing, apparel, and automotive sectors. Initial access vectors include exploitation of CVE-2019-1069 and CVE-2020-0618 RCE flaws, SQL Server xp_cmdshell abuse, and OneNote-based spam campaigns. Execution relies on WMIC-invoked PowerShell scripts to retrieve various payloads (TargetComp ransomware, Remcos backdoor, Negasteal, Snake Keylogger) and, since January 2022, reflective loading of a .NET downloader that decrypts and runs payloads in memory via XOR or inversion. For defense evasion, operators deploy GMER, PCHunter64 (YDArk.exe), Advance Process Termination, KILLAV, and killer.bat to disable AV and security services; discovery is achieved through network scans and Mimikatz credential dumping; lateral movement via RDP-based RCE; C2 evolved from an open Mallox directory to an Nginx-protected server. Impact involves ChaCha20 file encryption with keys generated by Curve25519 and AES-128, file extensions such as .mallox/.exploit/.avast and ransom notes titled “HOW TO RECOVER!!.TXT,” and potential data exfiltration. Their tactics span MITRE techniques T1190, T1059.001, T1047, T1562.001, T1003.001, T1071.001, T1486, and more. The group’s maturation—evidenced by reflective loading and possible RaaS adoption—underscores the urgency for organizations to enforce asset inventories, least-privilege access, prompt patching (or virtual patching), multifactor authentication, sandboxed email defenses, AI/ML-driven detection, regular backups, and continuous red-team testing to thwart this active threat.
hits.title: Ransomware Spotlight: TargetCompany | Trend Micro (US)

canonical_entities: enumerates SSH directories to harvest credentials
Persistence is achieved through multiple cronjobs
hits.text: Aqua Security’s Nautilus team has uncovered Hadooken, a new Linux malware targeting Oracle WebLogic servers via weak passwords. Post-compromise, attackers deploy redundant shell and Python scripts to ensure download and execution of Hadooken, which enumerates SSH directories to harvest credentials, moves laterally, and clears logs. Hadooken then drops a three-path cryptominer and a Tsunami backdoor with a randomized name, the latter reserved for potential later-stage attacks. Persistence is achieved through multiple cronjobs under varied names and frequencies stored across cron directories. The malware is hosted on two IPs—one German address linked to TeamTNT and Gang 8220, the other inactive in Russia—where researchers also identified a Mallox ransomware PowerShell loader targeting Windows. Static analysis links Hadooken to Rhombus and NoEscape families. With over 230,000 internet-connected WebLogic instances—hundreds of which expose vulnerable admin consoles—this campaign underscores the dual risk of cryptojacking and ransomware across Linux and Windows environments.
hits.title: New 'Hadooken' Linux Malware Targets WebLogic Servers - SecurityWeek

canonical_entities: spear-phishing attacks against European embassies in Seoul (March–July 2025)
exfiltrated ... over HTTPS to the attackers’ private GitHub repo via the Contents API
hits.text: Between March and July 2025, DPRK-linked Kimsuky operators executed at least 19 highly tailored spear-phishing attacks against Western, Central, Eastern and Southern European embassies in Seoul, spoofing real diplomats and embedding password-protected ZIPs delivered via Dropbox, Daum or Google Drive. Victims unwittingly launched malicious .LNK shortcuts that triggered obfuscated PowerShell scripts to decode and in-memory execute a Confuser-Core-obfuscated XenoRAT (MoonPeak) payload—identified by GUID 12DE1212-167D-45BA-1284-780DA98CF901 and mutex “Dansweit_Hk65-PSAccerdle”—leveraging scheduled tasks for persistence. Reconnaissance data (OS build, IP, process list) was exfiltrated as base64-encoded text files over HTTPS to the attackers’ private GitHub repo via the Contents API, while C2 instructions (e.g., onf.txt) directed dynamic payload rotations hosted on Dropbox with rapid header-fix GZIP routines. This ongoing campaign provided full system control—including keystroke logging, screenshots and remote shells—and underscores the need to monitor abnormal GitHub API usage, cloud-based archive downloads and anomalous PowerShell invocations.
hits.title: The Coordinated Embassy Hunt: Unmasking the DPRK-linked GitHub C2 Espionage Campaign

canonical_entities: lateral movement to additional cloud resources
hits.text: Attackers exploited an unpatched SQL injection vulnerability in an application to gain elevated permissions on a Microsoft SQL Server instance running in an Azure VM, then enumerated databases, schemas, network settings and enabled xp_cmdshell via “sp_configure” commands to execute OS-level commands, deploy encoded PowerShell scripts, establish persistence via scheduled tasks, dump SAM and SECURITY hives, and exfiltrate data discreetly using webhook[.]site. In a novel twist on known techniques, they attempted lateral movement to additional cloud resources by querying the Azure Instance Metadata Service (169.254.169.254) to obtain the managed identity’s OAuth2 token and abuse its privileges, but the move failed due to an error. Microsoft Defender for SQL triggered alerts for potential SQL injection, abnormal shell spawning, and IMDS calls from SQL Server, while Defender for Cloud and Defender for Endpoint provide further visibility into anomalous cloud-identity and xp_cmdshell activity. Although no breach of downstream cloud services was confirmed, this case underscores the critical need to enforce least privilege on managed identities, disable or tightly control xp_cmdshell, patch applications, monitor metadata endpoint access, and leverage Defender XDR’s detection capabilities to thwart SQL Server–to-cloud lateral movement.
hits.title: Defending new vectors: Threat actors attempt SQL Server to cloud lateral movement | Microsoft Security Blog

hits.text: Microsoft’s analysis of the PipeMagic backdoor—a modular, in-memory framework masquerading as an open-source ChatGPT desktop app—reveals a stealthy, extensible architecture that Storm-2460 (linked to RansomEXX ransomware) has leveraged since early 2025 to exploit a Windows zero-day (CVE-2025-29824) across targets in the US, Europe, South America and the Middle East. PipeMagic offloads C&C communication and core tasks to discrete modules delivered via named pipes and organized in four doubly linked list structures in memory (for raw payloads, loaded modules, networking code and dynamic calls), allowing granular control over execution, module enumeration, deletion and persistent C&C connectivity without touching disk. Once the networking module establishes contact, the backdoor harvests extensive system telemetry, awaits operator commands to load or invoke specific modules, and can self-terminate or shut down communications on demand. Microsoft warns that PipeMagic’s in-memory, modular design presents significant detection challenges and underscores the need for pipeline-level monitoring and memory forensics to disrupt this financially motivated threat.
hits.title: Microsoft Dissects PipeMagic Modular Backdoor

canonical_entities: installing Sagerunex variants in the Windows Registry
hits.text: The Lotus Blossom APT (aka Lotus Panda, Billbug, Spring Dragon) has stepped up cyberespionage against APAC government targets by deploying new Sagerunex backdoor variants and abusing Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) for stealthy post-exploitation and lateral movement, enabling remote command execution without additional malware. Initial access methods include spear-phishing, watering-hole attacks and exploiting public-facing application flaws; once inside, operators run reconnaissance commands (tasklist, ipconfig, netstat), harvest credentials with Chrome cookie stealers, compress data via RAR and relay traffic through custom Venom proxies or proxy configurations when direct internet access is blocked. Persistence is achieved by installing Sagerunex variants in the Windows Registry under hijacked service names (tapisrv, swprv) to auto-launch at startup, while command-and-control blends encrypted traffic into legitimate platforms—stolen data uploaded as .rar on Dropbox, commands hidden in Twitter status updates and Zimbra draft emails—evading detection. Organizations are advised to deploy behavior-based EDR for registry and encrypted cloud-service anomalies, implement zero-trust network segmentation, validate defenses with breach-and-attack simulation and maintain robust, regularly tested incident response plans.
hits.title: Lotus Blossom APT Exploits WMI for Post-Exploitation Activities

retrieval_events.query: How is Magniber ransomware being distributed and what techniques are the attackers using to evade detection?

retrieved_context.text: In 2022 Magniber ransomware attacks accelerated from fewer than 20 monthly attempts in Q1 to a peak of 1,482 detections in September and 508 in December, with Trend Micro data showing Taiwan as the hardest-hit nation (204 attempts, ~76.1% of total), followed by South Korea (15), Australia (9), Turkey and Japan (6) and emerging targets beyond Asia; industry-wise education, government and manufacturing bore the brunt (987 detections), then healthcare and technology, with energy, transportation and real estate also affected. Attackers gain initial access via exploit kits and public-facing flaws—CVE-2016-0189, CVE-2018-8174, CVE-2019-1367, CVE-2020-0968, CVE-2021-26411, CVE-2021-40444, PrintNightmare (CVE-2021-34527) and CVE-2022-44698—delivering payloads through fake MSI and CPL installers, MSHTML/Regsvr32 proxy execution and Mark-of-the-Web bypass. They employ NtQuerySystemInformation for discovery, thread execution hijacking and process injection for defense evasion, UAC bypass via Fodhelper scripts that delete shadow copies, then encrypt files using AES per 1 MiB block and RSA-wrapped keys, inhibit recovery and append mutex-based extensions. Security teams should prioritize patching these CVEs, monitor anomalous Msiexec/Regsvr32 activity, script-based installers and registry modifications, and detect shadow-copy deletion or process injection to mitigate this streamlined yet potent ransomware chain.
retrieved_context.title: Ransomware Spotlight: Magniber | Trend Micro (US)

retrieved_context.text: Google’s Threat Analysis Group uncovered that Magniber ransomware operators exploited a previously unpatched SmartScreen bypass (CVE-2023-24880) to deliver MSI installers signed with malformed Authenticode certificates that trigger a parsing error in smartscreen.exe, causing shdocvw.dll’s DoSafeOpenPromptForShellExec to proceed without displaying warnings—resulting in over 100,000 downloads since January 2023 (80 percent in Europe) before Microsoft issued a Patch Tuesday fix; this mirrors a prior bypass (CVE-2022-44698) used in late 2022 to spread Magniber via JScript and later adopted by Qakbot, with virtually identical signatures suggesting shared tooling, and highlights a systemic root-cause in SmartScreen’s error-handling logic—specifically NULL cert_context or NULL psIndirectData paths—that attackers now exploit by corrupting the SPC_INDIRECT_DATA_OBJID ASN.1 identifier, demonstrating the urgent need for holistic SmartScreen hardening and end-to-end certificate validation.
retrieved_context.title: Magniber ransomware actors used a variant of Microsoft SmartScreen bypass

canonical_entities: Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Tools
retrieved_context.text: Since its emergence in 2021 and first detection on Trend Micro telemetry in March 2022, the TargetCompany ransomware group has launched 269 attempted attacks against 250 disclosed Trend customers—predominantly in Asia (notably India and Saudi Arabia)—while avoiding Kazakhstan, Russia, Qatar, and Ukraine, and focusing on manufacturing, retail, and telecommunications; their November 2022–May 2023 leak site lists 20 confirmed victims (mostly small businesses) across the Asia-Pacific, Europe, and Middle East in IT, manufacturing, apparel, and automotive sectors. Initial access vectors include exploitation of CVE-2019-1069 and CVE-2020-0618 RCE flaws, SQL Server xp_cmdshell abuse, and OneNote-based spam campaigns. Execution relies on WMIC-invoked PowerShell scripts to retrieve various payloads (TargetComp ransomware, Remcos backdoor, Negasteal, Snake Keylogger) and, since January 2022, reflective loading of a .NET downloader that decrypts and runs payloads in memory via XOR or inversion. For defense evasion, operators deploy GMER, PCHunter64 (YDArk.exe), Advance Process Termination, KILLAV, and killer.bat to disable AV and security services; discovery is achieved through network scans and Mimikatz credential dumping; lateral movement via RDP-based RCE; C2 evolved from an open Mallox directory to an Nginx-protected server. Impact involves ChaCha20 file encryption with keys generated by Curve25519 and AES-128, file extensions such as .mallox/.exploit/.avast and ransom notes titled “HOW TO RECOVER!!.TXT,” and potential data exfiltration. Their tactics span MITRE techniques T1190, T1059.001, T1047, T1562.001, T1003.001, T1071.001, T1486, and more. The group’s maturation—evidenced by reflective loading and possible RaaS adoption—underscores the urgency for organizations to enforce asset inventories, least-privilege access, prompt patching (or virtual patching), multifactor authentication, sandboxed email defenses, AI/ML-driven detection, regular backups, and continuous red-team testing to thwart this active threat.
retrieved_context.title: Ransomware Spotlight: TargetCompany | Trend Micro (US)

canonical_entities: enumerates SSH directories to harvest credentials
Persistence is achieved through multiple cronjobs
retrieved_context.text: Aqua Security’s Nautilus team has uncovered Hadooken, a new Linux malware targeting Oracle WebLogic servers via weak passwords. Post-compromise, attackers deploy redundant shell and Python scripts to ensure download and execution of Hadooken, which enumerates SSH directories to harvest credentials, moves laterally, and clears logs. Hadooken then drops a three-path cryptominer and a Tsunami backdoor with a randomized name, the latter reserved for potential later-stage attacks. Persistence is achieved through multiple cronjobs under varied names and frequencies stored across cron directories. The malware is hosted on two IPs—one German address linked to TeamTNT and Gang 8220, the other inactive in Russia—where researchers also identified a Mallox ransomware PowerShell loader targeting Windows. Static analysis links Hadooken to Rhombus and NoEscape families. With over 230,000 internet-connected WebLogic instances—hundreds of which expose vulnerable admin consoles—this campaign underscores the dual risk of cryptojacking and ransomware across Linux and Windows environments.
retrieved_context.title: New 'Hadooken' Linux Malware Targets WebLogic Servers - SecurityWeek

canonical_entities: spear-phishing attacks against European embassies in Seoul (March–July 2025)
exfiltrated ... over HTTPS to the attackers’ private GitHub repo via the Contents API
retrieved_context.text: Between March and July 2025, DPRK-linked Kimsuky operators executed at least 19 highly tailored spear-phishing attacks against Western, Central, Eastern and Southern European embassies in Seoul, spoofing real diplomats and embedding password-protected ZIPs delivered via Dropbox, Daum or Google Drive. Victims unwittingly launched malicious .LNK shortcuts that triggered obfuscated PowerShell scripts to decode and in-memory execute a Confuser-Core-obfuscated XenoRAT (MoonPeak) payload—identified by GUID 12DE1212-167D-45BA-1284-780DA98CF901 and mutex “Dansweit_Hk65-PSAccerdle”—leveraging scheduled tasks for persistence. Reconnaissance data (OS build, IP, process list) was exfiltrated as base64-encoded text files over HTTPS to the attackers’ private GitHub repo via the Contents API, while C2 instructions (e.g., onf.txt) directed dynamic payload rotations hosted on Dropbox with rapid header-fix GZIP routines. This ongoing campaign provided full system control—including keystroke logging, screenshots and remote shells—and underscores the need to monitor abnormal GitHub API usage, cloud-based archive downloads and anomalous PowerShell invocations.
retrieved_context.title: The Coordinated Embassy Hunt: Unmasking the DPRK-linked GitHub C2 Espionage Campaign

canonical_entities: lateral movement to additional cloud resources
retrieved_context.text: Attackers exploited an unpatched SQL injection vulnerability in an application to gain elevated permissions on a Microsoft SQL Server instance running in an Azure VM, then enumerated databases, schemas, network settings and enabled xp_cmdshell via “sp_configure” commands to execute OS-level commands, deploy encoded PowerShell scripts, establish persistence via scheduled tasks, dump SAM and SECURITY hives, and exfiltrate data discreetly using webhook[.]site. In a novel twist on known techniques, they attempted lateral movement to additional cloud resources by querying the Azure Instance Metadata Service (169.254.169.254) to obtain the managed identity’s OAuth2 token and abuse its privileges, but the move failed due to an error. Microsoft Defender for SQL triggered alerts for potential SQL injection, abnormal shell spawning, and IMDS calls from SQL Server, while Defender for Cloud and Defender for Endpoint provide further visibility into anomalous cloud-identity and xp_cmdshell activity. Although no breach of downstream cloud services was confirmed, this case underscores the critical need to enforce least privilege on managed identities, disable or tightly control xp_cmdshell, patch applications, monitor metadata endpoint access, and leverage Defender XDR’s detection capabilities to thwart SQL Server–to-cloud lateral movement.
retrieved_context.title: Defending new vectors: Threat actors attempt SQL Server to cloud lateral movement | Microsoft Security Blog

canonical_entities: Korean American National Coordinating Council domain
retrieved_context.text: Trend Micro’s “Operation Earth Kitsune” report reveals that the SLUB threat actor recently pivoted from abusing Slack and GitHub to using an on-premise Mattermost instance—complete with five C&C servers and 15 user accounts—to coordinate a sophisticated watering-hole campaign against GNUBoard CMS sites (notably the Korean American National Coordinating Council domain), redirecting visitors to a weaponized proof-of-concept for CVE-2019-5782 (Chrome) that loads shellcode to fetch three backdoors (“1.jpg,” “2.jpg,” “3.jpg”) and exploiting CVE-2020-0674 (Internet Explorer) via a PowerShell loader (with optional LPE via CVE-2019-1458), alongside prior flaws CVE-2016-0189 and CVE-2019-1458; two new malware variants (dneSpy and agfSpy) extend system-information exfiltration and remote-control capabilities, underscoring the need for organizations to patch affected browsers, CMS platforms, audit Mattermost usage for unauthorized channels, and monitor for anomalous shellcode or PowerShell activity to disrupt SLUB’s evolving toolkit.
retrieved_context.title: Operation Earth Kitsune: Tracking SLUB’s Current Operations | Trend Micro (US)

retrieved_context.text: After a year-long investigation researchers at Lumen’s Black Lotus Labs dissected the Ngioweb botnet—first observed in 2017—which uses a loader network and roughly 15 n-day exploits to deploy malware that contacts C2 domains generated via a domain generation algorithm (augmented by DNS TXT records to resist sinkholing), evaluates device traffic capacity, and links compromised Zyxel, Reolink, Alpha Technologies and, increasingly, Netgear routers (now 10 % of bots) to over 180 “backconnect” C2 nodes that provide at least 80 % of the 35,000 residential proxies in the NSOCKS[.]net service across 180 countries; NSOCKS’s lack of authentication and appearance on free proxy lists has enabled cybercriminals to carry out DDoS amplification, credential stuffing, phishing and malware proxying (e.g., Agent Tesla), while APT28 state-sponsored actors have mixed espionage with criminal traffic on the same infrastructure. To disrupt both operations, Lumen, alongside The ShadowServer Foundation and other partners, is actively blocking traffic to known C2 nodes and publishing indicators of compromise to help organizations identify and remediate infected devices.
retrieved_context.title: Botnet fueling residential proxies disrupted in cybercrime crackdown

retrieved_context.text: Microsoft’s analysis of the PipeMagic backdoor—a modular, in-memory framework masquerading as an open-source ChatGPT desktop app—reveals a stealthy, extensible architecture that Storm-2460 (linked to RansomEXX ransomware) has leveraged since early 2025 to exploit a Windows zero-day (CVE-2025-29824) across targets in the US, Europe, South America and the Middle East. PipeMagic offloads C&C communication and core tasks to discrete modules delivered via named pipes and organized in four doubly linked list structures in memory (for raw payloads, loaded modules, networking code and dynamic calls), allowing granular control over execution, module enumeration, deletion and persistent C&C connectivity without touching disk. Once the networking module establishes contact, the backdoor harvests extensive system telemetry, awaits operator commands to load or invoke specific modules, and can self-terminate or shut down communications on demand. Microsoft warns that PipeMagic’s in-memory, modular design presents significant detection challenges and underscores the need for pipeline-level monitoring and memory forensics to disrupt this financially motivated threat.
retrieved_context.title: Microsoft Dissects PipeMagic Modular Backdoor

hits.text: A zero-day VPN vulnerability provided initial access for a sophisticated threat actor who employed publicly available penetration‐testing and exploitation tools—SoftPerfect Network Scanner for network discovery, PsExec to deploy ServeManager.exe (the FiveHands ransomware variant using lattice-based NTRUEncrypt public key cryptography), and SombRAT for remote information theft—alongside RouterScan, grabff.exe, rclone.exe, and s3browser-9-5-3.exe to harvest credentials and exfiltrate data. Once inside, the attacker leveraged Windows Management Instrumentation (T1047) to enumerate and delete Volume Shadow Copies (Inhibit System Recovery, T1490), encrypted files (including those in recovery folders) for impact (T1486), and dropped ransom notes across directories, demanding payment to restore access. Post-encryption activities align with MITRE techniques such as Access Token Manipulation, Boot or Logon Autostart, PowerShell command and scripting interpreter, Domain Trust Discovery, Process Discovery, Screen Capture, and Kerberoasting. The combined use of FiveHands ransomware and SombRAT RAT resulted in both data theft and destruction of backup artifacts, underscoring the need for proactive patch management, network segmentation, strict credential hygiene, and rapid incident response to mitigate novel lattice-based encryption threats.
hits.title: FiveHands Ransomware Overview

hits.text: Trend Micro’s investigation into the LockBit ransomware-as-a-service operation, tracked as intrusion set Water Selkie, reveals the group’s marketing of its lightning-fast AES-128 head-only file encryption (first 4 KB) with RSA-wrapped keys, deployed via versatile affiliate-driven campaigns that source initial access through phishing (T1566), CVE-2018-13379 Fortinet VPN exploits (T1190) and compromised RDP/VPN accounts (T1078), then execute payloads via PowerShell Empire, Meterpreter, scheduled tasks or signed binaries (T1059, T1218), evade defenses with Mimikatz, GMER, Process Hacker or disabled Windows Defender (T1562), discover network shares and AD servers (T1083, T1135), laterally propagate via SMB or Cobalt Strike (T1570), exfiltrate data using StealBit or cloud storage (T1567) and encrypt data for impact (T1486), often on weekdays (~78%). Between July 2021 and January 2022 LockBit attempts surged globally—chiefly the US, India and Brazil—targeting healthcare and education yet boasting 41 leak-site victims (Dec 2021–Jan 2022) primarily SMBs (65.9%) across North America, Europe and APAC. With a professional affiliate program fueling continuous innovation and predicted upticks in supply-chain attacks in 2022, organizations should implement comprehensive asset inventory, least-privilege access, regular patching (including Fortinet CVE-2018-13379), RDP/VPN lockdown, application allow-listing, multifactor authentication, offline backups and MITRE TTP monitoring to detect and disrupt LockBit activity.
hits.title: Ransomware Spotlight: LockBit | Trend Micro (US)

canonical_entities: ZIP files masquerading as legitimate updates
hits.text: Unit 42 has observed a sharp rise in post-intrusion WastedLocker ransomware attacks by the Evil Corp group—already known for Dridex—against large U.S. organizations in sectors from manufacturing to legal services, with initial compromise typically via ZIP files masquerading as legitimate updates that deploy a SocGholish JavaScript loader to profile systems and invoke PowerShell-based Cobalt Strike payloads; attackers then leverage WMI and PsExec for lateral movement, identify high-value and backup systems, elevate privileges, disable Windows Defender, delete shadow copies, install WastedLocker as a service, and encrypt files using a “.<victim_name>wasted” extension while appending ransom notes (“.<victim_name>wasted_info”) with contact addresses on ProtonMail, Airmail and others. Palo Alto Networks’ WildFire, Cortex XDR (anti-ransomware and behavioral threat protection), NGFW DNS signatures and AutoFocus tagging detect and prevent WastedLocker activity; organizations are urged to implement robust, off-site backup strategies and hardened cybersecurity controls to mitigate this high-impact targeted ransomware threat.
hits.title: Threat Assessment: WastedLocker Ransomware

canonical_entities: U.S. energy, oil and gas utilities
U.S. law firm Hunter Taubman Fischer & Li
Indicator Removal on Host: Clear Windows Event Logs
hits.text: Lynx ransomware, emerging in July 2024 as the INC ransomware successor under a Ransomware-as-a-Service model, employs a sophisticated double-extortion strategy—exfiltrating data prior to encryption and threatening publication on a leak site—and reuses significant INC source code. Between July and November 2024, it disrupted U.S. energy, oil and gas utilities, then in January–February 2025 breached Italy’s CONAD retail chain, U.S. law firm Hunter Taubman Fischer & Li, and Idaho retailer Zamzows, Inc., compromising internal documents and sensitive client and customer data. Initial access leverages phishing (T1566.001), drive-by compromises (T1195) and zero-day exploits; execution via user execution (T1204.002) and scripting interpreters (T1059.001); persistence through autostart mechanisms (T1070.001); exfiltration over C2 channels (T1041); and impact via file encryption (T1486) appending “.LYNX.” Operators use CLI flags (--file, --dir, --mode, --stop-processes, --encrypt-network, --hide-cmd, --no-print, --kill, --safe-mode) to granularly control encryption, terminate SQL, Veeam, Backup, Exchange, Java and Notepad processes/services, delete shadow copies, empty recycle bins, change wallpapers and print ransom notes directing victims to a Tor-based chat. Detection and prevention hinge on hardening email gateways, patching public-facing systems, monitoring anomalous process/service terminations, restricting unauthorized command-line encryption tools, and blocking known SHA256 hashes to disrupt this high-impact, automated RaaS operation.
hits.title: Lynx Ransomware: INC Ransomware Reincarnated - Threat Actors

hits.text: Following the December 9 disclosure of critical Log4j flaws (CVE-2021-44228 “Log4Shell,” CVE-2021-45046 and CVE-2021-45105), Symantec observed widespread exploitation via obfuscated jndi lookups over LDAP and RMI (with ${env}, ${lower}, ${::-} tricks) and secondary scans over IIOP, DNS, HTTP and NIS, delivering payloads from Muhstik botnet Java class files that drop ELF installers, XMRig miners via PowerShell, Java backdoors awaiting remote commands, reverse Bash shells and public threats including Dridex, Orcus RAT, Khonsari and Conti ransomware; between December 9–21, its IPS blocked 93 million Log4Shell attempts on 270 000 endpoints and 18 million on 60 000 servers—primarily targeting systems in the U.S. and U.K. and originating from the U.S., Germany, Russia, the U.K. and China—highlighting rapid global weaponization; actionable defenses include enforcing multi-layered DCS policies to prevent malware execution from temp or writable paths, sandboxing Java apps, restricting outbound LDAP/HTTP connections, whitelisting necessary proxy tools (*/curl, */wget), and updating detection rules to flag jndi:* patterns in web and Log4j logs for immediate alerting and mitigation.
hits.title: Log4j Vulnerabilities: Attack Insights | Symantec Enterprise Blogs

hits.text: On Oct. 10, 2023, Citrix released patches for Netscaler ADC and Gateway to address Citrix Bleed (CVE-2023-4966, CVSS 9.4), a memory-leak vulnerability allowing unauthenticated attackers to exfiltrate session tokens via crafted requests and hijack sessions; public proof-of-concept code from Assetnote and Python exploit scripts rapidly empowered ransomware affiliates and other threat actors to gain footholds, with Unit 42 Incident Response and Managed Threat Hunting teams observing exploitation-linked remote PowerShell sessions spawning cmd.exe, reconnaissance commands (whoami, WMIC, tasklist, net user), deployment of XScan (s.exe), Python HTTP servers, and mRemoteNG on VDI hosts—though no lateral movement beyond VDI was detected. Cortex Xpanse identified nearly 8,000 exposed Netscaler Gateway and 6,000 ADC IPs worldwide (3,100 US, 800 Germany, 450 China, 400 UK), prompting addition to the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog. Palo Alto Networks advises immediate patching (including CVE-2023-4967), engagement of Unit 42 for incident response and continuous hunting, deployment of Next-Generation Firewalls with Advanced Threat Prevention signature 94483, updated Advanced WildFire ML models, Cortex Xpanse Threat Response Event, and Cortex XDR/XSIAM behavioral, anti-webshell, and credential-gathering protections to detect and block post-exploitation activity.
hits.title: Threat Brief: Citrix Bleed CVE-2023-4966

hits.text: Following ConnectWise’s February 19 disclosure of two critical ScreenConnect flaws—CVE-2024-1709 (CVSS 10.0 authentication bypass) and CVE-2024-1708 (CVSS 8.4 path traversal)—an updated advisory two days later warned of active exploitation, and by week’s end a public SlashAndGrab PoC enabled threat actors to mimic admin roles, delete users and seize control. Trend Micro reports Black Basta leveraging these bugs for reconnaissance, AD discovery, privilege escalation, creation of new admin accounts, deployment of Cobalt Strike beacons and scripts to trace recent AD connections before dropping ransomware. Bl00dy similarly abused leaked Conti and LockBit builders to plant ransom notes, while other groups installed XWorm RAT, disabled Windows Defender real-time protection and deployed alternate RMM tools (Atera, Syncro). Immediate patching to ScreenConnect 23.9.8 is critical to halt ongoing remote-access intrusions, ransomware deployment and potential data theft.
hits.title: Black Basta, Bl00dy Ransomware Exploiting Recent ScreenConnect Flaws - SecurityWeek

canonical_entities: military and government organizations in Hong Kong, Taiwan, Vietnam, the Philippines and Indonesia
hits.text: In their June 16, 2015 report, Unit 42 unveiled Operation Lotus Blossom, a three-year, state-sponsored cyber-espionage campaign against military and government organizations in Hong Kong, Taiwan, Vietnam, the Philippines and Indonesia, in which over 50 spearphishing attacks exploited enticing subject lines and decoy personnel-roster documents to deploy the custom “Elise” Trojan backdoor in three variants capable of evading virtual-machine analysis, contacting C2 servers for instructions and exfiltrating data; Unit 42’s use of Palo Alto Networks’ AutoFocus and WildFire platforms enabled the rapid correlation of samples and the deployment of IPS signature 14358 to block Elise, and they recommend that defenders review the published indicators of compromise in the full report and GitHub repo, bolster email security controls and ensure WildFire and Threat Prevention signatures are properly implemented to thwart future Lotus Blossom intrusions.
hits.title: Operation Lotus Blossom: A New Nation-State Cyberthreat?

canonical_entities: Palo Alto Networks NGFW Advanced Threat Prevention
hits.text: Since its debut in 2017 as an advanced .NET second-stage backdoor, Kazuar—attributed to Russian FSB–linked Pensive Ursa (Turla)—reemerged in July 2023 targeting Ukraine’s defense sector alongside a new Capibar first-stage loader, marking its first wild appearance since late 2020. This upgraded variant features extensive stealth and anti-analysis countermeasures—fake 2008 compilation timestamps, custom multi-layer string encryption, assembly-location checks and GUID-based pseudorandom directory and mutex generation—and boasts 45 C2-driven commands for comprehensive system profiling, data collection and credential theft from cloud platforms, source control and Signal. It supports six injection modes (inject, zombify, combined, remote, single and non-interactive), a multithreaded architecture for asynchronous task execution, and a hybrid AES–RSA encryption scheme for task/result files, complicating forensic recovery. Organizations can detect and block Kazuar with Palo Alto Networks NGFW Advanced Threat Prevention, Cortex XDR/XSIAM and WildFire, and engage Unit 42 Incident Response teams for targeted hunting and mitigation guidance.
hits.title: Over the Kazuar’s Nest: Cracking Down on a Freshly Hatched Backdoor Used by Pensive Ursa (Aka Turla)

hits.text: CL0P, a prolific ransomware affiliate of TA505 that exploited the MOVEit Transfer zero-day in May 2023 to compromise over 3,000 U.S. and 8,000 global organizations, has shifted its data-leak operations from slow Tor-hosted zip downloads to decentralized BitTorrent distribution using magnet links and DHT trackers to handle terabytes of stolen data and re-pressure non-paying victims, enabling researchers to rapidly join swarms and identify 100 percent seeders by monitoring leak-site announcements, capturing peer IPs, torrent client fingerprints and connection metadata; this technique not only exposes CL0P’s initial seeding infrastructure and tradecraft opsec gaps but also underscores the need for organizations to deploy behavioral threat protection (e.g., Cortex XDR/XSIAM), continuously scan for MOVEit Transfer exposures (Cortex Xpanse), and engage Unit 42 incident response for tailored threat hunting and mitigation.
hits.title: CL0P Seeds ^_- Gotta Catch Em All!

Initial access leverages phishing (T1566.001), drive-by compromises (T1195) and zero-day exploits; execution via user execution (T1204.002) and scripting interpreters (T1059.001); persistence through autostart mechanisms (T1070.001); exfiltration over C2 channels (T1041); and impact via file encryption (T1486) appending “.LYNX.” Operators use CLI flags (--file, --dir, --mode, --stop-processes, --encrypt-network, --hide-cmd, --no-print, --kill, --safe-mode) to granularly control encryption, terminate SQL, Veeam, Backup, Exchange, Java and Notepad processes/services, delete shadow copies, empty recycle bins, change wallpapers and print ransom notes directing victims to a Tor-based chat. Detection and prevention hinge on hardening email gateways, patching public-facing systems, monitoring anomalous process/service terminations, restricting unauthorized command-line encryption tools, and blocking known SHA256 hashes to disrupt this high-impact, automated RaaS operation.
retrieved_context.title: Lynx Ransomware: INC Ransomware Reincarnated - Threat Actors

retrieved_context.text: Following the December 9 disclosure of critical Log4j flaws (CVE-2021-44228 “Log4Shell,” CVE-2021-45046 and CVE-2021-45105), Symantec observed widespread exploitation via obfuscated jndi lookups over LDAP and RMI (with ${env}, ${lower}, ${::-} tricks) and secondary scans over IIOP, DNS, HTTP and NIS, delivering payloads from Muhstik botnet Java class files that drop ELF installers, XMRig miners via PowerShell, Java backdoors awaiting remote commands, reverse Bash shells and public threats including Dridex, Orcus RAT, Khonsari and Conti ransomware; between December 9–21, its IPS blocked 93 million Log4Shell attempts on 270 000 endpoints and 18 million on 60 000 servers—primarily targeting systems in the U.S. and U.K. and originating from the U.S., Germany, Russia, the U.K. and China—highlighting rapid global weaponization; actionable defenses include enforcing multi-layered DCS policies to prevent malware execution from temp or writable paths, sandboxing Java apps, restricting outbound LDAP/HTTP connections, whitelisting necessary proxy tools (*/curl, */wget), and updating detection rules to flag jndi:* patterns in web and Log4j logs for immediate alerting and mitigation.
retrieved_context.title: Log4j Vulnerabilities: Attack Insights | Symantec Enterprise Blogs

retrieved_context.text: On Oct. 10, 2023, Citrix released patches for Netscaler ADC and Gateway to address Citrix Bleed (CVE-2023-4966, CVSS 9.4), a memory-leak vulnerability allowing unauthenticated attackers to exfiltrate session tokens via crafted requests and hijack sessions; public proof-of-concept code from Assetnote and Python exploit scripts rapidly empowered ransomware affiliates and other threat actors to gain footholds, with Unit 42 Incident Response and Managed Threat Hunting teams observing exploitation-linked remote PowerShell sessions spawning cmd.exe, reconnaissance commands (whoami, WMIC, tasklist, net user), deployment of XScan (s.exe), Python HTTP servers, and mRemoteNG on VDI hosts—though no lateral movement beyond VDI was detected. Cortex Xpanse identified nearly 8,000 exposed Netscaler Gateway and 6,000 ADC IPs worldwide (3,100 US, 800 Germany, 450 China, 400 UK), prompting addition to the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog. Palo Alto Networks advises immediate patching (including CVE-2023-4967), engagement of Unit 42 for incident response and continuous hunting, deployment of Next-Generation Firewalls with Advanced Threat Prevention signature 94483, updated Advanced WildFire ML models, Cortex Xpanse Threat Response Event, and Cortex XDR/XSIAM behavioral, anti-webshell, and credential-gathering protections to detect and block post-exploitation activity.
retrieved_context.title: Threat Brief: Citrix Bleed CVE-2023-4966

retrieved_context.text: Following ConnectWise’s February 19 disclosure of two critical ScreenConnect flaws—CVE-2024-1709 (CVSS 10.0 authentication bypass) and CVE-2024-1708 (CVSS 8.4 path traversal)—an updated advisory two days later warned of active exploitation, and by week’s end a public SlashAndGrab PoC enabled threat actors to mimic admin roles, delete users and seize control. Trend Micro reports Black Basta leveraging these bugs for reconnaissance, AD discovery, privilege escalation, creation of new admin accounts, deployment of Cobalt Strike beacons and scripts to trace recent AD connections before dropping ransomware. Bl00dy similarly abused leaked Conti and LockBit builders to plant ransom notes, while other groups installed XWorm RAT, disabled Windows Defender real-time protection and deployed alternate RMM tools (Atera, Syncro). Immediate patching to ScreenConnect 23.9.8 is critical to halt ongoing remote-access intrusions, ransomware deployment and potential data theft.
retrieved_context.title: Black Basta, Bl00dy Ransomware Exploiting Recent ScreenConnect Flaws - SecurityWeek

canonical_entities: military and government organizations in Hong Kong, Taiwan, Vietnam, the Philippines and Indonesia
retrieved_context.text: In their June 16, 2015 report, Unit 42 unveiled Operation Lotus Blossom, a three-year, state-sponsored cyber-espionage campaign against military and government organizations in Hong Kong, Taiwan, Vietnam, the Philippines and Indonesia, in which over 50 spearphishing attacks exploited enticing subject lines and decoy personnel-roster documents to deploy the custom “Elise” Trojan backdoor in three variants capable of evading virtual-machine analysis, contacting C2 servers for instructions and exfiltrating data; Unit 42’s use of Palo Alto Networks’ AutoFocus and WildFire platforms enabled the rapid correlation of samples and the deployment of IPS signature 14358 to block Elise, and they recommend that defenders review the published indicators of compromise in the full report and GitHub repo, bolster email security controls and ensure WildFire and Threat Prevention signatures are properly implemented to thwart future Lotus Blossom intrusions.
retrieved_context.title: Operation Lotus Blossom: A New Nation-State Cyberthreat?

canonical_entities: Palo Alto Networks NGFW Advanced Threat Prevention
retrieved_context.text: Since its debut in 2017 as an advanced .NET second-stage backdoor, Kazuar—attributed to Russian FSB–linked Pensive Ursa (Turla)—reemerged in July 2023 targeting Ukraine’s defense sector alongside a new Capibar first-stage loader, marking its first wild appearance since late 2020. This upgraded variant features extensive stealth and anti-analysis countermeasures—fake 2008 compilation timestamps, custom multi-layer string encryption, assembly-location checks and GUID-based pseudorandom directory and mutex generation—and boasts 45 C2-driven commands for comprehensive system profiling, data collection and credential theft from cloud platforms, source control and Signal. It supports six injection modes (inject, zombify, combined, remote, single and non-interactive), a multithreaded architecture for asynchronous task execution, and a hybrid AES–RSA encryption scheme for task/result files, complicating forensic recovery. Organizations can detect and block Kazuar with Palo Alto Networks NGFW Advanced Threat Prevention, Cortex XDR/XSIAM and WildFire, and engage Unit 42 Incident Response teams for targeted hunting and mitigation guidance.
retrieved_context.title: Over the Kazuar’s Nest: Cracking Down on a Freshly Hatched Backdoor Used by Pensive Ursa (Aka Turla)

retrieved_context.text: CL0P, a prolific ransomware affiliate of TA505 that exploited the MOVEit Transfer zero-day in May 2023 to compromise over 3,000 U.S. and 8,000 global organizations, has shifted its data-leak operations from slow Tor-hosted zip downloads to decentralized BitTorrent distribution using magnet links and DHT trackers to handle terabytes of stolen data and re-pressure non-paying victims, enabling researchers to rapidly join swarms and identify 100 percent seeders by monitoring leak-site announcements, capturing peer IPs, torrent client fingerprints and connection metadata; this technique not only exposes CL0P’s initial seeding infrastructure and tradecraft opsec gaps but also underscores the need for organizations to deploy behavioral threat protection (e.g., Cortex XDR/XSIAM), continuously scan for MOVEit Transfer exposures (Cortex Xpanse), and engage Unit 42 incident response for tailored threat hunting and mitigation.
retrieved_context.title: CL0P Seeds ^_- Gotta Catch Em All!

hits.text: A zero-day VPN vulnerability provided initial access for a sophisticated threat actor who employed publicly available penetration‐testing and exploitation tools—SoftPerfect Network Scanner for network discovery, PsExec to deploy ServeManager.exe (the FiveHands ransomware variant using lattice-based NTRUEncrypt public key cryptography), and SombRAT for remote information theft—alongside RouterScan, grabff.exe, rclone.exe, and s3browser-9-5-3.exe to harvest credentials and exfiltrate data. Once inside, the attacker leveraged Windows Management Instrumentation (T1047) to enumerate and delete Volume Shadow Copies (Inhibit System Recovery, T1490), encrypted files (including those in recovery folders) for impact (T1486), and dropped ransom notes across directories, demanding payment to restore access. Post-encryption activities align with MITRE techniques such as Access Token Manipulation, Boot or Logon Autostart, PowerShell command and scripting interpreter, Domain Trust Discovery, Process Discovery, Screen Capture, and Kerberoasting. The combined use of FiveHands ransomware and SombRAT RAT resulted in both data theft and destruction of backup artifacts, underscoring the need for proactive patch management, network segmentation, strict credential hygiene, and rapid incident response to mitigate novel lattice-based encryption threats.
hits.title: FiveHands Ransomware Overview

hits.text: Trend Micro’s investigation into the LockBit ransomware-as-a-service operation, tracked as intrusion set Water Selkie, reveals the group’s marketing of its lightning-fast AES-128 head-only file encryption (first 4 KB) with RSA-wrapped keys, deployed via versatile affiliate-driven campaigns that source initial access through phishing (T1566), CVE-2018-13379 Fortinet VPN exploits (T1190) and compromised RDP/VPN accounts (T1078), then execute payloads via PowerShell Empire, Meterpreter, scheduled tasks or signed binaries (T1059, T1218), evade defenses with Mimikatz, GMER, Process Hacker or disabled Windows Defender (T1562), discover network shares and AD servers (T1083, T1135), laterally propagate via SMB or Cobalt Strike (T1570), exfiltrate data using StealBit or cloud storage (T1567) and encrypt data for impact (T1486), often on weekdays (~78%). Between July 2021 and January 2022 LockBit attempts surged globally—chiefly the US, India and Brazil—targeting healthcare and education yet boasting 41 leak-site victims (Dec 2021–Jan 2022) primarily SMBs (65.9%) across North America, Europe and APAC. With a professional affiliate program fueling continuous innovation and predicted upticks in supply-chain attacks in 2022, organizations should implement comprehensive asset inventory, least-privilege access, regular patching (including Fortinet CVE-2018-13379), RDP/VPN lockdown, application allow-listing, multifactor authentication, offline backups and MITRE TTP monitoring to detect and disrupt LockBit activity.
hits.title: Ransomware Spotlight: LockBit | Trend Micro (US)

hits.text: Unit 42 has observed a sharp rise in post-intrusion WastedLocker ransomware attacks by the Evil Corp group—already known for Dridex—against large U.S. organizations in sectors from manufacturing to legal services, with initial compromise typically via ZIP files masquerading as legitimate updates that deploy a SocGholish JavaScript loader to profile systems and invoke PowerShell-based Cobalt Strike payloads; attackers then leverage WMI and PsExec for lateral movement, identify high-value and backup systems, elevate privileges, disable Windows Defender, delete shadow copies, install WastedLocker as a service, and encrypt files using a “.<victim_name>wasted” extension while appending ransom notes (“.<victim_name>wasted_info”) with contact addresses on ProtonMail, Airmail and others. Palo Alto Networks’ WildFire, Cortex XDR (anti-ransomware and behavioral threat protection), NGFW DNS signatures and AutoFocus tagging detect and prevent WastedLocker activity; organizations are urged to implement robust, off-site backup strategies and hardened cybersecurity controls to mitigate this high-impact targeted ransomware threat.

This upgraded variant features extensive stealth and anti-analysis countermeasures—fake 2008 compilation timestamps, custom multi-layer string encryption, assembly-location checks and GUID-based pseudorandom directory and mutex generation—and boasts 45 C2-driven commands for comprehensive system profiling, data collection and credential theft from cloud platforms, source control and Signal. It supports six injection modes (inject, zombify, combined, remote, single and non-interactive), a multithreaded architecture for asynchronous task execution, and a hybrid AES–RSA encryption scheme for task/result files, complicating forensic recovery. Organizations can detect and block Kazuar with Palo Alto Networks NGFW Advanced Threat Prevention, Cortex XDR/XSIAM and WildFire, and engage Unit 42 Incident Response teams for targeted hunting and mitigation guidance.
retrieved_context.title: Over the Kazuar’s Nest: Cracking Down on a Freshly Hatched Backdoor Used by Pensive Ursa (Aka Turla)

retrieved_context.text: CL0P, a prolific ransomware affiliate of TA505 that exploited the MOVEit Transfer zero-day in May 2023 to compromise over 3,000 U.S. and 8,000 global organizations, has shifted its data-leak operations from slow Tor-hosted zip downloads to decentralized BitTorrent distribution using magnet links and DHT trackers to handle terabytes of stolen data and re-pressure non-paying victims, enabling researchers to rapidly join swarms and identify 100 percent seeders by monitoring leak-site announcements, capturing peer IPs, torrent client fingerprints and connection metadata; this technique not only exposes CL0P’s initial seeding infrastructure and tradecraft opsec gaps but also underscores the need for organizations to deploy behavioral threat protection (e.g., Cortex XDR/XSIAM), continuously scan for MOVEit Transfer exposures (Cortex Xpanse), and engage Unit 42 incident response for tailored threat hunting and mitigation.
retrieved_context.title: CL0P Seeds ^_- Gotta Catch Em All!

hits.text: A zero-day VPN vulnerability provided initial access for a sophisticated threat actor who employed publicly available penetration‐testing and exploitation tools—SoftPerfect Network Scanner for network discovery, PsExec to deploy ServeManager.exe (the FiveHands ransomware variant using lattice-based NTRUEncrypt public key cryptography), and SombRAT for remote information theft—alongside RouterScan, grabff.exe, rclone.exe, and s3browser-9-5-3.exe to harvest credentials and exfiltrate data. Once inside, the attacker leveraged Windows Management Instrumentation (T1047) to enumerate and delete Volume Shadow Copies (Inhibit System Recovery, T1490), encrypted files (including those in recovery folders) for impact (T1486), and dropped ransom notes across directories, demanding payment to restore access. Post-encryption activities align with MITRE techniques such as Access Token Manipulation, Boot or Logon Autostart, PowerShell command and scripting interpreter, Domain Trust Discovery, Process Discovery, Screen Capture, and Kerberoasting. The combined use of FiveHands ransomware and SombRAT RAT resulted in both data theft and destruction of backup artifacts, underscoring the need for proactive patch management, network segmentation, strict credential hygiene, and rapid incident response to mitigate novel lattice-based encryption threats.
hits.title: FiveHands Ransomware Overview

hits.text: Trend Micro’s investigation into the LockBit ransomware-as-a-service operation, tracked as intrusion set Water Selkie, reveals the group’s marketing of its lightning-fast AES-128 head-only file encryption (first 4 KB) with RSA-wrapped keys, deployed via versatile affiliate-driven campaigns that source initial access through phishing (T1566), CVE-2018-13379 Fortinet VPN exploits (T1190) and compromised RDP/VPN accounts (T1078), then execute payloads via PowerShell Empire, Meterpreter, scheduled tasks or signed binaries (T1059, T1218), evade defenses with Mimikatz, GMER, Process Hacker or disabled Windows Defender (T1562), discover network shares and AD servers (T1083, T1135), laterally propagate via SMB or Cobalt Strike (T1570), exfiltrate data using StealBit or cloud storage (T1567) and encrypt data for impact (T1486), often on weekdays (~78%). Between July 2021 and January 2022 LockBit attempts surged globally—chiefly the US, India and Brazil—targeting healthcare and education yet boasting 41 leak-site victims (Dec 2021–Jan 2022) primarily SMBs (65.9%) across North America, Europe and APAC. With a professional affiliate program fueling continuous innovation and predicted upticks in supply-chain attacks in 2022, organizations should implement comprehensive asset inventory, least-privilege access, regular patching (including Fortinet CVE-2018-13379), RDP/VPN lockdown, application allow-listing, multifactor authentication, offline backups and MITRE TTP monitoring to detect and disrupt LockBit activity.
hits.title: Ransomware Spotlight: LockBit | Trend Micro (US)

hits.text: Unit 42 has observed a sharp rise in post-intrusion WastedLocker ransomware attacks by the Evil Corp group—already known for Dridex—against large U.S. organizations in sectors from manufacturing to legal services, with initial compromise typically via ZIP files masquerading as legitimate updates that deploy a SocGholish JavaScript loader to profile systems and invoke PowerShell-based Cobalt Strike payloads; attackers then leverage WMI and PsExec for lateral movement, identify high-value and backup systems, elevate privileges, disable Windows Defender, delete shadow copies, install WastedLocker as a service, and encrypt files using a “.<victim_name>wasted” extension while appending ransom notes (“.<victim_name>wasted_info”) with contact addresses on ProtonMail, Airmail and others. Palo Alto Networks’ WildFire, Cortex XDR (anti-ransomware and behavioral threat protection), NGFW DNS signatures and AutoFocus tagging detect and prevent WastedLocker activity; organizations are urged to implement robust, off-site backup strategies and hardened cybersecurity controls to mitigate this high-impact targeted ransomware threat.

hits.text: On Oct. 10, 2023, Citrix released patches for Netscaler ADC and Gateway to address Citrix Bleed (CVE-2023-4966, CVSS 9.4), a memory-leak vulnerability allowing unauthenticated attackers to exfiltrate session tokens via crafted requests and hijack sessions; public proof-of-concept code from Assetnote and Python exploit scripts rapidly empowered ransomware affiliates and other threat actors to gain footholds, with Unit 42 Incident Response and Managed Threat Hunting teams observing exploitation-linked remote PowerShell sessions spawning cmd.exe, reconnaissance commands (whoami, WMIC, tasklist, net user), deployment of XScan (s.exe), Python HTTP servers, and mRemoteNG on VDI hosts—though no lateral movement beyond VDI was detected. Cortex Xpanse identified nearly 8,000 exposed Netscaler Gateway and 6,000 ADC IPs worldwide (3,100 US, 800 Germany, 450 China, 400 UK), prompting addition to the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog. Palo Alto Networks advises immediate patching (including CVE-2023-4967), engagement of Unit 42 for incident response and continuous hunting, deployment of Next-Generation Firewalls with Advanced Threat Prevention signature 94483, updated Advanced WildFire ML models, Cortex Xpanse Threat Response Event, and Cortex XDR/XSIAM behavioral, anti-webshell, and credential-gathering protections to detect and block post-exploitation activity.

canonical_entities: Launch EC2 instances across regions via VPN
hits.text: Unit42’s “EleKtra-Leak” campaign, active since December 2020, uses automated scripts to clone public GitHub repos every few minutes, extract exposed AWS IAM keys within five minutes, then—if not blocked by GitHub-AWS quarantine policies—execute rapid AWS reconnaissance (DescribeRegions), create security groups, and launch hundreds of EC2 instances across regions via VPN for Monero cryptojacking, generating over 400 API calls in seven minutes. Between Aug. 30 and Oct. 6, 2023, researchers tracked 474 actor-controlled miners. The actor employs custom mining software and blocklists high-profile AWS account IDs to avoid honey traps. Leveraging the Prisma Cloud HoneyCloud project’s ephemeral key leaks and policy overrides, Unit42 obtained full visibility, informing Prisma Cloud Secrets Security, CI/CD IaC scanning, Cortex XDR, and recommendations for independent repo scanning, strict IAM policies, and continuous monitoring.
hits.title: CloudKeys in the Air: Tracking Malicious Operations of Exposed IAM Keys

hits.text: Unit 42 researchers uncovered a targeted Lampion infostealer campaign in late 2024–early 2025 against Portuguese government, finance and transportation organizations that reuses infrastructure and TTPs dating back to 2019 while introducing ClickFix social-engineering lures—victims receive a phishing email with a malicious ZIP attachment containing an HTML redirect to autoridade-tributaria[.]com, where they are duped into copying a “#Habilitar Visualização de ficheiro” PowerShell command into the Run dialog; this command downloads an obfuscated Visual Basic script (stage 1) that writes a second-stage downloader in %TEMP% and schedules its execution, which in turn fetches a third-stage 30–50 MB VBS stager responsible for reconnaissance (WMI AV checks, VM/sandbox detection, MD5-based victim ID Base64 exfiltration) and constructs a hostname-named .cmd file in the Startup folder to trigger system shutdown and launch a fourth-stage >700 MB DLL loader via rundll32.exe using Portuguese-named exports, although the final Lampion payload download was commented out—this dispersed, highly obfuscated multi-stage chain highlights the need for enhanced PowerShell/VBScript monitoring, advanced detection (Cortex XDR VBS Local Analysis, WildFire, URL Filtering, DNS Security) and ClickFix awareness training to thwart sophisticated banking-credential theft.
hits.title: Lampion Is Back With ClickFix Lures

hits.text: In a Unit 42 incident response to a suspected Black Basta breach, analysts discovered a novel USB-spreading variant of the decade-old Chinese-linked PlugX implant alongside GootLoader and Brute Ratel C4, revealing that attackers hijack the digitally-signed x32dbg.exe debugger via DLL side-loading (MITRE T1574.002) by deploying a malicious, unsigned x32bridge.dll to load an encrypted payload (x32bridge.dat) into memory, then infect both host and attached removable media by creating hidden no-break space (U+00A0) directory trees (e.g., \\u00A0\\u00A0\\RECYCLER.BIN\\files) with custom desktop.ini icons and obfuscated .lnk shortcuts that execute via %comspec%/q/c to evade Windows Explorer and cmd.exe (visible only through Unix-like mounts or forensic tools); a related PlugX variant further exfiltrates Adobe PDF and Word files into a concealed “da520e5” subfolder, underscoring evolving persistence, lateral-spread and data-theft capabilities used in high-profile incidents (e.g., the 2015 OPM breach), and highlighting the need for robust detection and prevention via solutions like Cortex XDR and WildFire.
hits.title: Chinese PlugX Malware Hidden in Your USB Devices?

canonical_entities: RansomEXX activity from March 31, 2021 to March 31, 2022
Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Tools
hits.text: Trend Micro’s analysis of RansomEXX activity from March 31, 2021 to March 31, 2022 reveals a predominantly human-operated ransomware campaign that hit the manufacturing sector hardest (followed by education and banking) with the highest attack attempts observed in the U.S., France, and Brazil—driven in part by a high-profile 2021 breach of a Taiwanese hardware manufacturer. Initial access is achieved via malspam delivering multi-stage payloads that leverage IcedID and TrickBot for footholds, deploy Cobalt Strike beacons and PyXie RAT for code execution and data exfiltration, use SMB to propagate a VATET loader for lateral movement, and employ Mimikatz and LaZagne for credential harvesting. Upon execution, RansomEXX evades defense by disabling tools (T1562.001), skipping encryption of critical Windows paths, file names, and extensions, and terminating hundreds of business and security processes to maximize impact (T1486, T1490), then encrypts data and demands ransom. Recommended mitigations include strict audit and asset inventory, hardened configurations and least-privilege access, macro and email sandboxing to block malspam entry, regular patching and virtual patching, multifactor authentication, advanced behavior-based detection (e.g., Trend Micro Vision One™), and continuous employee training and red-team testing to disrupt the ransomware kill chain and protect against future RansomEXX intrusions.
hits.title: Ransomware Spotlight: RansomEXX | Trend Micro (US)
