hits.text: In their June 16, 2015 report, Unit 42 unveiled Operation Lotus Blossom, a three-year, state-sponsored cyber-espionage campaign against military and government organizations in Hong Kong, Taiwan, Vietnam, the Philippines and Indonesia, in which over 50 spearphishing attacks exploited enticing subject lines and decoy personnel-roster documents to deploy the custom “Elise” Trojan backdoor in three variants capable of evading virtual-machine analysis, contacting C2 servers for instructions and exfiltrating data; Unit 42’s use of Palo Alto Networks’ AutoFocus and WildFire platforms enabled the rapid correlation of samples and the deployment of IPS signature 14358 to block Elise, and they recommend that defenders review the published indicators of compromise in the full report and GitHub repo, bolster email security controls and ensure WildFire and Threat Prevention signatures are properly implemented to thwart future Lotus Blossom intrusions.
hits.title: Operation Lotus Blossom: A New Nation-State Cyberthreat?

hits.text: Following ConnectWise’s February 19 disclosure of two critical ScreenConnect flaws—CVE-2024-1709 (CVSS 10.0 authentication bypass) and CVE-2024-1708 (CVSS 8.4 path traversal)—an updated advisory two days later warned of active exploitation, and by week’s end a public SlashAndGrab PoC enabled threat actors to mimic admin roles, delete users and seize control. Trend Micro reports Black Basta leveraging these bugs for reconnaissance, AD discovery, privilege escalation, creation of new admin accounts, deployment of Cobalt Strike beacons and scripts to trace recent AD connections before dropping ransomware. Bl00dy similarly abused leaked Conti and LockBit builders to plant ransom notes, while other groups installed XWorm RAT, disabled Windows Defender real-time protection and deployed alternate RMM tools (Atera, Syncro). Immediate patching to ScreenConnect 23.9.8 is critical to halt ongoing remote-access intrusions, ransomware deployment and potential data theft.
hits.title: Black Basta, Bl00dy Ransomware Exploiting Recent ScreenConnect Flaws - SecurityWeek

hits.text: On Oct. 10, 2023, Citrix released patches for Netscaler ADC and Gateway to address Citrix Bleed (CVE-2023-4966, CVSS 9.4), a memory-leak vulnerability allowing unauthenticated attackers to exfiltrate session tokens via crafted requests and hijack sessions; public proof-of-concept code from Assetnote and Python exploit scripts rapidly empowered ransomware affiliates and other threat actors to gain footholds, with Unit 42 Incident Response and Managed Threat Hunting teams observing exploitation-linked remote PowerShell sessions spawning cmd.exe, reconnaissance commands (whoami, WMIC, tasklist, net user), deployment of XScan (s.exe), Python HTTP servers, and mRemoteNG on VDI hosts—though no lateral movement beyond VDI was detected. Cortex Xpanse identified nearly 8,000 exposed Netscaler Gateway and 6,000 ADC IPs worldwide (3,100 US, 800 Germany, 450 China, 400 UK), prompting addition to the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog. Palo Alto Networks advises immediate patching (including CVE-2023-4967), engagement of Unit 42 for incident response and continuous hunting, deployment of Next-Generation Firewalls with Advanced Threat Prevention signature 94483, updated Advanced WildFire ML models, Cortex Xpanse Threat Response Event, and Cortex XDR/XSIAM behavioral, anti-webshell, and credential-gathering protections to detect and block post-exploitation activity.
hits.title: Threat Brief: Citrix Bleed CVE-2023-4966

hits.text: Following the December 9 disclosure of critical Log4j flaws (CVE-2021-44228 “Log4Shell,” CVE-2021-45046 and CVE-2021-45105), Symantec observed widespread exploitation via obfuscated jndi lookups over LDAP and RMI (with ${env}, ${lower}, ${::-} tricks) and secondary scans over IIOP, DNS, HTTP and NIS, delivering payloads from Muhstik botnet Java class files that drop ELF installers, XMRig miners via PowerShell, Java backdoors awaiting remote commands, reverse Bash shells and public threats including Dridex, Orcus RAT, Khonsari and Conti ransomware; between December 9–21, its IPS blocked 93 million Log4Shell attempts on 270 000 endpoints and 18 million on 60 000 servers—primarily targeting systems in the U.S. and U.K. and originating from the U.S., Germany, Russia, the U.K. and China—highlighting rapid global weaponization; actionable defenses include enforcing multi-layered DCS policies to prevent malware execution from temp or writable paths, sandboxing Java apps, restricting outbound LDAP/HTTP connections, whitelisting necessary proxy tools (*/curl, */wget), and updating detection rules to flag jndi:* patterns in web and Log4j logs for immediate alerting and mitigation.
hits.title: Log4j Vulnerabilities: Attack Insights | Symantec Enterprise Blogs

hits.text: Lynx ransomware, a Ransomware-as-a-Service strain first seen in mid-2024 that repurposes INC source code, has targeted finance, architecture and manufacturing organizations—later expanding into energy and APAC retail—via phishing emails that deploy malware to exfiltrate sensitive data for double-extortion (including timed “drip” leaks) before encrypting files with a “.LYNX” extension; Darktrace observed initial lateral movement through SMB enumeration on port 445 and Nmap scans, exploitation of default “admin”/“administrator” credentials via NTLM and Kerberos for privilege escalation, anomalous internal transfers of ~150 GiB over port 3260 and large uploads to wt-prod-euwest1-storm.s3.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com, plus AnyDesk-based remote sessions to aid operator actions, culminating in thousands of encrypted files detected by parallel SMB read/write anomalies and extension appends—Darktrace’s Autonomous Response models, if fully enabled, would automatically block suspicious SMB activity, unusual privileged user behavior and anomalous outbound connections to contain the threat and preserve business continuity.
hits.title: New Threat on the Prowl: Investigating Lynx Ransomware

canonical_entities: Palo Alto Networks NGFW Advanced Threat Prevention
hits.text: Since its debut in 2017 as an advanced .NET second-stage backdoor, Kazuar—attributed to Russian FSB–linked Pensive Ursa (Turla)—reemerged in July 2023 targeting Ukraine’s defense sector alongside a new Capibar first-stage loader, marking its first wild appearance since late 2020. This upgraded variant features extensive stealth and anti-analysis countermeasures—fake 2008 compilation timestamps, custom multi-layer string encryption, assembly-location checks and GUID-based pseudorandom directory and mutex generation—and boasts 45 C2-driven commands for comprehensive system profiling, data collection and credential theft from cloud platforms, source control and Signal. It supports six injection modes (inject, zombify, combined, remote, single and non-interactive), a multithreaded architecture for asynchronous task execution, and a hybrid AES–RSA encryption scheme for task/result files, complicating forensic recovery. Organizations can detect and block Kazuar with Palo Alto Networks NGFW Advanced Threat Prevention, Cortex XDR/XSIAM and WildFire, and engage Unit 42 Incident Response teams for targeted hunting and mitigation guidance.
hits.title: Over the Kazuar’s Nest: Cracking Down on a Freshly Hatched Backdoor Used by Pensive Ursa (Aka Turla)

canonical_entities: Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Tools
hits.text: Trend Micro data shows BlackCat executed 39.3% of its 176 manufacturing detections against US targets and confirmed 173 leak-site compromises from December 2021 to September 2022—58.7% US-based—favoring finance, professional, legal, technology, energy, utilities, construction, and manufacturing sectors, with small (52%) and midsize (26%) businesses most targeted. Initial access was achieved via Exchange CVE-2021-26855/26857/26858/27065 exploits, ConnectWise RCE, and SSH key abuse. Execution leverages COBEACON to inject the Rust-based ransomware into ntoskrnl.exe, evading detection; defense evasion includes disabling AV, using AdFind/ADRecon/SoftPerfect, Process Hacker, Mimikatz, WMIC, Netstat, and LSASS credential dumping. Lateral movement exploits embedded PsExec, RDP, MobaXterm, and BITSAdmin transfers of zzz.exe/xxx.exe/yyy.exe/sv.exe. C2 communication uses Base64-encoded PowerShell with a Cobalt Strike SMB beacon over named pipes. Exfiltration employs ExMatter (upgraded September 2022), 7-Zip, Rclone, MEGASync, WinSCP, and FreeFileSync for double extortion. The payload defaces backgrounds, terminates backup/AV/DB/Internet/VM services, disables recovery (shadow copy deletion, safe-mode variant), and appends variable Sphynx extensions while avoiding critical directories and file types. BlackCat maps to MITRE ATT&CK T1190, T1078, T1562.001/009, T1003.001, T1021.002, T1486, T1490, T1489, T1048/T1567. Security teams should patch Exchange CVEs, secure MSP tools, enforce least privilege, segment networks, monitor PowerShell injections, and vet outbound file transfers to disrupt this evolving affiliate-driven operation.

canonical_entities: ZIP files masquerading as legitimate updates
retrieved_context.text: Unit 42 has observed a sharp rise in post-intrusion WastedLocker ransomware attacks by the Evil Corp group—already known for Dridex—against large U.S. organizations in sectors from manufacturing to legal services, with initial compromise typically via ZIP files masquerading as legitimate updates that deploy a SocGholish JavaScript loader to profile systems and invoke PowerShell-based Cobalt Strike payloads; attackers then leverage WMI and PsExec for lateral movement, identify high-value and backup systems, elevate privileges, disable Windows Defender, delete shadow copies, install WastedLocker as a service, and encrypt files using a “.<victim_name>wasted” extension while appending ransom notes (“.<victim_name>wasted_info”) with contact addresses on ProtonMail, Airmail and others. Palo Alto Networks’ WildFire, Cortex XDR (anti-ransomware and behavioral threat protection), NGFW DNS signatures and AutoFocus tagging detect and prevent WastedLocker activity; organizations are urged to implement robust, off-site backup strategies and hardened cybersecurity controls to mitigate this high-impact targeted ransomware threat.
retrieved_context.title: Threat Assessment: WastedLocker Ransomware

retrieved_context.text: Trend Micro’s investigation into the LockBit ransomware-as-a-service operation, tracked as intrusion set Water Selkie, reveals the group’s marketing of its lightning-fast AES-128 head-only file encryption (first 4 KB) with RSA-wrapped keys, deployed via versatile affiliate-driven campaigns that source initial access through phishing (T1566), CVE-2018-13379 Fortinet VPN exploits (T1190) and compromised RDP/VPN accounts (T1078), then execute payloads via PowerShell Empire, Meterpreter, scheduled tasks or signed binaries (T1059, T1218), evade defenses with Mimikatz, GMER, Process Hacker or disabled Windows Defender (T1562), discover network shares and AD servers (T1083, T1135), laterally propagate via SMB or Cobalt Strike (T1570), exfiltrate data using StealBit or cloud storage (T1567) and encrypt data for impact (T1486), often on weekdays (~78%). Between July 2021 and January 2022 LockBit attempts surged globally—chiefly the US, India and Brazil—targeting healthcare and education yet boasting 41 leak-site victims (Dec 2021–Jan 2022) primarily SMBs (65.9%) across North America, Europe and APAC. With a professional affiliate program fueling continuous innovation and predicted upticks in supply-chain attacks in 2022, organizations should implement comprehensive asset inventory, least-privilege access, regular patching (including Fortinet CVE-2018-13379), RDP/VPN lockdown, application allow-listing, multifactor authentication, offline backups and MITRE TTP monitoring to detect and disrupt LockBit activity.
retrieved_context.title: Ransomware Spotlight: LockBit | Trend Micro (US)

retrieved_context.text: A zero-day VPN vulnerability provided initial access for a sophisticated threat actor who employed publicly available penetration‐testing and exploitation tools—SoftPerfect Network Scanner for network discovery, PsExec to deploy ServeManager.exe (the FiveHands ransomware variant using lattice-based NTRUEncrypt public key cryptography), and SombRAT for remote information theft—alongside RouterScan, grabff.exe, rclone.exe, and s3browser-9-5-3.exe to harvest credentials and exfiltrate data. Once inside, the attacker leveraged Windows Management Instrumentation (T1047) to enumerate and delete Volume Shadow Copies (Inhibit System Recovery, T1490), encrypted files (including those in recovery folders) for impact (T1486), and dropped ransom notes across directories, demanding payment to restore access. Post-encryption activities align with MITRE techniques such as Access Token Manipulation, Boot or Logon Autostart, PowerShell command and scripting interpreter, Domain Trust Discovery, Process Discovery, Screen Capture, and Kerberoasting. The combined use of FiveHands ransomware and SombRAT RAT resulted in both data theft and destruction of backup artifacts, underscoring the need for proactive patch management, network segmentation, strict credential hygiene, and rapid incident response to mitigate novel lattice-based encryption threats.
retrieved_context.title: FiveHands Ransomware Overview

hits.text: In early 2023, ransomware postings dropped 41% month-on-month yet LockBit stayed dominant, and despite predictions of waning ROI, Q3 saw a surge—driven by CL0P’s mass exploits of file-transfer flaws—that surpassed the combined victim counts of 2021–22 and hit law firms, government, manufacturing, oil & gas, and logistics hardest. In Q4 two new strains surfaced: CACTUS, first observed by Kroll in March 2023, leverages critical Qlik Sense vulnerabilities (CVE-2023-41266, ‑41265, ‑48365) or VPN appliance flaws for initial access; embeds a decryption key in ntuser.dat via scheduled tasks; uses SoftPerfect Network Scanner, PowerShell, Cobalt Strike, Splashtop, AnyDesk and Chisel for reconnaissance, persistence and lateral movement; exfiltrates data over Tox and Rclone; and encrypts files with AES/OpenSSL (.cts1 extension) accompanied by cAcTuS.readme.txt demands. When a LockBit affiliate’s deployment failed, they defaulted to 3AM, a new Rust-based backup encryptor that halts services, deletes VSS snapshots, appends .threeamtime and a “0x666” marker, exfiltrates via Wput to FTP, and issues Tor-based ransom negotiations. To counter these evolving threats, organizations must patch VPN and Qlik Sense flaws, enforce least-privilege RDP with MFA, restrict unauthorized remote access tools, monitor for anomalous scheduled tasks, scanner and Tox/Rclone traffic, deploy EDR to flag Cobalt Strike and script-based execution, and maintain secure, offline backups.
hits.title: New Ransomware Strains - CACTUS and 3AM

hits.text: Symantec has warned that extortion actors, notably the Clop ransomware operation (aka Snakefly/TA505/FIN11), have been exploiting a zero-day SQL injection vulnerability in the MOVEit Transfer web application (CVE-2023-34362) since May 27, 2023, enabling supply-chain attacks across multiple organizations; although first patched on May 31, additional vulnerabilities (CVEs pending) were disclosed on June 9. Attackers deploy a bespoke web shell, Lemurloot (detected as JS.Malscript!g1, Trojan.Gen.2, WS.Malware), to authenticate via hard-coded credentials, execute SQL statements to alter or delete database elements, exfiltrate records and Azure settings, and manipulate user accounts. With proof-of-concept code now public, secondary threat actors face elevated risk of exploitation and data theft. Clop has since threatened data leaks unless ransoms are paid, reflecting its shift from encryption to extortion. Symantec mitigations include file-based and ML detections, network-based attack signatures, and Data Center Security policy controls that harden MS SQL, IIS and sandbox environments to prevent web-shell deployment and unauthorized software execution.
hits.title: MOVEit Vulnerabilities: What You Need to Know | Symantec Enterprise Blogs

hits.text: On December 4 Fortra issued a private advisory on CVE-2024-0204, a critical authentication bypass in its GoAnywhere MFT 7.x, and silently patched it on December 7 in version 7.4.1 but only publicly disclosed the flaw today; now Horizon3’s Attack Team has released a proof-of-concept exploit that leverages a path traversal vulnerability to access the /InitialAccountSetup.xhtml endpoint and create unauthorized administrator accounts on unpatched instances, prompting defenders to immediately upgrade or delete/replace the InitialAccountSetup.xhtml file, restart services, and monitor the GoAnywhere “Admin Users” list for new entries. While Fortra reports no confirmed exploits in the wild, the public PoC is expected to trigger widespread scanning and compromises, echoing Clop’s January 2023 campaign that abused a GoAnywhere RCE (CVE-2023-0669) to breach over 100 organizations—including Community Health Systems, Procter & Gamble, Rubrik and the City of Toronto—and underscoring a broader pattern of MFT platform assaults seen in the 2020 Accellion FTA, 2021 SolarWinds Serv-U and 2023 MOVEit Transfer incidents.
hits.title: Exploit released for Fortra GoAnywhere MFT auth bypass bug

hits.text: Fortra has disclosed CVE-2024-0204, a critical (CVSS 9.8) authentication-bypass flaw in GoAnywhere MFT versions 6.0.1–7.4.0 that enables remote attackers to create arbitrary admin users via the web administration portal, potentially leading to full device takeover, data theft, malware deployment, and lateral movement; discovered December 1, 2023 by Mohammed Eldeeb and Islam Elrfai of Spark Engineering Consultants, it was patched in GoAnywhere MFT 7.4.1 on December 7 2023, and users unable to upgrade immediately can mitigate by deleting or emptying the InitialAccountSetup.xhtml file and restarting services. Although no in-the-wild exploitation has been observed, the publication of mitigations may spur PoC releases. This advisory follows January–February 2023 Clop ransomware attacks leveraging the unpatched CVE-2023-0669 remote-code-execution flaw to breach 130 organizations—including Crown Resorts, CHS, Hatch Bank, Rubrik, City of Toronto, Hitachi Energy, Procter & Gamble, and Saks Fifth Avenue—underscoring the critical need for timely patching and monitoring of MFT environments.
hits.title: Fortra warns of new critical GoAnywhere MFT auth bypass, patch now

hits.text: CL0P, a prolific ransomware affiliate of TA505 that exploited the MOVEit Transfer zero-day in May 2023 to compromise over 3,000 U.S. and 8,000 global organizations, has shifted its data-leak operations from slow Tor-hosted zip downloads to decentralized BitTorrent distribution using magnet links and DHT trackers to handle terabytes of stolen data and re-pressure non-paying victims, enabling researchers to rapidly join swarms and identify 100 percent seeders by monitoring leak-site announcements, capturing peer IPs, torrent client fingerprints and connection metadata; this technique not only exposes CL0P’s initial seeding infrastructure and tradecraft opsec gaps but also underscores the need for organizations to deploy behavioral threat protection (e.g., Cortex XDR/XSIAM), continuously scan for MOVEit Transfer exposures (Cortex Xpanse), and engage Unit 42 incident response for tailored threat hunting and mitigation.
hits.title: CL0P Seeds ^_- Gotta Catch Em All!

hits.text: Researchers at Mandiant Intelligence have identified UNC2165—the latest evolution of the U.S.-sanctioned Evil Corp—as leveraging the FakeUpdates infection chain to gain initial access, followed by deployment of LockBit ransomware to obscure attribution and monetize extortion efforts. After OFAC sanctions in December 2019 crippled Evil Corp’s ability to profit from Dridex and its WastedLocker strain, the group briefly resurfaced under PayloadBin (likely a WastedLocker rebrand) and used HTML redirectors in malicious Excel files, then adopted Hades ransomware with code overlaps to distance itself further. By aligning with LockBit’s RaaS model—already proven effective against high-profile victims such as Accenture and Bangkok Air—UNC2165 can blend in with legitimate affiliates, reduce development overhead, and bypass sanctions enforcement that deters U.S. entities from negotiating ransoms with known Evil Corp actors. This shift underscores the need for defenders to monitor FakeUpdates chains and LockBit activity for potential Evil Corp–linked intrusions and to enhance detection of rebranded ransomware variants despite attribution obfuscation tactics.
hits.title: Evil Corp Pivots LockBit to Dodge U.S. Sanctions | Threatpost

hits.text: Since at least August 2021, the Yanluowang ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) operation has targeted U.S. financial firms and other sectors—including manufacturing, IT services, consultancy, and engineering—using a toolkit and playbook that mirror veteran groups Thieflock and Fivehands and suggesting possible affiliate ties; Symantec’s Threat Hunter Team first observed an underdeveloped October 2021 deployment in which attackers used AdFind for Active Directory reconnaissance, then refined their approach with PowerShell-driven BazarLoader implants, registry-based RDP enablement, ConnectWise for persistent access, and SoftPerfect Network Scanner for lateral movement, followed by credential theft via KeeThief, custom secretdump.exe, and deployment of Cobalt Strike Beacon, culminating in file encryption and double-extortion ransom notes threatening DDoS, employee calls, repeated attacks, and data deletion if law enforcement or negotiation firms are engaged; this operation contributes to the $590 million in ransomware payments recorded in 2021 and 314 global double-extortion incidents in October alone, underscoring the need for hardened Active Directory security, RDP restrictions, EDR with credential-dump detection, network monitoring for AdFind and BazarLoader activity, and adherence to FBI/CISA incident response recommendations.
hits.title: An In-Depth Look at Yanluowang Ransomware

hits.text: During a recent incident, a LockBit affiliate conducted initial intrusions using gpresult for policy dumping, Cobalt Strike loaders and PsExec for privilege escalation, followed by reconnaissance (whoami, netstat, quser, net view), lateral movement, persistence via a new user account, and data exfiltration over FTP with Wput; when deployment of LockBit (SHA256 079b99f6…) was blocked on the target network, the attacker pivoted to a newly observed Rust-written ransomware family dubbed 3AM (SHA256 307a1217…), which appends “.threeamtime” to encrypted files, stops over 100 security and backup services via net stop and wbadmin/bcdedit/wmic commands, deletes Volume Shadow copies with vssadmin.exe delete shadows /all /quiet, and drops a Tor‐accessible ransom note requiring a 32-character “-k” access key and offering decryption/mystical-themed extortion; although 3AM encryption succeeded on only one of three attempted hosts, its Conti-style “-m” (local/net) and “-h” parameters, heavy service-termination payload, and aggressive VSS wipe underscore its potential as a fallback vector—defenders should update Symantec/Broadcom signatures, monitor for the .threeamtime extension, suspicious Rust binaries, command-line flags “-k” and “-m”, and mass service stoppage activity, and block associated IOCs (185.202.0[.]111, 212.18.104[.]6, 85.159.229[.]62) to mitigate future 3AM use.

hits.text: Dragos researchers, in collaboration with Ukraine’s CSSC, unearthed FrostyGoop—an ICS-specific malware first spotted in April and used in January to disrupt central heating in over 600 Lviv apartment buildings—marking the first known malware to leverage Modbus TCP for read/write operations on operational technology. Attackers gained initial access in April 2023 by exploiting a MikroTik router vulnerability, deployed a webshell on the router’s web server, and maintained persistence via Tor and L2TP tunnels to Moscow-based IPs. After spending months conducting reconnaissance, they extracted credentials by dumping the SAM registry hive in December, then directly issued scripted Modbus commands—read from a JSON configuration file—to publicly exposed ENCO heating controllers, even downgrading firmware to disable monitoring and force inaccurate measurements that halted heating services for nearly two days amid subzero temperatures. This incident underscores the threat posed by internet-exposed ICS devices—over 46,000 globally using Modbus—and highlights poor network segmentation, unpatched ICS CVEs, and the ease with which FrostyGoop’s protocol-agnostic payload can be repurposed against diverse industrial controllers, necessitating immediate network segmentation, firmware monitoring, and patch management in OT environments.
hits.title: ICS malware FrostyGoop disrupted heating in Ukraine, remains threat to OT worldwide

retrieved_context.text: In early 2023, ransomware postings dropped 41% month-on-month yet LockBit stayed dominant, and despite predictions of waning ROI, Q3 saw a surge—driven by CL0P’s mass exploits of file-transfer flaws—that surpassed the combined victim counts of 2021–22 and hit law firms, government, manufacturing, oil & gas, and logistics hardest. In Q4 two new strains surfaced: CACTUS, first observed by Kroll in March 2023, leverages critical Qlik Sense vulnerabilities (CVE-2023-41266, ‑41265, ‑48365) or VPN appliance flaws for initial access; embeds a decryption key in ntuser.dat via scheduled tasks; uses SoftPerfect Network Scanner, PowerShell, Cobalt Strike, Splashtop, AnyDesk and Chisel for reconnaissance, persistence and lateral movement; exfiltrates data over Tox and Rclone; and encrypts files with AES/OpenSSL (.cts1 extension) accompanied by cAcTuS.readme.txt demands. When a LockBit affiliate’s deployment failed, they defaulted to 3AM, a new Rust-based backup encryptor that halts services, deletes VSS snapshots, appends .threeamtime and a “0x666” marker, exfiltrates via Wput to FTP, and issues Tor-based ransom negotiations. To counter these evolving threats, organizations must patch VPN and Qlik Sense flaws, enforce least-privilege RDP with MFA, restrict unauthorized remote access tools, monitor for anomalous scheduled tasks, scanner and Tox/Rclone traffic, deploy EDR to flag Cobalt Strike and script-based execution, and maintain secure, offline backups.
retrieved_context.title: New Ransomware Strains - CACTUS and 3AM

retrieved_context.text: Symantec has warned that extortion actors, notably the Clop ransomware operation (aka Snakefly/TA505/FIN11), have been exploiting a zero-day SQL injection vulnerability in the MOVEit Transfer web application (CVE-2023-34362) since May 27, 2023, enabling supply-chain attacks across multiple organizations; although first patched on May 31, additional vulnerabilities (CVEs pending) were disclosed on June 9. Attackers deploy a bespoke web shell, Lemurloot (detected as JS.Malscript!g1, Trojan.Gen.2, WS.Malware), to authenticate via hard-coded credentials, execute SQL statements to alter or delete database elements, exfiltrate records and Azure settings, and manipulate user accounts. With proof-of-concept code now public, secondary threat actors face elevated risk of exploitation and data theft. Clop has since threatened data leaks unless ransoms are paid, reflecting its shift from encryption to extortion. Symantec mitigations include file-based and ML detections, network-based attack signatures, and Data Center Security policy controls that harden MS SQL, IIS and sandbox environments to prevent web-shell deployment and unauthorized software execution.
retrieved_context.title: MOVEit Vulnerabilities: What You Need to Know | Symantec Enterprise Blogs

retrieved_context.text: On December 4 Fortra issued a private advisory on CVE-2024-0204, a critical authentication bypass in its GoAnywhere MFT 7.x, and silently patched it on December 7 in version 7.4.1 but only publicly disclosed the flaw today; now Horizon3’s Attack Team has released a proof-of-concept exploit that leverages a path traversal vulnerability to access the /InitialAccountSetup.xhtml endpoint and create unauthorized administrator accounts on unpatched instances, prompting defenders to immediately upgrade or delete/replace the InitialAccountSetup.xhtml file, restart services, and monitor the GoAnywhere “Admin Users” list for new entries. While Fortra reports no confirmed exploits in the wild, the public PoC is expected to trigger widespread scanning and compromises, echoing Clop’s January 2023 campaign that abused a GoAnywhere RCE (CVE-2023-0669) to breach over 100 organizations—including Community Health Systems, Procter & Gamble, Rubrik and the City of Toronto—and underscoring a broader pattern of MFT platform assaults seen in the 2020 Accellion FTA, 2021 SolarWinds Serv-U and 2023 MOVEit Transfer incidents.
retrieved_context.title: Exploit released for Fortra GoAnywhere MFT auth bypass bug

retrieved_context.text: Fortra has disclosed CVE-2024-0204, a critical (CVSS 9.8) authentication-bypass flaw in GoAnywhere MFT versions 6.0.1–7.4.0 that enables remote attackers to create arbitrary admin users via the web administration portal, potentially leading to full device takeover, data theft, malware deployment, and lateral movement; discovered December 1, 2023 by Mohammed Eldeeb and Islam Elrfai of Spark Engineering Consultants, it was patched in GoAnywhere MFT 7.4.1 on December 7 2023, and users unable to upgrade immediately can mitigate by deleting or emptying the InitialAccountSetup.xhtml file and restarting services. Although no in-the-wild exploitation has been observed, the publication of mitigations may spur PoC releases. This advisory follows January–February 2023 Clop ransomware attacks leveraging the unpatched CVE-2023-0669 remote-code-execution flaw to breach 130 organizations—including Crown Resorts, CHS, Hatch Bank, Rubrik, City of Toronto, Hitachi Energy, Procter & Gamble, and Saks Fifth Avenue—underscoring the critical need for timely patching and monitoring of MFT environments.
retrieved_context.title: Fortra warns of new critical GoAnywhere MFT auth bypass, patch now

retrieved_context.text: CL0P, a prolific ransomware affiliate of TA505 that exploited the MOVEit Transfer zero-day in May 2023 to compromise over 3,000 U.S. and 8,000 global organizations, has shifted its data-leak operations from slow Tor-hosted zip downloads to decentralized BitTorrent distribution using magnet links and DHT trackers to handle terabytes of stolen data and re-pressure non-paying victims, enabling researchers to rapidly join swarms and identify 100 percent seeders by monitoring leak-site announcements, capturing peer IPs, torrent client fingerprints and connection metadata; this technique not only exposes CL0P’s initial seeding infrastructure and tradecraft opsec gaps but also underscores the need for organizations to deploy behavioral threat protection (e.g., Cortex XDR/XSIAM), continuously scan for MOVEit Transfer exposures (Cortex Xpanse), and engage Unit 42 incident response for tailored threat hunting and mitigation.
retrieved_context.title: CL0P Seeds ^_- Gotta Catch Em All!

retrieved_context.text: Trend Micro’s investigation into the LockBit ransomware-as-a-service operation, tracked as intrusion set Water Selkie, reveals the group’s marketing of its lightning-fast AES-128 head-only file encryption (first 4 KB) with RSA-wrapped keys, deployed via versatile affiliate-driven campaigns that source initial access through phishing (T1566), CVE-2018-13379 Fortinet VPN exploits (T1190) and compromised RDP/VPN accounts (T1078), then execute payloads via PowerShell Empire, Meterpreter, scheduled tasks or signed binaries (T1059, T1218), evade defenses with Mimikatz, GMER, Process Hacker or disabled Windows Defender (T1562), discover network shares and AD servers (T1083, T1135), laterally propagate via SMB or Cobalt Strike (T1570), exfiltrate data using StealBit or cloud storage (T1567) and encrypt data for impact (T1486), often on weekdays (~78%). Between July 2021 and January 2022 LockBit attempts surged globally—chiefly the US, India and Brazil—targeting healthcare and education yet boasting 41 leak-site victims (Dec 2021–Jan 2022) primarily SMBs (65.9%) across North America, Europe and APAC. With a professional affiliate program fueling continuous innovation and predicted upticks in supply-chain attacks in 2022, organizations should implement comprehensive asset inventory, least-privilege access, regular patching (including Fortinet CVE-2018-13379), RDP/VPN lockdown, application allow-listing, multifactor authentication, offline backups and MITRE TTP monitoring to detect and disrupt LockBit activity.
retrieved_context.title: Ransomware Spotlight: LockBit | Trend Micro (US)

retrieved_context.text: Researchers at Mandiant Intelligence have identified UNC2165—the latest evolution of the U.S.-sanctioned Evil Corp—as leveraging the FakeUpdates infection chain to gain initial access, followed by deployment of LockBit ransomware to obscure attribution and monetize extortion efforts. After OFAC sanctions in December 2019 crippled Evil Corp’s ability to profit from Dridex and its WastedLocker strain, the group briefly resurfaced under PayloadBin (likely a WastedLocker rebrand) and used HTML redirectors in malicious Excel files, then adopted Hades ransomware with code overlaps to distance itself further. By aligning with LockBit’s RaaS model—already proven effective against high-profile victims such as Accenture and Bangkok Air—UNC2165 can blend in with legitimate affiliates, reduce development overhead, and bypass sanctions enforcement that deters U.S. entities from negotiating ransoms with known Evil Corp actors. This shift underscores the need for defenders to monitor FakeUpdates chains and LockBit activity for potential Evil Corp–linked intrusions and to enhance detection of rebranded ransomware variants despite attribution obfuscation tactics.
retrieved_context.title: Evil Corp Pivots LockBit to Dodge U.S. Sanctions | Threatpost

hits.text: Silent Push researchers uncovered FIN7’s largest-ever infrastructure, identifying over 4,000 malicious IOFA domains and associated IP addresses used to fuel a global phishing and malware campaign that hit high-profile targets such as the Louvre, Meta and Reuters. Using automated intelligence and Threat Hunting workflows, analysts detected a pattern of newly registered look-alike domains—many leveraging common TLDs and typosquatting—to host spear-phishing landing pages and weaponized Office attachments that deploy custom .NET droppers and Cobalt Strike beacons. Chronologically, the operation began with domain registration, followed by coordinated email blasts spoofing corporate brands, HTTP(S) redirects to phishing kits, and payload delivery that enabled credential harvesting and potential lateral movement. Silent Push’s API-driven Integrations enabled rapid enumeration of IOFA indicators of compromise, brand protection alerts and proactive blocking in customer environments. Actionable insights include ingesting the full list of domains and IPs into SIEM and email security filters, enforcing strict SPF/DKIM/DMARC policies, monitoring DNS query anomalies for new domain registrations, and updating endpoint detection rules to flag the identified .NET loader behaviors.
hits.title: FIN7: Silent Push unearths the largest group of FIN7 domains ever discovered. 4000+ IOFA domains and IPs found. Louvre, Meta, and Reuters targeted in massive global phishing and malware campaigns.

hits.text: On Aug. 17, 2023, the Zero Day Initiative publicly reported an RCE vulnerability in WinRAR (CVE-2023-40477) originally disclosed to the vendor on June 8; just four days later, an actor using the alias whalersplonk published a fake PoC on GitHub that repurposed a GeoServer CVE-2023-25157 exploit script to launch an infection chain rather than trigger the WinRAR flaw. Analysis of poc.py shows it writes a batch file to %TEMP%, executes an encoded PowerShell script that downloads c.ps1 and, subsequently, a VenomRAT v6.0.3 payload named Windows.Gaming.Preview.exe from checkblacklistwords[.]eu, installs it under %APPDATA%\Drivers, creates a scheduled task for persistence, enables keylogging to %APPDATA%\MyData\DataLogs_keylog_offline.txt, and contacts C2 at 94.156.253.109:4449. This RAT supports HVNC, stealer, grabber and commands such as plu_gin, HVNCStop, loadofflinelog, keylogsetting, filterinfo, and Po_ng. The malicious domain was registered at least 10 days before the CVE’s disclosure, indicating pre-positioned infrastructure aimed at opportunistically compromising researchers or other miscreants, not end users directly. Although the fake PoC repo was removed by the time of analysis, Palo Alto Networks WildFire and Advanced URL Filtering had already auto-categorized the domain as malicious and blocked the chain. Unit 42 researchers, alongside CTA partner Broadcom/Symantec, have published full IoCs and SHA lists on GitHub to support proactive defenses across WinRAR’s 500 million-strong user base.
hits.title: Fake CVE-2023-40477 Proof of Concept Leads to VenomRAT

In Q4 two new strains surfaced: CACTUS, first observed by Kroll in March 2023, leverages critical Qlik Sense vulnerabilities (CVE-2023-41266, ‑41265, ‑48365) or VPN appliance flaws for initial access; embeds a decryption key in ntuser.dat via scheduled tasks; uses SoftPerfect Network Scanner, PowerShell, Cobalt Strike, Splashtop, AnyDesk and Chisel for reconnaissance, persistence and lateral movement; exfiltrates data over Tox and Rclone; and encrypts files with AES/OpenSSL (.cts1 extension) accompanied by cAcTuS.readme.txt demands. When a LockBit affiliate’s deployment failed, they defaulted to 3AM, a new Rust-based backup encryptor that halts services, deletes VSS snapshots, appends .threeamtime and a “0x666” marker, exfiltrates via Wput to FTP, and issues Tor-based ransom negotiations. To counter these evolving threats, organizations must patch VPN and Qlik Sense flaws, enforce least-privilege RDP with MFA, restrict unauthorized remote access tools, monitor for anomalous scheduled tasks, scanner and Tox/Rclone traffic, deploy EDR to flag Cobalt Strike and script-based execution, and maintain secure, offline backups.

retrieved_context.text: Fortra has disclosed CVE-2024-0204, a critical (CVSS 9.8) authentication-bypass flaw in GoAnywhere MFT versions 6.0.1–7.4.0 that enables remote attackers to create arbitrary admin users via the web administration portal, potentially leading to full device takeover, data theft, malware deployment, and lateral movement; discovered December 1, 2023 by Mohammed Eldeeb and Islam Elrfai of Spark Engineering Consultants, it was patched in GoAnywhere MFT 7.4.1 on December 7 2023, and users unable to upgrade immediately can mitigate by deleting or emptying the InitialAccountSetup.xhtml file and restarting services. Although no in-the-wild exploitation has been observed, the publication of mitigations may spur PoC releases. This advisory follows January–February 2023 Clop ransomware attacks leveraging the unpatched CVE-2023-0669 remote-code-execution flaw to breach 130 organizations—including Crown Resorts, CHS, Hatch Bank, Rubrik, City of Toronto, Hitachi Energy, Procter & Gamble, and Saks Fifth Avenue—underscoring the critical need for timely patching and monitoring of MFT environments.

retrieved_context.text: Silent Push researchers uncovered FIN7’s largest-ever infrastructure, identifying over 4,000 malicious IOFA domains and associated IP addresses used to fuel a global phishing and malware campaign that hit high-profile targets such as the Louvre, Meta and Reuters. Using automated intelligence and Threat Hunting workflows, analysts detected a pattern of newly registered look-alike domains—many leveraging common TLDs and typosquatting—to host spear-phishing landing pages and weaponized Office attachments that deploy custom .NET droppers and Cobalt Strike beacons. Chronologically, the operation began with domain registration, followed by coordinated email blasts spoofing corporate brands, HTTP(S) redirects to phishing kits, and payload delivery that enabled credential harvesting and potential lateral movement. Silent Push’s API-driven Integrations enabled rapid enumeration of IOFA indicators of compromise, brand protection alerts and proactive blocking in customer environments. Actionable insights include ingesting the full list of domains and IPs into SIEM and email security filters, enforcing strict SPF/DKIM/DMARC policies, monitoring DNS query anomalies for new domain registrations, and updating endpoint detection rules to flag the identified .NET loader behaviors.
retrieved_context.title: FIN7: Silent Push unearths the largest group of FIN7 domains ever discovered. 4000+ IOFA domains and IPs found. Louvre, Meta, and Reuters targeted in massive global phishing and malware campaigns.

retrieved_context.text: Trend Micro’s investigation into the LockBit ransomware-as-a-service operation, tracked as intrusion set Water Selkie, reveals the group’s marketing of its lightning-fast AES-128 head-only file encryption (first 4 KB) with RSA-wrapped keys, deployed via versatile affiliate-driven campaigns that source initial access through phishing (T1566), CVE-2018-13379 Fortinet VPN exploits (T1190) and compromised RDP/VPN accounts (T1078), then execute payloads via PowerShell Empire, Meterpreter, scheduled tasks or signed binaries (T1059, T1218), evade defenses with Mimikatz, GMER, Process Hacker or disabled Windows Defender (T1562), discover network shares and AD servers (T1083, T1135), laterally propagate via SMB or Cobalt Strike (T1570), exfiltrate data using StealBit or cloud storage (T1567) and encrypt data for impact (T1486), often on weekdays (~78%). Between July 2021 and January 2022 LockBit attempts surged globally—chiefly the US, India and Brazil—targeting healthcare and education yet boasting 41 leak-site victims (Dec 2021–Jan 2022) primarily SMBs (65.9%) across North America, Europe and APAC. With a professional affiliate program fueling continuous innovation and predicted upticks in supply-chain attacks in 2022, organizations should implement comprehensive asset inventory, least-privilege access, regular patching (including Fortinet CVE-2018-13379), RDP/VPN lockdown, application allow-listing, multifactor authentication, offline backups and MITRE TTP monitoring to detect and disrupt LockBit activity.
retrieved_context.title: Ransomware Spotlight: LockBit | Trend Micro (US)

retrieved_context.text: Researchers at Accenture Security exposed Q3 2021 proliferation of Karakurt, a financially motivated data‐extortion group first identified in June 2021 upon registering two domains and launching a Twitter handle, which compromised over 40 primarily North American (95 percent) organizations across random sectors between September and November by sourcing or phishing VPN credentials for initial access, establishing persistence with Cobalt Strike beacons or AnyDesk, then harvesting administrator privileges via Mimikatz to evade EDR solutions; they compress stolen data with 7zip or WinZip and exfiltrate it to Mega.io using Rclone or FileZilla, foregoing ransomware encryption in favor of public leak threats, a low-overhead approach that can still cripple victims—underscoring the need for robust VPN credential management, continuous monitoring for living-off-the-land tools, and preventative controls to detect and disrupt such intrusions before data exfiltration.
retrieved_context.title: New 'Karakurt' hacking group focuses on data theft and extortion

retrieved_context.text: On December 4 Fortra issued a private advisory on CVE-2024-0204, a critical authentication bypass in its GoAnywhere MFT 7.x, and silently patched it on December 7 in version 7.4.1 but only publicly disclosed the flaw today; now Horizon3’s Attack Team has released a proof-of-concept exploit that leverages a path traversal vulnerability to access the /InitialAccountSetup.xhtml endpoint and create unauthorized administrator accounts on unpatched instances, prompting defenders to immediately upgrade or delete/replace the InitialAccountSetup.xhtml file, restart services, and monitor the GoAnywhere “Admin Users” list for new entries. While Fortra reports no confirmed exploits in the wild, the public PoC is expected to trigger widespread scanning and compromises, echoing Clop’s January 2023 campaign that abused a GoAnywhere RCE (CVE-2023-0669) to breach over 100 organizations—including Community Health Systems, Procter & Gamble, Rubrik and the City of Toronto—and underscoring a broader pattern of MFT platform assaults seen in the 2020 Accellion FTA, 2021 SolarWinds Serv-U and 2023 MOVEit Transfer incidents.
retrieved_context.title: Exploit released for Fortra GoAnywhere MFT auth bypass bug

retrieved_context.text: During a recent incident, a LockBit affiliate conducted initial intrusions using gpresult for policy dumping, Cobalt Strike loaders and PsExec for privilege escalation, followed by reconnaissance (whoami, netstat, quser, net view), lateral movement, persistence via a new user account, and data exfiltration over FTP with Wput; when deployment of LockBit (SHA256 079b99f6…) was blocked on the target network, the attacker pivoted to a newly observed Rust-written ransomware family dubbed 3AM (SHA256 307a1217…), which appends “.threeamtime” to encrypted files, stops over 100 security and backup services via net stop and wbadmin/bcdedit/wmic commands, deletes Volume Shadow copies with vssadmin.exe delete shadows /all /quiet, and drops a Tor‐accessible ransom note requiring a 32-character “-k” access key and offering decryption/mystical-themed extortion; although 3AM encryption succeeded on only one of three attempted hosts, its Conti-style “-m” (local/net) and “-h” parameters, heavy service-termination payload, and aggressive VSS wipe underscore its potential as a fallback vector—defenders should update Symantec/Broadcom signatures, monitor for the .threeamtime extension, suspicious Rust binaries, command-line flags “-k” and “-m”, and mass service stoppage activity, and block associated IOCs (185.202.0[.]111, 212.18.104[.]6, 85.159.229[.]62) to mitigate future 3AM use.

retrieved_context.text: Researchers at Mandiant Intelligence have identified UNC2165—the latest evolution of the U.S.-sanctioned Evil Corp—as leveraging the FakeUpdates infection chain to gain initial access, followed by deployment of LockBit ransomware to obscure attribution and monetize extortion efforts. After OFAC sanctions in December 2019 crippled Evil Corp’s ability to profit from Dridex and its WastedLocker strain, the group briefly resurfaced under PayloadBin (likely a WastedLocker rebrand) and used HTML redirectors in malicious Excel files, then adopted Hades ransomware with code overlaps to distance itself further. By aligning with LockBit’s RaaS model—already proven effective against high-profile victims such as Accenture and Bangkok Air—UNC2165 can blend in with legitimate affiliates, reduce development overhead, and bypass sanctions enforcement that deters U.S. entities from negotiating ransoms with known Evil Corp actors. This shift underscores the need for defenders to monitor FakeUpdates chains and LockBit activity for potential Evil Corp–linked intrusions and to enhance detection of rebranded ransomware variants despite attribution obfuscation tactics.
retrieved_context.title: Evil Corp Pivots LockBit to Dodge U.S. Sanctions | Threatpost

canonical_entities: creates a scheduled task for persistence
retrieved_context.text: On Aug. 17, 2023, the Zero Day Initiative publicly reported an RCE vulnerability in WinRAR (CVE-2023-40477) originally disclosed to the vendor on June 8; just four days later, an actor using the alias whalersplonk published a fake PoC on GitHub that repurposed a GeoServer CVE-2023-25157 exploit script to launch an infection chain rather than trigger the WinRAR flaw. Analysis of poc.py shows it writes a batch file to %TEMP%, executes an encoded PowerShell script that downloads c.ps1 and, subsequently, a VenomRAT v6.0.3 payload named Windows.Gaming.Preview.exe from checkblacklistwords[.]eu, installs it under %APPDATA%\Drivers, creates a scheduled task for persistence, enables keylogging to %APPDATA%\MyData\DataLogs_keylog_offline.txt, and contacts C2 at 94.156.253.109:4449. This RAT supports HVNC, stealer, grabber and commands such as plu_gin, HVNCStop, loadofflinelog, keylogsetting, filterinfo, and Po_ng. The malicious domain was registered at least 10 days before the CVE’s disclosure, indicating pre-positioned infrastructure aimed at opportunistically compromising researchers or other miscreants, not end users directly. Although the fake PoC repo was removed by the time of analysis, Palo Alto Networks WildFire and Advanced URL Filtering had already auto-categorized the domain as malicious and blocked the chain. Unit 42 researchers, alongside CTA partner Broadcom/Symantec, have published full IoCs and SHA lists on GitHub to support proactive defenses across WinRAR’s 500 million-strong user base.
retrieved_context.title: Fake CVE-2023-40477 Proof of Concept Leads to VenomRAT

hits.text: Symantec has warned that extortion actors, notably the Clop ransomware operation (aka Snakefly/TA505/FIN11), have been exploiting a zero-day SQL injection vulnerability in the MOVEit Transfer web application (CVE-2023-34362) since May 27, 2023, enabling supply-chain attacks across multiple organizations; although first patched on May 31, additional vulnerabilities (CVEs pending) were disclosed on June 9. Attackers deploy a bespoke web shell, Lemurloot (detected as JS.Malscript!g1, Trojan.Gen.2, WS.Malware), to authenticate via hard-coded credentials, execute SQL statements to alter or delete database elements, exfiltrate records and Azure settings, and manipulate user accounts. With proof-of-concept code now public, secondary threat actors face elevated risk of exploitation and data theft. Clop has since threatened data leaks unless ransoms are paid, reflecting its shift from encryption to extortion. Symantec mitigations include file-based and ML detections, network-based attack signatures, and Data Center Security policy controls that harden MS SQL, IIS and sandbox environments to prevent web-shell deployment and unauthorized software execution.
hits.title: MOVEit Vulnerabilities: What You Need to Know | Symantec Enterprise Blogs

hits.text: Since its emergence in 2021 and first detection on Trend Micro telemetry in March 2022, the TargetCompany ransomware group has launched 269 attempted attacks against 250 disclosed Trend customers—predominantly in Asia (notably India and Saudi Arabia)—while avoiding Kazakhstan, Russia, Qatar, and Ukraine, and focusing on manufacturing, retail, and telecommunications; their November 2022–May 2023 leak site lists 20 confirmed victims (mostly small businesses) across the Asia-Pacific, Europe, and Middle East in IT, manufacturing, apparel, and automotive sectors. Initial access vectors include exploitation of CVE-2019-1069 and CVE-2020-0618 RCE flaws, SQL Server xp_cmdshell abuse, and OneNote-based spam campaigns. Execution relies on WMIC-invoked PowerShell scripts to retrieve various payloads (TargetComp ransomware, Remcos backdoor, Negasteal, Snake Keylogger) and, since January 2022, reflective loading of a .NET downloader that decrypts and runs payloads in memory via XOR or inversion. For defense evasion, operators deploy GMER, PCHunter64 (YDArk.exe), Advance Process Termination, KILLAV, and killer.bat to disable AV and security services; discovery is achieved through network scans and Mimikatz credential dumping; lateral movement via RDP-based RCE; C2 evolved from an open Mallox directory to an Nginx-protected server. Impact involves ChaCha20 file encryption with keys generated by Curve25519 and AES-128, file extensions such as .mallox/.exploit/.avast and ransom notes titled “HOW TO RECOVER!!.TXT,” and potential data exfiltration. Their tactics span MITRE techniques T1190, T1059.001, T1047, T1562.001, T1003.001, T1071.001, T1486, and more. The group’s maturation—evidenced by reflective loading and possible RaaS adoption—underscores the urgency for organizations to enforce asset inventories, least-privilege access, prompt patching (or virtual patching), multifactor authentication, sandboxed email defenses, AI/ML-driven detection, regular backups, and continuous red-team testing to thwart this active threat.
hits.title: Ransomware Spotlight: TargetCompany | Trend Micro (US)

canonical_entities: Lorenz ransomware group exploiting CVE-2022-29499 against Mitel MiVoice Connect
harvested local and domain admin credentials
hits.text: In mid-2022, Arctic Wolf researchers discovered the Lorenz ransomware group exploiting CVE-2022-29499, a remote code execution flaw in Mitel MiVoice Connect VoIP appliances disclosed in April and patched in July, to gain an initial reverse shell. Once inside, the attackers used the compromised Mitel Service Appliance’s CLI to create a hidden directory, download and rename the Golang-based Chisel tunneling tool via Wget, and establish a fast TCP/UDP SOCKS proxy over HTTP (skipping TLS verification) to evade firewalls. After lying dormant for nearly a month and deploying a “pdf_import_export.php” web shell for persistence, they harvested local and domain admin credentials, moved laterally via RDP to a domain controller, exfiltrated data via FileZilla for double-extortion, and encrypted ESXi hosts using BitLocker and Lorenz ransomware. Targeting primarily US SMBs (with outliers in China and Mexico), this campaign underscores the critical need for timely patching of IoT/VoIP devices, comprehensive asset discovery and hardening, network segmentation, and robust PowerShell and module logging with centralized log management.
hits.title: Lorenz Ransomware Goes After SMBs via Mitel VoIP Phone Systems

retrieved_context.text: Trend Micro’s investigation into the LockBit ransomware-as-a-service operation, tracked as intrusion set Water Selkie, reveals the group’s marketing of its lightning-fast AES-128 head-only file encryption (first 4 KB) with RSA-wrapped keys, deployed via versatile affiliate-driven campaigns that source initial access through phishing (T1566), CVE-2018-13379 Fortinet VPN exploits (T1190) and compromised RDP/VPN accounts (T1078), then execute payloads via PowerShell Empire, Meterpreter, scheduled tasks or signed binaries (T1059, T1218), evade defenses with Mimikatz, GMER, Process Hacker or disabled Windows Defender (T1562), discover network shares and AD servers (T1083, T1135), laterally propagate via SMB or Cobalt Strike (T1570), exfiltrate data using StealBit or cloud storage (T1567) and encrypt data for impact (T1486), often on weekdays (~78%). Between July 2021 and January 2022 LockBit attempts surged globally—chiefly the US, India and Brazil—targeting healthcare and education yet boasting 41 leak-site victims (Dec 2021–Jan 2022) primarily SMBs (65.9%) across North America, Europe and APAC. With a professional affiliate program fueling continuous innovation and predicted upticks in supply-chain attacks in 2022, organizations should implement comprehensive asset inventory, least-privilege access, regular patching (including Fortinet CVE-2018-13379), RDP/VPN lockdown, application allow-listing, multifactor authentication, offline backups and MITRE TTP monitoring to detect and disrupt LockBit activity.

retrieved_context.text: Researchers at Mandiant Intelligence have identified UNC2165—the latest evolution of the U.S.-sanctioned Evil Corp—as leveraging the FakeUpdates infection chain to gain initial access, followed by deployment of LockBit ransomware to obscure attribution and monetize extortion efforts. After OFAC sanctions in December 2019 crippled Evil Corp’s ability to profit from Dridex and its WastedLocker strain, the group briefly resurfaced under PayloadBin (likely a WastedLocker rebrand) and used HTML redirectors in malicious Excel files, then adopted Hades ransomware with code overlaps to distance itself further. retrieved_context.text: Since its emergence in 2021 and first detection on Trend Micro telemetry in March 2022, the TargetCompany ransomware group has launched 269 attempted attacks against 250 disclosed Trend customers—predominantly in Asia (notably India and Saudi Arabia)—while avoiding Kazakhstan, Russia, Qatar, and Ukraine, and focusing on manufacturing, retail, and telecommunications; their November 2022–May 2023 leak site lists 20 confirmed victims (mostly small businesses) across the Asia-Pacific, Europe, and Middle East in IT, manufacturing, apparel, and automotive sectors. Initial access vectors include exploitation of CVE-2019-1069 and CVE-2020-0618 RCE flaws, SQL Server xp_cmdshell abuse, and OneNote-based spam campaigns. Execution relies on WMIC-invoked PowerShell scripts to retrieve various payloads (TargetComp ransomware, Remcos backdoor, Negasteal, Snake Keylogger) and, since January 2022, reflective loading of a .NET downloader that decrypts and runs payloads in memory via XOR or inversion. For defense evasion, operators deploy GMER, PCHunter64 (YDArk.exe), Advance Process Termination, KILLAV, and killer.bat to disable AV and security services; discovery is achieved through network scans and Mimikatz credential dumping; lateral movement via RDP-based RCE; C2 evolved from an open Mallox directory to an Nginx-protected server. Impact involves ChaCha20 file encryption with keys generated by Curve25519 and AES-128, file extensions such as .mallox/.exploit/.avast and ransom notes titled “HOW TO RECOVER!!.TXT,” and potential data exfiltration. Their tactics span MITRE techniques T1190, T1059.001, T1047, T1562.001, T1003.001, T1071.001, T1486, and more. The group’s maturation—evidenced by reflective loading and possible RaaS adoption—underscores the urgency for organizations to enforce asset inventories, least-privilege access, prompt patching (or virtual patching), multifactor authentication, sandboxed email defenses, AI/ML-driven detection, regular backups, and continuous red-team testing to thwart this active threat.

retrieved_context.text: In mid-2022, Arctic Wolf researchers discovered the Lorenz ransomware group exploiting CVE-2022-29499, a remote code execution flaw in Mitel MiVoice Connect VoIP appliances disclosed in April and patched in July, to gain an initial reverse shell. Once inside, the attackers used the compromised Mitel Service Appliance’s CLI to create a hidden directory, download and rename the Golang-based Chisel tunneling tool via Wget, and establish a fast TCP/UDP SOCKS proxy over HTTP (skipping TLS verification) to evade firewalls. After lying dormant for nearly a month and deploying a “pdf_import_export.php” web shell for persistence, they harvested local and domain admin credentials, moved laterally via RDP to a domain controller, exfiltrated data via FileZilla for double-extortion, and encrypted ESXi hosts using BitLocker and Lorenz ransomware. Targeting primarily US SMBs (with outliers in China and Mexico), this campaign underscores the critical need for timely patching of IoT/VoIP devices, comprehensive asset discovery and hardening, network segmentation, and robust PowerShell and module logging with centralized log management.
retrieved_context.title: Lorenz Ransomware Goes After SMBs via Mitel VoIP Phone Systems

retrieved_context.text: During a recent incident, a LockBit affiliate conducted initial intrusions using gpresult for policy dumping, Cobalt Strike loaders and PsExec for privilege escalation, followed by reconnaissance (whoami, netstat, quser, net view), lateral movement, persistence via a new user account, and data exfiltration over FTP with Wput; when deployment of LockBit (SHA256 079b99f6…) was blocked on the target network, the attacker pivoted to a newly observed Rust-written ransomware family dubbed 3AM (SHA256 307a1217…), which appends “.threeamtime” to encrypted files, stops over 100 security and backup services via net stop and wbadmin/bcdedit/wmic commands, deletes Volume Shadow copies with vssadmin.exe delete shadows /all /quiet, and drops a Tor‐accessible ransom note requiring a 32-character “-k” access key and offering decryption/mystical-themed extortion; although 3AM encryption succeeded on only one of three attempted hosts, its Conti-style “-m” (local/net) and “-h” parameters, heavy service-termination payload, and aggressive VSS wipe underscore its potential as a fallback vector—defenders should update Symantec/Broadcom signatures, monitor for the .threeamtime extension, suspicious Rust binaries, command-line flags “-k” and “-m”, and mass service stoppage activity, and block associated IOCs (185.202.0[.]111, 212.18.104[.]6, 85.159.229[.]62) to mitigate future 3AM use.

hits.text: Symantec has warned that extortion actors, notably the Clop ransomware operation (aka Snakefly/TA505/FIN11), have been exploiting a zero-day SQL injection vulnerability in the MOVEit Transfer web application (CVE-2023-34362) since May 27, 2023, enabling supply-chain attacks across multiple organizations; although first patched on May 31, additional vulnerabilities (CVEs pending) were disclosed on June 9. Attackers deploy a bespoke web shell, Lemurloot (detected as JS.Malscript!g1, Trojan.Gen.2, WS.Malware), to authenticate via hard-coded credentials, execute SQL statements to alter or delete database elements, exfiltrate records and Azure settings, and manipulate user accounts. With proof-of-concept code now public, secondary threat actors face elevated risk of exploitation and data theft. Clop has since threatened data leaks unless ransoms are paid, reflecting its shift from encryption to extortion. Symantec mitigations include file-based and ML detections, network-based attack signatures, and Data Center Security policy controls that harden MS SQL, IIS and sandbox environments to prevent web-shell deployment and unauthorized software execution.
hits.title: MOVEit Vulnerabilities: What You Need to Know | Symantec Enterprise Blogs

hits.text: In early 2023, ransomware postings dropped 41% month-on-month yet LockBit stayed dominant, and despite predictions of waning ROI, Q3 saw a surge—driven by CL0P’s mass exploits of file-transfer flaws—that surpassed the combined victim counts of 2021–22 and hit law firms, government, manufacturing, oil & gas, and logistics hardest. hits.text: Fortra has disclosed CVE-2024-0204, a critical (CVSS 9.8) authentication-bypass flaw in GoAnywhere MFT versions 6.0.1–7.4.0 that enables remote attackers to create arbitrary admin users via the web administration portal, potentially leading to full device takeover, data theft, malware deployment, and lateral movement; discovered December 1, 2023 by Mohammed Eldeeb and Islam Elrfai of Spark Engineering Consultants, it was patched in GoAnywhere MFT 7.4.1 on December 7 2023, and users unable to upgrade immediately can mitigate by deleting or emptying the InitialAccountSetup.xhtml file and restarting services. Although no in-the-wild exploitation has been observed, the publication of mitigations may spur PoC releases. This advisory follows January–February 2023 Clop ransomware attacks leveraging the unpatched CVE-2023-0669 remote-code-execution flaw to breach 130 organizations—including Crown Resorts, CHS, Hatch Bank, Rubrik, City of Toronto, Hitachi Energy, Procter & Gamble, and Saks Fifth Avenue—underscoring the critical need for timely patching and monitoring of MFT environments.
hits.title: Fortra warns of new critical GoAnywhere MFT auth bypass, patch now

hits.text: Silent Push researchers uncovered FIN7’s largest-ever infrastructure, identifying over 4,000 malicious IOFA domains and associated IP addresses used to fuel a global phishing and malware campaign that hit high-profile targets such as the Louvre, Meta and Reuters. Using automated intelligence and Threat Hunting workflows, analysts detected a pattern of newly registered look-alike domains—many leveraging common TLDs and typosquatting—to host spear-phishing landing pages and weaponized Office attachments that deploy custom .NET droppers and Cobalt Strike beacons. hits.text: Since at least August 2023, threat actors have exploited CVE-2023-4966 (CitrixBleed), a 7.5-rated flaw in Citrix NetScaler ADC and Gateway, culminating in an October 16–19 breach at Comcast Xfinity that exposed 35,879,455 customers’ usernames, hashed passwords, names, contact details, last four SSN digits, dates of birth and security Q&A; despite Citrix’s October 10 patch and Comcast’s claim of prompt mitigation, attackers used publicly available proofs-of-concept and rumored Python automation scripts to extract session tokens from device memory, hijack active sessions and bypass authentication, a tactic linked by ReliaQuest to at least five threat groups including LockBit; this incident highlights the necessity not only of timely patching and reboots but also of invalidating all active and persistent session tokens, enforcing multi-factor authentication, resetting credentials and maintaining continuous 24x7 monitoring to prevent further data exfiltration and ransomware deployment.

hits.text: On December 4 Fortra issued a private advisory on CVE-2024-0204, a critical authentication bypass in its GoAnywhere MFT 7.x, and silently patched it on December 7 in version 7.4.1 but only publicly disclosed the flaw today; now Horizon3’s Attack Team has released a proof-of-concept exploit that leverages a path traversal vulnerability to access the /InitialAccountSetup.xhtml endpoint and create unauthorized administrator accounts on unpatched instances, prompting defenders to immediately upgrade or delete/replace the InitialAccountSetup.xhtml file, restart services, and monitor the GoAnywhere “Admin Users” list for new entries. While Fortra reports no confirmed exploits in the wild, the public PoC is expected to trigger widespread scanning and compromises, echoing Clop’s January 2023 campaign that abused a GoAnywhere RCE (CVE-2023-0669) to breach over 100 organizations—including Community Health Systems, Procter & Gamble, Rubrik and the City of Toronto—and underscoring a broader pattern of MFT platform assaults seen in the 2020 Accellion FTA, 2021 SolarWinds Serv-U and 2023 MOVEit Transfer incidents.

hits.text: ESET’s 2024 analysis shows that in the wake of law-enforcement-led Operation Cronos and the collapse of LockBit and BlackCat, RansomHub emerged in February as the dominant RaaS operator—driving a 15 percent rise in leak-site victims even as overall ransomware payments fell 35 percent—and by November had eclipsed LockBit in cumulative victim postings. By tracing unique victim IDs and builder tool fingerprints, researchers linked RansomHub to established gangs Play, Medusa and BianLian and revealed that its multiplatform encryptor (Windows, Linux, ESXi) repurposes Knight source code and is protected by a unique 64-character password per sample. In May, operators added “EDRKillShifter,” a custom EDR killer that abuses at least two publicly known vulnerable drivers and uses password-encrypted shellcode to disable security products, all delivered via RansomHub’s web panel under the same affiliate-specific password model. Affiliates—who keep 90 percent of ransoms and enroll via recommendation, reputation proof or a refundable US $5 000 deposit—negotiate exclusively over Tor, post detailed ransom notes to victims, and benefit from free trial decryptions. Key mitigations include strict driver allow-listing, monitoring for anomalous driver loads, hardening EDR self-protection, blocking known Tor endpoints, and correlating builder requests and password probes to detect emerging RansomHub activity.
hits.title: Shifting the sands of RansomHub’s EDRKillShifter
