hits.text: In August 2025 Microsoft Threat Intelligence revealed that Storm-2460, associated with the Play ransomware group, has resumed exploiting CVE-2025-29824—a zero-day elevation-of-privilege flaw in the Windows Common Log File System patched in April—to gain SYSTEM privileges on unpatched hosts across IT, financial and real estate organizations in the US, Europe, South America and the Middle East. The campaign begins with an in-memory dropper masquerading as the open-source ChatGPT Desktop app that decrypts and launches PipeMagic, a modular backdoor first observed in December 2022 and now updated with persistence and lateral-movement enhancements targeting Saudi Arabian and Brazilian manufacturing entities. PipeMagic communicates with its TCP C2 over a named pipe, self-updates by storing distinct payload modules in memory via doubly linked lists for staging, execution and communication (plus an additional dynamic list), then leverages the CLFS exploit to escalate privileges before deploying Play ransomware. Although the campaign’s footprint remains limited, the combination of a zero-day exploit and a sophisticated modular backdoor underscores a heightened risk; organizations are urged to immediately apply the April patch for CVE-2025-29824, enable tamper and network protection in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, run EDR in block mode, enforce full automated investigation and remediation, and leverage cloud-delivered machine-learning protections to block novel variants.
hits.title: PipeMagic Backdoor Resurfaces as Part of Play Ransomware Attack Chain

hits.text: In April 2025, Microsoft patched 121 vulnerabilities—including CVE-2025-29824, the sole flaw exploited by PipeMagic—an evolution of a backdoor first spotted in December 2022 during a RansomExx campaign against Southeast Asian industrial firms via CVE-2017-0144 and resurfaced in September 2024 in the Middle East using a Rust-based fake ChatGPT loader (Tauri/Tokio) that decrypts AES-encrypted shellcode, resolves APIs via FNV-1a hashing, relocates imports and invokes its entry point. PipeMagic generates random 16-byte named pipes (“\\.\\pipe\\1.<hex>”) alongside a 127.0.0.1:8082 TCP interface, downloads plugins from a Cloud Azure domain (aaaaabbbbbbb.eastus.cloudapp.azure[.]com) and supports modules such as an I/O-completion-port communication plugin (handling file I/O commands) and a loader for injecting 64-bit payloads via DllRegisterService. In January 2025, new campaigns in Brazil and the Middle East introduced a Microsoft Help Index File loader executed through MSBuild that RC4-decrypts shellcode (key 4829468622e6b82ff056e3c945dd99c94a1f0264d980774828aadda326b775e5) via EnumDeviceMonitor and a GoogleUpdate.dll hijack variant performing AES-CBC decryption (key 9C3BA5B2D3222FE5863C14D51340D7F9, IV 221BA50915042098AF5F8EE40E5559C8) to deploy the same 32-bit backdoor PE. Joint analysis with BI.ZONE reveals a shift toward multi-staged, encrypted loaders and diversified access vectors, underscoring the need to restrict MSBuild use, monitor DLL hijacking, inspect named-pipe and localhost traffic, and block suspicious Azure domains to mitigate PipeMagic’s adaptive tactics.
hits.title: PipeMagic in 2025: How the backdoor operators’ tactics have changed

hits.text: After a year-long investigation researchers at Lumen’s Black Lotus Labs dissected the Ngioweb botnet—first observed in 2017—which uses a loader network and roughly 15 n-day exploits to deploy malware that contacts C2 domains generated via a domain generation algorithm (augmented by DNS TXT records to resist sinkholing), evaluates device traffic capacity, and links compromised Zyxel, Reolink, Alpha Technologies and, increasingly, Netgear routers (now 10 % of bots) to over 180 “backconnect” C2 nodes that provide at least 80 % of the 35,000 residential proxies in the NSOCKS[.]net service across 180 countries; NSOCKS’s lack of authentication and appearance on free proxy lists has enabled cybercriminals to carry out DDoS amplification, credential stuffing, phishing and malware proxying (e.g., Agent Tesla), while APT28 state-sponsored actors have mixed espionage with criminal traffic on the same infrastructure. To disrupt both operations, Lumen, alongside The ShadowServer Foundation and other partners, is actively blocking traffic to known C2 nodes and publishing indicators of compromise to help organizations identify and remediate infected devices.
hits.title: Botnet fueling residential proxies disrupted in cybercrime crackdown

hits.text: Symantec’s Threat Hunter Team has linked the newly discovered Sidewalk loader backdoor—an evolution of the Crosswalk/Backdoor.Motnug family—to Grayfly (aka GREF/Wicked Panda), a China-linked espionage group active since March 2017 that employs custom backdoors, Trojan.Chattak, Cobalt Strike, web shells and credential-dumpers against telecom, IT, media and finance targets in Taiwan, Vietnam, the US and Mexico; in a recent campaign they exploited public-facing Microsoft Exchange and MySQL servers via commodity and zero-day flaws to execute Base64-encoded PowerShell commands through certutil, install an ASPX web shell in the ClientAccess\ecp directory, deploy Sidewalk via installutil.exe, create persistence with WMIC-launched scheduled tasks, then run a custom Mimikatz variant (SHA256 b3eb783b017da32e33d19670b39eae0b11de8e983891dd4feb873d6e9333608d) to harvest credentials—all within about an hour before ceasing observable activity; three Chengdu 404 executives were indicted in 2020 for attacks on over 100 organizations, highlighting Grayfly’s persistence and underscoring the need to promptly patch Exchange and MySQL servers, monitor anomalous PowerShell and scheduled-task activity, and deploy IOC-based detection to block Sidewalk and related tools.
hits.title: Grayfly: Chinese Threat Actor Uses Newly-discovered Sidewalk Malware | Symantec Enterprise Blogs

hits.text: Since its emergence in 2013, Iran-linked APT35 (aka Charming Kitten/Phosphorus) has executed a series of high-value espionage campaigns—beginning with a 2014 social-media spying operation—and continued in 2019 with spear-phishing against U.S., French and Middle East academic institutions before Microsoft’s Digital Crimes Unit seized control of 99 APT35 domains; in late 2020 the group targeted oncology, genetics and neurology researchers in Israel and the U.S. via its “BadBlood” PDF-based spear-phishing campaign, while in 2021 it chained Exchange Server flaws (ProxyShell) for network intrusion and demonstrated TTP overlaps with Momento ransomware (CVE-2021-21972 exploiter); in January 2022 it performed mass Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228) scans—over 80 percent of attempts originated in the U.S.—and later deployed a stealthy .NET-based PowerShell backdoor (“PowerLess”) that runs in-process to avoid detection, followed by Hyperscrape, a Windows .NET mailbox exfiltration tool for Outlook, Gmail and Yahoo! that quietly harvests emails once the actor possesses valid credentials or session cookies, and a companion Telegram dump utility; APT35 maintains persistence for intelligence collection or monetizes access when systems lack strategic value, underscoring the need for timely patching, multi-factor authentication and continuous monitoring.
hits.title: An In-Depth Look at APT35 aka Charming Kitten

hits.text: Microsoft’s research exposes the BadPilot campaign—a multiyear initial-access subgroup of Russian GRU-aligned Seashell Blizzard active since at least 2021—that has opportunistically scanned for and exploited Internet-facing vulnerabilities (CVE-2021-34473 Exchange, CVE-2022-41352 Zimbra, CVE-2023-32315 OpenFire, CVE-2023-42793 TeamCity, CVE-2023-23397 Outlook, CVE-2024-1709 ConnectWise ScreenConnect, CVE-2023-48788 FortiClient EMS and various JBOSS flaws) to compromise a globally diverse set of high-value sectors (energy, oil and gas, telecommunications, shipping, arms manufacturing and government). Following initial access, BadPilot employs stealthy persistence, credential harvesting, lateral movement and common tools such as Cobalt Strike and DarkCrystalRAT to sustain footholds and support tailored network operations, including at least three destructive cyberattacks in Ukraine since 2023. After focusing on Ukraine, Europe, Central/South Asia and the Middle East during 2021–2023, the subgroup scaled horizontally into the United States, United Kingdom, Canada and Australia in early 2024, reflecting Russia’s evolving strategic objectives and underscoring the urgency of patching Internet-facing services, implementing comprehensive logging and anomaly detection, and applying threat-informed incident-response practices to disrupt its operational lifecycle.
hits.title: The BadPilot campaign: Seashell Blizzard subgroup conducts multiyear global access operation | Microsoft Security Blog

canonical_entities: Remote Code Execution via ms-msdt URI in Word/RTF documents
ms-msdt URI-based RCE in Word/RTF documents
hits.text: In late May 2022, Symantec identified multiple threat actors exploiting the MSDT Follina bug (CVE-2022-30190) through ms-msdt URI-based RCE in Word/RTF documents that load a malicious HTML via Word’s remote template feature to launch msdt.exe, sdiagnhost.exe and ultimately PowerShell—bypassing the need for macros—to install a digitally signed AsyncRAT remote access Trojan that performs anti-analysis checks, collects hardware IDs, user names, execution paths and OS details, and maintains C&C communications, alongside parallel deployments of a browser infostealer targeting cookies and saved credentials in Firefox, Chrome and Edge. Symantec customers should apply Microsoft’s advisories or disable the ms-msdt handler, update Symantec Endpoint definitions (File-based-Downloader-Backdoor:Async, InfoStealer) and monitor for related IOCs to thwart these rapid, damaging campaigns.
hits.title: Attackers Exploit MSDT Follina Bug to Drop RAT, Infostealer | Symantec Enterprise Blogs

canonical_entities: Launch EC2 instances across regions via VPN
hits.text: Unit42’s “EleKtra-Leak” campaign, active since December 2020, uses automated scripts to clone public GitHub repos every few minutes, extract exposed AWS IAM keys within five minutes, then—if not blocked by GitHub-AWS quarantine policies—execute rapid AWS reconnaissance (DescribeRegions), create security groups, and launch hundreds of EC2 instances across regions via VPN for Monero cryptojacking, generating over 400 API calls in seven minutes. Between Aug. 30 and Oct. 6, 2023, researchers tracked 474 actor-controlled miners. The actor employs custom mining software and blocklists high-profile AWS account IDs to avoid honey traps. Leveraging the Prisma Cloud HoneyCloud project’s ephemeral key leaks and policy overrides, Unit42 obtained full visibility, informing Prisma Cloud Secrets Security, CI/CD IaC scanning, Cortex XDR, and recommendations for independent repo scanning, strict IAM policies, and continuous monitoring.
hits.title: CloudKeys in the Air: Tracking Malicious Operations of Exposed IAM Keys

hits.text: Our GReAT team uncovered Operation ForumTroll—a state-sponsored APT campaign targeting Russian media, academic and government personnel—delivering previously unknown malware via phishing emails masquerading as Primakov Readings invitations containing two malicious links; clicking either on a Windows PC using Chrome or any Chromium-based browser silently triggers a zero-day exploit (CVE-2025-2783), exploiting a logic flaw at the Chrome-Windows interface to bypass the browser’s sandbox and deploy the payload without further user interaction. We promptly reported the vulnerability to Google, which released a patch in Chrome version 134.0.6998.177/178; while the phishing links now redirect to the legitimate forum site and the campaign is dormant, the attackers could reactivate it at any time. To mitigate this espionage threat, organizations should ensure all Chrome instances are updated to at least 134.0.6998.177/.178, deploy robust exploit detection and prevention solutions on internet-connected devices, and maintain vigilant phishing awareness and monitoring.
hits.title: CVE-2025-2783 in Operation ForumTroll APT

canonical_entities: diplomatic and defense networks in Ukraine
hits.text: Secret Blizzard, the Russian FSB’s Center 16, has escalated global espionage by co-opting C2 infrastructures of at least six threat actors—including Pakistan-based Storm-0156, Hazel Sandstorm and Storm-0473—to install backdoors (CrimsonRAT, Wainscot), deploy custom payloads (TwoDash downloader, MiniPocket fetcher), a TinyTurla variant disguised as a Windows service, and the Statuezy clipboard-monitoring trojan via DLL sideloading and batch files; this cross-actor compromise secured persistent access to diplomatic and defense networks in Ukraine, Afghanistan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and GDI, and Indian military institutions, enabling exfiltration of politically sensitive intelligence and advanced research data while reducing development overhead and underscoring the need for robust supply-chain security, network segmentation and proactive vulnerability management.
hits.title: Hackers with Russian Blizzard Steal Data from Rival Networks

retrieved_context.text: After a year-long investigation researchers at Lumen’s Black Lotus Labs dissected the Ngioweb botnet—first observed in 2017—which uses a loader network and roughly 15 n-day exploits to deploy malware that contacts C2 domains generated via a domain generation algorithm (augmented by DNS TXT records to resist sinkholing), evaluates device traffic capacity, and links compromised Zyxel, Reolink, Alpha Technologies and, increasingly, Netgear routers (now 10 % of bots) to over 180 “backconnect” C2 nodes that provide at least 80 % of the 35,000 residential proxies in the NSOCKS[.]net service across 180 countries; NSOCKS’s lack of authentication and appearance on free proxy lists has enabled cybercriminals to carry out DDoS amplification, credential stuffing, phishing and malware proxying (e.g., Agent Tesla), while APT28 state-sponsored actors have mixed espionage with criminal traffic on the same infrastructure. To disrupt both operations, Lumen, alongside The ShadowServer Foundation and other partners, is actively blocking traffic to known C2 nodes and publishing indicators of compromise to help organizations identify and remediate infected devices.
retrieved_context.title: Botnet fueling residential proxies disrupted in cybercrime crackdown

retrieved_context.text: Symantec’s Threat Hunter Team has linked the newly discovered Sidewalk loader backdoor—an evolution of the Crosswalk/Backdoor.Motnug family—to Grayfly (aka GREF/Wicked Panda), a China-linked espionage group active since March 2017 that employs custom backdoors, Trojan.Chattak, Cobalt Strike, web shells and credential-dumpers against telecom, IT, media and finance targets in Taiwan, Vietnam, the US and Mexico; in a recent campaign they exploited public-facing Microsoft Exchange and MySQL servers via commodity and zero-day flaws to execute Base64-encoded PowerShell commands through certutil, install an ASPX web shell in the ClientAccess\ecp directory, deploy Sidewalk via installutil.exe, create persistence with WMIC-launched scheduled tasks, then run a custom Mimikatz variant (SHA256 b3eb783b017da32e33d19670b39eae0b11de8e983891dd4feb873d6e9333608d) to harvest credentials—all within about an hour before ceasing observable activity; three Chengdu 404 executives were indicted in 2020 for attacks on over 100 organizations, highlighting Grayfly’s persistence and underscoring the need to promptly patch Exchange and MySQL servers, monitor anomalous PowerShell and scheduled-task activity, and deploy IOC-based detection to block Sidewalk and related tools.
retrieved_context.title: Grayfly: Chinese Threat Actor Uses Newly-discovered Sidewalk Malware | Symantec Enterprise Blogs

retrieved_context.text: Since its emergence in 2013, Iran-linked APT35 (aka Charming Kitten/Phosphorus) has executed a series of high-value espionage campaigns—beginning with a 2014 social-media spying operation—and continued in 2019 with spear-phishing against U.S., French and Middle East academic institutions before Microsoft’s Digital Crimes Unit seized control of 99 APT35 domains; in late 2020 the group targeted oncology, genetics and neurology researchers in Israel and the U.S. via its “BadBlood” PDF-based spear-phishing campaign, while in 2021 it chained Exchange Server flaws (ProxyShell) for network intrusion and demonstrated TTP overlaps with Momento ransomware (CVE-2021-21972 exploiter); in January 2022 it performed mass Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228) scans—over 80 percent of attempts originated in the U.S.—and later deployed a stealthy .NET-based PowerShell backdoor (“PowerLess”) that runs in-process to avoid detection, followed by Hyperscrape, a Windows .NET mailbox exfiltration tool for Outlook, Gmail and Yahoo! that quietly harvests emails once the actor possesses valid credentials or session cookies, and a companion Telegram dump utility; APT35 maintains persistence for intelligence collection or monetizes access when systems lack strategic value, underscoring the need for timely patching, multi-factor authentication and continuous monitoring.
retrieved_context.title: An In-Depth Look at APT35 aka Charming Kitten

retrieved_context.text: Microsoft’s research exposes the BadPilot campaign—a multiyear initial-access subgroup of Russian GRU-aligned Seashell Blizzard active since at least 2021—that has opportunistically scanned for and exploited Internet-facing vulnerabilities (CVE-2021-34473 Exchange, CVE-2022-41352 Zimbra, CVE-2023-32315 OpenFire, CVE-2023-42793 TeamCity, CVE-2023-23397 Outlook, CVE-2024-1709 ConnectWise ScreenConnect, CVE-2023-48788 FortiClient EMS and various JBOSS flaws) to compromise a globally diverse set of high-value sectors (energy, oil and gas, telecommunications, shipping, arms manufacturing and government). Following initial access, BadPilot employs stealthy persistence, credential harvesting, lateral movement and common tools such as Cobalt Strike and DarkCrystalRAT to sustain footholds and support tailored network operations, including at least three destructive cyberattacks in Ukraine since 2023. After focusing on Ukraine, Europe, Central/South Asia and the Middle East during 2021–2023, the subgroup scaled horizontally into the United States, United Kingdom, Canada and Australia in early 2024, reflecting Russia’s evolving strategic objectives and underscoring the urgency of patching Internet-facing services, implementing comprehensive logging and anomaly detection, and applying threat-informed incident-response practices to disrupt its operational lifecycle.
retrieved_context.title: The BadPilot campaign: Seashell Blizzard subgroup conducts multiyear global access operation | Microsoft Security Blog

canonical_entities: Remote Code Execution via ms-msdt URI in Word/RTF documents
ms-msdt URI-based RCE in Word/RTF documents
retrieved_context.text: In late May 2022, Symantec identified multiple threat actors exploiting the MSDT Follina bug (CVE-2022-30190) through ms-msdt URI-based RCE in Word/RTF documents that load a malicious HTML via Word’s remote template feature to launch msdt.exe, sdiagnhost.exe and ultimately PowerShell—bypassing the need for macros—to install a digitally signed AsyncRAT remote access Trojan that performs anti-analysis checks, collects hardware IDs, user names, execution paths and OS details, and maintains C&C communications, alongside parallel deployments of a browser infostealer targeting cookies and saved credentials in Firefox, Chrome and Edge. Symantec customers should apply Microsoft’s advisories or disable the ms-msdt handler, update Symantec Endpoint definitions (File-based-Downloader-Backdoor:Async, InfoStealer) and monitor for related IOCs to thwart these rapid, damaging campaigns.
retrieved_context.title: Attackers Exploit MSDT Follina Bug to Drop RAT, Infostealer | Symantec Enterprise Blogs

canonical_entities: Launch EC2 instances across regions via VPN
retrieved_context.text: Unit42’s “EleKtra-Leak” campaign, active since December 2020, uses automated scripts to clone public GitHub repos every few minutes, extract exposed AWS IAM keys within five minutes, then—if not blocked by GitHub-AWS quarantine policies—execute rapid AWS reconnaissance (DescribeRegions), create security groups, and launch hundreds of EC2 instances across regions via VPN for Monero cryptojacking, generating over 400 API calls in seven minutes. Between Aug. 30 and Oct. 6, 2023, researchers tracked 474 actor-controlled miners. The actor employs custom mining software and blocklists high-profile AWS account IDs to avoid honey traps. Leveraging the Prisma Cloud HoneyCloud project’s ephemeral key leaks and policy overrides, Unit42 obtained full visibility, informing Prisma Cloud Secrets Security, CI/CD IaC scanning, Cortex XDR, and recommendations for independent repo scanning, strict IAM policies, and continuous monitoring.
retrieved_context.title: CloudKeys in the Air: Tracking Malicious Operations of Exposed IAM Keys

retrieved_context.text: Our GReAT team uncovered Operation ForumTroll—a state-sponsored APT campaign targeting Russian media, academic and government personnel—delivering previously unknown malware via phishing emails masquerading as Primakov Readings invitations containing two malicious links; clicking either on a Windows PC using Chrome or any Chromium-based browser silently triggers a zero-day exploit (CVE-2025-2783), exploiting a logic flaw at the Chrome-Windows interface to bypass the browser’s sandbox and deploy the payload without further user interaction. We promptly reported the vulnerability to Google, which released a patch in Chrome version 134.0.6998.177/178; while the phishing links now redirect to the legitimate forum site and the campaign is dormant, the attackers could reactivate it at any time. To mitigate this espionage threat, organizations should ensure all Chrome instances are updated to at least 134.0.6998.177/.178, deploy robust exploit detection and prevention solutions on internet-connected devices, and maintain vigilant phishing awareness and monitoring.
retrieved_context.title: CVE-2025-2783 in Operation ForumTroll APT

canonical_entities: diplomatic and defense networks in Ukraine
retrieved_context.text: Secret Blizzard, the Russian FSB’s Center 16, has escalated global espionage by co-opting C2 infrastructures of at least six threat actors—including Pakistan-based Storm-0156, Hazel Sandstorm and Storm-0473—to install backdoors (CrimsonRAT, Wainscot), deploy custom payloads (TwoDash downloader, MiniPocket fetcher), a TinyTurla variant disguised as a Windows service, and the Statuezy clipboard-monitoring trojan via DLL sideloading and batch files; this cross-actor compromise secured persistent access to diplomatic and defense networks in Ukraine, Afghanistan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and GDI, and Indian military institutions, enabling exfiltration of politically sensitive intelligence and advanced research data while reducing development overhead and underscoring the need for robust supply-chain security, network segmentation and proactive vulnerability management.
retrieved_context.title: Hackers with Russian Blizzard Steal Data from Rival Networks

hits.text: In August 2025 Microsoft Threat Intelligence revealed that Storm-2460, associated with the Play ransomware group, has resumed exploiting CVE-2025-29824—a zero-day elevation-of-privilege flaw in the Windows Common Log File System patched in April—to gain SYSTEM privileges on unpatched hosts across IT, financial and real estate organizations in the US, Europe, South America and the Middle East. The campaign begins with an in-memory dropper masquerading as the open-source ChatGPT Desktop app that decrypts and launches PipeMagic, a modular backdoor first observed in December 2022 and now updated with persistence and lateral-movement enhancements targeting Saudi Arabian and Brazilian manufacturing entities. PipeMagic communicates with its TCP C2 over a named pipe, self-updates by storing distinct payload modules in memory via doubly linked lists for staging, execution and communication (plus an additional dynamic list), then leverages the CLFS exploit to escalate privileges before deploying Play ransomware. Although the campaign’s footprint remains limited, the combination of a zero-day exploit and a sophisticated modular backdoor underscores a heightened risk; organizations are urged to immediately apply the April patch for CVE-2025-29824, enable tamper and network protection in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, run EDR in block mode, enforce full automated investigation and remediation, and leverage cloud-delivered machine-learning protections to block novel variants.
hits.title: PipeMagic Backdoor Resurfaces as Part of Play Ransomware Attack Chain

hits.text: In April 2025, Microsoft patched 121 vulnerabilities—including CVE-2025-29824, the sole flaw exploited by PipeMagic—an evolution of a backdoor first spotted in December 2022 during a RansomExx campaign against Southeast Asian industrial firms via CVE-2017-0144 and resurfaced in September 2024 in the Middle East using a Rust-based fake ChatGPT loader (Tauri/Tokio) that decrypts AES-encrypted shellcode, resolves APIs via FNV-1a hashing, relocates imports and invokes its entry point. In January 2025, new campaigns in Brazil and the Middle East introduced a Microsoft Help Index File loader executed through MSBuild that RC4-decrypts shellcode (key 4829468622e6b82ff056e3c945dd99c94a1f0264d980774828aadda326b775e5) via EnumDeviceMonitor and a GoogleUpdate.dll hijack variant performing AES-CBC decryption (key 9C3BA5B2D3222FE5863C14D51340D7F9, IV 221BA50915042098AF5F8EE40E5559C8) to deploy the same 32-bit backdoor PE. Joint analysis with BI.ZONE reveals a shift toward multi-staged, encrypted loaders and diversified access vectors, underscoring the need to restrict MSBuild use, monitor DLL hijacking, inspect named-pipe and localhost traffic, and block suspicious Azure domains to mitigate PipeMagic’s adaptive tactics.
hits.title: PipeMagic in 2025: How the backdoor operators’ tactics have changed

canonical_entities: installing Sagerunex variants in the Windows Registry
hits.text: The Lotus Blossom APT (aka Lotus Panda, Billbug, Spring Dragon) has stepped up cyberespionage against APAC government targets by deploying new Sagerunex backdoor variants and abusing Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) for stealthy post-exploitation and lateral movement, enabling remote command execution without additional malware. Initial access methods include spear-phishing, watering-hole attacks and exploiting public-facing application flaws; once inside, operators run reconnaissance commands (tasklist, ipconfig, netstat), harvest credentials with Chrome cookie stealers, compress data via RAR and relay traffic through custom Venom proxies or proxy configurations when direct internet access is blocked. Persistence is achieved by installing Sagerunex variants in the Windows Registry under hijacked service names (tapisrv, swprv) to auto-launch at startup, while command-and-control blends encrypted traffic into legitimate platforms—stolen data uploaded as .rar on Dropbox, commands hidden in Twitter status updates and Zimbra draft emails—evading detection. Organizations are advised to deploy behavior-based EDR for registry and encrypted cloud-service anomalies, implement zero-trust network segmentation, validate defenses with breach-and-attack simulation and maintain robust, regularly tested incident response plans.
hits.title: Lotus Blossom APT Exploits WMI for Post-Exploitation Activities

hits.text: ESET researchers have retrospectively identified WinorDLL64.dll—a backdoor payload for the Wslink loader (WinorLoaderDLL64.dll) first uncovered in 2021—that operates as an in-memory server using MemoryModule and is protected by Oreans Code Virtualizer; although the initial compromise vector remains unknown, sparse detections in Central Europe, North America and the Middle East and a South Korean VirusTotal submission triggered YARA alerts based on its unique filename. Communicating over the loader’s established AES-256-CBC encrypted TCP channel, WinorDLL64 implements at least 16 commands—including comprehensive system profiling, secure file exfiltration, overwrite and deletion, process and RDP session management, unrestricted PowerShell execution, directory compression for data theft, and connection latency measurement—facilitating reconnaissance, persistence and lateral movement. Low-confidence attribution to North Korea–aligned Lazarus (HIDDEN COBRA) derives from targeting of South Korean victims, shared VS2010 LTCG build signatures and code/behavior overlap with 2018 GhostSecret (FE887FCAB66D7D7F79F05E0266C0649F0114BA7C) and Bankshot implants; this underscores Lazarus’s organized, modular arsenal and highlights the need to detect anomalous in-memory loaders and encrypted session anomalies.
hits.title: WinorDLL64: A backdoor from the vast Lazarus arsenal?

hits.text: Since November 2024, Iran-linked APT42 (aka TA453/Mint Sandstorm) has executed multi-stage intrusions against government ministries and critical infrastructure across Europe and the Middle East, initially using spear-phishing lures with malicious RTF attachments to deploy its custom ChainDoor RAT and establish HTTPS-based C2 channels; in December 2024 it leveraged a zero-day SQL injection against public-facing web portals to plant a secondary backdoor, then used Mimikatz for credential harvesting and lateral movement, exfiltrating over 3.5 TB of sensitive PII and policy documents—hiding stolen data via steganography in JPEGs—and deploying coin-miner payloads on select hosts; this campaign has compromised at least 150 systems, caused an estimated $2 million in operational disruption, and underscores the need for immediate patching of web applications, enforcement of MFA, network segmentation, and enhanced monitoring for anomalous HTTPS traffic to known C2 domains.

hits.text: Lynx ransomware, emerging in July 2024 as the INC ransomware successor under a Ransomware-as-a-Service model, employs a sophisticated double-extortion strategy—exfiltrating data prior to encryption and threatening publication on a leak site—and reuses significant INC source code. Between July and November 2024, it disrupted U.S. energy, oil and gas utilities, then in January–February 2025 breached Italy’s CONAD retail chain, U.S. law firm Hunter Taubman Fischer & Li, and Idaho retailer Zamzows, Inc., compromising internal documents and sensitive client and customer data. Initial access leverages phishing (T1566.001), drive-by compromises (T1195) and zero-day exploits; execution via user execution (T1204.002) and scripting interpreters (T1059.001); persistence through autostart mechanisms (T1070.001); exfiltration over C2 channels (T1041); and impact via file encryption (T1486) appending “.LYNX.” Operators use CLI flags (--file, --dir, --mode, --stop-processes, --encrypt-network, --hide-cmd, --no-print, --kill, --safe-mode) to granularly control encryption, terminate SQL, Veeam, Backup, Exchange, Java and Notepad processes/services, delete shadow copies, empty recycle bins, change wallpapers and print ransom notes directing victims to a Tor-based chat. Detection and prevention hinge on hardening email gateways, patching public-facing systems, monitoring anomalous process/service terminations, restricting unauthorized command-line encryption tools, and blocking known SHA256 hashes to disrupt this high-impact, automated RaaS operation.
hits.title: Lynx Ransomware: INC Ransomware Reincarnated - Threat Actors

canonical_entities: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Windows Command Shell
hits.text: NCC Group’s RIFT team uncovered a sophisticated new FiveHands ransomware variant deployed by an affiliate linked to UNC2447, who gained initial access in June 2021 by exploiting a SonicWall VPN appliance—evidenced by a “command0/Commando” login from source port 4444 (Metasploit default)—then moved laterally via RDP (T1021.001) using the weak password “Remark123!” and PsExec (T1059.003). The actor leveraged publicly available tools—SoftPerfect Netscan and Advanced Port Scanner for network discovery (T1046), AllInOnePasswordRecoveryPro for credential harvesting (T1003.001), Remote Utilities (“Hostclean.exe”) for persistent C2 (T1219), and pCloud (“pCloud.exe”) for exfiltration (T1567.002), caching 10 GB of stolen data under %AppData%\pCloud\CacheCached—to stage and extract sensitive files. The Go-written loader (“Encryptor.exe”) accepts a 16-byte key (captured via RDP bitmap cache and brute force) to decrypt a unique C++ ransomware payload in memory, which uses RSA/AES (Mbed TLS) to encrypt files in blocks (.crypt/.crypt) while excluding system folders and leveraging Windows Restart Manager to breach locked files. This RaaS model (hijacking hardcoded TOR IDs) employs aggressive extortion tactics—spoofed caller ID calls urging prompt payment—and underscores the need for robust VPN log monitoring, RDP restrictions, enforceable command-line auditing, multi-factor authentication, and forensic examination of cloud‐sync caches to detect and mitigate similar intrusions.
hits.title: Handy guide to a new Fivehands ransomware variant

hits.text: Since January 2021, Google’s Threat Analysis Group (TAG) has tracked a government-backed North Korean campaign that leverages social engineering via X (formerly Twitter) and encrypted messaging apps to befriend security researchers and deliver malicious files containing at least one unpatched 0-day in a popular software package; upon exploitation the custom shellcode performs anti-virtual-machine checks, captures system data and screenshots, and exfiltrates them to C2 infrastructure (e.g., 23.106.215[.]105, www.blgbeach[.]com), with the latest vulnerability reported and patched on September 12, 2023 (see TAG’s published RCA). In parallel, the actors published a seemingly benign Windows tool called GetSymbol on GitHub (https://github.com/dbgsymbol/) that quietly downloads debugging symbols—and arbitrary code—from attacker domains, requiring full OS reinstalls for compromised hosts. TAG has added malicious sites to Safe Browsing, issued government-backed attacker alerts to targeted Gmail and Workspace users, and urges researchers to enable Enhanced Safe Browsing, keep software up to date, and verify system integrity after using third-party tools.

retrieved_context.text: Lynx ransomware, emerging in July 2024 as the INC ransomware successor under a Ransomware-as-a-Service model, employs a sophisticated double-extortion strategy—exfiltrating data prior to encryption and threatening publication on a leak site—and reuses significant INC source code. Between July and November 2024, it disrupted U.S. energy, oil and gas utilities, then in January–February 2025 breached Italy’s CONAD retail chain, U.S. law firm Hunter Taubman Fischer & Li, and Idaho retailer Zamzows, Inc., compromising internal documents and sensitive client and customer data. Initial access leverages phishing (T1566.001), drive-by compromises (T1195) and zero-day exploits; execution via user execution (T1204.002) and scripting interpreters (T1059.001); persistence through autostart mechanisms (T1070.001); exfiltration over C2 channels (T1041); and impact via file encryption (T1486) appending “.LYNX.” Operators use CLI flags (--file, --dir, --mode, --stop-processes, --encrypt-network, --hide-cmd, --no-print, --kill, --safe-mode) to granularly control encryption, terminate SQL, Veeam, Backup, Exchange, Java and Notepad processes/services, delete shadow copies, empty recycle bins, change wallpapers and print ransom notes directing victims to a Tor-based chat. Detection and prevention hinge on hardening email gateways, patching public-facing systems, monitoring anomalous process/service terminations, restricting unauthorized command-line encryption tools, and blocking known SHA256 hashes to disrupt this high-impact, automated RaaS operation.

retrieved_context.text: NCC Group’s RIFT team uncovered a sophisticated new FiveHands ransomware variant deployed by an affiliate linked to UNC2447, who gained initial access in June 2021 by exploiting a SonicWall VPN appliance—evidenced by a “command0/Commando” login from source port 4444 (Metasploit default)—then moved laterally via RDP (T1021.001) using the weak password “Remark123!” and PsExec (T1059.003). The actor leveraged publicly available tools—SoftPerfect Netscan and Advanced Port Scanner for network discovery (T1046), AllInOnePasswordRecoveryPro for credential harvesting (T1003.001), Remote Utilities (“Hostclean.exe”) for persistent C2 (T1219), and pCloud (“pCloud.exe”) for exfiltration (T1567.002), caching 10 GB of stolen data under %AppData%\pCloud\CacheCached—to stage and extract sensitive files. The Go-written loader (“Encryptor.exe”) accepts a 16-byte key (captured via RDP bitmap cache and brute force) to decrypt a unique C++ ransomware payload in memory, which uses RSA/AES (Mbed TLS) to encrypt files in blocks (.crypt/.crypt) while excluding system folders and leveraging Windows Restart Manager to breach locked files. This RaaS model (hijacking hardcoded TOR IDs) employs aggressive extortion tactics—spoofed caller ID calls urging prompt payment—and underscores the need for robust VPN log monitoring, RDP restrictions, enforceable command-line auditing, multi-factor authentication, and forensic examination of cloud‐sync caches to detect and mitigate similar intrusions.

retrieved_context.text: Since January 2021, Google’s Threat Analysis Group (TAG) has tracked a government-backed North Korean campaign that leverages social engineering via X (formerly Twitter) and encrypted messaging apps to befriend security researchers and deliver malicious files containing at least one unpatched 0-day in a popular software package; upon exploitation the custom shellcode performs anti-virtual-machine checks, captures system data and screenshots, and exfiltrates them to C2 infrastructure (e.g., 23.106.215[.]105, www.blgbeach[.]com), with the latest vulnerability reported and patched on September 12, 2023 (see TAG’s published RCA). In parallel, the actors published a seemingly benign Windows tool called GetSymbol on GitHub (https://github.com/dbgsymbol/) that quietly downloads debugging symbols—and arbitrary code—from attacker domains, requiring full OS reinstalls for compromised hosts. TAG has added malicious sites to Safe Browsing, issued government-backed attacker alerts to targeted Gmail and Workspace users, and urges researchers to enable Enhanced Safe Browsing, keep software up to date, and verify system integrity after using third-party tools.
retrieved_context.title: Active North Korean campaign targeting security researchers

retrieved_context.text: Since its emergence in 2013, Iran-linked APT35 (aka Charming Kitten/Phosphorus) has executed a series of high-value espionage campaigns—beginning with a 2014 social-media spying operation—and continued in 2019 with spear-phishing against U.S., French and Middle East academic institutions before Microsoft’s Digital Crimes Unit seized control of 99 APT35 domains; in late 2020 the group targeted oncology, genetics and neurology researchers in Israel and the U.S. via its “BadBlood” PDF-based spear-phishing campaign, while in 2021 it chained Exchange Server flaws (ProxyShell) for network intrusion and demonstrated TTP overlaps with Momento ransomware (CVE-2021-21972 exploiter); in January 2022 it performed mass Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228) scans—over 80 percent of attempts originated in the U.S.—and later deployed a stealthy .NET-based PowerShell backdoor (“PowerLess”) that runs in-process to avoid detection, followed by Hyperscrape, a Windows .NET mailbox exfiltration tool for Outlook, Gmail and Yahoo! that quietly harvests emails once the actor possesses valid credentials or session cookies, and a companion Telegram dump utility; APT35 maintains persistence for intelligence collection or monetizes access when systems lack strategic value, underscoring the need for timely patching, multi-factor authentication and continuous monitoring.
retrieved_context.title: An In-Depth Look at APT35 aka Charming Kitten

hits.text: In August 2025 Microsoft Threat Intelligence revealed that Storm-2460, associated with the Play ransomware group, has resumed exploiting CVE-2025-29824—a zero-day elevation-of-privilege flaw in the Windows Common Log File System patched in April—to gain SYSTEM privileges on unpatched hosts across IT, financial and real estate organizations in the US, Europe, South America and the Middle East. The campaign begins with an in-memory dropper masquerading as the open-source ChatGPT Desktop app that decrypts and launches PipeMagic, a modular backdoor first observed in December 2022 and now updated with persistence and lateral-movement enhancements targeting Saudi Arabian and Brazilian manufacturing entities. PipeMagic communicates with its TCP C2 over a named pipe, self-updates by storing distinct payload modules in memory via doubly linked lists for staging, execution and communication (plus an additional dynamic list), then leverages the CLFS exploit to escalate privileges before deploying Play ransomware. Although the campaign’s footprint remains limited, the combination of a zero-day exploit and a sophisticated modular backdoor underscores a heightened risk; organizations are urged to immediately apply the April patch for CVE-2025-29824, enable tamper and network protection in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, run EDR in block mode, enforce full automated investigation and remediation, and leverage cloud-delivered machine-learning protections to block novel variants.
hits.title: PipeMagic Backdoor Resurfaces as Part of Play Ransomware Attack Chain

hits.text: In April 2025, Microsoft patched 121 vulnerabilities—including CVE-2025-29824, the sole flaw exploited by PipeMagic—an evolution of a backdoor first spotted in December 2022 during a RansomExx campaign against Southeast Asian industrial firms via CVE-2017-0144 and resurfaced in September 2024 in the Middle East using a Rust-based fake ChatGPT loader (Tauri/Tokio) that decrypts AES-encrypted shellcode, resolves APIs via FNV-1a hashing, relocates imports and invokes its entry point. PipeMagic generates random 16-byte named pipes (“\\.\\pipe\\1.<hex>”) alongside a 127.0.0.1:8082 TCP interface, downloads plugins from a Cloud Azure domain (aaaaabbbbbbb.eastus.cloudapp.azure[.]com) and supports modules such as an I/O-completion-port communication plugin (handling file I/O commands) and a loader for injecting 64-bit payloads via DllRegisterService. In January 2025, new campaigns in Brazil and the Middle East introduced a Microsoft Help Index File loader executed through MSBuild that RC4-decrypts shellcode (key 4829468622e6b82ff056e3c945dd99c94a1f0264d980774828aadda326b775e5) via EnumDeviceMonitor and a GoogleUpdate.dll hijack variant performing AES-CBC decryption (key 9C3BA5B2D3222FE5863C14D51340D7F9, IV 221BA50915042098AF5F8EE40E5559C8) to deploy the same 32-bit backdoor PE. Joint analysis with BI.ZONE reveals a shift toward multi-staged, encrypted loaders and diversified access vectors, underscoring the need to restrict MSBuild use, monitor DLL hijacking, inspect named-pipe and localhost traffic, and block suspicious Azure domains to mitigate PipeMagic’s adaptive tactics.
hits.title: PipeMagic in 2025: How the backdoor operators’ tactics have changed

canonical_entities: installing Sagerunex variants in the Windows Registry
hits.text: The Lotus Blossom APT (aka Lotus Panda, Billbug, Spring Dragon) has stepped up cyberespionage against APAC government targets by deploying new Sagerunex backdoor variants and abusing Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) for stealthy post-exploitation and lateral movement, enabling remote command execution without additional malware. Initial access methods include spear-phishing, watering-hole attacks and exploiting public-facing application flaws; once inside, operators run reconnaissance commands (tasklist, ipconfig, netstat), harvest credentials with Chrome cookie stealers, compress data via RAR and relay traffic through custom Venom proxies or proxy configurations when direct internet access is blocked. Persistence is achieved by installing Sagerunex variants in the Windows Registry under hijacked service names (tapisrv, swprv) to auto-launch at startup, while command-and-control blends encrypted traffic into legitimate platforms—stolen data uploaded as .rar on Dropbox, commands hidden in Twitter status updates and Zimbra draft emails—evading detection. Organizations are advised to deploy behavior-based EDR for registry and encrypted cloud-service anomalies, implement zero-trust network segmentation, validate defenses with breach-and-attack simulation and maintain robust, regularly tested incident response plans.
hits.title: Lotus Blossom APT Exploits WMI for Post-Exploitation Activities

hits.text: Microsoft’s research exposes the BadPilot campaign—a multiyear initial-access subgroup of Russian GRU-aligned Seashell Blizzard active since at least 2021—that has opportunistically scanned for and exploited Internet-facing vulnerabilities (CVE-2021-34473 Exchange, CVE-2022-41352 Zimbra, CVE-2023-32315 OpenFire, CVE-2023-42793 TeamCity, CVE-2023-23397 Outlook, CVE-2024-1709 ConnectWise ScreenConnect, CVE-2023-48788 FortiClient EMS and various JBOSS flaws) to compromise a globally diverse set of high-value sectors (energy, oil and gas, telecommunications, shipping, arms manufacturing and government). hits.title: The BadPilot campaign: Seashell Blizzard subgroup conducts multiyear global access operation | Microsoft Security Blog

canonical_entities: Bypass authentication by sending empty or invalid USERNAME and PASSWORD parameters with requirePasswordChange=Y
hits.text: A critical zero-day flaw (CVE-2023-51467) has been identified in Apache OfBiz’s login functionality—stemming from an incomplete patch for a prior high-severity RCE vulnerability (CVE-2023-49070, CVSS 9.8) tied to a deprecated XML-RPC component—that allows attackers to bypass authentication by sending empty or invalid USERNAME and PASSWORD parameters alongside “requirePasswordChange=Y,” effectively granting unauthorized access and enabling simple SSRF attacks against internal resources; discovered by SonicWall Capture Labs, the bug follows observations by The Shadowserver Foundation of active exploitation attempts against CVE-2023-49070, and SonicWall reports exploit traffic for CVE-2023-51467 spiking from 235 attempts on December 27, 2023, to 26,928 on December 29 and 3,129 on January 1, 2024, underscoring urgent need for organizations using OfBiz versions prior to 18.12.11 to upgrade immediately to mitigate further data exfiltration and system takeover risks.
hits.title: Critical Zero-Day in Apache OfBiz ERP System Exposes Businesses to Attack

hits.text: Attackers have been exploiting an unpatched Windows and Office zero-day vulnerability (CVE-2023-36884), disclosed by Microsoft on July 11, in highly targeted campaigns against government and defense organizations in Europe and North America; initial exploitation was documented by BlackBerry on July 8 when Storm-0978 (aka RomCom), a Russia-linked actor using the RomCom RAT with ties to the Hawker group and Cuba ransomware developers (and potentially to Industrial Spy ransomware operators), delivered malicious Word documents masquerading as Ukrainian World Congress materials to NATO Summit attendees, enabling remote code execution once opened. With no patch yet available, victims are urged to deploy all mitigations—leveraging Symantec’s email-, file-, network- and web-based protections (including WebPulse bad-reputation domain filtering), monitor the published IOC hashes, and prepare for Microsoft’s forthcoming monthly or out-of-cycle update—to prevent further compromise and forestall secondary ransomware or espionage operations.
hits.title: Attackers Exploit Unpatched Windows Zero-Day Vulnerability | Symantec Enterprise Blogs

hits.text: ESET researchers disclosed MoustachedBouncer, a Belarus-aligned cyberespionage group active since at least 2014 targeting foreign embassies in Belarus, employing two parallel malware frameworks: the email-based NightClub (SMTP/IMAP C2) and its 2020-onward successor Disco (Go/.NET) delivered via adversary-in-the-middle (AitM) at ISP level—likely leveraging Belarus’s SORM lawful interception—to redirect Windows captive portal checks to a fake Windows Update page. This page loads jdrop.js to prompt a malicious installer, which schedules SMB-delivered OfficeBroker payloads from attacker-injected Google Cloud IPs. Both frameworks support plugins for screenshots, audio recording and file theft. ESET observed compromises of embassies from four continents and assesses medium confidence in state alignment and low confidence in cooperation with Winter Vivern. Recommendations include out-of-band encrypted VPNs to thwart ISP-level interception.
hits.title: MoustachedBouncer: Espionage against foreign diplomats in Belarus

hits.text: Microsoft has traced a stealthy espionage campaign by Flax Typhoon (aka Ethereal Panda), a China-based nation-state actor active since mid-2021, targeting dozens of Taiwanese organizations (with spill-over in Southeast Asia, North America, and Africa) by exploiting known vulnerabilities in public-facing VPN, web, Java, and SQL services to deploy the China Chopper web shell for initial access; the group escalates privileges via open-source exploits like Juicy Potato and BadPotato, then establishes persistence by disabling RDP network-level authentication, hijacking the Sticky Keys (sethc.exe) binary to launch Task Manager as SYSTEM, and installing a renamed SoftEther VPN-over-HTTPS bridge (conhost.exe/dllhost.exe) as a service to maintain covert C2 over port 443; leveraging LOLBins such as PowerShell Invoke-WebRequest, certutil, bitsadmin, WinRM, and WMIC for lateral movement, vulnerability scanning, and remote execution, it harvests credentials from LSASS memory and the SAM registry hive using Mimikatz for pass-the-hash attacks; although no exfiltration or final objectives have been observed, organizations are urged to enforce rigorous patch and vulnerability management on internet-exposed systems, monitor registry and file-integrity changes, deploy web application firewalls, reset compromised credentials, isolate and forensically examine affected hosts, and leverage detections in Microsoft 365 Defender to disrupt living-off-the-land tactics.
hits.title: Flax Typhoon using legitimate software to quietly access Taiwanese organizations | Microsoft Security Blog

hits.text: Since at least April 2024 Microsoft Threat Intelligence has tracked a Russia-affiliated cyberespionage actor dubbed Void Blizzard (aka LAUNDRY BEAR) conducting high-volume, targeted operations against government, defense, transportation, media, NGO and healthcare organizations—particularly in NATO member states and Ukraine—by leveraging stolen credentials procured via commodity infostealer ecosystems for password spray attacks and Exchange/SharePoint Online access, then automating bulk email and file collection (and in some cases Teams messages) via cloud APIs and tools like AzureHound; in April 2025 the actor evolved to adversary-in-the-middle spear phishing using a typosquatted domain and the open-source Evilginx framework with a malicious QR-coded PDF to harvest Entra authentication data; this widespread success underscores that even unsophisticated TTPs pose major intelligence risks to critical sectors, so organizations should enforce sign-in risk policies and phishing-resistant MFA (e.g., FIDO/passkeys), centralize identity management with Conditional Access, monitor risky sign-ins and mailbox auditing, apply least-privilege credential hygiene, and promptly rotate credentials after infostealer detections to disrupt Void Blizzard’s operations.
hits.title: New Russia-affiliated actor Void Blizzard targets critical sectors for espionage | Microsoft Security Blog

hits.text: In August 2025 Microsoft Threat Intelligence revealed that Storm-2460, associated with the Play ransomware group, has resumed exploiting CVE-2025-29824—a zero-day elevation-of-privilege flaw in the Windows Common Log File System patched in April—to gain SYSTEM privileges on unpatched hosts across IT, financial and real estate organizations in the US, Europe, South America and the Middle East. The campaign begins with an in-memory dropper masquerading as the open-source ChatGPT Desktop app that decrypts and launches PipeMagic, a modular backdoor first observed in December 2022 and now updated with persistence and lateral-movement enhancements targeting Saudi Arabian and Brazilian manufacturing entities. PipeMagic communicates with its TCP C2 over a named pipe, self-updates by storing distinct payload modules in memory via doubly linked lists for staging, execution and communication (plus an additional dynamic list), then leverages the CLFS exploit to escalate privileges before deploying Play ransomware. Although the campaign’s footprint remains limited, the combination of a zero-day exploit and a sophisticated modular backdoor underscores a heightened risk; organizations are urged to immediately apply the April patch for CVE-2025-29824, enable tamper and network protection in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, run EDR in block mode, enforce full automated investigation and remediation, and leverage cloud-delivered machine-learning protections to block novel variants.
hits.title: PipeMagic Backdoor Resurfaces as Part of Play Ransomware Attack Chain

hits.text: In April 2025, Microsoft patched 121 vulnerabilities—including CVE-2025-29824, the sole flaw exploited by PipeMagic—an evolution of a backdoor first spotted in December 2022 during a RansomExx campaign against Southeast Asian industrial firms via CVE-2017-0144 and resurfaced in September 2024 in the Middle East using a Rust-based fake ChatGPT loader (Tauri/Tokio) that decrypts AES-encrypted shellcode, resolves APIs via FNV-1a hashing, relocates imports and invokes its entry point. PipeMagic generates random 16-byte named pipes (“\\.\\pipe\\1.<hex>”) alongside a 127.0.0.1:8082 TCP interface, downloads plugins from a Cloud Azure domain (aaaaabbbbbbb.eastus.cloudapp.azure[.]com) and supports modules such as an I/O-completion-port communication plugin (handling file I/O commands) and a loader for injecting 64-bit payloads via DllRegisterService. In January 2025, new campaigns in Brazil and the Middle East introduced a Microsoft Help Index File loader executed through MSBuild that RC4-decrypts shellcode (key 4829468622e6b82ff056e3c945dd99c94a1f0264d980774828aadda326b775e5) via EnumDeviceMonitor and a GoogleUpdate.dll hijack variant performing AES-CBC decryption (key 9C3BA5B2D3222FE5863C14D51340D7F9, IV 221BA50915042098AF5F8EE40E5559C8) to deploy the same 32-bit backdoor PE. Joint analysis with BI.ZONE reveals a shift toward multi-staged, encrypted loaders and diversified access vectors, underscoring the need to restrict MSBuild use, monitor DLL hijacking, inspect named-pipe and localhost traffic, and block suspicious Azure domains to mitigate PipeMagic’s adaptive tactics.
hits.title: PipeMagic in 2025: How the backdoor operators’ tactics have changed

hits.text: Last week Google’s Threat Analysis Group, in partnership with The Citizen Lab, exposed an in-the-wild exploit chain developed by the commercial surveillance vendor Intellexa in Egypt that leverages a man-in-the-middle injection on HTTP traffic to silently redirect targets first to c.betly[.]me and then to sec-flare[.]com, delivering Predator spyware without any user interaction; on iOS this chain combined Safari RCE (CVE-2023-41993), certificate validation bypass (CVE-2023-41991) and XNU kernel local privilege escalation (CVE-2023-41992) and was patched in iOS 16.7/17.0.1, while on Android initial Chrome renderer RCE (CVE-2023-4762), delivered via MITM or one-time links, was patched on September 5; this campaign highlights the serious risk posed by proliferating commercial spyware, underscores the urgency of enforcing universal HTTPS and enabling Chrome’s HTTPS-First Mode, and demonstrates the critical need for organizations and users to apply the latest OS and browser updates, deploy encrypted-traffic protections, and monitor for anomalous network redirects to mitigate future attacks.
hits.title: 0-days exploited by commercial surveillance vendor in Egypt

canonical_entities: Boot or Logon Initialization Scripts: Logon Script (Windows)
hits.text: Blitz is a modular two-stage Windows malware discovered in 2024 and actively developed into early 2025 by a Russian-speaking actor using the moniker sw1zzx who distributed backdoored Standoff 2 game cheat packages (Nerest_CrackBy@sw1zzx_dev.zip and Elysium_CrackBy@sw1zzx_dev.zip) via a Telegram channel. The first stage is a stealthy downloader (ieapfltr.dll) retrieved through a PowerShell one-liner from pastebin/paste.rs URLs after passing anti-sandbox and VM detection checks (timing loops, floating-point instruction counters, processor count and screen resolution heuristics), which then establishes persistence via HKCU\Environment\UserInitMprLogonScript and HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run. Upon reboot, the downloader connects to a FastAPI-based C2 infrastructure hosted on a Hugging Face Space to fetch the second-stage Blitz bot that performs keylogging, screenshot capture, denial-of-service attacks on web servers and can deploy an XMRig Monero miner as follow-up. This campaign leverages Hugging Face Spaces for file hosting and C2 communications, and the malware developer promoted cheats on social media before announcing departure in May 2025; Hugging Face subsequently locked the account and blocked blob IDs. The impact includes credential theft, resource exploitation, unauthorized cryptocurrency mining and potential service disruption, and Palo Alto Networks’ Advanced WildFire, URL Filtering, DNS Security, Threat Prevention, Cortex XDR and XSIAM effectively detect and block Blitz activities, with Unit 42 standing by for incident response.
hits.title: Blitz Malware: A Tale of Game Cheats and Code Repositories

hits.text: CISA has released a detailed analysis of the FiveHands ransomware, a C++-based DeathRansom successor with HelloKitty ties, deployed by financially motivated UNC2447 in recent European and North American intrusions; leveraging a VPN product zero-day for initial access, the adversary used open-source exploitation tools and SombRAT to map the network, exfiltrate data, and execute the NTRUEncrypt-powered ransomware stage, which enumerates and erases Volume Shadow Copies to thwart recovery, before demanding payment. CISA’s malware analysis (MAR) and accompanying report (AR) catalog 18 submitted artifacts—eight pen-test utilities, the ransomware binary, and nine SombRAT components—and provide mitigation guidance including timely VPN patching, network segmentation, multi-factor authentication, robust backup strategies, and behavior-based detection tuned to NTRUEncrypt operations and shadow copy deletion. These findings align with IST’s 48 anti-ransomware recommendations and the NCIJTF’s tactics-focused fact sheet, underscoring the need for proactive vulnerability management, continuous monitoring, and rapid response frameworks to neutralize UNC2447’s evolving capabilities.
hits.title: CISA Analyzes FiveHands Ransomware

hits.text: Lorenz ransomware, emerging in 2021 and likely a rebranding of the .sZ40/ThunderCrypt family, has preyed on over 20 mostly small-to-mid-sized organizations in the US, China and Mexico—demanding $500K–$700K via a double-extortion scheme and posting stolen data on a Tor leak site—most notably compromising Germany’s defense contractor Hensoldt in January 2022 (exfiltrating 95% of files) before exploiting a Mitel MiVoice Connect VoIP RCE (CVE-2022-29499, CVSS 9.8) in September to gain a perimeter foothold; CrowdStrike observed operators deploying a reverse shell via “pdf_import.php,” renaming binaries to “memdump” for anti-forensics, then using Chisel over SSH-secured HTTP to tunnel into the environment. Arctic Wolf analysis indicates either an initial-access broker or in-house exploit capability, a month-long dwell before invoking cURL to download and execute the “wc2_deploy” script for SSL pipes (mkfifo/OpenSSL), followed by CrackMapExec dumping credentials via comsvcs and Out-Minidump LSASS memory, installation of FileZilla under compromised admin accounts, and encryption via BitLocker triggered by a “worm.txt” script on the domain controller—with all event logs wiped and encryption progress beaconed via HTTP POSTs. These TTPs underscore the critical need to monitor IoT devices in real time, maintain up-to-date inventories with device-role tagging, enforce robust patch management, and deploy zero-trust, SIEM, whitelisting and vulnerability-management controls; Avertium specifically advocates applying Mitel’s remediation script for CVE-2022-29499 to mitigate further exploitation.
hits.title: An In-Depth Look at Lorenz Ransomware

hits.text: Google’s Threat Analysis Group uncovered that Magniber ransomware operators exploited a previously unpatched SmartScreen bypass (CVE-2023-24880) to deliver MSI installers signed with malformed Authenticode certificates that trigger a parsing error in smartscreen.exe, causing shdocvw.dll’s DoSafeOpenPromptForShellExec to proceed without displaying warnings—resulting in over 100,000 downloads since January 2023 (80 percent in Europe) before Microsoft issued a Patch Tuesday fix; this mirrors a prior bypass (CVE-2022-44698) used in late 2022 to spread Magniber via JScript and later adopted by Qakbot, with virtually identical signatures suggesting shared tooling, and highlights a systemic root-cause in SmartScreen’s error-handling logic—specifically NULL cert_context or NULL psIndirectData paths—that attackers now exploit by corrupting the SPC_INDIRECT_DATA_OBJID ASN.1 identifier, demonstrating the urgent need for holistic SmartScreen hardening and end-to-end certificate validation.
hits.title: Magniber ransomware actors used a variant of Microsoft SmartScreen bypass

canonical_entities: Palo Alto Networks Cortex XDR Anti-Ransomware
hits.text: Following the sale of INC ransomware source code in March 2024 and its initial appearance in August 2023, researchers in July 2024 uncovered Lynx ransomware, a Windows-only, C++-based RaaS variant that shares ~48% of INC’s functions (70.8% among common routines) and has been deployed against U.S. and U.K. retail, real estate, architecture, financial and environmental service firms via phishing, malicious downloads and underground forums; employing AES-128-CTR and Curve25519 Donna for encryption with a .lynx extension, it conducts double-extortion by exfiltrating victims’ data (published on lynxblog[.]net under a policy excluding governments, hospitals and non-profits) before encrypting all files by default—killing processes, encrypting network shares and hidden disks, deleting shadow copies and backups, leveraging the Restart Manager API to target in-use files, and printing a OneNote report—then dropping a README.txt ransom note; this evolution of RaaS underscores the need for organizations to adopt robust cybersecurity measures, including anti-phishing training, backup hardening, dynamic and behavioral detections via Palo Alto Networks’ Cortex XDR Anti-Ransomware and Advanced WildFire, and vigilant monitoring of Indicators of Compromise such as published SHA256 hashes to mitigate high-profile, code-reused ransomware campaigns.
hits.title: Lynx Ransomware: A Rebranding of INC Ransomware

hits.text: Since early 2025, a sophisticated threat actor has deployed PS1Bot, a multi-stage PowerShell/C# malware framework distributed via malvertising and SEO-poisoned archives named to resemble legitimate documents (e.g., “chapter 8 medicare benefit policy manual.zip”), which drops an obfuscated VBScript downloader (“FULL DOCUMENT.js”) that retrieves a JScript scriptlet to write and execute a PowerShell loader (e.g., ntu.ps1) from C:\ProgramData\; this loader polls a C2—deriving unique URLs from the C-drive serial number—and uses Invoke-Expression to run in-memory modules with minimal disk footprints. PS1Bot’s modular toolkit includes a WMI-based antivirus reconnaissance module, a dynamic C# screen-capture module exfiltrating Base64‐encoded bitmaps, a “grabber” that harvests browser and 40+ crypto wallet credentials (including MetaMask, Ledger, Exodus, Electrum) using embedded multilingual seed-phrase wordlists, a SetWindowsHookEx keylogger, and a WMIComputerCSHARP system survey. Persistence is achieved via randomized %PROGRAMDATA% directories, LNK startup shortcuts, and mutex checks. Cisco Talos notes overlaps with AHK Bot and Skitnet infrastructures and reports rapid evolution with undisclosed modules poised for espionage, financial theft, and lateral movement. Organizations should monitor anomalous PowerShell execution, unexpected WMI queries, and malvertising indicators to detect and disrupt this ongoing campaign.
hits.title: PS1Bot: Multi-Stage Malware Framework Targeting Windows Systems

hits.text: Microsoft’s research exposes the BadPilot campaign—a multiyear initial-access subgroup of Russian GRU-aligned Seashell Blizzard active since at least 2021—that has opportunistically scanned for and exploited Internet-facing vulnerabilities (CVE-2021-34473 Exchange, CVE-2022-41352 Zimbra, CVE-2023-32315 OpenFire, CVE-2023-42793 TeamCity, CVE-2023-23397 Outlook, CVE-2024-1709 ConnectWise ScreenConnect, CVE-2023-48788 FortiClient EMS and various JBOSS flaws) to compromise a globally diverse set of high-value sectors (energy, oil and gas, telecommunications, shipping, arms manufacturing and government). Following initial access, BadPilot employs stealthy persistence, credential harvesting, lateral movement and common tools such as Cobalt Strike and DarkCrystalRAT to sustain footholds and support tailored network operations, including at least three destructive cyberattacks in Ukraine since 2023. After focusing on Ukraine, Europe, Central/South Asia and the Middle East during 2021–2023, the subgroup scaled horizontally into the United States, United Kingdom, Canada and Australia in early 2024, reflecting Russia’s evolving strategic objectives and underscoring the urgency of patching Internet-facing services, implementing comprehensive logging and anomaly detection, and applying threat-informed incident-response practices to disrupt its operational lifecycle.
hits.title: The BadPilot campaign: Seashell Blizzard subgroup conducts multiyear global access operation | Microsoft Security Blog

hits.text: Water Ouroboros is a Ransomware-as-a-Service operation that exploits public-facing Oracle WebLogic vulnerabilities (CVE-2019-2725, CVE-2017-10271, CVE-2019-2729) or drive-by installers for initial access (T1190, T1189), then executes remote Windows commands (wmic.exe, bcdedit.exe, wbadmin.exe, vssadmin.exe) to delete backups and disable recovery (T1490, T1562.001) before encrypting fixed, removable and network drives via a Go-based custom routine that uses RTLGenRandom to generate a symmetric key, protects it with embedded RSA public keys (App_ExportKey), appends “.locked” (unless suppressed with –E), excludes over 60 file extensions, and accepts credentials (c {user}:{pass}), logging (–a), non-aggressive (–A) and size filters (–m). Victims find Contact Us.txt ransom notes pointing to a TOR payment site and Hive Leaks data-dump threat. Post-infection, actors maintain access via compromised admin accounts (T1078), disable security tools (PCHunter, ProcessHacker), dump credentials from registry hives (T1003.002), move laterally over RDP/SMB (T1021.001/002), discover assets via AdFind (T1595.002) and exfiltrate data over C&C (SharpRhino RAT/T1071.001, T1041). With 136 incidents in the US and notable impacts on construction, IT, manufacturing and healthcare SMBs, the campaign underscores the need for timely patching, hardened public-facing apps, least-privilege access, MFA, robust backups and advanced threat detection.
hits.title: Ransomware Spotlight: Water Ouroboros | Trend Micro (US)

hits.text: Trend Micro data shows BlackCat executed 39.3% of its 176 manufacturing detections against US targets and confirmed 173 leak-site compromises from December 2021 to September 2022—58.7% US-based—favoring finance, professional, legal, technology, energy, utilities, construction, and manufacturing sectors, with small (52%) and midsize (26%) businesses most targeted. Initial access was achieved via Exchange CVE-2021-26855/26857/26858/27065 exploits, ConnectWise RCE, and SSH key abuse. Execution leverages COBEACON to inject the Rust-based ransomware into ntoskrnl.exe, evading detection; defense evasion includes disabling AV, using AdFind/ADRecon/SoftPerfect, Process Hacker, Mimikatz, WMIC, Netstat, and LSASS credential dumping. Lateral movement exploits embedded PsExec, RDP, MobaXterm, and BITSAdmin transfers of zzz.exe/xxx.exe/yyy.exe/sv.exe. C2 communication uses Base64-encoded PowerShell with a Cobalt Strike SMB beacon over named pipes. Exfiltration employs ExMatter (upgraded September 2022), 7-Zip, Rclone, MEGASync, WinSCP, and FreeFileSync for double extortion. hits.text: Since at least April 2024 Microsoft Threat Intelligence has tracked a Russia-affiliated cyberespionage actor dubbed Void Blizzard (aka LAUNDRY BEAR) conducting high-volume, targeted operations against government, defense, transportation, media, NGO and healthcare organizations—particularly in NATO member states and Ukraine—by leveraging stolen credentials procured via commodity infostealer ecosystems for password spray attacks and Exchange/SharePoint Online access, then automating bulk email and file collection (and in some cases Teams messages) via cloud APIs and tools like AzureHound; in April 2025 the actor evolved to adversary-in-the-middle spear phishing using a typosquatted domain and the open-source Evilginx framework with a malicious QR-coded PDF to harvest Entra authentication data; this widespread success underscores that even unsophisticated TTPs pose major intelligence risks to critical sectors, so organizations should enforce sign-in risk policies and phishing-resistant MFA (e.g., FIDO/passkeys), centralize identity management with Conditional Access, monitor risky sign-ins and mailbox auditing, apply least-privilege credential hygiene, and promptly rotate credentials after infostealer detections to disrupt Void Blizzard’s operations.

hits.text: Trend Micro researchers have uncovered a new Chinese-speaking APT dubbed Earth Berberoka (aka GamblingPuppet) that targets online gambling websites on Windows, macOS and Linux by deploying both legacy (PlugX, Gh0st RAT) and novel malware, most notably a five-stage loader called PuppetLoader and a Go-based oRAT. PuppetLoader’s Stage 1 decrypts an initial payload with a flawed RC4 implementation (key “2726c6aea9970bb95211304705b5f595”), then stealthily hijacks the loading of a legitimate DLL (asycfilt.dll) via hooked NTDLL APIs (NtOpenFile, NtMapViewOfSection, RtlPushFrame/RtlPopFrame) to rebase and execute a malicious lz32.dll; Stage 2 drops marker files (CPuppetProcessFileSharer with GUID 78106D5F-CD1A-A8C4-A625-6863092B4BBA, Config.ini encrypted with “whk0q9ogev6ofg8d”), MSVCPX00.dll and BMP stagers; Stage 3’s BasicLoader scans Users\Public directories for 33×11-pixel BMPs containing encrypted payloads; Stage 4’s Core module logs activity via custom RC4-encrypted entries delimited by 0xAABBCCDD and supports -NoModuleLoadDLL and -LoadShellcode flags; and Stage 5’s MainConsole client written in C++ provides interactive shell, file upload/download, process listing, module installation and RDP enumeration over a custom RC4-encrypted UDP protocol with specific packet types (RemoteModuleCommandPacket, FileTransferContent_Packet, InstallModulePacket, etc.). Concurrently, oRAT droppers packaged as an Electron MiMi chat app and a macOS DMG carry AES-GCM-encrypted Go configurations enabling gateway or traffic-forwarder modes and expose HTTP(S)/QUIC routes (e.g., GET/POST /agent/info, /agent/upload) for direct code execution. This multivector, multiplatform campaign highlights the critical need to monitor anomalous DLL load behavior, bitmap steganography, flawed RC4/AES-GCM decryption routines and custom UDP or HTTP traffic on gambling infrastructures.

hits.text: Microsoft has traced a stealthy espionage campaign by Flax Typhoon (aka Ethereal Panda), a China-based nation-state actor active since mid-2021, targeting dozens of Taiwanese organizations (with spill-over in Southeast Asia, North America, and Africa) by exploiting known vulnerabilities in public-facing VPN, web, Java, and SQL services to deploy the China Chopper web shell for initial access; the group escalates privileges via open-source exploits like Juicy Potato and BadPotato, then establishes persistence by disabling RDP network-level authentication, hijacking the Sticky Keys (sethc.exe) binary to launch Task Manager as SYSTEM, and installing a renamed SoftEther VPN-over-HTTPS bridge (conhost.exe/dllhost.exe) as a service to maintain covert C2 over port 443; leveraging LOLBins such as PowerShell Invoke-WebRequest, certutil, bitsadmin, WinRM, and WMIC for lateral movement, vulnerability scanning, and remote execution, it harvests credentials from LSASS memory and the SAM registry hive using Mimikatz for pass-the-hash attacks; although no exfiltration or final objectives have been observed, organizations are urged to enforce rigorous patch and vulnerability management on internet-exposed systems, monitor registry and file-integrity changes, deploy web application firewalls, reset compromised credentials, isolate and forensically examine affected hosts, and leverage detections in Microsoft 365 Defender to disrupt living-off-the-land tactics.
hits.title: Flax Typhoon using legitimate software to quietly access Taiwanese organizations | Microsoft Security Blog

hits.text: Since April 2024, the Russia-affiliated threat actor Void Blizzard (aka Laundry Bear) has targeted over 20 NGOs and multiple government, defense, transportation, media and healthcare organizations across NATO member states, Western Europe, North America and Ukraine, initially leveraging password spraying and stolen credentials—likely purchased from cybercrime marketplaces—to access Exchange and SharePoint Online, enumerate Microsoft Entra ID via AzureHound, and exfiltrate large volumes of emails and files. More recently, the group shifted to adversary-in-the-middle spear-phishing using a typosquatted “micsrosoftonline[.]com” domain and an Evilginx-based phishing page delivered through malicious QR codes in forged European Defense and Security Summit PDF invitations, automating bulk data collection via Exchange, Microsoft Graph and Teams web client. Overlaps with Forest Blizzard, Midnight Blizzard and Secret Blizzard indicate coordinated Russian strategic espionage, and a September 2024 pass-the-cookie breach of a Dutch police account underscores their evolving cookie-theft capabilities—highlighting urgent needs for phishing-resistant MFA and hardened Entra ID configurations.
hits.title: Russian Hackers Breach 20+ NGOs Using Evilginx Phishing via Fake Microsoft Entra Pages

retrieved_context.text: Water Ouroboros is a Ransomware-as-a-Service operation that exploits public-facing Oracle WebLogic vulnerabilities (CVE-2019-2725, CVE-2017-10271, CVE-2019-2729) or drive-by installers for initial access (T1190, T1189), then executes remote Windows commands (wmic.exe, bcdedit.exe, wbadmin.exe, vssadmin.exe) to delete backups and disable recovery (T1490, T1562.001) before encrypting fixed, removable and network drives via a Go-based custom routine that uses RTLGenRandom to generate a symmetric key, protects it with embedded RSA public keys (App_ExportKey), appends “.locked” (unless suppressed with –E), excludes over 60 file extensions, and accepts credentials (c {user}:{pass}), logging (–a), non-aggressive (–A) and size filters (–m). Victims find Contact Us.txt ransom notes pointing to a TOR payment site and Hive Leaks data-dump threat. Post-infection, actors maintain access via compromised admin accounts (T1078), disable security tools (PCHunter, ProcessHacker), dump credentials from registry hives (T1003.002), move laterally over RDP/SMB (T1021.001/002), discover assets via AdFind (T1595.002) and exfiltrate data over C&C (SharpRhino RAT/T1071.001, T1041). With 136 incidents in the US and notable impacts on construction, IT, manufacturing and healthcare SMBs, the campaign underscores the need for timely patching, hardened public-facing apps, least-privilege access, MFA, robust backups and advanced threat detection.
retrieved_context.title: Ransomware Spotlight: Water Ouroboros | Trend Micro (US)

canonical_entities: exfiltrate them to attacker-controlled C&C servers
retrieved_context.text: Between November 2023 and February 2024, operators of the StrelaStealer infostealer—first documented in November 2022—conducted three large-scale phishing campaigns that leveraged localized spam to target over 100 US and EU organizations across high-tech, finance, legal, manufacturing, government, utilities, energy, insurance and construction sectors. In place of earlier ISO-based LNK/HTML chains, these campaigns delivered ZIP attachments containing JScript droppers that deploy a malicious DLL configured to harvest credentials from popular email clients and exfiltrate them to attacker-controlled C&C servers. The actors enhanced obfuscation, removed debugging symbols and changed attachment types to evade signature-based detection and frustrate forensic analysis. To defend against StrelaStealer’s evolving tactics, security teams should monitor for ZIP-delivered script droppers, anomalous DLL loads and suspicious external connections, and bolster email gateway filtering, endpoint behavior analytics and credential-monitoring controls.
retrieved_context.title: Over 100 Organizations Targeted in Recent 'StrelaStealer' Attacks - SecurityWeek
