retrieved_context.text: Trend Micro data shows BlackCat executed 39.3% of its 176 manufacturing detections against US targets and confirmed 173 leak-site compromises from December 2021 to September 2022—58.7% US-based—favoring finance, professional, legal, technology, energy, utilities, construction, and manufacturing sectors, with small (52%) and midsize (26%) businesses most targeted. Initial access was achieved via Exchange CVE-2021-26855/26857/26858/27065 exploits, ConnectWise RCE, and SSH key abuse. Execution leverages COBEACON to inject the Rust-based ransomware into ntoskrnl.exe, evading detection; defense evasion includes disabling AV, using AdFind/ADRecon/SoftPerfect, Process Hacker, Mimikatz, WMIC, Netstat, and LSASS credential dumping. Lateral movement exploits embedded PsExec, RDP, MobaXterm, and BITSAdmin transfers of zzz.exe/xxx.exe/yyy.exe/sv.exe. C2 communication uses Base64-encoded PowerShell with a Cobalt Strike SMB beacon over named pipes. Exfiltration employs ExMatter (upgraded September 2022), 7-Zip, Rclone, MEGASync, WinSCP, and FreeFileSync for double extortion. The payload defaces backgrounds, terminates backup/AV/DB/Internet/VM services, disables recovery (shadow copy deletion, safe-mode variant), and appends variable Sphynx extensions while avoiding critical directories and file types. BlackCat maps to MITRE ATT&CK T1190, T1078, T1562.001/009, T1003.001, T1021.002, T1486, T1490, T1489, T1048/T1567. Security teams should patch Exchange CVEs, secure MSP tools, enforce least privilege, segment networks, monitor PowerShell injections, and vet outbound file transfers to disrupt this evolving affiliate-driven operation.
retrieved_context.title: Ransomware Spotlight: BlackCat | Trend Micro (US)

retrieved_context.text: HC3’s November 2022 alert warns of human-operated Lorenz ransomware, first observed in February 2021 and linked to earlier sZ40 and ThunderCrypt activity, which specifically targets large healthcare organizations by customizing its executable code and following a kill chain of initial access, extended reconnaissance, lateral movement to Windows domain controllers for administrator credential theft, then encryption and extortion. Operators demand $500,000–$700,000 and employ a non-typical leak site where stolen data is first offered for sale to other threat actors, then distributed in password-protected archives or, if sales fail, released publicly. With relatively limited public intelligence on Lorenz, HC3 emphasizes that victims should address common ransomware vectors—phishing, exploitation of known vulnerabilities, remote-access compromise and distributed attacks—by reinforcing patch management, intrusion detection, access controls and incident-response planning, especially in light of concurrent Hive ransomware warnings issued by HHS, FBI and CISA.
retrieved_context.title: Lorenz Ransomware Targets Large Healthcare Orgs, HC3 Warns | TechTarget

retrieved_context.text: ESET researchers have traced the China-aligned hacker group FishMonger, aka Aquatic Panda, and its global espionage campaign “FishMedley” back to the iSoon APT contractor (Axun Information Technology) operating under the Ministry of Public Security, Ministry of State Security and PLA, following the U.S. DOJ’s addition of key members to the FBI’s Most Wanted list; FishMonger’s modus operandi relies on compromising high-privilege user accounts—likely harvested via phishing or credential theft—to gain domain administrator access, then deploying publicly available modular backdoors and loaders (ShadowPad, Spyder loader, SodaMaster) and the RPipeCommander reverse shell rather than zero-day exploits, enabling sustained infiltration of governmental bodies, Catholic charities, NGOs and think tanks across Taiwan, Hungary, Turkey, Thailand, the U.S. and France; while technically unsophisticated, the group’s efficient use of known tools has yielded consistent exfiltration of confidential data, underscoring the need for potential targets to hunt for these specific indicators of compromise and strengthen monitoring of privileged accounts.
retrieved_context.title: Chinese Hacker Group Tracked Back to iSoon APT Operation

retrieved_context.text: Researchers at Accenture Security exposed Q3 2021 proliferation of Karakurt, a financially motivated data‐extortion group first identified in June 2021 upon registering two domains and launching a Twitter handle, which compromised over 40 primarily North American (95 percent) organizations across random sectors between September and November by sourcing or phishing VPN credentials for initial access, establishing persistence with Cobalt Strike beacons or AnyDesk, then harvesting administrator privileges via Mimikatz to evade EDR solutions; they compress stolen data with 7zip or WinZip and exfiltrate it to Mega.io using Rclone or FileZilla, foregoing ransomware encryption in favor of public leak threats, a low-overhead approach that can still cripple victims—underscoring the need for robust VPN credential management, continuous monitoring for living-off-the-land tools, and preventative controls to detect and disrupt such intrusions before data exfiltration.
retrieved_context.title: New 'Karakurt' hacking group focuses on data theft and extortion

retrieved_context.text: Since at least April 2024 Microsoft Threat Intelligence has tracked a Russia-affiliated cyberespionage actor dubbed Void Blizzard (aka LAUNDRY BEAR) conducting high-volume, targeted operations against government, defense, transportation, media, NGO and healthcare organizations—particularly in NATO member states and Ukraine—by leveraging stolen credentials procured via commodity infostealer ecosystems for password spray attacks and Exchange/SharePoint Online access, then automating bulk email and file collection (and in some cases Teams messages) via cloud APIs and tools like AzureHound; in April 2025 the actor evolved to adversary-in-the-middle spear phishing using a typosquatted domain and the open-source Evilginx framework with a malicious QR-coded PDF to harvest Entra authentication data; this widespread success underscores that even unsophisticated TTPs pose major intelligence risks to critical sectors, so organizations should enforce sign-in risk policies and phishing-resistant MFA (e.g., FIDO/passkeys), centralize identity management with Conditional Access, monitor risky sign-ins and mailbox auditing, apply least-privilege credential hygiene, and promptly rotate credentials after infostealer detections to disrupt Void Blizzard’s operations.
retrieved_context.title: New Russia-affiliated actor Void Blizzard targets critical sectors for espionage | Microsoft Security Blog

canonical_entities: hijacks the loading of a legitimate DLL
retrieved_context.text: Trend Micro researchers have uncovered a new Chinese-speaking APT dubbed Earth Berberoka (aka GamblingPuppet) that targets online gambling websites on Windows, macOS and Linux by deploying both legacy (PlugX, Gh0st RAT) and novel malware, most notably a five-stage loader called PuppetLoader and a Go-based oRAT. PuppetLoader’s Stage 1 decrypts an initial payload with a flawed RC4 implementation (key “2726c6aea9970bb95211304705b5f595”), then stealthily hijacks the loading of a legitimate DLL (asycfilt.dll) via hooked NTDLL APIs (NtOpenFile, NtMapViewOfSection, RtlPushFrame/RtlPopFrame) to rebase and execute a malicious lz32.dll; Stage 2 drops marker files (CPuppetProcessFileSharer with GUID 78106D5F-CD1A-A8C4-A625-6863092B4BBA, Config.ini encrypted with “whk0q9ogev6ofg8d”), MSVCPX00.dll and BMP stagers; Stage 3’s BasicLoader scans Users\Public directories for 33×11-pixel BMPs containing encrypted payloads; Stage 4’s Core module logs activity via custom RC4-encrypted entries delimited by 0xAABBCCDD and supports -NoModuleLoadDLL and -LoadShellcode flags; and Stage 5’s MainConsole client written in C++ provides interactive shell, file upload/download, process listing, module installation and RDP enumeration over a custom RC4-encrypted UDP protocol with specific packet types (RemoteModuleCommandPacket, FileTransferContent_Packet, InstallModulePacket, etc.). Concurrently, oRAT droppers packaged as an Electron MiMi chat app and a macOS DMG carry AES-GCM-encrypted Go configurations enabling gateway or traffic-forwarder modes and expose HTTP(S)/QUIC routes (e.g., GET/POST /agent/info, /agent/upload) for direct code execution. This multivector, multiplatform campaign highlights the critical need to monitor anomalous DLL load behavior, bitmap steganography, flawed RC4/AES-GCM decryption routines and custom UDP or HTTP traffic on gambling infrastructures.
retrieved_context.title: New APT Group Earth Berberoka Targets Gambling Websites With Old and New Malware | Trend Micro (US)

hits.text: In mid-2022, Arctic Wolf researchers discovered the Lorenz ransomware group exploiting CVE-2022-29499, a remote code execution flaw in Mitel MiVoice Connect VoIP appliances disclosed in April and patched in July, to gain an initial reverse shell. Once inside, the attackers used the compromised Mitel Service Appliance’s CLI to create a hidden directory, download and rename the Golang-based Chisel tunneling tool via Wget, and establish a fast TCP/UDP SOCKS proxy over HTTP (skipping TLS verification) to evade firewalls. After lying dormant for nearly a month and deploying a “pdf_import_export.php” web shell for persistence, they harvested local and domain admin credentials, moved laterally via RDP to a domain controller, exfiltrated data via FileZilla for double-extortion, and encrypted ESXi hosts using BitLocker and Lorenz ransomware. Targeting primarily US SMBs (with outliers in China and Mexico), this campaign underscores the critical need for timely patching of IoT/VoIP devices, comprehensive asset discovery and hardening, network segmentation, and robust PowerShell and module logging with centralized log management.
hits.title: Lorenz Ransomware Goes After SMBs via Mitel VoIP Phone Systems

canonical_entities: injected commands via a malicious URL
hits.text: CrowdStrike researchers in April 2022 uncovered that ransomware actors exploited a critical remote code execution flaw (CVE-2022-29499) in unpatched Linux-based Mitel MiVoice appliances (SA 100, SA 400 and Virtual SA) to gain initial access, plant malware and pivot laterally: the exploit chain began with an external HTTP GET to a “get_url” parameter in a PHP file (to bypass IP restrictions) followed by a device-originated GET that injected commands via a malicious URL, enabling an SSL-enabled reverse shell (using mkfifo and openssl_client) and deployment of a “pdf_import.php” web shell and the Chisel tunneling tool. Although the threat actors deleted evidence from the VoIP filesystem, CrowdStrike recovered the undocumented exploit, downloaded tools and anti-forensic measures. With some 21,000 MITEL devices worldwide still exposed (per Kevin Beaumont’s Shodan string “http.html_hash:-1971546278”), organizations are urged to apply Mitel’s April advisory patches for MiVoice Connect 19.2 SP3 and earlier, enforce strict network segmentation around perimeter devices, conduct threat modeling to detect anomalous GET requests, and prioritize timely firmware updates to thwart zero-day exploitation.
hits.title: Mitel VoIP Bug Exploited in Ransomware Attacks | Threatpost

canonical_entities: installing Sagerunex variants in the Windows Registry
hits.text: The Lotus Blossom APT (aka Lotus Panda, Billbug, Spring Dragon) has stepped up cyberespionage against APAC government targets by deploying new Sagerunex backdoor variants and abusing Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) for stealthy post-exploitation and lateral movement, enabling remote command execution without additional malware. Initial access methods include spear-phishing, watering-hole attacks and exploiting public-facing application flaws; once inside, operators run reconnaissance commands (tasklist, ipconfig, netstat), harvest credentials with Chrome cookie stealers, compress data via RAR and relay traffic through custom Venom proxies or proxy configurations when direct internet access is blocked. Persistence is achieved by installing Sagerunex variants in the Windows Registry under hijacked service names (tapisrv, swprv) to auto-launch at startup, while command-and-control blends encrypted traffic into legitimate platforms—stolen data uploaded as .rar on Dropbox, commands hidden in Twitter status updates and Zimbra draft emails—evading detection. Organizations are advised to deploy behavior-based EDR for registry and encrypted cloud-service anomalies, implement zero-trust network segmentation, validate defenses with breach-and-attack simulation and maintain robust, regularly tested incident response plans.
hits.title: Lotus Blossom APT Exploits WMI for Post-Exploitation Activities

canonical_entities: Bypass authentication by sending empty or invalid USERNAME and PASSWORD parameters with requirePasswordChange=Y
hits.text: A critical zero-day flaw (CVE-2023-51467) has been identified in Apache OfBiz’s login functionality—stemming from an incomplete patch for a prior high-severity RCE vulnerability (CVE-2023-49070, CVSS 9.8) tied to a deprecated XML-RPC component—that allows attackers to bypass authentication by sending empty or invalid USERNAME and PASSWORD parameters alongside “requirePasswordChange=Y,” effectively granting unauthorized access and enabling simple SSRF attacks against internal resources; discovered by SonicWall Capture Labs, the bug follows observations by The Shadowserver Foundation of active exploitation attempts against CVE-2023-49070, and SonicWall reports exploit traffic for CVE-2023-51467 spiking from 235 attempts on December 27, 2023, to 26,928 on December 29 and 3,129 on January 1, 2024, underscoring urgent need for organizations using OfBiz versions prior to 18.12.11 to upgrade immediately to mitigate further data exfiltration and system takeover risks.
hits.title: Critical Zero-Day in Apache OfBiz ERP System Exposes Businesses to Attack

hits.text: Following the December 9 disclosure of critical Log4j flaws (CVE-2021-44228 “Log4Shell,” CVE-2021-45046 and CVE-2021-45105), Symantec observed widespread exploitation via obfuscated jndi lookups over LDAP and RMI (with ${env}, ${lower}, ${::-} tricks) and secondary scans over IIOP, DNS, HTTP and NIS, delivering payloads from Muhstik botnet Java class files that drop ELF installers, XMRig miners via PowerShell, Java backdoors awaiting remote commands, reverse Bash shells and public threats including Dridex, Orcus RAT, Khonsari and Conti ransomware; between December 9–21, its IPS blocked 93 million Log4Shell attempts on 270 000 endpoints and 18 million on 60 000 servers—primarily targeting systems in the U.S. and U.K. and originating from the U.S., Germany, Russia, the U.K. and China—highlighting rapid global weaponization; actionable defenses include enforcing multi-layered DCS policies to prevent malware execution from temp or writable paths, sandboxing Java apps, restricting outbound LDAP/HTTP connections, whitelisting necessary proxy tools (*/curl, */wget), and updating detection rules to flag jndi:* patterns in web and Log4j logs for immediate alerting and mitigation.
hits.title: Log4j Vulnerabilities: Attack Insights | Symantec Enterprise Blogs

hits.text: On January 11, 2024, GitLab released patches for CVE-2023-7028—a critical (CVSS 10.0) zero-click account-takeover flaw in Community and Enterprise Edition versions 16.1–16.7—that lets attackers send password reset emails to an adversary-controlled address and hijack any account lacking two-factor authentication; 13 days post-disclosure, ShadowServer reported 5,379 internet-exposed instances (964 in the US, 730 in Germany, 721 in Russia, 503 in China, 298 in France, 122 in the UK, 117 in India and 99 in Canada) still vulnerable, placing them at risk of supply-chain compromise, proprietary code and API-key exfiltration, and other malicious activities. Defenders should inspect gitlab-rails/production_json.log for `/users/password` requests with JSON arrays of multiple emails and gitlab-rails/audit_json.log for `PasswordsController#create` entries, apply the fixes in 16.7.2, 16.6.4 and 16.5.6 (or backports 16.1.6, 16.2.9, 16.3.7), enforce 2FA, rotate all credentials, API tokens, certificates and other secrets, and review source code and environment configurations per GitLab’s incident-response guide, since unpatched servers may already be compromised despite no confirmed active exploitation to date.
hits.title: Over 5,300 GitLab servers exposed to zero-click account takeover attacks

hits.text: Attackers have been exploiting an unpatched Windows and Office zero-day vulnerability (CVE-2023-36884), disclosed by Microsoft on July 11, in highly targeted campaigns against government and defense organizations in Europe and North America; initial exploitation was documented by BlackBerry on July 8 when Storm-0978 (aka RomCom), a Russia-linked actor using the RomCom RAT with ties to the Hawker group and Cuba ransomware developers (and potentially to Industrial Spy ransomware operators), delivered malicious Word documents masquerading as Ukrainian World Congress materials to NATO Summit attendees, enabling remote code execution once opened. With no patch yet available, victims are urged to deploy all mitigations—leveraging Symantec’s email-, file-, network- and web-based protections (including WebPulse bad-reputation domain filtering), monitor the published IOC hashes, and prepare for Microsoft’s forthcoming monthly or out-of-cycle update—to prevent further compromise and forestall secondary ransomware or espionage operations.
hits.title: Attackers Exploit Unpatched Windows Zero-Day Vulnerability | Symantec Enterprise Blogs

hits.text: CISA has added CVE-2022-22047—a high-severity (CVSS 7.8) elevation-of-privilege flaw in the Windows Client Server Runtime Subsystem used since Windows 7 through Windows 11 and Server 2008–2022—to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog and is urging federal agencies to install Microsoft’s July 5 Patch Tuesday update by August 2 after evidence emerged of in-the-wild exploitation; initially disclosed as a zero-day by Microsoft’s security team, the CSRSS bug enables adversaries who already hold local or physical access—or who gain remote code execution via malware or specially crafted Office/Adobe documents and macros—to escalate to SYSTEM privileges for lateral movement, although FortiGuard Labs rates the overall business threat as “medium” given the prerequisite foothold and available patch, while Trend Micro’s ZDI notes such elevation flaws are typically paired with a separate RCE vector and Microsoft has signaled future default blocking of VBA macros to mitigate this attack chain.
hits.title: CISA Urges Patch of Exploited Windows 11 Bug by Aug. 2 | Threatpost

retrieved_context.text: The Lotus Blossom APT (aka Lotus Panda, Billbug, Spring Dragon) has stepped up cyberespionage against APAC government targets by deploying new Sagerunex backdoor variants and abusing Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) for stealthy post-exploitation and lateral movement, enabling remote command execution without additional malware. Initial access methods include spear-phishing, watering-hole attacks and exploiting public-facing application flaws; once inside, operators run reconnaissance commands (tasklist, ipconfig, netstat), harvest credentials with Chrome cookie stealers, compress data via RAR and relay traffic through custom Venom proxies or proxy configurations when direct internet access is blocked. Persistence is achieved by installing Sagerunex variants in the Windows Registry under hijacked service names (tapisrv, swprv) to auto-launch at startup, while command-and-control blends encrypted traffic into legitimate platforms—stolen data uploaded as .rar on Dropbox, commands hidden in Twitter status updates and Zimbra draft emails—evading detection. Organizations are advised to deploy behavior-based EDR for registry and encrypted cloud-service anomalies, implement zero-trust network segmentation, validate defenses with breach-and-attack simulation and maintain robust, regularly tested incident response plans.
retrieved_context.title: Lotus Blossom APT Exploits WMI for Post-Exploitation Activities

canonical_entities: Bypass authentication by sending empty or invalid USERNAME and PASSWORD parameters with requirePasswordChange=Y
retrieved_context.text: A critical zero-day flaw (CVE-2023-51467) has been identified in Apache OfBiz’s login functionality—stemming from an incomplete patch for a prior high-severity RCE vulnerability (CVE-2023-49070, CVSS 9.8) tied to a deprecated XML-RPC component—that allows attackers to bypass authentication by sending empty or invalid USERNAME and PASSWORD parameters alongside “requirePasswordChange=Y,” effectively granting unauthorized access and enabling simple SSRF attacks against internal resources; discovered by SonicWall Capture Labs, the bug follows observations by The Shadowserver Foundation of active exploitation attempts against CVE-2023-49070, and SonicWall reports exploit traffic for CVE-2023-51467 spiking from 235 attempts on December 27, 2023, to 26,928 on December 29 and 3,129 on January 1, 2024, underscoring urgent need for organizations using OfBiz versions prior to 18.12.11 to upgrade immediately to mitigate further data exfiltration and system takeover risks.
retrieved_context.title: Critical Zero-Day in Apache OfBiz ERP System Exposes Businesses to Attack

retrieved_context.text: Following the December 9 disclosure of critical Log4j flaws (CVE-2021-44228 “Log4Shell,” CVE-2021-45046 and CVE-2021-45105), Symantec observed widespread exploitation via obfuscated jndi lookups over LDAP and RMI (with ${env}, ${lower}, ${::-} tricks) and secondary scans over IIOP, DNS, HTTP and NIS, delivering payloads from Muhstik botnet Java class files that drop ELF installers, XMRig miners via PowerShell, Java backdoors awaiting remote commands, reverse Bash shells and public threats including Dridex, Orcus RAT, Khonsari and Conti ransomware; between December 9–21, its IPS blocked 93 million Log4Shell attempts on 270 000 endpoints and 18 million on 60 000 servers—primarily targeting systems in the U.S. and U.K. and originating from the U.S., Germany, Russia, the U.K. and China—highlighting rapid global weaponization; actionable defenses include enforcing multi-layered DCS policies to prevent malware execution from temp or writable paths, sandboxing Java apps, restricting outbound LDAP/HTTP connections, whitelisting necessary proxy tools (*/curl, */wget), and updating detection rules to flag jndi:* patterns in web and Log4j logs for immediate alerting and mitigation.
retrieved_context.title: Log4j Vulnerabilities: Attack Insights | Symantec Enterprise Blogs

retrieved_context.text: On January 11, 2024, GitLab released patches for CVE-2023-7028—a critical (CVSS 10.0) zero-click account-takeover flaw in Community and Enterprise Edition versions 16.1–16.7—that lets attackers send password reset emails to an adversary-controlled address and hijack any account lacking two-factor authentication; 13 days post-disclosure, ShadowServer reported 5,379 internet-exposed instances (964 in the US, 730 in Germany, 721 in Russia, 503 in China, 298 in France, 122 in the UK, 117 in India and 99 in Canada) still vulnerable, placing them at risk of supply-chain compromise, proprietary code and API-key exfiltration, and other malicious activities. Defenders should inspect gitlab-rails/production_json.log for `/users/password` requests with JSON arrays of multiple emails and gitlab-rails/audit_json.log for `PasswordsController#create` entries, apply the fixes in 16.7.2, 16.6.4 and 16.5.6 (or backports 16.1.6, 16.2.9, 16.3.7), enforce 2FA, rotate all credentials, API tokens, certificates and other secrets, and review source code and environment configurations per GitLab’s incident-response guide, since unpatched servers may already be compromised despite no confirmed active exploitation to date.
retrieved_context.title: Over 5,300 GitLab servers exposed to zero-click account takeover attacks

canonical_entities: exploiting known vulnerabilities in public-facing VPN, web, Java, and SQL services
harvests credentials from LSASS memory and the SAM registry hive
retrieved_context.text: Microsoft has traced a stealthy espionage campaign by Flax Typhoon (aka Ethereal Panda), a China-based nation-state actor active since mid-2021, targeting dozens of Taiwanese organizations (with spill-over in Southeast Asia, North America, and Africa) by exploiting known vulnerabilities in public-facing VPN, web, Java, and SQL services to deploy the China Chopper web shell for initial access; the group escalates privileges via open-source exploits like Juicy Potato and BadPotato, then establishes persistence by disabling RDP network-level authentication, hijacking the Sticky Keys (sethc.exe) binary to launch Task Manager as SYSTEM, and installing a renamed SoftEther VPN-over-HTTPS bridge (conhost.exe/dllhost.exe) as a service to maintain covert C2 over port 443; leveraging LOLBins such as PowerShell Invoke-WebRequest, certutil, bitsadmin, WinRM, and WMIC for lateral movement, vulnerability scanning, and remote execution, it harvests credentials from LSASS memory and the SAM registry hive using Mimikatz for pass-the-hash attacks; although no exfiltration or final objectives have been observed, organizations are urged to enforce rigorous patch and vulnerability management on internet-exposed systems, monitor registry and file-integrity changes, deploy web application firewalls, reset compromised credentials, isolate and forensically examine affected hosts, and leverage detections in Microsoft 365 Defender to disrupt living-off-the-land tactics.
retrieved_context.title: Flax Typhoon using legitimate software to quietly access Taiwanese organizations | Microsoft Security Blog

retrieved_context.text: Attackers have been exploiting an unpatched Windows and Office zero-day vulnerability (CVE-2023-36884), disclosed by Microsoft on July 11, in highly targeted campaigns against government and defense organizations in Europe and North America; initial exploitation was documented by BlackBerry on July 8 when Storm-0978 (aka RomCom), a Russia-linked actor using the RomCom RAT with ties to the Hawker group and Cuba ransomware developers (and potentially to Industrial Spy ransomware operators), delivered malicious Word documents masquerading as Ukrainian World Congress materials to NATO Summit attendees, enabling remote code execution once opened. With no patch yet available, victims are urged to deploy all mitigations—leveraging Symantec’s email-, file-, network- and web-based protections (including WebPulse bad-reputation domain filtering), monitor the published IOC hashes, and prepare for Microsoft’s forthcoming monthly or out-of-cycle update—to prevent further compromise and forestall secondary ransomware or espionage operations.
retrieved_context.title: Attackers Exploit Unpatched Windows Zero-Day Vulnerability | Symantec Enterprise Blogs

retrieved_context.text: CISA has added CVE-2022-22047—a high-severity (CVSS 7.8) elevation-of-privilege flaw in the Windows Client Server Runtime Subsystem used since Windows 7 through Windows 11 and Server 2008–2022—to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog and is urging federal agencies to install Microsoft’s July 5 Patch Tuesday update by August 2 after evidence emerged of in-the-wild exploitation; initially disclosed as a zero-day by Microsoft’s security team, the CSRSS bug enables adversaries who already hold local or physical access—or who gain remote code execution via malware or specially crafted Office/Adobe documents and macros—to escalate to SYSTEM privileges for lateral movement, although FortiGuard Labs rates the overall business threat as “medium” given the prerequisite foothold and available patch, while Trend Micro’s ZDI notes such elevation flaws are typically paired with a separate RCE vector and Microsoft has signaled future default blocking of VBA macros to mitigate this attack chain.
retrieved_context.title: CISA Urges Patch of Exploited Windows 11 Bug by Aug. 2 | Threatpost

canonical_entities: Lorenz ransomware group exploiting CVE-2022-29499 against Mitel MiVoice Connect
harvested local and domain admin credentials
hits.text: In mid-2022, Arctic Wolf researchers discovered the Lorenz ransomware group exploiting CVE-2022-29499, a remote code execution flaw in Mitel MiVoice Connect VoIP appliances disclosed in April and patched in July, to gain an initial reverse shell. Once inside, the attackers used the compromised Mitel Service Appliance’s CLI to create a hidden directory, download and rename the Golang-based Chisel tunneling tool via Wget, and establish a fast TCP/UDP SOCKS proxy over HTTP (skipping TLS verification) to evade firewalls. After lying dormant for nearly a month and deploying a “pdf_import_export.php” web shell for persistence, they harvested local and domain admin credentials, moved laterally via RDP to a domain controller, exfiltrated data via FileZilla for double-extortion, and encrypted ESXi hosts using BitLocker and Lorenz ransomware. Targeting primarily US SMBs (with outliers in China and Mexico), this campaign underscores the critical need for timely patching of IoT/VoIP devices, comprehensive asset discovery and hardening, network segmentation, and robust PowerShell and module logging with centralized log management.
hits.title: Lorenz Ransomware Goes After SMBs via Mitel VoIP Phone Systems

hits.text: HC3’s November 2022 alert warns of human-operated Lorenz ransomware, first observed in February 2021 and linked to earlier sZ40 and ThunderCrypt activity, which specifically targets large healthcare organizations by customizing its executable code and following a kill chain of initial access, extended reconnaissance, lateral movement to Windows domain controllers for administrator credential theft, then encryption and extortion. Operators demand $500,000–$700,000 and employ a non-typical leak site where stolen data is first offered for sale to other threat actors, then distributed in password-protected archives or, if sales fail, released publicly. With relatively limited public intelligence on Lorenz, HC3 emphasizes that victims should address common ransomware vectors—phishing, exploitation of known vulnerabilities, remote-access compromise and distributed attacks—by reinforcing patch management, intrusion detection, access controls and incident-response planning, especially in light of concurrent Hive ransomware warnings issued by HHS, FBI and CISA.
hits.title: Lorenz Ransomware Targets Large Healthcare Orgs, HC3 Warns | TechTarget

canonical_entities: injected commands via a malicious URL
hits.text: CrowdStrike researchers in April 2022 uncovered that ransomware actors exploited a critical remote code execution flaw (CVE-2022-29499) in unpatched Linux-based Mitel MiVoice appliances (SA 100, SA 400 and Virtual SA) to gain initial access, plant malware and pivot laterally: the exploit chain began with an external HTTP GET to a “get_url” parameter in a PHP file (to bypass IP restrictions) followed by a device-originated GET that injected commands via a malicious URL, enabling an SSL-enabled reverse shell (using mkfifo and openssl_client) and deployment of a “pdf_import.php” web shell and the Chisel tunneling tool. Although the threat actors deleted evidence from the VoIP filesystem, CrowdStrike recovered the undocumented exploit, downloaded tools and anti-forensic measures. With some 21,000 MITEL devices worldwide still exposed (per Kevin Beaumont’s Shodan string “http.html_hash:-1971546278”), organizations are urged to apply Mitel’s April advisory patches for MiVoice Connect 19.2 SP3 and earlier, enforce strict network segmentation around perimeter devices, conduct threat modeling to detect anomalous GET requests, and prioritize timely firmware updates to thwart zero-day exploitation.
hits.title: Mitel VoIP Bug Exploited in Ransomware Attacks | Threatpost

canonical_entities: U.S. energy, oil and gas utilities
U.S. law firm Hunter Taubman Fischer & Li
Indicator Removal on Host: Clear Windows Event Logs
hits.text: Lynx ransomware, emerging in July 2024 as the INC ransomware successor under a Ransomware-as-a-Service model, employs a sophisticated double-extortion strategy—exfiltrating data prior to encryption and threatening publication on a leak site—and reuses significant INC source code. Between July and November 2024, it disrupted U.S. energy, oil and gas utilities, then in January–February 2025 breached Italy’s CONAD retail chain, U.S. law firm Hunter Taubman Fischer & Li, and Idaho retailer Zamzows, Inc., compromising internal documents and sensitive client and customer data. Initial access leverages phishing (T1566.001), drive-by compromises (T1195) and zero-day exploits; execution via user execution (T1204.002) and scripting interpreters (T1059.001); persistence through autostart mechanisms (T1070.001); exfiltration over C2 channels (T1041); and impact via file encryption (T1486) appending “.LYNX.” Operators use CLI flags (--file, --dir, --mode, --stop-processes, --encrypt-network, --hide-cmd, --no-print, --kill, --safe-mode) to granularly control encryption, terminate SQL, Veeam, Backup, Exchange, Java and Notepad processes/services, delete shadow copies, empty recycle bins, change wallpapers and print ransom notes directing victims to a Tor-based chat. Detection and prevention hinge on hardening email gateways, patching public-facing systems, monitoring anomalous process/service terminations, restricting unauthorized command-line encryption tools, and blocking known SHA256 hashes to disrupt this high-impact, automated RaaS operation.
hits.title: Lynx Ransomware: INC Ransomware Reincarnated - Threat Actors

canonical_entities: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Windows Command Shell
hits.text: NCC Group’s RIFT team uncovered a sophisticated new FiveHands ransomware variant deployed by an affiliate linked to UNC2447, who gained initial access in June 2021 by exploiting a SonicWall VPN appliance—evidenced by a “command0/Commando” login from source port 4444 (Metasploit default)—then moved laterally via RDP (T1021.001) using the weak password “Remark123!” and PsExec (T1059.003). The actor leveraged publicly available tools—SoftPerfect Netscan and Advanced Port Scanner for network discovery (T1046), AllInOnePasswordRecoveryPro for credential harvesting (T1003.001), Remote Utilities (“Hostclean.exe”) for persistent C2 (T1219), and pCloud (“pCloud.exe”) for exfiltration (T1567.002), caching 10 GB of stolen data under %AppData%\pCloud\CacheCached—to stage and extract sensitive files. The Go-written loader (“Encryptor.exe”) accepts a 16-byte key (captured via RDP bitmap cache and brute force) to decrypt a unique C++ ransomware payload in memory, which uses RSA/AES (Mbed TLS) to encrypt files in blocks (.crypt/.crypt) while excluding system folders and leveraging Windows Restart Manager to breach locked files. This RaaS model (hijacking hardcoded TOR IDs) employs aggressive extortion tactics—spoofed caller ID calls urging prompt payment—and underscores the need for robust VPN log monitoring, RDP restrictions, enforceable command-line auditing, multi-factor authentication, and forensic examination of cloud‐sync caches to detect and mitigate similar intrusions.
hits.title: Handy guide to a new Fivehands ransomware variant

hits.text: Since January 2021, Google’s Threat Analysis Group (TAG) has tracked a government-backed North Korean campaign that leverages social engineering via X (formerly Twitter) and encrypted messaging apps to befriend security researchers and deliver malicious files containing at least one unpatched 0-day in a popular software package; upon exploitation the custom shellcode performs anti-virtual-machine checks, captures system data and screenshots, and exfiltrates them to C2 infrastructure (e.g., 23.106.215[.]105, www.blgbeach[.]com), with the latest vulnerability reported and patched on September 12, 2023 (see TAG’s published RCA). In parallel, the actors published a seemingly benign Windows tool called GetSymbol on GitHub (https://github.com/dbgsymbol/) that quietly downloads debugging symbols—and arbitrary code—from attacker domains, requiring full OS reinstalls for compromised hosts. TAG has added malicious sites to Safe Browsing, issued government-backed attacker alerts to targeted Gmail and Workspace users, and urges researchers to enable Enhanced Safe Browsing, keep software up to date, and verify system integrity after using third-party tools.
hits.title: Active North Korean campaign targeting security researchers

hits.text: In early April, Palo Alto Networks’ Advanced WildFire and Cortex XDR uncovered SnipBot—a new v5.0 iteration of the RomCom RAT family—employing advanced window message–based control-flow obfuscation and anti-sandbox checks (filename hash and HKCU\…\RecentDocs entries) in a multi-stage chain beginning with a PDF-labeled EXE downloader signed using a likely stolen certificate; the downloader contacts xeontime[.]com for config-pdf.dll, which uses registry-based COM hijacking to load keyprov.dll from drvmcprotect[.]com into explorer.exe, decrypts payloads stored in HKCU\Software\AppDataSoft\Software, and opens a TCP listener on port 1342 for commands to update, delete, or execute modules. The main backdoor single.dll (mutex “SnipMutex”) supports 27 encrypted commands for drive and process enumeration, file upload/download, and remote module execution, facilitating network pivoting and targeted file exfiltration. Active since December 2023 (RomCom activity since 2022), SnipBot’s tactics, stolen certificates, unique obfuscation, and sophisticated loader underscore a high-risk threat actor likely focused on intelligence gathering; Palo Alto products classify its samples, URLs, and domains as malicious to prevent compromise.
hits.title: Inside SnipBot: The Latest RomCom Malware Variant

The Go-written loader (“Encryptor.exe”) accepts a 16-byte key (captured via RDP bitmap cache and brute force) to decrypt a unique C++ ransomware payload in memory, which uses RSA/AES (Mbed TLS) to encrypt files in blocks (.crypt/.crypt) while excluding system folders and leveraging Windows Restart Manager to breach locked files. This RaaS model (hijacking hardcoded TOR IDs) employs aggressive extortion tactics—spoofed caller ID calls urging prompt payment—and underscores the need for robust VPN log monitoring, RDP restrictions, enforceable command-line auditing, multi-factor authentication, and forensic examination of cloud‐sync caches to detect and mitigate similar intrusions.
retrieved_context.title: Handy guide to a new Fivehands ransomware variant

retrieved_context.text: Since January 2021, Google’s Threat Analysis Group (TAG) has tracked a government-backed North Korean campaign that leverages social engineering via X (formerly Twitter) and encrypted messaging apps to befriend security researchers and deliver malicious files containing at least one unpatched 0-day in a popular software package; upon exploitation the custom shellcode performs anti-virtual-machine checks, captures system data and screenshots, and exfiltrates them to C2 infrastructure (e.g., 23.106.215[.]105, www.blgbeach[.]com), with the latest vulnerability reported and patched on September 12, 2023 (see TAG’s published RCA). In parallel, the actors published a seemingly benign Windows tool called GetSymbol on GitHub (https://github.com/dbgsymbol/) that quietly downloads debugging symbols—and arbitrary code—from attacker domains, requiring full OS reinstalls for compromised hosts. TAG has added malicious sites to Safe Browsing, issued government-backed attacker alerts to targeted Gmail and Workspace users, and urges researchers to enable Enhanced Safe Browsing, keep software up to date, and verify system integrity after using third-party tools.
retrieved_context.title: Active North Korean campaign targeting security researchers

retrieved_context.text: In early April, Palo Alto Networks’ Advanced WildFire and Cortex XDR uncovered SnipBot—a new v5.0 iteration of the RomCom RAT family—employing advanced window message–based control-flow obfuscation and anti-sandbox checks (filename hash and HKCU\…\RecentDocs entries) in a multi-stage chain beginning with a PDF-labeled EXE downloader signed using a likely stolen certificate; the downloader contacts xeontime[.]com for config-pdf.dll, which uses registry-based COM hijacking to load keyprov.dll from drvmcprotect[.]com into explorer.exe, decrypts payloads stored in HKCU\Software\AppDataSoft\Software, and opens a TCP listener on port 1342 for commands to update, delete, or execute modules. The main backdoor single.dll (mutex “SnipMutex”) supports 27 encrypted commands for drive and process enumeration, file upload/download, and remote module execution, facilitating network pivoting and targeted file exfiltration. Active since December 2023 (RomCom activity since 2022), SnipBot’s tactics, stolen certificates, unique obfuscation, and sophisticated loader underscore a high-risk threat actor likely focused on intelligence gathering; Palo Alto products classify its samples, URLs, and domains as malicious to prevent compromise.
retrieved_context.title: Inside SnipBot: The Latest RomCom Malware Variant

canonical_entities: Lorenz ransomware group exploiting CVE-2022-29499 against Mitel MiVoice Connect
harvested local and domain admin credentials
hits.text: In mid-2022, Arctic Wolf researchers discovered the Lorenz ransomware group exploiting CVE-2022-29499, a remote code execution flaw in Mitel MiVoice Connect VoIP appliances disclosed in April and patched in July, to gain an initial reverse shell. Once inside, the attackers used the compromised Mitel Service Appliance’s CLI to create a hidden directory, download and rename the Golang-based Chisel tunneling tool via Wget, and establish a fast TCP/UDP SOCKS proxy over HTTP (skipping TLS verification) to evade firewalls. After lying dormant for nearly a month and deploying a “pdf_import_export.php” web shell for persistence, they harvested local and domain admin credentials, moved laterally via RDP to a domain controller, exfiltrated data via FileZilla for double-extortion, and encrypted ESXi hosts using BitLocker and Lorenz ransomware. Targeting primarily US SMBs (with outliers in China and Mexico), this campaign underscores the critical need for timely patching of IoT/VoIP devices, comprehensive asset discovery and hardening, network segmentation, and robust PowerShell and module logging with centralized log management.
hits.title: Lorenz Ransomware Goes After SMBs via Mitel VoIP Phone Systems

hits.text: HC3’s November 2022 alert warns of human-operated Lorenz ransomware, first observed in February 2021 and linked to earlier sZ40 and ThunderCrypt activity, which specifically targets large healthcare organizations by customizing its executable code and following a kill chain of initial access, extended reconnaissance, lateral movement to Windows domain controllers for administrator credential theft, then encryption and extortion. Operators demand $500,000–$700,000 and employ a non-typical leak site where stolen data is first offered for sale to other threat actors, then distributed in password-protected archives or, if sales fail, released publicly. With relatively limited public intelligence on Lorenz, HC3 emphasizes that victims should address common ransomware vectors—phishing, exploitation of known vulnerabilities, remote-access compromise and distributed attacks—by reinforcing patch management, intrusion detection, access controls and incident-response planning, especially in light of concurrent Hive ransomware warnings issued by HHS, FBI and CISA.
hits.title: Lorenz Ransomware Targets Large Healthcare Orgs, HC3 Warns | TechTarget

initial access via compromised VPN credentials

hits.text: Between April and August 2023, the newly emerged Akira ransomware group targeted 107 organizations—predominantly SMBs in North America (85.9%) and France (53.1% of detections), with additional impacts in the United States and Turkey—surging from just three recorded attempts in May to 508 in June; operators gain initial access via compromised VPN credentials (including exploitation of CVE-2023-20269 on Cisco ASA/FTD), employ third-party tools such as PCHunter, PowerTool, AdFind, Advanced IP Scanner and MASSCAN for defense evasion and discovery, dump credentials with Mimikatz and LaZagne, and establish persistence by creating new domain accounts, then move laterally via RDP, exfiltrate data through RClone, FTP clients (FileZilla, WinSCP), AnyDesk, Radmin, Cloudflare Tunnel, MobaXterm, RustDesk or Ngrok, and encrypt data using a hybrid ChaCha20/RSA scheme—avoiding system directories and common extensions, deleting shadow copies, and appending .akira to files before dropping akira_readme.txt—and to mitigate this threat organizations should prioritize patching and virtual patching of vulnerable VPN appliances, enforce multifactor authentication and least-privilege access, monitor anomalous use of administration and reconnaissance tools, implement comprehensive backup and recovery procedures, and deploy layered endpoint, network and email defenses with behavior-based detection.
hits.title: Ransomware Spotlight: Akira | Trend Micro (US)

canonical_entities: Remote Code Execution via ms-msdt URI in Word/RTF documents
ms-msdt URI-based RCE in Word/RTF documents
hits.text: In late May 2022, Symantec identified multiple threat actors exploiting the MSDT Follina bug (CVE-2022-30190) through ms-msdt URI-based RCE in Word/RTF documents that load a malicious HTML via Word’s remote template feature to launch msdt.exe, sdiagnhost.exe and ultimately PowerShell—bypassing the need for macros—to install a digitally signed AsyncRAT remote access Trojan that performs anti-analysis checks, collects hardware IDs, user names, execution paths and OS details, and maintains C&C communications, alongside parallel deployments of a browser infostealer targeting cookies and saved credentials in Firefox, Chrome and Edge. Symantec customers should apply Microsoft’s advisories or disable the ms-msdt handler, update Symantec Endpoint definitions (File-based-Downloader-Backdoor:Async, InfoStealer) and monitor for related IOCs to thwart these rapid, damaging campaigns.
hits.title: Attackers Exploit MSDT Follina Bug to Drop RAT, Infostealer | Symantec Enterprise Blogs

canonical_entities: Launch EC2 instances across regions via VPN
hits.text: Unit42’s “EleKtra-Leak” campaign, active since December 2020, uses automated scripts to clone public GitHub repos every few minutes, extract exposed AWS IAM keys within five minutes, then—if not blocked by GitHub-AWS quarantine policies—execute rapid AWS reconnaissance (DescribeRegions), create security groups, and launch hundreds of EC2 instances across regions via VPN for Monero cryptojacking, generating over 400 API calls in seven minutes. Between Aug. 30 and Oct. 6, 2023, researchers tracked 474 actor-controlled miners. The actor employs custom mining software and blocklists high-profile AWS account IDs to avoid honey traps. Leveraging the Prisma Cloud HoneyCloud project’s ephemeral key leaks and policy overrides, Unit42 obtained full visibility, informing Prisma Cloud Secrets Security, CI/CD IaC scanning, Cortex XDR, and recommendations for independent repo scanning, strict IAM policies, and continuous monitoring.
hits.title: CloudKeys in the Air: Tracking Malicious Operations of Exposed IAM Keys

canonical_entities: injected commands via a malicious URL
hits.text: CrowdStrike researchers in April 2022 uncovered that ransomware actors exploited a critical remote code execution flaw (CVE-2022-29499) in unpatched Linux-based Mitel MiVoice appliances (SA 100, SA 400 and Virtual SA) to gain initial access, plant malware and pivot laterally: the exploit chain began with an external HTTP GET to a “get_url” parameter in a PHP file (to bypass IP restrictions) followed by a device-originated GET that injected commands via a malicious URL, enabling an SSL-enabled reverse shell (using mkfifo and openssl_client) and deployment of a “pdf_import.php” web shell and the Chisel tunneling tool. Although the threat actors deleted evidence from the VoIP filesystem, CrowdStrike recovered the undocumented exploit, downloaded tools and anti-forensic measures. With some 21,000 MITEL devices worldwide still exposed (per Kevin Beaumont’s Shodan string “http.html_hash:-1971546278”), organizations are urged to apply Mitel’s April advisory patches for MiVoice Connect 19.2 SP3 and earlier, enforce strict network segmentation around perimeter devices, conduct threat modeling to detect anomalous GET requests, and prioritize timely firmware updates to thwart zero-day exploitation.
hits.title: Mitel VoIP Bug Exploited in Ransomware Attacks | Threatpost

hits.text: The North Korea-linked threat actor Slow Pisces (also tracked as Jade Sleet, PUKCHONG, TraderTraitor, and UNC4899) has been conducting a multi-stage malware campaign targeting cryptocurrency developers via LinkedIn job opportunity lures since at least June 2024, leveraging trojanized Python and JavaScript projects hosted on GitHub that employ YAML deserialization and EJS templating to execute gated payloads only to validated targets meeting specific criteria (IP address, geolocation, time, HTTP headers); the campaign delivers RN Loader and RN Stealer malware on macOS systems capable of harvesting system metadata, installed applications, SSH keys, AWS/Kubernetes/Google Cloud configuration files, and iCloud Keychain data, with payloads remaining memory-resident and deployed selectively to prevent analysis; Slow Pisces is assessed to be responsible for the February 2025 Bybit cryptocurrency exchange breach and operates alongside other North Korean clusters including Operation Dream Job, Contagious Interview, Alluring Pisces, and Moonstone Sleet, though with notably superior operational security practices involving heavily guarded payload delivery across infection stages.
hits.title: Crypto Developers Targeted by Python Malware Disguised as Coding Challenges

hits.text: Since at least 2015, Mandiant has identified APT42—an IRGC-linked Iranian state-sponsored threat actor also known as APT35—conducting over 30 spear-phishing operations across 14 countries against government officials, policymakers, journalists, academics and dissidents, evolving tactics from 2020 Oxford vaccinologist-themed pharmaceutical lures to 2021 fake interview requests using compromised U.S. media accounts for 37-day MFA-intercepting credential harvesting, and February 2022 phishes posing as a British news agency targeting political science professors; beyond credential theft via shortened URLs and PDF attachments directing victims to spoofed login portals, APT42 deploys custom Android spyware—spread via SMS links to messaging/VPN apps—to exfiltrate calls, SMS, audio recordings, images and GPS data in real time, while on Windows it employs lightweight custom malware for initial access, privilege escalation, reconnaissance, lateral movement through follow-on phishing, and persistence via scheduled tasks and registry keys; Mandiant further correlates APT42’s TTPs with November 2021 PHOSPHORUS BitLocker ransomware attempts against Fortinet FortiOS SSL VPN and unpatched Exchange servers, highlighting the group’s multi-platform espionage-to-ransom capabilities and real-world threat to high-value targets.
hits.title: New Iranian hacking group APT42 deploys custom Android spyware

hits.text: After a year-long investigation researchers at Lumen’s Black Lotus Labs dissected the Ngioweb botnet—first observed in 2017—which uses a loader network and roughly 15 n-day exploits to deploy malware that contacts C2 domains generated via a domain generation algorithm (augmented by DNS TXT records to resist sinkholing), evaluates device traffic capacity, and links compromised Zyxel, Reolink, Alpha Technologies and, increasingly, Netgear routers (now 10 % of bots) to over 180 “backconnect” C2 nodes that provide at least 80 % of the 35,000 residential proxies in the NSOCKS[.]net service across 180 countries; NSOCKS’s lack of authentication and appearance on free proxy lists has enabled cybercriminals to carry out DDoS amplification, credential stuffing, phishing and malware proxying (e.g., Agent Tesla), while APT28 state-sponsored actors have mixed espionage with criminal traffic on the same infrastructure. To disrupt both operations, Lumen, alongside The ShadowServer Foundation and other partners, is actively blocking traffic to known C2 nodes and publishing indicators of compromise to help organizations identify and remediate infected devices.
hits.title: Botnet fueling residential proxies disrupted in cybercrime crackdown

hits.text: Our GReAT team uncovered Operation ForumTroll—a state-sponsored APT campaign targeting Russian media, academic and government personnel—delivering previously unknown malware via phishing emails masquerading as Primakov Readings invitations containing two malicious links; clicking either on a Windows PC using Chrome or any Chromium-based browser silently triggers a zero-day exploit (CVE-2025-2783), exploiting a logic flaw at the Chrome-Windows interface to bypass the browser’s sandbox and deploy the payload without further user interaction. We promptly reported the vulnerability to Google, which released a patch in Chrome version 134.0.6998.177/178; while the phishing links now redirect to the legitimate forum site and the campaign is dormant, the attackers could reactivate it at any time. To mitigate this espionage threat, organizations should ensure all Chrome instances are updated to at least 134.0.6998.177/.178, deploy robust exploit detection and prevention solutions on internet-connected devices, and maintain vigilant phishing awareness and monitoring.
hits.title: CVE-2025-2783 in Operation ForumTroll APT

canonical_entities: Boot or Logon Initialization Scripts: Logon Script (Windows)
hits.text: Blitz is a modular two-stage Windows malware discovered in 2024 and actively developed into early 2025 by a Russian-speaking actor using the moniker sw1zzx who distributed backdoored Standoff 2 game cheat packages (Nerest_CrackBy@sw1zzx_dev.zip and Elysium_CrackBy@sw1zzx_dev.zip) via a Telegram channel. The first stage is a stealthy downloader (ieapfltr.dll) retrieved through a PowerShell one-liner from pastebin/paste.rs URLs after passing anti-sandbox and VM detection checks (timing loops, floating-point instruction counters, processor count and screen resolution heuristics), which then establishes persistence via HKCU\Environment\UserInitMprLogonScript and HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run. Upon reboot, the downloader connects to a FastAPI-based C2 infrastructure hosted on a Hugging Face Space to fetch the second-stage Blitz bot that performs keylogging, screenshot capture, denial-of-service attacks on web servers and can deploy an XMRig Monero miner as follow-up. This campaign leverages Hugging Face Spaces for file hosting and C2 communications, and the malware developer promoted cheats on social media before announcing departure in May 2025; Hugging Face subsequently locked the account and blocked blob IDs. The impact includes credential theft, resource exploitation, unauthorized cryptocurrency mining and potential service disruption, and Palo Alto Networks’ Advanced WildFire, URL Filtering, DNS Security, Threat Prevention, Cortex XDR and XSIAM effectively detect and block Blitz activities, with Unit 42 standing by for incident response.
hits.title: Blitz Malware: A Tale of Game Cheats and Code Repositories

retrieved_context.text: In mid-2022, Arctic Wolf researchers discovered the Lorenz ransomware group exploiting CVE-2022-29499, a remote code execution flaw in Mitel MiVoice Connect VoIP appliances disclosed in April and patched in July, to gain an initial reverse shell. Once inside, the attackers used the compromised Mitel Service Appliance’s CLI to create a hidden directory, download and rename the Golang-based Chisel tunneling tool via Wget, and establish a fast TCP/UDP SOCKS proxy over HTTP (skipping TLS verification) to evade firewalls. Targeting primarily US SMBs (with outliers in China and Mexico), this campaign underscores the critical need for timely patching of IoT/VoIP devices, comprehensive asset discovery and hardening, network segmentation, and robust PowerShell and module logging with centralized log management.

retrieved_context.text: HC3’s November 2022 alert warns of human-operated Lorenz ransomware, first observed in February 2021 and linked to earlier sZ40 and ThunderCrypt activity, which specifically targets large healthcare organizations by customizing its executable code and following a kill chain of initial access, extended reconnaissance, lateral movement to Windows domain controllers for administrator credential theft, then encryption and extortion. Operators demand $500,000–$700,000 and employ a non-typical leak site where stolen data is first offered for sale to other threat actors, then distributed in password-protected archives or, if sales fail, released publicly. With relatively limited public intelligence on Lorenz, HC3 emphasizes that victims should address common ransomware vectors—phishing, exploitation of known vulnerabilities, remote-access compromise and distributed attacks—by reinforcing patch management, intrusion detection, access controls and incident-response planning, especially in light of concurrent Hive ransomware warnings issued by HHS, FBI and CISA.

retrieved_context.text: Blitz is a modular two-stage Windows malware discovered in 2024 and actively developed into early 2025 by a Russian-speaking actor using the moniker sw1zzx who distributed backdoored Standoff 2 game cheat packages (Nerest_CrackBy@sw1zzx_dev.zip and Elysium_CrackBy@sw1zzx_dev.zip) via a Telegram channel. Upon reboot, the downloader connects to a FastAPI-based C2 infrastructure hosted on a Hugging Face Space to fetch the second-stage Blitz bot that performs keylogging, screenshot capture, denial-of-service attacks on web servers and can deploy an XMRig Monero miner as follow-up. This campaign leverages Hugging Face Spaces for file hosting and C2 communications, and the malware developer promoted cheats on social media before announcing departure in May 2025; Hugging Face subsequently locked the account and blocked blob IDs. The impact includes credential theft, resource exploitation, unauthorized cryptocurrency mining and potential service disruption, and Palo Alto Networks’ Advanced WildFire, URL Filtering, DNS Security, Threat Prevention, Cortex XDR and XSIAM effectively detect and block Blitz activities, with Unit 42 standing by for incident response.

encrypted recovery folders and user data
hits.text: On May 6, 2021, CISA disclosed that FiveHands ransomware actors exploited a zero-day VPN vulnerability for initial access, then used SoftPerfect Network Scanner for host discovery and PsExec to deploy ServeManager.exe (the NTRUEncrypt-based FiveHands payload) alongside SombRAT RAT, leveraging publicly available tools (RouterScan, grabff, rclone, s3browser) and PowerSploit modules for credential access, persistence, token manipulation, Kerberoasting, and exfiltration; once in place, FiveHands enumerated and deleted Volume Shadow Copies via WMI (T1490, T1047), encrypted recovery folders and user data (T1486), and dropped ransom notes across directories. The campaign caused direct financial losses (ransoms, legal fees, incident response, downtime, reputational harm) and exposed third-party partners. Mitigation hinges on patching/decommissioning unused VPN servers, enforcing MFA on remote and privileged accounts, maintaining up-to-date AV/OS, implementing robust backup and recovery routines, hunting for IoCs, and reinforcing employee training against phishing and malicious attachments.
hits.title: FiveHands Ransomware Overview

hits.text: A zero-day VPN vulnerability provided initial access for a sophisticated threat actor who employed publicly available penetration‐testing and exploitation tools—SoftPerfect Network Scanner for network discovery, PsExec to deploy ServeManager.exe (the FiveHands ransomware variant using lattice-based NTRUEncrypt public key cryptography), and SombRAT for remote information theft—alongside RouterScan, grabff.exe, rclone.exe, and s3browser-9-5-3.exe to harvest credentials and exfiltrate data. Once inside, the attacker leveraged Windows Management Instrumentation (T1047) to enumerate and delete Volume Shadow Copies (Inhibit System Recovery, T1490), encrypted files (including those in recovery folders) for impact (T1486), and dropped ransom notes across directories, demanding payment to restore access. Post-encryption activities align with MITRE techniques such as Access Token Manipulation, Boot or Logon Autostart, PowerShell command and scripting interpreter, Domain Trust Discovery, Process Discovery, Screen Capture, and Kerberoasting. The combined use of FiveHands ransomware and SombRAT RAT resulted in both data theft and destruction of backup artifacts, underscoring the need for proactive patch management, network segmentation, strict credential hygiene, and rapid incident response to mitigate novel lattice-based encryption threats.
hits.title: FiveHands Ransomware Overview

canonical_entities: Defense evasion via virtual machine execution
deployment of a VirtualBox VM running Windows XP to execute encryption, thereby evading host defenses
hits.text: Ragnar Locker, active since December 2019 and first flagged by the FBI in April 2020, is a hybrid ransomware strain and operator gang responsible for breaching 52 organizations across 10 critical infrastructure sectors—including energy, manufacturing, financial services, government, IT and agriculture—employing double-extortion by exfiltrating sensitive data before encryption and threatening public leaks if ransoms go unpaid. Intrusions begin with RDP access via brute-force or stolen credentials, privilege escalation through CVE-2017-0213, and deployment of a VirtualBox VM running Windows XP to execute encryption, thereby evading host defenses; they delete shadow copies, disable antivirus (e.g., Sophos, Veeam) and remote management tools (Kaseya, ConnectWise), and spread laterally via PowerShell. Obfuscation is achieved through junk code, encrypted PE-embedded configs (".keys"), runtime string decryption, locale checks to avoid CIS targets and a custom Salsa20 cipher with a bespoke 64-byte key matrix appending “_RAGNAR_” to footers. Major attacks include Campari Group (2 TB, $15 M), Energias de Portugal (10 TB, 1 580 BTC), Capcom (1 TB) and Dassault Falcon Jet, with the FBI warning of heightened risks to food/agriculture during planting/harvest. Ragnar Locker pressures victims to avoid law enforcement, yet paying ransoms funds criminality and fails to guarantee data deletion; mitigation requires hardened RDP/MFA, patching CVE-2017-0213, network segmentation, behavioral EDR, offline backups and timely incident reporting to the FBI.

hits.text: NCC Group’s CIRT has tracked Karakurt as an extortion-focused threat actor exploiting single-factor FortiGate VPNs via legitimate Active Directory credentials to achieve initial access, with an average dwell time of just over one month due to living-off-the-land techniques and lack of malware. Although the exact privilege escalation method remains unclear, Karakurt has attempted CVE-2020-1472 (Zerologon) and attained domain-admin rights, then used PsExec and RDP for lateral movement to the primary domain controller. Early in the breach they execute an encoded PowerShell DNS zone export—generating Microsoft-Windows-DNS-Server-Service Event ID 3150—and extract NTDS.dit via Volume Shadow Copy for further credential harvesting. After a brief exit, they re-enter to deploy AnyDesk for persistence, archive sensitive files with 7-Zip, and likely exfiltrate data via Rclone to cloud hosts. NCC Group recommends immediate FortiGate VPN MFA implementation, critical patching of domain controllers, and monitoring for Event ID 3150, unauthorized AnyDesk or PsExec usage, and VPN pool host authentications (e.g., DESKTOP-XXXXXX) to detect potential Karakurt intrusions.

hits.text: Trend Micro data shows BlackCat executed 39.3% of its 176 manufacturing detections against US targets and confirmed 173 leak-site compromises from December 2021 to September 2022—58.7% US-based—favoring finance, professional, legal, technology, energy, utilities, construction, and manufacturing sectors, with small (52%) and midsize (26%) businesses most targeted. Initial access was achieved via Exchange CVE-2021-26855/26857/26858/27065 exploits, ConnectWise RCE, and SSH key abuse. Execution leverages COBEACON to inject the Rust-based ransomware into ntoskrnl.exe, evading detection; defense evasion includes disabling AV, using AdFind/ADRecon/SoftPerfect, Process Hacker, Mimikatz, WMIC, Netstat, and LSASS credential dumping. Lateral movement exploits embedded PsExec, RDP, MobaXterm, and BITSAdmin transfers of zzz.exe/xxx.exe/yyy.exe/sv.exe. C2 communication uses Base64-encoded PowerShell with a Cobalt Strike SMB beacon over named pipes. Exfiltration employs ExMatter (upgraded September 2022), 7-Zip, Rclone, MEGASync, WinSCP, and FreeFileSync for double extortion. The payload defaces backgrounds, terminates backup/AV/DB/Internet/VM services, disables recovery (shadow copy deletion, safe-mode variant), and appends variable Sphynx extensions while avoiding critical directories and file types. BlackCat maps to MITRE ATT&CK T1190, T1078, T1562.001/009, T1003.001, T1021.002, T1486, T1490, T1489, T1048/T1567. Security teams should patch Exchange CVEs, secure MSP tools, enforce least privilege, segment networks, monitor PowerShell injections, and vet outbound file transfers to disrupt this evolving affiliate-driven operation.

retrieved_context.text: On May 6, 2021, CISA disclosed that FiveHands ransomware actors exploited a zero-day VPN vulnerability for initial access, then used SoftPerfect Network Scanner for host discovery and PsExec to deploy ServeManager.exe (the NTRUEncrypt-based FiveHands payload) alongside SombRAT RAT, leveraging publicly available tools (RouterScan, grabff, rclone, s3browser) and PowerSploit modules for credential access, persistence, token manipulation, Kerberoasting, and exfiltration; once in place, FiveHands enumerated and deleted Volume Shadow Copies via WMI (T1490, T1047), encrypted recovery folders and user data (T1486), and dropped ransom notes across directories. The campaign caused direct financial losses (ransoms, legal fees, incident response, downtime, reputational harm) and exposed third-party partners. Mitigation hinges on patching/decommissioning unused VPN servers, enforcing MFA on remote and privileged accounts, maintaining up-to-date AV/OS, implementing robust backup and recovery routines, hunting for IoCs, and reinforcing employee training against phishing and malicious attachments.
retrieved_context.title: FiveHands Ransomware Overview

retrieved_context.text: A zero-day VPN vulnerability provided initial access for a sophisticated threat actor who employed publicly available penetration‐testing and exploitation tools—SoftPerfect Network Scanner for network discovery, PsExec to deploy ServeManager.exe (the FiveHands ransomware variant using lattice-based NTRUEncrypt public key cryptography), and SombRAT for remote information theft—alongside RouterScan, grabff.exe, rclone.exe, and s3browser-9-5-3.exe to harvest credentials and exfiltrate data. Once inside, the attacker leveraged Windows Management Instrumentation (T1047) to enumerate and delete Volume Shadow Copies (Inhibit System Recovery, T1490), encrypted files (including those in recovery folders) for impact (T1486), and dropped ransom notes across directories, demanding payment to restore access. Post-encryption activities align with MITRE techniques such as Access Token Manipulation, Boot or Logon Autostart, PowerShell command and scripting interpreter, Domain Trust Discovery, Process Discovery, Screen Capture, and Kerberoasting. The combined use of FiveHands ransomware and SombRAT RAT resulted in both data theft and destruction of backup artifacts, underscoring the need for proactive patch management, network segmentation, strict credential hygiene, and rapid incident response to mitigate novel lattice-based encryption threats.
retrieved_context.title: FiveHands Ransomware Overview

canonical_entities: Defense evasion via virtual machine execution
deployment of a VirtualBox VM running Windows XP to execute encryption, thereby evading host defenses
retrieved_context.text: Ragnar Locker, active since December 2019 and first flagged by the FBI in April 2020, is a hybrid ransomware strain and operator gang responsible for breaching 52 organizations across 10 critical infrastructure sectors—including energy, manufacturing, financial services, government, IT and agriculture—employing double-extortion by exfiltrating sensitive data before encryption and threatening public leaks if ransoms go unpaid. Intrusions begin with RDP access via brute-force or stolen credentials, privilege escalation through CVE-2017-0213, and deployment of a VirtualBox VM running Windows XP to execute encryption, thereby evading host defenses; they delete shadow copies, disable antivirus (e.g., Sophos, Veeam) and remote management tools (Kaseya, ConnectWise), and spread laterally via PowerShell. Obfuscation is achieved through junk code, encrypted PE-embedded configs (".keys"), runtime string decryption, locale checks to avoid CIS targets and a custom Salsa20 cipher with a bespoke 64-byte key matrix appending “_RAGNAR_” to footers. Major attacks include Campari Group (2 TB, $15 M), Energias de Portugal (10 TB, 1 580 BTC), Capcom (1 TB) and Dassault Falcon Jet, with the FBI warning of heightened risks to food/agriculture during planting/harvest. Ragnar Locker pressures victims to avoid law enforcement, yet paying ransoms funds criminality and fails to guarantee data deletion; mitigation requires hardened RDP/MFA, patching CVE-2017-0213, network segmentation, behavioral EDR, offline backups and timely incident reporting to the FBI.
retrieved_context.title: Ragnar Locker Ransomware (Everything You Need To Know)

canonical_entities: Boot or Logon Initialization Scripts: Logon Script (Windows)
retrieved_context.text: Blitz is a modular two-stage Windows malware discovered in 2024 and actively developed into early 2025 by a Russian-speaking actor using the moniker sw1zzx who distributed backdoored Standoff 2 game cheat packages (Nerest_CrackBy@sw1zzx_dev.zip and Elysium_CrackBy@sw1zzx_dev.zip) via a Telegram channel. The first stage is a stealthy downloader (ieapfltr.dll) retrieved through a PowerShell one-liner from pastebin/paste.rs URLs after passing anti-sandbox and VM detection checks (timing loops, floating-point instruction counters, processor count and screen resolution heuristics), which then establishes persistence via HKCU\Environment\UserInitMprLogonScript and HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run. Upon reboot, the downloader connects to a FastAPI-based C2 infrastructure hosted on a Hugging Face Space to fetch the second-stage Blitz bot that performs keylogging, screenshot capture, denial-of-service attacks on web servers and can deploy an XMRig Monero miner as follow-up. This campaign leverages Hugging Face Spaces for file hosting and C2 communications, and the malware developer promoted cheats on social media before announcing departure in May 2025; Hugging Face subsequently locked the account and blocked blob IDs. The impact includes credential theft, resource exploitation, unauthorized cryptocurrency mining and potential service disruption, and Palo Alto Networks’ Advanced WildFire, URL Filtering, DNS Security, Threat Prevention, Cortex XDR and XSIAM effectively detect and block Blitz activities, with Unit 42 standing by for incident response.
retrieved_context.title: Blitz Malware: A Tale of Game Cheats and Code Repositories

retrieved_context.text: NCC Group’s CIRT has tracked Karakurt as an extortion-focused threat actor exploiting single-factor FortiGate VPNs via legitimate Active Directory credentials to achieve initial access, with an average dwell time of just over one month due to living-off-the-land techniques and lack of malware. Although the exact privilege escalation method remains unclear, Karakurt has attempted CVE-2020-1472 (Zerologon) and attained domain-admin rights, then used PsExec and RDP for lateral movement to the primary domain controller. Early in the breach they execute an encoded PowerShell DNS zone export—generating Microsoft-Windows-DNS-Server-Service Event ID 3150—and extract NTDS.dit via Volume Shadow Copy for further credential harvesting. After a brief exit, they re-enter to deploy AnyDesk for persistence, archive sensitive files with 7-Zip, and likely exfiltrate data via Rclone to cloud hosts. NCC Group recommends immediate FortiGate VPN MFA implementation, critical patching of domain controllers, and monitoring for Event ID 3150, unauthorized AnyDesk or PsExec usage, and VPN pool host authentications (e.g., DESKTOP-XXXXXX) to detect potential Karakurt intrusions.
retrieved_context.title: Detecting Karakurt – an extortion focused threat actor

retrieved_context.text: Proofpoint researchers led by Sherrod DeGrippo have uncovered state-sponsored actors exploiting CVE-2022-30190 (Follina), a Microsoft Office remote code execution flaw in the Windows Support Diagnostic Tool (MSDT) invoked via URL protocol, in phishing campaigns since mid-April targeting U.S. and E.U. government workers; following Shadow Chaser Group’s April 12 discovery and Microsoft’s May patch, adversaries dispatched over 1,000 recruitment-themed emails promising a “20% increase” and urging recipients to open a Word attachment that launches a PowerShell script to detect virtualized environments, perform extensive reconnaissance across browsers, mail clients and file shares, zip collected data for exfiltration, and enable arbitrary code execution with user-level privileges to install malware, manipulate or delete data, and create accounts—activities indicative of a state-aligned nexus that underscore the urgency of rapid patch deployment, user training and network-level MSDT exploit mitigations.
retrieved_context.title: Follina Exploited by State-Sponsored Hackers | Threatpost

retrieved_context.text: Last week Google’s Threat Analysis Group, in partnership with The Citizen Lab, exposed an in-the-wild exploit chain developed by the commercial surveillance vendor Intellexa in Egypt that leverages a man-in-the-middle injection on HTTP traffic to silently redirect targets first to c.betly[.]me and then to sec-flare[.]com, delivering Predator spyware without any user interaction; on iOS this chain combined Safari RCE (CVE-2023-41993), certificate validation bypass (CVE-2023-41991) and XNU kernel local privilege escalation (CVE-2023-41992) and was patched in iOS 16.7/17.0.1, while on Android initial Chrome renderer RCE (CVE-2023-4762), delivered via MITM or one-time links, was patched on September 5; this campaign highlights the serious risk posed by proliferating commercial spyware, underscores the urgency of enforcing universal HTTPS and enabling Chrome’s HTTPS-First Mode, and demonstrates the critical need for organizations and users to apply the latest OS and browser updates, deploy encrypted-traffic protections, and monitor for anomalous network redirects to mitigate future attacks.
