hits.text: Researchers at Accenture Security exposed Q3 2021 proliferation of Karakurt, a financially motivated data‐extortion group first identified in June 2021 upon registering two domains and launching a Twitter handle, which compromised over 40 primarily North American (95 percent) organizations across random sectors between September and November by sourcing or phishing VPN credentials for initial access, establishing persistence with Cobalt Strike beacons or AnyDesk, then harvesting administrator privileges via Mimikatz to evade EDR solutions; they compress stolen data with 7zip or WinZip and exfiltrate it to Mega.io using Rclone or FileZilla, foregoing ransomware encryption in favor of public leak threats, a low-overhead approach that can still cripple victims—underscoring the need for robust VPN credential management, continuous monitoring for living-off-the-land tools, and preventative controls to detect and disrupt such intrusions before data exfiltration.
hits.title: New 'Karakurt' hacking group focuses on data theft and extortion

hits.text: The North Korea-linked threat actor Slow Pisces (also tracked as Jade Sleet, PUKCHONG, TraderTraitor, and UNC4899) has been conducting a multi-stage malware campaign targeting cryptocurrency developers via LinkedIn job opportunity lures since at least June 2024, leveraging trojanized Python and JavaScript projects hosted on GitHub that employ YAML deserialization and EJS templating to execute gated payloads only to validated targets meeting specific criteria (IP address, geolocation, time, HTTP headers); the campaign delivers RN Loader and RN Stealer malware on macOS systems capable of harvesting system metadata, installed applications, SSH keys, AWS/Kubernetes/Google Cloud configuration files, and iCloud Keychain data, with payloads remaining memory-resident and deployed selectively to prevent analysis; Slow Pisces is assessed to be responsible for the February 2025 Bybit cryptocurrency exchange breach and operates alongside other North Korean clusters including Operation Dream Job, Contagious Interview, Alluring Pisces, and Moonstone Sleet, though with notably superior operational security practices involving heavily guarded payload delivery across infection stages.
hits.title: Crypto Developers Targeted by Python Malware Disguised as Coding Challenges

canonical_entities: Iran’s Ministry of Intelligence and Security
hits.text: US and UK agencies (CISA, FBI, CNMF, NCSC-UK and NSA) issued a joint advisory detailing how the Iranian-backed MuddyWater group—active since at least 2017 and linked to Iran’s Ministry of Intelligence and Security in January 2022—has expanded its arsenal beyond PowGoop, Canopy/Starwhale, Mori and POWERSTATS to include a new Python backdoor dubbed “Small Sieve” and a PowerShell backdoor that encrypts C2 channels; these tools target telecom, defense, local government and oil and gas organizations across Asia, Africa, Europe and North America, maintain persistence via custom string and traffic obfuscation (hex byte-swapping plus an obfuscated Base64 routine) over the Telegram Bot API via HTTPS, and facilitate lateral movement and data exfiltration, underscoring the need for defenders to monitor anomalous Telegram API calls, obfuscated Base64 traffic and encrypted PowerShell sessions.
hits.title: US and UK expose new malware used by MuddyWater hackers

canonical_entities: Launch EC2 instances across regions via VPN
hits.text: Unit42’s “EleKtra-Leak” campaign, active since December 2020, uses automated scripts to clone public GitHub repos every few minutes, extract exposed AWS IAM keys within five minutes, then—if not blocked by GitHub-AWS quarantine policies—execute rapid AWS reconnaissance (DescribeRegions), create security groups, and launch hundreds of EC2 instances across regions via VPN for Monero cryptojacking, generating over 400 API calls in seven minutes. Between Aug. 30 and Oct. 6, 2023, researchers tracked 474 actor-controlled miners. The actor employs custom mining software and blocklists high-profile AWS account IDs to avoid honey traps. Leveraging the Prisma Cloud HoneyCloud project’s ephemeral key leaks and policy overrides, Unit42 obtained full visibility, informing Prisma Cloud Secrets Security, CI/CD IaC scanning, Cortex XDR, and recommendations for independent repo scanning, strict IAM policies, and continuous monitoring.
hits.title: CloudKeys in the Air: Tracking Malicious Operations of Exposed IAM Keys

hits.text: After a year-long investigation researchers at Lumen’s Black Lotus Labs dissected the Ngioweb botnet—first observed in 2017—which uses a loader network and roughly 15 n-day exploits to deploy malware that contacts C2 domains generated via a domain generation algorithm (augmented by DNS TXT records to resist sinkholing), evaluates device traffic capacity, and links compromised Zyxel, Reolink, Alpha Technologies and, increasingly, Netgear routers (now 10 % of bots) to over 180 “backconnect” C2 nodes that provide at least 80 % of the 35,000 residential proxies in the NSOCKS[.]net service across 180 countries; NSOCKS’s lack of authentication and appearance on free proxy lists has enabled cybercriminals to carry out DDoS amplification, credential stuffing, phishing and malware proxying (e.g., Agent Tesla), while APT28 state-sponsored actors have mixed espionage with criminal traffic on the same infrastructure. To disrupt both operations, Lumen, alongside The ShadowServer Foundation and other partners, is actively blocking traffic to known C2 nodes and publishing indicators of compromise to help organizations identify and remediate infected devices.
hits.title: Botnet fueling residential proxies disrupted in cybercrime crackdown

hits.text: Our GReAT team uncovered Operation ForumTroll—a state-sponsored APT campaign targeting Russian media, academic and government personnel—delivering previously unknown malware via phishing emails masquerading as Primakov Readings invitations containing two malicious links; clicking either on a Windows PC using Chrome or any Chromium-based browser silently triggers a zero-day exploit (CVE-2025-2783), exploiting a logic flaw at the Chrome-Windows interface to bypass the browser’s sandbox and deploy the payload without further user interaction. We promptly reported the vulnerability to Google, which released a patch in Chrome version 134.0.6998.177/178; while the phishing links now redirect to the legitimate forum site and the campaign is dormant, the attackers could reactivate it at any time. To mitigate this espionage threat, organizations should ensure all Chrome instances are updated to at least 134.0.6998.177/.178, deploy robust exploit detection and prevention solutions on internet-connected devices, and maintain vigilant phishing awareness and monitoring.
hits.title: CVE-2025-2783 in Operation ForumTroll APT

canonical_entities: Remote Code Execution via ms-msdt URI in Word/RTF documents
ms-msdt URI-based RCE in Word/RTF documents
hits.text: In late May 2022, Symantec identified multiple threat actors exploiting the MSDT Follina bug (CVE-2022-30190) through ms-msdt URI-based RCE in Word/RTF documents that load a malicious HTML via Word’s remote template feature to launch msdt.exe, sdiagnhost.exe and ultimately PowerShell—bypassing the need for macros—to install a digitally signed AsyncRAT remote access Trojan that performs anti-analysis checks, collects hardware IDs, user names, execution paths and OS details, and maintains C&C communications, alongside parallel deployments of a browser infostealer targeting cookies and saved credentials in Firefox, Chrome and Edge. Symantec customers should apply Microsoft’s advisories or disable the ms-msdt handler, update Symantec Endpoint definitions (File-based-Downloader-Backdoor:Async, InfoStealer) and monitor for related IOCs to thwart these rapid, damaging campaigns.
hits.title: Attackers Exploit MSDT Follina Bug to Drop RAT, Infostealer | Symantec Enterprise Blogs

retrieved_context.text: Researchers at Accenture Security exposed Q3 2021 proliferation of Karakurt, a financially motivated data‐extortion group first identified in June 2021 upon registering two domains and launching a Twitter handle, which compromised over 40 primarily North American (95 percent) organizations across random sectors between September and November by sourcing or phishing VPN credentials for initial access, establishing persistence with Cobalt Strike beacons or AnyDesk, then harvesting administrator privileges via Mimikatz to evade EDR solutions; they compress stolen data with 7zip or WinZip and exfiltrate it to Mega.io using Rclone or FileZilla, foregoing ransomware encryption in favor of public leak threats, a low-overhead approach that can still cripple victims—underscoring the need for robust VPN credential management, continuous monitoring for living-off-the-land tools, and preventative controls to detect and disrupt such intrusions before data exfiltration.
retrieved_context.title: New 'Karakurt' hacking group focuses on data theft and extortion

retrieved_context.text: The North Korea-linked threat actor Slow Pisces (also tracked as Jade Sleet, PUKCHONG, TraderTraitor, and UNC4899) has been conducting a multi-stage malware campaign targeting cryptocurrency developers via LinkedIn job opportunity lures since at least June 2024, leveraging trojanized Python and JavaScript projects hosted on GitHub that employ YAML deserialization and EJS templating to execute gated payloads only to validated targets meeting specific criteria (IP address, geolocation, time, HTTP headers); the campaign delivers RN Loader and RN Stealer malware on macOS systems capable of harvesting system metadata, installed applications, SSH keys, AWS/Kubernetes/Google Cloud configuration files, and iCloud Keychain data, with payloads remaining memory-resident and deployed selectively to prevent analysis; Slow Pisces is assessed to be responsible for the February 2025 Bybit cryptocurrency exchange breach and operates alongside other North Korean clusters including Operation Dream Job, Contagious Interview, Alluring Pisces, and Moonstone Sleet, though with notably superior operational security practices involving heavily guarded payload delivery across infection stages.
retrieved_context.title: Crypto Developers Targeted by Python Malware Disguised as Coding Challenges

canonical_entities: Iran’s Ministry of Intelligence and Security
retrieved_context.text: US and UK agencies (CISA, FBI, CNMF, NCSC-UK and NSA) issued a joint advisory detailing how the Iranian-backed MuddyWater group—active since at least 2017 and linked to Iran’s Ministry of Intelligence and Security in January 2022—has expanded its arsenal beyond PowGoop, Canopy/Starwhale, Mori and POWERSTATS to include a new Python backdoor dubbed “Small Sieve” and a PowerShell backdoor that encrypts C2 channels; these tools target telecom, defense, local government and oil and gas organizations across Asia, Africa, Europe and North America, maintain persistence via custom string and traffic obfuscation (hex byte-swapping plus an obfuscated Base64 routine) over the Telegram Bot API via HTTPS, and facilitate lateral movement and data exfiltration, underscoring the need for defenders to monitor anomalous Telegram API calls, obfuscated Base64 traffic and encrypted PowerShell sessions.
retrieved_context.title: US and UK expose new malware used by MuddyWater hackers

canonical_entities: Launch EC2 instances across regions via VPN
retrieved_context.text: Unit42’s “EleKtra-Leak” campaign, active since December 2020, uses automated scripts to clone public GitHub repos every few minutes, extract exposed AWS IAM keys within five minutes, then—if not blocked by GitHub-AWS quarantine policies—execute rapid AWS reconnaissance (DescribeRegions), create security groups, and launch hundreds of EC2 instances across regions via VPN for Monero cryptojacking, generating over 400 API calls in seven minutes. Between Aug. 30 and Oct. 6, 2023, researchers tracked 474 actor-controlled miners. The actor employs custom mining software and blocklists high-profile AWS account IDs to avoid honey traps. Leveraging the Prisma Cloud HoneyCloud project’s ephemeral key leaks and policy overrides, Unit42 obtained full visibility, informing Prisma Cloud Secrets Security, CI/CD IaC scanning, Cortex XDR, and recommendations for independent repo scanning, strict IAM policies, and continuous monitoring.
retrieved_context.title: CloudKeys in the Air: Tracking Malicious Operations of Exposed IAM Keys

retrieved_context.text: After a year-long investigation researchers at Lumen’s Black Lotus Labs dissected the Ngioweb botnet—first observed in 2017—which uses a loader network and roughly 15 n-day exploits to deploy malware that contacts C2 domains generated via a domain generation algorithm (augmented by DNS TXT records to resist sinkholing), evaluates device traffic capacity, and links compromised Zyxel, Reolink, Alpha Technologies and, increasingly, Netgear routers (now 10 % of bots) to over 180 “backconnect” C2 nodes that provide at least 80 % of the 35,000 residential proxies in the NSOCKS[.]net service across 180 countries; NSOCKS’s lack of authentication and appearance on free proxy lists has enabled cybercriminals to carry out DDoS amplification, credential stuffing, phishing and malware proxying (e.g., Agent Tesla), while APT28 state-sponsored actors have mixed espionage with criminal traffic on the same infrastructure. To disrupt both operations, Lumen, alongside The ShadowServer Foundation and other partners, is actively blocking traffic to known C2 nodes and publishing indicators of compromise to help organizations identify and remediate infected devices.
retrieved_context.title: Botnet fueling residential proxies disrupted in cybercrime crackdown

retrieved_context.text: Our GReAT team uncovered Operation ForumTroll—a state-sponsored APT campaign targeting Russian media, academic and government personnel—delivering previously unknown malware via phishing emails masquerading as Primakov Readings invitations containing two malicious links; clicking either on a Windows PC using Chrome or any Chromium-based browser silently triggers a zero-day exploit (CVE-2025-2783), exploiting a logic flaw at the Chrome-Windows interface to bypass the browser’s sandbox and deploy the payload without further user interaction. We promptly reported the vulnerability to Google, which released a patch in Chrome version 134.0.6998.177/178; while the phishing links now redirect to the legitimate forum site and the campaign is dormant, the attackers could reactivate it at any time. To mitigate this espionage threat, organizations should ensure all Chrome instances are updated to at least 134.0.6998.177/.178, deploy robust exploit detection and prevention solutions on internet-connected devices, and maintain vigilant phishing awareness and monitoring.
retrieved_context.title: CVE-2025-2783 in Operation ForumTroll APT

canonical_entities: Remote Code Execution via ms-msdt URI in Word/RTF documents
ms-msdt URI-based RCE in Word/RTF documents
retrieved_context.text: In late May 2022, Symantec identified multiple threat actors exploiting the MSDT Follina bug (CVE-2022-30190) through ms-msdt URI-based RCE in Word/RTF documents that load a malicious HTML via Word’s remote template feature to launch msdt.exe, sdiagnhost.exe and ultimately PowerShell—bypassing the need for macros—to install a digitally signed AsyncRAT remote access Trojan that performs anti-analysis checks, collects hardware IDs, user names, execution paths and OS details, and maintains C&C communications, alongside parallel deployments of a browser infostealer targeting cookies and saved credentials in Firefox, Chrome and Edge. Symantec customers should apply Microsoft’s advisories or disable the ms-msdt handler, update Symantec Endpoint definitions (File-based-Downloader-Backdoor:Async, InfoStealer) and monitor for related IOCs to thwart these rapid, damaging campaigns.
retrieved_context.title: Attackers Exploit MSDT Follina Bug to Drop RAT, Infostealer | Symantec Enterprise Blogs

retrieved_context.text: NCC Group’s CIRT has tracked Karakurt as an extortion-focused threat actor exploiting single-factor FortiGate VPNs via legitimate Active Directory credentials to achieve initial access, with an average dwell time of just over one month due to living-off-the-land techniques and lack of malware. Although the exact privilege escalation method remains unclear, Karakurt has attempted CVE-2020-1472 (Zerologon) and attained domain-admin rights, then used PsExec and RDP for lateral movement to the primary domain controller. Early in the breach they execute an encoded PowerShell DNS zone export—generating Microsoft-Windows-DNS-Server-Service Event ID 3150—and extract NTDS.dit via Volume Shadow Copy for further credential harvesting. After a brief exit, they re-enter to deploy AnyDesk for persistence, archive sensitive files with 7-Zip, and likely exfiltrate data via Rclone to cloud hosts. NCC Group recommends immediate FortiGate VPN MFA implementation, critical patching of domain controllers, and monitoring for Event ID 3150, unauthorized AnyDesk or PsExec usage, and VPN pool host authentications (e.g., DESKTOP-XXXXXX) to detect potential Karakurt intrusions.
retrieved_context.title: Detecting Karakurt – an extortion focused threat actor

hits.text: On May 6, 2021, CISA disclosed that FiveHands ransomware actors exploited a zero-day VPN vulnerability for initial access, then used SoftPerfect Network Scanner for host discovery and PsExec to deploy ServeManager.exe (the NTRUEncrypt-based FiveHands payload) alongside SombRAT RAT, leveraging publicly available tools (RouterScan, grabff, rclone, s3browser) and PowerSploit modules for credential access, persistence, token manipulation, Kerberoasting, and exfiltration; once in place, FiveHands enumerated and deleted Volume Shadow Copies via WMI (T1490, T1047), encrypted recovery folders and user data (T1486), and dropped ransom notes across directories. The campaign caused direct financial losses (ransoms, legal fees, incident response, downtime, reputational harm) and exposed third-party partners. Mitigation hinges on patching/decommissioning unused VPN servers, enforcing MFA on remote and privileged accounts, maintaining up-to-date AV/OS, implementing robust backup and recovery routines, hunting for IoCs, and reinforcing employee training against phishing and malicious attachments.
hits.title: FiveHands Ransomware Overview

hits.text: A zero-day VPN vulnerability provided initial access for a sophisticated threat actor who employed publicly available penetration‐testing and exploitation tools—SoftPerfect Network Scanner for network discovery, PsExec to deploy ServeManager.exe (the FiveHands ransomware variant using lattice-based NTRUEncrypt public key cryptography), and SombRAT for remote information theft—alongside RouterScan, grabff.exe, rclone.exe, and s3browser-9-5-3.exe to harvest credentials and exfiltrate data. Once inside, the attacker leveraged Windows Management Instrumentation (T1047) to enumerate and delete Volume Shadow Copies (Inhibit System Recovery, T1490), encrypted files (including those in recovery folders) for impact (T1486), and dropped ransom notes across directories, demanding payment to restore access. Post-encryption activities align with MITRE techniques such as Access Token Manipulation, Boot or Logon Autostart, PowerShell command and scripting interpreter, Domain Trust Discovery, Process Discovery, Screen Capture, and Kerberoasting. The combined use of FiveHands ransomware and SombRAT RAT resulted in both data theft and destruction of backup artifacts, underscoring the need for proactive patch management, network segmentation, strict credential hygiene, and rapid incident response to mitigate novel lattice-based encryption threats.

canonical_entities: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Windows Command Shell
hits.text: NCC Group’s RIFT team uncovered a sophisticated new FiveHands ransomware variant deployed by an affiliate linked to UNC2447, who gained initial access in June 2021 by exploiting a SonicWall VPN appliance—evidenced by a “command0/Commando” login from source port 4444 (Metasploit default)—then moved laterally via RDP (T1021.001) using the weak password “Remark123!” and PsExec (T1059.003). The Go-written loader (“Encryptor.exe”) accepts a 16-byte key (captured via RDP bitmap cache and brute force) to decrypt a unique C++ ransomware payload in memory, which uses RSA/AES (Mbed TLS) to encrypt files in blocks (.crypt/.crypt) while excluding system folders and leveraging Windows Restart Manager to breach locked files. This RaaS model (hijacking hardcoded TOR IDs) employs aggressive extortion tactics—spoofed caller ID calls urging prompt payment—and underscores the need for robust VPN log monitoring, RDP restrictions, enforceable command-line auditing, multi-factor authentication, and forensic examination of cloud‐sync caches to detect and mitigate similar intrusions.

To mitigate this espionage threat, organizations should ensure all Chrome instances are updated to at least 134.0.6998.177/.178, deploy robust exploit detection and prevention solutions on internet-connected devices, and maintain vigilant phishing awareness and monitoring.

hits.text: On May 6, 2021, CISA disclosed that FiveHands ransomware actors exploited a zero-day VPN vulnerability for initial access, then used SoftPerfect Network Scanner for host discovery and PsExec to deploy ServeManager.exe (the NTRUEncrypt-based FiveHands payload) alongside SombRAT RAT, leveraging publicly available tools (RouterScan, grabff, rclone, s3browser) and PowerSploit modules for credential access, persistence, token manipulation, Kerberoasting, and exfiltration; once in place, FiveHands enumerated and deleted Volume Shadow Copies via WMI (T1490, T1047), encrypted recovery folders and user data (T1486), and dropped ransom notes across directories. The campaign caused direct financial losses (ransoms, legal fees, incident response, downtime, reputational harm) and exposed third-party partners. Mitigation hinges on patching/decommissioning unused VPN servers, enforcing MFA on remote and privileged accounts, maintaining up-to-date AV/OS, implementing robust backup and recovery routines, hunting for IoCs, and reinforcing employee training against phishing and malicious attachments.
hits.title: FiveHands Ransomware Overview

hits.text: A zero-day VPN vulnerability provided initial access for a sophisticated threat actor who employed publicly available penetration‐testing and exploitation tools—SoftPerfect Network Scanner for network discovery, PsExec to deploy ServeManager.exe (the FiveHands ransomware variant using lattice-based NTRUEncrypt public key cryptography), and SombRAT for remote information theft—alongside RouterScan, grabff.exe, rclone.exe, and s3browser-9-5-3.exe to harvest credentials and exfiltrate data. Once inside, the attacker leveraged Windows Management Instrumentation (T1047) to enumerate and delete Volume Shadow Copies (Inhibit System Recovery, T1490), encrypted files (including those in recovery folders) for impact (T1486), and dropped ransom notes across directories, demanding payment to restore access. Post-encryption activities align with MITRE techniques such as Access Token Manipulation, Boot or Logon Autostart, PowerShell command and scripting interpreter, Domain Trust Discovery, Process Discovery, Screen Capture, and Kerberoasting. The combined use of FiveHands ransomware and SombRAT RAT resulted in both data theft and destruction of backup artifacts, underscoring the need for proactive patch management, network segmentation, strict credential hygiene, and rapid incident response to mitigate novel lattice-based encryption threats.

canonical_entities: installing Sagerunex variants in the Windows Registry
hits.text: The Lotus Blossom APT (aka Lotus Panda, Billbug, Spring Dragon) has stepped up cyberespionage against APAC government targets by deploying new Sagerunex backdoor variants and abusing Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) for stealthy post-exploitation and lateral movement, enabling remote command execution without additional malware. Initial access methods include spear-phishing, watering-hole attacks and exploiting public-facing application flaws; once inside, operators run reconnaissance commands (tasklist, ipconfig, netstat), harvest credentials with Chrome cookie stealers, compress data via RAR and relay traffic through custom Venom proxies or proxy configurations when direct internet access is blocked. Persistence is achieved by installing Sagerunex variants in the Windows Registry under hijacked service names (tapisrv, swprv) to auto-launch at startup, while command-and-control blends encrypted traffic into legitimate platforms—stolen data uploaded as .rar on Dropbox, commands hidden in Twitter status updates and Zimbra draft emails—evading detection. Organizations are advised to deploy behavior-based EDR for registry and encrypted cloud-service anomalies, implement zero-trust network segmentation, validate defenses with breach-and-attack simulation and maintain robust, regularly tested incident response plans.
hits.title: Lotus Blossom APT Exploits WMI for Post-Exploitation Activities

canonical_entities: Bypass authentication by sending empty or invalid USERNAME and PASSWORD parameters with requirePasswordChange=Y
hits.text: A critical zero-day flaw (CVE-2023-51467) has been identified in Apache OfBiz’s login functionality—stemming from an incomplete patch for a prior high-severity RCE vulnerability (CVE-2023-49070, CVSS 9.8) tied to a deprecated XML-RPC component—that allows attackers to bypass authentication by sending empty or invalid USERNAME and PASSWORD parameters alongside “requirePasswordChange=Y,” effectively granting unauthorized access and enabling simple SSRF attacks against internal resources; discovered by SonicWall Capture Labs, the bug follows observations by The Shadowserver Foundation of active exploitation attempts against CVE-2023-49070, and SonicWall reports exploit traffic for CVE-2023-51467 spiking from 235 attempts on December 27, 2023, to 26,928 on December 29 and 3,129 on January 1, 2024, underscoring urgent need for organizations using OfBiz versions prior to 18.12.11 to upgrade immediately to mitigate further data exfiltration and system takeover risks.

hits.text: NCC Group’s CIRT has tracked Karakurt as an extortion-focused threat actor exploiting single-factor FortiGate VPNs via legitimate Active Directory credentials to achieve initial access, with an average dwell time of just over one month due to living-off-the-land techniques and lack of malware. Although the exact privilege escalation method remains unclear, Karakurt has attempted CVE-2020-1472 (Zerologon) and attained domain-admin rights, then used PsExec and RDP for lateral movement to the primary domain controller. Early in the breach they execute an encoded PowerShell DNS zone export—generating Microsoft-Windows-DNS-Server-Service Event ID 3150—and extract NTDS.dit via Volume Shadow Copy for further credential harvesting. After a brief exit, they re-enter to deploy AnyDesk for persistence, archive sensitive files with 7-Zip, and likely exfiltrate data via Rclone to cloud hosts. NCC Group recommends immediate FortiGate VPN MFA implementation, critical patching of domain controllers, and monitoring for Event ID 3150, unauthorized AnyDesk or PsExec usage, and VPN pool host authentications (e.g., DESKTOP-XXXXXX) to detect potential Karakurt intrusions.
hits.title: Detecting Karakurt – an extortion focused threat actor

hits.text: On Oct. 27 the Apache Software Foundation disclosed CVE-2023-46604, a critical (CVSS 10.0) insecure-deserialization flaw in Apache ActiveMQ (all versions prior to 5.18.3 and Legacy OpenWire Module before 5.17.6) that enables unauthenticated remote code execution, and by Nov. 2 threat actors had begun exploiting publicly available proof-of-concept code to drop HelloKitty ransomware on at least two Rapid7 customer networks; ShadowServer data show some 3,329 internet-exposed brokers remain unpatched, making small and midsize organizations running outdated ActiveMQ instances prime targets, and the attackers—characterized by Rapid7 as “clumsy” due to repeated failed encryption attempts—have employed rudimentary double-extortion tactics, prompting ASF to release patched versions and urgent recommendations to upgrade immediately to mitigate widespread ransomware impact.
hits.title: Attackers Target Max-Severity Apache ActiveMQ Bug to Drop Ransomware

hits.text: Proofpoint researchers led by Sherrod DeGrippo have uncovered state-sponsored actors exploiting CVE-2022-30190 (Follina), a Microsoft Office remote code execution flaw in the Windows Support Diagnostic Tool (MSDT) invoked via URL protocol, in phishing campaigns since mid-April targeting U.S. and E.U. government workers; following Shadow Chaser Group’s April 12 discovery and Microsoft’s May patch, adversaries dispatched over 1,000 recruitment-themed emails promising a “20% increase” and urging recipients to open a Word attachment that launches a PowerShell script to detect virtualized environments, perform extensive reconnaissance across browsers, mail clients and file shares, zip collected data for exfiltration, and enable arbitrary code execution with user-level privileges to install malware, manipulate or delete data, and create accounts—activities indicative of a state-aligned nexus that underscore the urgency of rapid patch deployment, user training and network-level MSDT exploit mitigations.
hits.title: Follina Exploited by State-Sponsored Hackers | Threatpost

hits.text: Fortra has disclosed CVE-2024-0204, a critical (CVSS 9.8) authentication-bypass flaw in GoAnywhere MFT versions 6.0.1–7.4.0 that enables remote attackers to create arbitrary admin users via the web administration portal, potentially leading to full device takeover, data theft, malware deployment, and lateral movement; discovered December 1, 2023 by Mohammed Eldeeb and Islam Elrfai of Spark Engineering Consultants, it was patched in GoAnywhere MFT 7.4.1 on December 7 2023, and users unable to upgrade immediately can mitigate by deleting or emptying the InitialAccountSetup.xhtml file and restarting services. Although no in-the-wild exploitation has been observed, the publication of mitigations may spur PoC releases. This advisory follows January–February 2023 Clop ransomware attacks leveraging the unpatched CVE-2023-0669 remote-code-execution flaw to breach 130 organizations—including Crown Resorts, CHS, Hatch Bank, Rubrik, City of Toronto, Hitachi Energy, Procter & Gamble, and Saks Fifth Avenue—underscoring the critical need for timely patching and monitoring of MFT environments.
hits.title: Fortra warns of new critical GoAnywhere MFT auth bypass, patch now

canonical_entities: Defense evasion via virtual machine execution
deployment of a VirtualBox VM running Windows XP to execute encryption, thereby evading host defenses
hits.text: Ragnar Locker, active since December 2019 and first flagged by the FBI in April 2020, is a hybrid ransomware strain and operator gang responsible for breaching 52 organizations across 10 critical infrastructure sectors—including energy, manufacturing, financial services, government, IT and agriculture—employing double-extortion by exfiltrating sensitive data before encryption and threatening public leaks if ransoms go unpaid. Intrusions begin with RDP access via brute-force or stolen credentials, privilege escalation through CVE-2017-0213, and deployment of a VirtualBox VM running Windows XP to execute encryption, thereby evading host defenses; they delete shadow copies, disable antivirus (e.g., Sophos, Veeam) and remote management tools (Kaseya, ConnectWise), and spread laterally via PowerShell. Obfuscation is achieved through junk code, encrypted PE-embedded configs (".keys"), runtime string decryption, locale checks to avoid CIS targets and a custom Salsa20 cipher with a bespoke 64-byte key matrix appending “_RAGNAR_” to footers. Major attacks include Campari Group (2 TB, $15 M), Energias de Portugal (10 TB, 1 580 BTC), Capcom (1 TB) and Dassault Falcon Jet, with the FBI warning of heightened risks to food/agriculture during planting/harvest. Ragnar Locker pressures victims to avoid law enforcement, yet paying ransoms funds criminality and fails to guarantee data deletion; mitigation requires hardened RDP/MFA, patching CVE-2017-0213, network segmentation, behavioral EDR, offline backups and timely incident reporting to the FBI.
hits.title: Ragnar Locker Ransomware (Everything You Need To Know)

hits.text: In late August 2021, TAG uncovered a sophisticated, state-backed watering-hole campaign targeting Hong Kong media and pro-democracy sites that leveraged dual iframes to deliver encrypted iOS exploits (partial chain using CVE-2019-8506 in Safari) and a full macOS exploit chain against Catalina (10.15), combining an n-day WebKit RCE (CVE-2021-1789) with a 0-day XNU local privilege escalation (CVE-2021-30869) to load a patched, embedded Mach-O via Capstone.js, escape the Safari sandbox, elevate to root through a port-type confusion variant of CVE-2020-27932, and deploy a highly modular “MACMA” backdoor over DDS for fingerprinting, file transfer, keylogging, screen/audio capture and remote command execution; with rid counters in the 200s confirming scale, researchers disclosed IOCs (e.g. 103[.]255[.]44[.]56, appleid-server[.]com) to enable blocking and urged immediate application of Apple’s Jan 5 and Sept 23 patches.

hits.text: On March 2, 2025, CyberMaterial’s report on Void Manticore (aka Storm-0842, linked to the cybercriminal Storm-1811 cluster) details a coordinated espionage campaign that began in late 2024 against aerospace, defense and government organizations in Europe and North America: operators initiated intrusions via spear-phishing emails embedding weaponized RTFs exploiting CVE-2024-4113 to drop a custom loader (“VoidLoader”), which in turn deployed the “ManticoreShell” backdoor; post-compromise activities included credential harvesting (Mimikatz), lateral movement via PSExec and WMI, privilege escalation through a signed kernel-mode driver exploit, and persistence using registry Run keys and scheduled tasks; C2 communications leveraged HTTPS with a domain generation algorithm (DGA) and fallback to TOR. Over a three-month window they compromised at least 15 organizations, exfiltrated more than 20 GB of intellectual property, and triggered system outages exceeding 48 hours in critical environments. Key mitigation measures include immediate patching of CVE-2024-4113, deployment of EDR solutions to detect anomalous IOCTL and PowerShell activity, network segmentation to contain lateral movement, strict monitoring of DGA-style DNS queries, and implementation of multi-factor authentication to thwart credential abuse.
hits.title: Void Manticore (Storm-0842) – Threat Actor - CyberMaterial

hits.text: Microsoft has identified a China-based nation-state threat actor tracked as Flax Typhoon (aka Ethereal Panda) conducting espionage against dozens of Taiwanese organizations since mid-2021 by exploiting known vulnerabilities in public-facing VPN, web, Java and SQL servers to deploy the China Chopper web shell, escalate privileges with Juicy Potato and BadPotato, and establish persistence by disabling RDP network-level authentication, hijacking the Sticky Keys binary to launch Task Manager as SYSTEM, and installing a renamed SoftEther VPN bridge over HTTPS on port 443 for stealthy command-and-control. Once inside, the actor leverages WinRM and WMIC for lateral movement and deploys Mimikatz to dump LSASS and SAM for pass-the-hash attacks, yet conducts minimal post-persistence activity, suggesting long-term credential harvesting rather than immediate data exfiltration. To mitigate, organizations must enforce rigorous patch management, monitor registry changes and RDP configurations, deploy file integrity and behavioral monitoring on public-facing servers, isolate and forensically examine compromised systems, and rotate or disable exposed credentials.
hits.title: Flax Typhoon using legitimate software to quietly access Taiwanese organizations | Microsoft Security Blog

canonical_entities: ZIP files masquerading as legitimate updates
hits.text: Unit 42 has observed a sharp rise in post-intrusion WastedLocker ransomware attacks by the Evil Corp group—already known for Dridex—against large U.S. organizations in sectors from manufacturing to legal services, with initial compromise typically via ZIP files masquerading as legitimate updates that deploy a SocGholish JavaScript loader to profile systems and invoke PowerShell-based Cobalt Strike payloads; attackers then leverage WMI and PsExec for lateral movement, identify high-value and backup systems, elevate privileges, disable Windows Defender, delete shadow copies, install WastedLocker as a service, and encrypt files using a “.<victim_name>wasted” extension while appending ransom notes (“.<victim_name>wasted_info”) with contact addresses on ProtonMail, Airmail and others. Palo Alto Networks’ WildFire, Cortex XDR (anti-ransomware and behavioral threat protection), NGFW DNS signatures and AutoFocus tagging detect and prevent WastedLocker activity; organizations are urged to implement robust, off-site backup strategies and hardened cybersecurity controls to mitigate this high-impact targeted ransomware threat.
hits.title: Threat Assessment: WastedLocker Ransomware

hits.text: Microsoft has traced a stealthy espionage campaign by Flax Typhoon (aka Ethereal Panda), a China-based nation-state actor active since mid-2021, targeting dozens of Taiwanese organizations (with spill-over in Southeast Asia, North America, and Africa) by exploiting known vulnerabilities in public-facing VPN, web, Java, and SQL services to deploy the China Chopper web shell for initial access; the group escalates privileges via open-source exploits like Juicy Potato and BadPotato, then establishes persistence by disabling RDP network-level authentication, hijacking the Sticky Keys (sethc.exe) binary to launch Task Manager as SYSTEM, and installing a renamed SoftEther VPN-over-HTTPS bridge (conhost.exe/dllhost.exe) as a service to maintain covert C2 over port 443; leveraging LOLBins such as PowerShell Invoke-WebRequest, certutil, bitsadmin, WinRM, and WMIC for lateral movement, vulnerability scanning, and remote execution, it harvests credentials from LSASS memory and the SAM registry hive using Mimikatz for pass-the-hash attacks; although no exfiltration or final objectives have been observed, organizations are urged to enforce rigorous patch and vulnerability management on internet-exposed systems, monitor registry and file-integrity changes, deploy web application firewalls, reset compromised credentials, isolate and forensically examine affected hosts, and leverage detections in Microsoft 365 Defender to disrupt living-off-the-land tactics.
hits.title: Flax Typhoon using legitimate software to quietly access Taiwanese organizations | Microsoft Security Blog

canonical_entities: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Windows Command Shell
hits.text: NCC Group’s RIFT team uncovered a sophisticated new FiveHands ransomware variant deployed by an affiliate linked to UNC2447, who gained initial access in June 2021 by exploiting a SonicWall VPN appliance—evidenced by a “command0/Commando” login from source port 4444 (Metasploit default)—then moved laterally via RDP (T1021.001) using the weak password “Remark123!” and PsExec (T1059.003). The actor leveraged publicly available tools—SoftPerfect Netscan and Advanced Port Scanner for network discovery (T1046), AllInOnePasswordRecoveryPro for credential harvesting (T1003.001), Remote Utilities (“Hostclean.exe”) for persistent C2 (T1219), and pCloud (“pCloud.exe”) for exfiltration (T1567.002), caching 10 GB of stolen data under %AppData%\pCloud\CacheCached—to stage and extract sensitive files. The Go-written loader (“Encryptor.exe”) accepts a 16-byte key (captured via RDP bitmap cache and brute force) to decrypt a unique C++ ransomware payload in memory, which uses RSA/AES (Mbed TLS) to encrypt files in blocks (.crypt/.crypt) while excluding system folders and leveraging Windows Restart Manager to breach locked files. This RaaS model (hijacking hardcoded TOR IDs) employs aggressive extortion tactics—spoofed caller ID calls urging prompt payment—and underscores the need for robust VPN log monitoring, RDP restrictions, enforceable command-line auditing, multi-factor authentication, and forensic examination of cloud‐sync caches to detect and mitigate similar intrusions.
hits.title: Handy guide to a new Fivehands ransomware variant

hits.text: Microsoft Threat Intelligence Center has attributed the emerging H0lyGh0st ransomware, active since June 2021 and tracked as DEV-0530, to financially motivated North Korean state-sponsored actors with ties to PLUTONIUM (DarkSeoul/Andariel), which has compromised small-to-mid-sized businesses—including manufacturers, banks, schools and event planners—across multiple countries since September 2021 by deploying custom SiennaPurple (C++ BTLC_C.exe) and SiennaBlue (Go-based HolyRS.exe, HolyLock.exe, BLTC.exe) families that encrypt Windows files with a .h0lyenc extension, use string obfuscation and public-key management, and enforce persistence via a scheduled task called “lockertask”; victims receive a ransom note delivered over a .onion portal demanding Bitcoin payment under double-extortion threats to publish stolen data if unpaid; between October 2021 and May 2022 MSTIC observed iterative Go-based SiennaBlue variants sharing core encryption and network/intranet connectivity functions, and in April 2022 the group rolled out its latest BTLC.exe, which hard-codes ServerBaseURL fallback credentials for network shares, uploads victim public keys to a C2 server, and encrypts all drive files—underscoring the need for defenders to monitor anomalous scheduled tasks, default-credential share connections, .onion traffic, and the appearance of .h0lyenc files to detect and disrupt this evolving threat.
hits.title: Emerging H0lyGh0st Ransomware Tied to North Korea | Threatpost

hits.text: A zero-day VPN vulnerability provided initial access for a sophisticated threat actor who employed publicly available penetration‐testing and exploitation tools—SoftPerfect Network Scanner for network discovery, PsExec to deploy ServeManager.exe (the FiveHands ransomware variant using lattice-based NTRUEncrypt public key cryptography), and SombRAT for remote information theft—alongside RouterScan, grabff.exe, rclone.exe, and s3browser-9-5-3.exe to harvest credentials and exfiltrate data. Once inside, the attacker leveraged Windows Management Instrumentation (T1047) to enumerate and delete Volume Shadow Copies (Inhibit System Recovery, T1490), encrypted files (including those in recovery folders) for impact (T1486), and dropped ransom notes across directories, demanding payment to restore access. Post-encryption activities align with MITRE techniques such as Access Token Manipulation, Boot or Logon Autostart, PowerShell command and scripting interpreter, Domain Trust Discovery, Process Discovery, Screen Capture, and Kerberoasting. The combined use of FiveHands ransomware and SombRAT RAT resulted in both data theft and destruction of backup artifacts, underscoring the need for proactive patch management, network segmentation, strict credential hygiene, and rapid incident response to mitigate novel lattice-based encryption threats.
hits.title: FiveHands Ransomware Overview

hits.text: Researchers at Mandiant Intelligence have identified UNC2165—the latest evolution of the U.S.-sanctioned Evil Corp—as leveraging the FakeUpdates infection chain to gain initial access, followed by deployment of LockBit ransomware to obscure attribution and monetize extortion efforts. After OFAC sanctions in December 2019 crippled Evil Corp’s ability to profit from Dridex and its WastedLocker strain, the group briefly resurfaced under PayloadBin (likely a WastedLocker rebrand) and used HTML redirectors in malicious Excel files, then adopted Hades ransomware with code overlaps to distance itself further. By aligning with LockBit’s RaaS model—already proven effective against high-profile victims such as Accenture and Bangkok Air—UNC2165 can blend in with legitimate affiliates, reduce development overhead, and bypass sanctions enforcement that deters U.S. entities from negotiating ransoms with known Evil Corp actors. This shift underscores the need for defenders to monitor FakeUpdates chains and LockBit activity for potential Evil Corp–linked intrusions and to enhance detection of rebranded ransomware variants despite attribution obfuscation tactics.
hits.title: Evil Corp Pivots LockBit to Dodge U.S. Sanctions | Threatpost

hits.text: Since mid-2021, Microsoft has tracked Volt Typhoon, a China-linked state-sponsored actor, conducting stealthy living-off-the-land campaigns against U.S. critical infrastructure—spanning communications, utilities, transportation, manufacturing, government and education—aimed at post-compromise credential access, network discovery and long-term espionage with an eye toward potential disruption of Asia-U.S. communications in future crises. Initial access is achieved via internet-exposed Fortinet FortiGuard devices, whose AD credentials are harvested to move laterally; all traffic is proxied through compromised SOHO routers, firewalls and VPN hardware (ASUS, Cisco, D-Link, NETGEAR, Zyxel) to blend with legitimate activity. Post-compromise hands-on-keyboard operations rely almost exclusively on LOLBins and valid credentials to dump LSASS memory and use Ntdsutil.exe to create domain controller installation media for offline hash cracking, enumerate systems via PowerShell, WMIC and ping, collect browser and system data into staged archives, then exfiltrate via password-protected files. In rare cases, Volt Typhoon deploys custom Impacket or FRP-based C2 over portproxy, observable as unusual successful sign-ins and command-line activity from anomalous IPs. Detection is challenging due to use of built-in binaries and normal sign-in channels; Microsoft 365 Defender and cloud-delivered Microsoft Defender Antivirus yield behavioral alerts (e.g., SuspPowershellExec, SuspNtdsUtilUsage), while Defender for Endpoint flags suspicious LSASS dumps, wmic.exe executions and domain-controller media creation. Mitigation hinges on closing or rotating compromised accounts, enforcing strong MFA or passwordless authentication, disabling internet-facing device management interfaces, enabling LSASS Protective Process Light and Credential Guard on Windows 11, applying attack surface reduction rules to block LSASS and PSExec/WMI abuse, and running EDR in block mode to thwart post-compromise artifacts.
hits.title: Volt Typhoon targets US critical infrastructure with living-off-the-land techniques | Microsoft Security Blog

hits.text: The Lotus Blossom APT (aka Lotus Panda, Billbug, Spring Dragon) has stepped up cyberespionage against APAC government targets by deploying new Sagerunex backdoor variants and abusing Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) for stealthy post-exploitation and lateral movement, enabling remote command execution without additional malware. Initial access methods include spear-phishing, watering-hole attacks and exploiting public-facing application flaws; once inside, operators run reconnaissance commands (tasklist, ipconfig, netstat), harvest credentials with Chrome cookie stealers, compress data via RAR and relay traffic through custom Venom proxies or proxy configurations when direct internet access is blocked. Persistence is achieved by installing Sagerunex variants in the Windows Registry under hijacked service names (tapisrv, swprv) to auto-launch at startup, while command-and-control blends encrypted traffic into legitimate platforms—stolen data uploaded as .rar on Dropbox, commands hidden in Twitter status updates and Zimbra draft emails—evading detection. Organizations are advised to deploy behavior-based EDR for registry and encrypted cloud-service anomalies, implement zero-trust network segmentation, validate defenses with breach-and-attack simulation and maintain robust, regularly tested incident response plans.
hits.title: Lotus Blossom APT Exploits WMI for Post-Exploitation Activities

retrieved_context.text: On March 2, 2025, CyberMaterial’s report on Void Manticore (aka Storm-0842, linked to the cybercriminal Storm-1811 cluster) details a coordinated espionage campaign that began in late 2024 against aerospace, defense and government organizations in Europe and North America: operators initiated intrusions via spear-phishing emails embedding weaponized RTFs exploiting CVE-2024-4113 to drop a custom loader (“VoidLoader”), which in turn deployed the “ManticoreShell” backdoor; post-compromise activities included credential harvesting (Mimikatz), lateral movement via PSExec and WMI, privilege escalation through a signed kernel-mode driver exploit, and persistence using registry Run keys and scheduled tasks; C2 communications leveraged HTTPS with a domain generation algorithm (DGA) and fallback to TOR. Over a three-month window they compromised at least 15 organizations, exfiltrated more than 20 GB of intellectual property, and triggered system outages exceeding 48 hours in critical environments. Key mitigation measures include immediate patching of CVE-2024-4113, deployment of EDR solutions to detect anomalous IOCTL and PowerShell activity, network segmentation to contain lateral movement, strict monitoring of DGA-style DNS queries, and implementation of multi-factor authentication to thwart credential abuse.

retrieved_context.text: Microsoft has identified a China-based nation-state threat actor tracked as Flax Typhoon (aka Ethereal Panda) conducting espionage against dozens of Taiwanese organizations since mid-2021 by exploiting known vulnerabilities in public-facing VPN, web, Java and SQL servers to deploy the China Chopper web shell, escalate privileges with Juicy Potato and BadPotato, and establish persistence by disabling RDP network-level authentication, hijacking the Sticky Keys binary to launch Task Manager as SYSTEM, and installing a renamed SoftEther VPN bridge over HTTPS on port 443 for stealthy command-and-control. Once inside, the actor leverages WinRM and WMIC for lateral movement and deploys Mimikatz to dump LSASS and SAM for pass-the-hash attacks, yet conducts minimal post-persistence activity, suggesting long-term credential harvesting rather than immediate data exfiltration. To mitigate, organizations must enforce rigorous patch management, monitor registry changes and RDP configurations, deploy file integrity and behavioral monitoring on public-facing servers, isolate and forensically examine compromised systems, and rotate or disable exposed credentials.

retrieved_context.text: Unit 42 has observed a sharp rise in post-intrusion WastedLocker ransomware attacks by the Evil Corp group—already known for Dridex—against large U.S. organizations in sectors from manufacturing to legal services, with initial compromise typically via ZIP files masquerading as legitimate updates that deploy a SocGholish JavaScript loader to profile systems and invoke PowerShell-based Cobalt Strike payloads; attackers then leverage WMI and PsExec for lateral movement, identify high-value and backup systems, elevate privileges, disable Windows Defender, delete shadow copies, install WastedLocker as a service, and encrypt files using a “.<victim_name>wasted” extension while appending ransom notes (“.<victim_name>wasted_info”) with contact addresses on ProtonMail, Airmail and others. retrieved_context.text: NCC Group’s RIFT team uncovered a sophisticated new FiveHands ransomware variant deployed by an affiliate linked to UNC2447, who gained initial access in June 2021 by exploiting a SonicWall VPN appliance—evidenced by a “command0/Commando” login from source port 4444 (Metasploit default)—then moved laterally via RDP (T1021.001) using the weak password “Remark123!” and PsExec (T1059.003). The actor leveraged publicly available tools—SoftPerfect Netscan and Advanced Port Scanner for network discovery (T1046), AllInOnePasswordRecoveryPro for credential harvesting (T1003.001), Remote Utilities (“Hostclean.exe”) for persistent C2 (T1219), and pCloud (“pCloud.exe”) for exfiltration (T1567.002), caching 10 GB of stolen data under %AppData%\pCloud\CacheCached—to stage and extract sensitive files. The Go-written loader (“Encryptor.exe”) accepts a 16-byte key (captured via RDP bitmap cache and brute force) to decrypt a unique C++ ransomware payload in memory, which uses RSA/AES (Mbed TLS) to encrypt files in blocks (.crypt/.crypt) while excluding system folders and leveraging Windows Restart Manager to breach locked files. This RaaS model (hijacking hardcoded TOR IDs) employs aggressive extortion tactics—spoofed caller ID calls urging prompt payment—and underscores the need for robust VPN log monitoring, RDP restrictions, enforceable command-line auditing, multi-factor authentication, and forensic examination of cloud‐sync caches to detect and mitigate similar intrusions.

canonical_entities: creates a scheduled task for persistence
hits.text: On Aug. 17, 2023, the Zero Day Initiative publicly reported an RCE vulnerability in WinRAR (CVE-2023-40477) originally disclosed to the vendor on June 8; just four days later, an actor using the alias whalersplonk published a fake PoC on GitHub that repurposed a GeoServer CVE-2023-25157 exploit script to launch an infection chain rather than trigger the WinRAR flaw. Analysis of poc.py shows it writes a batch file to %TEMP%, executes an encoded PowerShell script that downloads c.ps1 and, subsequently, a VenomRAT v6.0.3 payload named Windows.Gaming.Preview.exe from checkblacklistwords[.]eu, installs it under %APPDATA%\Drivers, creates a scheduled task for persistence, enables keylogging to %APPDATA%\MyData\DataLogs_keylog_offline.txt, and contacts C2 at 94.156.253.109:4449. This RAT supports HVNC, stealer, grabber and commands such as plu_gin, HVNCStop, loadofflinelog, keylogsetting, filterinfo, and Po_ng. The malicious domain was registered at least 10 days before the CVE’s disclosure, indicating pre-positioned infrastructure aimed at opportunistically compromising researchers or other miscreants, not end users directly. Although the fake PoC repo was removed by the time of analysis, Palo Alto Networks WildFire and Advanced URL Filtering had already auto-categorized the domain as malicious and blocked the chain. Unit 42 researchers, alongside CTA partner Broadcom/Symantec, have published full IoCs and SHA lists on GitHub to support proactive defenses across WinRAR’s 500 million-strong user base.
hits.title: Fake CVE-2023-40477 Proof of Concept Leads to VenomRAT

canonical_entities: enumerates SSH directories to harvest credentials
Persistence is achieved through multiple cronjobs
hits.text: Aqua Security’s Nautilus team has uncovered Hadooken, a new Linux malware targeting Oracle WebLogic servers via weak passwords. Post-compromise, attackers deploy redundant shell and Python scripts to ensure download and execution of Hadooken, which enumerates SSH directories to harvest credentials, moves laterally, and clears logs. Hadooken then drops a three-path cryptominer and a Tsunami backdoor with a randomized name, the latter reserved for potential later-stage attacks. Persistence is achieved through multiple cronjobs under varied names and frequencies stored across cron directories. The malware is hosted on two IPs—one German address linked to TeamTNT and Gang 8220, the other inactive in Russia—where researchers also identified a Mallox ransomware PowerShell loader targeting Windows. Static analysis links Hadooken to Rhombus and NoEscape families. With over 230,000 internet-connected WebLogic instances—hundreds of which expose vulnerable admin consoles—this campaign underscores the dual risk of cryptojacking and ransomware across Linux and Windows environments.
hits.title: New 'Hadooken' Linux Malware Targets WebLogic Servers - SecurityWeek

canonical_entities: spear-phishing attacks against European embassies in Seoul (March–July 2025)
exfiltrated ... over HTTPS to the attackers’ private GitHub repo via the Contents API
hits.text: Between March and July 2025, DPRK-linked Kimsuky operators executed at least 19 highly tailored spear-phishing attacks against Western, Central, Eastern and Southern European embassies in Seoul, spoofing real diplomats and embedding password-protected ZIPs delivered via Dropbox, Daum or Google Drive. Victims unwittingly launched malicious .LNK shortcuts that triggered obfuscated PowerShell scripts to decode and in-memory execute a Confuser-Core-obfuscated XenoRAT (MoonPeak) payload—identified by GUID 12DE1212-167D-45BA-1284-780DA98CF901 and mutex “Dansweit_Hk65-PSAccerdle”—leveraging scheduled tasks for persistence. Reconnaissance data (OS build, IP, process list) was exfiltrated as base64-encoded text files over HTTPS to the attackers’ private GitHub repo via the Contents API, while C2 instructions (e.g., onf.txt) directed dynamic payload rotations hosted on Dropbox with rapid header-fix GZIP routines. This ongoing campaign provided full system control—including keystroke logging, screenshots and remote shells—and underscores the need to monitor abnormal GitHub API usage, cloud-based archive downloads and anomalous PowerShell invocations.

After OFAC sanctions in December 2019 crippled Evil Corp’s ability to profit from Dridex and its WastedLocker strain, the group briefly resurfaced under PayloadBin (likely a WastedLocker rebrand) and used HTML redirectors in malicious Excel files, then adopted Hades ransomware with code overlaps to distance itself further. By aligning with LockBit’s RaaS model—already proven effective against high-profile victims such as Accenture and Bangkok Air—UNC2165 can blend in with legitimate affiliates, reduce development overhead, and bypass sanctions enforcement that deters U.S. entities from negotiating ransoms with known Evil Corp actors. This shift underscores the need for defenders to monitor FakeUpdates chains and LockBit activity for potential Evil Corp–linked intrusions and to enhance detection of rebranded ransomware variants despite attribution obfuscation tactics.
hits.title: Evil Corp Pivots LockBit to Dodge U.S. Sanctions | Threatpost

hits.text: Moses Staff, an Iran-linked APT active since September 2021, has conducted politically motivated sabotage campaigns—initially against Israeli organizations and later targets in India, Germany, the U.S., Italy, Chile, Turkey and the UAE—by exploiting known public-facing server vulnerabilities (e.g., Microsoft Exchange), moving laterally with PsExec, WMIC and PowerShell, and deploying a two-stage destructive toolkit: a Python-based loader (PyDCrypt) that installs a custom DiskCryptor variant (DCSrv) to encrypt files and disrupt operations without ransom demands, and, as newly documented by Cybereason, the StrifeWater RAT masquerading as calc.exe to establish early footholds, harvest system metadata (machine name, OS version, CPU architecture, user privileges, time zone), execute commands, capture screens, maintain persistence via scheduled tasks, and download auxiliary modules before self-removal—all while communicating with hard-coded C2 IPs, URLs and domain names—to evade detection; organizations should urgently patch exposed servers, monitor anomalous calc.exe and scheduled-task activity, and enhance EDR rules to detect PyDCrypt, DCSrv and StrifeWater behaviors to thwart data exfiltration and infrastructure damage.

retrieved_context.text: On March 2, 2025, CyberMaterial’s report on Void Manticore (aka Storm-0842, linked to the cybercriminal Storm-1811 cluster) details a coordinated espionage campaign that began in late 2024 against aerospace, defense and government organizations in Europe and North America: operators initiated intrusions via spear-phishing emails embedding weaponized RTFs exploiting CVE-2024-4113 to drop a custom loader (“VoidLoader”), which in turn deployed the “ManticoreShell” backdoor; post-compromise activities included credential harvesting (Mimikatz), lateral movement via PSExec and WMI, privilege escalation through a signed kernel-mode driver exploit, and persistence using registry Run keys and scheduled tasks; C2 communications leveraged HTTPS with a domain generation algorithm (DGA) and fallback to TOR. Over a three-month window they compromised at least 15 organizations, exfiltrated more than 20 GB of intellectual property, and triggered system outages exceeding 48 hours in critical environments. Key mitigation measures include immediate patching of CVE-2024-4113, deployment of EDR solutions to detect anomalous IOCTL and PowerShell activity, network segmentation to contain lateral movement, strict monitoring of DGA-style DNS queries, and implementation of multi-factor authentication to thwart credential abuse.
retrieved_context.title: Void Manticore (Storm-0842) – Threat Actor - CyberMaterial

retrieved_context.text: Microsoft has identified a China-based nation-state threat actor tracked as Flax Typhoon (aka Ethereal Panda) conducting espionage against dozens of Taiwanese organizations since mid-2021 by exploiting known vulnerabilities in public-facing VPN, web, Java and SQL servers to deploy the China Chopper web shell, escalate privileges with Juicy Potato and BadPotato, and establish persistence by disabling RDP network-level authentication, hijacking the Sticky Keys binary to launch Task Manager as SYSTEM, and installing a renamed SoftEther VPN bridge over HTTPS on port 443 for stealthy command-and-control. Once inside, the actor leverages WinRM and WMIC for lateral movement and deploys Mimikatz to dump LSASS and SAM for pass-the-hash attacks, yet conducts minimal post-persistence activity, suggesting long-term credential harvesting rather than immediate data exfiltration. To mitigate, organizations must enforce rigorous patch management, monitor registry changes and RDP configurations, deploy file integrity and behavioral monitoring on public-facing servers, isolate and forensically examine compromised systems, and rotate or disable exposed credentials.
retrieved_context.title: Flax Typhoon using legitimate software to quietly access Taiwanese organizations | Microsoft Security Blog

retrieved_context.text: Unit 42 has observed a sharp rise in post-intrusion WastedLocker ransomware attacks by the Evil Corp group—already known for Dridex—against large U.S. organizations in sectors from manufacturing to legal services, with initial compromise typically via ZIP files masquerading as legitimate updates that deploy a SocGholish JavaScript loader to profile systems and invoke PowerShell-based Cobalt Strike payloads; attackers then leverage WMI and PsExec for lateral movement, identify high-value and backup systems, elevate privileges, disable Windows Defender, delete shadow copies, install WastedLocker as a service, and encrypt files using a “.<victim_name>wasted” extension while appending ransom notes (“.<victim_name>wasted_info”) with contact addresses on ProtonMail, Airmail and others. Palo Alto Networks’ WildFire, Cortex XDR (anti-ransomware and behavioral threat protection), NGFW DNS signatures and AutoFocus tagging detect and prevent WastedLocker activity; organizations are urged to implement robust, off-site backup strategies and hardened cybersecurity controls to mitigate this high-impact targeted ransomware threat.

retrieved_context.text: Microsoft Threat Intelligence Center has attributed the emerging H0lyGh0st ransomware, active since June 2021 and tracked as DEV-0530, to financially motivated North Korean state-sponsored actors with ties to PLUTONIUM (DarkSeoul/Andariel), which has compromised small-to-mid-sized businesses—including manufacturers, banks, schools and event planners—across multiple countries since September 2021 by deploying custom SiennaPurple (C++ BTLC_C.exe) and SiennaBlue (Go-based HolyRS.exe, HolyLock.exe, BLTC.exe) families that encrypt Windows files with a .h0lyenc extension, use string obfuscation and public-key management, and enforce persistence via a scheduled task called “lockertask”; victims receive a ransom note delivered over a .onion portal demanding Bitcoin payment under double-extortion threats to publish stolen data if unpaid; between October 2021 and May 2022 MSTIC observed iterative Go-based SiennaBlue variants sharing core encryption and network/intranet connectivity functions, and in April 2022 the group rolled out its latest BTLC.exe, which hard-codes ServerBaseURL fallback credentials for network shares, uploads victim public keys to a C2 server, and encrypts all drive files—underscoring the need for defenders to monitor anomalous scheduled tasks, default-credential share connections, .onion traffic, and the appearance of .h0lyenc files to detect and disrupt this evolving threat.
retrieved_context.title: Emerging H0lyGh0st Ransomware Tied to North Korea | Threatpost

canonical_entities: creates a scheduled task for persistence
retrieved_context.text: On Aug. 17, 2023, the Zero Day Initiative publicly reported an RCE vulnerability in WinRAR (CVE-2023-40477) originally disclosed to the vendor on June 8; just four days later, an actor using the alias whalersplonk published a fake PoC on GitHub that repurposed a GeoServer CVE-2023-25157 exploit script to launch an infection chain rather than trigger the WinRAR flaw. Analysis of poc.py shows it writes a batch file to %TEMP%, executes an encoded PowerShell script that downloads c.ps1 and, subsequently, a VenomRAT v6.0.3 payload named Windows.Gaming.Preview.exe from checkblacklistwords[.]eu, installs it under %APPDATA%\Drivers, creates a scheduled task for persistence, enables keylogging to %APPDATA%\MyData\DataLogs_keylog_offline.txt, and contacts C2 at 94.156.253.109:4449. This RAT supports HVNC, stealer, grabber and commands such as plu_gin, HVNCStop, loadofflinelog, keylogsetting, filterinfo, and Po_ng. The malicious domain was registered at least 10 days before the CVE’s disclosure, indicating pre-positioned infrastructure aimed at opportunistically compromising researchers or other miscreants, not end users directly. Although the fake PoC repo was removed by the time of analysis, Palo Alto Networks WildFire and Advanced URL Filtering had already auto-categorized the domain as malicious and blocked the chain. Unit 42 researchers, alongside CTA partner Broadcom/Symantec, have published full IoCs and SHA lists on GitHub to support proactive defenses across WinRAR’s 500 million-strong user base.
retrieved_context.title: Fake CVE-2023-40477 Proof of Concept Leads to VenomRAT

canonical_entities: enumerates SSH directories to harvest credentials
Persistence is achieved through multiple cronjobs
retrieved_context.text: Aqua Security’s Nautilus team has uncovered Hadooken, a new Linux malware targeting Oracle WebLogic servers via weak passwords. Post-compromise, attackers deploy redundant shell and Python scripts to ensure download and execution of Hadooken, which enumerates SSH directories to harvest credentials, moves laterally, and clears logs. Hadooken then drops a three-path cryptominer and a Tsunami backdoor with a randomized name, the latter reserved for potential later-stage attacks. Persistence is achieved through multiple cronjobs under varied names and frequencies stored across cron directories. The malware is hosted on two IPs—one German address linked to TeamTNT and Gang 8220, the other inactive in Russia—where researchers also identified a Mallox ransomware PowerShell loader targeting Windows. Static analysis links Hadooken to Rhombus and NoEscape families. With over 230,000 internet-connected WebLogic instances—hundreds of which expose vulnerable admin consoles—this campaign underscores the dual risk of cryptojacking and ransomware across Linux and Windows environments.
retrieved_context.title: New 'Hadooken' Linux Malware Targets WebLogic Servers - SecurityWeek

retrieved_context.text: Microsoft has traced a stealthy espionage campaign by Flax Typhoon (aka Ethereal Panda), a China-based nation-state actor active since mid-2021, targeting dozens of Taiwanese organizations (with spill-over in Southeast Asia, North America, and Africa) by exploiting known vulnerabilities in public-facing VPN, web, Java, and SQL services to deploy the China Chopper web shell for initial access; the group escalates privileges via open-source exploits like Juicy Potato and BadPotato, then establishes persistence by disabling RDP network-level authentication, hijacking the Sticky Keys (sethc.exe) binary to launch Task Manager as SYSTEM, and installing a renamed SoftEther VPN-over-HTTPS bridge (conhost.exe/dllhost.exe) as a service to maintain covert C2 over port 443; leveraging LOLBins such as PowerShell Invoke-WebRequest, certutil, bitsadmin, WinRM, and WMIC for lateral movement, vulnerability scanning, and remote execution, it harvests credentials from LSASS memory and the SAM registry hive using Mimikatz for pass-the-hash attacks; although no exfiltration or final objectives have been observed, organizations are urged to enforce rigorous patch and vulnerability management on internet-exposed systems, monitor registry and file-integrity changes, deploy web application firewalls, reset compromised credentials, isolate and forensically examine affected hosts, and leverage detections in Microsoft 365 Defender to disrupt living-off-the-land tactics.
retrieved_context.title: Flax Typhoon using legitimate software to quietly access Taiwanese organizations | Microsoft Security Blog

canonical_entities: spear-phishing attacks against European embassies in Seoul (March–July 2025)
exfiltrated ... over HTTPS to the attackers’ private GitHub repo via the Contents API
retrieved_context.text: Between March and July 2025, DPRK-linked Kimsuky operators executed at least 19 highly tailored spear-phishing attacks against Western, Central, Eastern and Southern European embassies in Seoul, spoofing real diplomats and embedding password-protected ZIPs delivered via Dropbox, Daum or Google Drive. Victims unwittingly launched malicious .LNK shortcuts that triggered obfuscated PowerShell scripts to decode and in-memory execute a Confuser-Core-obfuscated XenoRAT (MoonPeak) payload—identified by GUID 12DE1212-167D-45BA-1284-780DA98CF901 and mutex “Dansweit_Hk65-PSAccerdle”—leveraging scheduled tasks for persistence. Reconnaissance data (OS build, IP, process list) was exfiltrated as base64-encoded text files over HTTPS to the attackers’ private GitHub repo via the Contents API, while C2 instructions (e.g., onf.txt) directed dynamic payload rotations hosted on Dropbox with rapid header-fix GZIP routines. This ongoing campaign provided full system control—including keystroke logging, screenshots and remote shells—and underscores the need to monitor abnormal GitHub API usage, cloud-based archive downloads and anomalous PowerShell invocations.
retrieved_context.title: The Coordinated Embassy Hunt: Unmasking the DPRK-linked GitHub C2 Espionage Campaign

hits.text: A zero-day VPN vulnerability provided initial access for a sophisticated threat actor who employed publicly available penetration‐testing and exploitation tools—SoftPerfect Network Scanner for network discovery, PsExec to deploy ServeManager.exe (the FiveHands ransomware variant using lattice-based NTRUEncrypt public key cryptography), and SombRAT for remote information theft—alongside RouterScan, grabff.exe, rclone.exe, and s3browser-9-5-3.exe to harvest credentials and exfiltrate data. Once inside, the attacker leveraged Windows Management Instrumentation (T1047) to enumerate and delete Volume Shadow Copies (Inhibit System Recovery, T1490), encrypted files (including those in recovery folders) for impact (T1486), and dropped ransom notes across directories, demanding payment to restore access. Post-encryption activities align with MITRE techniques such as Access Token Manipulation, Boot or Logon Autostart, PowerShell command and scripting interpreter, Domain Trust Discovery, Process Discovery, Screen Capture, and Kerberoasting. The combined use of FiveHands ransomware and SombRAT RAT resulted in both data theft and destruction of backup artifacts, underscoring the need for proactive patch management, network segmentation, strict credential hygiene, and rapid incident response to mitigate novel lattice-based encryption threats.
hits.title: FiveHands Ransomware Overview

canonical_entities: registered variables in the Windows Registry
hits.text: In June 2024, HP’s Threat Research team led by Patrick Schlapfer intercepted a low-grade phishing campaign leveraging HTML smuggling via an AES-encrypted HTML attachment containing JavaScript-embedded decryption logic—a novel twist on typical encrypted archives—which, when decrypted, mimicked a legitimate website but dropped a fully commented, French-language VBScript that registered variables in the Windows Registry, staged a JavaScript payload as a scheduled task, and invoked a PowerShell script to deploy the freely available AsyncRAT infostealer. Schlapfer and co-lead Alex Holland’s analysis, including comparison with generative-AI–produced code, concluded the well-structured, human-readable script was likely authored by gen-AI by a low-skill newcomer benefitting from reduced entry barriers, with no obfuscation or complex infrastructure beyond a single C2 server. This first definitive proof of AI-generated malware in the wild underscores the need for defenders to adapt detection strategies to AI-crafted droppers, monitor anomalous AES-in-JavaScript decryption patterns, and anticipate more sophisticated AI-generated payloads poised to emerge within the next two years, thereby heightening the risk to network and endpoint security.
hits.title: AI-Generated Malware Found in the Wild - SecurityWeek

canonical_entities: installing Sagerunex variants in the Windows Registry
hits.text: The Lotus Blossom APT (aka Lotus Panda, Billbug, Spring Dragon) has stepped up cyberespionage against APAC government targets by deploying new Sagerunex backdoor variants and abusing Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) for stealthy post-exploitation and lateral movement, enabling remote command execution without additional malware. Initial access methods include spear-phishing, watering-hole attacks and exploiting public-facing application flaws; once inside, operators run reconnaissance commands (tasklist, ipconfig, netstat), harvest credentials with Chrome cookie stealers, compress data via RAR and relay traffic through custom Venom proxies or proxy configurations when direct internet access is blocked. Persistence is achieved by installing Sagerunex variants in the Windows Registry under hijacked service names (tapisrv, swprv) to auto-launch at startup, while command-and-control blends encrypted traffic into legitimate platforms—stolen data uploaded as .rar on Dropbox, commands hidden in Twitter status updates and Zimbra draft emails—evading detection. Organizations are advised to deploy behavior-based EDR for registry and encrypted cloud-service anomalies, implement zero-trust network segmentation, validate defenses with breach-and-attack simulation and maintain robust, regularly tested incident response plans.
hits.title: Lotus Blossom APT Exploits WMI for Post-Exploitation Activities

canonical_entities: enumerated and deleted Volume Shadow Copies
encrypted recovery folders and user data
hits.text: On May 6, 2021, CISA disclosed that FiveHands ransomware actors exploited a zero-day VPN vulnerability for initial access, then used SoftPerfect Network Scanner for host discovery and PsExec to deploy ServeManager.exe (the NTRUEncrypt-based FiveHands payload) alongside SombRAT RAT, leveraging publicly available tools (RouterScan, grabff, rclone, s3browser) and PowerSploit modules for credential access, persistence, token manipulation, Kerberoasting, and exfiltration; once in place, FiveHands enumerated and deleted Volume Shadow Copies via WMI (T1490, T1047), encrypted recovery folders and user data (T1486), and dropped ransom notes across directories. The campaign caused direct financial losses (ransoms, legal fees, incident response, downtime, reputational harm) and exposed third-party partners. Mitigation hinges on patching/decommissioning unused VPN servers, enforcing MFA on remote and privileged accounts, maintaining up-to-date AV/OS, implementing robust backup and recovery routines, hunting for IoCs, and reinforcing employee training against phishing and malicious attachments.
hits.title: FiveHands Ransomware Overview

retrieved_context.text: Researchers at Mandiant Intelligence have identified UNC2165—the latest evolution of the U.S.-sanctioned Evil Corp—as leveraging the FakeUpdates infection chain to gain initial access, followed by deployment of LockBit ransomware to obscure attribution and monetize extortion efforts. After OFAC sanctions in December 2019 crippled Evil Corp’s ability to profit from Dridex and its WastedLocker strain, the group briefly resurfaced under PayloadBin (likely a WastedLocker rebrand) and used HTML redirectors in malicious Excel files, then adopted Hades ransomware with code overlaps to distance itself further. By aligning with LockBit’s RaaS model—already proven effective against high-profile victims such as Accenture and Bangkok Air—UNC2165 can blend in with legitimate affiliates, reduce development overhead, and bypass sanctions enforcement that deters U.S. entities from negotiating ransoms with known Evil Corp actors. This shift underscores the need for defenders to monitor FakeUpdates chains and LockBit activity for potential Evil Corp–linked intrusions and to enhance detection of rebranded ransomware variants despite attribution obfuscation tactics.
retrieved_context.title: Evil Corp Pivots LockBit to Dodge U.S. Sanctions | Threatpost

retrieved_context.text: A zero-day VPN vulnerability provided initial access for a sophisticated threat actor who employed publicly available penetration‐testing and exploitation tools—SoftPerfect Network Scanner for network discovery, PsExec to deploy ServeManager.exe (the FiveHands ransomware variant using lattice-based NTRUEncrypt public key cryptography), and SombRAT for remote information theft—alongside RouterScan, grabff.exe, rclone.exe, and s3browser-9-5-3.exe to harvest credentials and exfiltrate data. Once inside, the attacker leveraged Windows Management Instrumentation (T1047) to enumerate and delete Volume Shadow Copies (Inhibit System Recovery, T1490), encrypted files (including those in recovery folders) for impact (T1486), and dropped ransom notes across directories, demanding payment to restore access. Post-encryption activities align with MITRE techniques such as Access Token Manipulation, Boot or Logon Autostart, PowerShell command and scripting interpreter, Domain Trust Discovery, Process Discovery, Screen Capture, and Kerberoasting. The combined use of FiveHands ransomware and SombRAT RAT resulted in both data theft and destruction of backup artifacts, underscoring the need for proactive patch management, network segmentation, strict credential hygiene, and rapid incident response to mitigate novel lattice-based encryption threats.
