retrieved_context.text: In June 2024, HP’s Threat Research team led by Patrick Schlapfer intercepted a low-grade phishing campaign leveraging HTML smuggling via an AES-encrypted HTML attachment containing JavaScript-embedded decryption logic—a novel twist on typical encrypted archives—which, when decrypted, mimicked a legitimate website but dropped a fully commented, French-language VBScript that registered variables in the Windows Registry, staged a JavaScript payload as a scheduled task, and invoked a PowerShell script to deploy the freely available AsyncRAT infostealer. Schlapfer and co-lead Alex Holland’s analysis, including comparison with generative-AI–produced code, concluded the well-structured, human-readable script was likely authored by gen-AI by a low-skill newcomer benefitting from reduced entry barriers, with no obfuscation or complex infrastructure beyond a single C2 server. This first definitive proof of AI-generated malware in the wild underscores the need for defenders to adapt detection strategies to AI-crafted droppers, monitor anomalous AES-in-JavaScript decryption patterns, and anticipate more sophisticated AI-generated payloads poised to emerge within the next two years, thereby heightening the risk to network and endpoint security.
retrieved_context.title: AI-Generated Malware Found in the Wild - SecurityWeek

retrieved_context.text: Moses Staff, an Iran-linked APT active since September 2021, has conducted politically motivated sabotage campaigns—initially against Israeli organizations and later targets in India, Germany, the U.S., Italy, Chile, Turkey and the UAE—by exploiting known public-facing server vulnerabilities (e.g., Microsoft Exchange), moving laterally with PsExec, WMIC and PowerShell, and deploying a two-stage destructive toolkit: a Python-based loader (PyDCrypt) that installs a custom DiskCryptor variant (DCSrv) to encrypt files and disrupt operations without ransom demands, and, as newly documented by Cybereason, the StrifeWater RAT masquerading as calc.exe to establish early footholds, harvest system metadata (machine name, OS version, CPU architecture, user privileges, time zone), execute commands, capture screens, maintain persistence via scheduled tasks, and download auxiliary modules before self-removal—all while communicating with hard-coded C2 IPs, URLs and domain names—to evade detection; organizations should urgently patch exposed servers, monitor anomalous calc.exe and scheduled-task activity, and enhance EDR rules to detect PyDCrypt, DCSrv and StrifeWater behaviors to thwart data exfiltration and infrastructure damage.

canonical_entities: installing Sagerunex variants in the Windows Registry
retrieved_context.text: The Lotus Blossom APT (aka Lotus Panda, Billbug, Spring Dragon) has stepped up cyberespionage against APAC government targets by deploying new Sagerunex backdoor variants and abusing Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) for stealthy post-exploitation and lateral movement, enabling remote command execution without additional malware. Initial access methods include spear-phishing, watering-hole attacks and exploiting public-facing application flaws; once inside, operators run reconnaissance commands (tasklist, ipconfig, netstat), harvest credentials with Chrome cookie stealers, compress data via RAR and relay traffic through custom Venom proxies or proxy configurations when direct internet access is blocked. Persistence is achieved by installing Sagerunex variants in the Windows Registry under hijacked service names (tapisrv, swprv) to auto-launch at startup, while command-and-control blends encrypted traffic into legitimate platforms—stolen data uploaded as .rar on Dropbox, commands hidden in Twitter status updates and Zimbra draft emails—evading detection. Organizations are advised to deploy behavior-based EDR for registry and encrypted cloud-service anomalies, implement zero-trust network segmentation, validate defenses with breach-and-attack simulation and maintain robust, regularly tested incident response plans.
retrieved_context.title: Lotus Blossom APT Exploits WMI for Post-Exploitation Activities

retrieved_context.text: On May 6, 2021, CISA disclosed that FiveHands ransomware actors exploited a zero-day VPN vulnerability for initial access, then used SoftPerfect Network Scanner for host discovery and PsExec to deploy ServeManager.exe (the NTRUEncrypt-based FiveHands payload) alongside SombRAT RAT, leveraging publicly available tools (RouterScan, grabff, rclone, s3browser) and PowerSploit modules for credential access, persistence, token manipulation, Kerberoasting, and exfiltration; once in place, FiveHands enumerated and deleted Volume Shadow Copies via WMI (T1490, T1047), encrypted recovery folders and user data (T1486), and dropped ransom notes across directories. The campaign caused direct financial losses (ransoms, legal fees, incident response, downtime, reputational harm) and exposed third-party partners. Mitigation hinges on patching/decommissioning unused VPN servers, enforcing MFA on remote and privileged accounts, maintaining up-to-date AV/OS, implementing robust backup and recovery routines, hunting for IoCs, and reinforcing employee training against phishing and malicious attachments.

hits.text: On March 2, 2025, CyberMaterial’s report on Void Manticore (aka Storm-0842, linked to the cybercriminal Storm-1811 cluster) details a coordinated espionage campaign that began in late 2024 against aerospace, defense and government organizations in Europe and North America: operators initiated intrusions via spear-phishing emails embedding weaponized RTFs exploiting CVE-2024-4113 to drop a custom loader (“VoidLoader”), which in turn deployed the “ManticoreShell” backdoor; post-compromise activities included credential harvesting (Mimikatz), lateral movement via PSExec and WMI, privilege escalation through a signed kernel-mode driver exploit, and persistence using registry Run keys and scheduled tasks; C2 communications leveraged HTTPS with a domain generation algorithm (DGA) and fallback to TOR. Over a three-month window they compromised at least 15 organizations, exfiltrated more than 20 GB of intellectual property, and triggered system outages exceeding 48 hours in critical environments. Key mitigation measures include immediate patching of CVE-2024-4113, deployment of EDR solutions to detect anomalous IOCTL and PowerShell activity, network segmentation to contain lateral movement, strict monitoring of DGA-style DNS queries, and implementation of multi-factor authentication to thwart credential abuse.
hits.title: Void Manticore (Storm-0842) – Threat Actor - CyberMaterial

hits.text: Microsoft has identified a China-based nation-state threat actor tracked as Flax Typhoon (aka Ethereal Panda) conducting espionage against dozens of Taiwanese organizations since mid-2021 by exploiting known vulnerabilities in public-facing VPN, web, Java and SQL servers to deploy the China Chopper web shell, escalate privileges with Juicy Potato and BadPotato, and establish persistence by disabling RDP network-level authentication, hijacking the Sticky Keys binary to launch Task Manager as SYSTEM, and installing a renamed SoftEther VPN bridge over HTTPS on port 443 for stealthy command-and-control. Once inside, the actor leverages WinRM and WMIC for lateral movement and deploys Mimikatz to dump LSASS and SAM for pass-the-hash attacks, yet conducts minimal post-persistence activity, suggesting long-term credential harvesting rather than immediate data exfiltration. To mitigate, organizations must enforce rigorous patch management, monitor registry changes and RDP configurations, deploy file integrity and behavioral monitoring on public-facing servers, isolate and forensically examine compromised systems, and rotate or disable exposed credentials.

hits.text: Last week Google’s Threat Analysis Group, in partnership with The Citizen Lab, exposed an in-the-wild exploit chain developed by the commercial surveillance vendor Intellexa in Egypt that leverages a man-in-the-middle injection on HTTP traffic to silently redirect targets first to c.betly[.]me and then to sec-flare[.]com, delivering Predator spyware without any user interaction; on iOS this chain combined Safari RCE (CVE-2023-41993), certificate validation bypass (CVE-2023-41991) and XNU kernel local privilege escalation (CVE-2023-41992) and was patched in iOS 16.7/17.0.1, while on Android initial Chrome renderer RCE (CVE-2023-4762), delivered via MITM or one-time links, was patched on September 5; this campaign highlights the serious risk posed by proliferating commercial spyware, underscores the urgency of enforcing universal HTTPS and enabling Chrome’s HTTPS-First Mode, and demonstrates the critical need for organizations and users to apply the latest OS and browser updates, deploy encrypted-traffic protections, and monitor for anomalous network redirects to mitigate future attacks.

hits.text: Dragos researchers, in collaboration with Ukraine’s CSSC, unearthed FrostyGoop—an ICS-specific malware first spotted in April and used in January to disrupt central heating in over 600 Lviv apartment buildings—marking the first known malware to leverage Modbus TCP for read/write operations on operational technology. Attackers gained initial access in April 2023 by exploiting a MikroTik router vulnerability, deployed a webshell on the router’s web server, and maintained persistence via Tor and L2TP tunnels to Moscow-based IPs. After spending months conducting reconnaissance, they extracted credentials by dumping the SAM registry hive in December, then directly issued scripted Modbus commands—read from a JSON configuration file—to publicly exposed ENCO heating controllers, even downgrading firmware to disable monitoring and force inaccurate measurements that halted heating services for nearly two days amid subzero temperatures. This incident underscores the threat posed by internet-exposed ICS devices—over 46,000 globally using Modbus—and highlights poor network segmentation, unpatched ICS CVEs, and the ease with which FrostyGoop’s protocol-agnostic payload can be repurposed against diverse industrial controllers, necessitating immediate network segmentation, firmware monitoring, and patch management in OT environments.

hits.text: After a year-long investigation researchers at Lumen’s Black Lotus Labs dissected the Ngioweb botnet—first observed in 2017—which uses a loader network and roughly 15 n-day exploits to deploy malware that contacts C2 domains generated via a domain generation algorithm (augmented by DNS TXT records to resist sinkholing), evaluates device traffic capacity, and links compromised Zyxel, Reolink, Alpha Technologies and, increasingly, Netgear routers (now 10 % of bots) to over 180 “backconnect” C2 nodes that provide at least 80 % of the 35,000 residential proxies in the NSOCKS[.]net service across 180 countries; NSOCKS’s lack of authentication and appearance on free proxy lists has enabled cybercriminals to carry out DDoS amplification, credential stuffing, phishing and malware proxying (e.g., Agent Tesla), while APT28 state-sponsored actors have mixed espionage with criminal traffic on the same infrastructure. To disrupt both operations, Lumen, alongside The ShadowServer Foundation and other partners, is actively blocking traffic to known C2 nodes and publishing indicators of compromise to help organizations identify and remediate infected devices.

hits.text: Unit42’s “EleKtra-Leak” campaign, active since December 2020, uses automated scripts to clone public GitHub repos every few minutes, extract exposed AWS IAM keys within five minutes, then—if not blocked by GitHub-AWS quarantine policies—execute rapid AWS reconnaissance (DescribeRegions), create security groups, and launch hundreds of EC2 instances across regions via VPN for Monero cryptojacking, generating over 400 API calls in seven minutes. Between Aug. 30 and Oct. 6, 2023, researchers tracked 474 actor-controlled miners. The actor employs custom mining software and blocklists high-profile AWS account IDs to avoid honey traps. Leveraging the Prisma Cloud HoneyCloud project’s ephemeral key leaks and policy overrides, Unit42 obtained full visibility, informing Prisma Cloud Secrets Security, CI/CD IaC scanning, Cortex XDR, and recommendations for independent repo scanning, strict IAM policies, and continuous monitoring.

hits.text: In late May 2022, Symantec identified multiple threat actors exploiting the MSDT Follina bug (CVE-2022-30190) through ms-msdt URI-based RCE in Word/RTF documents that load a malicious HTML via Word’s remote template feature to launch msdt.exe, sdiagnhost.exe and ultimately PowerShell—bypassing the need for macros—to install a digitally signed AsyncRAT remote access Trojan that performs anti-analysis checks, collects hardware IDs, user names, execution paths and OS details, and maintains C&C communications, alongside parallel deployments of a browser infostealer targeting cookies and saved credentials in Firefox, Chrome and Edge. hits.text: In August 2019 Dragos and SecureWorks detailed a protracted (since April 2018) campaign by the Lyceum/Hexane threat group targeting Middle East critical infrastructure with straightforward but effective tactics: initial password‐spraying and brute‐force attacks on corporate email accounts, followed by spear-phishing from compromised internal accounts to executives, HR and IT staff using malicious Excel macros that deploy the DanBot RAT; once inside, operators run PoshC2-sourced PowerShell scripts—Decrypt-RDCMan.ps1 to extract RDCMan-stored passwords and Get-LAPSP.ps1 to harvest Active Directory credentials via LDAP—enabling environment reconnaissance and lateral movement. Despite its reliance on common techniques rather than novel malware or zero-days, Lyceum’s persistence highlights the urgency of enforcing multi-factor authentication, disabling macros, monitoring for unauthorized PowerShell/PoshC2 activity and training high-value users to detect spear-phishing, thereby mitigating the group’s primary objective of information collection before any potential pivot into OT/ICS environments.

hits.text: Since at least August 2023, threat actors have exploited CVE-2023-4966 (CitrixBleed), a 7.5-rated flaw in Citrix NetScaler ADC and Gateway, culminating in an October 16–19 breach at Comcast Xfinity that exposed 35,879,455 customers’ usernames, hashed passwords, names, contact details, last four SSN digits, dates of birth and security Q&A; despite Citrix’s October 10 patch and Comcast’s claim of prompt mitigation, attackers used publicly available proofs-of-concept and rumored Python automation scripts to extract session tokens from device memory, hijack active sessions and bypass authentication, a tactic linked by ReliaQuest to at least five threat groups including LockBit; this incident highlights the necessity not only of timely patching and reboots but also of invalidating all active and persistent session tokens, enforcing multi-factor authentication, resetting credentials and maintaining continuous 24x7 monitoring to prevent further data exfiltration and ransomware deployment.

hits.text: The North Korea-linked threat actor Slow Pisces (also tracked as Jade Sleet, PUKCHONG, TraderTraitor, and UNC4899) has been conducting a multi-stage malware campaign targeting cryptocurrency developers via LinkedIn job opportunity lures since at least June 2024, leveraging trojanized Python and JavaScript projects hosted on GitHub that employ YAML deserialization and EJS templating to execute gated payloads only to validated targets meeting specific criteria (IP address, geolocation, time, HTTP headers); the campaign delivers RN Loader and RN Stealer malware on macOS systems capable of harvesting system metadata, installed applications, SSH keys, AWS/Kubernetes/Google Cloud configuration files, and iCloud Keychain data, with payloads remaining memory-resident and deployed selectively to prevent analysis; Slow Pisces is assessed to be responsible for the February 2025 Bybit cryptocurrency exchange breach and operates alongside other North Korean clusters including Operation Dream Job, Contagious Interview, Alluring Pisces, and Moonstone Sleet, though with notably superior operational security practices involving heavily guarded payload delivery across infection stages.
hits.title: Crypto Developers Targeted by Python Malware Disguised as Coding Challenges

hits.text: Symantec’s Threat Hunter Team has linked the newly discovered Sidewalk loader backdoor—an evolution of the Crosswalk/Backdoor.Motnug family—to Grayfly (aka GREF/Wicked Panda), a China-linked espionage group active since March 2017 that employs custom backdoors, Trojan.Chattak, Cobalt Strike, web shells and credential-dumpers against telecom, IT, media and finance targets in Taiwan, Vietnam, the US and Mexico; in a recent campaign they exploited public-facing Microsoft Exchange and MySQL servers via commodity and zero-day flaws to execute Base64-encoded PowerShell commands through certutil, install an ASPX web shell in the ClientAccess\ecp directory, deploy Sidewalk via installutil.exe, create persistence with WMIC-launched scheduled tasks, then run a custom Mimikatz variant (SHA256 b3eb783b017da32e33d19670b39eae0b11de8e983891dd4feb873d6e9333608d) to harvest credentials—all within about an hour before ceasing observable activity; three Chengdu 404 executives were indicted in 2020 for attacks on over 100 organizations, highlighting Grayfly’s persistence and underscoring the need to promptly patch Exchange and MySQL servers, monitor anomalous PowerShell and scheduled-task activity, and deploy IOC-based detection to block Sidewalk and related tools.
hits.title: Grayfly: Chinese Threat Actor Uses Newly-discovered Sidewalk Malware | Symantec Enterprise Blogs

hits.text: During a recent incident, a LockBit affiliate conducted initial intrusions using gpresult for policy dumping, Cobalt Strike loaders and PsExec for privilege escalation, followed by reconnaissance (whoami, netstat, quser, net view), lateral movement, persistence via a new user account, and data exfiltration over FTP with Wput; when deployment of LockBit (SHA256 079b99f6…) was blocked on the target network, the attacker pivoted to a newly observed Rust-written ransomware family dubbed 3AM (SHA256 307a1217…), which appends “.threeamtime” to encrypted files, stops over 100 security and backup services via net stop and wbadmin/bcdedit/wmic commands, deletes Volume Shadow copies with vssadmin.exe delete shadows /all /quiet, and drops a Tor‐accessible ransom note requiring a 32-character “-k” access key and offering decryption/mystical-themed extortion; although 3AM encryption succeeded on only one of three attempted hosts, its Conti-style “-m” (local/net) and “-h” parameters, heavy service-termination payload, and aggressive VSS wipe underscore its potential as a fallback vector—defenders should update Symantec/Broadcom signatures, monitor for the .threeamtime extension, suspicious Rust binaries, command-line flags “-k” and “-m”, and mass service stoppage activity, and block associated IOCs (185.202.0[.]111, 212.18.104[.]6, 85.159.229[.]62) to mitigate future 3AM use.
hits.title: 3AM: New Ransomware Family Used As Fallback in Failed LockBit Attack | Symantec Enterprise Blogs

hits.text: Blitz is a modular two-stage Windows malware discovered in 2024 and actively developed into early 2025 by a Russian-speaking actor using the moniker sw1zzx who distributed backdoored Standoff 2 game cheat packages (Nerest_CrackBy@sw1zzx_dev.zip and Elysium_CrackBy@sw1zzx_dev.zip) via a Telegram channel. The first stage is a stealthy downloader (ieapfltr.dll) retrieved through a PowerShell one-liner from pastebin/paste.rs URLs after passing anti-sandbox and VM detection checks (timing loops, floating-point instruction counters, processor count and screen resolution heuristics), which then establishes persistence via HKCU\Environment\UserInitMprLogonScript and HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run. Upon reboot, the downloader connects to a FastAPI-based C2 infrastructure hosted on a Hugging Face Space to fetch the second-stage Blitz bot that performs keylogging, screenshot capture, denial-of-service attacks on web servers and can deploy an XMRig Monero miner as follow-up. This campaign leverages Hugging Face Spaces for file hosting and C2 communications, and the malware developer promoted cheats on social media before announcing departure in May 2025; Hugging Face subsequently locked the account and blocked blob IDs. The impact includes credential theft, resource exploitation, unauthorized cryptocurrency mining and potential service disruption, and Palo Alto Networks’ Advanced WildFire, URL Filtering, DNS Security, Threat Prevention, Cortex XDR and XSIAM effectively detect and block Blitz activities, with Unit 42 standing by for incident response.

hits.text: In Q1 2023, Google’s Threat Analysis Group (TAG) found that over 60 percent of Russian state-backed phishing campaigns were aimed at Ukraine, led by FROZENBARENTS (aka Sandworm, GRU Unit 74455), which abused globally compromised EXIM mail servers, SMS-delivered phishing links and fake Windows update payloads deploying the Rhadamanthys stealer, then maintained persistence via webshells and Adminer to exfiltrate data to the CyberArmyofRussia_Reborn Telegram channel across government, defense, energy (notably the Caspian Pipeline Consortium), transport, education and humanitarian sectors while conducting information operations. Simultaneously, FROZENLAKE (APT28) leveraged reflected XSS on Ukrainian government sites to redirect users to phishing domains hosted on free services, with harvested credentials sent to compromised Ubiquiti devices; Belarusian PUSHCHA continued targeted low-volume campaigns against regional webmail providers; and IRA-linked actors deployed coordinated YouTube Shorts and Blogger posts to amplify pro-Wagner, anti-Ukrainian narratives. Financially motivated Cuba ransomware affiliates pivoted to intelligence collection using RomCom malware via ChatGPT/OpenAI-spoofed domains against conference attendees. TAG’s takedowns and Safe Browsing protections, coupled with targeted Gmail alerts, underscore the need for organizations to enable Enhanced Safe Browsing, patch mail servers, monitor for unauthorized EXIM access, and guard against reflected XSS and SMS phishing.
hits.title: Ukraine remains Russia’s biggest cyber focus in 2023

canonical_entities: Scanning the Internet for IoT devices with open Telnet/SSH ports
Use of default or weak credentials
Encrypted SOCKS5 tunneling to proxy infrastructure
hits.text: Researchers have uncovered that since early 2024 a previously undocumented botnet, dubbed Ngioweb, has been systematically scanning the Internet for IoT devices—primarily DVRs, IP cameras and home routers—with open Telnet/SSH ports and default or weak credentials, exploiting known firmware vulnerabilities to deploy a lightweight Go-based loader that establishes encrypted SOCKS5 tunnels back to a resilient NSOCKS residential proxy network of over 150,000 infected nodes. Once a device is compromised, Ngioweb drops a persistent agent that connects to fast-flux C2 domains via HTTPS, retrieves updated encryption keys and proxy configuration, and registers the node for NSOCKS’ tiered subscription service (starting at $25/month), which reportedly generates upwards of $500K in monthly revenue by fueling large-scale credential-stuffing campaigns, ad fraud and DDoS-for-hire operations. The actors behind Ngioweb continually rotate fallback C2 domains, employ encryption and obfuscation to evade signature-based detection, and monitor infection success rates in real time, enabling rapid retooling and expansion. Defenders are urged to enforce strong, unique credentials on all IoT assets, disable unused management interfaces, apply timely firmware updates, implement network segmentation and deploy behavioral analytics or honeypots to detect anomalous outbound proxy traffic.
hits.title: Ngioweb Botnet Fuels NSOCKS Residential Proxy Network Exploiting IoT Devices

hits.text: CISA has released a detailed analysis of the FiveHands ransomware, a C++-based DeathRansom successor with HelloKitty ties, deployed by financially motivated UNC2447 in recent European and North American intrusions; leveraging a VPN product zero-day for initial access, the adversary used open-source exploitation tools and SombRAT to map the network, exfiltrate data, and execute the NTRUEncrypt-powered ransomware stage, which enumerates and erases Volume Shadow Copies to thwart recovery, before demanding payment. CISA’s malware analysis (MAR) and accompanying report (AR) catalog 18 submitted artifacts—eight pen-test utilities, the ransomware binary, and nine SombRAT components—and provide mitigation guidance including timely VPN patching, network segmentation, multi-factor authentication, robust backup strategies, and behavior-based detection tuned to NTRUEncrypt operations and shadow copy deletion. These findings align with IST’s 48 anti-ransomware recommendations and the NCIJTF’s tactics-focused fact sheet, underscoring the need for proactive vulnerability management, continuous monitoring, and rapid response frameworks to neutralize UNC2447’s evolving capabilities.
hits.title: CISA Analyzes FiveHands Ransomware

hits.text: Following the sale of INC ransomware source code in March 2024 and its initial appearance in August 2023, researchers in July 2024 uncovered Lynx ransomware, a Windows-only, C++-based RaaS variant that shares ~48% of INC’s functions (70.8% among common routines) and has been deployed against U.S. and U.K. retail, real estate, architecture, financial and environmental service firms via phishing, malicious downloads and underground forums; employing AES-128-CTR and Curve25519 Donna for encryption with a .lynx extension, it conducts double-extortion by exfiltrating victims’ data (published on lynxblog[.]net under a policy excluding governments, hospitals and non-profits) before encrypting all files by default—killing processes, encrypting network shares and hidden disks, deleting shadow copies and backups, leveraging the Restart Manager API to target in-use files, and printing a OneNote report—then dropping a README.txt ransom note; this evolution of RaaS underscores the need for organizations to adopt robust cybersecurity measures, including anti-phishing training, backup hardening, dynamic and behavioral detections via Palo Alto Networks’ Cortex XDR Anti-Ransomware and Advanced WildFire, and vigilant monitoring of Indicators of Compromise such as published SHA256 hashes to mitigate high-profile, code-reused ransomware campaigns.
hits.title: Lynx Ransomware: A Rebranding of INC Ransomware

hits.text: In July 2024, evolving from an early-year attack on a Ukrainian municipal energy provider disclosed by Ukraine’s CSSC, the Russian-linked OT malware FrostyGoop (aka BUSTLEBERM) exploited an obscure Go-based Modbus TCP library, goccy’s go-json encoder/decoder and an open-source ‘queues’ execution controller—delivered via compromised MikroTik routers or internet-exposed OT devices—to issue bespoke Modbus read/write commands that disrupted heating services to over 600 apartment buildings for two days in sub-zero conditions. FrostyGoop accepts JSON or command-line arguments to configure operation codes, addresses, counts, values and timing, includes a PEB BeingDebugged flag check for anti-analysis, and our telemetry reveals 1,088,175 Modbus TCP devices exposed from Sept. 2–Oct. 2, 2024 (6,211,623 total), including 32 ENCO control devices with Telnet-accessible TCP/23 in Romania and Ukraine. Concurrently, we identified a co-occurring Golang sample, go-encrypt.exe, using AES-CFB to encrypt/decrypt JSON files—likely for concealing FrostyGoop configs—that first appeared with task_test.json on Oct. 10, 2023. These insights highlight the need for ICS-centric detection—signatures for the unique Modbus library and JSON schema, monitoring for PEB debug checks and encrypted JSON usage—and rigorous network segmentation to mitigate the growing OT threat.
hits.title: FrostyGoop’s Zoom-In: A Closer Look into the Malware Artifacts, Behaviors and Network Communications

hits.text: At least four distinct campaigns exploited CVE-2023-37580, a reflected XSS zero-day in Zimbra Collaboration Suite, to siphon emails, attachments, user credentials and authentication tokens from government organizations worldwide before the July 5 hotfix and July 25 official patch; in chronological order, unidentified actors targeted Greece on June 29 via malicious URLs that, when clicked during active Zimbra sessions, deployed a data-theft framework and auto-forward rules, Winter Vivern’s APT leveraged unique exploit links to hit Moldova and Tunisia between July 11 and 25, another group used a phishing-style XSS link in Vietnam to harvest webmail credentials and exfiltrate them to a compromised government domain, and on August 25 unknown attackers employed an N-day variant to steal tokens from Pakistan’s mail servers; Google’s Threat Analysis Group warns these campaigns underscore the urgency of promptly applying open-source fixes, hardening mail-server code to prevent XSS, and maintaining vigilant patch management as attackers continuously monitor public repositories for unpatched vulnerabilities.
hits.title: APTs Swarm Zimbra Zero-Day to Steal Government Info Worldwide

retrieved_context.text: Dragos researchers, in collaboration with Ukraine’s CSSC, unearthed FrostyGoop—an ICS-specific malware first spotted in April and used in January to disrupt central heating in over 600 Lviv apartment buildings—marking the first known malware to leverage Modbus TCP for read/write operations on operational technology. Attackers gained initial access in April 2023 by exploiting a MikroTik router vulnerability, deployed a webshell on the router’s web server, and maintained persistence via Tor and L2TP tunnels to Moscow-based IPs. After spending months conducting reconnaissance, they extracted credentials by dumping the SAM registry hive in December, then directly issued scripted Modbus commands—read from a JSON configuration file—to publicly exposed ENCO heating controllers, even downgrading firmware to disable monitoring and force inaccurate measurements that halted heating services for nearly two days amid subzero temperatures. This incident underscores the threat posed by internet-exposed ICS devices—over 46,000 globally using Modbus—and highlights poor network segmentation, unpatched ICS CVEs, and the ease with which FrostyGoop’s protocol-agnostic payload can be repurposed against diverse industrial controllers, necessitating immediate network segmentation, firmware monitoring, and patch management in OT environments.
retrieved_context.title: ICS malware FrostyGoop disrupted heating in Ukraine, remains threat to OT worldwide

retrieved_context.text: Blitz is a modular two-stage Windows malware discovered in 2024 and actively developed into early 2025 by a Russian-speaking actor using the moniker sw1zzx who distributed backdoored Standoff 2 game cheat packages (Nerest_CrackBy@sw1zzx_dev.zip and Elysium_CrackBy@sw1zzx_dev.zip) via a Telegram channel. The first stage is a stealthy downloader (ieapfltr.dll) retrieved through a PowerShell one-liner from pastebin/paste.rs URLs after passing anti-sandbox and VM detection checks (timing loops, floating-point instruction counters, processor count and screen resolution heuristics), which then establishes persistence via HKCU\Environment\UserInitMprLogonScript and HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run. Upon reboot, the downloader connects to a FastAPI-based C2 infrastructure hosted on a Hugging Face Space to fetch the second-stage Blitz bot that performs keylogging, screenshot capture, denial-of-service attacks on web servers and can deploy an XMRig Monero miner as follow-up. This campaign leverages Hugging Face Spaces for file hosting and C2 communications, and the malware developer promoted cheats on social media before announcing departure in May 2025; Hugging Face subsequently locked the account and blocked blob IDs. The impact includes credential theft, resource exploitation, unauthorized cryptocurrency mining and potential service disruption, and Palo Alto Networks’ Advanced WildFire, URL Filtering, DNS Security, Threat Prevention, Cortex XDR and XSIAM effectively detect and block Blitz activities, with Unit 42 standing by for incident response.
retrieved_context.title: Blitz Malware: A Tale of Game Cheats and Code Repositories

retrieved_context.text: Last week Google’s Threat Analysis Group, in partnership with The Citizen Lab, exposed an in-the-wild exploit chain developed by the commercial surveillance vendor Intellexa in Egypt that leverages a man-in-the-middle injection on HTTP traffic to silently redirect targets first to c.betly[.]me and then to sec-flare[.]com, delivering Predator spyware without any user interaction; on iOS this chain combined Safari RCE (CVE-2023-41993), certificate validation bypass (CVE-2023-41991) and XNU kernel local privilege escalation (CVE-2023-41992) and was patched in iOS 16.7/17.0.1, while on Android initial Chrome renderer RCE (CVE-2023-4762), delivered via MITM or one-time links, was patched on September 5; this campaign highlights the serious risk posed by proliferating commercial spyware, underscores the urgency of enforcing universal HTTPS and enabling Chrome’s HTTPS-First Mode, and demonstrates the critical need for organizations and users to apply the latest OS and browser updates, deploy encrypted-traffic protections, and monitor for anomalous network redirects to mitigate future attacks.
retrieved_context.title: 0-days exploited by commercial surveillance vendor in Egypt

retrieved_context.text: In August 2019 Dragos and SecureWorks detailed a protracted (since April 2018) campaign by the Lyceum/Hexane threat group targeting Middle East critical infrastructure with straightforward but effective tactics: initial password‐spraying and brute‐force attacks on corporate email accounts, followed by spear-phishing from compromised internal accounts to executives, HR and IT staff using malicious Excel macros that deploy the DanBot RAT; once inside, operators run PoshC2-sourced PowerShell scripts—Decrypt-RDCMan.ps1 to extract RDCMan-stored passwords and Get-LAPSP.ps1 to harvest Active Directory credentials via LDAP—enabling environment reconnaissance and lateral movement. Despite its reliance on common techniques rather than novel malware or zero-days, Lyceum’s persistence highlights the urgency of enforcing multi-factor authentication, disabling macros, monitoring for unauthorized PowerShell/PoshC2 activity and training high-value users to detect spear-phishing, thereby mitigating the group’s primary objective of information collection before any potential pivot into OT/ICS environments.
retrieved_context.title: Lyceum/Hexane Threat Group Uses Common Hacking Tactics

retrieved_context.text: In Q1 2023, Google’s Threat Analysis Group (TAG) found that over 60 percent of Russian state-backed phishing campaigns were aimed at Ukraine, led by FROZENBARENTS (aka Sandworm, GRU Unit 74455), which abused globally compromised EXIM mail servers, SMS-delivered phishing links and fake Windows update payloads deploying the Rhadamanthys stealer, then maintained persistence via webshells and Adminer to exfiltrate data to the CyberArmyofRussia_Reborn Telegram channel across government, defense, energy (notably the Caspian Pipeline Consortium), transport, education and humanitarian sectors while conducting information operations. Simultaneously, FROZENLAKE (APT28) leveraged reflected XSS on Ukrainian government sites to redirect users to phishing domains hosted on free services, with harvested credentials sent to compromised Ubiquiti devices; Belarusian PUSHCHA continued targeted low-volume campaigns against regional webmail providers; and IRA-linked actors deployed coordinated YouTube Shorts and Blogger posts to amplify pro-Wagner, anti-Ukrainian narratives. Financially motivated Cuba ransomware affiliates pivoted to intelligence collection using RomCom malware via ChatGPT/OpenAI-spoofed domains against conference attendees. TAG’s takedowns and Safe Browsing protections, coupled with targeted Gmail alerts, underscore the need for organizations to enable Enhanced Safe Browsing, patch mail servers, monitor for unauthorized EXIM access, and guard against reflected XSS and SMS phishing.
retrieved_context.title: Ukraine remains Russia’s biggest cyber focus in 2023

hits.text: Since November 2024, Iran-linked APT42 (aka TA453/Mint Sandstorm) has executed multi-stage intrusions against government ministries and critical infrastructure across Europe and the Middle East, initially using spear-phishing lures with malicious RTF attachments to deploy its custom ChainDoor RAT and establish HTTPS-based C2 channels; in December 2024 it leveraged a zero-day SQL injection against public-facing web portals to plant a secondary backdoor, then used Mimikatz for credential harvesting and lateral movement, exfiltrating over 3.5 TB of sensitive PII and policy documents—hiding stolen data via steganography in JPEGs—and deploying coin-miner payloads on select hosts; this campaign has compromised at least 150 systems, caused an estimated $2 million in operational disruption, and underscores the need for immediate patching of web applications, enforcement of MFA, network segmentation, and enhanced monitoring for anomalous HTTPS traffic to known C2 domains.
hits.title: APT42 – TA453, Mint Sandstorm – IRAN - CyberMaterial

hits.text: In February 2022, CISA, the FBI, US Cyber Command CNMF, NCSC-UK and NSA issued a joint advisory on Iranian Ministry of Intelligence–linked APT MuddyWater (aka MERCURY, Earth Vetala, Static Kitten, Seedworm, TEMP.Zagros), active since 2018 and focused on cyber espionage, intellectual property theft and ransomware against defense, oil & gas, government and telecom sectors across Asia, Africa, Europe and North America. Exploiting publicly disclosed vulnerabilities and open-source tools, MuddyWater delivers malicious PDFs with embedded links that display error messages prompting users to download Excel maldocs or Windows executables; these files host VBA macros that drop WSF scripts to execute PowerShell and VB payloads, leverage LoLBins, and stage RATs and malware families including PowGoop, Canopy, Small Sieve, POWERSTATS and Mori while communicating with C2 over HTTP and DNS and persisting via Registry Run keys. Cisco Talos observed regional campaigns in Turkey (Nov 2021), Pakistan (Aug 2021) and Armenia (Jun 2021) using decoy documents, signaling tokens and a consistent TTP set, suggesting a conglomerate of subgroups migrating techniques across regions. The resultant network access and data exfiltration underscore the imperative for proactive DFIR readiness, deployment of XDR/MDR platforms, rigorous vulnerability management, macro execution restrictions, PowerShell/LoLBin monitoring and ongoing user awareness training reinforced by incident response tabletop exercises.
hits.title: An In-Depth Look at Iranian APT "MuddyWater"

canonical_entities: installing Sagerunex variants in the Windows Registry
hits.text: The Lotus Blossom APT (aka Lotus Panda, Billbug, Spring Dragon) has stepped up cyberespionage against APAC government targets by deploying new Sagerunex backdoor variants and abusing Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) for stealthy post-exploitation and lateral movement, enabling remote command execution without additional malware. Initial access methods include spear-phishing, watering-hole attacks and exploiting public-facing application flaws; once inside, operators run reconnaissance commands (tasklist, ipconfig, netstat), harvest credentials with Chrome cookie stealers, compress data via RAR and relay traffic through custom Venom proxies or proxy configurations when direct internet access is blocked. Persistence is achieved by installing Sagerunex variants in the Windows Registry under hijacked service names (tapisrv, swprv) to auto-launch at startup, while command-and-control blends encrypted traffic into legitimate platforms—stolen data uploaded as .rar on Dropbox, commands hidden in Twitter status updates and Zimbra draft emails—evading detection. Organizations are advised to deploy behavior-based EDR for registry and encrypted cloud-service anomalies, implement zero-trust network segmentation, validate defenses with breach-and-attack simulation and maintain robust, regularly tested incident response plans.
hits.title: Lotus Blossom APT Exploits WMI for Post-Exploitation Activities

hits.text: Since January 2021, Google’s Threat Analysis Group (TAG) has tracked a government-backed North Korean campaign that leverages social engineering via X (formerly Twitter) and encrypted messaging apps to befriend security researchers and deliver malicious files containing at least one unpatched 0-day in a popular software package; upon exploitation the custom shellcode performs anti-virtual-machine checks, captures system data and screenshots, and exfiltrates them to C2 infrastructure (e.g., 23.106.215[.]105, www.blgbeach[.]com), with the latest vulnerability reported and patched on September 12, 2023 (see TAG’s published RCA). In parallel, the actors published a seemingly benign Windows tool called GetSymbol on GitHub (https://github.com/dbgsymbol/) that quietly downloads debugging symbols—and arbitrary code—from attacker domains, requiring full OS reinstalls for compromised hosts. TAG has added malicious sites to Safe Browsing, issued government-backed attacker alerts to targeted Gmail and Workspace users, and urges researchers to enable Enhanced Safe Browsing, keep software up to date, and verify system integrity after using third-party tools.
hits.title: Active North Korean campaign targeting security researchers

hits.text: Lynx ransomware, emerging in July 2024 as the INC ransomware successor under a Ransomware-as-a-Service model, employs a sophisticated double-extortion strategy—exfiltrating data prior to encryption and threatening publication on a leak site—and reuses significant INC source code. Between July and November 2024, it disrupted U.S. energy, oil and gas utilities, then in January–February 2025 breached Italy’s CONAD retail chain, U.S. law firm Hunter Taubman Fischer & Li, and Idaho retailer Zamzows, Inc., compromising internal documents and sensitive client and customer data. Initial access leverages phishing (T1566.001), drive-by compromises (T1195) and zero-day exploits; execution via user execution (T1204.002) and scripting interpreters (T1059.001); persistence through autostart mechanisms (T1070.001); exfiltration over C2 channels (T1041); and impact via file encryption (T1486) appending “.LYNX.” Operators use CLI flags (--file, --dir, --mode, --stop-processes, --encrypt-network, --hide-cmd, --no-print, --kill, --safe-mode) to granularly control encryption, terminate SQL, Veeam, Backup, Exchange, Java and Notepad processes/services, delete shadow copies, empty recycle bins, change wallpapers and print ransom notes directing victims to a Tor-based chat. Detection and prevention hinge on hardening email gateways, patching public-facing systems, monitoring anomalous process/service terminations, restricting unauthorized command-line encryption tools, and blocking known SHA256 hashes to disrupt this high-impact, automated RaaS operation.
hits.title: Lynx Ransomware: INC Ransomware Reincarnated - Threat Actors

hits.text: Operation RoundPress, attributed with medium confidence to Russian state-sponsored APT28 (Fancy Bear), has since 2023 exploited stored and reflected XSS flaws in widely used webmail platforms—initially leveraging Roundcube CVE-2020-35730 to inject malicious JavaScript into email bodies, then CVE-2023-43770 and additional n-day vulnerabilities in Roundcube, Horde, MDaemon and Zimbra in early 2024—to execute upon email open without clicks or redirects. Through spear-phishing emails crafted with timely political or news excerpts, the hidden script auto-fills victim credentials via invisible input fields, scrapes DOM content—including emails, contacts, webmail settings, login history, 2FA tokens and passwords—and exfiltrates data via HTTP POST to hardcoded C2 servers. Targets span high-value government entities in Greece, Ukraine, Serbia and Cameroon, military units in Ukraine and Ecuador, defense contractors in Ukraine, Bulgaria and Romania, and critical infrastructure in Ukraine and Bulgaria. The lack of persistence mechanisms confines execution to session scope but underscores the necessity for timely patching of XSS vulnerabilities, disabling HTML rendering in webmail clients, enforcing strict input sanitization and multifactor authentication, and monitoring anomalous outbound traffic to mitigate credential theft and data exfiltration.
hits.title: Government webmail hacked via XSS bugs in global spy campaign

hits.text: ESET researchers have retrospectively identified WinorDLL64.dll—a backdoor payload for the Wslink loader (WinorLoaderDLL64.dll) first uncovered in 2021—that operates as an in-memory server using MemoryModule and is protected by Oreans Code Virtualizer; although the initial compromise vector remains unknown, sparse detections in Central Europe, North America and the Middle East and a South Korean VirusTotal submission triggered YARA alerts based on its unique filename. Communicating over the loader’s established AES-256-CBC encrypted TCP channel, WinorDLL64 implements at least 16 commands—including comprehensive system profiling, secure file exfiltration, overwrite and deletion, process and RDP session management, unrestricted PowerShell execution, directory compression for data theft, and connection latency measurement—facilitating reconnaissance, persistence and lateral movement. retrieved_context.text: Researchers have uncovered that since early 2024 a previously undocumented botnet, dubbed Ngioweb, has been systematically scanning the Internet for IoT devices—primarily DVRs, IP cameras and home routers—with open Telnet/SSH ports and default or weak credentials, exploiting known firmware vulnerabilities to deploy a lightweight Go-based loader that establishes encrypted SOCKS5 tunnels back to a resilient NSOCKS residential proxy network of over 150,000 infected nodes. Once a device is compromised, Ngioweb drops a persistent agent that connects to fast-flux C2 domains via HTTPS, retrieves updated encryption keys and proxy configuration, and registers the node for NSOCKS’ tiered subscription service (starting at $25/month), which reportedly generates upwards of $500K in monthly revenue by fueling large-scale credential-stuffing campaigns, ad fraud and DDoS-for-hire operations. The actors behind Ngioweb continually rotate fallback C2 domains, employ encryption and obfuscation to evade signature-based detection, and monitor infection success rates in real time, enabling rapid retooling and expansion. Defenders are urged to enforce strong, unique credentials on all IoT assets, disable unused management interfaces, apply timely firmware updates, implement network segmentation and deploy behavioral analytics or honeypots to detect anomalous outbound proxy traffic.

retrieved_context.text: Since January 2021, Google’s Threat Analysis Group (TAG) has tracked a government-backed North Korean campaign that leverages social engineering via X (formerly Twitter) and encrypted messaging apps to befriend security researchers and deliver malicious files containing at least one unpatched 0-day in a popular software package; upon exploitation the custom shellcode performs anti-virtual-machine checks, captures system data and screenshots, and exfiltrates them to C2 infrastructure (e.g., 23.106.215[.]105, www.blgbeach[.]com), with the latest vulnerability reported and patched on September 12, 2023 (see TAG’s published RCA). In parallel, the actors published a seemingly benign Windows tool called GetSymbol on GitHub (https://github.com/dbgsymbol/) that quietly downloads debugging symbols—and arbitrary code—from attacker domains, requiring full OS reinstalls for compromised hosts. TAG has added malicious sites to Safe Browsing, issued government-backed attacker alerts to targeted Gmail and Workspace users, and urges researchers to enable Enhanced Safe Browsing, keep software up to date, and verify system integrity after using third-party tools.

retrieved_context.text: Lynx ransomware, emerging in July 2024 as the INC ransomware successor under a Ransomware-as-a-Service model, employs a sophisticated double-extortion strategy—exfiltrating data prior to encryption and threatening publication on a leak site—and reuses significant INC source code. Between July and November 2024, it disrupted U.S. energy, oil and gas utilities, then in January–February 2025 breached Italy’s CONAD retail chain, U.S. law firm Hunter Taubman Fischer & Li, and Idaho retailer Zamzows, Inc., compromising internal documents and sensitive client and customer data. Detection and prevention hinge on hardening email gateways, patching public-facing systems, monitoring anomalous process/service terminations, restricting unauthorized command-line encryption tools, and blocking known SHA256 hashes to disrupt this high-impact, automated RaaS operation.

retrieved_context.text: Operation RoundPress, attributed with medium confidence to Russian state-sponsored APT28 (Fancy Bear), has since 2023 exploited stored and reflected XSS flaws in widely used webmail platforms—initially leveraging Roundcube CVE-2020-35730 to inject malicious JavaScript into email bodies, then CVE-2023-43770 and additional n-day vulnerabilities in Roundcube, Horde, MDaemon and Zimbra in early 2024—to execute upon email open without clicks or redirects. Through spear-phishing emails crafted with timely political or news excerpts, the hidden script auto-fills victim credentials via invisible input fields, scrapes DOM content—including emails, contacts, webmail settings, login history, 2FA tokens and passwords—and exfiltrates data via HTTP POST to hardcoded C2 servers. Targets span high-value government entities in Greece, Ukraine, Serbia and Cameroon, military units in Ukraine and Ecuador, defense contractors in Ukraine, Bulgaria and Romania, and critical infrastructure in Ukraine and Bulgaria. The lack of persistence mechanisms confines execution to session scope but underscores the necessity for timely patching of XSS vulnerabilities, disabling HTML rendering in webmail clients, enforcing strict input sanitization and multifactor authentication, and monitoring anomalous outbound traffic to mitigate credential theft and data exfiltration.
retrieved_context.title: Government webmail hacked via XSS bugs in global spy campaign

retrieved_context.text: ESET researchers have retrospectively identified WinorDLL64.dll—a backdoor payload for the Wslink loader (WinorLoaderDLL64.dll) first uncovered in 2021—that operates as an in-memory server using MemoryModule and is protected by Oreans Code Virtualizer; although the initial compromise vector remains unknown, sparse detections in Central Europe, North America and the Middle East and a South Korean VirusTotal submission triggered YARA alerts based on its unique filename. hits.text: McAfee researchers at RSA Conference 2019 revealed that Operation Sharpshooter—a previously disclosed December 2018 espionage campaign first observed via October 25 weaponized macro-laden Dropbox documents—actually began as early as September 2017, using embedded shellcode in Microsoft Word to deploy a modular, in-memory second-stage implant dubbed “Rising Sun.” Rising Sun, which reuses source code from the Lazarus Group’s Duuzer backdoor, performs reconnaissance, encrypts and exfiltrates system data (computer names, IP addresses, native OS details) and communicates with multiple newly identified command-and-control servers. hits.text: First observed in September 2024 and active through at least August 12, 2025, the GodRAT campaign—attributed to an APT likely linked to Winnti—targets financial institutions, particularly trading and brokerage firms in Hong Kong, the UAE, Jordan, Lebanon and Malaysia, by distributing malicious .scr and .pif files via Skype messenger disguised as legitimate financial documents. Evolving from the AwesomePuppet RAT on a Gh0st RAT codebase, GodRAT employs a two-stage loader architecture: an initial stub invokes SDL2.dll to allocate memory and extract XOR-decoded (key 0x63) shellcode hidden via steganography in image files named to mimic authentic financial reports, then searches for the “godinfo” marker and uses the authentication string “GETGOD” to contact C2 servers, download UPX-packed GodRAT DLL modules and launch browser credential-stealing and remote-access payloads. This advanced steganographic delivery evades signature-based defenses and underscores the need to inspect .scr/.pif attachments, monitor Skype channels, and deploy detection rules for “godinfo,” “GETGOD” and related shellcode patterns.

Exploiting publicly disclosed vulnerabilities and open-source tools, MuddyWater delivers malicious PDFs with embedded links that display error messages prompting users to download Excel maldocs or Windows executables; these files host VBA macros that drop WSF scripts to execute PowerShell and VB payloads, leverage LoLBins, and stage RATs and malware families including PowGoop, Canopy, Small Sieve, POWERSTATS and Mori while communicating with C2 over HTTP and DNS and persisting via Registry Run keys. Cisco Talos observed regional campaigns in Turkey (Nov 2021), Pakistan (Aug 2021) and Armenia (Jun 2021) using decoy documents, signaling tokens and a consistent TTP set, suggesting a conglomerate of subgroups migrating techniques across regions. The resultant network access and data exfiltration underscore the imperative for proactive DFIR readiness, deployment of XDR/MDR platforms, rigorous vulnerability management, macro execution restrictions, PowerShell/LoLBin monitoring and ongoing user awareness training reinforced by incident response tabletop exercises.
retrieved_context.title: An In-Depth Look at Iranian APT "MuddyWater"

canonical_entities: installing Sagerunex variants in the Windows Registry
retrieved_context.text: The Lotus Blossom APT (aka Lotus Panda, Billbug, Spring Dragon) has stepped up cyberespionage against APAC government targets by deploying new Sagerunex backdoor variants and abusing Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) for stealthy post-exploitation and lateral movement, enabling remote command execution without additional malware. Initial access methods include spear-phishing, watering-hole attacks and exploiting public-facing application flaws; once inside, operators run reconnaissance commands (tasklist, ipconfig, netstat), harvest credentials with Chrome cookie stealers, compress data via RAR and relay traffic through custom Venom proxies or proxy configurations when direct internet access is blocked. Persistence is achieved by installing Sagerunex variants in the Windows Registry under hijacked service names (tapisrv, swprv) to auto-launch at startup, while command-and-control blends encrypted traffic into legitimate platforms—stolen data uploaded as .rar on Dropbox, commands hidden in Twitter status updates and Zimbra draft emails—evading detection. Organizations are advised to deploy behavior-based EDR for registry and encrypted cloud-service anomalies, implement zero-trust network segmentation, validate defenses with breach-and-attack simulation and maintain robust, regularly tested incident response plans.
retrieved_context.title: Lotus Blossom APT Exploits WMI for Post-Exploitation Activities

retrieved_context.text: McAfee researchers at RSA Conference 2019 revealed that Operation Sharpshooter—a previously disclosed December 2018 espionage campaign first observed via October 25 weaponized macro-laden Dropbox documents—actually began as early as September 2017, using embedded shellcode in Microsoft Word to deploy a modular, in-memory second-stage implant dubbed “Rising Sun.” Rising Sun, which reuses source code from the Lazarus Group’s Duuzer backdoor, performs reconnaissance, encrypts and exfiltrates system data (computer names, IP addresses, native OS details) and communicates with multiple newly identified command-and-control servers. Initially detected in 87 global organizations—50 percent in U.S. defense, nuclear, energy and financial sectors—the ongoing campaign has expanded to target financial services, government and critical infrastructure in Germany, Turkey, the U.K. and the U.S., exhibiting TTP overlaps and code reuse linking it to Lazarus operations. These findings underscore the need for strengthened macro and memory-resident malware defenses, proactive C2 infrastructure takedown efforts and enhanced attribution methodologies.
retrieved_context.title: RSAC 2019: New Operation Sharpshooter Data Reveals Higher Complexity, Scope | Threatpost

retrieved_context.text: ESET researchers have retrospectively identified WinorDLL64.dll—a backdoor payload for the Wslink loader (WinorLoaderDLL64.dll) first uncovered in 2021—that operates as an in-memory server using MemoryModule and is protected by Oreans Code Virtualizer; although the initial compromise vector remains unknown, sparse detections in Central Europe, North America and the Middle East and a South Korean VirusTotal submission triggered YARA alerts based on its unique filename. Communicating over the loader’s established AES-256-CBC encrypted TCP channel, WinorDLL64 implements at least 16 commands—including comprehensive system profiling, secure file exfiltration, overwrite and deletion, process and RDP session management, unrestricted PowerShell execution, directory compression for data theft, and connection latency measurement—facilitating reconnaissance, persistence and lateral movement. Low-confidence attribution to North Korea–aligned Lazarus (HIDDEN COBRA) derives from targeting of South Korean victims, shared VS2010 LTCG build signatures and code/behavior overlap with 2018 GhostSecret (FE887FCAB66D7D7F79F05E0266C0649F0114BA7C) and Bankshot implants; this underscores Lazarus’s organized, modular arsenal and highlights the need to detect anomalous in-memory loaders and encrypted session anomalies.
retrieved_context.title: WinorDLL64: A backdoor from the vast Lazarus arsenal?

retrieved_context.text: Lynx ransomware, emerging in July 2024 as the INC ransomware successor under a Ransomware-as-a-Service model, employs a sophisticated double-extortion strategy—exfiltrating data prior to encryption and threatening publication on a leak site—and reuses significant INC source code. Between July and November 2024, it disrupted U.S. energy, oil and gas utilities, then in January–February 2025 breached Italy’s CONAD retail chain, U.S. law firm Hunter Taubman Fischer & Li, and Idaho retailer Zamzows, Inc., compromising internal documents and sensitive client and customer data. Initial access leverages phishing (T1566.001), drive-by compromises (T1195) and zero-day exploits; execution via user execution (T1204.002) and scripting interpreters (T1059.001); persistence through autostart mechanisms (T1070.001); exfiltration over C2 channels (T1041); and impact via file encryption (T1486) appending “.LYNX.” Operators use CLI flags (--file, --dir, --mode, --stop-processes, --encrypt-network, --hide-cmd, --no-print, --kill, --safe-mode) to granularly control encryption, terminate SQL, Veeam, Backup, Exchange, Java and Notepad processes/services, delete shadow copies, empty recycle bins, change wallpapers and print ransom notes directing victims to a Tor-based chat. Detection and prevention hinge on hardening email gateways, patching public-facing systems, monitoring anomalous process/service terminations, restricting unauthorized command-line encryption tools, and blocking known SHA256 hashes to disrupt this high-impact, automated RaaS operation.
retrieved_context.title: Lynx Ransomware: INC Ransomware Reincarnated - Threat Actors

canonical_entities: trading and brokerage firms in Hong Kong, the UAE, Jordan, Lebanon and Malaysia
retrieved_context.text: First observed in September 2024 and active through at least August 12, 2025, the GodRAT campaign—attributed to an APT likely linked to Winnti—targets financial institutions, particularly trading and brokerage firms in Hong Kong, the UAE, Jordan, Lebanon and Malaysia, by distributing malicious .scr and .pif files via Skype messenger disguised as legitimate financial documents. Evolving from the AwesomePuppet RAT on a Gh0st RAT codebase, GodRAT employs a two-stage loader architecture: an initial stub invokes SDL2.dll to allocate memory and extract XOR-decoded (key 0x63) shellcode hidden via steganography in image files named to mimic authentic financial reports, then searches for the “godinfo” marker and uses the authentication string “GETGOD” to contact C2 servers, download UPX-packed GodRAT DLL modules and launch browser credential-stealing and remote-access payloads. This advanced steganographic delivery evades signature-based defenses and underscores the need to inspect .scr/.pif attachments, monitor Skype channels, and deploy detection rules for “godinfo,” “GETGOD” and related shellcode patterns.
retrieved_context.title: New GodRAT Weaponizing Screen Saver and Program Files to Attack Organizations
